text:
Trump’s Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) wants to gut the standards that require oil and gas companies to find and fix methane leaks caused by their drilling operations.

Methane is 28 times more potent than carbon dioxide — and the second-largest contributor to climate change. And the same leaks pump cancer-causing, smog-forming pollutants straight into the air of communities living next to oil and gas sites.

Most oil and gas companies already check for leaks. This proposal is a free pass for the worst polluters who won’t. The EPA’s reckless plan would:

Hand a loophole to the dirtiest well sites, which supply less than 5% of the nation’s oil and gas but cause more than half of the industry’s methane pollution

Kill the EPA’s super emitter program, which catches massive leaks so they get fixed

Let companies flare more, burning off excess gas and fouling the air nearby communities breathe

Zeldin didn’t at first announce this to the public. He announced it to a room full of oil and gas executives. Now it’s our turn to be heard.

title: Government Belatedly Scrambles to Revive EVs as Chinese-Made Rivals Surge
description:
As Chinese-made electric vehicles mount an increasingly strong challenge in the domestic market, the government has decided to support finished-vehicle production.
At the time, Deputy Prime Minister Koo Yun-cheol identified batteries and high-performance cathode materials as the core sources of competitiveness for electric vehicles.
◆Urgent need to strengthen price competitiveness against Chinese automakers... A deepening sense of crisis= The need for production tax credits has become increasingly apparent as the influence of Chinese automakers grows.
Domestic automakers now face the dual challenges of expanding sales while maintaining domestic production and strengthening price competitiveness.
◆Tax credits alone have limits... Future-vehicle technology and parts competitiveness must be supported= Even if domestic production tax credits are introduced, competitiveness will not recover immediately.
text:
As Chinese-made electric vehicles mount an increasingly strong challenge in the domestic market, the government has decided to support finished-vehicle production. The tax reform plan announced in August excluded finished electric vehicles from the domestic production tax credit, but the policy direction has shifted amid growing concerns over the declining market share of domestic vehicles and their weakening price competitiveness. After meeting with Euisun Chung, Executive Chair of Hyundai Motor Group, to discuss support measures for the auto industry, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and Economy Lee Hyung-il has also decided to take an active part in legislative discussions on related tax credits. Parliamentary discussions are gaining momentum as lawmakers from both the ruling and opposition parties introduce related bills and build consensus.

◆Support for batteries and materials, but not finished vehicles... A changing market landscape= In its tax reform plan announced in August, the government selected six sectors for domestic production tax credits: solar power, wind power, secondary batteries, semiconductors, key materials, and artificial intelligence (AI) robot components. The aim was to focus support on sectors with a weak domestic production base or strategic importance to economic security, but finished electric vehicles were not included. At the time, Deputy Prime Minister Koo Yun-cheol identified batteries and high-performance cathode materials as the core sources of competitiveness for electric vehicles. The government also considered that finished-vehicle manufacturers already had production facilities and sales networks, that incentives such as purchase subsidies were already in place, and that direct support could trigger trade friction.

However, industry and academic circles had called for support for finished-vehicle production even before the tax reform plan was announced. In April, the Korea Automobile & Mobility Association (KAMA), together with the Korea Auto Industries Cooperative Association and the Korean Metal Workers' Union, issued a joint labor-management proposal calling for the introduction of a tax incentive to promote domestic production of electric vehicles. In May, Oh Moon-sung, president of the Korea Tax Policy Association, also proposed at a tax policy seminar that output-based tax credits be introduced for nationally strategic sectors, including electric and hydrogen vehicles. Nevertheless, finished vehicles were ultimately left out of the August tax reform plan.

◆Urgent need to strengthen price competitiveness against Chinese automakers... A deepening sense of crisis= The need for production tax credits has become increasingly apparent as the influence of Chinese automakers grows. Domestic automakers now face the dual challenges of expanding sales while maintaining domestic production and strengthening price competitiveness. An official from the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy said, "Price competitiveness is also why domestic production tax credits are regarded by the industry as the most effective measure." The idea is that using the tax credit to lower vehicle prices could narrow the price gap with Chinese-made vehicles.

Lawmakers from both the ruling and opposition parties have introduced amendments to the Restriction of Special Taxation Act that would include electric vehicles among the eligible products. Measures under discussion include tax credits of up to 4 million won per domestically produced electric vehicle, and a proposal has also been made to apply a preferential coefficient for production outside the Seoul metropolitan area. An official from the Ministry of Finance and Economy said, "Deputy Prime Minister Lee has stated since his confirmation hearing that he would consider various support measures, including production tax credits for electric vehicles." The official added, "The specific details of the related bills will be determined during the National Assembly's review of the tax code amendments, and the government will actively participate in the discussions."

◆Tax credits alone have limits... Future-vehicle technology and parts competitiveness must be supported= Even if domestic production tax credits are introduced, competitiveness will not recover immediately. If support amounts only to tax benefits for existing production volumes, its impact could be limited. The credits should therefore be designed to be linked to new investment, increased production, domestic parts sourcing, and employment retention. To ensure that support for finished-vehicle manufacturers benefits parts suppliers and local economies, the government should support the transition of internal-combustion-engine parts suppliers to new businesses and retrain their workers, while also strengthening domestic supply chains for key components. An official from the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy said, "The share of internal-combustion-engine vehicles is declining further, and the market is being reshaped around future vehicles such as autonomous and electric vehicles." The official added, "Whether Korea secures a leading position in the future-vehicle market will determine the competitiveness of the Korean auto industry." The official continued, "Hyundai Motor will also invest, and the government is seeking to provide as much support as possible for research and development (R&D) investment."

text:
Washington, D.C. — The League of Conservation Voters (LCV) congratulates Senator Jon Ossoff and Representative-elect Jasmine Clark (GA-13) on their wins in Georgia.

“Georgians know firsthand the impacts of extreme weather, air and water pollution, and rising energy costs on their families and communities, and tonight they chose leaders who will fight for a healthier, more affordable future,” said LCV President Pete Maysmith. “Senator Ossoff and Representative-elect Clark will fight to hold polluters accountable, to expand clean energy to lower our costs, to create good jobs and to protect a free and fair democracy. We congratulate these climate champions and look forward to working with them to protect Georgia communities, hold Big Polluters accountable, and defend our democracy.”

LCV Victory Fund named Mike Collins to the 2026 Dirty Dozen list of candidates who consistently side against the environment and are running in competitive races that have a serious chance to affect the outcome. Mike Collins earned his spot for his votes in support of the Republican Tax Law, gutting the Inflation Reduction Act clean energy tax credits, and for authoring the PERMIT ACT, which limits the Clean Water Act and expands exemptions for agricultural and pesticide pollution.

LCV’s GreenRoots member mobilization program turned out LCV members to volunteer for Senator Ossoff’s campaign as part of a nationwide field program to help elect environmental champions that drove over 32,500 volunteer shifts that turned out voters through 1,200,000 door knocks, phone calls, and letters.

Environmental donors contributed $1,035,000 to Georgia candidates via GiveGreen. GiveGreen — a partnership between LCV Victory Fund and NRDC Action Votes that helps grassroots donors directly contribute to pro-environment candidates — raised $28.8 million for the 2026 cycle.

These are just some of the climate champions who won up and down the ballot in Georgia, reaffirming that addressing the climate crisis and affordable clean energy solutions are winning issues for voters.

text:
Waaree Solar Americas Inc. (WSA), the U.S. manufacturing arm of India’s Waaree Energies Limited, has initiated commercial operations on two new solar module lines at its facility in Brookshire, Texas.

Each new line adds 800 MW of annual capacity, effectively doubling the Texas plant’s total output from 1.6 GW to 3.2 GW. Commercial production officially started on October 29, 2026, following board expansion approval granted in April 2025.

The Brookshire expansion is central to the group’s “Make in U.S. for U.S.” domestic supply strategy. Alongside an ongoing upgrade at its Arizona module plant, which is expanding from 1 GW to 1.6 GW, Waaree is targeting an aggregate U.S. manufacturing capacity of 4.8 GW during FY27.

Revenue from Waaree’s U.S. manufacturing operations increased to $154.8 million in Q2 FY27, up from $87.1 million in the corresponding prior-year period. U.S. domestic supply contracts now represent 43.8% of Waaree’s total consolidated order book of $7.05 billion, growing from 36% in Q1 FY27. Across all global markets, Waaree’s cumulative module backlog stands above 25 GW.

“Shifting trade policy has strengthened the case for local manufacturing, and that is exactly where we have invested,” said Sunil Rathi, Director at Waaree Group. “With Brookshire now at 3.2 GW and Arizona expanding, we are serving American customers from American factories, and our U.S. order book continues to grow every quarter.”

For Q2 FY27, Waaree Energies reported a 23.9% year-on-year increase in consolidated revenue from operations, reaching $895 million.

Alongside its U.S. manufacturing investments, the company is executing a dual-track strategy to scale backward integration in India. Waaree plans to increase domestic cell production capacity from 5.4 GW to 15.4 GW in FY27, while laying the groundwork for a 10 GW ingot and wafer manufacturing plant targeted for FY28 operational readiness.

According to data from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA), the broader U.S. solar and storage manufacturing sector has achieved substantial growth, reaching an operational U.S. module manufacturing capacity of 75.3 GWdc and an operational battery cell manufacturing capacity of 62.4 GWh. SEIA reports that the industry has attracted $41.9 billion in cumulative announced investments and supports a potential total of 74,626 jobs across the domestic supply chain.

title: If The US Military Gets Solar Power, Why Can't We? - CleanTechnica
description:
In the topsy-turvy world of today’s federal energy policy, solar power is a bad thing.
Various members of the President’s cabinet have advised that solar is “unreliable,” and that solar power plants routinely experience “catastrophic failure” with every sunset.
At 700 kW, the new array is peanuts compared to the megawatt scale common among modern solar power plants.
Circling back around to military applications, it’s not surprising to see solar power resurfacing as a resilient energy resource over at the Defense Department, regardless of last year’s sharp U-turn in federal energy policy.
Resiliency was front and center in the early 2000’s, when the Defense Department began pushing the envelope on solar power while the civilian market was still spinning its wheels.
text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

In the topsy-turvy world of today’s federal energy policy, solar power is a bad thing. Various members of the President’s cabinet have advised that solar is “unreliable,” and that solar power plants routinely experience “catastrophic failure” with every sunset. So why does the US Department of Defense continue to pursue solar-enabled microgrids at its facilities? Asking for a friend…

More Solar Power For White Sands Missile Range

Though some solar projects at military facilities are relatively small, they are stamped with the seal of approval from the Defense Department, and that can have an outsized influence on public perceptions about the reliability, security, and durability of photovoltaic systems.

The history-making White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico is a case in point. In February of 2025 the facility celebrated the launch of a new, 700-kilowatt solar array designed and built by the joint venture HSGS-Ameresco.

At 700 kW, the new array is peanuts compared to the megawatt scale common among modern solar power plants. However, a little can go a long way in some cases, particularly when solar is integrated with other energy resources in a microgrid that can operate independently, without interruption, if the local distribution grid goes down.

“The innovative microgrid system, which integrates a 700kW solar photovoltaic array, a 500kW natural gas generator, and a 500kW lithium-ion battery system, will provide backup power to four groundwater wells on the range,” Ameresco explained in a press statement last year, in which it described the White Sands project.

The four wells are the primary source of potable water to the main post at White Sands. The new microgrid meets a US Army requirement for up to 14 days of independent water and power delivery to the post in case of a grid outage.

“This self-sufficient energy system, designed to serve a specific geographic area, helps ensure that critical missions at WSMR can proceed without interruption,” Ameresco elaborates, adding that the microgrid underscores White Sands’s commitment to building more resilient energy systems into its future construction projects.

Ameresco also indicated that the now-familiar combineation of solar power and BESS (battery energy storage systems) will do most of the heavy lifting, with the gas generator playing a back-up role if necessary.

“The solar array captures energy from the sun during the day, while the natural gas generator provides a dependable backup power source. The lithium-ion battery system efficiently stores excess energy generated by the solar array and releases it when needed, helping to ensure an uninterrupted power supply,” Ameresco emphasized.

What Catastrophic Failure?

The role of a lithium-ion battery in the new microgrid may come as quite a shock to US Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who has somehow failed to get memo about energy storage systems for solar power. Energy storage is an actual thing that exists in the space-time continuum here on Earth, but apparently not in Burgum’s corner of the mulitverse.

“And of course, when the sun goes down, you have a catastrophic failure called sunset and there’s no solar energy produced, and yet we’re subsidizing these things that are intermittent, unreliable, and expensive,” Burgum told a Fox News audience in July of 2025.

Whether Burgum believes it or not, the HGSG-Ameresco project is living proof that solar power is just as reliable as any other energy resource, with a mature supply chain and knowledge base to back it up.

Take the Florida-based firm Cantsink, for example. A specialist in piling specialist infrastructure, Cantskin installed the supports for the solar racking system in the new microgrid.

“Cantsink delivered a foundation system engineered to withstand the demanding conditions of a military testing range,” the company reports in a recap of the project on its website.

“Given the site conditions, pull testing was performed to determine pile requirements, which confirmed that 17’6″ piles were needed to support the racking system,” Cantsink further explains.

Among other details, Cantsink notes that the racking system is supported by 193 8×10 piles measuring 17’6″ long. “Every bolt used had a torque requirement that was inspected by a vendor appointed third party,” Cantsink emphasizes.

Next Steps For Solar Power At White Sands, And Beyond

Evidently the people in charge of energy systems at White Sands were satisfied with the results of their new microgrid, and the facility is on track to receive another solar-enabled microgrid. On November 3, the Kentucky-based global-facing engineering and infrastructure firm ABM described a new microgrid in the planning stages at White Sands, consisting of a carport-mounted solar power plant, BESS, and dispatchable on-site generators, presumably meaning gas generators for backup power.

The construction contract for the facility was assigned to ABM’s joint venture partner, AACON-RavenVolt. The AACON part of the venture is a general contractor based in Louisville, Kentucky. Ravenvolt is a subsidiary of ABM based in Georgia, having been acquired by the firm in 2022.

The relationship with RavenVolt is significant because ABM has positioned the partnership to zero in on microgrid opportunities throughout the federal government. “The partnership provides federal agencies with dependable, end-to-end energy resilience and infrastructure construction capabilities,” ABM notes.

Implications For Solar Power And EVs, Too

Keep an eye on ABM and RavenVolt moving forward, as EV stakeholders in the US anticipate an uptick in sales following President Donald Trump’s decision to start a war against Iran last February. That will increase the demand for kilowatts, and RavenVolt is among those advocating for solar-enabled microgrids to avoid grid-related bottlenecks.

“It’s all about the easy integration of on-site renewables, whether that’s solar, battery or ensuring on-site resiliency and expansion capability,” explains RavenVolt co-founder and President of Sales Cody George. The company’s microgrid model is designed for ease of installation, combining whole-of-system standardization while tailoring the switchgear to customer-specific applications.

“We’re not beholden to one technology, so our customers aren’t locked into outdated infrastructure forcing them to completely retool,” George adds.

Circling back around to military applications, it’s not surprising to see solar power resurfacing as a resilient energy resource over at the Defense Department, regardless of last year’s sharp U-turn in federal energy policy. Resiliency was front and center in the early 2000’s, when the Defense Department began pushing the envelope on solar power while the civilian market was still spinning its wheels. Solar panels were still relatively expensive back then, and the civilian market was slow on the uptake. Energy storage systems were more expensive, too.

As one indication that the Defense Department is still carving out its own energy destiny, get a load of Defense Secretary Pete Hesgeth’s new “FORTRESS America” resiliency plan. The goal is to make major Defense Department facilities in the US energy independent for at least 90 days, alongside other emergency stockpiling measures.

Nuclear and fossil fuels are part of the plan, but keep an eye on the solar-plus-storage combo to be first out of the box on a speed-to-power basis.

title: Riding the new Amtrak Cascades to Vancouver, BC, and back/ Meanderings by Mindy Stern
description:

When I arrived at the beautifully restored King Street station, its white walls glowed in ultra-white light.

Aside from the environmental benefits, travel on Amtrak Cascades allows you to read, write, walk around, stretch your legs and enjoy a dining car.
text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

“Can I help you with that?” a uniformed porter offered to hoist my carry-on bag up the stairs, then guided me into the coach car on an Amtrak Cascades train that would take me from Seattle’s King Street Station to Vancouver, BC. “Sit anywhere you’d like,” he advised. I picked a single seat at the very back of the train’s last car, and put my laptop and water bottle on the table separating me from two facing seats, only one of which was occupied. The train on this new Amtrak Cascades service had a “new car smell.” I marveled at the large, clean windows, and settled in for the four-hour journey north.

When I arrived at the beautifully restored King Street station, its white walls glowed in ultra-white light. My suitcase rolled effortlessly over the tiled floor. But the hard surfaces and tall ceilings provide no sound absorption, making it a challenge to understand announcements. Which track? What line to stand on? The amplified words bounce off the walls, rendering them difficult to make out. So, passengers confer with one another, figuring out that Gate 5 is where to line up for the Amtrak Cascades Train, #516, with its brand-spanking-new Airo cars. Replacing an aging fleet that was getting harder and harder to maintain, the Airos are Amtrak Cascade’s first revamp in 55 years. It was worth the wait.

The ticket booth at King Street is tucked away in an alcove. I’d gotten an email confirming my booking, but no link to print the ticket or save it to my phone. Presenting my passport instantly brought up my itinerary and I was handed a printed roundtrip ticket and a yellow, bookmark-sized slip. “Show this to the gate agent and keep it with you on the train. It means we’ve seen your passport and you’re approved for boarding.”

One week before traveling, I’d purchased a “flexible” ticket, which allowed for cancellations or changes. It cost $135 round trip, way less than a tank of gas. For the return trip, I upgraded to business car. New total: $182. Had I driven my electric car, I’d have to find an EV charging station, plus wait while until the battery reached full capacity. The train is relatively fast and affordable.

After walking down the platform with the other coach travelers and being helped into the car, I was instantly impressed. The lighting is bright and welcoming. The windows are large and clean. There’s ample luggage storage and the overhead shelf has a transparent bottom, making it less likely you’d forget something up there. Each seat has a little tray for watching movies on small devices, a USB-C port for each passenger, and a lever for reclining. Super comfortable.

There are open spaces and adjustable tables for wheelchairs in every car, and mechanical lifts to reach car level. The restrooms are enormous, making it possible for a wheelchair to turn around. Bikes can be accommodated –- by pre-arrangement –- in vertical racks, though without a ramp, help is needed to hoist the bike onto the train.

The Amtrak Cascades Cascade Café Car features grab-and-go sandwiches, salads, and a selection of hot items from Pacific Northwest icons including Alki Bakery, Bob’s Red Mill and Ivar’s, plus a water bottle refill station and table seating.

For my northbound ride in coach, I sat on the left side of the train and enjoyed the water views to the west. To accommodate its wider seats, the business car is configured differently: two seats on one side, and a row of singles on the other. As a solo traveler, I was assigned a single for my return trip in Business. This $47 upgrade provided even more leg room, a leg rest, adjustable lighting, retractable coat hook, early boarding, and a $3 coupon for the Café Car.

The new Airo trains were built in California and North Carolina to “Buy America” standards using components from 31 U.S. states. The Amtrak Cascades line from Eugene, Oregon, to Vancouver, BC, which debuted on Sept. 30, is their first roll-out.

Aside from the environmental benefits, travel on Amtrak Cascades allows you to read, write, walk around, stretch your legs and enjoy a dining car. It’s a friendly way to travel. And the views can’t be beat.

Meanderings is an award-winning travel column by Mercer Island resident, Mindy Stern. For more essays, or to comment, visit her website www.mindysternauthor.com

title: Beyond BS - The Times of India
description:
Environmental policies must be carefully planned before they are put into action.
To fight air pollution, Delhi has chosen the second approach – but in a rather strange way.
It has banned cars and buses below BS VI standards from entering the city if they come from neighbouring states.
But Delhi's own BS IV vehicles can continue to run freely.
Environmental policies must be based on sound research and careful thinking.
text:
Good intentions are not enough. Environmental policies must be carefully planned before they are put into action. To cool a hot kitchen on a sunny day, you can close the curtains or switch off the stove. To fight air pollution, Delhi has chosen the second approach – but in a rather strange way. It has banned cars and buses below BS VI standards from entering the city if they come from neighbouring states. This ban could affect the daily movement of thousands of people between Delhi and its surrounding areas. Such movement is important for the entire region's economy and daily life. The government believes that if older, more polluting vehicles from outside Delhi stay away, the city's air will become cleaner. But Delhi's own BS IV vehicles can continue to run freely. So, a vehicle's right to enter Delhi depends on where it comes from, not on its age, technology or condition. This is unfair and poorly planned. Sadly, many environmental rules seem to be announced without enough thought. Look at Tamil Nadu's order to recycle liquor bottles. It has caused confusion over the past few days. If empty glass bottles have any value, your raddiwala will happily buy them. They can then be recycled or used again. But if companies do not find these bottles worth collecting, adding a refundable deposit of ₹10 to every bottle will not suddenly create a recycling system. It will only create trouble for buyers and sellers, who will have to collect and return the money. Big environmental announcements may make governments look serious about protecting nature. But badly planned policies can cause serious damage. In 2021, Sri Lanka banned chemical fertilisers and pesticides and tried to move completely to organic farming. The result? Farm production fell sharply, and the country's economy suffered. In 2009, during the financial crisis, the US announced large tax benefits to encourage people to buy electric vehicles. But there were very few electric cars available then. As a result, taxpayers' money ended up supporting golf carts that had been fitted with seatbelts, headlights and rearview mirrors so they could be driven on public roads. India's effort to promote green firecrackers has also failed. Rules that make people pay a penalty for cutting down trees have even discouraged landowners from allowing new trees to grow on their empty plots. Now consider Delhi's annual ban on older vehicles. It has never made any real difference to the city's air quality. Governments need to keep up with new scientific research. The Centre and state governments focus heavily on smoke coming out of vehicle exhausts. But pollution also comes from tyres rubbing against roads, brakes wearing out and roads themselves getting damaged. These are called non-exhaust emissions. Some laboratory studies suggest that these particles can damage lung tissue more than diesel fumes. They may also make up as much as 60% of pollution particles produced by vehicles. This problem could get worse as cars and SUVs become heavier. Many now weigh around two tonnes. Heavier vehicles produce more particles through tyre and brake wear. So, it is time to take another look at the environmental costs and benefits of cars. Simply announcing bans and other big-sounding measures will not solve the problem. Environmental policies must be based on sound research and careful thinking.

title: Disneyland forced to pull plug on Autopia gas engines ahead of California mandate
description:
Disneyland will replace the gas-powered cars on its classic Autopia attraction with electric vehicles ahead of a looming deadline.
“It’s very different.” Vehicles on the ride have been gas-powered since it first debuted at Disneyland in 1955.
The park has been in trouble for the gas-powered vehicles before.
“The dirtiest place on Earth is the Autopia attraction at Disneyland in the city of Anaheim.” Autopia last received a major renovation in 2016 when Honda came on as a sponsor.
Disneyland first announced plans to convert the ride to electric powered vehicles in 2024.
text:
They’re going green.

Disneyland will replace the gas-powered cars on its classic Autopia attraction with electric vehicles ahead of a looming deadline. The change comes just months before the state’s Feb. 1 deadline to retire the cars or shut the ride down completely.

“It will be electric, but not the conventional idea of a battery in a car,” Disney legend Bob Gurr, who designed the ride, revealed to the New York Times in a new interview. “It’s very different.”

Vehicles on the ride have been gas-powered since it first debuted at Disneyland in 1955. Cars on the ride currently run on 8.5 horsepower Honda four-stroke engines. Honda will continue to sponsor the ride after the remodel, according to Gurr.

“Our current sponsorship agreement with Disneyland Resort runs through early 2027,” a Honda spokesperson told the Times. “Discussions regarding the future of the partnership and sponsorship of the Autopia attraction are currently ongoing.”

The ride was previously sponsored by Richfiled Oil from 1955 to 1970, and Chevron Oil from 2000 to 2012.

Disneyland is currently testing a fully-electric vehicle prototype for the ride.

The park has been in trouble for the gas-powered vehicles before. In 2024, Disneyland paid a $56,000 settlement to the California Air Resources Board after it was discovered that the ride’s cars were operating without certified emissions controls. The park says the fine was the result of “administrative oversight” and corrections were made without impact to the environment.

Gurr says the ride’s switch to electric a long time coming. The designer has been advocating for it since 2000.

“For 26 years, I’ve been arguing, ‘When are you going to do anything to get rid of that gasoline?’” Gurr told the Times. “The dirtiest place on Earth is the Autopia attraction at Disneyland in the city of Anaheim.”

Autopia last received a major renovation in 2016 when Honda came on as a sponsor. Disneyland first announced plans to convert the ride to electric powered vehicles in 2024.

The park says the switch is part of its commitment to reach net zero emissions by 2030 by increasing its usage. renewable energy sources.

text:
POSCO Group and Hyundai Motor Group are expanding their strategic alliance beyond steel into the core components of electric vehicle manufacturing. POSCO Future M announced on Dec. 3 that it has signed a Letter of Intent (LOI) with Hyundai Motor Group to collaborate on a synthetic graphite anode business in Vietnam.

Under this agreement, Hyundai Motor Group is reviewing a 100 billion won (approximately $73 million) equity investment in POSCO Future M’s Vietnamese synthetic graphite anode project. The automaker also plans to secure priority purchasing rights to acquire the manufactured output first. However, specific details regarding the exact equity stake, mass production timeline, and applicable vehicle models have not yet been finalized.

This collaboration serves as a follow-up to the memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed by both groups in April of last year, which focused on mutual cooperation in the steel and secondary battery sectors. While the previous agreement centered on a joint venture for Hyundai Steel’s electric arc furnace steel plant in Louisiana, USA, this marks their first cooperative venture in secondary battery materials.

While cathode materials determine a battery’s capacity and voltage, anode materials directly impact charging speed and lifespan. Graphite, the primary material used in anodes, is divided into natural graphite mined from the earth and synthetic graphite processed from petroleum and coal-based raw materials. Synthetic graphite offers distinct advantages in fast-charging performance and longevity, making it increasingly crucial as electric vehicle technology advances.

Chinese companies currently dominate the global anode market, accounting for over 90% of production. Meanwhile, the United States classifies entities linked to countries of concern, such as China, as Foreign Entities of Concern (FEOC). Battery and automaker compliance requires minimizing components sourced from these entities to qualify for production tax credits under local regulations. Consequently, automakers and battery cell manufacturers alike are rapidly expanding their engagement with domestic and allied material suppliers.

POSCO Future M commenced construction on its synthetic graphite anode plant in Thai Nguyen, northern Vietnam, earlier this year with an investment of approximately 357 billion won. Following this, the company signed a massive supply agreement worth about 1.15 trillion won with a global automaker last March, targeting full-scale mass production by 2028.

text:
Global electrification means batteries are in demand, and new analysis shows Australia has the capacity to become a battery manufacturing powerhouse.

The future of Australian battery manufacturing: Cell cans and current collector foils report by CSIRO identifies where local industry has the skills, materials, and expertise to make key components for lithium-ion and emerging sodium-ion batteries.

The report looks beyond Australia’s critical-minerals strengths to ask a more practical question: what would it take to turn more of those local resources into the parts that make up every battery cell?

Related article: New portable battery moves towards local manufacturing

CSIRO Advanced Battery Manufacturing lead Dr Adam Best said the work combines expertise in advanced manufacturing, battery materials, and industrial process assessment, bringing together knowledge of how battery components are made with a practical understanding of what Australian industry can already do.

“That combination is central to the report’s message that Australia’s battery opportunity is not only about what lies in the ground, but what can be made here from it,” Dr Best said.

With the bulk of our critical minerals being exported, much of the battery value chain ends up offshore. CSIRO’s work shows Australia has a pathway to change that story by building sovereign capability in selected parts of the battery supply chain.

“Bringing more of the value chain onshore would mean Australia could move beyond exporting raw and refined materials alone, towards creating higher-value products, supporting skilled manufacturing jobs and strengthening supply chains for technologies that will underpin the clean energy transition,” Dr Best said.

Rather than attempting to build every part of a battery industry at once, the report points to two promising first steps: making prismatic battery cell cans from Australian aluminium using the impact extrusion process, and producing copper current collector foil using electrolytic deposition.

CSIRO researcher Geoff de Looze said, “Australia has many of the building blocks needed for a battery manufacturing sector. The question is where we can take the most practical next steps.

“This work identifies areas where Australian materials, existing industrial capability and targeted investment could come together to create a stronger domestic supply chain.”

Battery cell cans are the thin metal cases housing a cell’s active parts. Although apparently simple, they must withstand internal pressure changes and crash loads, remain compatible with electrolyte chemicals, minimise weight and leave maximum space for energy storage—all at low cost. Australia could feasibly make any of the cylindrical, prismatic or ‘blade’ cell formats, although some pathways would require major investment in production of nickel-plated steel and aluminium sheet.

A practical first step for Australia could be producing prismatic battery cans from aluminium. Australia already has a strong aluminium industry and experience manufacturing similar products, including aerosol cans. The report recommends investing in facilities and production equipment tailored to making battery cans locally.

A battery’s current collector foils support the cell’s electrochemical core and carry current to its terminals. The copper foil on a lithium-ion battery’s negative electrode is typically just six microns thick—about one-tenth the thickness of a human hair— while the aluminium foil on the other side is about twice as thick. These highly engineered components are critical to battery performance, safety and production.

The report identifies electrolytically deposited copper foil as a viable first priority for establishing a local lithium-ion battery manufacturing sector. It would build on Australia’s copper production and refining capability, can be scaled by adding production cells over time, and is less capital-intensive than rolling routes.

“Australia is already a critical minerals powerhouse, but the next opportunity is to capture more value through manufacturing,” Dr Best said.

“By focusing on practical, technically achievable steps, Australia can build capability, support industry growth and contribute to more resilient battery supply chains both domestically and internationally.”

Rebuilding lost or reduced downstream capability will require careful technical, commercial and market analysis, particularly where facilities need high utilisation to be viable. But CSIRO’s analysis shows that Australia is not starting from scratch. It has the minerals, parts of the industrial base and growing national interest in clean energy manufacturing. With targeted investment, it could turn more local resources into battery components made here, supporting jobs, supply-chain resilience and long-term energy security.

Related article: ARENA initiative to grow Aussie battery manufacturing

With this in mind, CSIRO has recently established the Australian Battery Safety Facility (ABSF), strengthening Australia’s capability to test and understand battery safety as the country builds its domestic battery industry.

The facility will play an important role in supporting a safe and competitive local lithium-ion battery manufacturing sector, helping Australian-made battery technologies meet the performance and safety expectations needed for domestic and international markets.

text:
Client Alert | November 3, 2026

We are pleased to provide you with Gibson Dunn’s ESG Risk, Litigation, and Reporting update covering the following key developments during September 2026. Please click on the links below for further details.

I. GLOBAL

The International Organization for Standardization’s proposed net zero standard does not receive approval needed to advance

On September 10, 2026, a vote on the International Organization for Standardization’s (ISO) proposed Net Zero Aligned Organizations Standard (ISO 14060) failed to obtain the level of approval needed to become a final standard. ISO launched a 12-week public consultation on the initial draft on June 17, 2026, and received nearly 5,000 comments from ISO national members in over 170 countries by the submission deadline. The proposed standard builds on ISO’s 2022 Net Zero Guidelines and was developed over two years, incorporating feedback from experts across “business, government, academia, civil society and standards bodies worldwide.” ISO 14060 would provide guidance to organizations in “adapting business models for the global transition to net zero” while addressing “supply chain disruption, market volatility and evolving investor and regulatory expectations” and helping organizations prioritize energy security, manage emissions reductions, and integrate transition planning into their business strategy. Following ISO 14060’s failure to reach the requisite vote, ISO is reportedly reviewing the comments received in the consultation and will consider what next steps are appropriate.

U.S. Department of Energy hosts G20 energy ministers at Energy Abundance Ministerial

From September 14 to September 16, 2026, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), together with the White House National Energy Dominance Council, the U.S. Department of the Interior, and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), hosted the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial in Houston, Texas. The Trump Administration advanced its agenda regarding U.S. energy policy priorities, which focuses on the role of hydrocarbons, nuclear energy, and advanced technologies in delivering energy. The G20 ministers were able to reach consensus on the following four items: (i) advancing clean cooking access (committing members to expand clean cooking access and highlighting the role of liquefied petroleum gas and other energy sources in this effort), (ii) permitting and regulatory efficiency (committing members to improve the domestic permitting and regulatory processes for energy infrastructure, including by exploring the “use of artificial intelligence and other digital tools,” while maintaining national sovereignty and the existing economic, social, and environmental priorities of member countries), (iii) a water reuse initiative (establishing a voluntary framework for exchanging best practices on a “fit for purpose” water reuse approach), and (iv) a critical minerals statement (establishing voluntary cooperation to build “resilient, affordable, secure, and diversified critical minerals value chains” through information sharing, capacity building, innovation, investment, and technology transfer).

The G20 energy ministers also issued a Chair’s Statement setting out the G20 Voluntary Energy Security Principles organized around five themes: advancing affordability (adequately investing in energy systems and supply chains to address scarcity risks, global market dynamics, and excessive price volatility), expanding energy supply to meet structural demand growth (investing in energy infrastructure and a diverse range of energy sources and technologies to address increases in demand), diversifying energy systems (incorporating a diversified mix of energy sources and technologies), strengthening infrastructure and resilience (expanding and modernizing transmission, storage, and distribution infrastructure and retrofitting, expanding, and modernizing grid backups), and enabling innovation (supporting research, development, deployment, and scaling of a wide range of energy technologies and solutions). All G20 members present agreed to the statement with the exception of Brazil.

Other highlights:

From September 14 to September 18, 2026, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) held its 70th General Conference in Vienna, including representatives from 160 IAEA Member States. The conference featured discussions, events, and activities centered around nuclear topics. IAEA Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi emphasized the projected growth of global nuclear power capacity, driven in part by electrification and demand from artificial intelligence data centers, as well as the agency’s continued nuclear safety work in Ukraine and its lack of verification access in Iran. During the conference, the Member States elected 11 countries to the IAEA Board of Governors for 2026–2027.

On September 23, 2026, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres convened the Climate Summit 2026, an annual event focused on climate action and a just transition, which included global leaders from government, business, finance, civil society, and other sectors. Participants discussed scaling up existing climate solutions, “accelerat[ing] the transition to clean energy, expand[ing] access to affordable climate finance and strengthen[ing] communities’ resilience to climate impacts” as well as the importance of maintaining international cooperation.

II. UNITED KINGDOM

United Kingdom consults on modernizing corporate reporting, proposes removal of environmental and social topics from the strategic report

On September 7, 2026, the UK government launched a consultation, “Modernising Corporate Reporting to support long-term economic growth,” which closes on November 30, 2026. The consultation forms part of a wider program to simplify reporting obligations, while reducing administrative burdens on business.

The consultation proposes replacing most existing strategic report requirements with five baseline narrative disclosures covering a company’s business model, performance, resources and relationships, strategy, and principal risk exposures. The following would be removed as express statutory requirements, currently set out in section 414CB(1) of the Companies Act 2006, which requires in-scope companies to report on each listed topic as a minimum: (i) environmental matters, including the impact of a company’s business on the environment; (ii) employee matters, including employment policies, engagement, and diversity; (iii) social and community matters; (iv) respect for human rights; and (v) anti-corruption and anti-bribery matters.

The government stated that companies may still be required to report on these topics where they are financially material, in which case the obligation would arise from the general requirement to disclose information necessary to understand the business rather than from a list of named topics. Many of these topics are addressed in the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) Standards, and a recommendation on whether the UK should adopt mandatory ISSB-aligned reporting more broadly is expected in 2027.

Financial Conduct Authority finalizes rules requiring listed issuers to report against the UK Sustainability Reporting Standards

On September 30, 2026, the United Kingdom’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) published Policy Statement PS26/19 (PS26/19), containing final rules requiring listed issuers to report against the UK Sustainability Reporting Standards (UK SRS), the UK-endorsed version of the ISSB Standards. The UK SRS replace the existing Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD)-aligned rules. The rules apply to accounting periods beginning on or after January 1, 2027, with first reporting commencing in 2028.

The final rules depart from the FCA’s consultation on PS26/19 in two respects. The FCA initially proposed that climate disclosures under UK SRS S2 be mandatory. However, following feedback that this could burden smaller issuers disproportionately, issuers may now explain rather than comply with the requirement to disclose across the whole of the UK SRS. The comply-or-explain model is available to all issuers within the scope of the rules; an issuer that does not make a disclosure required by the UK SRS must state that it has not done so, and explain why, in its annual financial report. The FCA has not prescribed the form that explanation must take, and has reminded issuers that climate and sustainability matters falling within their principal risks and uncertainties must still be disclosed as such. The FCA also extended the regime to international commercial companies with a secondary listing and to depositary receipt issuers, which it had proposed should merely signpost their home-jurisdiction requirements, affecting an estimated 89 issuers.

Guidance on the level of detail of issuer disclosure expected was consulted on in Primary Market Bulletin 66 (as discussed in more detail below), with public feedback invited by October 28, 2026.

Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office publishes guidance on marine genetic resources under the Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction Act 2026

On September 21, 2026, the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) published guidance on the collection and utilization of marine genetic resources (MGR) under the Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction Act 2026 (BBNJ Act). The BBNJ Act implements the UK’s obligations under the Agreement under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ Agreement). The UK ratified the BBNJ Agreement in July 2026, and it entered into force in the UK on August 9, 2026.

The collection requirements apply where a UK craft is used to collect MGR in areas beyond national jurisdiction after that date. A pre-collection information form must be submitted to the UK BBNJ Focal Point at least seven months before collection begins, except for collection due to start on or before May 8, 2027, where shorter transitional periods apply. Post-collection information must be provided as soon as it is available and, in any event, before the end of 11 months after the last day of collection.

Other highlights:

On September 9, 2026, the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (Emissions and Verification) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/995) were presented to the House of Commons. The Regulations establish the emissions and verification framework for the UK Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and will come into force on January 1, 2027.

The Employment Rights Act 2025 (Commencement No. 5 and Transitional Provisions) (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/954) were made on September 1, 2026. These Regulations brought section 152 of, and Schedule 12 to, the Employment Rights Act 2025 into force on October 1, 2026, extending the time limit for instituting most employment tribunal claims from three to six months.

Alongside PS26/19, the FCA published Primary Market Bulletin 66 on September 30, 2026, consulting on a proposed new Technical Note setting out the FCA’s expectations for issuers under the new sustainability disclosure regime, including the level of detail expected where an issuer chooses to explain rather than comply.

III. EUROPE

Final revised European Sustainability Reporting Standards officially published

On September 21, 2026, the revised European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) (Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1563) and the Voluntary Sustainability Reporting Standard (Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1560), adopted by the European Commission on July 3, 2026, were published in the Official Journal of the European Union. Publication in the Official Journal is the final step required for the delegated acts to enter into force; it does not, however, alter the application dates set out in the delegated acts. For an overview of the key changes, see our June 2026 ESG Update and our client alert on the European Financial Reporting Advisory Group’s draft simplified ESRS.

The revised ESRS enter into force on November 10, 2026, and apply to financial years beginning on or after January 1, 2027. For financial years beginning in 2026, undertakings may apply the existing ESRS, the revised ESRS, or the existing ESRS with specified reliefs, and must disclose which option they have chosen. The Voluntary Sustainability Reporting Standard entered into force on September 24, 2026.

Anti-Greenwashing Directive now applicable across the EU with last-minute alleviation in Germany for products already on the market

On September 27, 2026, the Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive (Directive (EU) 2024/825, EmpCo Directive) became applicable. The EmpCo Directive applies generally to business-to-consumer communications, bans unverified generic environmental claims, and restricts the use of sustainability labels to those based on official certification schemes or those established by public authorities. Sustainability statements required to be prepared under the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) do not fall within the EmpCo Directive, in contrast to consumer-facing marketing that reuses the content of such statements. Member States were required to transpose the EmpCo Directive by March 27, 2026, though several had not completed transposition by then. On September 22, 2026, the European Commission published guidance on the EmpCo Directive in the form of updated Questions and Answers, which cover topics including the scope of the EmpCo Directive, what is considered an environmental claim, and specific prohibited practices.

On September 24, 2026, Germany followed with national legislation, introducing a limited transitional provision for goods placed on the market before September 27, 2026, requiring that injunctive and removal claims relating to such goods be asserted in good faith and in a proportionate manner. Subject to further legislative approval, the legislation is to apply retroactively from September 27, 2026, through September 27, 2028.

France: Paris Judicial Court holds first merits hearing in duty of vigilance case concerning Indigenous rights

On September 24, 2026, the Paris Judicial Court held a merits hearing in proceedings brought under France’s 2017 duty of vigilance law (LDV) against a French energy company (Company) in connection with a proposed wind farm in Unión Hidalgo, Oaxaca, Mexico. The claim was brought in 2020 by representatives of the Indigenous Zapotec community of Unión Hidalgo, together with two human rights organizations. The claimants allege that the Company failed to adequately identify, prevent, and mitigate risks associated with the project, including risks to the community’s collective land rights, its right to free, prior and informed consent, and the safety of human rights defenders.

The case raises a novel question under the LDV – whether companies must address, in their vigilance plans, risks relating specifically to the rights of Indigenous peoples, including the principle of free, prior and informed consent. The claimants argue that such rights should fall within the scope of the LDV, while the Company disputes that position, noting in particular that France has not ratified ILO Convention No. 169.

The Court’s decision, expected on January 21, 2027, may provide guidance on whether, and to what extent, the LDV requires companies to identify and address risks relating to internationally recognized Indigenous and collective rights in connection with overseas projects. It may also clarify whether the principle of free, prior and informed consent forms part of the human rights considerations that companies must incorporate into their vigilance plans.

Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation: Negotiating position on the revision adopted by the European Parliament’s Economic and Monetary Affairs Committee

On September 10, 2026, the European Parliament’s Committee on Economic and Monetary Affairs (ECON) adopted its negotiating position on the European Commission’s proposal to revise the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR), discussed in our November 2025 ESG Update. The European Council adopted its general approach on June 24, 2026.

Both ECON and the European Council broadly support the Commission’s proposal to replace the current complex Article 8 and Article 9 disclosure regime with three defined product categories (“Sustainable,” “Transition,” and “ESG Basics”). Financial products may only use these categories if they meet uniform minimum criteria, with differences between the institutions remaining, in particular, on the treatment of fossil fuel investments in the “Transition” category. The European Parliament confirmed the mandate at its plenary session in early October 2026, and trilogue negotiations are expected to begin shortly. The revised rules are not expected to apply before 2029.

Other highlights:

On September 30, 2026, the European Council agreed on its negotiating position on the proposed regulation to speed up environmental assessments, part of the Environmental Omnibus, and agreed to explore a targeted solution for extended producer responsibility obligations under the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2025/40) for small producers, in line with a proposal by the German Federal Government (see our August 2026 ESG Update).

On September 15, 2026, the European Parliament adopted its negotiating position on extending the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism to downstream steel- and aluminum-intensive goods, going significantly beyond the scope proposed by the European Commission and the European Council. Trilogue negotiations are expected to follow.

Transposition Tracker: An overview of the current transposition status of the CSRD into national laws, the Omnibus Directive, and the “Stop-the-Clock” process under the Omnibus simplification package can be found here.

IV. NORTH AMERICA

Teneo publishes its sixth annual report on sustainability disclosures of S&P 500 companies

On September 11, 2026, Teneo released its annual sustainability report entitled “Staying the Course: Our Sixth Annual State of U.S. Sustainability Reports,” which reviewed 250 sustainability reports published by S&P 500 companies between January 1, 2026, and August 31, 2026. The report tracked how sustainability reporting practices have changed year over year. According to the report, 87% of companies that had issued a sustainability report by the same point in 2025 also issued one in 2026. The report found that the term “ESG” appeared in the titles of only 4% of reports, down from a peak of 35% in 2022, and that its usage in the reports themselves had decreased 50% since 2025. The report also found that many companies were following international standards, with increasing numbers of companies (51%) completing or in the process of completing a double materiality assessment and, of those, 44% referencing CSRD requirements, and 14% of companies aligning their disclosures with ISSB Standards. The companies surveyed are increasingly disclosing standalone sustainability data tables, and the percentage of companies disclosing sustainability goals remained steady at 30% from 2025. The percentage of companies indicating that they were not on track to meet certain ESG goals increased from 9% to 12% since 2025.

The Environmental Protection Agency finalizes its repeal of most of the 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards and proposes to repeal all remaining greenhouse gas standards for power plants

On September 14, 2026, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced that the EPA had issued a final rule repealing most provisions of the 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards (CPS) for greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from fossil fuel-fired power plants under the Clean Air Act (CAA). It eliminates three sets of requirements: (i) the emission guidelines for fossil fuel-fired steam generating units; (ii) the carbon capture and sequestration/storage (CCS)-based standards for coal-fired steam generating units undertaking a large modification; and (iii) the CCS-based standards for new base load stationary combustion turbines. The EPA estimates that the final rule will save companies in the power sector more than $300 billion in compliance costs through 2047 and asserts that it will decrease energy costs to consumers throughout the country. The final rule will take effect on November 16, 2026.

The EPA also issued a supplement to its proposal to repeal all remaining GHG emissions requirements for fossil fuel-fired electric generating units under the CAA. This proposal would rescind the EPA’s 2015 findings and determinations supporting those standards. The EPA asserts that the CAA “does not authorize the EPA to regulate emissions from power plants in response to global climate change concerns.”

Securities and Exchange Commission staff issues no-action letter setting out a universal framework for issuer voluntary retail voting programs

On September 29, 2026, the staff (Staff) of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) issued a no-action letter to Tesla, Inc. (Tesla) regarding Tesla’s proposed issuer voluntary retail voting program (IVRVP). The Staff indicated that other companies that operate an IVRVP in the same manner described in Tesla’s letter may rely on the no-action relief outlined in the letter.

Generally, under Tesla’s IVRVP, a retail shareholder may give a standing voting instruction to vote its shares in line with the board’s recommendations at each shareholder meeting. The instruction can cover either all matters, or all matters other than contested director elections and acquisitions, mergers, or divestitures that require shareholder approval under state law or stock exchange rules. There is no option under the IVRVP to provide standing instructions to vote against the board’s recommendations. Votes under a standing instruction are submitted once the issuer files its definitive proxy statement, before the proxy statement is distributed to shareholders.

The Tesla no-action letter follows two other recent no-action letters related to similar retail voting programs. The Tesla letter, however, is characterized as a “framework letter,” which Tesla states was developed over months of discussions with the Staff, and the Staff’s response states that its position applies to any issuer operating an IVRVP in the same manner described in Tesla’s letter. A company that wishes to adopt a program under the Tesla letter must include the following features in its program: (i) participation is free; (ii) every shareholder, including each participant, continues to receive the full proxy materials for each meeting; (iii) a participant can override the standing instruction on any proposal, at no cost, simply by voting using the proxy materials received for that meeting; (iv) a participant can cancel the standing instruction at any time and at no cost for future meetings; (v) a participant receives a reminder at least once a year, outside any solicitation period, that states that the participant is enrolled, which standing instruction the participant selected, and that the participant can cancel at any time and at no cost for future meetings, with an additional reminder before any meeting involving a contested director election or a shareholder-approved acquisition, merger, or divestiture; and (vi) the company fully describes the program and each of these features on its website and in each proxy statement, and files its program communications with the SEC as soliciting material under Rule 14a-12(b).

Other highlights:

On September 18, 2026, the Federal Court of Canada dismissed the Attorney General of Canada’s motion to strike an application by three individual climate advocates and two environmental organizations seeking to compel the Minister of Environment, Climate Change and Nature to amend Canada’s 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan under the Canadian Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act. The Court found that the parties’ competing interpretations of whether the Act imposes a duty to amend the plan should be decided on a full record.

On September 18, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island vacated the EPA’s August 2025 termination of the $7 billion Solar for All grant program, which provided grants to states, nonprofits, tribes, and other organizations to help decrease electricity costs in lower-income households. The Court held that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act did not rescind grant funds that had already been obligated and that the termination exceeded the EPA’s statutory authority.

On September 24, 2026, Glass Lewis and Clarity AI, a provider of AI-based sustainability data and analytics, announced their merger, stating the combination will expand the combined company’s ability to serve institutional investors and companies in Europe using Clarity AI’s strong European market presence and advanced technology, combined with Glass Lewis’s expertise in corporate governance and proxy voting.

The SEC issued a Section 21(a) report on October 7, 2026, regarding its investigation into activities undertaken in advance of a contested election of directors at ExxonMobil’s 2021 Annual Shareholder Meeting. The Commission determined that no enforcement action was warranted. It issued guidance on how, when interpreting its disclosure requirements under Schedules 13D, 13G, and 14A, it will approach the questions of when investors formed a “group,” whether they had an intent to “control” an issuer, and whether they were “participants” in a proxy solicitation.

In case you missed it…

The Gibson Dunn Workplace DEI Task Force has published its updates summarizing the latest key developments, media coverage, case updates, and legislation related to diversity, equity, and inclusion.

A collection of our analyses of the legal and industry impacts from the current administration is available here.

V. APAC

Thailand announces US$1.52 billion financing program for residential rooftop solar panels

On September 9, 2026, it was reported that Thailand’s Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister would launch a THB 50 billion (approximately US$1.52 billion) program to finance rooftop solar installations for an initial one million households. The program is expected to launch in mid-October 2026. Through state-owned financial institutions, it will provide eligible households with up to approximately US$1,520 per installation. It will also exempt certain imported solar panels from tax. The goal is to address high upfront costs, which the government sees as a major barrier to solar adoption. Households will use the power they generate and sell any surplus to the grid. Electricity authorities will put the revenue from those purchases toward the households’ loan repayments, so participants may not need to invest anything themselves. The program is part of Thailand’s broader Power Development Plan, and the government expects it to create jobs and support domestic businesses.

Hong Kong Monetary Authority publishes Phase 2B model of taxonomy for sustainable finance

On September 7, 2026, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) published its Phase 2B prototype of the Hong Kong Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance, which builds on Phase 2A published in January 2026. Phase 2B adds 10 new climate change mitigation activities. Together with the re-categorization of some Phase 2A activities, this brings the total climate change mitigation activities to 39 economic activities, up from 25. The new activities include battery manufacturing and recycling, and Phase 2B also adds transition pathways for hard-to-abate sectors such as air transport and iron and steel. It also introduces a process-based approach to climate change adaptation, with 24 adaptation measures that initially focus on shoreline protection and flood management. Public comments were due by October 7, 2026.

Other highlights:

On September 28, 2026, Hong Kong priced its fourth digital green bond offering. The offering was worth about HK$20 billion (approximately US$2.6 billion) and set a new record as the world’s largest digital bond issuance. It followed a virtual roadshow and was split into four tranches in Hong Kong dollars, renminbi, U.S. dollars, and euros. Proceeds will fund eligible projects under the government’s Green Bond Framework.

ISELIN, N.J., Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Cenntro Inc. (NASDAQ: CENN) ("Cenntro" or the "Company"), an electric commercial vehicle company offering purpose-built vehicles, today announced deliveries of its LS450 electric trucks in the United States under government incentive programs that support commercial fleet electrification.

Cenntro has delivered 20 LS450 electric trucks under the New York Truck Voucher Incentive Program (NYTVIP), generating more than $2.44 million in total revenue. The Company plans to deliver LS450 trucks under the New York City Clean Trucks Program (NYCCTP), extending its participation in programs designed to help fleet operators adopt cleaner commercial vehicles.

In addition, the LS450 has qualified for and been listed under the California Clean Fuel Reward (CCFR) and the New Jersey Zero-Emission Incentive Program (NJ ZIP). These qualifications broaden the opportunities for eligible customers to access incentives when purchasing the Company's electric trucks.

Incentive programs can help reduce the upfront cost of electric commercial vehicles, making it easier for fleet operators to evaluate and pursue electrification. Cenntro views participation in these programs as an important part of its efforts to expand LS450 adoption in the U.S. market. Customer incentives remain subject to each program's eligibility requirements, funding availability and approval process.

"Delivering 20 LS450 trucks under New York State's incentive program is an important step in expanding our U.S. commercial vehicle business," said Peter Wang, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Cenntro. "These programs help lower the upfront investment for eligible customers and support their transition to electric vehicles. With deliveries underway under New York programs and eligibility in California and New Jersey, we see opportunities to bring the LS450 to more fleet operators."

Cenntro expects these program qualifications to support additional LS450 deliveries as it continues to develop its U.S. commercial vehicle business.

Cenntro (NASDAQ: CENN) is a pioneering maker and provider of electric commercial vehicles ("ECVs"). Cenntro's purpose-built ECVs are designed to serve a variety of commercial applications inclusive of its line of class 1 to class 4 trucks. Cenntro is building a globalized supply-chain, as well as the manufacturing, distribution, and service capabilities for its innovative and reliable products. title: Econili Secures Vynn Capital Investment to Strengthen Battery Recycling Operations
description:
The investment comes as Malaysia develops its battery recycling industry alongside the expansion of electric vehicles and battery manufacturing.
Econili targets higher throughput at existing facilities Econili is a lithium-ion battery recycler and the country’s first licensed mineral recovery plant.
Malaysia’s battery recycling market is still developing.
Southeast Asia is also seeking a larger role in battery processing and supply chains as manufacturers diversify sourcing and production locations.
Econili was founded by Dr. Jayden Goh, whom the company describes as a pioneer in lithium-ion battery recycling since 2014.
text:
The investment brings Econili’s total funding to RM8 million, with the Malaysian recycler planning to use the latest capital to secure additional battery feedstock and increase processing throughput at its existing facilities.

Vynn Capital has led an extension funding round in Econili Battery New Energy, a Malaysian lithium-ion battery recycler and black-mass refinery, bringing the company’s total funding raised to RM8 million as it seeks to increase processing throughput and strengthen its access to battery feedstock. The latest investment amount was not disclosed. The funding follows an earlier round led by Kumpulan Modal Perdana (KMP) and will be deployed as working capital to secure additional end-of-life batteries and battery production scrap for Econili’s existing processing facilities in Ipoh, Perak.

The investment comes as Malaysia develops its battery recycling industry alongside the expansion of electric vehicles and battery manufacturing. The country’s growing industrial ecosystem could create opportunities for recovering lithium, nickel and cobalt, although the availability of recyclable materials and the economics of processing remain important considerations for operators.

Malaysia generated 13,743.15 metric tonnes of battery waste classified under SW103 between 2021 and 2025, according to figures reported by Bernama citing the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability. The category includes several battery types and is not limited to electric vehicle batteries.

Econili targets higher throughput at existing facilities

Econili is a lithium-ion battery recycler and the country’s first licensed mineral recovery plant. Its operations in Ipoh include battery treatment capacity of 24,000 metric tonnes and critical-mineral recovery capacity of 12,000 metric tonnes.

The company processes end-of-life lithium-ion batteries and battery manufacturing scrap to recover materials including lithium, nickel and cobalt. These minerals are used in the production of cathode active materials, which form a key component of batteries for electric vehicles and energy-storage systems.

The company’s processing model combines mechanical shredding with hydrometallurgical refining. Mechanical processing produces black mass, an intermediate material containing valuable battery metals, which is subsequently refined to recover usable mineral compounds. Econili’s two-stage process produces lithium carbonate, mixed hydroxide precipitate and lithium phosphate, according to the company. It says the recovered materials are supplied to Tier-1 global supply chains through a cost-efficient operating model.

The company also claims its operating costs are 30% to 50% lower than those of Western peers. However, it has not disclosed comparative operating data, recovery yields or customer-level sales figures to independently substantiate the claim.

Battery recycling depends on feedstock availability

Recyclers require consistent access to batteries and production scrap, while collection, transportation, sorting and processing determine how efficiently material can move through the supply chain. Working capital can help operators secure feedstock, but the commercial impact depends on the quantity and quality of material available and the economics of recovering it.

Malaysia’s battery recycling market is still developing. Bernama reported estimates that approximately 40,000 electric vehicle batteries could require recycling in Malaysia by 2030, rising to 330,000 by 2040 and 870,000 by 2050. The projections assume an eight-year battery lifecycle and are based on EV registration trends. These estimates point to a longer-term opportunity rather than an immediate supply of recyclable EV batteries. Battery manufacturing scrap is also important because it can provide recycling feedstock before vehicles reach the end of their operating lives.

Econili’s stated focus on both battery waste and production scrap reflects this distinction. Its ability to secure material from different sources will be relevant to how effectively it uses its existing capacity.

Malaysia’s role in critical-mineral recovery

The expansion of battery manufacturing and electric mobility is increasing attention on the recovery of critical minerals. Recycling offers a way to return materials from discarded batteries and manufacturing waste into industrial supply chains, reducing the need to rely exclusively on newly mined resources.

Southeast Asia is also seeking a larger role in battery processing and supply chains as manufacturers diversify sourcing and production locations. Malaysia’s industrial base and proximity to regional battery markets provide a potential advantage, although developing a competitive recycling industry will require reliable feedstock, commercially viable processing and compliance with environmental regulations.

Econili is among the operators handling scheduled battery waste under Malaysia’s SW103 framework. The company says it is one of five licensed battery-recycling operators compliant with the protocol. Its hydrometallurgical process is designed to recover minerals for reuse in battery-related manufacturing. Econili says the method enables high recovery rates while consuming less energy and producing lower emissions than conventional processes. Those environmental performance claims have not been independently quantified in the announcement. The company aims to develop Malaysia into a black-mass processing hub, recovering critical materials and supplying them back into Asia’s battery value chain.

Vynn Capital sees opportunity in mobility and circular supply chains

Vynn Capital’s investment reflects its focus on companies operating across mobility, travel and supply chains. The firm sees battery recycling as part of the broader transition toward circular industrial systems, where materials can be recovered and reused rather than discarded.

Speaking with AsiaTechDaily, Vynn Capital Founding and Managing Partner Victor Chua said:

“Econili represents the kind of company we believe can redefine how industries think about growth and sustainability. As Southeast Asia continues to develop into one of the world’s most important economic regions, the transition towards a more circular economy is becoming both an environmental imperative and a significant commercial opportunity. We see tremendous potential for Econili to build solutions that can create meaningful impact at scale, particularly across the mobility ecosystem. What gives us further conviction is the strength and execution capabilities of the founding team. We are excited to partner with them as they build from Malaysia and pursue a much larger regional opportunity.”

The investment also reflects the importance of execution in an industry where future demand does not automatically translate into available material or profitable operations.

Econili was founded by Dr. Jayden Goh, whom the company describes as a pioneer in lithium-ion battery recycling since 2014. The company says its recovered materials are supplied to global supply chains, although it has not named customers or disclosed sales volumes.

Goh said:

“With global end-of-life battery volumes projected to surge from 1.1 million tonnes today to over 20 million tonnes by 2040, the demand for localised, cost-efficient refining capacity is virtually limitless. Econili is currently looking for strategic opportunities and expanding its capital footprint, actively bringing external investment into Malaysia to position the nation as a premier hub for sustainable battery recycling innovation.”

Econili’s latest funding is directed toward strengthening its existing operations rather than announcing a new plant or a disclosed increase in processing capacity.

text:
Used electric vehicles are getting more expensive and spending less time waiting for buyers, according to a new study from iSeeCars. While gasoline-powered vehicles have barely budged in price over the past year, used EVs have posted a nearly double-digit increase and now sell almost two weeks faster than their gasoline counterparts.
