title: The Value of Electric Power Transmission in a New Energy Context - Rhodium Group
description:
Because the regionality and scale of transmission benefits differ depending on energy market conditions, we evaluated the value of transmission expansion across a range of potential energy system futures.
Together, these scenarios represent a range of possible energy system outcomes given current energy market trends.
The expanded transmission environment allows us to evaluate how the US energy system would evolve with fewer barriers to transmission development.
We quantified the value of transmission expansion by comparing capacity additions, electricity prices, reliability costs, and transmission deployment in the expanded transmission and BAU environments for each scenario.
Our expanded transmission scenarios envision a world in which it’s easier and cheaper to build out transmission infrastructure, but this world is far from guaranteed.
text:
Surging electricity demand and constraints on generator supply are increasingly challenging access to affordable, reliable electricity in the US. Evolving natural gas dynamics at home and abroad also have implications for the power sector. Though considerable work has been appropriately focused on expanding new generation on the grid in response, a more robust transmission system also plays a critical role in meeting demand and reducing costs. We find that expanding transmission capacity has the potential to help mitigate rising electricity prices while supporting electricity reliability, especially under conditions that add extra strain on the grid. Easing transmission barriers reduces total US power system costs by $82-130 billion from 2026 to 2040, resulting in 2-3% lower electricity prices nationally in 2040, with greater price impacts in some regions. Expanded transmission drives these lower costs by enabling 9-43% more capacity deployment on the grid through 2040. More extensive interregional transmission networks also allow regions to meet reliability requirements at up to 12% lower costs, since they facilitate the sharing of capacity resources between regions. At the same time, expanded interregional transmission enables access to lower-cost sources of electricity in neighboring regions, driving different decisions on where generators are built and how they are operated.

Transmission value in a dynamic energy environment

After a couple of decades of effectively flat electricity demand growth, surging US electricity demand, largely driven by current and anticipated growth in large AI data centers, has increasingly dominated energy conversations and begun to reshape the US power sector. But electricity demand growth isn’t the only factor driving rapid change in the energy sector. Elsewhere on the grid, supply chain challenges, interconnection queue delays, and inflation are driving up the costs to bring new generating capacity onto the grid—at a time when the country needs all the electrons that it can get. Taken together, these dual challenges are intensifying the focus on rising electricity bills and what can be done about them. At the same time, demand for US liquefied natural gas (LNG) and the corresponding build-out of new LNG export terminals are reshaping domestic natural gas production trends and stand to put upward pressure on domestic gas prices. All of this is playing out against a backdrop of a dynamic energy policy environment, with legislative and executive decisions that are poised to shape how the US meets this increasing demand.

There has been considerable attention on how the US can expand electricity generating capacity in response to these trends—building more gas turbines, batteries, solar farms, and the like—but that only tells part of the story. These electrons need to move from generators to end users efficiently and in real time—underlining the critical importance of a robust transmission system for delivering affordable, reliable electricity. The recently released Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) includes meaningful improvements to federal policy to help bolster the transmission system, underscoring how important a strong grid is for meeting future energy needs. In this note, we briefly describe the new energy context the US is facing and then unpack modeling results that demonstrate how increasing transmission capacity on the grid can help bring more power to the grid, reduce costs, and contribute to reliability.

AI data centers are driving increasing electricity demand but are not the only source

The evolution of US electricity generation since 1960 can be divided into three distinct phases. From 1960 to 2005, electricity generation grew steadily, averaging just over 70 TWh per year, driven by economic and population growth, widespread adoption of electric appliances, and increasing commercial building floorspace (Figure 1). From 2005 through 2019, load growth was flat, averaging just 11 TWh (or about 0.1%) more demand per year due to increasing efficiency of appliances and lighting, a continued shift away from electricity-intensive manufacturing, and the Great Recession. The country is now on the precipice of increasing load growth that could dwarf the previous era of sustained growth, and has already seen a rebound to 50 TWh (2.1%) of year-on-year growth this decade.

AI data centers drive the bulk of future load growth, and assumptions around just how quickly that demand will materialize have an outsized impact on aggregate power demand. That said, the reshoring of electricity-intensive manufacturing (like chipmaking and battery manufacturing) and ongoing electrification of oil and gas operations in the Permian Basin also contribute step changes in demand growth. Increasing demand from large loads is superimposed on broader trends toward electrification via technologies like electric vehicles and heat pumps. All these factors contribute to higher electricity consumption, tighter reliability conditions, and greater pressure on electricity prices in many regions than the US has experienced over the past few decades.

This electricity demand growth varies meaningfully by region, largely driven by expectations around where data center development will take place and at what scale. Under our baseline data center assumptions, which represent a reasonably conservative pace of expansion compared to other recent data center demand projections, Virginia accounts for 23% of data center demand growth through 2040, doubling already high electricity growth rates in the South Atlantic. Data center expansion in Texas (15% of the total) helps maintain high levels of demand growth in West South Central, while expansion in Ohio and Indiana (11% of the total) more than doubles demand growth in East North Central.

Data center demand expectations are highly uncertain and vary widely. Under high data center demand assumptions aligned with the upper range of recent projections, the pace of national electricity demand growth could increase by 80% compared to baseline rates, widening regional differences. This new era of data center-driven demand growth raises the stakes for building cost-effective and rapid grid infrastructure to ensure delivery of reliable, affordable energy.

Abundant, low-cost US natural gas plays an increasingly prominent role in the global energy system

Alongside the need for more electrons, demand is also expanding for US natural gas abroad, and investments to increase export capacity that have been underway for years are well-timed to meet that increased demand. US LNG export volumes have surged in recent years, growing from effectively zero in 2015 to more than 5.5 trillion cubic feet—14% of domestic natural gas production­­—­in 2025. The war in Iran and ensuing closures and limitations on the Strait of Hormuz have amplified demand for US gas. From January through June 2026, LNG exports were up 23% compared to the same period in 2025, driven by increasing demand from Asian markets that were previously largely served by Qatari LNG. This trend looks poised to continue, enabled by currently under-construction projects coming online over the next few years. As discussed further below, we consider two LNG export capacity pathways and find volumes could more than double by 2040, increasing by 121-145% over 2025 levels (Figure 3).

This increasing demand for US LNG does not reduce the amount of natural gas available for use in the power sector. We model increasing demand for LNG along with demand from other sectors and estimate domestic production of gas will increase by 7-8 trillion cubic feet in 2040 (18-20%) in response, building on a period of immense growth in gas production over the last decade. Rather, this global demand drives producers to drill higher-cost wells and increases competition with domestic consumers. As a result, Henry Hub spot prices increase by 10% ($0.50) on average from 2030 to 2040 in the high LNG case compared to the baseline LNG case. In turn, the power sector makes somewhat different investment and operational choices, with power generation from natural gas decreasing by 7% in the high LNG case in 2040. As we unpack below, more available transmission has a different impact on this less gas-heavy grid.

The US needs a grid that provides affordable, reliable electricity

The grid is made up of three interconnected systems: generating assets that convert natural resources into electricity; the transmission system, which connects these generating assets to concentrations of electricity demand; and the distribution system, which moves electrons from the transmission system to end users. While adequate supply of generating capacity is necessary to provide affordable and reliable energy, the transmission system plays a crucial role in connecting supply and demand. It ensures that generation can meet load reliably, at the right time and place, and at the least cost. Our focus in this analysis is on the importance of transmission to the grid.

The transmission system can be further subdivided into three major categories of assets: lower-voltage lines that connect individual generators to the bulk power system (spur lines), medium-voltage lines that make up the bulk of the transmission system moving electricity around within an individual grid region (regional lines), and higher-voltage lines that connect larger grid regions together (interregional lines; in our case 25 individual electricity regions).

Taken together, these components add value to the grid in several important ways. First, the transmission system supports the reliability of the entire power system by enabling power to flow from places where it is abundant and cheap to places where it is needed—both of which might change depending on the time of day or time of year. By sharing resources across regions, the grid as a whole can meet its reliability standards at a lower overall cost.

Second, transmission can expand access to geographically diverse supplies. Some types of generators, especially renewables like solar, wind, geothermal, and hydroelectric power, have resource endowments that are not located proximate to population centers and other sources of load. Adding transmission can enable new and existing resources to meet increasing demand. Finally, transmission can help reduce costs by reducing congestion at key chokepoints on the grid, allowing lower-cost generation to places that would otherwise be reliant on more expensive generation, helping to improve grid asset utilization.

Despite the value that transmission brings to the power system, the US has been building less transmission in recent years (Figure 4). Part of this is because transmission expansion has been less critical in a period of low load growth. Beyond that, federal, state, and local siting and permitting challenges have also slowed the pace of deployment and now represent a major bottleneck in this new era of surging demand.

Despite these challenges, some meaningful transmission investments are moving forward. ERCOT, the grid operator in Texas, has plans to build a 765-kV transmission backbone across the state, largely to help serve increasing load associated with oil and gas production in the Permian Basin. The Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) approved nearly $22 billion in transmission investments aimed at improving reliability, interconnection, and market efficiency. And construction is underway on the TransWest Express transmission project to connect grid regions in the West.

Building new transmission lines represents one of a number of solutions that can improve the performance of the grid by increasing access to generation, relieving congestion, and enabling interregional sharing of resources. Deploying grid-enhancing technologies (like dynamic line rating and advanced power flow controls) and reconductoring existing transmission lines can all improve the efficiency of the existing grid. The use of high ampacity conductors in transmission expansion can maximize the impact of these investments. Increasing the installation of energy storage of a range of durations and scaling up grid flexibility efforts can help strategically shape the demand that the grid needs to serve. Though the focus of this report is specifically on transmission build-out, an all-of-the-above approach leveraging each of these solutions can help respond to emerging urgent energy system needs.

Scenarios to assess transmission value

There is a considerable body of work that discusses the importance of transmission to an efficient, reliable, low-cost power sector. We aim to add to that work by examining the importance of transmission specifically in the new energy context that we’ve described above, representing both the current federal and state policy environment and macro drivers of energy system change.

Because the regionality and scale of transmission benefits differ depending on energy market conditions, we evaluated the value of transmission expansion across a range of potential energy system futures. We developed a set of scenarios that capture uncertainty in key dimensions of the US energy system. The central scenario largely mirrors our mid emissions scenario from Taking Stock 2026 and assumes moderate oil and gas price projections, moderate clean technology costs, baseline data center demand growth, and planned LNG export capacity that includes all under-construction facilities. We also incorporated additional electricity demand in the Permian Basin from the ongoing electrification of oil and gas operations.

All other scenarios start from the central scenario assumptions and explore a more extreme outcome for one component of the energy system (Table 1). The high data center scenario assumes data center demand grows at a faster pace, with total data center demand rising 133% above the central scenario by 2035. The high LNG scenario assumes planned LNG export capacity that includes both under-construction and permitted facilities, increasing planned export capacity by 43% and increasing Henry Hub spot prices by 10% ($0.50) on average from 2030 to 2040 relative to central assumptions. The constrained supply scenario represents an environment where adding new generating capacity to the grid is more expensive by imposing a cost premium on all new additions when installations exceed thresholds derived from historical annual deployment levels. Together, these scenarios represent a range of possible energy system outcomes given current energy market trends.

To assess the value of transmission expansion, we used RHG-NEMS, Rhodium Group’s US energy system model, to model this set of scenarios under two transmission environments:

Business-as-usual (BAU): Transmission expansion continues at a similar pace to historical levels.

Expanded (Exp.): Interregional and intraregional transmission infrastructure, including spur lines, can be developed faster and at lower cost than today.

The expanded transmission environment allows us to evaluate how the US energy system would evolve with fewer barriers to transmission development. We quantified the value of transmission expansion by comparing capacity additions, electricity prices, reliability costs, and transmission deployment in the expanded transmission and BAU environments for each scenario.

BAAJA, the current bipartisan federal permitting reform bill, includes changes to transmission planning requirements, cost allocation approaches, and the federal government’s role in permitting interstate transmission lines. We modeled those transmission reforms as part of a broader set of policy changes and recently released a note discussing our findings. We do not model explicitly BAAJA provisions in this analysis and instead take a policy-neutral approach to representing the potential to increase transmission, but our findings here are generally consistent with our BAAJA modeling.

RHG-NEMS captures many benefits of transmission, and it has the advantage of reflecting dynamic natural gas prices to the grid—a key driver of power sector decision-making. However, its representation of transmission is limited relative to more specialized production cost models and, naturally, the actual electricity grid and its operations. RHG-NEMS does not capture benefits that play out on highly granular scales, either in terms of time or geography. RHG-NEMS does not capture within-region congestion, one well–documented source of costs that better transmission access can help improve. Similarly, recent work from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory has shown that around 40-60% of the benefits of expanded transmission accrue in just 5% of hours in a year (in their retrospective modeling approach)—and 20-30% accrue in just the top 1% of hours. RHG-NEMS takes a reduced-form approach to modeling hourly dispatch that doesn’t fully capture the benefits that occur in these narrow time slices. Similarly, RHG-NEMS does not anticipate unexpected weather events, which can strain the resilience of the grid and which can be at least partly mitigated by transmission investments. As a result of these limitations, this analysis provides a conservative estimate of the value of transmission.

Expanded transmission reduces prices and enables more capacity on the grid

We find that making transmission easier and cheaper to build reduces electricity prices by transforming the US electric grid. Capacity additions increase as it becomes easier to connect power plants to demand centers. The transmission network grows, strengthening existing connections and expanding to connect new regions. Increasing trade between regions impacts the capacity and generation mix while reducing reliability costs.

Lower electricity prices

Making transmission easier and cheaper to deploy reduces costs across the electricity system. We unpack changes to the grid in the sections that follow, but in general, increased solar and natural gas-fired capacity displaces generation from older, inefficient, more expensive fossil plants, reducing fuel costs. Increasing connections between regions allows regions to share resources for reserve margins. Trade between regions also impacts capacity deployment and operating decisions in ways that favor cheaper resources. Taken together, these dynamics combine to lower total system costs in the expanded transmission scenarios relative to BAU by $82-130 billion from 2026 to 2040, a 2-3% reduction.

This reduction in total system costs flows through to electricity prices. Electricity price represents the average amount customers ultimately pay per kilowatt-hour after accounting for the various components of their electricity rates, including fixed and volumetric charges. Between 2027 and 2040, expanded transmission decreases economy-wide national electricity prices modestly across all sectors, with average economy-wide prices falling by 1.6-3.4% (0.2-0.5 cents) in 2040 (Figure 5). Put another way, the average residential customer saves up to $40 on their electricity bill in 2040 with expanded transmission. These price gaps widen over time as cheaper transmission allows more renewable capacity and more efficient natural gas plants to come online, compounding the benefits of transmission investment. From 2035 to 2040, lower electricity prices save residential and commercial customers $4-5 billion and $5-9 billion per year on average, respectively. Like the dynamics in the previous section, transmission expansion reduces electricity prices most in scenarios where the electricity system is most strained: the constrained supply scenario sees the largest price impact, while the central scenario sees the smallest price impacts. Put another way, the affordability implications of expanded transmission are amplified if data center demand or LNG exports grow at a faster pace.

Unplanned solar additions increase by 20-24% (59-75 GW) in the central, high data center, and high LNG expanded transmission cases compared to BAU in 2040. In the constrained supply scenario, solar capacity doubles (170 GW) over the same period with expanded transmission, owing to lower transmission barriers and reduced spur line costs decreasing overall project costs, balancing this scenario’s higher supply-related costs and allowing solar capacity to deploy more readily.

Natural gas plants also benefit from a more connected grid. Unplanned natural gas-fired additions increase by 10-19 GW (7-21%) with expanded transmission relative to BAU. Combined cycle plants comprise most of these additions, but peaker plants deploy as well to balance the additional solar capacity and maintain grid reliability. Natural gas additions increase the most with expanded transmission in the high LNG scenario. In this scenario, higher LNG exports drive the average Henry Hub spot price up by 50 cents (10%) compared to prices in the central scenario from 2030 to 2040. As a result of higher natural gas prices, the high LNG scenario under BAU sees the lowest gas-fired capacity of all scenarios. Coming from this lower baseline, expanded transmission has a differential impact on natural gas additions in the high LNG scenario, but total natural gas capacity remains the lowest of all scenarios.

In our modeling, emerging clean technologies like nuclear technologies and enhanced geothermal systems remain too expensive to compete with more conventional resources: nuclear capacity doesn’t expand beyond planned uprates and restarts, and geothermal capacity grows meaningfully from today but still represents only a small share of the market by 2040. However, these technologies also benefit from expanded transmission, which can reduce the time and costs associated with grid connection. The economic viability of geothermal projects in particular, which are often located in rural areas, partially depends on the build-out of transmission infrastructure required to connect these resources to demand centers.

These capacity changes impact the generation mix in each scenario. Solar generation shares increase by 2-7% in 2040 relative to BAU, largely displacing gas generation shares despite the increase in gas capacity. Across scenarios, transmission expansion allows older, more inefficient gas-fired generators to run less frequently while increasing generation from new gas plants and solar capacity. Instead of retiring, these older gas plants stay online to provide reliability for growing shares of renewable energy and amid increasing demand. Coal generation also falls slightly as coal retirements increase modestly, and surviving plants operate at lower capacity factors. This shift towards zero-marginal cost resources and more efficient gas power plants reduces generation costs, which helps drive down electricity prices.

Meeting reliability targets at lower cost

Beyond reshaping the generation mix, making transmission cheaper and easier to deploy also lowers the cost of maintaining grid reliability. Across all scenarios, our model optimizes to meet the same targets for resource adequacy and spinning reserves. Expanded transmission reduces the costs of achieving these by up to 12.2% (Figure 8). Enhancing connections between regions allows regions to rely on some capacity in neighboring regions to meet reliability requirements, driving down costs associated with building out extra in-region peaking generation or long-term planning of generation to meet growing load. Regional grid operators currently utilize this strategy to cut costs. For instance, the Southwest Power Pool saved $8.5 billion in additional generation capacity investment in 2025 by sharing resources across its footprint. Expanded transmission allows for greater resource sharing and increased cost savings. In our modeling, the high LNG and constrained supply scenarios see the biggest reductions in reliability costs with expanded transmission, because transmission mitigates some of the high generation costs associated with high gas prices or a generation-limited power sector.

By 2035, regional transmission and spur lines together expand by 2.9-6.7 TW-mi (22-35%) relative to BAU scenarios. Like the interregional transmission results, the high data center scenario sees the greatest regional transmission and spur line impacts in 2035, as easier access to transmission allows grid capacity to expand and meet high electricity demand at lower cost. However, transmission impacts in this scenario fall after 2035 as the expanded grid becomes increasingly sufficient to accommodate load growth. By 2040, the constrained supply scenario experiences the greatest impacts to regional transmission and spur line build-out, with lower voltage transmission expanding by 53% compared to BAU. In this scenario, impacts accumulate over time as capacity additions continue to diverge from the supply-limited BAU.

Conclusions

In this era of surging US electricity demand—coupled with increasing pressure on natural gas prices from expanding LNG exports, elevated costs from supply chain inflation, and non-cost barriers like lengthy interconnection queues—energy reliability and affordability have become critical concerns across the country. A robust transmission network is an essential tool for alleviating some of these cost and supply pressures, as well as accommodating rapid electricity demand growth.

Expanded transmission lowers electricity prices by 2-3% in 2040 compared to BAU, though some regions see larger price impacts. While our modeling doesn’t capture local congestion, transmission expansion can also reduce price impacts from congestion, further reducing electricity prices beyond what we’ve modeled here. These price impacts result from changes in the grid mix and grid operations enabled by expanded transmission.

Strengthening and expanding transmission systems enables more capacity to connect to the grid—mostly solar and natural gas in our modeling. Enhancing interregional connections allows regions to share their generation more readily, improving the relative economics of certain types of power in areas with better-quality, cheaper resources than their neighbors.

The grid capacity build-out and changing electricity trade dynamics, driven by expanded transmission, improve electricity affordability. Expanded transmission enables more efficient natural gas plants and renewables to connect to the grid faster, allowing less-efficient, higher-cost resources to retire and reducing the total system costs required to meet growing demand. At the same time, greater trade between regions allows cheaper energy to be delivered to demand centers. Expanded interregional transmission also allows regions to share resources for reserve margins, reducing the costs required to meet reliability standards.

We find that transmission expansion offers the greatest benefits when the US energy system is stressed (e.g., by skyrocketing data center demand or constraints on supply of new capacity). As demand growth continues to accelerate, driven by AI proliferation, domestic manufacturing, and electrification, and global conflicts continue to strain supply chains, the risk of longer-term systemic stressors increases. Our expanded transmission scenarios envision a world in which it’s easier and cheaper to build out transmission infrastructure, but this world is far from guaranteed. The path from our current environment to this imagined world requires focused resources and policy development at the federal, state, and local levels.

text:
Two groups behind construction of a proposed $1-billion natural gas-fired power plant in northern Wisconsin told state officials they are pulling the plug on the project. Dairyland Power Cooperative, headquartered in La Crosse, Wisconsin, and South Shore Energy—a subsidiary of Allete—the parent of Minnesota Power—in a letter to Wisconsin's Public Service Commission told commissioners the groups would not move forward with the Nemadji Trail Energy Center (NTEC).The power plant was sited in Superior, in Douglas County, near Lake Superior, and also near Duluth, Minnesota. The letter to the PSC was filed Oct. 28 by Daniel McCourtney, manager of strategic environmental initiatives at Allete, which had distanced itself from the project late last year."No construction has occurred on NTEC or the [generation tie line]," McCourtney wrote in the letter to the PSC. "Accordingly, the owners respectfully request that the commission acknowledge their relinquishment of all rights associated with the [plant approvals]."[caption id="attachment_216052" align="alignnone" width="640"]

This is a rendering of the proposed Nemadji Trail Energy Center in Wisconsin. Construction of the natural gas-fired power plant, which was approved in 2020, was canceled in October 2026. Courtesy: Dairyland Power Cooperative[/caption]The PSC had approved the project in 2020. The commission had granted certificates of public convenience and necessity for construction of a natural gas-fired power plant with generation capacity of between 550 and 625 MW. The utilities had proposed the NTEC as a way to provide baseload electricity to replace retiring coal-fired generation, and support power reliability as they made more investments in renewable energy.

Several Gas-Fired Power Stations Move Forward

Other gas-fired power plant projects are moving forward in Wisconsin. Regulators recently approved Invenergy's request to build two new gas-fired stations in the southern part of the state, and We Energies—the state's largest electric utility—has said it would buy the plants. The Red Oak Ridge Energy Center project would be a nearly 1.2-GW facility; the Foundry Ridge Energy Center would have 324 MW of generation capacity.We Energies also received approval in 2025 for two new gas-fired facilities, in Oak Creek (1,100 MW) and Paris (128 MW). POWER previously reported on the utility's plan to build a gas-fired plant in Outagamie County; the Fox North Energy Center would have 750 MW of generation capacity.Invenergy in August filed an engineering plan with the PSC for two gas-fired stations in Calumet County in northeast Wisconsin that would have a combined generation capacity of nearly 2 GW. We Energies has included the power plants in its regulatory filings, and has said the 1,200-MW Forest Junction Energy Center and the 750-MW Union Depot Energy Center could be online by December 2031.

text:
With Hyundai-POSCO Louisiana Steel’s air permit approved, a coalition of residents and environmental and labor organizations is pressing the steelmaker for a legally binding agreement covering pollution protections, local hiring and compensation for affected homeowners.

The Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality approved the permit last week, clearing a major regulatory hurdle for the planned $5.8 billion mill at RiverPlex MegaPark near Donaldsonville. With the permit secured, Hyundai can advance authorized construction activities. Trial operations are slated for the fourth quarter of 2028, with commercial production still scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2029.

The permit decision followed a 4½-hour public hearing Sept. 1 that drew sharply divided testimony from supporters and opponents.

Jacob Horwitz, a New Orleans-based organizer with the United Steelworkers and the Good Neighbors Louisiana Coalition, says the decision was disappointing but does not end the group’s efforts to secure stronger protections for nearby communities.

The coalition welcomed Hyundai’s June permit revisions, which reduced projected emissions, but argues the company could adopt cleaner technologies. Its concerns include the lack of a firm timeline for transitioning from natural gas to green hydrogen, questions about carbon capture and safeguards against pollution incidents.

He says the coalition’s next priority is a community benefits agreement that would establish enforceable environmental safeguards, guarantee local employment opportunities and provide compensation for affected homeowners. The coalition plans to continue organizing residents and publicizing their concerns to press Hyundai into negotiations.

Hyundai has previously maintained that the facility will meet environmental standards and produce substantially fewer carbon emissions than conventional steelmaking methods.

“This marks an important step forward for the project and the community, as the construction phase is expected to bring significant additional economic growth and opportunities to the area,” HPLS said in an emailed statement after the approval.

Ascension Parish President Clint Cointment also welcomed the decision.

“The approval of the air permit by the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality marks a pivotal moment of progress for Hyundai-POSCO, Ascension Parish, and the entire River Region,” Cointment said in an emailed statement. “This milestone clears the path for a historic $5.8 billion capital investment that will anchor the RiverPlex MegaPark on our West Bank, bringing thousands of quality jobs, long-term economic stability, and advanced manufacturing opportunities to our residents.”

text:
Project demonstrates how drone technology can support transmission crews working across marshland, farmland, and difficult crossings

AUSTIN, Texas, November 03, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Infravision today announced the deployment of its drone stringing technology on Entergy's Amite South Reliability Project in Louisiana. Working alongside Utility Lines Construction Services (ULCS), Infravision is helping install pulling lines across challenging terrain while freeing up construction crews and equipment for other work.

Entergy's Amite South Reliability Project includes constructing new 230 kV and 500 kV transmission lines from Plaquemine, LA, to Westwego, LA, crossing more than 150 miles of rural farmland and marshland. Once energized, these lines will improve power flows across the region, enhance reliability and resiliency for customers in the Greater New Orleans area, and support growing industrial and commercial development on the west bank of the Mississippi River.

ULCS is incorporating Infravision's drone stringing system into its construction operations. The drone installs an initial pulling line through blocks mounted on transmission structures. Construction crews then use that line to pull the subsequent lines and conductor through.

The approach reduces work at height and the need to position crews and equipment at individual structures for initial line installation, particularly in areas with limited ground access. It also allows Infravision's drone team to execute work outside of the critical path of construction, freeing up ULCS crews to advance other activities.

"Safety innovation is about finding ways to perform high-risk tasks while reducing employee exposure. Our partnership with Infravision allows us to leverage technology that improves safety while enhancing operational efficiency," said Brett Crochet, director of safety operations for ULCS.

In field interviews, Entergy construction supervisors reported that drone installation cut rope installation time by approximately 75% on some sections, from about seven days to a day and a half. They also highlighted the reduced exposure for crews and the public at highway and bayou crossings.

"This is the first time we've integrated this technology into our transmission construction work, and it has meaningfully improved how we install lead lines and navigate challenging terrain," said Chris Gremillion, Entergy vice president of project delivery for capital projects. "It allows our crews to work more safely and efficiently, and it's rewarding to see long‑standing challenges addressed through practical innovation."

The Amite South Reliability Project is Infravision's largest U.S. project to date. The ongoing deployment offers an opportunity to demonstrate drone stringing as a routine part of major transmission line construction, with repeated use across successive line sections.

"On a project of this scale, the technology has to deliver day after day and fit the way construction crews work," said Matt Jones, chief commercial officer of Infravision. "At Amite South, we're working alongside ULCS to get pulling lines in place while their crews advance other construction activities. That's the opportunity we see across the U.S.: helping utilities and contractors build more transmission with the skilled crews and resources they have. We're proud to be putting that approach to work with Entergy and ULCS."

About Infravision

Infravision is transforming how critical power infrastructure is built, making transmission construction faster, safer, and more affordable. Its integrated system combines advanced drone technology, intelligent ground equipment, specialized stringing hardware, and experienced field crews to support the construction and maintenance of electricity infrastructure. Infravision operates internationally, supporting utilities and infrastructure providers as they expand and modernize the world's electric grid. For more information, visit infravisioninc.com.

ULCS is part of Asplundh Infrastructure Group. As an Asplundh company, ULCS is backed by a nearly 100-year-old, financially solid, privately held company with over 36,000 employees providing utilities with vegetation management services and transmission and distribution infrastructure services. Working with ULCS, you have access to the reach, resources and responsiveness that the scope, scale, and financial strength of Asplundh can offer—plus the peace of mind that comes with it.

title: What's on the Menu for the UN Climate Summit? | Article | EESI
description:
Key Takeaways: United Nations (UN) climate summit presidencies have the ability to highlight key issues they would like to see addressed in the summit’s Action Agenda.
In this role, Kurum is responsible for conference logistics and setting the COP31 Action Agenda.
An overview of several COP31 Action Agenda items and priorities follows.
These Action Agenda priority items also include deeper support for ocean research and coastal communities.
COP31 priority items for climate-resilient cities include achieving whole-life emission reductions by using more sustainable materials and making buildings more efficient.
text:
Key Takeaways:

United Nations (UN) climate summit presidencies have the ability to highlight key issues they would like to see addressed in the summit’s Action Agenda.

This year, COP31 President-Designate Murat Kurum of Türkiye has highlighted a handful of issues with particular importance to Türkiye and the world, including electrification, the clean energy transition, zero waste, protecting ecosystems, and building resilient cities

From November 9–20, 2026, representatives from around the world will gather in Antalya, Türkiye, to make decisions about our planet’s future at the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). The conference will be attended by representatives from national, subnational, and indigenous governments, as well as non-governmental organizations, trade associations, and academic institutions. Though the exact negotiation agenda is still up in the air, those following COP31 can look to the stated priorities of the COP31 President-Designate to get a sense of what might be in store.

The COP president is responsible for the event’s facility, logistics, and the substantive content and direction of both formal negotiations and informal commitments. Typically, the COP host country’s leader appoints the COP president. Countries bid for the right to host COP, rotating between the continents. At COP29, Australia and Türkiye each put in bids to host the COP31 conference, but negotiations stalled until the end of COP30, when the countries agreed to host the next conference jointly. In this arrangement, the conference will be led by two presidents. This dual-host model is unprecedented—the only comparable case is COP23, which was hosted by Germany to simplify logistics, but presided over by Fiji.

Both COP31 presidents have clear responsibilities. The first president is Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister for climate change and energy, who will serve as the president of negotiations. Bowen will be the main point of contact for delegations struggling to reach agreements and individuals with concerns about rules, procedures, or the inclusion of marginalized perspectives. The second president is Turkish Minister of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Murat Kurum, who will serve as the president-designate. In this role, Kurum is responsible for conference logistics and setting the COP31 Action Agenda.

The Action Agenda is the mechanism for all voluntary commitments from businesses, national and subnational governments, non-governmental organizations, and other actors outside of formal negotiations. The concept was originally introduced at COP20 in Lima, Peru, and runs alongside COP negotiations. The Action Agenda can also shed light on what the host country is most eager to see accomplished at COP, both within and outside the negotiations. The Action Agenda is strictly voluntary and non-binding, which differentiates its goals and action items from the obligatory agreements that come out of COP. Many Action Agenda items invite COP parties to collaborate with non-party actors and the United Nations on key goals. For example, the food security agenda item is introducing a voluntary program called the Turquoise Nexus, which aims to bring together countries and non-parties to collaborate under the United Nations’ Food and Agriculture Organization. An overview of several COP31 Action Agenda items and priorities follows.

Electrification

One of Türkiye’s primary interests at COP31 is electrification. Electrification is the process of moving away from technologies that directly burn fossil fuels—such as gasoline cars, diesel generators, or gas stoves—and towards electric alternatives. Electrification is a necessary part of the clean energy transition, as it makes it possible to replace fossil fuels with electricity generated from renewable energy.

As a part of the electrification priority and its corresponding Action Agenda item, COP31 has affirmed a target of achieving 35% electrification by 2035 in its proposed Global Electrification Pledge. Kurum introduced this target at Climate Week NYC in September 2026. It is designed to be voluntary for both parties to the UNFCCC and non-party actors, and also informs other voluntary programs COP31 is introducing. Türkiye itself has a long way to go when it comes to electrification. Only 22% of the country’s energy consumption came from electricity in 2024.

Other aspects of the electrification agenda item include broadening electricity access and strengthening the grid. Around the world, 730 million people do not yet have access to electric power, according to the Turkish presidency. This agenda item also prioritizes replacing fossil fuel power plants with clean energy generation. This is essential when considering the growing energy demands of data centers. For the same reason, efforts to strengthen the grid are especially timely. The presidency highlights solutions, such as infrastructure investments and storage technologies, that can help make the grid more resilient. The Action Agenda also includes the COP31 Global Electrification Initiative, which seeks to assist countries in the implementation of electrification and grid improvements.

Another focus area of this agenda item is clean cooking. According to the Clean Cooking Alliance, a quarter of the world population cooks on open flames. This process releases harmful pollutants and smoke that cause environmental pollution and human health impacts. Furthermore, burning wood for fuel accounts for 2% of global carbon emissions. Providing cleaner cooking alternatives to people who use open flames, including electric stoves, is an essential aspect of electrification.

Clean Energy Transition

Complementary to the presidency’s electrification goals are its overarching clean transition goals. A global transition to clean energy has been a major goal of climate diplomacy for many years, with the annual meeting of the parties to the Paris Agreement (CMA) sessions, held during COP, serving as the main venue for formal negotiations. The president-designate has heavily emphasized this goal in the months leading up to COP31. Coal is Türkiye’s largest energy source, generating 33% of its electricity, and has actually seen its share of Turkish electricity production rise in recent years, replacing a decline in hydropower.

The clean energy transition priority’s corresponding Action Agenda item includes more than just phasing out fossil fuels. Another core focus is sustainable cooling. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), air conditioning accounts for 10% of global energy consumption. This statistic does not include most of the developing world, where only 8% of people own air conditioners. As the developing world grows richer, enabling more of its inhabitants to embrace air conditioning, cooling technologies are projected to account for 37% of electricity demand growth through 2050. The IEA estimates that energy-efficient cooling technologies can reduce future electricity demand by 45%. Passive and sustainable cooling strategies, such as shade, insulation, ventilation, climate-smart landscaping, and evaporation, can also effectively lower the temperature through non-mechanical means. These solutions are also flexible and scalable, and can be tailored to different countries’ climates, resources, and architecture. This ties in with another focus, nationally grounded transitions. This goal recognizes that every country has its own distinct context, and what works for one country may not work for the next—accordingly, the best solutions are those that can be modified to the needs of any country.

Another key focus within this item is geothermal energy, the subject of the Global Geothermal Ambition Pledge. With this proposed pledge, the presidency seeks to increase the total electricity and heat produced via geothermal energy twelvefold by 2050 (compared to 2025 levels). Countries and non-party actors that sign on to this pledge will attempt to boost geothermal generation through actions like funding geothermal research, providing technical assistance to countries in need, and using geothermal heat directly in heating and cooling systems.

Waste and Circularity

Zero waste has long been a priority for the Turkish government, and now it features on the Action Agenda. In his third letter from the presidency, Kurum stated that under this priority, his goal would be to cut projected global annual municipal waste generation 50% by 2035.

This Action Agenda item aims to prevent food waste and promote circular economies. Food waste is one of the largest components of waste-related emissions, responsible for 219 metric tons of carbon dioxide and 2.59 million metric tons of methane emissions in the United States alone in 2024.

As a part of the related green industrialization priority, Kurum seeks to increase the global circular material use rate to 15% by 2035. Circular economy strategies allow items that might normally be thrown away to be repurposed, repaired, salvaged, and reused. Developing circularity pathways is especially useful for materials that are hard to source, such as critical minerals like lithium.

Waste is a key concern for Türkiye, which is a major importer of waste, particularly from the rest of Europe. In the waste trade, wealthier countries often export their waste to developing countries for processing. Those developing countries then deal with the consequences, including methane emissions, water pollution, and harm to wildlife. Countries like Mexico, Malaysia, and India also receive hundreds of millions of pounds of imported waste each year. Developing strategies to reduce, reuse, and recycle waste in its country of origin can improve both the environmental impacts of excess waste and the negative geopolitical impacts of exporting waste to developing countries. Key Turkish officials, including First Lady Emine Erdoğan, have been working on the challenge of zero waste, both domestically and internationally, for years. Erdoğan has campaigned to reduce waste since 2017, and founded the Zero Waste Foundation in 2023. She also serves on a UN Advisory Board on zero waste, having worked closely with Secretary-General António Guterres on the issue.

Protecting Natural Environments

Two stated priorities of the COP31 Presidency reflect international interest in protecting and restoring natural ecosystems. The first of these covers oceans and seas, and notes that 25% of human carbon emissions are absorbed by ocean ecosystems, which act as a carbon sink, so protecting them is critical to continued climate action. Within that priority is a focus item on acidification—when excess carbon dioxide is absorbed by seawater, creating an acidic byproduct—which also poses major ecosystem threats. Acidification can be limited by developing and protecting coastal blue carbon sinks, which is one of the focus items under the oceans and seas priority. Coastal blue carbon sinks are ecosystems that can sequester carbon in coastal plants like seagrasses and mangroves. Related to this priority is the commitment to building coastal ecosystem resilience. Coral reefs, for example, are highly sensitive to changes in water acidity and temperature, but critical to protecting coasts and marine life from storms and erosion.

These Action Agenda priority items also include deeper support for ocean research and coastal communities. The presidency notes that better ocean research can inform early-warning disaster communication and stronger climate policy. Better support can help coastal communities, which are vulnerable to flooding and erosion, take appropriate actions to limit the damage climate change may cause.

Türkiye is also developing a voluntary program to address marine litter. The Australian presidency has similarly emphasized the importance of oceans in COP discussions, appointing three Pacific climate envoys to highlight local climate solutions in Pacific island nations. Australia also hosted a pre-COP summit in Fiji and a world leaders event in Tuvalu.

The other presidential priority dedicated to protecting the natural environment is the Rio Synergy, a plan to implement “integrated solutions where climate, biodiversity, and desertification converge.” Focus areas here include protecting carbon sinks and biodiversity and improving wildfire management. These three goals build on priorities established at COP30 in Brazil.

Resilient Cities

Türkiye’s Murat Kurum has also emphasized the importance of city-level resilience and adaptation. In May, negotiators, including Kurum, adopted the Hatay Declaration, which committed signatories to building resilient cities, establishing financing mechanisms to fund urban sustainability, and implementing nature-based solutions. In its priority related to climate-resilient cities, the presidency highlights that 37% of all carbon dioxide emissions are from buildings and construction. Buildings are responsible for considerable emissions related to heating and cooling. Only 17% of worldwide building power demands are met with renewable energy. COP31 priority items for climate-resilient cities include achieving whole-life emission reductions by using more sustainable materials and making buildings more efficient. The promotion of green building certifications is one tool for reducing these emissions. The Action Agenda also highlights the need for finance mechanisms to improve cities’ disaster resilience infrastructure.

As it seeks to make cities climate resilient, the Action Agenda encourages buy-in to multiple programs, including the Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings, which would reduce the energy intensity of buildings globally by 25% by 2035. The presidency also launched the Sustainable Urban Resilience Financing Facility, in partnership with the Turkish development bank, İlbank. This program would help countries create and implement sustainable finance mechanisms and provide technical assistance for urban planning.

Other Priorities

The programs discussed above represent only part of a broader suite of initiatives that the Turkish presidency is using to advance climate action at COP31. Dialogue at COP31 may also include other topics explicit in the presidential priorities and in continued discussions from previous COPs, as well as topics like climate finance that are central to the UNFCCC’s work. As COP31 unfolds, EESI will cover key updates on Action Agenda items and negotiation issues. To keep up with everything COP31, sign up for our COP Dispatch newsletter and keep an eye on our COP31 Resources page.

The Office of Workforce Development, in partnership with the Metropolitan Area Planning Council, hosted a celebration on August 25 to mark the conclusion of the Good Jobs Metro Boston Coalition (GJMBC) and recognize the training providers, employers, community-based organizations, and partners who made it possible. The GJMBC was a four-year initiative created to train and place 4,618 unemployed and underemployed residents in the healthcare, clean energy, and child care industries. The initiative was funded by a $23 million grant from the Economic Development Administration (EDA) of the U.S. Department of Commerce. The City invested another $24 million in job training across sectors throughout the grant period.

“Over the past four years, we have supported over 4,000 workers in pathways to quality jobs with living wages, benefits, and career advancement opportunities,” said Chief of Worker Empowerment Trinh. “This accomplishment was made possible thanks to Mayor Wu’s leadership and the commitment of local employers, training providers, wraparound support providers, and industry stakeholders. Together, we will continue to create a City where the best talent can build careers with world-class employers.

The celebration highlighted the success of the coalition’s work. Beth Israel Lahey Health Assistant Vice President of Workforce Development Joanne Pokaski spoke about how this investment increased BILH’s staff capacity in critical roles and supported employees’ professional development along career pathways. Three GJMBC graduates participated in a panel to discuss their experiences with the GJMBC program, including Boston EMS EMT Jordy Gonzalez, lead teacher Mackendy Saveur, and contractor Nacius Magis.

Industry leaders from the Boston Healthcare Careers Consortium (healthcare), Benjamin Franklin Cummings Institute of Technology (clean energy), and CAYL Institute (child care) developed and implemented the strategy for their respective sectors. Commitments from employers were also critical to the GJMBC’s success. Top employers included Mass General Brigham with over 1,000 hires, Beth Israel Lahey Health, Boston EMS, Schneider Electric, Homeworks Energy, Bozzuto, Little Sprouts, YMCA, and Action for Boston Community Development.

“The Good Jobs Challenge was an important catalyst in addressing healthcare workforce shortages as our industry emerged from the pandemic, bringing together employers, educators, and community partners around a shared goal,” said Kristin Driscoll, Executive Director, Workforce Development, Human Resources, Mass General Brigham. “Mass General Brigham is proud to be included in this effort, helping expand access to healthcare careers, create opportunities for economic mobility, and build a stronger workforce for the future. Through the Good Jobs Challenge, we welcomed more than 1,000 individuals, each helping address critical staffing needs and ensuring we can continue delivering exceptional care to the patients and communities we serve."

text:
The United States Department of Energy (DOE) has announced $8.5m in funding for 28 research projects to advance commercial fusion energy.

The awards, delivered through its Innovation Network for Fusion Energy (INFUSE) programme, will support partnerships between private fusion companies, national laboratories and universities.

Funding will target scientific and technological challenges that must be overcome to make fusion energy commercially viable.

A total of 22 commercial enterprises will participate in the selected projects, which will investigate areas including materials science, plasma diagnostics, modelling and simulation.

The latest awards represent another step in the US Government’s efforts to accelerate fusion development through public-private collaboration, bringing together industry expertise and research capabilities to advance technologies needed for future fusion power plants.

Speaking on the investment, DOE Under Secretary for Science Darío Gil said: “The race to commercial fusion energy will not be won in isolation. It demands a seamless partnership between the pioneering intellect of our National Labs and universities and the speed and daring of private capital.

“Every challenge we solve through INFUSE brings us one step closer to an era of energy abundance that will transform our economy, revitalise manufacturing, and secure American leadership for generations.”

How does fusion energy work?

Fusion energy is produced by combining two light atomic nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy in the process. It is the same fundamental reaction that powers the Sun and other stars.

Replicating this process on Earth requires extremely high temperatures to create a state of matter known as plasma.

Controlling and sustaining this plasma, along with developing materials and technologies that can operate under demanding conditions, are among the challenges facing fusion researchers.

The long-term objective is to develop fusion power plants that can generate reliable electricity on a commercial scale.

Read our full fusion energy explainer here to learn more.

Research targets key fusion technology challenges

Of the 28 selected projects, 17 will be led by US National Laboratories, while universities will lead the remaining 11. Each project will receive between $100,000 and $500,000, with funding supporting research programmes lasting one or two years.

The selection process was managed by the INFUSE leadership team, comprising Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory.

Applications were assessed through a competitive peer-review process.

The programme is designed to give private fusion companies access to specialist research facilities and expertise, helping address technical barriers that could otherwise slow progress towards commercial deployment.

These activities also support the DOE’s Fusion Science and Technology roadmap, which sets out priorities for overcoming the scientific and engineering challenges associated with developing fusion energy.

INFUSE opens applications for 2027 funding

Alongside announcing the latest awards, the INFUSE programme management team has opened its fiscal year 2027 Request for Assistance (RFA).

The next funding round introduces expanded eligibility for consortia and a new review category covering preconceptual designs for fusion pilot plants.

The changes are intended to broaden opportunities for collaboration and support further progress towards commercial fusion energy.

However, the DOE has emphasised that selection does not guarantee funding. Successful applicants must first complete an award negotiation process, during which the department retains the right to withdraw selections or cancel negotiations.

A new call is now offering to support carbon dioxide removal (CDR) projects in Louisiana that will help position the state as a global leader in these technologies

The call is launched by Newlab, Shell GameChanger, and Louisiana Innovation, and is accepting applications by November 13, 2026

Eligible technologies include direct air capture (DAC), biomass-based approaches, enhanced rock weathering (ERW), marine CDR, and innovations in sensing, measurement, reporting, and verification

A new open call launched by Newlab, Shell GameChanger, and Louisiana Innovation is offering support for carbon removal pilot deployments in Louisiana across a range of different technologies.

The Louisiana Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) Initiative was announced last month as a public-private effort that aims to position Louisiana as a global leader for CO2 removal technology development and deployment.

Through this call, Newlab, Shell GameChanger, and Louisiana Innovation will back CDR technology companies and project developers, intending to demonstrate how Louisiana’s industrial, geological, coastal, and agricultural resources could support selected pathways while also identifying deployment opportunities and constraints.

The call is open to solutions centered around direct air capture (DAC) and hybrid pathways, biomass-based approaches, such as biochar, biomass storage, bio-oil, and bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS), marine CDR, enhanced rock weathering (ERW), and innovations in sensing, measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV).

Launched on October 16, 2026, the call will be accepting applications by November 13, 2026.

Projects eligible under this call

The call will support high-durability CDR projects at three different commercial and technical readiness levels.

In the first readiness tier, the call is looking for pilot-stage projects that have an indicative scale for their next deployment milestone of up to 1,000 tpa CO2.

The second tier is for projects that have reached a demonstration stage and and an indicative scale for the next deployment milestone of ~1,000 to 10,000 tpa CO2, while the projects in the third readiness tier need to be deployment-ready or near-commercial and pursuing an indicative scale of ~10,000 to 100,000+ tpa CO2.

Relevant: EPA Issues Second-Ever Marine Carbon Removal Pilot Permit In Louisiana

Call organizers highlight that any project would remain subject to technical validation, commercial evaluation, applicable permitting, and relevant environmental and regulatory requirements.

To qualify for this opportunity, applicants must exhibit a viable path to deployment within Louisiana and a dedicated willingness to collaborate onsite-specific deployment scenarios.

text:
Cleaner electricity helps advance zero-emission goals as power demand grows across the Seaport and OAK

Oakland, Calif. – November 3, 2026: The Port of Oakland announced that 84% of the electricity delivered by its publicly owned utility, Port Public Power, to Port tenants and facilities in 2025 came from renewable and zero-carbon sources. The Port’s Board of Commissioners approved the annual Power Source Disclosure Report and Power Content Label for submission to the California Energy Commission at its October 22 meeting.

The Port’s electricity supply also had less than half the greenhouse gas emissions intensity of the average California utility, supporting the Port’s efforts to reduce emissions as more operations transition to electric power.

Renewable energy exceeds state average

Renewable resources accounted for 61% of Port Public Power’s electricity supply in 2025, compared with a 46% average for California utilities. Geothermal energy was the largest renewable source, followed by solar, biomass and biogas, and eligible small hydroelectric power.

An additional 21% of the Port’s electricity came from large hydroelectric power, with other zero-carbon market purchases bringing the total share of renewable and zero-carbon electricity to 84%.

The Port’s electricity supply had a greenhouse gas intensity of 186 pounds of carbon dioxide equivalent per megawatt-hour, compared with 384 pounds for the average California utility.

Cleaner electricity supports Port electrification

As the Port works toward its zero-emission goals, cleaner electricity helps maximize the environmental benefits of replacing diesel-powered equipment and vehicles with electric alternatives. Electrification across the Seaport and Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport (OAK) can reduce local tailpipe emissions, while a cleaner electricity supply helps limit emissions associated with generating the power.

Port Public Power expects electricity demand on its system to grow four- to five-fold over the next five years as tenants electrify their operations. Total demand could reach as much as 100 megawatts.

“Every year, more of the Port runs on electricity, and our job is to make sure that electricity is clean, reliable and affordable,” said Andre Basler, Director of Utilities at the Port of Oakland. “Delivering 84% renewable and zero carbon power means that as our tenants electrify their trucks, equipment, and operations, they are moving onto one of the cleanest power supplies in California. We intend to keep that supply getting cleaner as demand grows.”

Investments prepare the power system for the future

The Port continues to modernize, expand and replace aging electrical infrastructure to improve reliability and support electrification and sustainable energy across Port properties.

In 2025, the Port’s Board approved a 20-year Energy Storage Service Agreement with Trolley Pass Project LLC, providing the Port with 4 megawatts of capacity at a battery energy storage facility in San Bernardino County. Energy storage can help the Port make better use of solar power, reduce reliance on market purchases and advance its transition to clean energy.

The Port’s efforts support California’s Senate Bill 100 goal of achieving 100% clean electricity by 2045. As a publicly owned utility and member of the Northern California Power Agency, Port Public Power works with other public power utilities across the region to secure reliable, affordable and sustainable electricity for the businesses it serves.

Port Public Power’s 2025 electricity mix and greenhouse gas intensity. Source: Port Power Content Label.

About the Port of Oakland

The Port of Oakland generates vital economic activity, community benefits, and environmental innovation as it decarbonizes its operations for a cleaner and greener future. Along with its partners, the Port supports more than 98,000 regional jobs and $174 billion in annual economic activity. The Port oversees the Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport (OAK), the Oakland Seaport, and nearly 20 miles of waterfront, including Jack London Square, and a publicly owned utility.
