text:
WASHINGTON — A group representing General Motors Co., Ford Motor Co., Stellantis NV and other major automakers on Monday, Nov. 2 backed the Trump administration in a legal challenge to its sharply lower vehicle fuel economy standards filed by California and other states.

Last month, the U.S. Transportation Department said it was finalizing a fleet-wide fuel economy average of 34.9 miles per ⁠gallon by 2031, down from 50.4 miles per gallon that had been approved under then-President Joe Biden in 2024.

The Alliance for Automotive Innovation, which represents most major automakers, backed the effort by President Donald Trump's administration after Michigan, California and two dozen other states, cities and counties sued last month.

"Automakers require certainty and stability in the standards," the group said in the filing with the 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals.

It added that if the standards were set aside, it "would affect automakers’ business, endangering the capital investment planning, product development, and performance validation for hundreds of new vehicle models intended for the U.S. market."

The states said the Trump administration was ignoring the presence of millions of electric vehicles, "leading to a ‌flawed, dramatically ⁠distorted analysis of the 'maximum feasible' fuel economy level." The automaker group said the court should reject those arguments.

The revised Trump administration standards seek to reverse Biden's push toward greater fuel efficiency and electric vehicles. A coalition of environmental ​and consumer groups also filed a separate lawsuit challenging the new rules.

The Transportation Department said the regulation reduces manufacturers' average cost per ​vehicle to comply by $1,289 but increases fuel costs by more than $1,600 over the life ​of the vehicles. ⁠

The department said the rule would increase U.S. gasoline consumption through 2050 by 4.6%, or about 121 billion gallons, compared with the Biden rules but also boost new car sales.

The American Petroleum Institute, an oil and natural gas industry trade group, also filed in support of the Trump administration's rules, saying they ensure the government sets standards that "do not force consumers to purchase vehicles that consume less fuel than they would otherwise choose."

name: Clean Energy
title: Workforce Development for a Clean Energy Future | The Climate Equity Fund
authors: Kimiko Vecchione, Eli Vargas, State Strategist
description:
Workforce Development Leadership within the Climate Equity Fund Network Climate Equity Fund grantees have had success in increasing funding, accessibility, and inclusive curriculum design for workforce development programs before and have paved the way for other communities to follow.
We heard from grantees that there was a recurring need across the states we work in for guidance on how they could work with labor partners to build clean energy, create high paying jobs, and bring BIPOC community members into the clean energy workforce.
So, we recently released a new policy playbook – Workforce Development for a Clean Energy Future.
Opportunities for Community-led Clean Energy Workforce Development While past federal climate legislation included tax credits that were contingent upon workforce development provisions meant to grow the clean energy workforce and economy, the majority of these credits have been sunsetted.
This will increase the construction of renewable energy projects in states, provide everyday ratepayers with access to low-cost electricity, and grow the clean energy workforce.
text:
Why is community-led workforce development key to climate justice?

Without community-led workforce development, a just transition away from fossil fuels is not possible. An equitable transition should allow communities that have borne the costs of the fossil fuel economy to shape and benefit from the clean energy economy. For example, in the Permian Basin many rural Latino immigrant fossil fuel workers are exposed to physical harm from heavy machinery resulting in debilitating injuries and even death. 83% of workers surveyed by our grantee, Somos Un Pueblo Unido, are worried their jobs will not be replaced in the transition away from fossil fuels. They also shared a desire to switch industries. However, many of these workers have not had the resources to do so on their own.

Workers are able to gain the skills to leave toxic and dangerous industries with expanded access to vocational training, education, and certification. Workers and communities already have knowledge about what a just economic transition should look like, but often lack access to the resources and policy pathways needed to realize it. Providing community-based organizations (CBOs) with the resources to lead how educational opportunities are designed and made accessible to workers increases agency and the likelihood their communities are able to transition out of this shuttering industry. This is key to climate justice.

Workforce Development Leadership within the Climate Equity Fund Network

Climate Equity Fund grantees have had success in increasing funding, accessibility, and inclusive curriculum design for workforce development programs before and have paved the way for other communities to follow. In New Mexico, grantees have advocated for the passage of the Energy Transition Act (ETA) of 2019, which mandates all investor-owned utilities achieve 100% clean energy mandates by 2045 and rural electric co-ops do so by 2045. The ETA provides funding to assist displaced fossil fuel workers and mandates apprenticeships for new clean energy projects. New Mexico grantees followed that up with the Community Benefits Fund in 2025, which provides $210 million dollars in funding for communities to adapt to the effects of climate change. These funds are also used towards increasing the ability of rural Latino communities in the Permian Basin to access skill development, vocational training, and certification programs. These programs target oil workers, providing them with the choice to seek alternative employment outside of the dangerous and unhealthy oil sector. Wrap around services like childcare, language, and transportation access help underserved communities benefit from these programs so they can gain meaningful employment.

Illinois People’s Action in partnership with other grassroots organizations worked to pass the landmark Climate and Equitable Jobs Act of 2021 (CEJA). This bill mandates the state of Illinois to meet 100% clean energy by 2050. This mandate drives a need for expansion of renewable energy projects as fossil fuel power plants are closed. CEJA creates workforce training hubs, directs funds to low-income communities, and directs assistance to workers affected by the closure of fossil fuel energy infrastructure.

These two examples highlight what CBOs can accomplish through coordinated efforts, grassroots involvement, and long-term flexible funding. The Climate Equity Fund has been proud to support our partners New Mexico and Illinois with this long-term, flexible support so they have the resources to build sustained community power over years and bring community members to the capital to pass legislation. They are then able to follow policy through the implementation processes to ensure their legislation is implemented equitably the way the community intended.

Policy Playbook

Our grantees are able to drive strong community informed and community-led policy, because they are trusted, community rooted organizations. Grantee staff have firsthand experience of the unique issues impacting workers in their communities and are best positioned to reach workers who traditional workforce systems miss because they understand the language, childcare, transportation, trust, and other barriers facing their communities.

We heard from grantees that there was a recurring need across the states we work in for guidance on how they could work with labor partners to build clean energy, create high paying jobs, and bring BIPOC community members into the clean energy workforce. So, we recently released a new policy playbook – Workforce Development for a Clean Energy Future. Through the playbook, CBOs can choose a policy pathway which best suits their specific state and locality’s needs including legislation, executive pathways, and community benefits agreements. In this playbook CBOs will find there is a pathway which they can implement across shifting political landscapes and geographies. CBOs can use this playbook to understand where strategic opportunities lie in their states and pursue workforce development priorities through the legislative, executive, or project development arenas. This playbook will show options for advocates to pursue job creation and create pathways for equitable workforce training so BIPOC communities can attain those jobs.

Opportunities for Community-led Clean Energy Workforce Development

While past federal climate legislation included tax credits that were contingent upon workforce development provisions meant to grow the clean energy workforce and economy, the majority of these credits have been sunsetted. There are still meaningful opportunities for states and CBOs to advance workforce development despite this such as through the following:

Community solar legislation focused on apprenticeships, prevailing wages and union friendly project labor agreement (PLA) mandates can grow the clean energy workforce, while encouraging the development of affordable solar for ratepayers.

Community benefits agreements (CBAs) for developers to prioritize apprenticeship programs, on-the-job training, local hiring, and payment of family sustaining wages. Projects like large solar arrays, battery energy storage facilities, and data centers can provide opportunities for CBAs.

State renewable energy legislation can also include mandates for apprenticeships, PLAs, and prevailing wage requirements into any potential legislation. This will increase the construction of renewable energy projects in states, provide everyday ratepayers with access to low-cost electricity, and grow the clean energy workforce.

With our support Climate Equity Fund grantees are able to take advantage of these opportunities to advance workforce development policy through partnerships with labor allies, base-building, and grassroots mobilization.

The Climate Equity Fund’s Place Within This

The Climate Equity Fund is uniquely positioned to support grassroots, frontline communities in key states across the country due to our intermediary model of flexible funding, state expertise, tailored technical assistance, and ability to provide connections to peer organizations and specialized issue expertise. As a State Strategist at the Climate Equity Fund I work one-on-one with our grantees to support their workforce advocacy efforts. I help grantees strategize how to translate worker needs into policy goals, campaigns, and wins. State Strategists at the Climate Equity Fund provide this support through strategy conversations, issue specific webinars, individualized policy research briefs, and connection to other technical assistance experts. This role within the movement is truly rewarding as it offers you the opportunity to see a community’s needs transformed into proposed policy, then into a campaign, and ultimately into life changing impact. That is the type of work the Climate Equity Fund supports and this dynamic of being a funder, technical assistance provider, and ally to CBOs across the country is what makes us unique. Communities are leading the way to realize a just transition through workforce development and the Climate Equity Fund holistically supports them to maximize their impact.

name: Congress
title: Al Gore on Midterms 2026: “To Solve the Climate Crisis, We Need to Address the Democracy Crisis”
description:
He has been steadfast in his determination to ring the alarm bells on the climate crisis, and held the first hearings in Congress on climate.
If we want to solve the climate issue, we need to build political power.
The climate crisis is connected to affordability.
SA: My goal is to solve the climate crisis.
It's all interconnected, and I've often said in order to solve the climate crisis, we need to address the democracy crisis.
text:
I watched Al Gore in An Inconvenient Truth in my eighth-grade US history class. It was the first time I learned about the depth of climate science, and it has stayed with me ever since. I have spent years organizing in the climate space, mobilizing the masses to vote, pushing for policy at the federal level, and consulting with the United Nations. While most registered voters would prefer to vote for a candidate who supports climate action, however, it often feels like much of the older generation has abandoned the issue.

Even so, Mr. Gore has become a beacon of what happens when you step into your own power. He has served as a congressman, senator, and vice president of the United States. He has been steadfast in his determination to ring the alarm bells on the climate crisis, and held the first hearings in Congress on climate.

Even after his tenure in political office, he has continued his work against the fossil fuel industry, building the Climate Reality Project, educating a new crop of climate leaders, and working with leaders across the globe. His work has won him the Presidential Medal of Freedom, a Nobel Prize, and the admiration of young people worldwide.

I’ve had the humbling, albeit dreamlike, honor of collaborating with Mr. Gore over the years. Despite our age difference, we agree on a lot, including that climate change is the defining issue of our time. It requires intergenerational collaboration to solve. And it’s not too late to take action.

Whether in Indonesia or Italy, Mexico or Morocco, citizens of the world are taking to the streets and demanding a better future. This week, Serbia’s nationalist leader was voted out after two years of sustained student protests. Brazil reelected Lula the same day, standing up for nature and against fascism. With the 2026 midterms underway, we have a chance to do the same in the United States.

Advertisement

These midterm elections will determine the balance of power in the House of Representatives and the Senate. And that means these elections will determine what policies will pass, and what policies will crumble. The past two years have presented us with demoralizing rollbacks: trampled endangered species protections, dissolved air pollution standards, and an all-out assault on climate justice.

Millions of voters have already cast their ballots in the midterm elections, using this chance to reclaim our power, mobilize our communities, and show up at the polls. You can find your polling place, see who is on your ballot, and find all the resources you need to vote here. If we want to solve the climate issue, we need to build political power.

Mr. Gore and I sat down to discuss the urgency of climate action, the need for all generations to get involved, and the importance of voting in this election. Ahead, read our conversation, which also addresses voting rights, clean energy, and more.

Saad Amer: It’s the 20th anniversary of An Inconvenient Truth, and I actually rewatched it yesterday. The film holds up incredibly well, and it's kind of shocking because it feels as if we've barely moved forward in these last 20 years, despite the groundswell of awareness. I'm so curious: How do you feel about the legacy of the film? And how do we make sure that within 20 years' time, this same delay isn't happening again?

The following conversation has been lightly copy-edited for clarity.

Al Gore: Thanks for watching the movie again 20 years after you were in middle school. I wish the movie had been wrong. I channeled the scientists who were very patient and took a lot of time to go over things many, many times with me so that I could simplify [the information] without distorting it. And they wish they were wrong, too, of course—but they weren't. And the fact that they were spot on 20 years ago should cause us to pay more attention to what they're warning us about now.

I know how it feels when progress on something important is not moving as fast as you would wish it to move. I experienced something similar when I was your age and younger during the Civil Rights Movement in the US back in the 1960s. Along with most of my generation, we felt like we hadn't moved forward fast enough toward racial justice. But like that movement—and like all of the morally based movements in humanity's future—there were times when advocates felt despair, but they kept going. In the anti-apartheid movement, Nelson Mandela [was] famously [attributed] with saying, "It always seems impossible until it's done.”

I can't deny, I'm disappointed that we have not yet fully deployed all of the solutions to the climate crisis that are right at our fingertips. They're available, they work, but I know we can do it.

Now, we have already come a good piece since 20 years ago. The energy transition is moving in the right direction pretty powerfully, and I don't think we can stop that momentum. Back in 2006, when An Inconvenient Truth was first released, the world had a grand total of seven gigawatts of solar capacity. Today our capacity is almost 3,000 gigawatts, which is more than 400 times what it was 20 years ago.

In 2006, 77% of all the new global power capacity was from fossil fuels. Only 23% was carbon-free, and a lot of that was hydro, which can't expand very much, and nuclear, which has unfortunately priced itself out of the market to an extent.

But look at the change. In 2025, if you look at all of the new global power capacity installed last year, 85% was renewables. And here in the US, the number was even higher. Renewables were 92% of all new power capacity added last year, so we're making progress. Twenty years ago, the US generated 49% of its electricity from coal, more than from any other source. But last year coal was responsible for about 17%, not almost 50%.

And this year feels like we really have reached a genuine turning point. The war in Iran— which is the second time in four years the fossil fuel supply chain has been disrupted and prices have spiked—this war has exposed just how vulnerable our dependence on fossil fuel makes us. And more and more people are choosing electric vehicles, heat pumps, which can now handle big loads in cold climates too, and renewables as alternatives to the rising oil and gas prices. So we need to keep up the momentum, and that means we need to continue to expand and grow the climate movement.

SA: I didn't realize that it was just seven gigawatts back when the film originally came out. That is such a revolution within my lifetime. My family's from Pakistan, and the way that people have been rapidly adopting solar and, for the first time, having electricity across the country in a way that didn't even require government intervention or massive subsidies… it was just the best economic choice.

AG: I was reading an article about some of the rural areas of Pakistan; the common dowry for a bride now is three panels and an inverter. In Africa, they're installing a hundred thousand panels per day. Nigeria is accelerating dramatically: 20 years ago it took a full year to install one gigawatt of solar, now it takes 13 hours, so it's a big change.

So let me ask you a question, Saad. We've worked together over the years, mobilizing young voters, training grassroots climate activists with the Climate Reality Project, and now raising alarm bells for climate action here with Teen Vogue, as you're doing. What do you think is the most important thing people can do right now to make a difference on climate, or for that matter, on any other issue they feel so strongly about?

SA: I mean, it's been an honor to collaborate with you over these years, and with just days until the election, the most important thing people can do is not just vote—but bring their friends out to vote too, right?

Early voting has already started in most states across the country. Millions of ballots have already been cast, and I frequently hear people being frustrated by affordability right now, by the influx of data centers taking people's land and polluting water and the air, and all of these environmental rollbacks that we're seeing nationwide. Right now, the most impactful thing a person can do is mobilize their community to get out and vote.

These policies don't shift unless we take in that power and get to the polls and shift things in the right direction. Yesterday, I was doing a text bank, and we were able to text 25,000 voters in Michigan. So many people were excited to get texts from us and were telling us that they had already voted. We had so many more people volunteer to tell their friends to get out and vote. One person told me that they were volunteering with Planned Parenthood and mobilizing voters, but that they had free time, and then they wanted to sign up for more shifts to mobilize people to vote.

Right now I think the name of the game is democracy. Come November 4, the day after the election, is when we get back to holding our elected officials accountable and making sure that they know which policies they need to implement and are actually doing their job and representing our communities.

AG: I was excited that just in the last week, young people and students were responsible for a huge surprise victory in Serbia, overturning the Putin-friendly dictator-wannabe there and electing a new democratically focused government. And the same day, basically, young people and students pulled off a surprise victory in the second round of the elections for president in Brazil. The son of Bolsonaro was the victor in the first round, and students got busy and turned that around, so that we have a progressive leader of Brazil now being reelected.

The one thing I would add to what you said is: We need more young people who care about climate action to become more active participants in our democracy. That means, of course, voting in this election—and not just for Congress. Make sure you do your research on your local races as well, to learn about the candidates and policies in your area…. Public service commissions determine a lot of energy choices and school boards.

And after the election, we need young people to continue making their voices heard so that we can see renewed ambition from what will hopefully be not only a new Congress, but a transformed Congress, and continue your activities at the local level. I would encourage anyone who wants to join Saad and me to sign up for Climate Reality's Climate Ambition Campaign, or join our weekly hour of action every Monday at climaterealityproject.org.

SA: I keep hearing this idea that climate isn't a popular voting issue, that we should ignore it, and there's this “climate-hushing" idea that has swept across the nation, kind of silencing a lot of the momentum that the climate movement has gained. You led the first hearings in Congress on climate change, and probably took a lot of political hits when it came to raising the alarm bells on this issue.

But I'm curious: Given that context of where you were, how do you see this current wave of climate hushing? Should we shift how we're talking about climate change to think more about affordability and education? How do we keep people focused on this issue?

AG: We need the opposite of climate hushing. We need to be shouting from the rooftops. The truth is the climate crisis is already deeply connected to almost every other important issue and challenge that we face, and including all the same issues that are on the ballot November 3.

The climate crisis is connected to affordability. Renewables [are] affordable abundance. It's connected to the cost of living, because the fossil fuels supply chain is so volatile that we're incredibly vulnerable to these price spikes coming every few years.

I saw a statistic the other day that found that the United States is paying, by far, the highest cost from the elevated fuel prices resulting from the war in Iran. That's the gasoline you have to put in your car. It's the diesel that farmers and truckers need to harvest food and drive the trucks that get that food to the grocery store and everything else. It's pushing prices up across the board.

So I think we need to do a better job at connecting the dots between the solutions to the climate crisis and their very positive impact on the affordability challenges that everybody's dealing with now. Since the Paris Agreement, the affordability of solar itself has gone down almost 80%. Wind energy's declined by more than two-thirds. The only energy source where prices have fallen faster than solar is utility scale batteries; they've fallen almost 90% in cost.

Saad, I want to switch gears just a bit:

You and I are from two different generations. I am proud and incredibly inspired to see young people leading the charge on climate, on resuscitating our democracy, and on so many other issues. But I'm curious to hear from you what you've learned from previous generations. What you think needs to change now? What does the next era of leadership demand? What do you hope to accomplish in your life in the next 20, 30, 40 years?

SA: My goal is to solve the climate crisis. I hope that in 20, 30, 40 years, we are not having this conversation anymore. I hope that it's something similar to what we saw with the ozone layer, where we saw this massive, global scientific issue impacting our planet; we listened to leading authorities; we quickly created policy; and we solved the issue.

AG: We're in the process of fixing it. It is beginning to heal now, and it is a great success story, but it's important to understand that we have to continue the actions that have led to such dramatic progress.

Honestly, Saad, it’s about standing on the shoulders of the giants who've come before us, who laid the groundwork for all of these years. I know that there's this public discourse that the climate movement has maybe taken a step back, but I feel the opposite; I feel like we're actually incredibly close to solving this issue.

Even though the United States is going back in many ways, I feel a big momentum shift. I feel quite hopeful about the results of not just these midterms, but even going into the next presidency, and the next. I feel like there is this hunger and desire for change in the US and across the world. There are protests in Argentina, France, and across the world right now. People are mobilizing from Mexico to Morocco in a way that I don't think people are willing to capitulate and lose their power.

SA: I feel like politics has maybe changed since you originally got into the space. I heard when you started running for office, you didn't even really have to do fundraisers. Now it feels like a lot of these campaigns are multibillion dollar advertising moments, and after Citizens United, there's been this big influx of dark money and oil money infiltrating our politics.

A lot of people feel disillusioned by those forces because they're so massive in their scale, and it feels like the machine is literally well-oiled, but for all the wrong reasons. How do you respond to what's happened with the influx of dark money?

AG: Well, my colleagues that I served with in the House and Senate some years ago, some of them are still there, and I hear from a lot that when the Citizens United decision came down from the Supreme Court in 2010—that's the one that just legalized donations of unlimited amounts of money anonymously—that put a stop to bipartisanship in the Congress on climate. And it's the single biggest marker of how much politics has changed since I ran for public office.

It certainly has changed since I ran for the first time in 1976. As you noted, I didn't have a single fundraiser way back then, but now members of Congress spend many hours every day making fundraising calls, catering to special interest groups and asking lobbyists for money.

That Citizens United ruling, it just opened the door for massive amounts of money from corporations and other special interests to really influence politicians in an unhealthy way and distort our political system. When the court said, "Okay, corporations, unlimited amounts anonymously," it reminded me of the old saying: "What could go wrong?" Well, we found out what could go wrong completely predictably.

SA: Younger people nowadays, we say, "F*ck around and find out."

AG: Well, [there’s] the ongoing struggle to pass good climate policies despite having a majority of Americans wanting action on this issue, feeling it should be given a much higher priority. The fossil fuel industry, as I said, they're better at capturing politicians and capturing emissions, and they've been using their wealth and legacy networks of political and economic influence to dominate the policy process and obstruct our democracy.

The fossil fuel industry's role in setting climate policy is actually illustrative of a broader trend. Just look at the way the gun industry has achieved control of policies related to trying to do something about the flood of guns that are killing so many people in the US—so many more per capita than any other country in the world—even though the overwhelming majority in both political parties, and independents as well, support tougher laws to try to limit the number of guns in the wrong hands.

It's all interconnected, and I've often said in order to solve the climate crisis, we need to address the democracy crisis. That means restoring power back to the people, not just as a slogan or a phrase, but in reality, to reinvigorate our democracy so that we can ensure that our government reflects the will of the people rather than special interests.

The bedrock of America is the saying that all just power is derived from the consent of the governed. But these special interests have used their money to take control of the system in an unhealthy way. We can take it back. This election in just a few days is a good chance to make a big first start on that.

That said, all too often, it feels like people in my generation shift the burden of action to younger generations like yours, and they say, "Oh, don't worry, they'll fix it." Well, I'd like to hear from you. What do young people need from my generation and from those who are in so many positions of leadership today to unlock this opportunity for you to empower you?

SA: Well, thank you for saying that, because it often feels like we'll go into these spaces and they'll say, "Young people are the future, and when you are in power, then you will fix this issue." And there's just this inherent irony to that because the person saying that is the person in power.

So I think what we need from a lot of these people in power is to: 1) Allow more young people into the room and create the space to facilitate those conversations; and 2), listen to the needs of young people, but also provide real support, whether that is funding organizations run by young people or hiring younger people and taking their ideas seriously.

There’s a whole new generation of people with great ideas and great momentum that just need the opportunity. I hope to see older generations take that more seriously. There's this accumulation of power, accumulation of wealth, and now you have a generation of young people that can't afford homes or [a nest] egg. So there's this discrepancy, I think, of a promise that young people were sold and being told, "Go to college, you'll get a good job," and now we have the most educated generation ever that is also incredibly unemployed.

AG: That's a great answer. I've been working on this issue for decades. So let's talk just a bit about motivation: What keeps you going? What do you think is next for the climate movement?

SA: What keeps me motivated is this beautiful planet and the beautiful people on it. I've had the opportunity to meet people from around the world, meet the kindest people living in the mountains of the Himalayas, and the most lovely people across Europe and here in the United States, and I see how nature and this Earth is this common force that brings us all together.

We all appreciate a walk outside. We all appreciate our communities coming together, and seeing people recognize how beautiful this planet is, how special, and it's something that I feel grateful to have experienced myself. But we all should have a right to be able to experience that. I don't think anyone or any company should have the ability to take that away.

Mr. Gore, you have been in this space for decades and decades, and you keep going even when, honestly, you could just not. The world would be in a much worse place, but if you did choose to take a step back, I think people would understand. And yet you keep going with the same passion you've had for decades. What keeps that spark alive in you?

AG: One reason is I find an incredible amount of optimism in the fact that we really do have the solutions we need. They're right in front of us. We can solve this crisis. I think we will. I'm confident we will.

The remaining question is whether we will solve it in time, because we're approaching some dangerous so-called negative tipping points, which could make it very hard to come back from if we cross them. So we've got to have a sense of urgency.

I also find an incredible amount of hope in climate science itself, because it's not all doom and gloom. In fact, a lot of people aren't aware of this, but the latest scientific models (that they're perfecting more and more every year) show that once we reach net-zero emissions, the temperatures on Earth will stop going up almost immediately, with a lag time of as little as three to five years.

It's a system with a thermostat, but the thermostat's not a round knob on the wall; it's the set of policy choices that we make that determine how much more fossil fuel resources we're going to burn and put the polluting residue in the sky, as if the sky is an open sewer.

Here's another positive bit of news from the scientists: Not only can we stop the temperatures from going up, but if we maintain net-zero emissions for as little as 30 years, about half of the human-caused CO2 will have fallen out of the atmosphere in a quarter-century or a little more.

So we can solve this. We have the ability to turn that thermostat—which is made up of the policy choices—down instead of continuing to turn the thermostat up. I'm optimistic that we will choose the policies that drive solutions to the climate crisis, and young people can turn that thermostat toward the solutions that will limit the warming of our planet.

And that starts with voting. It starts in the US. It starts with engaging with your elected officials and your communities. Just remember: We have everything we need. But if you ever doubt our ability to generate the political will necessary to bring about change, please also remember that political will is itself a renewable resource.

title: The Methane Regulatory Pendulum Swings Again: EPA Proposes Sweeping Changes ... - JD Supra
description:
Few environmental regulations better illustrate Washington’s regulatory “ping-pong” than EPA’s methane standards for the oil and natural gas sector.
I. EPA Proposes to Eliminate the Super Emitter Program Among the proposal’s most consequential changes is the complete elimination of the Super Emitter Program.
In response, EPA proposes to replace the existing capture-focused approach with a substantially more flexible standard.
EPA proposes to distinguish between deviations of the design requirements and deviations of the operational NIE requirements.
For certain high-pressure process controllers at transmission compressor stations, EPA proposes a separate regulatory approach based on its reassessment of technical feasibility and cost.
text:
Few environmental regulations better illustrate Washington’s regulatory “ping-pong” than EPA’s methane standards for the oil and natural gas sector. Over the last decade, successive administrations have repeatedly expanded, narrowed, rescinded, reinstated, and revised federal methane requirements, leaving industry to navigate a shifting compliance landscape with each change in administration. EPA’s October 27, 2026 proposal to reconsider significant portions of the 2024 oil and natural gas New Source Performance Standards (“NSPS”) and Emission Guidelines (“EG”) under Subparts OOOOb and OOOOc represents the latest swing of the regulatory pendulum. If finalized, the proposal would substantially reduce compliance obligations in several areas, particularly with respect to lower-producing wells, associated gas flaring, equipment and control-device standards, and the Super Emitter Program. EPA estimates that the proposal would result in approximately $45 billion in savings, while preserving what the agency considers appropriate methane emission controls. EPA’s proposal was published in the Federal Register on October 29, 2026. Comments must be received on or before December 16, 2026.

Significantly, EPA is not using this rulemaking to reconsider its general authority to regulate methane emissions from the oil and natural gas sector. Rather, the agency is addressing specific requirements adopted in the 2024 methane rule, while broader questions concerning greenhouse gas regulation are being addressed in separate proceedings. The present proposal therefore focuses on the appropriate design and scope of particular methane regulations, rather than resolving the threshold question of whether methane may be regulated under the Clean Air Act at all.

I. EPA Proposes to Eliminate the Super Emitter Program

Among the proposal’s most consequential changes is the complete elimination of the Super Emitter Program. Adopted in 2024, the program created a regulatory framework under which EPA-certified third parties could identify large methane releases using approved remote-sensing technologies. Upon receiving a qualifying notification from EPA, owners and operators were required to investigate the reported emissions event, report findings to EPA, and take corrective action where necessary.

EPA now proposes to repeal the Super Emitter Program in its entirety. The agency questions the program’s legal and policy foundations, including the role of third parties in identifying emissions events and triggering regulatory obligations. EPA also questions whether the program is necessary or effective given other requirements applicable to regulated sources and whether its expected emissions reductions justify its costs and implementation challenges. Because the program was incorporated into both the NSPS applicable to new, modified, and reconstructed sources and the EG applicable to existing sources, its removal would affect federal requirements as well as the presumptive requirements that States otherwise would be expected to address in Clean Air Act § 111(d) plans. Importantly, EPA’s proposed repeal does not prevent States from developing and implementing their own Super Emitter Program based on the existing requirements, which several states are already doing.

II. EPA Reconsiders Associated Gas Requirements

Another centerpiece of EPA’s proposal is its reconsideration of the 2024 rule’s restrictions on flaring associated gas from oil wells. The 2024 rule determined that the best system of emission reduction (“BSER”) generally required operators to capture and beneficially use associated gas by routing it to a sales line, using it onsite, or reinjecting it, rather than routinely flaring it. Although EPA provided certain transition periods and compliance flexibilities, particularly for wells facing infrastructure constraints, the rule ultimately established a framework strongly favoring capture and utilization over flaring. Since promulgation, EPA has received significant feedback regarding gathering-system limitations, gas quality issues, and other practical barriers operators face in securing outlets for associated gas.

In response, EPA proposes to replace the existing capture-focused approach with a substantially more flexible standard. EPA argues that the 2024 rule relied too heavily on the availability of third-party gathering and processing infrastructure that is often beyond an operator’s control, raising questions regarding achievability and cost-effectiveness. Under the proposal, BSER would be based on routing associated gas to a flare or other control device capable of achieving at least a 95 percent reduction in methane and volatile organic compound (“VOC”) emissions. Operators could continue to capture gas for sale, use it onsite, or reinject it where feasible, but those practices would no longer be required. EPA also proposes that if a portion of associated gas is routed to sales or used for another purpose, the remaining portion must comply with the 95 percent standard. For example, if a company can route 40 percent of its associated gas to a sales line, the company would need to route the other 60 percent to a control device with a 95 percent reduction, or to a flare.

EPA is also soliciting comment on less sweeping alternatives that would preserve the basic structure of the 2024 associated-gas program, while providing additional compliance flexibility. In particular, EPA requests comment on whether it should retain the current capture-and-sales framework but expand the circumstances under which temporary flaring is permitted or extend the duration of temporary flaring allowances where operators face infrastructure constraints. EPA appears to recognize that gathering-system availability, processing constraints, and other third-party factors can affect an operator's ability to route gas to sales, even where the operator ultimately intends to comply with the capture requirements. These requests for comment suggest that EPA is considering whether targeted revisions to the existing framework could address implementation concerns without fully abandoning the 2024 rule's underlying preference for gas capture and beneficial use.

III. EPA’s Reconsideration of the “No Identifiable Emissions” Standard

EPA's proposal would substantially revise the 2024 rule’s “no identifiable emissions” (“NIE”) requirements applicable to certain covers and closed vent systems (“CVS”) associated with storage tanks. Under the existing rule, covered equipment generally must operate without identifiable emissions, creating a compliance framework that focuses heavily on the absence of observable emissions rather than solely on equipment design or overall control effectiveness. Since promulgation, industry has argued that the standard effectively functions as a zero-emissions requirement that may be difficult to satisfy under all operating conditions, even where equipment and vapor control systems are properly designed, maintained, and operated. Moreover, EPA stated in the preamble to the 2024 rule that any identified emissions would constitute a deviation of the emissions limitation, resulting in a framework under which the observation of emissions could itself establish noncompliance.

EPA now proposes to separate the requirements into distinct design and operational components and to fundamentally alter how compliance with the operational NIE requirement is evaluated. EPA proposes to distinguish between deviations of the design requirements and deviations of the operational NIE requirements. Under the proposed approach, failure to repair an identified emission or defect within 24 hours would constitute a deviation of the design requirement, although not necessarily an underlying violation. Separately, operators could demonstrate compliance with the operational NIE requirement by making repairs as soon as practicable, with an initial repair attempt within five days and final repair within 30 days, or by qualifying for the existing delay-of-repair provisions. A deviation of the operational requirement would occur if the applicable repair deadlines are not met and the delay-of-repair provisions do not apply.

The proposal also establishes a new framework for addressing recurring or “chronic” emissions events. After the third emissions event or defect from the same cover or CVS within a year, the owner or operator would be required to conduct an investigative analysis within 10 days to determine whether the underlying cause relates to equipment design, operation, maintenance, or prior repair efforts. The results of that investigation would have important compliance implications. If recurring emissions are attributable to a design flaw, EPA would treat the issue as a deviation of the design requirements. If the emissions result from inadequate prior repairs, the deviation would be attributed to the repair requirements. If operations, maintenance, or other site practices are responsible, the deviation would be classified under the operational requirements. EPA would also require implementation of corrective measures identified through the analysis, including design modifications within 90 days and operational or maintenance-related corrective actions within 30 days. Taken together, these revisions would shift the NIE standard away from a framework in which the mere presence of emissions may establish noncompliance and toward one that focuses on whether operators identify emissions, complete timely repairs, investigate recurring problems, and address the root causes of repeated emissions events.

IV. Solicitation of Comment on “Legally and Practicably Enforceable” Standard

EPA is also soliciting comment on the definition of “legally and practicably enforceable” (“LPE”), which industry has identified as one of the more problematic existing requirements. Under the 2024 rule, EPA adopted an interpretation of LPE that many commenters argued effectively disqualifies numerous state regulatory programs, permits, and other federally enforceable mechanisms from serving as the basis for remaining below applicable Subpart OOOOb storage tank thresholds. In particular, stakeholders have asserted that the current LPE framework makes it difficult for state air permitting programs and other state regulatory requirements to satisfy EPA's criteria, thereby causing more storage tanks and other emission units to remain subject to Subpart OOOOb requirements than would otherwise be the case.

EPA now requests comment on whether its current interpretation of LPE is overly restrictive and whether alternative approaches would better account for the manner in which state permitting and regulatory programs are administered and enforced. The request is significant because a broader interpretation of LPE could allow a wider range of federally enforceable state permits and regulatory requirements to satisfy exemption criteria under OOOOb, potentially reducing the number of storage tanks and other sources subject to direct NSPS regulation. As a result, the LPE issue has implications that extend beyond compliance mechanics and could materially affect the scope of sources regulated under the federal methane program.

V. Revised Requirements for Marginal Wells

EPA is also proposing significant revisions to the treatment of lower-producing wells under Subparts OOOOb and OOOOc. The agency notes that marginal wells constitute a substantial portion of the nation’s producing well inventory but account for a relatively small share of overall production. At the same time, EPA discusses studies estimating that marginal wells contribute a disproportionate share of methane emissions from oil and natural gas production. The agency is evaluating whether the 2024 rule appropriately accounts for the operational characteristics, emissions profiles, and compliance costs associated with these wells.

To address those concerns, EPA is proposing two alternative approaches to well-site subcategorization. Under the first option, EPA would distinguish between marginal and non-marginal well sites. EPA proposes to define a marginal well as a well that produced no more than 15 barrels of oil equivalent (“BOE”) per day over the prior 12-month period and a marginal well site as a site consisting exclusively of marginal wells with total site-wide production of no more than 15 BOE per day over the same period. EPA is also soliciting comment on whether marginal wells should be further subdivided based on production levels, including a potential distinction between sites producing 6 BOE per day or less and sites producing more than 6 BOE but no more than 15 BOE per day, which could result in additional regulatory flexibility for the lowest-producing wells. Under the second option, EPA would distinguish between conventional and unconventional well sites and tailor requirements based on that classification, including reduced requirements for conventional wells. The agency is seeking comment on which framework better reflects the operational and emissions characteristics of different well sites, as well as whether additional subcategories should be established within the marginal-well population and the extent to which compliance requirements should differ among categories.

VI. LDAR, Pneumatic Controllers, Control Device Monitoring, and Facility Modifications

EPA's proposal also includes several targeted revisions to the 2024 rule's leak detection and repair (“LDAR”) requirements. Most notably, EPA proposes additional flexibility in the use of advanced monitoring technologies and seeks to move away from compliance frameworks that rely heavily on a single detection method. The agency is proposing changes intended to facilitate the use of multiple monitoring technologies, including optical gas imaging and other alternative detection approaches, and is seeking comment on whether technology-neutral compliance options can achieve equivalent emissions reductions at lower cost. EPA also proposes revisions for components and equipment that are particularly difficult to monitor using conventional LDAR methods, reflecting concerns that certain 2024 requirements may not be practical or cost-effective in the field. More broadly, EPA questions whether some of the monitoring frequencies adopted in 2024 appropriately balance compliance burdens and emissions-reduction benefits and seeks comment on additional opportunities to tailor LDAR obligations based on emissions risk and source characteristics.

EPA also proposes technical revisions to requirements governing control devices and related equipment. These include changes addressing continuous pilot-flame requirements, flame-monitoring data deviations, control-device alerts, visible-emissions test conditions, temporary or backup control devices, temporary process controllers, and control-device categories. The agency’s stated objective is to provide additional compliance flexibility while maintaining appropriate emissions controls. The practical effect will depend on the final requirements and the equipment and circumstances to which each amendment applies.

The proposal also addresses pneumatic controllers and equipment leaks at gas processing plants. For certain high-pressure process controllers at transmission compressor stations, EPA proposes a separate regulatory approach based on its reassessment of technical feasibility and cost. The proposal should not be read as establishing a general exemption for pneumatic controllers across the industry. EPA also proposes changes to other equipment-specific requirements, including requirements applicable to pumps, storage vessels, and equipment leaks at gas plants, in response to concerns raised following promulgation of the 2024 rule.

Finally, EPA proposes changes to certain requirements governing liquids unloading and other well-site operations, as well as technical corrections and clarifications to the existing regulatory text. These provisions form part of EPA’s broader effort to address implementation concerns and reassess the costs and expected emissions reductions associated with selected requirements in the 2024 rule. Operators should evaluate the specific proposed amendments applicable to their facilities rather than assume that the proposal would provide across-the-board relief from existing monitoring, equipment, or control-device obligations.

VII. Implications for States and Future Congressional or Administrative Action

EPA’s proposal would substantially revise several consequential elements of the 2024 methane rule, but it would not eliminate regulation of existing oil and natural gas sources under Clean Air Act § 111(d). As a result, states remain subject to the existing obligation to develop and submit plans for existing sources. If the proposed revisions are finalized, states currently developing those plans may need to reevaluate key program elements, including requirements relating to associated gas, well-site subcategories, the Super Emitter Program, and other compliance obligations. The proposal does not itself extend the January 22, 2027 deadline for state-plan submissions established under the existing framework.

The Congressional Review Act (“CRA”) remains a potential source of uncertainty. Depending on when EPA submits a final rule to Congress and the applicable congressional-session timing, a future Congress and President could seek to disapprove the rule under the CRA. A successful disapproval would invalidate the rule and generally restrict the agency from issuing a rule in substantially the same form absent subsequent statutory authorization. The CRA’s lookback provisions can affect the period during which a rule remains subject to congressional review, so the risk cannot be assessed solely by reference to the calendar year in which the rule is finalized. The timing of finalization and submission to Congress, together with the applicable congressional calendar, will determine the extent of that exposure.

Finally, unlike the CRA, which can nullify a recently promulgated rule through legislative action, a future administration seeking to unwind this rule would generally need to proceed through a new notice-and-comment rulemaking. EPA would need to revisit the underlying BSER determinations, cost analyses, technical feasibility findings, and enforceability conclusions that support the final rule. Because this proposal is grounded heavily in findings regarding achievability, legal and practical enforceability, and cost-effectiveness, a future administration would need to develop a sufficient record supporting different conclusions before reinstating more stringent requirements. Consequently, the final rule may prove more durable than prior pendulum swings, even if it remains politically controversial.

text:
Although there have been many strides taken at the state level to reduce the property tax burden, local governments’ incessant and reckless spending continues to drive up the bill.

Key points:

In May 2026, Texas voters considered 439 bonds. Of those, 233 were approved.

The passage rate for bond propositions for the May 2026 cycle was 63%.

Total repayment for every bond measure passed was $96.7 billion.

Denton County Municipal Utility District 7 approved Proposition C with only 1 person voting, approving $5.9 billion in total repayment.

The City of Saginaw approved Proposition B, 767 to 766, a margin of 1 vote, authorizing $9.6 million.

The Texas Legislature should consider establishing higher voter thresholds, requiring a minimum voter threshold, moving all bond elections to November, and increasing the transparency of ballot language in the 90th legislative session.

Click here to download the full research paper

Introduction

With principal and interest, the debt in Texas’s counties, cities, school districts, and special purpose districts now totals $552 billion (Quintero & Solin, 2025). This saddles every man, woman, and child in the state with $18,939 in debt.1 This debt is driven entirely by unrestrained local government spending. In a time when affordability of everything from groceries to housing is a kitchen table conversation in the homes of Texan families, it is necessary to examine how to relieve cost burdens.

Governments have a variety of tools to issue debt, which can be broken down into tax-supported debt, general obligation (GO) debt, or revenue-supported debt. GO debt is secured by a promise that the borrowing government entity will repay it with money collected through taxation. Those are the ways debt is secured, but debt can also be approved in different ways (Tex. Tax Code § 26.012). The statute that primarily covers bond elections is Chapter 1251 of the Texas Government Code (Texas Government Code Chapter 1251). This research will examine how reforming portions of Texas Government Code Chapter 1251 to spur voter turnout and increase the scrutiny required to pass a bond could reduce the debt local governments incur.

May 2026 Bond Election

The following report lists every bond passed in the May 2026 election cycle, organized by taxing entity. It synthesizes information from the BRB’s searchable bond election database. The BRB catalogs every bond proposed in a given cycle along with basic data on votes cast, principal amounts, estimated interest, and stated purposes taken from the various Voter Information Documents (VIDs) and financial disclosures provided by individual political subdivisions. These documents contain ballot language, existing debt profiles, projected tax impacts, and other legal information. The passage and implementation of House Bill (HB) 3526 mandated the creation of a database that provides consolidated information on bond elections, from which this research drew its data (HB 3526, 2025; Bond Review Board, n.d.).

Below is a high-level analysis of bond elections across cities, school districts, and special purpose districts in May of 2026. Each election is analyzed by issuer, bond purpose, total votes cast, votes for and against each proposition, approval status, total estimated repayment, and, if it passed, the percentage of voters who approved the bond.

Bonds that were “carried,” or passed, by voters are highlighted in green, and those carried by a threshold of 60% or greater are highlighted in red. Bonds for refunds, bonds that were canceled, or bonds pending at the time of research were included in the full count of bond elections but removed as the level of analysis increased. Refunding bonds were removed because they are not subject to the same election requirements as other bonds (Texas Government Code § 1251.006 (1), 1999). Canceled or pending elections were removed so that only elections that took place and had observable results were included in conclusions regarding total estimated repayment.

Results At a Glance

In this election cycle alone, 439 bond measures were proposed, worth nearly $133 billion in total repayment. Of those, 276 passed (a 63% passage rate), for a total repayment of $96.7 billion. Table 1, below, shows the aggregated bond election information for Cities, School Districts, and Special Purpose Districts. Two fields were added to examine the impact of a 60% voter approval threshold. 234 bonds were passed at the 60% approval threshold, 43 fewer than those approved with a simple majority, resulting in a reduction of $6.4 billion in total repayment.

Table 1

May 2026 Bond Election At a Glance

Note. Data from Local Bond Elections, by Bond Review Board, n.d. (https://brb.texas.gov/searchable-db.html#/datasets/local_elections) and author’s calculations.

City Bond Elections

In this cycle, as described in Table 2, 26 city bonds were proposed and considered by voters; Payne Springs, while displayed, was not included in calculations because it was a refunding bond. Of the 25 bonds in the calculation, 22 passed, giving cities an 88% passage rate. However, some of these bonds passed by relatively small margins. For example, 9 of the 25 city bonds passed with less than 60% approval. The bonds that passed will require as much as $2.78 billion to fully repay, $1.3 billion of which passed with less than 60% of the vote.

The defeated bonds included Carrollton’s Proposition D, La Grange Proposition A, and McCamey Proposition A. Proposition D sought $7.85 million for improvements to municipal court facilities, the smallest of five bond measures Carrollton placed on the May 2 ballot, which would have resulted in a total repayment of $12.6 million. La Grange Proposition A was defeated with a proposed amount of $90 million, which would have resulted in a total repayment of $159.6 million. McCamey Proposition A was also defeated with a proposed amount of $8 million, which would have resulted in a total repayment of $15.6 million.

The largest city bond passed was Fort Worth’s Proposition A, which asked for approval of $511 million and would have resulted in a total repayment of $821 million for street improvements. The City of Fort Worth simultaneously holds the title of the biggest spender in 2026, authorizing just over a billion dollars in total cost, nearly a third of all city bond spending statewide. It was the largest bond program in the city’s history, surpassing even the nearly $847 million total repayment package Fort Worth voters approved in 2022 (City of Fort Worth, 2022).

Table 2

City Bond Elections May 2026

Note. Data from Local Bond Elections, by Bond Review Board, n.d. (https://brb.texas.gov/searchable-db.html#/datasets/local_elections) and author’s calculations.

ISD Bond Elections

In the May 2026 Bond election cycle, the number of Independent School District (ISD) elections dwarfed city bond elections by just over a magnitude of 5. Before filtering out refunding bonds, 124 propositions were on the ballot compared to 26 city bonds. The total repayment amount proposed surpassed $24.7 billion. After removing refunding bonds, 122 bond propositions remained, with a proposed total repayment of $24.2 billion. 96 bonds passed, with a total repayment of $22.1 billion. However, if a 60% threshold were required to pass bonds, 63 bonds would have passed with a total repayment of $17.1 billion, eliminating $5 billion in total debt repayment and removing only one-third of the total bonds approved.

The largest single proposition was Dallas ISD’s Prop A, which carries a total repayment burden of more than $12 billion, which is 55%% of all ISD bond propositions that passed in this election cycle. It was part of a larger $12.5 billion bond package, the most expensive in Texas history, topping Dallas ISD’s previous package approved just six years before (Dallas Independent School District, n.d.). Voters approved all three2 propositions by wide margins, with Proposition A receiving 74.3% support (Dallas County Elections Department, 2026).

The largest defeated ISD proposition was Pilot Point ISD’s $295 million bond, which failed decisively. Of the 1,384 votes cast, 845 were against, and only 539 were in favor, a margin of roughly 61% to 39%. The measure would have funded Phase 1 of a new high school, a new elementary school, and renovations to existing campuses (Garcia, 2026).

ISD Bond Elections May 2026

SPD Bond Elections

In Texas, there are thousands of Special Purpose Districts (SPDs), which are independent entities of local government created to provide a specific service such as water and sewer service, toll roads, fire protection, hospital care, or community college education, among dozens of other purposes (Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts, n.d.). Despite their narrow scopes, SPDs have broad financial powers, including the authority to impose property taxes to service debt; because they carry taxing authority, SPDs must hold bond elections before taking on new debt, just as cities and ISDs do.

In the May 2026 bond elections, described in Table 4, there were 289 SPD propositions, more than twice the number of propositions for ISDs. Before removing refunding bonds, the total proposed repayment was $105.6 billion. After removing refunding bonds, canceled propositions, and elections with pending results, the 187 bonds had a total proposed repayment of $76.4 billion. The 160 bonds that passed had a total repayment of $71.6 billion. Of those 160 that passed, 158 passed with the 60% threshold, and their total repayment was $71.5 billion.

In practice, many SPD elections draw a tiny fraction of the turnout seen in city or ISD races. In the 2026 cycle, for example, only 5 of 289, or 1.7%, of SPD bond elections statewide had more than 250 voters participate, down from 6.3% the year before, meaning relatively few residents can authorize debt obligations worth tens or even hundreds of millions of dollars.

In this cycle, only one of the 228 SPD bonds passed with less than 60% approval: Harris County’s Water Control and Improvement District 109’s Proposition A, a total repayment of $107.3 million, passed with 56.9% of the vote. The contrast with ISDs is stark, as just over 1/3 of all ISD bonds passed this cycle faced significant voter opposition; SPD elections almost universally pass, often with unanimous margins.

SPD Elections May 2026

Recommendations

The May 2026 bond election cycle set a record for local bond debt authorized in a single May election. By comparison, May 2024 saw voters approve $33.3 billion in total bond repayment debt, which is less than half of the nearly $71 billion authorized in 2026 (Quintero, 2024). Texas local governments are increasingly willing to bring large debt packages to voters, and voters that show up are increasingly willing to approve them. The key phrase is “voters that show up.” As this report documents, many of these elections, especially in SPDs, are decided by a handful of residents, raising serious questions about whether the democratic check that bond elections are meant to provide is functioning as intended.

Legislators in the 90th legislative session should prioritize reforms that ensure voters not only have the opportunity to weigh in on debt but are also equipped to understand what they are approving and what it will cost them over the long term.

Implementing a Supermajority Threshold: The first, and perhaps most significant, reform the Legislature should pursue is raising the voter approval threshold required to pass a bond. Under current law, a simple majority is all that is needed to authorize debt (Tex. Educ. Code § 45.003). This report recommends the Legislature raise that threshold to a supermajority of 60%. If the 60% threshold had been in place in 2026, taxpayers would have been spared nearly $6.4 billion in authorized debt. Therefore, it is recommended that legislation similar to HB 96 (2025) be advanced in the 90th legislative session.

Establishing a Minimum Turnout Requirement: Along with a supermajority threshold, it is recommended that the Legislature adopt a minimum voter turnout requirement. Especially in SPDs, billions of dollars are adopted usually by just one or two people. For example, one singular person in the Denton County MUD 7 Proposition C election approved more than $5.9 billion in total repayment. This issue was explored briefly in 2017 through SB 702 (2017), which sought to require a minimum 30% participation in bond elections; however, the legislation failed. The 90th Legislature should revive and pass a similar requirement. A minimum turnout floor would ensure that decisions reflect a true community consensus rather than the preferences of a select few.

Uniform November Election Dates:Bond elections have notoriously low turnout. Tarrant County reported that only 4.1% of registered voters participated in the May 2026 bond election, yet in the November 2024 general election, 63.8% turned out, more than a 15-fold difference (Tarrant County Elections, 2024). This results from holding consequential fiscal elections in low-visibility, off-cycle windows when most voters are not paying attention. SB 1209 (2025) directly addressed this problem by eliminating the May uniform election date and requiring most elections to be held on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November, aligning with the federal election calendar. The 90th Legislature should revisit similar legislation.

Ballot Transparency: The final category of reform concerns what voters actually see when they walk into the voting booth. Current ballot language for bond measures is vague and structured in ways that obscure rather than illuminate the financial commitment being made. A ballot might ask voters to approve the issuance of general obligation bonds in a specific amount without ever telling them the total repayment cost. The 89th Legislature made meaningful progress, including SB 1025 (2025), HB103 (2025), and SB 843 (2025). But gaps remain: Ballot language still permits significant “bundling” of unrelated projects into single propositions, preventing voters from approving infrastructure they support while rejecting spending they oppose. The 90th Legislature should build on the 89th’s foundation by mandating universal VID distribution requirements across all taxing entities, prohibiting the bundling of substantively unrelated projects into a single proposition, and requiring all bond ballot language to include the estimated total repayment cost with interest so that voters understand the full price tag of what they are being asked to approve (Tex. Gov’t Code § 1251.052). Additionally, the same section of code should be amended to change the assumed property value used as the basis for estimations from $100,000 to better reflect the value of homes across the state, which is $339,000 according to the Texas Real Estate Research Center (TRERC, 2026).

Challenges

Issues with special purpose districts, particularly Municipal Utility Districts (MUDs), often stem from starting with a very low population. It is entirely possible to create a MUD with the petition of one person (Texas Water Code §54.014; 54.016; 54.016, 1971 and rev. 2023) and approve bonds with one vote. While bonds are necessary for a MUD’s development, they are expected to grow, and as they do, the debt is passed on to future residents. If a MUD is annexed before it pays off its debt, the city absorbs that debt, and its residents shoulder it. However, until then, bond debt stays within those districts. Limits on these districts should not prevent MUDs from being lawfully established, but should be enough to protect future residents from debt approved by a few voters.

One way to address this issue would be to exempt districts with a population less than 250 from the turnout or approval thresholds, similar to how districts with fewer than 250 people are exempt from providing a Voter Information Document (Tex. Gov’t Code § 1251.052). This would maintain the logical consistency of a reasonable population threshold to ensure MUDs can be created, but as they grow, debt decisions would face higher scrutiny.

One last challenge is whether changes to approval thresholds, turnout thresholds, and election dates would require constitutional amendments. Further research is needed to determine whether these provisions would conflict with Texas Constitution Article VIII, which governs taxation, particularly the prohibition on a state property tax and equity in valuation (Tex. Const. Art. VIII).

Conclusion

Debt directly contributes to Texans’ property tax bills. Increases in the I&S rate often must occur to service growing debt, or valuations may increase as a result of increasing debt. Changing approval thresholds, turnout thresholds, consolidating elections in November, and providing more transparency are not punitive measures against local governments, but ways to put the decision to incur debt more firmly in voters’ hands. The spirit of these changes is to increase voter turnout and ensure overwhelming voter support for bond measures with hefty price tags.

title: EPA Proposes Significant Revisions to Oil and Natural Gas Methane Standards Under Clean Air Act
authors: Matthew Z. Leopold, Ashley T.K. Phillips, Jason A. Hill, Clarissa Howley Mills, Aaron Aber, Evan Neustater
