text:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) published a proposed rule on October 29, 2026, titled "Additional Reconsideration Standards of Performance for New, Reconstructed, and Modified Sources and Emissions Guidelines for Existing Sources: Oil and Natural Gas Sector Climate Review" (Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OAR-2025-0163) that would revise the agency's 2024 New Source Performance Standards (NSPS) for new, modified and reconstructed oil and natural gas sources (40 C.F.R. Part 60, Subpart OOOOb) and existing sources (Subpart OOOOc) issued under Section 111 of the Clean Air Act (CAA), 42 U.S.C. § 7411 (collectively, the 2024 Rule). The proposal is EPA's second reconsideration package for the 2024 Rule.

This Holland & Knight alert summarizes the regulatory background, describes key components of the proposal and identifies considerations for regulated entities as the rulemaking proceeds.

Background

CAA Section 111 requires EPA to establish standards of performance for new, modified and reconstructed stationary sources based on the "best system of emission reduction" that has been "adequately demonstrated," taking into account cost, non-air quality health and environmental impacts and energy requirements. It also requires EPA to issue emission guidelines that states use to develop plans establishing standards for existing sources in the same source categories for which NSPS have been issued. For the oil and natural gas sector, EPA has implemented these provisions through a succession of rules, including Subparts OOOO (2012) and OOOOa (2016), which regulate emissions of volatile organic compounds (VOCs), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and, with OOOOa, methane.

In the 2024 Rule finalized under the Biden Administration, EPA phased out routine flaring of associated gas from new oil wells, required zero-emitting process controllers in most scenarios, strengthened leak detection and repair (LDAR) requirements at well sites and established a Super Emitter Program under which EPA-certified third parties could use remote sensing to identify large emission events and notify operators. The 2024 Rule also established emission guidelines for methane from existing sources, which states must implement through state plans. (See Holland & Knight's previous alert, "EPA Issues Final Methane Regulations for New and Existing Sources," December 6, 2023.)

On March 12, 2025, EPA announced that it would reconsider the 2024 Rule as part of a broad set of deregulatory actions. (See Holland & Knight's previous alert, "EPA Announces Deregulatory Initiative to 'Power the Great American Comeback'," March 17, 2025.) Since then, EPA has taken several interim actions:

On July 31, 2025, the agency issued an interim final rule (IFR) extending several compliance deadlines in the 2024 Rule.

In December 2025, EPA finalized a rule reaffirming those extensions, providing an additional 180-day extension for compliance dates related to net heating value monitoring of flares and enclosed combustion devices and providing a 360-day extension for submission of initial annual reports.

On April 9, 2026, EPA finalized revisions to provisions governing net heating value and the time limits and justifying circumstances for temporary flaring of associated gas.

On May 1, 2026, EPA issued a clarification that existing federal regulations permit flaring of associated gas at new oil wells in limited circumstances after the May 7, 2026, phase-out deadline.

The Proposed Rule

In a press release announcing the proposal, EPA said the proposed changes to OOOOb and OOOOc would yield economic benefits of approximately $45 billion1 and allow production of an estimated 210 million additional barrels of oil and 1.41 trillion additional cubic feet of natural gas. In the proposed rule, EPA finds that the 2024 Rule delivered "more modest emissions reductions and more significant costs" than expected and significant parts of some of its best system of emission reduction (BSER) determinations are "inappropriate." EPA also notes that industry has raised concerns about compliance with the 2024 Rule.

Key changes proposed by EPA are summarized below.

Subcategorization of Well Sites

EPA co-proposes two alternative approaches to subcategorizing well sites in OOOOb and OOOOc and may finalize only one. Under the first option, wells would be subcategorized as "marginal" if their combined production is 15 barrels of oil equivalent (BOE) per day or less over the prior 12 months. Under the second option, wells would be subcategorized as "conventional" based on their well formation. EPA says subcategorization may be warranted for these wells based on the high cost of compliance for these types of sources.

EPA proposes the same reduced standards for "marginal" and "conventional" wells:

quarterly audio, visual and olfactory inspections for fugitive component emissions

low-bleed devices for continuous bleed natural gas-driven pneumatic controllers

routing VOC and methane emissions from natural gas-driven pumps to a control device that reduces emissions by at least 95 percent where such a device is already available onsite

routing associated gas emissions to control devices only if their potential to emit exceeds certain thresholds (20 tons per year (tpy) methane for associated gas and 20 tpy methane or six tpy VOCs for storage vessels)

"Marginal" status would be based on the site's average daily oil and gas production over the prior 12 months. Modifications and other actions that increase production would require a new determination within 45 days, based on the first 30 days of production. Triggering activities would include drilling, fracturing or refracturing, stimulation or workovers, shutting in one well to boost another, adding even one gas-driven controller or pump, and certain tank battery changes. Zero-emission controllers and pumps already installed would have to stay, and any new units would also have to be zero-emission. Sites below the 20 tpy associated gas threshold would still need to demonstrate it. If EPA splits the subcategory at six BOE per day, the lower tier will likely avoid the associated gas control requirement, while larger sites in the upper tier would likely face annual optical gas imaging (OGI) plus quarterly audio, visual and olfactory. EPA noted in the proposal that subcategorizing as "conventional" rather than "marginal" wells would provide more regulatory certainty over time because it would avoid the additional and ongoing requirement to determine BOE per day to justify a marginal well classification.

EPA further proposes what would constitute "modification" of an existing conventional well and trigger applicability of OOOOb – for example, if a new well is drilled at an existing conventional well site, an existing conventional well is hydraulically fractured, or there is an increase in natural gas-driven process controllers.

EPA estimates that this co-proposal could result in compliance cost savings of approximately $39 billion (present value 2027-2050, at a 3 percent discount rate) but may also result in an additional 88 million short tons of methane emissions and 25 million short tons of VOC emissions.

EPA seeks comment on numerous aspects of this subcategorization co-proposal, including whether marginal wells should be subcategorized further based on average production levels of six BOE and 15 BOE and with respect to EPA's proposed BSER for these sources and the costs and assumptions used to determine the BSER for these sources.

Rescission of the Super Emitter Program

EPA proposes to rescind the Super Emitter Program for all NSPS Subpart OOOO programs (OOOO, OOOOa and OOOOb and OOOOc). EPA says the rescission is warranted because the program relies on "insufficient evidence of the nature and duration of super-emitter events";" adds little value on top of existing requirements; is overly broad and ineffective; and lacks adequate statutory authority, particularly for the role that third parties play. EPA notes that it can still use its CAA Section 114 information-collection authority to track compliance and that people may still submit methane data to the agency.

Storage Vessels and Centralized Production Facilities

EPA proposes to treat tank batteries at centralized production facilities the same as those at compressor stations and gas processing plants so that a reassessment of potential emissions would be triggered only if actual throughput exceeds the projected maximum average daily throughput or the throughput in a legally and practically enforceable (LPE) limit. EPA acknowledges that the 2024 modification provisions caused far more midstream storage vessels to be treated as modified than it had estimated and upstream changes unknown to the midstream operator could put sources out of compliance. EPA would also redefine "well site" and "centralized production facility" and base fugitive emissions modification triggers at centralized production facilities on actions within the operator's control. EPA solicits comments on whether the 2024 LPE criteria should be repealed and temporary shut-in sites could recalculate potential emissions for storage vessel control.

Covers and Closed Vent Systems

EPA proposes to divide the "no identifiable emissions" standard for covers and closed vent systems into separate design requirements and operational requirements. Under the proposal, the operational requirements would allow for repairs, rather than treating any identifiable emission as a potential deviation. That relief comes with new obligations that operators should plan for going forward. Routine leaks will have to be repaired within 24 hours, and sources not fixed on the spot would have to be tagged or otherwise documented and then resurveyed. Three or more events in a year would trigger an investigative analysis that EPA suggests could identify design flaws. The same approach would apply to self-contained process controllers. Because these provisions reach covers and closed vent systems at well sites, compressor stations and gas plants, they may significantly affect compliance and enforcement exposure across upstream and midstream operations. EPA has asked whether 24 hours is workable, making this a key comment issue.

Control Devices

Finally, EPA is proposing technical changes to provide flexibility, where appropriate, for continuous burning pilot flames, flame monitoring data deviations, control device alerts, visible emissions test conditions, control devices used on a temporary or backup basis and control device categories, and requests comment on whether automatic igniters perform comparably to continuously lit pilots. EPA would also allow temporary control devices during liquids unloading with streamlined compliance requirements and would let operators submit well closure notifications after closure is complete. The package also revises requirements for pumps and fugitives. These provisions have been a frequent source of operational difficulty and potential deviations under the 2024 Rule, and the proposed revisions could reduce the volume of reportable deviations associated with routine monitoring anomalies.

Associated Gas

EPA is proposing to drop "route to sales" as the BSER for associated gas from oil wells. In EPA's view, the 2024 approach depends on third-party midstream infrastructure that operators "cannot compel," making it "not an allowable form of BSER." For non-marginal wells, EPA would instead require routing associated gas to a control device or flare that achieves a 95 percent reduction, while associated gas at sites in the new subcategory would be subject to control only above the applicable threshold. EPA also requests comment on whether flaring during pipeline construction should be limited in duration (e.g., three years from when the well begins operation) and whether operators should report contractual arrangements and compliance schedules in annual reports. These are issues of direct interest to producers awaiting gathering capacity and midstream companies building it. The proposal would also remove the temporary flaring provisions addressed in EPA's April 2026 final rule.

Process Controllers at Transmission Compressor Stations

EPA is proposing to create a new subcategory for process controllers on high-pressure systems at transmission compressor stations, concluding that retrofitting to zero-emission controllers is not technically feasible or cost-effective. EPA's revised analysis estimates $2.4 million in capital costs and $33,100 per ton of methane reduced to convert these controllers to compressed air. Under the proposal, operators could either route controller emissions through a closed vent system to a control device achieving a 95 percent reduction or use low-bleed controllers in combination with intermittent vent controllers that are periodically monitored. Separately, temporary process controllers could use a low-bleed alternative for up to 60 additional operational days per site per year after the first 30 days, with recordkeeping.

Equipment Leaks at Gas Plants

For onshore natural gas processing plants, EPA proposes to allow a "first attempt at repair" of a leaking valve (such as tightening bolts or packing gland nuts) before requiring replacement or repacking with low-emission valves or packing. EPA also proposes to limit leak detection and repair applicability to equipment "in VOC service" (10 percent VOC by weight) or "in methane service" (1 percent methane by weight), restore "in wet gas service" to the equipment definition and allow OGI surveys under Appendix K.

Takeaways for Regulated Entities

The 2024 Rule Remains in Effect for Now. Companies' obligations under the 2024 Rule remain unchanged until this proposed rule is finalized.

Subcategorization Will Drive Applicability. Owners and operators should consider evaluating their well site portfolios under both co-proposed options, including the 15 BOE per day threshold and the potential six BOE per day split. The choice between a production-based and a formation-based approach and the specific thresholds and definitions EPA ultimately adopts may materially affect which sites qualify for the reduced standards. Stakeholders should also consider whether EPA's new profit-based cost reasonableness analysis is adequately supported.

Midstream Operators Should Review Modifications and Controller Provisions. Gathering, processing and transmission companies should evaluate the proposed throughput-based storage vessel modification triggers, high-pressure controller subcategory at transmission compressor stations, gas plant leak repair and applicability changes and 24-hour closed vent system repair timeline and consider submitting data supporting their positions.

State Plans. States developing plans to implement the Subpart OOOOc emission guidelines will need to assess how the proposal would affect their plan development and timelines.

Commenting Opportunity. Comments on the proposed rule are due December 16, 2026, and EPA will hold a virtual public hearing on November 13, 2026 (speaker preregistration closes November 10, 2026). Comments on information collection provisions are best submitted to the U.S. Office of Management and Budget by November 30, 2026. Given the short timeline and the dozens of specific comment questions posed, companies should consider preparing technical and economic data now to support their positions on the numerous issues for which EPA seeks input.

How Holland & Knight Can Help

Holland & Knight's Environmental Team regularly advises oil and natural gas producers, midstream companies and other stakeholders on CAA compliance, rulemaking participation and related litigation. For questions regarding EPA's proposal or assistance preparing comments, please contact the authors.

Notes

1 Present value for 2027-50 at 3 percent discount rate. In EPA's regulatory analysis, this figure represents net surplus, consisting of $42 billion in compliance cost savings and $3 billion in savings from energy market impacts.

title: President Trump Is Powering an American Manufacturing Renaissance - The White House
description:
American manufacturing is surging under President Donald J. Trump.
Manufacturing jobs are coming back.
Manufacturers have added 72,000 jobs this year, reversing the 202,000 manufacturing jobs lost in the final two years of the Biden Administration.
Employment in factory construction has climbed by nearly 112,000 since President Trump took office.
Under President Trump, American manufacturing is being rebuilt — and made great again.
text:
American manufacturing is surging under President Donald J. Trump. A new report shows the sector expanding for the tenth consecutive month, with production growing at its fastest pace in nearly five years. Factories are expanding. Jobs are returning. Paychecks are rising faster than inflation. And companies are investing trillions to build their futures in America.

Manufacturing jobs are coming back. Manufacturers have added 72,000 jobs this year, reversing the 202,000 manufacturing jobs lost in the final two years of the Biden Administration. Employment in factory construction has climbed by nearly 112,000 since President Trump took office.

Paychecks are growing. Manufacturing workers’ weekly earnings are up 5% over the past year — outpacing inflation and boosting purchasing power.

Investment is accelerating. Business investment jumped 12.7% in the third quarter of 2026, the fastest growth in 15 years. Private investment in plants and equipment rose 9.4% — more than twice the 2025 rate and triple the pace of Biden’s final year. Capital goods imports hit a record share of total goods imports in September while consumer goods imports fell to a historic low, signaling businesses are equipping American factories, not just importing finished products.

Demand for American machinery is strong. U.S. machine tool orders reached their third-highest monthly total on record, up more than 36% from a year earlier.

Companies are matching the momentum with major new commitments. In just the past few weeks:

Audi announced a $4 billion factory in Georgia — its first U.S. manufacturing plant — creating 4,500 jobs.

Westinghouse Electric announced a $1 billion investment in South Carolina to build a next-generation nuclear fuel factory.

U.S. Steel announced a $3 billion investment near Pittsburgh to construct a new hot strip mill and increase annual capacity by roughly 1.3 million tons.

Apple announced up to $100 million to strengthen American titanium production.

Bombardier announced $270 million in U.S. manufacturing investment, creating thousands of jobs.

Carrier announced more than $600 million in an advanced manufacturing facility in Fort Worth.

More jobs. Rising wages. New factories. Record investment. Under President Trump, American manufacturing is being rebuilt — and made great again.

name: Texas and Evs
title: Data reveals California dominates US electric vehicle adoption, with 20 of nation's top 25 counties
description:
California tops the nation for electric vehicle adoption, accounting for 20 of the top 25 U.S. counties, with the Bay Area claiming every spot in the top five.
Here's what to know Plug-in hybrids counted as EVs in the census survey, alongside all-electric vehicles.
Californians continued purchasing electric vehicles amid soaring gasoline prices, according to separate sales figures released by the California Energy Commission.
The commission noted that electric vehicles made up most zero-emission sales and accounted for 16.6% of all new car sales.
Tricia Holley, a Census Bureau survey statistician, said: "Western states have led the way in switching to electric vehicles."
text:
California tops the nation for electric vehicle adoption, accounting for 20 of the top 25 U.S. counties, with the Bay Area claiming every spot in the top five.

Here's what to know

Plug-in hybrids counted as EVs in the census survey, alongside all-electric vehicles. Almost 14% of California households had an EV in 2025, compared with 5.5% nationwide, according to U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey figures reported by KTVU.

Santa Clara County, home to a tech-heavy economy, ranked first nationally. About 24% of its households — roughly 163,000 — owned or leased at least one EV.

The next four counties were Marin, San Mateo, Alameda, and Contra Costa, in that order. Beyond the Bay Area, Orange County placed sixth, followed by Napa County.

More background

About 18% of homeowner households had an EV, compared with almost 9% of renter households, according to the survey.

Washington followed at 8.9%, ahead of Hawaii at 8.5%, Nevada at 8.2%, and Vermont at 7.7%.

At the other end of the rankings, North Dakota recorded the lowest share, at 1.3%. Wyoming and Louisiana each registered 1.6%, while South Dakota and Mississippi each reported 1.8%.

What's being done?

Californians continued purchasing electric vehicles amid soaring gasoline prices, according to separate sales figures released by the California Energy Commission.

Unlike the household survey, these figures track new purchases rather than the share of households that already have an EV.

"During the second quarter of 2026, Californians purchased 86,857 new zero-emission vehicles (ZEVs)," the commission said in a July news release. "This represents 19.1% of new car sales."

The commission noted that electric vehicles made up most zero-emission sales and accounted for 16.6% of all new car sales.

Tricia Holley, a Census Bureau survey statistician, said: "Western states have led the way in switching to electric vehicles."

Where can I learn more?

For Californians considering an EV, cost and access to charging are practical concerns. These stories cover state charging policies, regional rebates, and obstacles facing drivers.

• California signed an EV package to speed charger installation and expand access for renters.

• San Joaquin Valley buyers can receive up to $3,000 from California's remaining EV rebate funds.

• California drivers weigh $3,500 EV discounts against broken chargers, scarce mechanics, and power outages.

• California's Central Coast offers expanded rebates and assistance for EVs, chargers, and other electric equipment.

description:

The report identifies electrolytically deposited copper foil as a viable first priority for establishing a local lithium-ion battery manufacturing sector.
The facility will play an important role in supporting a safe and competitive local lithium-ion battery manufacturing sector, helping Australian-made battery technologies meet the performance and safety expectations needed for domestic and international markets.
The future of Australian battery manufacturing: Cell cans and current collector foils report was funded through the AU-USA Battery R&D Grant, an Australian Government-supported initiative.
Want to hear more about the opportunities in Australian battery manufacturing?
text:
4 November 2026 News Release

With electrification of our transport, energy system and industry driving global demand in batteries, new analysis reveals Australia already has the capacity to become a battery manufacturing powerhouse.

The future of Australian battery manufacturing: Cell cans and current collector foils, by Australia’s national science agency, CSIRO, identifies where local industry has the skills, materials and expertise to make key components for lithium-ion and emerging sodium-ion batteries.

The report looks beyond Australia’s critical-minerals strengths to ask a more practical question: what would it take to turn more of those local resources into the parts that make up every battery cell?

CSIRO Advanced Battery Manufacturing lead, Dr Adam Best, said the work combines expertise in advanced manufacturing, battery materials and industrial process assessment, bringing together knowledge of how battery components are made with a practical understanding of what Australian industry can already do.

“That combination is central to the report’s message that Australia’s battery opportunity is not only about what lies in the ground, but what can be made here from it,” Dr Best said.

McKinsey analysis projects the global lithium-ion battery value chain could grow to more than US$400 billion by 2030, while the Australian Government’s National Battery Strategy notes that 96 per cent of the total revenue opportunity is expected to occur downstream of mining. Today, much of that value is captured offshore, with the bulk of our critical minerals being exported. CSIRO’s work shows Australia has a pathway to change that story by building sovereign capability in selected parts of the battery supply chain.

“Bringing more of the value chain onshore would mean Australia could move beyond exporting raw and refined materials alone, towards creating higher-value products, supporting skilled manufacturing jobs and strengthening supply chains for technologies that will underpin the clean energy transition,” Dr Best said.

Rather than attempting to build every part of a battery industry at once, the report points to two promising first steps: making prismatic battery cell cans from Australian aluminium using the impact extrusion process, and producing copper current collector foil using electrolytic deposition.

Both opportunities align with Australia’s aluminium and copper resources and its metal-forming, packaging, electrorefining and electrowinning expertise.

CSIRO researcher Geoff de Looze said the study focused on realistic opportunities to move from minerals and materials into higher-value components.

“Australia has many of the building blocks needed for a battery manufacturing sector,” Mr de Looze said.

“The question is where we can take the most practical next steps. This work identifies areas where Australian materials, existing industrial capability and targeted investment could come together to create a stronger domestic supply chain.”

Battery cell cans are the thin metal cases housing a cell’s active parts. Although apparently simple, they must withstand internal pressure changes and crash loads, remain compatible with electrolyte chemicals, minimise weight and leave maximum space for energy storage - all at low cost. Australia could feasibly make any of the cylindrical, prismatic or ‘blade’ cell formats, although some pathways would require major investment in production of nickel-plated steel and aluminium sheet.

A practical first step for Australia could be producing prismatic battery cans from aluminium. Australia already has a strong aluminium industry and experience manufacturing similar products, including aerosol cans. The report recommends investing in facilities and production equipment tailored to making battery cans locally.

A battery’s current collector foils support the cell’s electrochemical core and carry current to its terminals. The copper foil on a lithium-ion battery’s negative electrode is typically just six microns thick - about one-tenth the thickness of a human hair - while the aluminium foil on the other side is about twice as thick. These highly engineered components are critical to battery performance, safety and production.

The report identifies electrolytically deposited copper foil as a viable first priority for establishing a local lithium-ion battery manufacturing sector. It would build on Australia’s copper production and refining capability, can be scaled by adding production cells over time, and is less capital-intensive than rolling routes.

“Australia is already a critical minerals powerhouse, but the next opportunity is to capture more value through manufacturing,” Dr Best said.

“By focusing on practical, technically achievable steps, Australia can build capability, support industry growth and contribute to more resilient battery supply chains both domestically and internationally.”

Rebuilding lost or reduced downstream capability will require careful technical, commercial and market analysis, particularly where facilities need high utilisation to be viable. But CSIRO’s analysis shows that Australia is not starting from scratch. It has the minerals, parts of the industrial base and growing national interest in clean energy manufacturing. With targeted investment, it could turn more local resources into battery components made here, supporting jobs, supply-chain resilience and long-term energy security.

With this in mind, CSIRO has recently established the Australian Battery Safety Facility (ABSF), strengthening Australia’s capability to test and understand battery safety as the country builds its domestic battery industry. The facility will play an important role in supporting a safe and competitive local lithium-ion battery manufacturing sector, helping Australian-made battery technologies meet the performance and safety expectations needed for domestic and international markets.

The future of Australian battery manufacturing: Cell cans and current collector foils report was funded through the AU-USA Battery R&D Grant, an Australian Government-supported initiative.

Rising energy demand for projects like data centers are forcing difficult conversations in Indiana.

Clinton County farmer Alan Dunn says energy affordability and local control are top concerns as energy infrastructure grows across the state.

“The grid, data centers, energy generation,” he says. “Don’t be closed minded. There’s an opportunity here that energy generation can be paid for by these large data centers in a way that we as a community would never be able to do.”

Last week, Indiana Governor Mike Braun and 22 other governors across the country signed onto President Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge to help lower energy bills in rural areas. Congress is also considering several pieces of legislation that could prevent large price hikes due to the increased use of data centers.

District 16 State Representative Kendell Culp says there has to be a balance between supporting economic growth and protecting rural landowners.

“If you decide you want or don’t want a data center, that’s a local community decision, but our energy needs will have to be met if we’re going to reach our future goals,” he says.

Both say finding policy solutions that balances economic development and farmland preservation remains a top priority heading into the 2027 state legislative session.

Brownfield interviewed Dunn and Culp during the 2026 Indiana Ag Policy Summit.

text:
Before the 1950s, raw sewage flowed into San Francisco Bay. It created a foul, polluted mess. East Bay communities turned to EBMUD for a regional solution.

This year, we mark our 75th year of providing wastewater treatment that protects public health and has helped transform the bay into a treasured natural resource.

A vote for the bay

When residents voted in 1944 for EBMUD to manage wastewater treatment, we built a plant in West Oakland and installed three massive underground interceptor pipes to capture flows from city sewers. Operations began in 1951.

EBMUD has continually improved treatment as environmental standards have evolved.

Pollution reductions

In the 1970s, EBMUD added biological processes to remove more organic matter and launched a program to control pollutants at their source. The result: a 90% reduction in toxic discharges.

Since 2020, EBMUD has significantly cut nitrogen discharges that can upset the ecological balance needed for healthy marine life, saving ratepayer dollars while improving bay water quality.

Sustainable operations

EBMUD recycles water, recovers nutrients used in soil amendments, and generates energy from waste materials. We became the first North American wastewater utility to produce more renewable energy than we consume.

The bay today

Decades of environmental stewardship by EBMUD and our regional partners have restored the marine ecosystem to support wildlife and recreation.

A team of over 50 EBMUD plant operators work around the clock to fulfill our mission of protecting public health and the environment for today’s 740,000 wastewater customers and for future generations.

text:
Samsung SDI posted its highest quarterly operating profit in three years in the third quarter of 2026, driven by utility-scale energy storage system (ESS) orders and battery backup units (BBUs) for artificial intelligence data centers.

Revenue rose 52.6% year-on-year, with operating profit reaching $304 million after an operating loss a year earlier. The battery division generated $3.28 billion, up 55.3% year-on-year, and posted a $269 million operating profit.

The turnaround is bolstered by data center demand for energy storage, but was anchored by the U.S. stationary storage market, where Samsung SDI said it secured more than 60 GWh of ESS battery orders in 2026. That tally includes a 1 GWh U.S. supply agreement with Alpha Omega Power for its nickel cobalt aluminum (NCA) Samsung Battery Box 1.7 and a U.S. cell supply arrangement with Sungrow.

The South Korean-headquartered company said that, as part of its two-track NCA and LFP chemistry strategy, it began mass production of LFP cells in October at its StarPlus Energy facility in Indiana.

U.S. electric vehicle demand remains slow enough that factories meant to supply cells and packs for mobility purposes are not as viable as when investment decisions were made.

Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solutions have both pivoted factory lines towards LFP for stationary storage, and Samsung said it is designating its Synergy Cells plant in Indiana as an ESS production hub, and further accelerating EV-to-LFP line conversions in the fourth quarter. LG did similar with its own JV with Stellantis.

To avoid Chinese import tariffs and meet Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) rules, it said it has “signed long-term supply agreements for LFP cathode materials with major Korean materials companies to meet U.S. demand for supply chains independent of China.”

Samsung SDI also recently launched cylindrical LFP cells for data center BBUs and aims to close additional long-term utility-scale ESS and uninterruptible power supply (UPS) contracts before year-end, alongside bidding in South Korea’s third government-led ESS procurement round.

text:
Wicomico County Executive Julie Giordano is pleased to announce continued progress on a groundbreaking renewable natural gas (RNG) project at the Newland Park Landfill in Salisbury, Maryland. This initiative represents another major step toward modernizing county infrastructure, expanding alternative energy production, and positioning Wicomico County as a leader in environmental stewardship. Following nearly a year of due diligence, Wicomico County finalized agreements with WAGA Energy to develop what is anticipated to be Maryland's first cryogenic distillation facility designed to convert landfill gases, including methane, into pipeline-quality renewable natural gas.

Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, and landfills are a significant source of emissions. By capturing and converting these gases into usable energy, Wicomico County is taking an innovative approach to environmental protection while maximizing the value of existing county resources.

"This project is another example of what can happen when we focus on innovation, responsible government, and long-term solutions," said County Executive Julie Giordano. "We are turning what was once considered a waste product into a valuable energy resource while strengthening our infrastructure and protecting our environment. I am incredibly proud of our Department of Public Works and the partnerships making this possible."

To further support the initiative, the county has engaged the Maryland Energy Administration through its Local Government Energy Modernization (L-GEM) Grant Program to assist with infrastructure planning and development.

Since November 2025, WAGA Energy, the county's existing landfill-gas-to-energy partner Archaea, and local utility providers have worked collaboratively to finalize easements, agreements, and natural gas interconnection plans. Engineering and facility development are currently underway, with renewable natural gas production anticipated to begin in the spring or summer of 2028.

title: Strong methane regulations are essential as Canada pushes new infrastructure projects forward
description:
These projects make Canada’s enhanced oil and gas methane regulations more important than ever.
The critical difference in methane emissions performance between the scenarios considered is whether methane regulations are fully implemented in the provinces.
An EDF analysis estimates that reducing oil and gas methane emissions by 75% would create 34,000 jobs, many of which are in the mitigation sector.
Strong, verifiable methane performance for Canadian energy will set our product apart on the international market.
If the government intends to move major energy and data-centre projects forward, it must pair that agenda with the strongest available safeguards.
text:
By Ari Pottens and Scott Seymour

The rupture in relations with the United States has created an existential challenge for Canada’s economic well-being. Its response is taking shape through a nation-building agenda meant to strengthen the economy, diversify trade, and strengthen Canadian sovereignty.

A central aspect of that agenda involves advancing major infrastructure projects that “reinforce Canadian sovereignty.” Canada’s climate agenda, however, is going to be immensely impacted by the additional greenhouse gas emissions required for the proposed buildout, including a one-million-barrel-per-day pipeline and natural-gas-powered data centres requiring 5.5 gigawatts of energy.

These projects make Canada’s enhanced oil and gas methane regulations more important than ever. If they are robustly implemented in every oil and gas producing province, they can significantly reduce emissions even as new emissions-intensive projects move forward. Strong methane rules will not erase the climate impact of expanded fossil-fuel infrastructure and use, but they are one of the fastest, most practical tools available to slow the rate of near-term warming.

Our analysis uses emissions data from the National Inventory Report and oil and gas production projections from Canada’s Energy Future to establish a baseline before adding production changes related to the proposed pipeline and gas-powered data centres. The critical difference in methane emissions performance between the scenarios considered is whether methane regulations are fully implemented in the provinces.

Methane has earned this special attention because it is more than 80 times as potent a climate warming as carbon dioxide over a 20-year period, meaning that methane mitigation can deliver an outsized benefit in the short-term. The proposal pipeline and data centre buildout is set to increase overall carbon dioxide emissions, but the government can still drastically reduce methane pollution from the oil and gas industry. And as a bonus, these mitigation efforts can drive growth in the Canadian economy.

Canada already has a strong domestic methane mitigation sector with more than 100 companies supplying the equipment and expertise to find and fix leaks and avoid unnecessary emissions from venting and flaring. Increasing methane performance stringency for oil and gas production will increase the demand for this equipment and expertise. An EDF analysis estimates that reducing oil and gas methane emissions by 75% would create 34,000 jobs, many of which are in the mitigation sector.

The benefits aren’t only for Canada’s air quality, climate resiliency, and domestic economy, however: the demand for low-methane energy is steadily increasing among large energy-buying countries in Europe and Asia. Strong, verifiable methane performance for Canadian energy will set our product apart on the international market.

Seizing this opportunity won’t be easy, but the way to do it is clear. The federal government needs to ensure that its ambition is matched by strong provincial rules in every producing jurisdiction, with a particular emphasis on credible emissions measurement.

Watering down the proposed regulations will hurt Canada’s goal of being the most responsible source of energy in North America, and building energy-intensive infrastructure without mitigating the emissions impacts undermine our reputation as an international climate leader.

Nation-building does not mean having to choose between ambitious projects and climate responsibility, or economic growth and pollution reduction. If the government intends to move major energy and data-centre projects forward, it must pair that agenda with the strongest available safeguards. Robust, measurement-based methane regulations—implemented consistently across the country—are an essential place to start.

text:
This story was originally published on Utility Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily Utility Dive newsletter.

The outcome of Tuesday's midterm elections could have serious implications for utilities, as candidates in both parties seek to capitalize on widespread concerns about energy affordability.

Policy areas that could see the biggest impact include data centers, energy tax credits and permitting reform, experts told Utility Dive.

Hasan Nazar, head of policy at Crux, a finance technology company that connects tax credit buyers and sellers, said he believes energy affordability will be "determinative" in this election.

Polls have given Democrats a strong chance of taking control of the House and possibly also flipping the Senate, but even if they do, Nazar noted that there would still be a split government with a Republican administration in place. He hopes broad support for reform will lead to bipartisan cooperation on energy policy.

"History shows us that energy crises create policy openings, and we think the conditions are probably in place for a window of policymaking," Nazar said.

What candidates are telling voters

All U.S. House seats are up for grabs, along with one-third of the Senate and 36 gubernatorial seats.

An Oct. 8 poll from Pew Research Center found that 74% of U.S. adults surveyed were concerned about the price of gasoline and energy, the largest share of concern among all surveyed issues.

As candidates campaigned this year, energy issues were central in many races.

During an Oct. 8 debate, Georgia Senate candidates Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., and Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., sought to tie each other to controversial data center projects, according to Atlanta News First. Collins said Ossoff had a "data center billionaire" donor and promised to protect Georgians from having their electricity infrastructure "destroyed" by the projects. Ossoff noted Collins had voted in favor of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and said the legislation contained a "data center tax scam."

In Wisconsin's gubernatorial race, David Crowley, D, has proposed requiring data centers to be powered with renewable energy, and a 2050 net zero goal for the state. His opponent Tom Tiffany, R, has strongly opposed data center development, saying "data centers, solar and wind farms should not be built on Wisconsin's farmland," the Wisconsin Examiner reported.

Ohio gubernatorial candidates Vivek Ramaswamy, R, and Amy Acton, D, have both campaigned on data center and energy issues — the next governor will appoint a full slate of commissioners to the Ohio Public Utilities Commission. Ramaswamy has promised free electricity to those who live near a data center, while Acton proposed a conditional moratorium on data centers if certain requirements aren't met, reported the Ohio Capital Journal.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, D, has applied pressure to utilities requesting rate hikes, while his opponent, state treasurer Stacy Garrity, R, proposed lowering rates by eliminating the state tax on electricity, and said she would intervene in a utility's rate case if she disagreed with a hike, according to reporting from Spotlight PA. An ad from Garrity's campaign said Shapiro "sold us out" to data center interests, while an ad from Shapiro's campaign called Garrity "Pennsylvania's No. 1 fan of data centers," The Hill reported.

Dylan Reed, Advanced Energy United's managing director overseeing federal and political affairs, said Pennsylvania's race is also significant given the role that Gov. Shapiro has played in the ongoing debate over the PJM Interconnection's surging prices.

In 2025, Shapiro was one of the PJM state governors who threatened to pull out of the grid operator's markets.

"Affordability is the message that we see out here very clearly," Reed said. "I think when you are looking at high prices when it comes to your utility bill, the number one office that can impact that right now is the governor."

How elections could shape federal policy

Nazar said he thinks that following the election, in Congress "there's probably going to be at least a discussion about new kinds of tax credit incentives that could be deployed."

In 2022, then-Vice President Kamala Harris cast the tie-breaking vote in the Senate to pass the Inflation Reduction Act, which received no Republican votes and established long-horizon tax credits for clean energy along with new tax credit mechanisms like transferability.

In 2025, a Republican-controlled Congress passed the OBBBA, which shortened the horizon for some of the IRA's clean energy benefits. Now, if Democrats take back control, they could seek to revise the OBBBA's impacts, observers say.

"A flipped Congress where both houses are with the Democrats could have a dramatic turn on the energy policy landscape, and particularly with federal energy tax credits," said Heather Cooper, a partner at the law firm McDermott Will & Schulte. "We have seen pretty dramatic flip-flopping in the last five years as Congress has gone back and forth."

However, Cooper — who advises clients on federal income tax issues related to the energy transition — said she thinks the clean energy industry is prepared for the possibility of future flip-flopping.

"Most of the players who are in this market … The reality is all of their business models are kind of used to a world where these tax credits have 1, 2, 3, 4-year horizons," she said.

The IRA, which created a longer runway for the first time, resulted in a "phenomenal amount of money poured into this industry," she added.

The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) has introduced a $237 million funding opportunity designed to increase manufacturing and strengthen supply chains for critical electric grid components.

The Grid Supply Chain Alternatives to Lead Energy Dominance (Grid SCALED) funding opportunity will incentivize the refurbishment and reuse of critical equipment and encourage the adoption of alternative materials and sub components that are sourced and made in America. These efforts will lower costs, strengthen grid reliability, and meet growing electricity demand.

“The Energy Department is investing in American-made technologies and modernizing our grid to reduce reliance on foreign suppliers and deliver affordable, reliable, electricity,” U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said.

The funding opportunity will support projects in two key areas:

Up to $50 million will be provided to projects that promote greater refurbishment and reuse of existing grid equipment and materials;

Up to $187 million will be provided to projects that will increase the use of alternative materials and subcomponents sourced and made in the U.S, reducing dependence on imports.

“America should never have to rely on foreign suppliers to keep the lights on,” Office of Electricity Assistant Secretary Katie Jereza said. “We’re putting American ingenuity to work, developing next-generation grid technologies that strengthen our domestic supply chain, help lower costs, and make our grid more reliable. The power to secure our energy future should be in our own hands.”

This is the first funding opportunity in the DOE’s Grid Supply Chain Program, which is authorized to provide up to $375 million to strengthen domestic supply chains for the manufacturing of distribution and power transformers, grid components, and materials.

In 2027, additional funding announcements are anticipated for next-generation technologies, including solid-state transformers, and promote common configurations to streamline manufacturing.

The investment is expected to deliver an estimated $125 million in annual utility savings. Further, it would keep about $50 million per year in the U.S. economy that would otherwise go to foreign suppliers.

Applicants must submit a concept paper by Nov. 20 to qualify to submit a full application. Full applications are due by Feb. 8, 2027.

text:
The election will also be a test of how voters respond to Democratic candidates tying the biggest issue of the election — affordability — to the climate crisis.

Here are five things to know about the climate crisis and the midterms:

1. If Democrats do well, they could gain leverage to oppose Trump’s anti-climate agenda

If Democrats take control of the House or Senate, they won’t be able to overturn previous Republican actions like gutting the Inflation Reduction Act, and they can’t pass new legislation that Trump would veto, but they will have more cards to play to oppose Trump’s pro-fossil fuel agenda going forward.

If Democrats take back the House, it will mean the White House has to compromise with Democrats in order to pass budgets. This would give Democrats the power to add climate provisions into appropriations legislation, said Michael Gerrard, founder and director of the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law. “Many appropriations begin in the House, and these are huge bills that have to pass, so it’s possible that some pro-climate provisions could be put in some of the appropriations legislation,” he said. “Often presidents sign appropriation bills that have provisions they don’t like because they need to get the budget passed.”

Democrats could also use their power in the House to launch investigations and subpoena witnesses and documents. Dan Farber, a law professor at the University of California, Berkeley, suggested they could investigate possible conflicts of interest or corruption, like the Trump administration intervening in a federal lawsuit to allow Elon Musk to continue using portable gas generators in his Mississippi data center, which the suit alleges is a violation of the Clean Air Act.

If Democrats win the Senate, they could oppose further confirmations of federal judges, cabinet officers, and sub-cabinet positions. “That gives [Democratic] senators some leverage to stop appointments they don’t want,” Farber said. “But you can also hold appointments hostage in return for other things.”

Preventing appointments of anti-climate judges would leave more vacancies for the next president to fill, he added. “That can have a big long-term effect on the environment.”

Gerrard said a power shift in the House and Senate could change negotiations around the permitting reform bill, which could clear hurdles for both clean energy and fossil fuels projects. The bill would significantly weaken the National Environmental Policy Act, making it impossible for a court to halt a project due to a Nepa violation, he said. “But if the Democrats are in charge of both the House and the Senate, that bill might look different.”

Farber and Gerrard said state climate policy was also hanging in the balance this November. The Cook Political Report found that Democrats could gain two-to-four governor’s seats this cycle. “If some of the governor’s offices flip from Republican to Democrat, that could yield a profound change in state climate policy,” Gerrard said.

2. If Republicans do well, expect more environmental rollbacks

If the Republicans buck polling predictions and manage to keep control of the House and Senate, it would embolden Trump to continue his anti-climate agenda.

Trump could continue his favoritism toward polluting companies, because Democrats would lack the investigative and subpoena powers to hold him accountable.

And he could continue appointing conservative justices: “Trump has been packing the lower courts with anti-regulatory, super conservative judges,” Farber said.

Under this administration, Republican lawmakers have backed Trump on policies that were unfavorable to their constituents — such as voting to repeal clean energy tax credits that created jobs in their districts. If Republicans win in the midterms, Republicans would continue to vote in support of Trump. “Maybe even more so, because I think this would be seen as a big win for him personally,” Farber said.

“They have not just been sitting on the sidelines ‚ they have helped Trump, in terms of repealing the Inflation Reduction Act from Biden, and overturning some specific regulations by Congress. We could see more of that kind of thing coming from them. So it would be another big step backwards,” Farber said.

“I keep thinking, how much worse could they do? But they always find something,” he added.

3. As affordability remains a key issue, voters feel the pinch of Trump’s anti-climate policies

The administration’s constraints on renewables are forcing consumers to spend more on energy. A study by Nera predicted that between 2027 and 2033, economy-wide household energy costs would increase on average by $11.6 billion annually from constraining the deployment of solar and wind. The region hardest hit by these constraints is Texas, where rates are forecast to rise as much as 22 percent, the study found.

Trump’s attacks on clean energy have also led to mass job losses, including many in battleground states. The US clean energy workforce lost nearly 37,000 jobs last year — the first annual job loss in America’s clean energy economy since the pandemic, according to a September report from E2, a business advocacy group for the clean economy that analyzed Department of Energy data.

A report from Climate Power puts that number even higher, with 173,000 clean energy jobs either cut or delayed since Trump took office. The report found that Texas saw the most jobs lost from Trump’s war on clean energy.

The Nera report found that increased reliance on natural gas capacity and generation raises reliability risks and increases exposure to price volatility. According to Climate Power, since Trump took office, gas and electric utilities have raised or sought to increase bills by more than $92 billion, affecting more than 100 million customers across the country.

4. Voters in battleground states want to hear more from candidates about the climate crisis

Polling shows that Democrats and Republicans in battleground states want candidates to talk more about the climate crisis. And even though one in three US adults have been directly affected by extreme weather, midterm candidates are avoiding talking directly about climate change in what’s known as “climate hushing.”

But researchers from the University of Michigan’s School for Environment and Sustainability have found that there are three groups of Democratic candidates and officeholders who are talking about the climate crisis in subtle instead of direct ways: energy populists like Democrat Sherrod Brown in Ohio are using data centers and utility bills to connect the issues of climate and affordability, climate champions like Arizona Democratic candidate JoAnna Mendoza are promising bold action like investing in clean energy, and candidates who are advocating for an “all-of-the-above” approach to energy, like Amy Acton in the Ohio governor’s race.

“The one thing that they all have in common is a focus on affordability … and talking about energy issues in the context of affordability,” said Geoffrey Henderson, an assistant environmental policy and planning professor at the University of Michigan.

He noted that a few candidates, like Democrat Josh Turek in Iowa, were emphasizing how extreme weather events worsened by the climate crisis are driving up the cost of insurance.

With various quiet climate messages being tested in battleground states, this election could be a test of how voters respond to these messages. Henderson expects political analysts will study the data after the election to draw lessons from it. “The climate message has in a number of ways been brought into alignment with the affordability question, and so I think this is a test of whether that combination resonates,” he said.

The issue of climate hushing has come up election after election, but Henderson believes it’s a positive thing that candidates are still finding ways to talk about climate, even indirectly. “It’s better that candidates are tying climate to affordability than not mentioning it at all, and I do see how different parts of the country lend themselves to different strategies.”

5. Whatever happens at the polls, some of the big US climate fights ahead will be in the courts

Environmental laws are being tested in US courts like never before. “We’re now at a stage where every significant environmental regulation is challenged in court by one side or the other,” Gerrard said.

The Trump administration has set out to weaken and revoke environmental regulations, triggering a wave of litigation attempting to undo those actions. If a future Democratic president tries to restore those regulations or issue new ones, they would also be challenged in court, Gerrard said.

Gerrard is closely watching the fight over Trump’s repeal of the endangerment finding, which stated that the buildup of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere endangers public health, allowing the Environmental Protection Agency to limit greenhouse gas pollution from various sources. “There’s a case before the DC circuit on Trump’s revocation of the endangerment finding — that’s a very big case,” he noted.

Samsung SDI has started mass production of LFP batteries at its $6.3 billion StarPlus Energy plant in Kokomo, Indiana. The company started prismatic LFP cell output in October. The step is part of a two-track approach for both LFP and NCA chemistries. The Indiana location is now Samsung SDI’s “ESS battery production hub.

The transfer is a solid quarter closer. In the third quarter of 2026, Samsung SDI reported its best operating profit for the quarter in three years. Revenue increased 52.6 percent from the previous year. After posting an operating loss last year, operating profit stood at KRW 407.8 billion, or $304 million. The battery division alone accounted for KRW 4.41 trillion in revenue, which rose by 55.3 percent, and an operating profit of KRW 361.9 billion.

Other Projects.

Another major energy project is taking place in Texas. Waaree Solar Americas has started commercial production on two new 800 MW solar module manufacturing lines at its Brookshire facility in Texas, USA. The expansion doubles the plant’s annual manufacturing capacity to 3.2 GW. Production on the new lines began on October 29, 2026. The development strengthens Waaree’s domestic manufacturing footprint as the company targets growing demand from US solar developers, utilities and engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractors.

Scope of implementation on the Samsung SDI StarPlus Energy Plant

The Kokomo complex houses two StarPlus Energy gigafactories, built with Stellantis under their battery joint venture. They have a combined investment of more than $6.3 billion and a combined capacity of 67 gigawatt hours. The first plant, which has a capacity of 33 GWh, was opened in early 2025. Stellantis schedules the second, at 34 GWh, to start production in early 2027. It will employ 1,400 more workers.

The pivot was driven by demand. The factories that produce mobility cells are no longer profitable in the United States, where EV sales have been sluggish. Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solutions have thus moved their lines towards LFP for stationary storage. LG made a similar move at its joint venture with Stellantis in Canada. Samsung will speed up the conversion of EVs to LFP in the fourth quarter.

The company has also ensured its supply chain. Next, supply chains. To avoid Chinese import tariffs and meet Foreign Entity of Concern rules, Samsung SDI said it has “signed long-term supply agreements for LFP cathode materials with major Korean materials companies.” The objective is to meet U.S. demand “independent of China.

Orders back the strategy. Samsung SDI has received over 60 GWh of orders for energy storage in the United States in 2026. The tally includes a 1 GWh agreement with Alpha Omega Power for its NCA-based Samsung Battery Box 1.7. It also includes a US cell supply deal with inverter manufacturer Sungrow.

Outlook for the Samsung SDI business

Today, data centers are driving the growth narrative. The turnaround was driven by orders for utility-scale ESS and battery backup units for AI facilities. Samsung SDI has also launched cylindrical LFP cells for data center BBUs.

Furthermore, the company is pursuing additional deals. It is looking to finalize more long-term ESS and UPS deals before the end of the year. It is also bidding in South Korea’s third government-led ESS procurement round.

The pieces therefore fit together. The cells come from Kokomo, the cathode chain is provided by Korean suppliers, and the output is taken by grid plus data center customers. Now Samsung SDI has to prove that the hub can operate at scale with the continued softness of EV demand. Despite this, it has a head start with the order book and the profit swing.

text:
Q&A with Adam Webb, Head of Battery Raw Materials, Benchmark Mineral Intelligence

Battery raw materials expert Adam Webb of Benchmark Mineral Intelligence says the long-term outlook for lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite, and phosphate remains strong despite a slowdown in electric vehicle (EV) growth. Webb argues that battery energy storage systems (BESS) have become a major demand driver, pushing lithium into deficit and helping lift prices as global battery deployment accelerates.

This interview explores how export restrictions are reshaping cobalt and nickel markets, where future supply is likely to emerge, and the key risks facing the sector. Webb identifies lithium as the standout battery metal, forecasting demand growth from around 2 million tonnes (Mt) today to 5Mt by 2040, requiring significant new mine supply globally.

To listen to the interview, click here:

Give us a quick introduction to yourself and your work in this space.

For those unfamiliar with Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, we cover critical minerals and are particularly focused on battery supply chains, as well as materials outside and adjacent to them, including copper and rare earths.

My role within the company is to look after our fundamental research into those raw materials, specifically looking at supply, demand, market balance forecasts, price forecasts, and cost analysis. This also covers a broad spectrum of critical minerals, including lithium, nickel, cobalt, and graphite.

There’s been a lot of talk about the EV revolution, which has gained pace in many ways, but also faltered in others. What are some of the broader trends you’re seeing today?

On the EV side, you’re right. The market has grown massively over recent years. We’ve seen a huge uptick in EV sales globally, but there has been somewhat of a slowdown in that growth this year.

But if you look at this on a regional basis, China, which is by far the biggest EV market, has seen growth almost flatline this year. That’s because certain subsidies were removed towards the end of last year.

In North America, we have a similar picture. The Trump administration removed some tax credits for EVs. So, we saw a big uptick in sales just before the tax credit was removed and then subsequently a downturn.

But if you look at Europe, EV sales have risen significantly this year. That’s because of high fuel prices driven by the war in Iran, subsidies in various European Union (EU) countries, and imports of Chinese EVs.

That picture is reflected in the rest of the world as well. For example, in Australia, New Zealand, and South America, sales are strong. This is again due to a combination of relatively competitively priced Chinese imports and high fuel prices.

So it’s a really mixed picture.

Overall, we’re expecting 7% growth in global EV sales this year. While there is a slowdown, there are different regional dynamics, and the market is still growing pretty strongly.

Let’s look at some of the supply and demand dynamics for some of the key metals that are needed like lithium, graphite, cobalt, etc. Where are the biggest supply gaps?

We look at the raw materials needed for batteries used in EVs, but also in BESS, which is another massively growing segment driving demand.

When we’re talking about raw materials, number one is lithium. It’s used in all lithium-ion (Li-ion) batteries, regardless of the battery type.

That’s probably the commodity most tied to this sector, with about 90% of lithium demand coming from batteries.

What we’re seeing for lithium is that the market has been in deficit this year, meaning demand has exceeded supply. That has been driven not by the EV sector, but by BESS. We’ve seen new BESS deployments increase by around 40% year-on-year. We’re expecting that this year, the supply of those batteries will increase at an even greater rate.

There’s been a big ramp-up of production, particularly of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries in China. That’s pushed up lithium demand significantly this year. We’re talking around 30% growth in terms of demand.

On the supply side, we’ve also seen growth as projects come online. Some projects that previously closed due to low lithium prices have also returned, particularly in Australia. This has pushed supply up by around 20%, but not at the same rate as demand.

The lithium market is in deficit and that’s caused prices to increase. We’ve seen prices more than double, rising from around US$10,000 ($14,170) per tonne of lithium carbonate in mid-2025 to above US$20,000 by mid-2026.

There’s been a recent pullback in prices, but we see that as more sentiment-driven. The fundamentals are still showing that the lithium market is in deficit.

The dynamic differs for other commodities. Nickel and cobalt, for example, are used in battery cathodes, but not in LFP batteries. Instead, they’re used in nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) batteries, which are used in EVs rather than the energy storage sector.

The dynamic that we’ve seen is the increase in the use of LFP batteries in EVs in China, particularly in the more economic models, and that means that the share of NCM batteries has fallen.

Even so, battery types that contain nickel and cobalt are still growing. For example, I think cobalt-containing batteries are expected to grow 10% this year, which feeds through to rising demand for nickel and cobalt.

There are a few dynamics that are quite interesting on the supply side.

About 75% of cobalt comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), which imposed an export ban early last year before introducing a quota system that has reduced how much cobalt can reach the market.

These measures have switched the market into a deficit, leading to a strong rally in cobalt prices. A couple of years ago, cobalt hydroxide was as low as US$14,000 per tonne, but this year, it’s reached as high as US$60,000.

It’s a similar picture for nickel, but for different reasons. That market is dominated by Indonesia, which has really ramped up its refining capacity in nickel and now accounts for around 60% of global supply.

Indonesia has introduced a quota system called the Rencana Kerja dan Anggaran Biaya (RKAB), which dictates how much ore can be mined to supply its smelters. The quota was significantly lower this year than the previous year and fell short of the smelters’ requirements.

So, we’ve seen some operations having to curtail production, with a resulting drop in Indonesian output.

In addition, the Fort Saskatchewan refinery in Canada has closed because the US imposed sanctions on Cuban oil imports. The refinery relied on a mine in Cuba and it basically ran out of fuel and couldn’t produce any ore.

So, for those two reasons, we’ve had a small drop in nickel output this year, around 1%. At the same time, demand has risen, driven by batteries and stainless steel, which remains the biggest demand sector for nickel. This has essentially balanced the market.

By our estimates, the market is in a very narrow deficit but to all intents and purposes remains balanced.

Again, that’s supported prices, which we’ve seen rise by about 15% from the 2025 average to the 2026 average.

Graphite is another interesting and often overlooked material. While the other materials that I’ve mentioned go into the cathode side of the battery, graphite goes into the anode.

There are two types of graphite: natural and synthetic. Synthetic graphite is produced from coke, so from the hydrocarbon industry, while natural graphite is mined as flake graphite.

We’ve seen rising demand from batteries, which account for about 40% of global graphite demand. There is also significant industrial demand for flake graphite, so demand is rising. However, 70% of supply comes from China. We’ve also seen a big ramp-up in production in East Africa, leaving the market in a bit of a surplus and weighing on prices.

Prices have been very stable. I would say that flake graphite prices for the -100 mesh, which goes into the battery supply chain, have remained at about US$400 per tonne, reflecting the industry’s price floor.

The last one to mention is purified phosphoric acid, which is important to LFP cells and is becoming more significant as LFP use rises. That market is essentially in deficit. It’s important to know that with purified phosphoric acid, there are a lot of other uses as well, including fertilisers. The battery use of phosphate rock is relatively small, but it’s an important raw material to consider, particularly with that rise in LFP.

You spoke about export bans and quotas in the DRC and Indonesia specifically. What’s the overall impact of these policies on the industry overall? Is substitution an option?

With cobalt, on the substitution side, the industry has been looking at that for a long time because cobalt is quite a volatile commodity. The market is small, with a total demand of about 300,000 tonnes. Compare that with lithium, which is at 2Mt, and nickel, at close to 4Mt. So, cobalt is a really small market.

What comes with that is price volatility. A small change in supply or demand can move prices significantly. For that reason, and because supply is concentrated in the DRC and linked to artisanal mining, original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) have been looking to move away from cobalt for quite some time. That’s one of the reasons why we’ve seen a shift from NCM chemistries containing more cobalt to those containing less.

In terms of the broader impact, I think nickel and cobalt are similar when it comes to pricing. If you have that much control of supply and can control how much reaches the market, you can influence supply and demand dynamics and, therefore, prices.

Cobalt hydroxide prices were as low as US$14,000 per tonne due to a massive glut of supply from primary copper mines in the DRC, which produce cobalt as a byproduct. The DRC Government wanted to generate more revenue from its cobalt resources, so it introduced export bans and quotas, which have led to prices rallying.

That was always the plan. The risk, though, is that pushing prices up increases the incentive to substitute cobalt with other materials.

I think there’s a balancing act on the nickel side of things. Indonesia’s RKAB quota system is another way to support the price. What we saw last year is nickel prices dropping to a point where a lot of the Indonesian nickel industry was not making any money or was operating at a loss.

The Indonesian Government can use the RKAB quota system to better manage its natural resources and prevent them from being overexploited. It can also control supply to support prices and keep the Indonesian nickel industry profitable.

But there is always the risk that if you pull that lever too much, it pushes the prices too high and then you destroy demand for the very thing you’re trying to monetise.

So, with these export controls and regulations in producing regions, where do you see emerging opportunities or projects?

While demand in the lithium market is currently around 2Mt, it’s expected to reach 5Mt by 2040. That means we’ll need to more than double supply to meet demand.

The scale of growth is similar for other commodities, although a little lower for nickel and cobalt. Natural graphite and purified phosphoric acid are also expected to see significant growth.

We’re going to need more supply to come online to meet that demand, which will naturally create opportunities for project developers across the world.

Where that supply comes from is based on geology and where the deposits are located.

For lithium, it’s quite a diverse supply landscape. The bottleneck is refining, particularly in China. In terms of mining, Australia is currently the biggest producer, with China the second- or third-largest. Then you’ve got Chile, Argentina, and Zimbabwe, so lithium is quite diverse in terms of where the mineral resources are located, with opportunities around the world.

At the moment, the biggest growth we’re seeing is in Argentina, where the country is becoming quite supportive of the industry, as well as in the US, particularly around the Smackover Formation in Arkansas, and in parts of Africa. We’re expecting AVZ Minerals’ (HM:3A2) Manono Lithium Project to come online in the DRC, along with several more projects in West Africa.

On the nickel front, this has become a clearly Indonesian-focused story. However, there are several projects in Canada, for example, that differ from those in Indonesia. They’re exploiting sulphide resources, whereas nickel resources in Indonesia are laterite.

Western governments have been looking to diversify away from Chinese supply, particularly. Within Indonesia, there’s also quite a heavy influence of Chinese companies through joint ventures. So there’s that strategic aspect as well.

We’re expecting growth in Indonesia to continue, particularly from high-pressure acid leach operations, which are feeding the battery supply chain. So, that’s where we’re seeing the biggest growth in terms of nickel.

For graphite, we’ve seen huge growth in East Africa, including Mozambique, Tanzania, and Madagascar, and we expect that to continue. In North America, Nouveau Monde Graphite (NYSE:NMG) has secured funding for its project, which is tied to this move away from Chinese control, particularly in graphite.

If you look at the natural graphite side, around 70% of mine supply is coming from China, with refined supply bringing that up to 90%. So, that’s part of a strategic move as well.

Finally, in the purified phosphoric acid industry, China accounts for around 40% of supply. Morocco is the second biggest producer, but if you look at the global reserve base, Morocco has about 70% of reserves. So, there’s a real opportunity there for Morocco to become a source for Western markets.

But, in terms of growth at the moment, China is still going to be the dominant player in that space.

What are some of the biggest risks for the future growth of the industry?

The opportunities for growth that I’ve outlined represent our base case — especially where we’re talking about a doubling of demand by 2040.

On the risk side of things, the number one risk is EV adoption and BESS rollouts. One risk that I’ve been talking about a lot this week is basically the oversupply of batteries, particularly within China, and this is largely on the BESS side.

This year, we’re expecting battery production to reach around 3 terawatt hours (TWh), but demand for those batteries is much lower, around 2.3TWh. So, we’re getting this oversupply.

Obviously, the production of the batteries is what dictates the demand for the raw materials. The risk is that if battery production is curtailed to bring it closer to demand, we may not see a decline in demand, but rather a slower rate of growth. This is because continuing to produce well above demand is not sustainable in the long term. However, this could be a gradual trend rather than a dramatic shift, and China has a history of overproducing in various sectors.

The other risk is technological. When we look at different battery types, there’s a lot of talk about sodium-ion batteries instead of Li-ion batteries. These are unlikely to be as relevant for EVs, although there may be some adoption. That’s because they tend to have lower energy density, meaning a car would have less range with the same size battery. However, they could have applications in BESS.

We’re seeing growth in the sodium-ion battery, but we’re not seeing it replacing LFP or Li-ion in the BESS space. There is a risk that if sodium-ion suddenly takes off, becomes commercialised, and costs less than LFP, it could displace some demand for Li-ion batteries, shifting requirements for raw materials.

To wrap it up, can you pick a favourite metal? What do you find most exciting?

I like looking at them all! They all have different dynamics when it comes to the energy transition and the EV and BESS market. Intrinsically, the one that is fundamental to all of this is lithium. As I said at the start, lithium is used in every single one of those Li-ion batteries and that’s a market that has grown massively.

By the time we get to 2040, that market is going to be 5Mt, which is more than the current nickel market, an established commodity.

We’ve seen the market grow from a very niche sector to the size of an established commodity. Along the way, we’ve seen projects emerge in various countries, different technologies being used, and even financial instruments, hedging, and futures contracts around lithium.

So, this rapid development of a niche or speciality commodity is quite exciting to be involved in.

Write to Amy Rotman at Mining.com.au
