text:
Houston-returned entrepreneur sees opportunities as Nigerian banks, telecom operators and major businesses reassess long-term energy costs.

HOUSTON, TX, UNITED STATES, November 3, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Nigeria’s longstanding electricity challenges may be creating one of the country’s most significant emerging private-sector investment opportunities as businesses increasingly evaluate solar generation, battery storage and independent power systems against the rising cost of conventional energy.

That is the outlook of Hakim Ali, an American-born Nigerian entrepreneur who relocated from Houston, Texas, to pursue opportunities in Nigeria’s renewable-energy and electric mobility industries.

Ali, a Director of Abuja-based Sora Green Energy Projects Limited, believes the next major shift in Nigeria’s renewable-energy market may come not only from households adopting solar power, but from banks, telecommunications operators, hospitals, hotels and other institutions reconsidering how they finance and manage electricity over the long term.

From Houston to Nigeria’s Energy Opportunity

Ali’s decision to relocate from the United States reflected his belief that Nigeria’s large population, expanding commercial requirements and persistent electricity challenges created opportunities for businesses capable of providing practical energy solutions.

However, entering the market required patience.

Customers unfamiliar with newer technologies often needed education about equipment reliability, battery performance, maintenance requirements and the economics of replacing conventional energy systems.

Ali believes this initial hesitation is gradually giving way to a more financially focused discussion.

For many Nigerian businesses, electricity is not simply a utility expense. It is an operating requirement that can involve generators, fuel purchases, equipment maintenance and the financial consequences of service interruptions.

He believes these recurring costs are encouraging more organizations to examine whether alternative energy systems can offer greater predictability over time.

Why Institutional Buyers Could Transform Solar Adoption

Ali sees particularly significant opportunities among institutions with substantial and recurring electricity requirements.

Banks operating multiple branches, telecommunications companies maintaining mobile network infrastructure, hospitals requiring dependable electricity and hotels serving customers around the clock all face different versions of the same challenge: maintaining reliable power while controlling operating expenses.

For these organizations, Ali believes the financial case for solar energy should be evaluated over five- to ten-year periods rather than solely through initial installation costs.

Such assessments can include electricity consumption, generator fuel expenditure, maintenance, financing, battery replacement, equipment lifespan and the cost of power interruptions.

Properly designed solar and battery-storage systems may offer financial advantages where the total cost of ownership compares favorably with existing arrangements.

The economics are not identical for every institution, and system design, financing terms and operating requirements remain important considerations.

Nevertheless, Ali believes institutional demand could become a significant driver of Nigeria’s renewable-energy market as more businesses incorporate long-term electricity costs into capital investment decisions.

Solar Energy and Electric Mobility Are Becoming Connected Markets

Sora Green’s operations illustrate another development Ali considers important: the growing relationship between renewable-energy infrastructure and electric transportation.

Solar energy remains the company’s original and principal business, providing residential and commercial electricity-generation and storage solutions.

The company has expanded into electric vehicle distribution, charging infrastructure and related automotive services.

According to management, Sora Green has delivered more than 300 electric vehicles since late 2024, including models from Hongqi, Xiaomi and Avatr, alongside its relationship with Chinese automotive manufacturer FAW.

Ali believes this combination of energy and transportation services reflects the practical requirements of Nigeria’s emerging electric mobility market.

Electric vehicles require dependable charging, while solar generation and battery storage can provide alternative electricity sources where grid supply is inconsistent.

Rather than treating the two industries as separate opportunities, Sora Green is developing services intended to address them together.

Off-Grid Charging Infrastructure in Abuja

The company’s planned electric vehicle charging facility in Maitama, Abuja, provides a practical example of this integrated approach.

Designed to operate independently of Nigeria’s national electricity grid, the facility is expected to combine more than one megawatt of solar generation capacity with over 1.3 megawatt-hours of battery storage.

Initial plans include four 120-kilowatt DC fast chargers, with the company also considering a future increase in charging capacity.

The project is intended to serve the wider electric vehicle market, including motorists who purchased vehicles from other distributors.

The facility is not yet operational, with an opening targeted for early 2027.

For Ali, the development illustrates how private investment in renewable-energy infrastructure may help address limitations that would otherwise slow electric vehicle adoption.

Financing and Commercial Partnerships

Ali believes access to financing will be important to the wider adoption of electric mobility and renewable-energy technology.

Sora Green reports an existing agreement with Jaiz Bank that provides financing facilities for eligible customers purchasing vehicles through the company.

According to management, Jaiz Bank has also purchased vehicles from Sora Green.

The company has additionally supplied vehicles to Nigeria’s Rural Electrification Agency.

These activities reflect the development of commercial relationships alongside the company’s energy and mobility operations.

Ali believes similar attention to financing and long-term operating economics will be important as institutional customers consider larger renewable-energy investments.

A Long-Term Opportunity Beyond Equipment Sales

Ali’s outlook extends beyond the immediate sale of solar panels, batteries or electric vehicles.

He believes Nigeria’s energy market may increasingly reward companies capable of delivering integrated solutions that combine equipment, technical support, maintenance, financing access and dependable long-term performance.

The transition is unlikely to happen immediately.

High initial costs, financing constraints, technical requirements and customer uncertainty remain important barriers.

Nevertheless, Ali believes the country’s energy challenges are creating incentives for businesses to reconsider conventional approaches to electricity supply.

For institutions facing substantial recurring energy expenditure, the decision to invest in alternative power infrastructure may increasingly become a question of financial planning rather than environmental preference alone.

Ali sees this as a potentially important shift in Nigeria’s energy economy: from treating electricity shortages primarily as an operating problem to evaluating dependable energy infrastructure as a long-term commercial investment.

About Sora Green Energy Projects Limited

Sora Green Energy Projects Limited is an Abuja-based renewable-energy and electric mobility company providing residential and commercial solar-energy solutions, electric vehicle distribution, charging infrastructure and automotive support services.

name: Clean Energy
title: Pulling together: A European partnership model for decarbonisation
description:
How to improve the EU’s offer The EU’s regulatory know-how can be most useful, for example, where pollution and heat are worst.
Another element could be the establishment of a green technology licensing mechanism within the UNFCCC Green Climate Fund, with appropriate financing.
Yet even big member states such as Germany cannot build strong enough partnerships to counter China’s dominance alone.
Such coordinators could sometimes be from member states with historical links, but more often it would be useful to avoid the tensions that might exist and have more “neutral” EU member states take the lead.
The European Climate Foundation cannot be held responsible for any use which may be made of the information contained or expressed therein.
text:
Summary

Europe’s transition to a green economy is going through a geopolitical blizzard. To cut through the adverse conditions and build a thriving clean economy, the EU should make a step change and work with a team of countries that are committed to decarbonisation, and that can also supply clean materials, components and tech to Europe.

The EU should start this sharper push with a few like-minded partners that have what it lacks. To entice them to become part of the team, Europeans should make them competitive offers. They have to beat rival bids using clear goals, money, technology and skills. The bloc has much to bring: packages tailored to each country’s interests, guarantees, green markets and know-how, among others.

There will be hurdles, to be sure. Speed, capital and coordination are familiar obstacles, but they can be overcome. Clear them, and a “green team” will deliver results on EU competitiveness, security and sustainability.

A relay to the rescue

In the winter of 1925, 20 dog sled teams ran a 674-mile relay through an Arctic blizzard to bring medicine to the town of Nome, in Alaska. Nome faced a deadly diphtheria outbreak with no way to get antitoxin serum through the sub-zero winter freeze. Officials judged that sled dogs offered the only chance of delivering the serum in time, but no single team could make the journey alone, so the authorities split the route into stages and passed the serum from team to team. That relay saved the residents of Nome.

The EU’s green transition also runs through a geopolitical blizzard, a period of rupture. America has broken with Europe and moved from being the guarantor of Western security and prosperity to a disruptor that rips up the rulebook, and weaponises all of its assets. China exploits the uncertainty, hyper-connectedness and asymmetric dependencies of this new moment to press ahead with its economic strategy and entrench its dominance of clean-technology supply chains and manufacturing. This is the storm that Europe needs to navigate to make it through to a planet that stays safe to live on, and a Europe that is stronger for helping to keep it so. But the bloc cannot make the journey alone. What it can do is build a “green relay” of countries that will move everyone towards a sustainable future: partners that can carry a stretch of the route, supplying the clean materials, components and tech that Europe lacks while decarbonising themselves.

The stakes are high. The EU will lose markets, jobs and investment if it simply accepts rivals’ monopoly of clean tech supply chains as the world decarbonises. Its security is at stake too, as the heat, floods and storms of a warming climate strain its infrastructure and energy systems. The bloc needs a stronger partner network to widen its options, and choosing where it sources materials and technology is how it keeps its agency over its green transition.

Europe can build that relay by turning its market access, finance, technology and skills into offers that partners find hard to resist. That would help underpin its own green transition and show other major powers that global decarbonisation is achievable despite the breakdown of global consensus on its necessity. This paper shows how the EU can pick its team in such a qualitative leap. We outline what Europe needs and from whom, lessons from other powers that are building their own teams, and eight ways to improve the EU’s offer. In the simple terms of Trumpian times, this paper lays out what the EU can put on the table to sign up its relay partners, and how to make sure they say yes.

How to choose relay partners

Over 90% of rare earth magnets, used in wind energy, are made in China, as are around 95% of heat pump compressors. This means that Europeans cannot be self-sufficient in delivering the green transition. The problem is not confined to these two sectors. In other areas critical for decarbonisation—for example, grid infrastructure, electric vehicle manufacturing, or battery development more broadly—the EU’s dependence is also high. That means the bloc will need partners to advance these areas and to decarbonise heavy industry such as cement, iron and steel. Think of a sled team: each dog can pull hard alone, but the sled moves only when the harnesses pull together.

Choosing the right partners is a key part of building a green relay team. The EU has a great many possible ones to consider. Just for its top five critical mineral imports in 2024—cobalt, copper, graphite, lithium and nickel—the EU traded with 16 different supplier countries, according to authors’ analysis of data from the World Integrated Trade Solution and UN Comtrade. Add components and engineered materials, and the list of possible suppliers becomes unwieldy. The EU can have many partners, but it needs to assemble a smaller group of priority countries to carry its green transition the full distance. The best relay partners will be global players that will repay investment in the relationship with predictable supplies for the EU’s green transition and have their own climate ambitions.

Research from Catalyse Europe and Ember, as well as earlier ECFR work, points to three areas where the EU needs reliable suppliers if it is to keep its choices open for its own transition:

critical raw materials for clean tech;

engineered materials such as green iron and steel; and,

components for key clean tech sectors.

China is at or near the top of the list for all three elements. However, the sheer scale of its supply chain dominance in the clean tech sector, its control of the production of the materials that feed it, and the centrality of this dominance to its long-term economic model, mean that dependence on China hands it more power to coerce the EU. Rather, the EU’s goal should be to diversify away from single-country dependency by investing in the partnerships that can supply it the materials it needs. Several major suppliers of the EU have committed to cutting their own emissions, so they could be reliable relay partners. Brazil, Canada, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and South Africa supply raw materials, including the iron ore and other minerals the EU needs for engineering materials. Indonesia, Morocco and Turkey offer other raw materials and manufacturing. Japan, South Korea and, to a lesser extent, India supply components.

Identifying sources of supply is only a part of the picture. The bigger challenge for the EU is winning partners over in a competitive world. Incomes and priorities vary across countries, so the EU will need distinct offers for low- and middle-income economies in the “global south” and for richer OECD countries. The EU is of course not starting from zero here. It already has laws and plans to secure its green industrial supplies, including the Net-Zero Industry Act, the European Critical Raw Materials Act, the Resource EU Action Plan and the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act. Laws alone will not secure supplies, so strengthening international partnerships is the third pillar of the EU economic security strategy. The EU has 16 bilateral mineral partnerships and has developed a joint action plan with the US to make critical mineral supply chains more resilient.

Learn from rival teams: Clear goals, serious money and shared tech

The EU is far from the only team on the course, and some rival teams are already well on the way. China’s approach is the biggest in investment and market access, the longest-running and the most systematic. But many other governments now offer resource-rich countries partnerships on critical minerals and clean-tech supply chains, because they too want to avoid relying on China alone. Japan has spent over 15 years making its supply chains more resilient, using state-backed market commitments and financing and strategic research and innovation cooperation. Other OECD countries also use the state more actively. America is investing directly in public-private partnerships. So the EU’s offer to relay partners has to be competitive. Five lessons from these rivals follow, each showing one way the EU can sharpen its offer.

Taken together, these lessons show that partners are won with clear public goals, substantial funding and shared technology. They can guide the EU, but the bloc will have to draw up its own approach to attracting relay partners, built on the assets it brings to each relationship.

How the EU can attract relay partners

As the world’s largest trading area and home to some of its wealthiest countries, the EU has plenty to put on the table, and often already uses the same approaches as the countries described in the previous section. The challenge is to bring its tools together and refine them into an offer that attracts partners. The International Energy Agency (IEA) said this summer that resilient, diversified supply chains need a coordinated package of policies. This package must tackle investment risk, market structure and gaps in technology and know-how, with incentives for both supply-side and demand-side development. The eight approaches below show what concrete steps the EU can take to create a competitive package.

1. Offer kits with tailored extras for each partner

The EU’s existing agreements are wide in scope but need strengthening in what they offer each partner. Economic development, including poverty reduction, matters to many partners, and the EU and its member states already have broad cooperation agreements with both resource-rich developing countries and wealthy OECD countries. However, these agreements could better reflect individual countries’ interests, which would increase their appeal.

How to improve the EU’s offer

EU green-industry and supply-chain offers should widen existing agreements to cover entire supply and industrial ecosystems and top them up with measures that address each partner’s domestic agenda.

Such measures, for example, should include biobased products and the circular economy for Brazil. Its decision-makers are keen to discuss how the EU can adapt existing EU rules, such as the taxonomy that classifies sustainable investments, and those on deforestation and biofuels. The EU should also cover social aspects, such as funding for a just transition in the Just Energy Transition Partnership (JETP) with South Africa.

China is one of those players whose offer is broad, spanning infrastructure, finance, trade and investment, especially to Africa. But breadth has not always translated into popularity. Complaints about debt traps, few local jobs, opaque contracts, harm to the environment and poor working conditions in Chinese companies have fuelled unease in some partner countries. Many governments would like to reduce dependency on China without ending cooperation altogether. That does not mean they want to be drawn into a contest between the West and China. Rather than asking partners to choose sides, the EU should present its offer as a way of expanding their room for manoeuvre. And while European policymakers should be open about their own interests, they should avoid creating the impression that engagement is driven solely by a desire to secure access to natural resources.

2. Line up like-minded partners first

Trade agreements are one of the EU’s main tools for building partnerships, but so far they have not been shown to secure the critical minerals it needs. Many of the EU’s trade agreements now include sustainability chapters and, more recently, provisions on access to critical minerals. The Mercosur agreement is such an example. By making sustainability commitments and adherence to the Paris climate agreement a core part of the deal, the EU has tied market access to environmental goals. Yet the European Court of Auditors found in 2026 that the commission cannot show that such deals have been effective in raising the EU’s supply of critical raw materials. The EU must therefore either implement its existing deals more effectively or negotiate new ones.

The EU’s newest trade tool shows promise, but so far it lacks the money and speed to matter. The Clean Trade and Investment Partnership (CTIP) is a new type of deal in which partners get easier trade and investment in return for climate commitments. The first, with South Africa, was signed in November 2025.

That is too slow, and one partner is too few. The EU needs to act faster in order to meet its climate goals before the damage to the environment becomes irreversible. The easiest places to widen the net are to make such agreements with like-minded OECD countries and neighbouring countries.

How to improve the EU’s offer

Donald Trump’s presidency has drawn other OECD members closer to the EU’s view that a rules-based order and green transitions matter. The EU can relatively easily deepen cooperation with these like-minded countries, which are at a similar stage of economic development. Japan and South Korea, for example, have the manufacturing and capital to help build clean-tech supply chains, while Canada and Australia have the raw materials to feed them. In her State of the Union address in September 2026, Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, even floated “associate membership” for Canada. The EU and Canada then held a summit on October 29th–30th, the outcome of which envisages far-reaching cooperation within a new Canada-EU Alliance for the Future. Follow-up has included an investment agreement, signed by the European Investment Bank and Canada, focused on critical minerals.

The EU should also use association agreements with neighbouring countries to secure supply chains for the green transition close to home. Neighbours are an obvious place to start, because companies there are often closely interlinked in European supply chains. The EU already has agreements with North African and Middle Eastern countries, for example, which largely eliminated tariffs on all industrial goods. Cooperation on energy and climate is playing a growing role in these agreements. With Morocco, the EU has had a green partnership since 2022, supported by the Global Gateway initiative. The partnership could go further by supporting low-carbon fertiliser production with renewable energy. Similarly, the EU could work with other countries as it does with Egypt, where cooperation on electricity grids, green hydrogen and renewable energy can serve climate goals for both sides.

3. Clear the course for clean markets, and guard them judiciously

Access to the EU’s internal market of 450 million people is its biggest draw for partners to supply its green transition, but the bloc’s measures to protect European industry deter them. Restrictions such as its carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM), which puts a carbon price on imports such as steel and cement, and deforestation rules, which bar imports of soy, beef and similar goods from recently cleared land, could push suppliers away. More friction is on its way, from “Made in Europe” criteria in forthcoming laws, which would require EU-made content in government buying. The Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed in March 2026, would also require European-made content in publicly funded purchases of goods such as steel and solar panels. Revised public-procurement rules would do likewise. Such measures are sometimes necessary to protect European clean-tech firms from unfair competition, especially from China, but good relations with partner countries should be a more significant part of the equation.

How to improve the EU’s offer

By continuing its green transition, the EU can create markets that serve partners’ companies as well as European ones. One way to do this is to set up “lead markets”, where early demand lets new technologies scale up and cut costs. Carbon pricing, for example, makes polluting products dearer and so draws buyers to clean ones. Criteria in public procurement (as currently discussed) and quotas for certain products can do the same. That leaves room for both “Made in Europe” products and close cooperation with trusted partners.

Yet building lead markets that partners can use means the EU must stop protecting every domestic company and accept that “creative destruction” should be part of industrial development. It should limit trade protection to areas where it is truly necessary and where European firms have a good chance of winning market share on a level playing field. It should not use trade barriers to prop up firms with little hope of competing in the long run.

4. Secure the harnesses by guaranteeing returns on investments

To draw investors into new supply chains for the green transition, the EU should guarantee them a market. Its members can promise to take what partners produce. When Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine set off an energy crisis, the EU created a joint platform for buying liquefied natural gas. Member states already do this on a smaller scale. Germany and the Netherlands do it for low-carbon hydrogen. Partners outside Europe need the same assurance before they commit to new capacity. The Team Europe initiative on green iron in Brazil, a Global Gateway project that pairs cheap Brazilian hydrogen with Vale’s iron ore to make green steel in the EU, shows scope for an offtake agreement. Southern Africa, centred on South Africa, also has great potential. Namibia shows this potential in practice, as it already has an offtake agreement for green iron with a German company.

The commission is now extending joint purchasing to critical raw materials. The EU Energy and Raw Materials Platform, which matches buyers with suppliers, was launched in July 2025, but the commission wants to go further, with a public body that buys and stockpiles critical raw materials itself. It has advocated a European Critical Raw Materials Centre, like Japan’s state agency that finances overseas mining and stockpiles metals, the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security (JOGMEC). Von der Leyen’s State of the Union speech also proposed a European Corporation on Critical Raw Materials. The idea is to add public joint purchasing and stockpiling to the private matchmaking that the Raw Materials Mechanism already does. A public buyer of this kind would give investors in partner countries the demand guarantee they need.

How to improve the EU’s offer

Member states are negotiating the funding for these investments in the Council of the EU, but the talks are tangled up in a wider dispute over the next EU budget. They should settle the funding quickly and get public joint purchasing and stockpiling in place.

The EU must also fund the purchasing and stockpiling. The quickest route is to write them into the Competitiveness Fund, which the Council and the European Parliament are now negotiating. The European Parliament’s proposal for a European Critical Raw Materials Fund, with a €2bn budget, is a step in the right direction. Failing that, the bloc could turn to the Industrial Decarbonisation Bank or a new resilience charge on imports from dominant producers such as China.

Suppliers outside China often struggle to compete on price. National governments and the EU should therefore guarantee minimum prices for trusted suppliers, as advocated by the IEA, and use regulation to promote diversification away from China, including in the processing and refining of minerals. MP Materials in the United States and Nouveau Monde Graphite in Canada show how such support can work. The US government guarantees MP Materials a minimum price of $110 a kg for neodymium and praseodymium, two rare earths used in magnets, for 10 years, to help its mine turn a profit. Coordinated public procurement can also create markets in other areas, such as low-carbon iron and ammonia.

5. Pay for the run with carbon markets and guarantees

The EU and its member states together are the world’s biggest development donor, but the need is far larger than their budgets and risk further cuts, which would weaken the EU’s hand with partners. The EU could instead go further with guarantees that reduce risks for investors and carbon credits that pay partners for cutting emissions.

The EU’s financial offer is already broad, spanning grants, guarantees and loans from both Brussels and member states. The bloc pays directly for infrastructure, such as electricity grids and railways. It also offers guarantees, through the European Fund for Sustainable Development Plus (EFSD+), that shield private investors from some of the risk. France and Germany add their own state development banks, AFD and KfW. The EU’s financing is visible in two flagship deals. The first is the JETP with South Africa, where the EU, together with France and Germany, has made €3bn available since 2022, though much remains unspent. The second is the EU-Mercosur agreement, where the EU has pledged €1.8bn to Global Gateway projects in the countries concerned, including for green transitions.

Yet these sums are small amounts in relation to what is needed. The OECD and the IEA estimate that low-carbon steel and cement alone need more than €300bn of investment in emerging and developing economies to reach net zero by 2050. India’s bill is larger still: the think-tank Council on Energy, Environment and Water says net-zero steel and cement will require $627bn (about €560bn) of investment, much of which needs backing from international partners, including through guarantees and subsidised loans. Indonesia and Vietnam would need $122bn and $120bn respectively, according to analysis by the World Bank.

How to improve the EU’s offer

The EU should prioritise adequate funding in the next Global Europe Instrument, now under negotiation as part of the next seven-year EU budget. But it can also stretch its funds by doing more to derisk private investments. Green guarantees, which promise to cover an investor’s losses if a project fails, are one promising way of reducing the risks of investing in high-risk markets. Donor countries and multilateral development banks can, for example, offer guarantees against exchange rate risk. They can also provide first-loss guarantees, which take the first hit if a project fails, to companies that are beginning to use new technologies, such as producing steel using hydrogen. Germany and Nigeria already do this through the Green Guarantees Group, a platform launched in 2024 that brings together governments, guarantee providers and investors to scale up guarantees for emerging economies. The EU as a whole should do more of this. In the next seven-year budget, the EU should also expand the EFSD+ programme while improving coordination with European export credit agencies, state-backed bodies that insure and finance exports and can also help reduce investment risks.

The bloc already has an instrument to use to this effect. The European Investment Bank (EIB) is the EU’s natural lender for the risks that private investors shun, and EIB Global, its arm for projects outside the EU, could take first-loss risk on green projects in partner countries. It already funds renewable projects, but mostly safer ones. For example, with Germany’s KfW it provides up to €216m for renewable hydrogen projects in Chile. The recent rise in its gearing ratio—the cap on lending relative to its capital—gives it more room to lend, though not necessarily to take more risk. Member states have good reason to increase the EIB’s capital, which would give it a bigger cushion against losses on riskier projects. In addition, better coordination between the EIB, Global Europe and financing from member states is needed. A pilot project with a few partner countries could bring together the EIB, the commission and the biggest national development banks in closer coordination of activities.

International carbon credits could be another source of finance, with EU buyers paying partners for cutting emissions. The EU has decided to use up to 5% of 1990 EU net emissions of “high-quality” international credits under Article 6 of the Paris climate agreement from 2036 to 2040, in order to reach its 2040 climate target. A pilot will run from 2031 to 2035. This mechanism will create billions in euro transfers to other countries that cut their emissions, including in carbon-intensive industries.

Credits could become a real source of finance for partners, but only if the EU settles who buys them, how, and on what terms. First, it is unclear whether member states share the commission’s view that purchases of such credits should be coordinated at EU level. Second, the EU must choose between project-based methods, like Japan’s Joint Crediting Mechanism, and broader agreements with countries that have, for example, a high enough carbon price. Either way, international credits could help the EU’s resilience and its supply of low-carbon inputs, though in different ways. The catch is that partners may hold off on their own cuts until credits from the EU start paying them.

6. Build stronger teams through joint research ties and training

Partner countries aim to build their own research and industrial know-how, not only buy European technology. The EU’s main offer so far is access to Horizon Europe, its research and innovation programme, which lets partners’ researchers and firms compete for grants on the same terms as European ones. Partners value it. South Africa was eager to include such participation in the recent CTIP. But other partners could also gain from similar offers. The EU should expand who it offers cooperation on research and other know-how based on partners’ long-term economic and political value, not only for their science today.

How to improve the EU’s offer

In addition to Horizon Europe access, which is mainly a chance to compete for grants, the EU should learn from China and offer more help to build long-term research and innovation ecosystems in partner countries.

Such ecosystems should include establishing joint research institutes in areas important for green transitions and adding value to natural resources. The EU and its member states could support European institutes that establish such joint ventures. Brazil and South Africa are natural places to host the first institutes, since both already have deep research ties with the EU and active Team Europe projects. The EU could also do more to build institutional capacity, improve research infrastructure and subsidise test beds for new products.

Yet talks on the next seven-year budget are already shaping how Horizon Europe and the new Competitiveness Fund will work, and the proposals so far would shrink Horizon Europe and limit cross-border research collaboration. Member states will need to step up and coordinate bilateral support for green innovation ecosystems in partner countries if there is no agreement for sufficient action at the EU level.

European private companies could also do more to build skills in partner countries, as Theophilus Acheampong has suggested for Africa in another ECFR publication. If companies do too little themselves, EU policymakers could impose conditions on financial support and derisking tools and sometimes give grants to companies and research institutes that invest in joint innovation and skills development.

7. Share your knowledge of the trail

The EU’s most underused offer may be its know-how in creating regulation: how to write, enforce and finance green rules. Partners that want to cut emissions need working institutions and sound regulation, and the EU has decades of experience in building both. The bloc has created a comprehensive legislative framework and administrative capacity for environmental protection and climate transitions. It has similar experience in the internal market and innovation policy. Sharing this experience and supporting institutional capacity in partner countries is an important part of what the EU can offer.

How to improve the EU’s offer

The EU’s regulatory know-how can be most useful, for example, where pollution and heat are worst. European countries can share their experience of tackling air pollution and help partners do the same in emerging markets with poor air quality, such as India. The same is true for other green policy areas, such as water efficiency and cooling buildings in India and Indonesia. In environmental monitoring, the EU’s Copernicus Earth-observation programme is a major asset, for example in work with Brazil. More generally, partner countries are looking for support in improving cybersecurity and managing the rapid development of artificial intelligence.

Knowing how to write rules only pays off if they can be enforced, and enforcement needs money and people, so the EU should offer partners help with financing them, setting up enforcement infrastructure and training personnel. For example, the EU Task Force for International Carbon Pricing and Markets Diplomacy, set up in 2024, works with more than 40 partner countries to help them adopt carbon pricing and build carbon markets. However, it does not address how Europeans can help develop the infrastructure, access to finance, intellectual property rights and personnel skills necessary for industrial decarbonisation. The EU could do this through “twinning” with government agencies in member states. Twinning, which pairs institutions in EU member states with counterparts in candidate countries through staff exchanges and joint seminars, has worked well in Europe. But programmes that support this kind of cooperation with countries in other parts of the world are still far too limited. For example, as noted by the Observer Research Foundation, many partner countries lack mature systems for carbon accounting and the monitoring, reporting and verification of emissions needed to comply with CBAM. The EU can and should support the development of such systems through assistance to both authorities and companies in partner countries, for example with India.

The need for support is particularly strong for small and medium enterprises that struggle to meet CBAM and deforestation rules. India, for example, has many small steel companies, as do Brazil and Indonesia. Priority should go to scaling technical assistance for smaller companies and co-developing digital tools with partner-country authorities.

8. Run as a pack with coalitions and frameworks

“Coalitions of the willing” now drive much of global green industrial policy, but the EU as such is largely absent from them even if some member states play important roles. Several such groups have appeared in recent years for critical minerals and low-carbon industry, as cooperation through the UN climate convention (UNFCCC) has grown harder because US–China rivalry is spilling into climate talks. Examples include the Minerals Security Partnership, a 2022 US-led effort to diversify critical-minerals supply chains and, more recently, the Forum on Resource Geostrategic Engagement, a US-backed trade and investment coalition launched in 2026 that succeeds the Minerals Security Partnership. The EU should join the coalitions that are gaining momentum, or lead new ones, rather than watch from the sidelines.

The emergence of these coalitions is partly because countries want more say and to see more action in green industrial transitions. Potential partner countries already play prominent roles in coalitions of the willing, for example Canada, Indonesia, South Korea and Turkey in the Climate Club. Many developing countries also call for better technology cooperation. India pressed hard for this at COP30 in Brazil last year. Brazil, Indonesia and South Africa also signed the Belém Declaration on Global Green Industrialisation, a COP30 framework for industrial decarbonisation, alongside EU member states, Australia, South Korea, industry and academia, urging more action and cooperation.

How to improve the EU’s offer

The EU should take a more active part in coalitions and minilateral groups, because they can accelerate the climate transition. Creating demand for low-carbon products in smaller “clubs” is one way to speed up industrial decarbonisation, as advocated in the IEA Breakthrough Agenda 2026 report on iron and steel. The IEA also recommends such actions in its recent report, for example on fertilisers. Improving recycling of critical minerals can be another important area for international cooperation.

The EU can widen coalitions through partners that carry weight in other regions. Brazil, South Africa and India have legitimacy in the global south and are not burdened by a history of being colonial powers. The EU could build on this by pursuing “triangular” cooperation with middle powers and global south states, such as sustainable mining with Brazil and African countries.

Coalitions can also be linked to the UN system. The EU could play a key role in negotiating a Global Green Industrialisation Agenda at COP31 in Antalya. Turkey wants the agenda to be prominent there too. Together with key partners such as Brazil, Canada, India, Japan and South Africa, the EU can work for stronger links between UN institutions and coalitions of the willing.

The EU and its member states should also help put into practice what these coalitions agree. For example, they could increase their contributions to the industry decarbonisation programme of the Climate Investment Funds, and press multilateral development banks to prioritise low-carbon industry. Another element could be the establishment of a green technology licensing mechanism within the UNFCCC Green Climate Fund, with appropriate financing. They can also show commitment with more funding for the UN Industrial Development Organization, the UN Environment Programme and the Climate Technology Centre.

Three hurdles on the route: Speed, capital and coordination

To complete the run with its relay partners, the EU faces three cross-cutting challenges.

The first challenge is speed. The turnaround times at all levels, from finance to legislation to permitting, are too slow to compete with China, the Gulf states and others. The EU is capable of working faster. When it came to vaccine procurement in tackling the covid-19 pandemic, or the energy crisis starting in 2021, the EU mobilised its machinery quickly. To attract partners also focused on their own transition, the EU should recategorise this challenge as urgent. Von der Leyen’s 2026 State of the Union speech, which framed climate change along with artificial intelligence as the two “tipping points of our time”, was an important change of tone.

The second challenge is mobilising sufficient capital to put behind these partnerships. The European Central Bank estimates that investment equivalent to 2.7–3.7% of EU GDP will be needed every year from 2026 to 2030 in order to shift from carbon-intensive to carbon-free technologies. This is a very tall order in the current geopolitical environment. Security, a national competence, now tops the priority list of policymakers, given the war in Ukraine and more frequent threats within the EU. Rising living costs, volatile energy prices and food supply worries leave every EU government focused on showing results on jobs and poverty. Germany leads a backlash against the commission’s plan to lift the next seven-year budget to €2trn. This makes an increase in EU spending seem unlikely, but framing the transition as urgent for economic and security reasons can help policymakers earmark sufficient amounts for it. Without a bigger budget, other tools include more EIB lending, using emissions trading revenue for external relations, and co-financing joint procurement with member states.

The final cross-cutting challenge is the need to improve internal EU coordination in engagement with third countries. Partner countries often find the EU confusing. Big member states such as Germany and France often have a more visible presence than the EU, with many national initiatives on resilient supply chains and low-carbon transformations of industry in parallel to EU-level action. For example, as noted in one interview for this paper, India has signed over 30 memoranda of understanding on climate and clean energy with 14 individual EU member states and Britain. In parallel, India has critical-minerals agreements with Germany and France regarding joint exploration, processing technology and research on rare-earth recycling, among others. This diversity can sometimes help the EU, but fragmentation more often lets partners play one part of the EU against another and slows EU action. Brazil is a case in point. European countries often compete with each other there for contracts, which weakens the EU’s hand. Contacts in Brazil single out Germany, Spain and Britain as the European partners that help them move into higher-value production, but these countries do not coordinate their efforts.[1]

Team Europe, the EU’s framing of national governments and EU institutions working in concert, still lacks a clear strategy, so member states often act in an uncoordinated way. Yet even big member states such as Germany cannot build strong enough partnerships to counter China’s dominance alone. This makes coordination all the more important. One option, as in formal climate negotiations, is to name coordinators from different member states to approach different key countries—not to replace bilateral contacts but to improve synergies and information flow. Such coordinators could sometimes be from member states with historical links, but more often it would be useful to avoid the tensions that might exist and have more “neutral” EU member states take the lead.

An alternative, or complementary, route comes from the German Institute of Development and Sustainability, which proposes improving dialogue among member states and forming more issue-specific, informal groups to strengthen cooperation.

The two methods can be combined. Either way, the EU should add staff for climate and economic security diplomacy in Brussels and at its delegations, and sharpen coordination at the core of the commission, working closely with the European External Action Service. Above all, leaders must feel political urgency and accept that no single member state can meet these challenges alone.

A relay can carry the transition

There is a clear geoeconomic and geopolitical case for global partnerships around the green transition. Yet the EU does not signal that decarbonisation is central to its interests in the way that it approaches relationships with partner countries. Like the sled teams that carried the serum to Nome, the EU must mobilise around this goal to ensure that the run is completed.

A relay team can deliver competitiveness, security and decarbonisation to Europeans and beyond, so the EU must prioritise building its relay team around the partners this paper identifies. In all these partnerships, it should go in with scale and speed, and use every tool this paper sets out, from tailored offers and green markets to guarantees, research and training, regulatory know-how and coalitions. With so many immediate crises and tensions in today’s geopolitics, too few leaders are willing to speak out in favour of action to mitigate the climate crisis, which is the most consequential for the world of tomorrow. The beauty of a relay partnership approach for the EU is that it will speak for itself, achieving results on security and prosperity, and slowing climate breakdown.

Carla Moll’s and Marissa Gillwald’s expert management of the research project leading up to it has been invaluable. Kat Fytatzi’s brilliant editing and creative imagery have really brought the argument to life.

About the authors

Susi Dennison is a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations and director of ECFR’s European Power programme. Her topics of focus include strategy, politics and cohesion in European foreign policy; climate and energy; migration; and the toolkit for Europe as a global actor.

He has been involved in EU policymaking and analysis since the 1980s, including as deputy state secretary at the Swedish Ministry for the Environment and as a political adviser to the foreign minister.

text:
CARROLLTON, Texas, Nov. 03, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- ACT-ion Battery Technologies, Inc. (“ACT-ion”), an innovator in battery material manufacturing, today celebrated the grand opening of its pilot plant at 1200 Tappan Circle in Carrollton, Texas. The facility is now fully commissioned and ready to produce cathode active materials (CAM) in the United States using ACT-ion’s proprietary ACT-ivate™ process, a clean, high-throughput manufacturing method developed to reduce the cost, environmental impact, and production time of next-generation battery components.

CAM is the fine black powder at the heart of every lithium-ion battery. It forms the cathode, the electrode that largely determines a battery’s energy, power, lifespan, and cost. CAM is also the single biggest contributor to a battery cell’s cost, accounting for about 50 percent of cell production costs, depending on battery chemistry, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).

Yet production of this critical material is highly concentrated abroad. In 2025, about 85 percent of the world’s CAM used in electric car batteries was produced offshore, according to the IEA. That leaves U.S. battery makers, automakers, and grid-storage developers dependent on foreign supply for a material essential to electric vehicles, energy storage, and consumer electronics.

ACT-ion’s Carrollton plant is built to change that. By producing CAM here in the United States, ACT-ion is reducing reliance on offshore materials and strengthening the domestic supply chain for critical battery materials, so batteries powering vehicles, businesses, and homes can be built with American-made components.

“Officially opening our doors today is proof that the vision we shared a year ago is now reality,” noted Mark McGough, CEO of ACT-ion. “This facility increases our capacity 10 times, to 20 tons per annum, making it the largest all-American phosphate-based CAM producer in the USA.”

“One of the most powerful advantages of our ACT-ivate technology is its unprecedented feedstock flexibility,” explained Jin Lim, Founder and CTO of ACT-ion. “We incorporated lower-cost domestic inputs like industrial-grade chemicals and recycled black mass, allowing us to reduce costs while delivering the high-quality materials the market demands.“

Scaling the ACT-ivate process is central to that milestone. The continuous platform is designed to lower costs and shrink environmental impact by using less energy and water and eliminating harmful byproducts, while delivering higher throughput and a more streamlined manufacturing flow than traditional methods. ACT-ion’s innovation earned the prestigious R&D 100 Award in 2024.

The process is also “chemistry-agnostic.” While many manufacturers are locked into specific battery chemistries, ACT-ion has demonstrated the ACT-ivate process across a range of materials, including cost-effective lithium iron phosphate (LFP) and high-performance nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM), allowing the company to adapt to market trends and serve a broader customer base. The company is also applying the technology to next-generation materials such as lithium manganese iron phosphate (LFMP) and sodium-ion battery materials.

The U.S. Department of Energy’s Advanced Materials & Manufacturing Technologies Office (AMMTO) and Vehicle Technologies Office (VTO) continue to support the pilot plant scale-up.

text:
As electric vehicles (EV) drive up electricity demand, charging habits are becoming central to power grid planning. When left unmanaged, home charging tends to bundle together, dangerously intensifying evening peak hours. Meanwhile, commercial fast-charging hubs drop sudden, massive demands onto the grid, increasing equipment wear and upgrade costs. Consequently, utilities are shifting managed charging off-peak and integrating EV forecasts into distribution planning, says GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform.

GlobalData’s latest report, “Strategic Intelligence: Electric Vehicles in Power (2026)” reveals that public direct current (DC) fast charging is replacing slower Level 2 AC charging as the primary investment focus. By delivering substantial energy during short stops, DC hubs support long-distance travel, commercial fleets, and high-utilization vehicles, drastically improving site economics and serving more drivers.

Fast-charging networks operated by companies including Tesla, IONITY, Electrify America, EVgo, BP Pulse, and Shell Recharge reflect the increasing importance of hub-based, high-throughput charging models.

On the utilities side, Enel, Iberdrola and Korea Electric Power Corporation are deploying DC or ultra-fast charging hubs on key routes and in urban areas. Fleet electrification is further strengthening the role of DC charging. In Europe, the development of high-power truck-charging networks, including initiatives such as Milence, indicates that fast charging is becoming essential to commercial transport electrification as well as passenger-vehicle adoption.

Rehaan Shiledar, Power Analyst at GlobalData, comments: “Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) will continue to gain traction as utilities and grid operators seek fast, distributed flexibility to balance renewable variability, relieve local congestion, and support grid stability. Commercialization is moving from pilots toward scaled deployment. This shift is driven by aggregators, including digital intermediaries, energy technology companies, and utilities, which coordinate EV batteries as virtual power plants.”

Additionally, progress is being supported by clearer ancillary-services revenue pathways, improving bidirectional hardware, and converging standards such as ISO 15118. Recent milestones include Toyota Industries’ AC V2G hardware verification with RISE and DEFA, Valeo and Nissan’s agreement to commercialize bidirectional chargers across Europe starting in the UK, and Vattenfall Netherlands’ V2G household pilot with Kia and Hyundai for up to 80 homes.

Shiledar adds: “The industry is advancing new charging models that reduce grid stress and improve deployment flexibility. Battery-buffered charging hubs pair fast chargers with on-site storage that charges steadily from the grid and delivers high-power bursts to vehicles helping avoid costly upgrades, cut demand charges, and enable fast charging in constrained locations.”

In parallel, Electric Road Systems (ERS), which charge vehicles in motion via inductive, conductive, or overhead catenary technologies are moving from pilots toward planning at scale. ERS is progressing across Sweden, France, Germany, Italy, Israel, and the US.

Shiledar continues: “Government policies are accelerating charging buildout by lowering investment risk, setting technical standards, and steering deployment toward underserved areas which are crucial in a market that requires coordination among utilities, site hosts, local authorities, original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), and equipment suppliers.”

The US, European Union (EU), UK, China, and India are using massive funding, tax credits, and harmonized regulations to aggressively scale their EV charging networks. These coordinated policies mandate minimum power, cross-border interoperability, and utility integration while targeting underserved drivers to secure long-term project economics.

Shiledar concludes: “Future EV charging success depends on treating infrastructure as a flexible grid asset rather than mere electricity demand. By matching deployment with distribution planning via smart tariffs, managed charging, and bidirectional vehicles, markets can ensure reliable charging, cut grid costs, maximize renewable energy use, and strengthen transport electrification economics.”

text:
Hydrogen (H2) is an important energy source for a low-carbon future because it only emits water when burned. However, present methods of hydrogen production emit greenhouse gases. Over 90% of hydrogen is produced as "gray" with steam methane reforming (SMR) or "blue" with carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS).

Image Credit: FOTOGRIN/Shutterstock.com

Only a small percentage is "green" hydrogen, which is created renewably through electrolysis. Integrating hydrogen also presents obstacles such as high production costs, storage constraints, and flammability issues.

Significant investment is required to develop production and distribution. As a gas analysis leader, Servomex offers cutting-edge solutions to accelerate hydrogen adoption, including air separation unit (ASU) applications.

This helps to ensure regulatory compliance, operating efficiency, and safety, making it suitable for all industrial applications.

Introduction

Worldwide, 97 million tons (Mt) of hydrogen are consumed each year.1 Refineries absorb half of the global supply, converting crude oil into products such as gasoline and diesel.2

However, the gas could now replace the very fossil fuels it has contributed to producing. As a result, the demand for H2 is expected to increase sixfold over the next 25 years, reaching 125–585 Mt per year.3 This represents a massive financial opportunity, but it also poses technical problems.

A multifaceted strategy will be required to achieve net zero emissions by 2050. It is thought that energy efficiency, electrification, and renewable power can reduce emissions by up to 70%.4

However, decarbonizing heavy industries that produce critical materials such as steel, cement, and aluminum requires a different approach. Simply using less is not an option. In fact, demand for these materials is increasing rapidly, projected to rise by up to 80% by 2050, owing in part to the development of renewable energy infrastructure.5,6

The Essential Guide to Modern Gas Analysis eBook

This eBook covers modern gas analysis technologies, measurement challenges, and applications.

Temperatures beyond 1000 °C are frequently required in production, making it challenging to power production solely with renewable energy sources. Carbon dioxide (CO2) is a natural byproduct of various chemical processes, including plastics, cement, and steel production.7

As a highly reactive element and known energy transporter, H2 provides a solution. Industry can burn the gas to generate extreme heat, with only water vapor as a byproduct. It can also replace fossil fuels in reduction and reaction processes.8

For example, replacing coal with hydrogen in iron ore processing can lower steel-making emissions by 80%.9 Importantly, industrial processes and infrastructure that presently use natural gas can be converted to use H2.10

This enables businesses to use their existing equipment with minimal modification, reducing the need for entirely new systems. As a result, one UK study indicated that the gas might replace 40% of the fossil fuels used in manufacturing by 2040.10

The Need for Accurate Gas Analysis

Despite these advantages, hydrogen is not a miracle worker. The way it is currently manufactured is quite carbon-intensive, so increasing gas use risks canceling out the benefits of switching.

The same properties that make H2 an excellent fuel for heavy industry also make it extremely harmful. The gas has a much lower flashpoint than gasoline, at -43 °C, so extra measures must be taken.10

It is also the lightest element with a low volumetric energy density. This makes it difficult to store and transport H2 unless it is compressed or liquefied.10 However, these obstacles can be overcome.

This article will discuss how air separation units (ASUs) and precise gas analysis can ensure that H2 production is safe, efficient, and, ultimately, sustainable. It will explore how these technologies are critical to making hydrogen a realistic component of our energy future.

The Role of SMR in H2 Production

The majority of H2 is produced by unregulated fossil fuels, particularly natural gas. Steam methane reforming (SMR) is the process of combining natural gas and heated water to produce steam. The product is H2, but for every ton generated, roughly 12 tons of CO2 are discharged into the atmosphere.11

This process accounts for over 2% of global carbon emissions each year.12 However, it does not have to be that way. Electrolysis, which uses an electric current to split water into oxygen (O2) and hydrogen (H2), can generate pure "green hydrogen" using only solar or wind power.

This is still a developing business, and it will take time to expand electrolyzer capacity globally. In the battle to meet emissions objectives, so-called "blue hydrogen" offers a practical, implementable solution.

New Technologies, New Opportunities

Blue hydrogen also produces hydrogen from fossil fuels, but carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) limits emissions. This is compatible with conventional SMR, making it easier to convert current manufacturing units. However, other technologies are being investigated, notably autothermal reforming (ATR).

Similar to SMR, this method generates energy by burning a portion of the fuel with O2. When paired with CCUS, this can lead to improved energy efficiency, lower investment costs, and a simpler manufacturing process. While not completely net zero, this technology can absorb 99% of carbon emissions.13

Using O2 as a feedstock offers up new possibilities for ASUs. This technology separates ambient air into its essential components: oxygen (O2), nitrogen (N2), and argon (Ar). The cryogenic distillation process is the most common way of accomplishing this, producing high-quality, high-volume liquid and gaseous products.

JUNO BEACH, Fla., Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- NextEra Energy, Inc. (NYSE: NEE) and Dominion Energy, Inc. (NYSE: D) have filed rebuttal testimony with the Virginia State Corporation Commission strengthening their proposed combination with additional customer and financial protections.

The companies' testimony reflects strong alignment with key conditions proposed by the Virginia State Corporation Commission Staff and the Office of the Attorney General Division of Consumer Counsel (Consumer Counsel) ensuring robust financial safeguards and independence for Dominion Energy Virginia. Of the 117 conditions proposed by the Commission Staff and the Consumer Counsel, the companies have accepted 101 conditions as proposed and another 13 conditions with enhancements or modifications.

As a result, the companies have strengthened the enhanced package with additional financial and governance safeguards. These measures reinforce Dominion Energy Virginia's financial separation from affiliated businesses, add independent oversight, strengthen Virginia representation on its board and protect the utility's financial strength — all while preserving access to NextEra Energy's capital.

The companies remain confident the merger satisfies Virginia's legal standard that adequate service to the public at just and reasonable rates will not be impaired or jeopardized by the proposed transaction. In fact, the proposal exceeds the standard by proposing significant benefits in terms of customer affordability, jobs in our service area and development of needed energy resources, as well as in terms of strengthening the parent that would be backing Virginia's largest utility.

A word from John Ketchum, chairman and CEO of NextEra Energy

"We have already put forward a historic package of benefits for Dominion Energy Virginia customers, workers and communities, and we are going even further. Virginia should not have to choose between relief on electric bills today and affordable, reliable power tomorrow. Our proposal delivers four years of shareholder-funded bill credits for Dominion Energy Virginia customers while putting NextEra Energy's scale, financial strength and operating experience behind the local Dominion Energy team Virginians know and trust. We have listened carefully to stakeholders, and our filing accepts the vast majority of the additional protections proposed by Commission Staff and the Consumer Counsel while offering targeted alternatives to a limited number of remaining provisions. Together, these commitments strengthen protections for customers while preserving the financial and operating capabilities needed to build and finance Virginia's energy future more efficiently."

A word from Bob Blue, chair, president and CEO of Dominion Energy

"Dominion Energy has proudly served Virginia for more than a century. This combination is about building on that legacy. Dominion Energy Virginia would remain locally led and accountable to the State Corporation Commission, supported by NextEra Energy's financial strength and operational expertise. These additional protections reinforce our commitment to our customers as we continue to reliably and affordably meet Virginia's growing energy needs."

The companies' rebuttal testimony outlines additional commitments designed to address concerns raised by Commission Staff and the Consumer Counsel while preserving Dominion Energy Virginia's financial strength and ability to serve customers. For the limited number of provisions not accepted as proposed, the companies offered targeted alternatives designed to address the underlying concerns without unnecessarily increasing costs or restricting parent company capital or operational efficiencies that should benefit customers.

Protecting affordability while meeting Virginia's growing energy needs

The companies' proposal is designed to deliver both immediate bill relief and long-term affordability. Customers will not pay one cent for this combination. Four years of shareholder-funded residential bill credits and an additional $100 million for EnergyShare would provide near-term assistance, while the combined company's ability to buy, build, finance and operate more efficiently would help manage customer costs as Virginia's energy needs continue to grow.

Virginia's extraordinary growth in electricity demand will require significant investments in new generation, transmission and grid infrastructure, regardless of whether the proposed combination moves forward. Dominion Energy Virginia would be better positioned to meet those challenges with NextEra Energy's financial strength, scale and proven operating capabilities, helping to manage costs for customers over the long term.

NextEra Energy's track record at its Florida utility, Florida Power & Light Company (FPL), demonstrates how those capabilities benefit customers. FPL's typical residential bills are 37% below the national average and 20% lower than two decades ago in inflation-adjusted dollars, while its reliability is more than 60% better than the national average.

A generational investment in Virginia

The proposed combination includes commitments to:

Provide four years of shareholder-funded bill credits.

Contribute $100 million for EnergyShare for energy assistance and weatherization.

Invest $100 million for workforce development and skilled-trades training.

Create 1,000 new jobs, including 600 NextEra Energy jobs and approximately 400 jobs with suppliers, contractors and service providers.

Maintain Dominion Energy's current Virginia employee headcount for at least five years.

Build a new shareholder-funded office tower in downtown Richmond and maintain dual headquarters.

Spend up to $5 billion over five years with Virginia-based manufacturers, contractors, suppliers and service providers through a new Virginia Supplier Program.

Together, these commitments would provide immediate customer relief, support long-term affordability and create significant economic opportunities across the Commonwealth—all while preserving Dominion Energy Virginia's local leadership, separate regulation and full accountability to the State Corporation Commission.

The proposed combination remains subject to required regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions. The companies continue to expect the transaction to close in the second half of 2027.

Additional information about the proposed combination, including the filing, is available at DominionNextEraFuture.com.

NextEra Energy, Inc. (NYSE: NEE) is the largest electric power and energy infrastructure company in North America and is a leading provider of electricity to American homes and businesses. Headquartered in Juno Beach, Florida, NextEra Energy is a Fortune 200 company that owns Florida Power & Light Company, America's largest electric utility, which provides reliable electricity to approximately 12 million people across Florida. NextEra Energy also owns the largest energy infrastructure development company in the U.S., NextEra Energy Resources, LLC. NextEra Energy and its affiliated entities are meeting America's growing energy needs with a diverse mix of energy sources, including natural gas, nuclear, renewable energy and battery storage. title: Here's how solar and wind developers can hold on to tax credits - Canary Media
description:
When Congress passed the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) in August 2022, solar and wind developers celebrated something that had historically been elusive: long-term certainty about federal tax incentives.
But one of its most immediate effects was to create confusion over who could still access the tax credits, for how long, and what requirements wind and solar companies must meet.
The OBBBA gave solar and wind projects one year to begin construction to retain tax credit eligibility, a countdown that ended July 4, 2026.
That turned out not to be true for wind and solar, and the OBBBA cut short the long-term support the IRA promised.
Though not exactly a strategy for securing tax credits, it is a reminder that this year’s midterms and the 2028 presidential election could fundamentally reshape the federal incentive landscape yet again.
text:
When Congress passed the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) in August 2022, solar and wind developers celebrated something that had historically been elusive: long-term certainty about federal tax incentives. Companies accustomed to the waxing and waning of political support for the investment tax credit (ITC) and production tax credit (PTC) now had a decade of reliable access to both. One analysis after the law’s passage projected an additional 155 gigawatts of solar and wind capacity by 2030 and more than $270 billion in additional investments.

That certainty was short-lived. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed into law in July 2025, sharply shortened the timeline for wind and solar projects to claim the ITC and PTC and tightened the requirements to qualify. The OBBBA was expected to crush clean-energy growth. It didn’t. But one of its most immediate effects was to create confusion over who could still access the tax credits, for how long, and what requirements wind and solar companies must meet.

Dates to remember

A recent Canary Media Forum, ​“Hold onto Your Tax Credits: How to Get Ahead of the 2027 Deadline,” aimed to cut through that confusion and offer strategies for accessing federal incentives. The event was sponsored by Intersolar & Energy Storage North America (IESNA) and brought together a tax attorney, a project developer, a procurement specialist, and a manufacturer, who shared their perspectives on lingering uncertainties about qualifying for credits, steps to take now, and what could change in the future.

As the webinar’s title suggests, the end of 2027 is the deadline that matters most. ​“Those credits go away if your project isn’t placed into service by the end of 2027,” said Heather Cooper, a partner at the law firm McDermott Will & Schulte.

There is one exception to that 2027 cutoff. The OBBBA gave solar and wind projects one year to begin construction to retain tax credit eligibility, a countdown that ended July 4, 2026. Projects that met the July 4 deadline face a clock of their own. They generally have four calendar years after construction began to be placed in service. For projects that started this year, that means the end of 2030.

Question marks and strategies

Those hard dates suggest that claiming the ITC and PTC is a black-and-white matter. It is not. Definitions for key terms such as ​“placed in service” and ​“begin construction” leave room for interpretation. For example, The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) lists five factors it considers when determining whether a project is in service, including whether it has secured the necessary permits and licenses, completed critical preoperation tests, and synchronized with the power grid.

Because the IRS evaluates those factors case by case, Cooper said, a project doesn’t necessarily have to satisfy all five. That makes it hard to be certain when a project meets the criteria. Similarly, beginning construction doesn’t necessarily mean a project had modules installed by July 4.

Under IRS rules, one way to begin construction is to perform significant physical work, either on the project site or away from it. Another way to qualify is to pay or incur at least 5 percent of total project costs, often by purchasing modules or other equipment. And a developer that missed the July 4 deadline on paper may not be out of luck. Cooper said that reviewing what was done before that date, such as securing smaller equipment contracts, tracking internal costs, or starting early site work, may support a claim that construction had already begun.

Prioritizing your portfolio

For projects that didn’t begin construction by July 4, the end-of-2027 deadline forces hard choices. Rohit Patil, senior director of design engineering at New Leaf Energy, said developers should review their entire portfolio to identify which projects have a realistic path to being placed in service by then and which are worth accelerating.

“The placed-in-service deadline doesn’t necessarily turn a marginal project into a good project,” he said. ​“Projects with borderline economics are particularly vulnerable because they have little room to absorb any additional costs and delays.”

For many developers, the key factor that will determine whether a project can meet the in-service deadline is the utility interconnection timeline. Kleber Facchini, senior director of CC&I products and applications at SolarEdge Technologies, said customers that build both ground-mounted and rooftop systems are shifting toward rooftop projects. Those connect to the distribution grid near cities and tend to interconnect faster than ground-mounted projects, which are often sited in rural areas with weaker grids.

Purchasing with purpose

Equipment decisions also shape whether a project keeps its credits in two ways. The first is timing: A project can’t be placed in service by the end of 2027 without all its equipment on site.

That means ordering equipment now. Facchini said transformers have especially long lead times and urged developers to procure modules, racking, and trackers as well. Another reason to secure modules quickly: New Section 232 tariffs on imported polysilicon and solar products, including modules, take effect on December 4. ​“Any sort of modules that land after that date will cost you more,” said Ravi Manghani, senior director of strategic sourcing at Anza Renewables.

The second is compliance with the OBBBA’s foreign entity of concern (FEOC) rules, which can disqualify a project even if it is on schedule. The rules include denying credits to projects with too much ownership, debt, or control tied to China, Russia, North Korea, or Iran. For projects that began construction in 2026 or later, FEOC rules also cap the share of equipment that can come from manufacturers tied to those countries.

Elections matter

The underlying assumption behind the IRA was that the law would endure because many of its benefits were directed toward Republican constituencies. That turned out not to be true for wind and solar, and the OBBBA cut short the long-term support the IRA promised.

One lesson from both the rollback of the IRA and past tax credit challenges is that federal energy tax policy is rarely a static and settled matter. ​“Folks who’ve been in the industry long enough know that an ITC cliff is not necessarily an ITC cliff,” Manghani said. Though not exactly a strategy for securing tax credits, it is a reminder that this year’s midterms and the 2028 presidential election could fundamentally reshape the federal incentive landscape yet again.
