title: Arevon Energy secures $120 million Wells Fargo tax equity deal for its 124 MW Big Muddy ...
description:
Arevon Energy just closed a $120 million tax equity commitment with Wells Fargo Bank for its 124 MW Big Muddy Solar Project in Jackson County, Illinois.
Arevon and Wells Fargo close $120 million tax equity deal for Illinois solar project This commitment didn’t arrive in isolation.
Why the tax equity structure was used Tax equity financing is a well-established tool in U.S. renewable energy.
What this deal means for Big Muddy Solar’s path to completion The $120 million tax equity commitment fills a key piece of Big Muddy Solar’s financing structure.
For Wells Fargo, it deepens a partnership that has now produced two tax equity deals with the same developer.
text:
Arevon Energy just closed a $120 million tax equity commitment with Wells Fargo Bank for its 124 MW Big Muddy Solar Project in Jackson County, Illinois. The deal was announced on October 27, 2026, marking the second tax equity transaction between the two companies. It also pushes Arevon’s total project financings past $5.2 billion over the last several years.

Arevon and Wells Fargo close $120 million tax equity deal for Illinois solar project

This commitment didn’t arrive in isolation. Back in February 2026, Arevon announced a $183 million debt package for the same project — and together, those two deals give Big Muddy Solar a substantial combined financing stack as it heads toward completion.

The fact that this is the second tax equity deal between the two companies says something. It signals confidence on Wells Fargo’s side and a consistent financing playbook on Arevon’s.

Arevon also developed and managed construction of the 251 MWdc Gibson Solar Project and the 228 MWdc Posey Solar Project in Indiana on behalf of local utilities.

Why the tax equity structure was used

Tax equity financing is a well-established tool in U.S. renewable energy. The basic logic works like this: a project like Big Muddy Solar generates significant federal tax benefits — investment tax credits and depreciation — but the developer might not carry enough tax liability to use them fully. A tax equity investor like Wells Fargo steps in, absorbs those credits, and takes a financial stake in return. The structure lets Arevon monetize tax attributes it couldn’t otherwise capture.

This isn’t a workaround. It’s how most utility-scale solar projects in the U.S. get financed.

Wells Fargo’s Renewable Energy & Environmental Finance division structured the deal. Andrew Kho, a Managing Director in that group, described it as part of an “expanding relationship” with Arevon — phrasing that suggests more transactions could follow.

Project construction progress and expected community impact

Big Muddy Solar broke ground in 2025, employing more than 250 workers during construction. Commercial operations are expected before the end of 2026.

The economic footprint extends well beyond the construction crew. Throughout the build phase, workers spending at local stores, hotels, and restaurants generated meaningful activity across the Jackson County area. Over the project’s operating life, Big Muddy Solar is projected to deliver more than $12.6 million in property tax payments — funds expected to support local schools, roads, and community initiatives.

Once operational, the facility should generate enough electricity to power more than 24,000 Illinois homes annually. At 124 MWdc, the output is real and the scale is utility-grade.

Denise Tait, Arevon’s Chief Investment Officer and Interim CFO, put it plainly: “Together, we remain focused on advancing American-made energy projects that create jobs, generate tax revenue for schools and local governments, and deliver long-term value for both our financial partners and host communities.”

Arevon’s broader Midwest expansion and company profile

Big Muddy Solar is Arevon’s first utility-scale project in Illinois, but it fits into a wider Midwest push that’s already delivering results. The company recently reached commercial operations at its 430 MWdc Kelso Solar Project in Missouri. In Indiana, the 264 MWdc combined Ratts 1 and Heirloom Solar Projects are operational and picked up the 2025 Proximo North America Solar Deal of the Year award. Arevon also developed and managed construction of the 251 MWdc Gibson Solar Project and the 228 MWdc Posey Solar Project in Indiana on behalf of local utilities.

Illinois has more in the pipeline too. Arevon has secured three 20-year renewable energy credit contracts for its Panther Energy Project — a 200 MWac/275 MWdc facility currently under development in the state.

Nationally, Arevon owns and operates more than 6.3 gigawatts of solar and energy storage projects across 18 states, with 370 MW of new capacity under construction and what the company describes as a robust development pipeline. Headquarters are in Scottsdale, Arizona, with a regional office in New York City.

What this deal means for Big Muddy Solar’s path to completion

The $120 million tax equity commitment fills a key piece of Big Muddy Solar’s financing structure. Paired with the $183 million debt package closed earlier in 2026, the project now has the capital it needs to reach commercial operations before year-end.

For Arevon, this adds another data point to a track record of closing complex transactions at scale — more than $5.2 billion in cumulative project financings over recent years. For Wells Fargo, it deepens a partnership that has now produced two tax equity deals with the same developer.

When Big Muddy Solar comes online, it’ll be Arevon’s first operational utility-scale project in Illinois, delivering clean electricity to more than 24,000 homes and starting to generate the property tax revenue that Jackson County communities are counting on.

title: Despite setbacks, NC's clean energy sector still has plenty of charge - Wilmington Star-News
description:
That could have many wondering if the clean energy sector is running out of steam, including in North Carolina.
But clean energy advocates say that's hardly the case.
That has helped cushion some of the state's job losses in the clean energy sector tied to policy decisions coming out of Washington.
That hasn't been the case in recent years, with the Trump administration putting the brakes on much of the momentum for the clean energy sector adopted under the Biden administration.
"Yes, it is still growing and the industry remains strong in North Carolina," Andrew Whiteman, senior policy manager with CleanAIRE NC, said of the state's clean energy sector.
text:
Rising electricity costs and data center power demands have renewed interest in solar and battery storage.

The electric vehicle market has slowed due to policy changes, impacting manufacturing plans in the state.

Advocates state that clear, long-term policies are needed to reduce uncertainty and spur growth in the industry.

At sea, the chance for Southeastern North Carolina to see wind farms off its coast blew away in 2026 when first French-based TotalEnergies and then Duke Energy sold their offshore leases roughly 20 miles south of Brunswick County back to the federal government.

While on land, the cancelation of a generous federal tax break for buyers of new electric vehicles (EVs) under the "Big Beautiful Bill" pushed by President Trump have seen national sales of EVs fall by more than 30% through the first half of 2026.

That could have many wondering if the clean energy sector is running out of steam, including in North Carolina.

But clean energy advocates say that's hardly the case. While some sectors of the industry might have slowed down, several factors − including concerns over the power needs of data centers and rising fuel prices tied to the ongoing conflict with Iran − have seen renewed interest in many "green" power options by both homeowners and businesses.

Polls also show the public continues to favor renewable energy and remains concerned about the impacts of climate change.

"It's no secret that there's been quite a bit of headwinds from a policy perspective over the past 24 months or so," said Matt Abele, executive director of the N.C. Sustainable Energy Association. "But no matter what happens in D.C., North Carolina has consistently proven that clean energy is a resource choice that's seen as favorable on both sides of the political aisle."

Solar heats up

Growing concerns in North Carolina over the power needs of data centers amid electricity bills that are already increasing on a seemingly annual basis have many, including state politicians, looking for answers that protect existing customers from shouldering the burden.

That has refocused attention on solar power and battery storage systems, with Gov. Josh Stein saying data centers should have to bring clean energy options to the table to provide electricity to their power-hungry projects instead of simply relying on grid upgrades to meet their needs.

The sector also is drawing interest from other customers as Duke Energy raises rates to upgrade the power grid and meet surging demand.

"The story we're hearing is that inquiries around solar and battery storage are increasing because of increasing electricity costs," Abele said, noting that a tax credit for large solar projects that is set to expire in mid-2027 also is driving demand. "Rate increases do not appear to be slowing, so households and businesses are looking for opportunities to mitigate those rising costs."

That has helped cushion some of the state's job losses in the clean energy sector tied to policy decisions coming out of Washington. Abele said North Carolina has seen an estimated 1,000 job losses in the sector, with employment falling to roughly 111,000, since late 2025. While the loss of federal tax credits has seen residential solar companies take a hit, the state has seen job growth in the energy efficiency sector, like HVAC and residential insulation improvements.

Solar and battery storage power also can be brought online much faster than a natural gas or nuclear plant, and are increasing their cost advantage over more traditional power sources every year.

Stuck in neutral?

While interest in solar appears to be heating up, the same can't be said for the EV industry.

Policy changes in Washington and uncertainty about the industry's future have seen EV sales drop sharply. Citing the market volatility, VinFast has frozen plans to open a vehicle manufacturing plant that would have employed thousands in Chatham County near the Triangle. Indian-based Epsilon Advanced Materials also has pushed back plans to build a EV battery materials plant in Brunswick County.

But not all "green" automotive sectors are struggling. Fueled by strong demand for its hybrid vehicles, Toyota has opened the first phase of its $14 billion battery plant near Greensboro and employs more than 3,000 people at the sprawling facility. The slowdown in EV growth also is allowing North Carolina to build out its charging network, filling in holes in rural and other areas that will make EVs enticing to more consumers once the industry bounces back. Much of that charging infrastructure is built in the Tar Heel State.

Surging gasoline prices since February 2026 also has seen some uptick in interest in EVs, with Tesla attracting most of the growth as legacy automakers slow their own plans to enter the EV market.

Seeking clarity

What the clean energy sector needs, though, to really get back on track are coherent policies coming out of Washington and Raleigh that allow companies to make long-term plans and commitments.

That hasn't been the case in recent years, with the Trump administration putting the brakes on much of the momentum for the clean energy sector adopted under the Biden administration. In North Carolina, the state has backed away from its aggressive carbon-reduction goals adopted earlier this decade, with the N.C. General Assembly citing economic and power generation needs in its decision to scrap interim carbon-reduction goals that were supposed to come into force by 2030.

"Yes, it is still growing and the industry remains strong in North Carolina," Andrew Whiteman, senior policy manager with CleanAIRE NC, said of the state's clean energy sector. "But there's a lot of uncertainty out there, so we're hoping we can see greater clarity at both the federal and state levels in the coming years."

Reporter Gareth McGrath can be reached at GMcGrath@usatodayco.com or @GarethMcGrathSN on X/Twitter. This story was produced with financial support from Journalism Funding Partners. The USA TODAY Network maintains full editorial control of the work.

text:
A new Nordic research initiative will develop artificial intelligence-based solutions to help power grid operators optimise the use of existing grid infrastructure, handle growing uncertainty and keep power grids resilient as electricity demand increases.

The Novo Nordisk Foundation is awarding up to DKK 100 million (EUR 13.3 million) over four years to establish AI4GRIDS, a Nordic research initiative led by universities in Denmark, Sweden and Norway. The aim of the project is to optimise the use of the existing Nordic energy grids, thus enabling the safer and smoother integration of renewable and weather-dependent energy sources such as wind and solar power.

As societies electrify and electricity demand rises, power grids must accommodate far more renewable energy sources, alongside a growing number of batteries, electric vehicles, heat pumps, data centres and other electricity assets. These developments are putting increasing pressure on existing infrastructure and making power systems more complex to operate safely and efficiently, while potentially increasing the risk of so-called brownouts and blackouts.

“The increasing energy demand challenges the current energy grid, which was built to meet entirely different needs. Until we scale up the capacity of the energy grid, there is an urgent need to optimise the use of the existing grid. At the Novo Nordisk Foundation, we see AI as an obvious enabler for achieving this, as it can help us make critical decisions on how to balance energy production and demand so that our energy systems become more resilient and ready for future needs,” says Lene Oddershede, Chief Scientific Officer, Novo Nordisk Foundation.

New operating methods for a changing electricity system

Most operational power system principles and methods applied today were originally developed for systems with a relatively small number of centralised power plants. Today’s systems are increasingly decentralised, weather-dependent and complex.

Building on the Nordic countries’ closely connected electricity systems, AI4GRIDS will bring together leading researchers in power systems, AI, energy data and control theory to develop new methods for optimising the operation of future grids. By combining AI with mathematical models of how electricity grids behave, the project aims to make grid operation more reliable and better suited to safety- and time-critical decisions.

The Technical University of Denmark (DTU) is leading the initiative in partnership with Lund University in Sweden and the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

“The electricity grid is becoming vastly more complex, while society is becoming more dependent on it. We want to fundamentally rethink how power systems are operated. Our vision is a self-operating grid where trustworthy AI can help make decisions at a speed and scale beyond what is possible today, while humans remain in a supervisory role,” says Spyros Chatzivasileiadis, Professor at DTU Wind and Energy Systems.

The ambition is to equip operators with the best possible response options when imminent risks arise from a range of potential scenarios. Human operators will remain in charge, supported by AI-based tools that can perform computations up to 100 times faster, enhance power controllers and energy markets with safe autonomy and unlock demand-side flexibility.

Nordic expertise with a shared challenge

AI4GRIDS builds on complementary expertise across the Nordic region. DTU contributes expertise in power systems, trustworthy AI, energy data and computing. Lund University brings expertise in mathematical statistics, forecasting and control, and NTNU contributes expertise in energy markets, optimisation and decision-making under uncertainty. Together, the partners aim to develop technologies and operating principles that can scale across Europe’s interconnected electricity systems, energy markets and varying grid conditions.

The collaboration builds on the close links between Nordic electricity systems and the region’s cross-border cooperation in energy research and innovation. Over the next four years, AI4GRIDS will train more than 30 PhD students, postdoctoral researchers and other specialists across the partner institutions. The initiative will also bring researchers together with power system operators, technology developers, regulators and other stakeholders to ensure that the research remains connected to future needs. By building the scientific foundation for more resilient and efficient power system operations, AI4GRIDS aims to help prepare electricity systems for the demands ahead, strengthening Nordic and European leadership at the intersection of energy, AI and critical infrastructure.

Watch CSO Lene Oddershede and Professor Spyros Chatzivasileiadis explain more about AI4GRIDS in the video here.

The project is expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027.

name: EPA
title: Mid-term in the United States: seven reasons for being (moderately) optimistic about the ...
authors: José Pablo Martínez, Carmen González Enríquez
description:
The United States still has a wide variety of institutional, territorial, economic and societal checks and balances that curb the concentration of presidential power.
The autonomy of civil and military bureaucracy The US federal administration constitutes another major source of resistance to the concentration of political power.
The federal structure as a safety net The federal structure of the United States probably constitutes one of the most important obstacles to the concentration of presidential power.
Similarly, certain business groups may benefit from their proximity to political power and choose to comply with its demands.
There are organisations advocating liberal pluralism and others that actively endorse expansionist interpretations of presidential power.
text:
During Donald Trump’s first term (2017-2021), and even more so in the second, inaugurated in January 2025, American democracy has undergone a significant downturn. According to Freedom House, America slipped from a score of 86 points out of 100 in 2017 to 81 in 2025. The V-Dem Institute’s liberal democracy index also recorded a significant decline, with a fall from 0.75 in 2024 to 0.57 in 2025, dropping from 20th to 51st in the international rankings. Moreover, the Economist Intelligence Unit, which describes the United States as a ‘flawed democracy’, awarded it 7.65 out of 10 points in 2025, as opposed to 8.22 in 2006. Despite their differing methodologies, these studies concur in highlighting problems related to the expansion of presidential power, the dilution of institutional controls, and growing pressures regarding the rule of law and public freedoms.

The American system’s main source of resilience lies in one of the characteristics that often hampers its governability: the extraordinary dispersal of power.

Democratic erosion does not necessarily entail an irreversible drift towards authoritarianism, however. The United States still has a wide variety of institutional, territorial, economic and societal checks and balances that curb the concentration of presidential power. The regular holding of competitive elections, the autonomy of the civil and military administrations, the independence of the judiciary, federalism, the political clout of then larger cities, the diversity of the private sector and the strength of civil society constitute seven reasons for being moderately optimistic about the future of its democracy.

Paradoxically, the American system’s main source of resilience lies in one of the characteristics that often hampers its governability: the extraordinary dispersal of power. This fragmentation can give rise to stalemates and conflicts, but it also hinders a president from forcing the main centres of political, economic and societal decision-making to bend to his will simultaneously. Although some of these checks and balances have undergone significant erosion, their resilience enables the gloomiest forecasts about the future of American democracy to be viewed from a more nuanced perspective.

1. Electoral resilience and the role of legislative checks and balances

The fact that contested elections are held on a regular basis continues to be one of the main mechanisms for curbing presidential power in the United States. The mid-term elections being held on 3 November 2026 offer voters the chance of substantially altering the balance of power in Washington and placing fresh constraints on the Trump administration.

At the time of writing, everything seems to suggest that the elections will take place normally thanks to the existence of numerous institutional, technological and legal mechanisms designed to ensure the trustworthiness of the vote and the verification of the outcome. As the US Election Assistance Commission (EAC) recently pointed out, a fundamental characteristic of the American system is that elections are not overseen by a single federal authority, since the task of running them fundamentally rests with state and local authorities. This means that thousands of jurisdictions administer their own electoral processes, and there is no single centralised computer system that manages all the results. According to the latest EAC press release, more than 98% of electoral jurisdictions use systems that generate a paper record of every vote cast. Moreover, the voting equipment, which is stored in secure premises, is subjected to testing prior to the elections. Furthermore, a recent report issued by the National Conference of State Legislatures (NCSL), a bipartisan organisation that brings together state legislatures, notes that all 50 states undertake audits once the elections are over. While it is true that the Trump administration has tried to introduce significant restrictions on the distribution of postal ballots, several federal courts have intervened to ensure that such restrictions do not apply to the elections to be held on 3 November.

The importance of these elections lies not only in the fact of their being held but also in the real possibility of new majorities emerging in one or both houses of Congress. Although the electoral process does not in itself provide a guarantee of democratic quality, the enduring existence of real political competition constitutes a necessary condition for curbing any drift towards the concentration of power.

If the Democrats were to regain the House of Representatives, they would acquire a considerable ability to audit the behaviour of the executive branch, instigate enquiries and have a significant say in the adoption of certain legislative and budgetary initiatives. Control of the Senate would significantly increase such powers, especially in terms of confirming nominations. In the event of both houses falling into the hands of the Democrats, Trump would face a scenario of divided government that would significantly hamper the execution of a large part of his legislative programme (or what remains of it) and restrict his room for manoeuvre during the last two years of his term in office.

Despite this, the extent and scope of such checks and balances should not be exaggerated. The president enjoys ample executive powers that can be wielded without passing new laws, and partisan polarisation has considerably reduced the possibility of striking bilateral deals. Moreover, controlling one or both houses does not automatically guarantee the ability to place real restraints on the executive, especially when the latter resorts to expansionist interpretations of presidential powers.

That said, the possibility of legislative elections substantially altering the president’s scope for action remains a fundamental characteristic of the US political system. Changes in the composition of both legislative chambers remain a real possibility, and with it, voters’ ability to modify the institutional balance of power.

2. The autonomy of civil and military bureaucracy

The US federal administration constitutes another major source of resistance to the concentration of political power. Its organisational complexity, the existence of entrenched administrative procedures and the professionalism of a large proportion of its employees obstruct the transformation of the state apparatus into an instrument subject to the president’s personal preferences.

The federal administration has undergone profound restructuring during Trump’s second term, initially instigated by the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) under Elon Musk. According to figures provided by the Office of Personnel Management (OPM), the net reduction in the federal civil service amounted to 264,029 employees between January 2025 and August 2026, accounting for around 12% of the total. This contraction affected federal agencies in a highly uneven fashion: whereas USAID lost approximately 98% of its staff and the Department of Education more than 45%, other organisations, such as the Department of Homeland Security, escaped relatively unscathed.

These cutbacks have laid bare the vulnerability of certain federal institutions, especially those that are most dependent on the spending priorities of the White House. However, they have also revealed the difficulties of carrying out an administrative transformation on such a sweeping scale. The procedures surrounding hiring and firing, the powers assigned to certain agencies by legislation and the possibility of launching legal challenges to government decisions have impeded the implementation of some measures.

The story of DOGE is instructive. Regarding the savings of $215 billion announced by the organisation itself, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) has reported major methodological flaws and problems of transparency that prevented it from confirming a substantial proportion of the amount declared. The report issued by the GAO in 2026 found accounting errors in a number of contracts, savings attributed to operations that had never been put into effect and insufficient information regarding costs linked to some layoffs. When DOGE was wound up in July 2026, without submitting a final report evaluating the results of its efforts, it laid bare the difficulties of translating a political offensive against the federal bureaucracy into coherent and sustainable administrative reform.

Interpreting these events as an unequivocal victory for the civil service would be unjustified, however. The loss of specialist expertise and the undermining of certain agencies may well have lasting consequences. Bureaucratic resilience consists not only of preserving the formal existence of the institutions concerned but also of maintaining their professional and operational capabilities.

A particularly sensitive issue in this debate is the relationship between civilian power and the armed forces. At the behest of Pete Hegseth, the Trump administration has brought about changes in the highest echelons of the military and in the Pentagon’s organisational priorities, accompanied by an attack on certain diversity and inclusion policies. The administration’s initial proposals floated the idea of a substantial reduction in the number of officers and a review of promotion criteria and internal organisation matters, raising concerns regarding the politicisation of the armed forces.

Nevertheless, the US armed forces boast a professional tradition and institutional culture that stand in the way of attempts at partisan instrumentalisation. Military obedience to the legitimately constituted civilian authority is an essential principle of any democracy, but this is not the same as a duty to execute illegal orders or the acceptance of essentially partisan considerations in the discharge of military functions.

The decisive issue therefore is not whether the military hierarchy is capable of resisting the president’s political preferences but whether it manages to preserve its institutional neutrality, its professional procedures and its respect for constitutional legality. Although recent pressures have put these principles to the test, the existence of a well-established command structure and entrenched professional standards continues to represent a bulwark against the unfettered politicisation of the armed forces.

In short, America’s civilian and military bureaucracies have shown themselves to be vulnerable to presidential pressures, but also more resistant to being swiftly and unilaterally transformed than might have initially been supposed.

3. Judicial independence and the defence of the constitution

The judiciary constitutes one of the main checks to the Trump administration’s more arbitrary initiatives. The decentralised structure of federal courts, the formal independence of their judges and the longstanding US tradition of constitutional litigation provide numerous opportinities for challenging the decisions of the executive branch.

The current makeup of the Supreme Court, with a six-to-three majority of conservative judges over their progressive counterparts, adds another layer of complexity. Although three of their number were nominated by Trump himself, their stances on jurisprudence do not necessarily ensure unconditional submission to the will of the White House. Indeed, some of the thorniest controversies arising during his second term have made it clear that the textualist and originalist interpretations advocated by some of the conservative judged may induce them to curb presidential powers.

Thus, in the case of Trump v. Barbara, the Supreme Court rejected the president’s attempt to implement an executive order that would unilaterally suppress the right of citizenship by birth enshrined by the Fourteenth Amendment to the constitution. Simillarly, in Learning Resources v. Trump, the Supreme Court rejected the argument that his emergency economic powers enabled the president to impose certain tariffs without legislative approval. Other disputes have revolved around the autonomy of the Federal Reserve and the limitations placed on the president’s ability to deploy the National Guard, as in the case of Trump v. Illinois.

These cases demonstrate the importance of the separation of powers and the continued existence of judicial curbs on presidential action. They particularly illustrate the fact that the conservative majority in the Supreme Court does not necessarily constitute a bloc that will automatically accede to any expansionist interpretation of executive powers.

However, it would be equally mistaken to portray the Supreme Court as a systematic counterweight to the Trump administration. Some of their decisions have favoured broad interpretations of presidential prerogatives, while others have limited the possibility of obtaining broad-ranging judicial redress for the actions of the executive. Recent judicial rulings therefore reveal a finely poised balance, where the judges’ ideological outlook coexists with different notions of the separation of powers.

It is also important to distinguish between the provisional suspension of a measure and its definitive withdrawal. A court ruling can delay the implementation of a policy while failing to prevent the executive from imposing it through other procedures. Moreover, in the final analysis the efficacy of judicial oversight depends on the extent to which its sentences are actually obeyed.

Despite these limitations, the existence of an independent judiciary which the states, local authorities, businesses, universities and other organisations can turn to continues to act as a major restraint on the arbitrary exercise of power. Its importance lies not so much in the administration suffering legal reverses as in the fact that it is obliged to give a legal justification for its decisions and submit them to the scrutiny of institutions that it does not directly control.

4. The federal structure as a safety net

The federal structure of the United States probably constitutes one of the most important obstacles to the concentration of presidential power. The existence of 50 states equipped with their own institutions, constitutionally recognised powers and independent democratic legitimacy significantly hampers any blanket imposition of policy initiatives emanating from Washington.

In the US system, states are not mere administrative offshoots of the federal executive. Their governors, legislatures and judiciaries are accountable to their own electorates and play a significant policy-making role in areas such as education, law and order, healthcare, economic regulation and environmental policy. This territorial distribution of power has taken on special importance during Trump’s second term. Several Democrat-run states have turned to their regulatory powers and the courts to challenge federal decisions in areas such as immigration, environmental protection and the funding of public services.

California represents a particularly significant example. When the Trump administration revoked the special authorisations included in the Clean Air Act enabling states to impose more stringent emissions standards on new vehicles, its attorney general coordinated a legal challenge supported by 26 states, counties and cities. The dispute provided a clear illustration of state governments’ ability to challenge federal decisions when they are deemed to undermine their regulatory powers.

Similarly, a coalition of 21 states and four cities, spearheaded by New York, challenged the decision of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to postpone certain restrictions on greenhouse gas emissions for coal-fired and gas-powered power stations. Another 15 states went to court to challenge the ‘energy emergency’ measures advocated by the White House, arguing that they would allow it to bypass the environmental assessments required by federal legislation.

State-led resistance is not restricted to the judicial domain. California has advocated the continued existence of its emissions-trading programmes and bolstered its participation in international climate cooperation networks. The fact that it has joined the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) as a sub-national member is especially noteworthy. With an economy that accounts for approximately 14% of the US’s GDP, California wields a capacity for international influence that clearly transcends its borders.

Such autonomy is subject to significant limitations, however. The constitution assigns exclusive powers to the federal government in certain areas, and federal legislation can prevail over state regulations when their competences overlap. Moreover, the dependence of certain state programmes on federal funding can significantly restrict their room for manoeuvre.

Furthermore, it should not be forgotten that federalism can contribute to both the protection and limitation of certain rights. Some states have used their autonomy to strengthen certain freedoms, while others have passed controversial measures in areas such as reproductive rights, the regulation of elections and immigration.

Federalism cannot therefore be construed as an automatic guarantor of liberal democracy. Its contribution to democratic resilience lies in its multiplication of decision-making centres with their own legitimacy, capable of offering political alternatives, challenging federal decisions and hindering an unjustified geographical concentration of power.

5. Checks and balances at the municipal level

The larger US cities account for an additional dimension of the geographical dispersal of power. Although their legal autonomy depends largely on state legislation, city halls wield significant administrative, budgetary and regulatory powers that can have considerable impact on the implementation of federal policies.

The importance of this counterweight is strengthened by the country’s current political landscape. At the time of writing, 67 of the 100 largest US cities have Democrat mayors, and Democrats run nine out of the ten most populated conurbations. Cities such as New York, Los Angeles and Chicago combine significant economic resources, large populations, sophisticated infrastructure and highly developed administrative capabilities that lend them considerable political influence.

One of the areas in which municipal autonomy has emerged in an especially pronounced way is migration policy. Cities such as Los Angeles and Chicago have passed resolutions that restrict voluntary collaboration between their police forces and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). This does not necessarily prevent the federal government from exercising its powers, but it may hinder certain operations and force federal agencies to incur greater administrative and operating costs.

The conflicts provoked by the deployment of the National Guard and the intervention of federal forces in large cities have also highlighted the importance of local governments as political and judicial actors. Local administrations in places such as Portland and Chicago have appealed to the courts to challenge certain initiatives emanating from Washington, invoking constitutional and legal limits to federal involvement in matters of law and order.

Environmental policy offers another striking example. A network of more than 400 mayors has made commitments to cutting emissions in keeping with the Paris Agreement targets, despite the U-turn in federal climate policy. Numerous cities have used public transport electrification programmes, energy efficiency and the decarbonisation of buildings to continue pushing the green transition agenda at the local level. In areas such as housing, planning and social services, local governments can also pursue their own policies, which partly offset the consequences of certain changes in federal funding and regulation.

Local autonomy should not be mistaken for sovereignty, however. State governments can curb the powers of cities by means of specific legislation, and dependence on federal and state funding affects their ability to operate. Moreover, the large urban areas do not represent the entirety of American society, and their political priorities may differ substantially from those of rural areas.

Despite these limitations, local power represents a significant counterweight. Its importance lies not so much in its ability to block presidential decisions as in hindering their uniform implementation, preserving spaces for political experimentation and providing alternative institutional platforms where opposition to the executive branch can operate.

6. The diversity of the private sector and the autonomy of the market economy

The size, complexity, wealth and heterogeneity of the US economy constitute another barrier to the concentration of political power. The existence of giant multinational corporations, small and medium-sized companies, professional associations, financial institutions and capital markets that are deeply integrated with the international economy makes it difficult for economic activity in its entirety to be subordinated to the political preferences of a specific administration.

Although certain business sectors have explicitly backed some of Trump’s initiatives, especially in the areas of deregulation and taxation, others have expressed reservations about policies they regard as prejudicial to their interests. Restrictions on migration, the uncertainty surrounding tariffs and specific government initiatives affecting the way markets operate have created acute tensions between the White House and various economic actors.

Migration policy is especially illuminating. The large tech companies depend very significantly on their ability to attract highly qualified professionals from abroad. This is why corporations such as Apple and Google have devised legal protection mechanisms and carried out internal reorganisations of their workers subject to H-1B visas, while others such as Microsoft and Adobe have lodged legal challenges to certain administrative restrictions that affect the hiring of foreign workers.

The most labour-intensive sectors of the economy, such as agriculture and construction, have also expressed concern about the economic consequences of a tightening of immigration controls. Business associations such as the Associated General Contractors of America (AGC) have expressed their reservations about the compulsory application of certain employment verification mechanisms, such as E-Verify, and have advocated solutions which will guarantee the availability of workers for their companies.

Despite this, it is important to differentiate between the defence of economic interests and a commitment to liberal democracy. A company may oppose a migration policy for reasons of profitability without challenging other governmental actions that weaken institutional controls. Similarly, certain business groups may benefit from their proximity to political power and choose to comply with its demands. The relationship between the Trump administration and large US corporations has brought this ambivalence to the fore. While some companies have publicly proclaimed their autonomy or challenged specific policies, others have sought agreements with the White House or adapted their priorities to the executive’s preferences.

The private sector should not therefore be viewed as a homogeneous bloc of democratic resistance. Its contribution to institutional resilience is more indirect and structural: the multiplicity of economic interests, the competition between companies, membership of international markets and the existence of financial resources that are relatively independent of the federal state are obstacles standing tin the way of the concentration of economic power in the hands of the executive.

This autonomy does not guarantee that companies will act in defence of public liberties, but it does limit the president’s ability to impose his political preferences on the entirety of the economy.

7. The strength of civil society

The density, diversity and autonomy of US civil society organisations constitute one of the main sources of resistance to any weakening of democratic institutions. Universities, foundations, organisations devoted to the defence of civil rights, professional associations, the news media and civic movements constitute an extensive network of actors capable of mobilising resources, voicing demands and subjecting government decisions to public scrutiny.

An especially important feature of the US system is the existence of private organisations with sufficient financial and legal resources to embark upon strategic litigation against the federal government. Entities such as the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) have the resources and experience needed to petition the courts, mobilise experts and pursue prolonged legal suits. This capacity is essential to understanding the efficacy of the judiciary as a constitutional counterweight: the independence of the courts would be far less relevant if there were no non-governmental organisations capable of resorting to them.

Universities constitute another important battleground. During Trump’s second term, a number of prominent academic institutions have faced pressures related to federal funding, their internal policies and their handling of politically controversial issues. Some, such as Columbia and the University of Pennsylvania, have chosen to negotiate with the administration, while others have turned to the courts to defend their autonomy.

The case of Harvard is particularly striking. The university won several legal rulings in its favour after appealing against the withdrawal of $2.2 billion in federal research funding, which the courts viewed as unwarranted government interference in its institutional autonomy. These controversies have revealed both the universities’ ability to overturn the decisions of the executive branch and their financial vulnerability in the face of threats to withdraw public funding.

Freedom of information is another highly contested arena. In September 2025, the Pentagon introduced new restrictions for journalists accredited to the Department of War, demanding commitments regarding the obtaining and publishing of non-authorised information, even if it was unclassified. These measures triggered a strong reaction from the news media and professional organisations concerned, which challenged their compatibility with the rights enshrined in the First Amendment. The controversies surrounding the withdrawal of credentials and the restrictions on access to certain federal institutions have also triggered court cases instigated by media outlets and organisations concerned with defending press freedoms. Although the court rulings in question have not always led to definitive victories for the media, they have demonstrated the existence of a means of challenging government pressure.

Organisations devoted to the defence of digital rights have also played an important role. For example, the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) has questioned the automated surveillance and monitoring programmes that social media companies have applied to foreign residents, obtaining the judicial review of specific security protocols devised by the Department of Homeland Security.

In addition to the activities of these institutional actors, there is a broad and longstanding US tradition of civic mobilisation. Demonstrations, protest campaigns, community initiatives and activist networks provide an outlet for political discontent beyond strictly electoral channels. Their ability to influence government decisions is uneven, but they help to keep public participation alive.

It is of course worth noting, in this regard, that America’s civil society does not constitute a homogeneous ideological bloc. There are organisations advocating liberal pluralism and others that actively endorse expansionist interpretations of presidential power. This is why the organisational strength of civil society does not in and of itself ensure the preservation of democracy. Its fundamental contribution lies in the existence of multiple forums for association, mobilisation and funding that do not depend directly on the federal government. This pluralism hinders the administration’s ability to dominate public debate and allows different forms of political and societal opposition to survive, even when certain state institutions are being subjected to major pressures.

Conclusions: the limits of presidential power and US democratic resilience

This brief analysis of seven clearly differentiated spheres of activity provides grounds to view the most pessimistic diagnoses of the future of US democracy to be viewed in a more nuanced manner. Although Trump’s second term has accelerated certain worrying trends regarding the concentration of presidential power and the undermining of certain institutional controls, the United States continues to have a plurality of relatively autonomous power centres capable of challenging, curbing and, in certain circumstances, overturning the decisions of the executive branch.

The US political system’s main source of resilience lies in an extraordinary dispersal of political, geographical, economic and societal power. The same characteristics that often hinder the country’s governability — its institutional fragmentation, federal structure, the autonomy of local governments and the existence of multiple social actors with the ability to initiate action — also represent a significant hindrance to the political system as a whole being subjugated to the presidential will.

Nevertheless, this capacity for resistance should not be confused with a guarantee of democratic recovery. The periodic holding of elections, the independence of the judiciary, federalism and the strength of civil society create favourable conditions for the survival of political pluralism, but their efficacy depends both on the resources at their disposal and on the will of political actors to respect the constitutional rules of the game.

Nor should it be forgotten that some of these checks and balances have suffered considerable attrition. The cuts to administrative capabilities, the pressures exerted on universities, the polarisation of the judiciary and the hoops that some economic actors have jumped through to meet certain presidential preferences reveal that institutional resilience is uneven and subject to significant vulnerabilities.

This is why it is essential to distinguish between three dimensions of democratic resilience: the ability to challenge the decisions of the executive branch, the likelihood of effectively curbing their application and the possibility of reversing their consequences. The existence of court cases, protests and institutional conflicts shows that pluralism remains alive, but this does not guarantee that existing checks and balances will preserve their powers intact or succeed in reestablishing the rights that have already been eroded.

The future of US democracy will therefore depend to a large extent on three conditions: that the elections — and in particular the mid-term elections of 3 November — continue being genuinely contested and that their results are respected; that judicial decisions are respected and properly implemented by the executive; and that the organisations and institutions capable of performing supervisory duties retain the necessary resources and autonomy to discharge them.

From this perspective, guarded optimism about the future of the United States should not depend on the alleged superiority of its institutions or the assumption that constitutional checks and balances will operate automatically. It should instead be based on the realisation that presidential power continues to face a range of deeply entrenched and relatively autonomous obstacles whose existence hinders any authoritarian transformation of the US political system.

American democracy is not immune from the authoritarian tendencies that are increasingly in evidence elsewhere, but it retains sufficient institutional and societal bulwarks to render its recovery possible. Whether or not this possibility can become a reality will depend on the resilience of its institutions and the ability of American society to defend the traditions and practices that have hitherto underpinned alternation in power, the rule of law and the full exercise of fundamental freedoms.

title: Texas used to be 'the best place' to build data centers — but not anymore
authors: Arcelia Martin, Inside Climate News, Arcelia Martin, Inside Climate News

text:
This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.

When BaRupOn LLC, a California-based developer, bought land in East Texas for a 700-acre industrial campus in 2023, the company received a warm welcome from the state. The developer set out to build numerous data centers and rare-earth manufacturing facilities at the site, as well as its own power plants.

At first, Gov. Greg Abbott’s office worked closely with BaRupOn, said Balaji Tammabattula, the chief operating officer.

The governor’s office staff would recommend site locations for future projects and which county officials they should get in touch with, Tammabattula said. Developers were encouraged to seek out incentives and tax breaks. The governor’s office, which was just a phone call away, even gave the planned industrial campus, in Liberty, Texas, the codename of “Project Tough,” Tammabattula said.

“Texas used to be the best place,” he said. “Fast forward to 2026, it’s impossible to have [the governor’s office] respond to our emails.”

The climate around data centers has soured so severely that new developments in Texas are essentially on pause until after November’s elections. The land, energy and water usage of the large warehouses filled with server racks have elicited strong protest across the country—even becoming a bipartisan issue among midterm election candidates, including in Texas.

Abbott has gone against his typical business-first approach and led some companies to rethink their major data center investments in Texas, analysts and developers said. Those seeking to keep their spot in the lengthy line for grid power are laboring to not only secure state permits but social permission from communities across the state.

The data center industry flocked to invest billions of dollars in the state to quickly construct the physical infrastructure required for tech companies to develop the most mature artificial intelligence and other advanced technologies. The developers, many of whom were new to the industry, saw a state not only open to doing business but a grid committed to connecting projects to power faster than anywhere else. Texas became the epicenter of A.I. development as Abbott willed last year. But that tune changed fast.

The state has long been seen as the best place for business development in the country, with its previously unfussy regulatory environment. It’s a reputation that’s carried throughout Abbott’s 11 years in office. Yet that’s changed amid the staunch opposition data centers have ignited and a race which could result in a Democrat representing Texas in the U.S. Senate for the first time in more than 30 years. And there’s another unanticipated outcome for Abbott: his own unusually tight race for reelection against Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa from Austin.

Andrew Mahaleris, Abbott’s press secretary, said Abbott has taken decisive action to set clear guardrails to protect Texans against intrusive data center development.

In August, he ordered the state’s utilities regulator, the Public Utility Commission, and its grid operator, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, to audit how much power and water every data center project being developed would consume. In September, he ordered the Texas Water Development Board to enforce water-use reporting requirements on data center projects.

“Data centers must pay their own way, protect our grid and water, and complete the ERCOT and TWDB audits,” Mahaleris said in a statement to Inside Climate News. “Until they do, no state agency will issue related permits, and any project that fails those standards will be denied.”

Abbott’s audit and directive to pause all environmental permits is on top of new regulations and planning processes implemented after the last legislative session, which seek to verify the validity of the massive amounts of data center projects trying to connect to the grid.

Six months ago, the industry in Texas was most concerned about how fast their projects could get interconnected to the grid, said Olivier Beaufils, a head researcher at Aurora Energy Research. Now, the industry is nervous, Beaufils said, because there’s more political uncertainty than there was earlier this year, when developers were solely dealing with the wave of new rules.

“Political backlash and political risk was sort of a remote risk that people weren’t considering as their core problem they had to deal with,” Beaufils said. “That has shifted very rapidly.”

There’s anguish within the industry over whether the political issues they’re facing today will subside after the midterms are over, or whether they will multiply during the legislative session in January, Beaufils said.

“I think there’s a recognition that this is not a risk that is going to disappear in November,” Beaufils said. “This is something they’re going to have to engage with over the next six months until there’s a bit more clarity.”

After Diode Ventures, a data center developer, withdrew its plans for a data center near a residential community in Henderson County as a result of Abbott’s directives and community pushback about its water usage, Abbott celebrated the company’s decision.

“Data centers that want to do business in Texas must meet a clear standard. This project did not,” Abbott said in a July statement. “Diode did the right thing by withdrawing their project. If other data center developments refuse to meet these standards, I expect them to do the same.”

A spokesperson for Diode said due diligence findings, as well as feedback from community members, local leaders and stakeholders informed the decision to not advance the project beyond preliminary planning.

“We share Governor Abbott’s emphasis on responsible infrastructure development and the importance of considering community priorities, natural resources and infrastructure impacts,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “These considerations are part of Diode’s approach to evaluating potential development sites.”

Beaufils said he expects to see more projects withdrawn as there’s more community opposition.

Abbott stated that he plans to seek legislation to require large data centers to annually report electricity and water usage data to the PUC and repeal any sales tax exemptions or other outdated or unnecessary incentives for the facilities.

Despite environmental and community groups, and many Democrats, seeing eye-to-eye with much of what amounts to Abbott’s data center moratorium, there’s skepticism among them about whether the directives, like reusing water and data centers bringing their own power, will become legislation that Abbott will sign once the midterms have passed. There’s also widespread skepticism among them about the timing of Abbott’s audit.

Texans understand Gov. Abbott rolled out the red carpet for data centers with some of the largest tax breaks in the country, said Jacob Long, a spokesman for Texas Democrats, in a statement.

“Greg Abbott is desperately trying to rewrite his own record, but Texans will not be fooled by his election year flip flops,” Long said. “Data centers will get every green light under the sun if Greg Abbott gets four more years.”

Tammabattula said the wider industry acknowledges the political moment the governor is in and expects that if Abbott is reelected, the new rules outlined in his directives would eventually be relaxed. “But it’s not going to be the same,” Tammabattula said. “It won’t be the same Texas anymore—where Texas is the best place and easy to do business for data centers—I don’t think so.”

Industry forced to ask permission

For a long time, the data center industry, which built server closets in office basements and supported early web services, like online banking, flew under the radar of the general public. Now, the opposite is true as tech companies race to develop AI systems that require massive data centers that sprawl across large tracts of land.

“They say that all publicity is good publicity, but that’s really only true when engagement is the bottom line,” Matt Richesin, an analyst for S&P Global Energy Horizon’s 451 Research, said at a webinar on artificial intelligence infrastructure earlier this month. “For the data center industry, at least the developmental arm of it,” engagement has now become a battleground with both political parties in Texas vowing strong opposition.

Ongoing concerns in Texas about electricity and water use, air quality and further community impact has driven interest in more data center regulation both on the state level and within local communities, said Lilli Flynn, a senior analyst at DC Byte, a data center market intelligence firm.

That’s as data center capacity has tripled between 2020 and 2025 across the U.S., said Tony Lenoir, the market research firm’s associate director of data centers and energy. It’s expected to grow the same share, three times larger, by 2030.

Yet about two-thirds of the data center projects the research firm is tracking across the country are at risk from community pushback or pending legislation, said Dan Thompson, research director of data center services and infrastructure at 451 Research.

The opposition data centers have garnered in the last year is much stronger than garden variety “not in my backyard” syndrome, in which people agree a development has merit, as long as it’s not too close to where they live, Richesin said. Now, people want developers to build no data centers anywhere, near anyone, or anything. The opposition, Richesin said, is “a bit more extreme and straightforward.”

The industry traditionally approaches early-stage planning by following a decide, announce, then defend, process. “That’s probably not going to work well now with the opposition the way that it is,” Richesin said.

Developers can no longer count on overcoming communities’ opposition, Richesin said. No matter what developers say, there are likely some communities that just don’t want data centers anywhere near them. “There’s not a whole lot that’s going to be able to be done,” Richesin said.

The industry is learning that it needs new engagement strategies in this era of near-total opposition if it is going to achieve its growth objectives in Texas, and across the country, Beaufils said. “I think we’re seeing a change in behavior there, right?”

In 2023 and 2024, BaRupOn didn’t do any community events, Tammabattula said. In 2025, they did two. And so far in 2026, they’ve done eight. Tammabattula said his colleagues now dread working community-outreach events, as nearby residents have hard-set views against data centers.

When it comes to their East Texas campus, Tammabattula said that communication with residents has tended to feel like a one-way conversation. “That’s an unfortunate thing where they are so angry they don’t want to even engage into any kind of dialogue,” Tammabattula said.

Even though these town hall events result in heated discussions, Tammabattula said they still have to be done in the hope that some new understanding can emerge.

When BaRupOn began looking to develop a new project in Gillette, Wyoming, given the opposition it faced in Texas, they met with all the neighbors. For a prospective facility in North Dakota, BaRupOn is planning to make the landowners small equity owners of the project. Involving the community ahead of purchasing land has become a new best practice to avoid pushback down the road, he said.

Since the pause of environmental permits in Texas, Tammabattula said his firm has redirected its priority to developing sites outside the state.

But Beautfils said that only so many developers will seek to move to states with more available space, lower land costs and more supportive legislatures. Because while states like Wyoming, North Dakota and New Mexico may now be offering developers faster scenarios, they are all limited in how many huge hyperscale data centers they can handle, and offer a less-developed grid than Texas.

“If there is too much crowding in one given area, then we’ll probably see the same problem emerge again,” Beaufils said.

At Aurora Energy Research, more than half of the 277 gigawatts of project capacity the research firm is tracking across the country—most of it in Texas—is from companies that have never developed a data center before. Only 81 gigawatts were being developed by what the researchers called proven operators—companies like Meta, Beaufils said, that had developed data centers before.

Some 145 gigawatts of capacity, which have submitted interconnection requests and have the land or permits necessary to advance, are newcomers, and have no operational capacity, Beaufils said. The more than 400-gigawatt pipeline in Texas is full of speculative projects, he said. It’s clearly vastly more than what the industry is capable of building and paying for, Beaufils added.

“They’re coming into this business as it looks attractive and juicy,” Beaufils said. “As it becomes more difficult, I would expect a number of these projects to just disappear.”

description:

text:
Opinion Piece by Illari Aragon, Global Policy and Advocacy Lead, Christian Aid,

Co-chair, ACT Alliance Climate Justice Reference Group.

COP31 will take place in Antalya, Turkiye, from the 9-20 November. It will test whether governments can turn existing climate commitments into funded action for the countries and communities most affected by climate change. Four priorities will be critical: a just transition away from fossil fuels, finance to adapt to climate impacts, support for countries facing loss and damage and meaningful progress on the finance negotiations.

The need for decisive action on the climate crisis could not be clearer. The chance of holding global warming below 1.5 is now gone. The latest scientific evidence indicates that the world is set to cross the 1.5°C warming limit within the next few years, with projections for warming that could reach 2.8 °C by the end of the century. Above 1.5°C, risks and impacts can increase dramatically, including intensified extreme weather events, ecosystem loss, damage to human health, food and water security.

On top of this, a supersized El Niño is underway – a natural phenomenon whose impacts are only compounded by climate change. El Nino will bring intensified droughts, floods, crop losses, food insecurity, and displacement across many parts of the world. Governments and communities need stronger early warning systems, resilient infrastructure, greater access to adaptation finance, and timely support for disaster response and recovery.

COP31 must turn political commitments into practical, adequately funded action. Four areas will be critical to watch:

Keeping fossil fuels on the agenda

One of the disappointments of COP30 in Brazil was the failure to secure an explicit reference to phasing out fossil fuels in the final negotiated outcome. Yet momentum for a transition away from fossil fuels continues to build outside the formal COP process.

Earlier this year, 57 governments met in Colombia for the first International Conference on the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels, demonstrating growing international support for addressing one of the root causes of the climate crisis.

COP31 should continue to place this consequential issue at the centre of the talks and its outcomes.

The challenge is ensuring that this transition is genuinely just. Too often, climate discussions focus narrowly on reducing emissions while overlooking a fundamental reality: more than 560 million people in sub-Saharan Africa alone live without electricity. This is more than the entire population of the European Union.

For many developing countries, the challenge is not simply about transitioning from one energy source to another but about expanding access to clean, affordable and reliable energy for the first time.

A just transition must therefore be judged not only by how quickly fossil fuel use declines, but whether it also expands access to clean energy for all.

This is where the new Just Transition Mechanism, agreed at COP30, could prove critical. The Mechanism has the potential to help countries pursue low-carbon development and ensure that equity and energy access remain central. However, key questions around the Mechanism’s governance, financing, and implementation remain unresolved. It is yet to be decided how the Mechanism will support countries in practice.

COP31 should deliver a well-resourced mechanism capable of supporting countries through finance, technology transfer, capacity building, and international cooperation. Without this, a “just transition” could remain aspiration rather than becoming a reality.

More broadly, for a transition to be genuinely just, it must avoid creating new forms of injustice. Demand for critical minerals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel, and copper will continue to grow as countries expand renewable energy and electric vehicle technologies. While this presents important economic opportunities for mineral-rich developing countries (many in the global south), it also carries environmental and social risks. A just transition requires responsible mining, respect for community rights, and greater investment in local industries so that producing countries can capture more of the benefits. They should not simply supply the minerals that power the clean energy transition elsewhere, they should also benefit through better access to energy, decent jobs, and broader economic opportunities for their own people.

Ultimately, the success of the energy transition will depend not only on how quickly the world moves away from fossil fuels, but on whether the benefits of that transition are shared equitably.

2. Adaptation finance: the most urgent gap

Adaptation remains one of the most underfunded areas of climate action. Last year’s agreement at COP30 to triple adaptation finance by 2035 was a significant political achievement. But this commitment remains unclear. Governments have not agreed on an exact financial target or at least a baseline year to calculate the tripling, nor a roadmap for delivery and accountability. Without these details, the commitment risks becoming another headline announcement that fails to translate into tangible support for vulnerable countries.

The scale of the challenge is sobering. According to latest estimates, international public adaptation finance flowing to developing countries stands at approximately $26 billion annually (AGR2025.pdf page xiii). At the same time, adaptation needs are projected to reach between $310 billion and $365 billion per year by 2035. Even if adaptation finance were successfully tripled, it would still fall well short of projected needs.

Equally important is the quality of finance. Much international climate finance continues to be provided through loans. Yet adaptation projects often do not generate revenue capable of servicing loans. Building flood defences, developing drought-resistant agriculture, or protecting communities from extreme heat are essential adaptations to climate change, but they do not generate profits in the traditional sense. That is why adaptation support must increasingly come in the form of grants rather than loans.

3. Loss and damage can’t be ignored

The devastating floods that struck Nepal this year offer a reminder that some climate impacts cannot be prevented through mitigation or adaptation alone. Communities need support not only to prepare for climate disasters, but also to recover from them.

The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) is one of the most important achievements of recent climate diplomacy. Created to support countries facing irreversible climate impacts, the fund is now operational and has begun receiving requests for support this year. However, the gap between available resources and actual needs is already huge.

By June 2026, the fund had received 176 funding requests covering 119 countries, totalling $2.8 billion. The FRLD’s start-up phase had a total allocation of $342 million, highlighting the substantial gap between the support requested and the funding available.

Nepal has become the first country to test the emergency procedures of the FRLD following its devastating floods and reconstruction needs estimated in the billions of dollars. This should serve as a warning. As global temperatures continue to rise, demand for loss and damage finance will grow significantly. COP31 must therefore generate political momentum for new and ambitious pledges for the FRLD while reinforcing the urgent need to cut greenhouse gas emissions.

4. The finance conversation that COP31 can’t avoid

Climate finance always influences the success or failure of any COP. This COP31 will be no different.

Negotiations this year will be heavily influenced by the newly established Climate Finance Work Programme, which could become an important forum for resolving long-standing debates about how developed countries will deliver on their obligations under the Paris Agreement.

Developing countries are seeking clearer commitments on the provision of public finance. Many fear that growing emphasis on mobilizing private investment risks obscuring the continued responsibility of developed countries to provide direct financial support, enshrined in article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement. Private finance undoubtedly has a role, but it cannot replace public funding, particularly for adaptation, loss and damage, and support for the poorest and most vulnerable countries. COP31 must therefore reaffirm the importance of public finance and deliver clearer commitments to scale it up.

At COP31 governments must demonstrate that international cooperation can still deliver meaningful action. For millions of people already living with the consequences of climate change, the decisions taken in Antalya will matter far beyond the negotiating rooms.

title: Pushing the Envelope - RMI
authors: Eva Rosenbloom, Maggie Huang, Brett Webster
description:
Envelope retrofits, which seal and insulate a building’s exterior barrier, are at the heart of that effort.
Many envelope retrofit strategies already exist to make buildings more energy-efficient, however, they vary in market maturity and remain difficult to implement at scale.
Envelope Retrofit Strategies New York’s diverse building stock calls for a range of retrofit pathways, as no single solution applies universally across building types, conditions, and ownership structures.
Scaling Envelope Retrofits Despite growing solution development and deployment, persistent barriers make envelope retrofit projects difficult to advance and repeat.
A durable retrofit market requires coordinated progress across the industry beyond addressing individual challenges in policy, financing, or workforce.
text:
Improving the performance of existing buildings is one of the most critical actions states can take to meet their climate goals — in tandem with increasing housing affordability, resilience, and energy efficiency jobs. Envelope retrofits, which seal and insulate a building’s exterior barrier, are at the heart of that effort. They lower the heating and cooling loads of a building, which reduces the electricity demand on the grid and makes electrification more cost-effective. They also extend the life of aging buildings and improve comfort, helping people stay safely in their homes longer during extreme weather or power outages. Many envelope retrofit strategies already exist to make buildings more energy-efficient, however, they vary in market maturity and remain difficult to implement at scale.

Sponsored by the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) and prepared by RMI, this report is primarily directed at project delivery stakeholders, including building owners, project team members, and manufacturers. It provides a granular assessment of envelope solutions for New York’s building stock (with a focus on multifamily buildings and some applicability to office buildings), key suitability considerations for decision-making, and resources to guide project teams, while also touching on the current market, key challenges, and recommendations to promote affordable, scalable solutions that accelerate market growth. Although focused on New York, many of the challenges and lessons are not unique to this state and can inform efforts in other cold climate regions.

Envelope Retrofit Strategies

New York’s diverse building stock calls for a range of retrofit pathways, as no single solution applies universally across building types, conditions, and ownership structures. Most approaches fall into three primary categories:

Light-touch interventions (targeted weatherization)

Full retrofits from the interior

Full retrofit from the exterior (over-cladding), including site-built and prefabricated approaches

The report outlines how each approach performs across key considerations such as cost, constructability, disruption, durability, and operational impact. It also highlights where each strategy is most appropriate and how building-specific constraints, including structural capacity, occupancy, site conditions, and regulatory requirements, influence feasibility and selection.

Scaling Envelope Retrofits

Despite growing solution development and deployment, persistent barriers make envelope retrofit projects difficult to advance and repeat. Getting projects off the ground remains challenging; costs are high, uncertain, and poorly understood; retrofit value is not fully recognized; demand is too fragmented to support investment; and workforce and delivery capabilities need to mature alongside solutions.

Scaling deployment requires more than continued technical innovation. It will also require more streamlined delivery conditions and stronger market organization, so that both proven and emerging solutions are easier to select, finance, install, verify, and repeat.

Repeatable Project Delivery

A consistent indicator of retrofit success is whether an owner would pursue the same strategy again. Lessons from early projects suggest that repeatability depends less on peak performance and more on predictability, manageable disruption, and alignment with long-term asset planning. Projects that deliver durable improvements, minimize tenant disruption, and remain predictable in cost and schedule are more likely to be replicated. Integrated design and delivery, contingency planning, standardized approaches, alignment with capital cycles, and tenant management strategies can support more reliable outcomes and deployment at scale.

Creating Market Conditions for Scale

Building-specific conditions will continue to shape individual retrofit projects, but scaling requires solutions to be delivered more consistently and repeatedly across buildings and portfolios. Achieving this depends on broader market conditions that support sustained demand and industry investment. A durable retrofit market requires coordinated progress across the industry beyond addressing individual challenges in policy, financing, or workforce. The three improvement areas can be summarized as follows:

Create a favorable landscape: Align policy, incentives, financing, and risk allocation to enable investment and reduce barriers to entry.

Simplify the retrofit process: Reduce complexity across planning, decision-making, and delivery to improve project clarity and predictability.

Build market capacity: Expand workforce capability, manufacturing readiness, and supply-chain coordination to support scalable deployment.

The current and future opportunity is to better align these elements to support repeatability, reduce costs and uncertainty, and build confidence across the market. Together, these efforts can enable a shift from fragmented, project-by-project implementation toward more standardized and scalable delivery, positioning envelope retrofits as a core pathway for decarbonizing New York’s and other states’ existing building stocks.
