text:
Inox Solar Americas has confirmed that its planned photovoltaic (PV) cell manufacturing facility in Greenville, North Carolina, is on track to begin production in the second quarter (Q2) of 2027.

The US-based company states that the new plant will have an annual capacity of 3GW and occupy 515,460ft².

The facility forms a core element of Inox Solar Americas’ efforts to develop a vertically integrated domestic solar manufacturing platform within the US.

According to the company, producing PV cells domestically will complement its current US-based PV module output, increasing access for customers to solar technology made in the country and expanding the transparency and resilience of the domestic supply chain.

Inox Solar Americas’ manufacturing strategy emphasises domestic content across its products. The company says this will help customers address shifting requirements related to domestic content, “Foreign Entity of Concern” and “Prohibited Foreign Entity” considerations, relevant trade regulations, and provisions stemming from federal energy policy.

The company is focused on documented manufacturing procedures, qualified sourcing, and compliance readiness intended to assist customers managing complex procurement and project planning.

Integrating PV cell and PV module production in the US is also expected to help improve visibility and control throughout the solar supply chain.

The company indicates it is strengthening processes for supplier qualification, sourcing documentation, traceability of materials, and due diligence, to offer customers clearer insight into the origins and manufacturing details of their products.

Increasing domestic production is also intended to reduce reliance on imported PV cells and limit exposure to global supply disruptions or trade-related risks.

The Greenville facility will feature the company’s Galaxion monocrystalline PV cell technology, alongside its Gamma Series monofacial and Vega Series bifacial PV modules.

Inox Solar Americas reports that the plant will use automated manufacturing systems and process controls to maintain consistent quality and production traceability from PV cell fabrication through to finished modules.

Inox Solar Americas president and CEO Ashok Nair said: “By bringing advanced cell technology, high-performance module manufacturing, and rigorous quality control together within our US manufacturing platform, we are strengthening our ability to support customers with reliable supply and the bankability required for their project pipelines.”

text:
Input

2026-11-03 10:45:32

Updated

2026-11-03 10:45:32

[Financial News] Ruling and opposition lawmakers united in calling for electric vehicles to be included among the beneficiaries of the government’s proposed ‘Korean version of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA).’ With lawmakers from both sides demanding tax support for domestic EV production at last month’s parliamentary audit, this month’s National Assembly review of the tax amendment bill has emerged as a turning point. As Chinese-made EVs’ share of the domestic market has surpassed 40%, policy measures to protect the production base for domestically made vehicles are emerging as a key issue.

■ Ruling and opposition parties introduce 24 bills ... November review to be pivotal

According to the auto industry on the 3rd, lawmakers from both sides repeatedly called for electric vehicles to be included among those eligible for the domestic production tax credit during the parliamentary audit, which concluded on the 30th of last month. In particular, lawmakers held intensive questioning over the government’s plan to exclude EVs from support during the comprehensive audit of the Ministry of Economy and Finance by the National Assembly’s Finance and Economy Planning Committee, held on the 22nd of last month.

People Power Party lawmaker Ahn Sang-hoon pointed out, ‘Major developed countries are pulling out all the stops—tariffs, tax credits and subsidies—to protect their domestic EV industries,’ adding, ‘There seems to be virtually no country that has protected its market without an active response.’ Fellow party lawmaker Bae Joon-young also stressed the need for policy support for the EV industry, saying, ‘When the semiconductor industry was struggling in the past, the government acted as a catalyst.’

Similar calls came from the Democratic Party of Korea. Lawmaker Yoon Hoo-deok called for expanding eligibility for the tax credit, saying, ‘Chinese-made EVs are rapidly taking over domestic and international markets, putting the domestic EV industry in a crisis.’ Lawmaker Moon Jin-seok criticized the government’s proposal, saying, ‘It seems to be pushing domestic automakers to the brink as they compete with Chinese automakers, which have strong price competitiveness.’

At the National Assembly Committee on Climate, Energy, Environment and Labor, People Power Party lawmaker Na Kyung-won also said, ‘The United States and Europe are defending their domestic industries with tariffs and other measures, while we are effectively using no such tools,’ and called for measures to boost the competitiveness of domestically made EVs.

In response, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyung-il said at the Hyundai Motor-Kia technical research institute he visited on the 2nd, ‘The next battleground for a rebound in potential growth is EVs,’ adding, ‘The government will also actively participate in the National Assembly’s discussions and continue to engage in in-depth deliberations.’

The tax reform plan announced by the government last August included six sectors—solar power, wind power, secondary batteries, semiconductors, key materials, and artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics components—but excluded electric vehicles.

By contrast, a total of 24 bills to include future-oriented vehicles such as EVs among the eligible support targets were introduced in the 22nd National Assembly. Of these, 11 were introduced by members of the Finance and Economy Planning Committee, and 8 were sponsored by members of the Tax Subcommittee. Whether to include EVs is expected to be discussed in earnest at the Tax Subcommittee’s review this month.

■ Chinese-made EVs surge ... domestically made cars lose their majority share

Behind the growing calls to expand tax support is the rapid encroachment of Chinese-made EVs into the market. According to statistics from the Korea Automobile & Mobility Association (KAMA) and the Korea Automobile Importers & Distributors Association (KAIDA), 112,417 Chinese-made passenger EVs were newly registered in South Korea from January through September this year, 2.2 times the 51,535 registered in the same period a year earlier.

Chinese-made passenger EVs captured 43.5% of the market, up 8.4 percentage points from the same period a year earlier. By contrast, the market share of domestically made passenger EVs fell 6.2 percentage points to 48.7%, dropping below half. This has raised concerns that intensifying competition in the EV market could also affect the foundations of domestic production and employment.

An auto industry official emphasized, ‘Chinese-made EVs have secured price competitiveness across their supply chains, including materials, parts and batteries,’ adding, ‘Given that South Korea’s export-oriented industrial structure makes it difficult to take trade measures like those of major economies, policy support—including the domestic production tax credit—needs to be provided in a timely manner.’

title: Louisiana's accidental blueprint for restoring its coast - Grist
description:

Since 2007, CPRA has completed just three diversion projects totaling $47 million, according to the agency’s 2027 annual plan.
After canceling the Mid-Barataria Sediment Diversion, the agency dusted off an earlier, much smaller version of the project: the Medium Diversion at Myrtle Grove.

text:
Arthur Matherne is used to speeding his airboat across a southeastern stretch of the Louisiana coast where lakes and bayous have widened as the Gulf of Mexico’s salty water has moved in, dissolving marshes and swamps.

But in one tucked-away patch of the Barataria Basin’s 1.6 million acres, the semi-retired tour guide eases off the throttle as he tries to remember his way through channels that have grown tighter by the year. Grasses are overtaking the shallows, and oak branches are spreading overhead, dangling Spanish moss over waterways he once barreled through.

“All this, it’s filling in,” Matherne said after shutting off his airboat’s roaring propeller. “Right here, it used to be three feet of water. Now it’s three inches.”

What Matherne is seeing is a striking reversal of a pattern that has defined south Louisiana for the past century. While much of the coastal zone has receded at about 11 square miles per year from erosion and other forces compounded by climate change, the wetlands here are gaining ground.

The reason is just a few miles away. Near Luling in St. Charles Parish, the Davis Pond Freshwater Diversion has funneled Mississippi River water into the basin since the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers built it in 2002 to combat saltwater intrusion. But something unexpected happened. The diversion also carried the muddy river’s sediment into the wetlands, raising the bottom and helping create new land.

“It’s had this unintended consequence of building land,” said Jacob Berkowitz, an Army Corps of Engineers wetland scientist. “This became one of the strategies that’s considered a key to addressing coastal land loss in Louisiana.”

Yet even as Davis Pond demonstrates the land-building potential of river diversions, Louisiana has abandoned its most ambitious attempt to put that approach to work. Last year, the state canceled the massive Mid-Barataria Sediment Diversion, a $3 billion project inspired by Davis Pond and once heralded by the state as “the largest and boldest environmental restoration project in U.S. history.” Though it broke ground in 2023, work stopped shortly after Governor Jeff Landry, a Republican and one of the diversion’s most prominent critics, took office in 2024. He officially terminated the project, which would have been located 20 miles south of New Orleans, in July 2025.

Landry called the diversion a costly and ineffective “experiment” that would harm the commercial fishing industry by flooding parts of Barataria Bay with too much freshwater and sediment, pushing out shrimp and burying oysters.

“This project is going to break our culture,” Landry told state lawmakers in 2024. “It will destroy the shrimping industry – which is already struggling – and destroy the oyster beds.”

Landry’s administration also canceled a companion project – the $1.8 billion Mid-Breton Sediment Diversion, aimed at reviving dying wetlands southeast of New Orleans.

Despite Landry’s opposition to these projects, his administration is quietly planning more diversions along the Mississippi, albeit on a smaller scale.

Officials with the Louisiana Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority declined to discuss the state’s diversion plans, but a Verite News review of the authority’s budget documents indicates the state plans to spend at least $340 million on five projects over the next several years that would divert Mississippi River water to restore coastal wetlands. That represents a big increase over past spending on diversions. Since 2007, CPRA has completed just three diversion projects totaling $47 million, according to the agency’s 2027 annual plan.

While some state leaders may disparage diversions, CPRA scientists still believe using river water to rebuild land and restore wetlands is a sound approach. At its core, a diversion mimics how the Mississippi functioned before levees walled off its floodplain, preventing the river from overflowing its banks or breaking through them at points called crevasses, according to Brian Gossman, a CPRA coastal scientist, speaking during a public lecture in March.

“The natural process that we’re attempting to harness is the Delta cycle,” Gossman said. “It’s the same process that built all of coastal Louisiana over millennia. We’re just using it in a targeted way.”

Nearly all of the authority’s diversion spending would go to one project — the restoration of Maurepas Swamp, a Chicago-sized wetland along the west edge of Lake Pontchartrain, about 25 miles from New Orleans.

The $334 million project, which broke ground in 2024, will install gates in the Mississippi River levee near Garyville in St. John the Baptist Parish and channel up to 2,000 cubic feet per second of water into Maurepas, which remains one of the country’s largest swamps despite losing thousands of acres of cypress and tupelo forest. Levees built in the early 1900s cut the swamp off from freshwater and sediment, leaving its trees vulnerable to saltwater intrusion.

According to the CPRA, the diversion will rebuild lost land and flush out stagnant, salty water, rejuvenating about 45,000 acres. It’s set for completion late next year.

The authority hasn’t totally given up on diverting sediment into the Barataria Basin. After canceling the Mid-Barataria Sediment Diversion, the agency dusted off an earlier, much smaller version of the project: the Medium Diversion at Myrtle Grove. Proposed more than 25 years ago, the project would divert up to 15,000 cubic feet of river water per second into the basin — about one-third of Mid-Barataria’s typical operating rate. To speed up the creation of marsh, the authority would also dredge sediment from the Mississippi and pump it directly into the basin.

The Myrtle Grove project’s timeline and budget are unclear. CPRA’s budget documents indicate about $1.7 million could be spent on it between 2027 and 2029, but the full cost will likely be much more. In 2012, the project was estimated at $278 million, or about $480 million in today’s dollars.

CPRA’s spending plans would also boost the Davis Pond diversion. The agency has proposed spending $3 million, shared with the Army Corps, to study how the diversion could be operated to build more land.

Research led by Tulane University in 2019 suggested that boosting the diversion’s average flow from 1,000 cubic feet per second to between 4,000 and 7,000 cubic feet per second could deliver more sediment to nearby wetlands. But if the flow is too high, researchers warned, the sediment will be flushed away.

In St. Charles Parish, home to Davis Pond, finding ways to increase the diversion’s flows has strong support. In its 2025 habitat restoration plan, the parish endorsed the proposed CPRA study, citing criticism that the diversion’s operations were “not being aggressive enough” to maximize its benefits.

Watching Davis Pond’s silty flows creep past his airboat, Matherne agreed the diversion should release more water and sediment. “Right now, it’s like pissing in an Olympic-size swimming pool,” he said. “We need more flow.”

The Army Corps built the diversion to improve oyster beds that had become too salty as coastal marshes receded. Oyster abundance in the area has fluctuated since the diversion was built, but recent monitoring data suggests populations on public beds were above their 10-year averages in 2024, according to Danielle Richardi, a CPRA coastal scientist. Shrimp catches south of the diversion hit a nearly four-decade high that same year, she said.

Matherne said he’s seen a marked increase in wildlife. Alligators are more plentiful, he said, pointing out more than a dozen of the reptiles as his boat traveled the maze of waterways near the diversion. “All the alligators you see – that’s a fraction of what’s out there,” he said. “Come back at night, and you’ll see their eyes shining all over.”

Several studies have documented how accumulated sediment has built land near the diversion, although researchers in recent years have reached conflicting conclusions about the overall impact on wetland acreage.

In 2019, Louisiana State University coastal sciences professor Eugene Turner challenged conventional thinking about river diversions with a study linking Davis Pond to increased wetland loss. Turner found that the annual rate of wetland loss near Davis Pond nearly tripled after the diversion began operating, increasing from 0.36 percent to more than 1 percent. The increase was greater than in nearby wetlands unaffected by the diversion.

One explanation might have to do with what’s in the water. While the diversion was intended to restore the Mississippi’s pre-levee connections to surrounding wetlands, the river’s water has changed dramatically over the past century. It now carries high concentrations of nitrogen and phosphorus, much of it from fertilizer and manure runoff from farms and wastewater discharged by cities upstream. Turner argues that the excess nutrients produce wetland plants that are, essentially, flabby and weak.

“If your garden is fertilized too much, it puts all its growth aboveground,” he said. “It falls over because its roots never had to work hard.”

Turner believes that lower nutrient levels encourage plants to develop stronger root systems, making marshes more resistant to erosion. He likens some of the apparent land gains from diversions to a “green toupee.” The wetlands may look as though they’re filling in, but strong winds or currents can easily strip away the vegetation.

Two of Turner’s colleagues disputed his findings in a 2023 study. John White and John Day, also LSU coastal sciences professors, found that the first 20 years of Davis Pond’s operations had actually led to a net gain of 1.3 square miles of land. Their study said Turner came to an “erroneous conclusion” by incorrectly using data “that was clearly labeled as inappropriate for the task.”

The researchers asserted that Turner’s satellite data were too imprecise to distinguish small patches of wetlands from open water, potentially making land appear to have disappeared when it hadn’t.

Turner stands by his findings, arguing they more accurately portray how diversions affect coastal wetlands and warn of the damage they can cause if poorly managed.

Opponents of the Mid-Barataria diversion regularly cited Turner’s research and added several more concerns, including the CPRA’s projections that the huge diversion could bury oyster beds under sediment and that added freshwater would likely push shrimp farther offshore, making them harder to catch. Combined with the project’s $3 billion price tag, those concerns cratered political support.

“Considering the uncertainties and questionable environmental outcomes recognized by various agencies … it was necessary to abandon the current project,” CPRA Chairman Gordon Dove wrote in a column in The Times Picayune.

Although the CPRA has yet to fully explain its new approach to diversions, smaller and cheaper projects appear to be a priority. Turner welcomes that shift, but argues diversions should also operate at lower flows to avoid washing away vegetation that he believes excessive nutrients have weakened. He also recommends building diversions in areas with sandy soils rather than the soft, unstable soil in many marshes.

“It’s not that they won’t work,” Turner said. “These diversions give you lessons. We should learn from them.”

Background and Context

Founded in 2026, Inox Solar Americas operates as part of the broader renewable energy platform of Inox Clean Energy and the India-headquartered INOXGFL Group. Key Details

The latest update confirms that the 3 GW annual-capacity solar cell manufacturing plant has successfully moved into the equipment installation phase. This development builds upon Inox Solar Americas’ acquisition of Boviet Solar’s U.S. PV manufacturing assets in Greenville, which already included 3 GW of annual PV module manufacturing capacity. Once fully operational in the second quarter of 2027, the new facility will integrate advanced Galaxion™ monocrystalline PV cell technologies with the company’s existing module production lines. The manufacturing site is designed to incorporate advanced automation, precision cell processing, integrated inspection, rigorous testing protocols, and complete production traceability to ensure high quality and regulatory compliance.

What This Means for EPCs and Developers

For EPC contractors, solar developers, and procurement professionals operating in regulated markets, localized manufacturing asset integration is crucial. The addition of domestic PV cell manufacturing capabilities directly addresses complex U.S. procurement hurdles, including evolving domestic-content requirements, Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC), Prohibited Foreign Entity (PFE) considerations, and federal energy policy provisions. By securing a transparent, resilient, and reliable domestic supply chain, buyers can mitigate trade risks and streamline project deployment across residential, commercial, industrial, community solar, and utility-scale applications.

What Happens Next

With the project now entering the equipment installation phase, focus shifts toward completing internal assembly lines and initiating trial runs ahead of the Q2 2027 production target. Meanwhile, as Indian conglomerates continue to expand their clean energy manufacturing footprints internationally, the broader Indian renewable energy sector watches closely how domestic players scale advanced photovoltaic technologies across global markets.

title: Will Clean Energy Stocks Get Their Credits Back? - Trefis
description:
Enphase is 61% below its 52-week high and Plug Power 68% below.
The homeowner solar credit expired at the end of 2025.
The credits that survived, like the factory credit that helps First Solar, can’t be cut again without the House.
A Democratic House can protect what survived and question the Treasury’s rules.
The clean-energy stocks to watch are tied to power demand and to the President’s trade calls, not to the vote count.
text:
For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Part of our midterms guide. Start here: what the vote really changes for your money.

Betting markets give Democrats about a 94% chance of winning the House on Tuesday, and about three in four of taking the Senate. Clean-energy investors hope that means the subsidies return. President Trump keeps his veto, and Democrats won’t have the votes to override it. So the credits that are gone stay gone, at least until 2029.

Company Value 12-month return What drives it now Exposure to the vote NextEra Energy (NEE) $178B +7% Power demand from data centers Low First Solar (FSLR) $20B −32% Manufacturing credit it kept; new import price floors Medium Rivian (RIVN) $19B −3% R2 launch without the $7,500 credit Low-medium Enphase (ENPH) $3.7B −8% Home solar after the homeowner credit expired Medium Plug Power (PLUG) $1.8B −51% Hydrogen credit timeline; cash Medium

The winner is the one that sells power, not panels.

Enphase is 61% below its 52-week high and Plug Power 68% below. NextEra is 12% below.

See more lines: how we rated exposure

Exposure is our judgment of how much Tuesday’s outcome can change each company’s revenue or costs, given that a Democratic House can hold hearings, write budgets and block bills, but can’t pass laws past a veto. Values and 12-month returns are at the Nov 2 close (Trefis market data).

What Did The 2025 Law Take Away?

Three big things. The $7,500 EV credit ended for vehicles bought after Sept 30, 2025. The homeowner solar credit expired at the end of 2025. And wind and solar projects that start construction after July 4, 2026 lose the main production and investment credits unless running by the end of 2027. The damage shows. Enphase’s third-quarter revenue fell 29% from a year earlier, and U.S. sales of its products to installers fell 35%.

What Can A Democratic House Actually Do?

Restore credits? No. That needs a bill the President signs. He won’t.

Stop further cuts? Yes. The credits that survived, like the factory credit that helps First Solar, can’t be cut again without the House. That protects what’s left. It doesn’t add anything.

Oversight. The Treasury writes the fine print: what counts as “starting construction,” and which Chinese parts disqualify a project. A Democratic House can question those rules. It can’t rewrite them.

The 2027 debt limit. Democrats get leverage when the borrowing limit must be raised. Their first ask is health care money, not solar. Clean-energy credits are a long shot in that deal.

Who Decides What Really Moves These Stocks?

The President, on tariffs. In August he set import price floors on polysilicon, solar cells and panels, plus a 15% tariff on some products. They take effect Dec 4. Floors on imported panels help a U.S. maker like First Solar and raise costs for installers. Congress had no vote.

The market, on power demand. NextEra says it has signed deals to build about 16.5 gigawatts of power at three hubs for large data-center sites, and its backlog of renewables and storage is about 36.7 gigawatts. Tech giants need electricity fast, and solar plus batteries is quick to build. That demand doesn’t care who runs the House.

Buyers, on EVs. Rivian raised its 2026 delivery outlook to 67,000 to 70,000 last week, credit or not. Its test is the R2’s price, not Congress.

What Could Go Wrong?

Tariffs bite. The Dec 4 floors could raise panel prices for home installers, Enphase’s customers.

Rates stay high. Home solar is financed. Enphase blamed high rates as well as the lost credit.

Dilution. Plug Power trades at about $1.31 a share. Companies that need capital often raise it by selling stock, and that hurts holders whoever wins.

The AI trade cools. If data-center spending slows, NextEra’s best story slows with it.

The credits aren’t coming back on Tuesday. A Democratic House can protect what survived and question the Treasury’s rules. It can’t restore what was cut, and it has no say on tariffs. The clean-energy stocks to watch are tied to power demand and to the President’s trade calls, not to the vote count.

Related: Tesla and the midterms · Which sectors win, which lose.

description:

Microreactors are compact nuclear reactors that could produce up to 20 megawatts of thermal energy.
The study also looks at small modular reactors along with other types of energy generation, Falin said.
While much of energy generation in the coalfields still comes from fossil fuels, like coal and natural gas, localities are looking toward opportunities for renewable energy, Falin said.
“I think as things start to shift in Virginia to more renewable energy and clean energy policies, that’s driving the industry to look at that too,” Falin said.
text:
The last public meeting for Wise County’s microreactor feasibility study will be held on Thursday.

The meeting, at 6 p.m. at The Inn at Wise, will review the results of the community feedback portion of the study as well as a “high level outline” of the final report, said Brian Falin, director of the county’s industrial development authority. The report is planned for release in mid-December.

The study, funded by a $100,000 grant from the Go Virginia Region 1 Council and led by the Virginia Innovative Nuclear, or VIN, Hub, started early this year and looks at the feasibility of building microreactors in Wise County. Microreactors are compact nuclear reactors that could produce up to 20 megawatts of thermal energy. While several companies are developing designs for them, none have been built in the U.S.

The study also looks at small modular reactors along with other types of energy generation, Falin said. Then-Gov. Glenn Youngkin said in October 2022 that he wanted to bring the nation’s first SMR to the coalfields, but he reversed course in 2024, when he said that they were better suited elsewhere.

So far with the study, there have been two public meetings and two rounds of surveys, which brought almost 500 responses, Falin said. Safety, public health and environmental concerns have emerged as main themes from the engagement up to this point, he said, particularly when it comes to the handling of nuclear waste. Job creation has been another focus, he added.

The meeting will be centered on a presentation by the VIN Hub, and it will also act as a round of public comment that will be factored into the final report.

While the study is speculative and there are no active projects, Falin said the hope is that the report gives Wise County a tool it can refer to in future decision-making. Thomas Lawson, a regional planner at LENOWISCO Planning District Commission, told Cardinal News the study weighs several factors, including the demand for power, considerations for siting them and community impacts.

While much of energy generation in the coalfields still comes from fossil fuels, like coal and natural gas, localities are looking toward opportunities for renewable energy, Falin said. But he added that a study like this helps determine if the area will be conducive to supplying the hardware and manufacturing necessary to meet the demand.

“I think as things start to shift in Virginia to more renewable energy and clean energy policies, that’s driving the industry to look at that too,” Falin said.

name: American Energy
title: On Wall Street, the 'energy transition' includes natural gas and data centers | Grist
description:
Blackstone’s is one of several energy transition funds at private equity firms that have consistently grown over the past decade.
Colloquially, “energy transition” refers to the shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy that is necessary to limit the worst impacts of climate change.
Some transition funds — including Blackstone’s — see opportunities for profit in natural gas, data centers, and rising electricity costs.
In the financial industry, the energy transition has grown into a sophisticated economic trend with established players and markets, said Dan Cohn, an energy finance analyst with the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, a think tank focused on the energy transition.
Off Wall Street, the question of whether natural gas and data centers have a role to play in the energy transition is hotly debated.
text:
Blackstone, one of the largest private equity firms in the world, officially changed the name of its dedicated energy investment fund to include the phrase “energy transition” in 2022, having already ceased investing in oil and gas production five years earlier. The pivot toward a new energy future has not diminished interest in the fund. In mid-October, Blackstone announced that the fund pulled in $8.7 billion in investor money this year, reportedly turning away an additional $3 billion to stay under its maximum investment cap.

Blackstone’s is one of several energy transition funds at private equity firms that have consistently grown over the past decade. That growth has continued even as general climate-oriented investment has fallen over the last few years. Colloquially, “energy transition” refers to the shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy that is necessary to limit the worst impacts of climate change. But on Wall Street, the term can mean something a bit different. Some transition funds — including Blackstone’s — see opportunities for profit in natural gas, data centers, and rising electricity costs.

“I know a lot of the investors out there do consider gas a transition fuel,” said Ryan Loughead, a senior associate and former climate solutions analyst for BloombergNEF, an energy research firm.

Private equity funds take new investor money every few years, and then use it to buy existing companies, maximize their profits, and then sell them, returning the money from the sale to investors. Unlike publicly traded companies, whose stocks are available for anyone to buy, private equity firms typically only take investments from large organizations, like pension funds, or very wealthy individuals, and they have faced criticism for prioritizing returns at the expense of workers and the environment.

The transition to renewable energy has been a booming business for private equity firms. “Transition funds” in private equity have raked in $178 billion between 2021 and the beginning of 2026, triple the amount raised by comparable funds dedicated to fossil fuels and general energy, according to Loughead’s research. They’ve maintained their popularity even as other forms of climate-related investments have flagged in the United States, with climate-related venture capital on track to suffer its worst year this decade. (While private equity funds buy out established companies, venture capital funds make smaller investments in startups.)

These shifts have coincided with changes in federal policy, as well as the overall economy. The Biden administration’s signature climate law once spurred innovation in new technologies, but Republicans in Congress repealed most of that legislation last year. Meanwhile, the tech industry’s data center buildout is creating surging demand for electricity and drawing trillions of dollars from investors.

In the financial industry, the energy transition has grown into a sophisticated economic trend with established players and markets, said Dan Cohn, an energy finance analyst with the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, a think tank focused on the energy transition. Private equity funds don’t typically demonstrate investor interest in a budding industry so much as a view that the industry is becoming economically important.

“Investors are sensing oncoming scarcity [of electricity] and are positioning themselves accordingly,” Cohn said. “That speaks to both the moment of rising electricity demand, but also the maturity of clean energy technologies.”

But while these funds seek to capitalize on high demand for electricity, they don’t all show a clear commitment to reducing emissions. Blackstone’s fund is explicit in its view that methane gas, a fossil fuel, is an essential component of the energy transition. The fund no longer invests in oil and gas fields, but it does invest in natural gas plants. When Blackstone rebranded the fund in 2022, the fund’s director, David Foley, explained why natural gas plants were still on the table. “A lot of the capital invested in the energy transition is going into simple renewable power generation assets like solar and wind,” he told an industry publication. “While this is important, just adding renewables to the grid doesn’t necessarily mean you can shut down and remove existing sources of power, such as coal and gas.”

This year, the fund announced investments in six companies, including a natural gas plant operator and a data center cooling technology company, alongside a company focused on renewable energy development and some transmission and grid technology companies. Blackstone did not reply to a request for comment.

Meanwhile, the private equity firm Brookfield governs its transition funds partly through an explicit commitment to decarbonization and emissions reductions. The company has said it can invest in natural gas in cases where it replaces dirtier fossil fuels, but Brookfield has also drawn criticism for describing gas expansion as part of the energy transition.

Similar funds in Europe, like Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners’ Energy Transition Fund, are far more focused on clean energy sources like green hydrogen, with little emphasis on natural gas.

“‘Energy transition’ is a flexible term,” Cohn said. “And I’m unsurprised to see either the gas or electrical equipment and data center-related companies in some of these funds. That is perfectly consistent with how I know some investors think about the energy transition.”

BlackRock, another private equity giant unrelated to Blackstone, explicitly defines “transition” investing as something different from “sustainable” investing: “not all sustainable strategies are transition, and not all transition strategies are sustainable,” its website reads.

That partial overlap could complicate investors’ claims about how sustainable their portfolios are.

At least three major government-managed investors in Blackstone’s energy transition fund have explicit climate investing goals. The Oregon Treasury, Minnesota State Board of Investment, and San Francisco Employees’ Retirement System all have some form of climate-related goal or plan for their investments. Combined, these entities have committed a combined $525 million to the fund, according to Private Equity International, an analytics firm.

These investors did not reply to requests for comment before publication of this article, but the wide range of standards for climate- and energy-related investments has already created confusion. In Oregon, a state representative formally asked the state’s treasury this year to more clearly define what it reports as “climate-positive” investments, which it uses as a category in its public reports.

Investors may have a financial incentive to include gas in their view of the energy transition. Transition funds that include gas tend to have slightly higher returns than those that don’t, Loughead said. And Loughead and Cohn both said the massive rush to invest in the data center boom has permeated funds nominally concerned with the clean energy transition.

Off Wall Street, the question of whether natural gas and data centers have a role to play in the energy transition is hotly debated. Natural gas has cut emissions from the power sector when it has replaced coal, while data centers have spurred investment in grid improvements and clean energy sources. But using natural gas still produces significant emissions — both when it’s burned and when it leaks out of infrastructure — and data centers are spurring more fossil fuel use, potentially slowing progress on global power sector emissions. Plus, some grids are already finding ways to provide reliability with cleaner alternatives to gas, like batteries, which can store renewable energy to use when the sun isn’t shining and the wind isn’t blowing. Most climate and environmental groups argue emphatically that gas should not be seen as a transition fuel.

“Natural gas no longer functions as a credible bridge in the energy transition,” wrote Shruti Shukla, a senior advocate on international energy at the Natural Resources Defense Council in a 2025 article, adding that the fuel “risks slowing decarbonization, raising system costs, and locking economies into avoidable volatility.”

And in the long run, it may not even come to be seen on Wall Street as a questionable investment, according to Cohn. As fuel price spikes continue driving the world toward renewables, fossil fuels may become less and less attractive as investment opportunities.

“There are other very prominent solutions like solar, wind, and batteries, which will mature and continue to see price declines, and so the view that you need gas is increasingly contested,” Cohn said.”

title: Why batteries, not gas plants, should be data centers' first choice - Canary Media
description:
Developers and utilities are building tons of gas generation to power the data center boom.
Overall, U.S. utilities are planning more than 60 gigawatts of new gas plants to serve data center demand, and around 90 GW of behind-the-meter gas generators for data centers have been proposed nationwide.
They’re also inherently modular and flexible in ways that gas power plants are not, which allows planners to increase or cut back on deployment if data center demand shifts sharply.
Data center demand is pushing much of that growth.
So, what can state decision-makers do to further encourage data centers to opt for batteries?
text:
Developers and utilities are building tons of gas generation to power the data center boom. It’s an expansion that could cost them and the rest of us dearly, both in terms of climate change and money that may end up wasted if computing demand fails to materialize.

But there’s a cleaner, cheaper, and faster-to-deploy alternative: batteries.

That’s the conclusion of a new report from researchers at Georgetown and Duke universities, which lays out the ways states can push utilities and tech firms to opt for energy storage over fossil fuels whenever possible.

Fossil fuel power — whether in the form of giant utility-scale plants or generators installed behind the meter at data centers — has become the go-to for many in the AI industry. That’s because gas generation offers round-the-clock power in a single package. Overall, U.S. utilities are planning more than 60 gigawatts of new gas plants to serve data center demand, and around 90 GW of behind-the-meter gas generators for data centers have been proposed nationwide.

“At the moment, there’s a lot of inertia and status quo pressure for much of the behind-the-meter resources being natural gas,” said Ian Hitchcock, report co-author and senior program coordinator at the Duke Initiative for Science and Society.

Moving ahead with those gas power plans does more than spell climate disaster. If data center proposals fall through or shut down early, other utility customers could be on the hook for the cost of overbuilding gas. That’s called ​“stranded asset” risk — and states have only begun to tackle it, even amid mounting fears that the AI sector is a bubble about to pop.

Batteries ​“can act as a hedge against that risk,” last week’s report explains. Batteries are much cheaper than round-the-clock gas generation in situations where hours of stored energy can solve near-term needs. They’re also inherently modular and flexible in ways that gas power plants are not, which allows planners to increase or cut back on deployment if data center demand shifts sharply.

Plus, batteries can help avoid the need for costly grid buildouts that would otherwise be used to serve increasing electricity demand, and can act as shock absorbers to cushion the grid against data centers’ massive and fast-changing computing loads.

While lithium-ion batteries can’t provide round-the-clock power, they can meet large portions of data center electricity needs, said Jackson Ewing, director of energy and climate policy at Duke University’s Nicholas Institute of Energy, Environment & Sustainability. And unlike more future-forward solutions — such as advanced geothermal, next-generation nuclear, and novel long-duration energy storage technologies — ​“batteries are already showing serious momentum in terms of their deployment trajectory.”

In fact, utilities and data center developers are increasingly embracing batteries, even as they pursue gas. A new forecast from BloombergNEF sees U.S. energy storage deployment surpassing 11,000 gigawatt-hours by 2036, a 30% increase from its 10-year forecast from just six months ago. Data center demand is pushing much of that growth.

So, what can state decision-makers do to further encourage data centers to opt for batteries?

States that directly regulate utility investments can craft ​“bring your own new clean energy” tariff structures. These regulations can set minimum requirements for data centers to procure or pay for enough carbon-free generation and energy storage to cover some or all of their electricity needs. Certain jurisdictions are already moving ahead with this approach; Google, for example, has signed onto such tariffs with regulators in Nevada and Minnesota.

Things get more complicated in states with ​“restructured” energy markets. In these places, regulators have limited authority over the independent power producers that build big generation and battery projects and sell power into wholesale electricity markets. Still, the report highlights several ways that these states can encourage battery development to serve data centers, including via state energy storage mandates like those launched in Illinois, Maryland and New Jersey, and engaging in state energy planning in conjunction with regional grid operators.

“There is not a jurisdiction that has no potential action items if they’re serious about trying to deploy this,” Hitchcock said.

title: Trump cuts have left tribes without millions of dollars for clean energy - Canary Media
description:
“We’re pretty much at the mercy of world markets,” Chad Nordlum, who is the energy project manager for the Native Village of Kotzebue, told Grist.
According to Brookings, despite historic investments flowing into Indian Country after the pandemic, a massive underinvestment in Indigenous communities continues.
The report authors are calling for policy changes that would ensure tribes receive funding, regardless of political winds.
That funding, which came under the Biden administration, included over $700 million in climate, energy, and infrastructure funding for tribes.
Maxim says that funding for Indigenous communities is a federal obligation based on treaties and other agreements with tribes and should be standard and irrevocable.
text:
This story was originally published by Grist. Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter.

Every year, Kotzebue, a small city in northwest Alaska, has a three-month window to receive all the diesel fuel it will use throughout the following year. It sits on a gravel spit that juts into Kotzebue Sound just north of the Arctic Circle, and is accessible only by air and sea. Ice keeps freight barges from reaching it for most of the year.

The community relies on diesel for 75% of its power, and residents put about 20% of their income toward buying it. That’s more than three times the average energy burden for low-income households nationwide.

“We’re pretty much at the mercy of world markets,” Chad Nordlum, who is the energy project manager for the Native Village of Kotzebue, told Grist. ​“Right now, with the Iran war going on, the diesel prices are very high and we’re locked in to much higher prices than we’ve had in the past. There’s really nothing the community can do about diesel prices, but what we can do is produce our own energy.”

That’s why Nordlum was so excited about a $20 million grant from the Environmental Protection Agency to support a wind energy project. The funding, announced in 2024, was part of a larger $150 million allocation for tribal infrastructure in Alaska. Nordlum says it would have lowered the community’s reliance on diesel to about 40% to 50% and given the tribe more control over energy and economic decisions.

But the Trump administration canceled the grant in May 2025. More than a year later, the project remains paused.

That cut was among hundreds of millions of dollars the Department of Government Efficiency pulled from Indian Country, and part of a broader pattern of funding rollbacks and underinvestment in Indigenous communities. Two new reports from the Brookings Institution show that the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act killed many of the funding streams established by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, while DOGE eliminated another $468 million, about half of which was allocated for environmental and natural resources. Another 11% targeted agriculture. Those projects include climate resiliency plans, renewable energy projects, and jobs programs.

According to Brookings, despite historic investments flowing into Indian Country after the pandemic, a massive underinvestment in Indigenous communities continues. Not only is that a violation of the federal government’s trust and treaty obligations to tribes; it is hindering Indigenous efforts to protect the environment and address climate change. The report authors are calling for policy changes that would ensure tribes receive funding, regardless of political winds.

Rob Maxim, who is Mashpee Wampanoag and a fellow at Brookings Metro, said climate and environmental funding is especially crucial for Indigenous communities because they are often the most severely impacted by climate change, especially after years of underinvestment.

“The actions that the Trump administration is taking are particularly significant, but it’s not totally out of trend with previous administrations,” he said. ​“And what we wanted to show was that actually this underinvestment is kind of the default for the U.S. rather than a blip.”

The true aberration was the unprecedented levels of funding after the pandemic. That funding, which came under the Biden administration, included over $700 million in climate, energy, and infrastructure funding for tribes. It covered projects like development of climate action plans, food systems analysis, and more. For example, the Hopi Tribe was to receive a $25 million grant to install solar panels for 600 homes. That grant and the entire $7 billion Solar for All program were cut.

Maxim says that funding for Indigenous communities is a federal obligation based on treaties and other agreements with tribes and should be standard and irrevocable. ​“The funding that was flowing to Indian Country was not being done on the basis of race or DEI, and it was absolutely not illegal,” he said. ​“It was aimed at the promotion of tribal sovereignty and the well-being of tribal citizens and tribal communities, and so that is, you know, an obligation that the U.S. government maintains.”

The White House and the EPA did respond to requests for comment.

Glencora Haskins, a senior research associate and applied research manager at Brookings Metro, said that the administration had targeted funding to tribes, with ​“tribal” being the most frequently flagged term. ​“I think that there was a very surface-level view of what a lot of these programs were doing, rather than any deep interrogation of the types of systemic infrastructure deficits that programs were trying to fix,” Haskins said.

In Native communities throughout Alaska, and around the country, energy and infrastructure needs are especially acute because of increasingly frequent and destructive storms, wildfires, and other climate-driven disasters.

Haskins and Maxim recommend that Congress pass legislation that bars the cancellation of grants and contracts for tribes, and stipulates that all funding for Indigenous nations and communities is in service of trust and treaty obligations even if it is from a program with a different stated purpose. They also call for a statutory requirement that money should flow directly to tribes rather than having them seek reimbursement from the U.S. Treasury.

In Kotzebue, Chad Nordlum hopes the political tide will turn enough to get the funding for the wind project moving. In the meantime, he is working on a smaller solar project that he hopes will help alleviate the community’s energy challenges.

“Our main goals are energy security and economic development for the tribe, which is ultimately being able to invest in our own community, help make the lives of people here a little more sustainable,” Nordlum said. ​“We want our community to continue on into the future. We have to get a handle on our energy prices and availability.”

text:
Highlights

General Motors draws attention as fresh quarterly results reach the market.

Raised full-year guidance and a recalibrated electric-vehicle plan anchor the story.

A deep lineup of trucks and crossovers keeps the automaker squarely in view among value names.

General Motors (NYSE:GM) Consumer Cyclical General Motors Company (NYSE:GM) 88.74 USD -1.201 ↓ 1.335% moved into sharper focus as fresh quarterly results reached the market and traders weighed how the Detroit automaker is balancing a strong core truck business against a recalibrated electric-vehicle plan. As one of the largest vehicle makers in the United States, each update from the company tends to draw a wave of commentary across financial and automotive media.

The renewed attention reflects the breadth of a business that spans pickup trucks, full-size crossovers, a growing battery-electric lineup, financing operations and software-led services. That spread means the group is read as a barometer for the health of the American consumer, the pace of the electric transition and the resilience of industrial earnings all at once.

Interest also owes something to the backdrop. With the wider market tracked by the S&P 500 absorbed in technology earnings and heavy spending on data-center power, cyclical names such as automakers have traded more on their own fundamentals, and market watchers parsed this update closely for evidence of how the company is navigating a shifting demand picture.

Recent Numbers

The central event drawing eyes was the arrival of fresh results that came in firmer than many had braced for, prompting the company to lift its full-year guidance even as it absorbed pressure from import duties and a recalibrated electric-vehicle schedule. Rather than any single headline figure, the update read as a progress check on how the core business is faring.

Reporting periods for the big automakers are closely parsed because they touch so many corners of the economy at once. Vehicle demand, pricing, factory utilization and the pace of the electric transition all feed into the picture, and the latest update offered a clearer look at how each of those threads is trending as the year moves toward its close.

Framed this way, the news matters less for one number and more for the direction of travel. A resilient truck franchise, disciplined pricing and a more measured approach to battery-electric spending combined to shape how the quarter was received, and the timing, arriving amid a busy earnings season, kept the spotlight firmly on the automaker.

Industry Climate At Play

Value-oriented names have drawn steady interest as the market's attention swings between high-flying technology themes and more established businesses trading at modest multiples. Large automakers often feature in that conversation, framed as mature, cyclical franchises whose fortunes track the real economy rather than the latest wave of artificial-intelligence enthusiasm.

Within that value frame, General Motors is frequently cited as a company working to defend its core earnings while navigating the costly shift toward electric vehicles. That narrative gives the group a distinct flavor among value-tilted industrial names, where the emphasis falls on steady execution and capital discipline rather than rapid, unproven expansion.

The broader mood across value stocks has been shaped by the strength of the consumer, the path of borrowing costs and the pace of the electric transition. Each shift in those conditions tends to move sentiment across the whole group rather than any single name in isolation, keeping the conversation around established automakers lively and giving updates from a maker of this size added weight.

Revenue Segments Overview

General Motors operates across several connected arms, spanning its core gasoline vehicle business, a growing battery-electric lineup, a captive financing operation and a suite of software and connected-services offerings. That spread gives the group one of the broadest footprints in the American auto industry, reaching millions of households through a vast dealer network.

The truck and full-size crossover business anchors much of the story, built around well-known nameplates that command loyal followings and firm pricing. This engine provides a steady foundation of earnings that helps fund the heavy spending required to bring new electric models and software features to market.

Alongside the core lineup, the company runs a financing arm that supports vehicle sales and a technology effort spanning driver-assistance systems, connected services and recurring software revenue. This blend of durable vehicle earnings and emerging digital lines defines how the group is framed by those tracking it.

The financing arm deserves particular attention, since it helps buyers afford vehicles while generating a steadier stream of fee revenue that smooths the cyclical swings of the core auto business. The Shifting Electric-Vehicle Strategy

The electric-vehicle plan has become a central thread in how the market reads General Motors. That recalibration reflects a broader cooling in the pace of electric adoption, as buyers weigh charging access, pricing and the appeal of hybrids. The company has signaled a willingness to adjust factory plans and model timing to protect earnings while keeping a foothold in the technologies expected to define the next era of driving.

Market watchers have read this reset as a pragmatic move rather than a retreat, framing it as an effort to balance near-term earnings with long-run positioning. How cleanly the company manages that balance is likely to stay a defining question for the stock in the quarters ahead.

The group has also leaned on a flexible manufacturing approach, aiming to build both gasoline and electric models on shared lines so it can shift production as demand dictates. That adaptability is framed as a hedge against misjudging the tempo of the transition, allowing the company to lean toward whichever powertrain buyers favor without stranding large pools of capital.

A deep lineup, a vast dealer network and a diversified mix of gasoline, electric and software lines form the core of that message. Each arm is framed as a way to diversify revenue and reduce reliance on any single engine, a structure the group argues gives it steadier footing than narrower rivals.

The direction of travel, as described by the group, is toward an automaker that pairs dependable truck earnings with a carefully paced electric push and a growing software layer, able to lean on whichever engine the conditions favor while guarding costs and capital.

Market Challenges Ahead

The auto industry remains exposed to several demanding forces, from swings in consumer demand to shifting trade measures and the heavy cost of the electric transition. Import duties on parts and vehicles can squeeze margins quickly, making trade conditions a constant point of attention for every large automaker.

The pace of electric adoption adds its own uncertainty, as buyers weigh charging access, pricing and the appeal of hybrids. Automakers that misjudge that tempo can be left with idle capacity or stranded spending, making the calibration of electric plans a delicate balancing act.

Competition and supply chains add further pressure. Rivals at home and abroad compete fiercely on price, features and technology, while the availability of chips, batteries and raw materials can shape production. Navigating that landscape while sustaining steady results is a continual challenge for a company of this scale.

Labor and input costs round out the pressures, as wages, materials and logistics all feed into what it costs to build a vehicle. When those costs climb faster than prices, margins can compress quickly, making disciplined manufacturing and careful pricing central to how the company defends its earnings across the cycle.

The heavy capital demands of the transition sit atop all of this. Designing new platforms, building battery capacity and developing software all require sustained spending years before the revenue arrives, so the company must fund tomorrow's vehicles while keeping today's business healthy, a juggling act that defines the modern auto industry.

The Competitive Road Ahead

The auto field remains crowded, with legacy American and international automakers, fast-moving electric specialists and emerging overseas entrants all competing for buyers. Scale, brand strength, a deep dealer network and the ability to fund new technology set the competitive terms across the industry.

Within this field, General Motors is often positioned as a scale leader in trucks and full-size vehicles, a framing it leans into through its well-known nameplates and loyal demand. That strength in the most durable part of the market sets it apart from rivals more concentrated in smaller, lower-margin segments.

Competition also plays out across technology, where driver-assistance features, connected services and the quality of electric offerings increasingly shape where buyers turn. The ability to pair dependable trucks with credible electric and software options has become a meaningful differentiator, and it is a balance the company works hard to strike as newer entrants press on price and features.

text:
Oakland, California – Protesters dressed as cardboard robots chanted and danced to a drumbeat as they protested against new data centres outside Oakland City Hall last month.

Their concerns largely focused on how the centres — which process large amounts of digital information — might strain the energy grid.

The result, they argued, would not only be environmental harm but also sky-high electricity bills for local households.

“Power prices have gone up so much in Oakland that some people are thinking of shutting off their power,” said Carlos Gutierrez, an activist for Communities for a Better Environment, an environmental justice group.

“And the city is planning to provide power to a data centre instead.”

Opposition to data centres is growing across the United States, as residents express concern about their rapid expansion.

More than 3,000 data centres already operate in the country, with more than 1,500 others in development, according to the Pew Research Center.

But the backlash is perhaps most striking in California’s San Francisco Bay Area, a region considered to be the heart of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.

Major AI companies such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta are based in the Bay Area, and the industry’s growth has been credited with fuelling a local economic renaissance.

Data centres house the advanced computer chips and servers needed to run AI-powered services such as Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s ChatGPT.

But they also require 24-hour power and a large supply of water to cool their processors.

Even with such cooling technology, data centres are notorious for emitting heat, leading to an increase in land surface temperatures as high as 9 degrees Celsius (16 degrees Fahrenheit).

A midterm election issue

Concerns about the cost of rapid data centre growth, both environmentally and financially, have catapulted the issue into the discourse around Tuesday’s midterm elections.

In the final two months before the vote, at least seven Bay Area cities, including San Francisco and Richmond, have passed temporary moratoriums on data centre construction.

They include Oakland, which passed a data centre moratorium on October 6, after days of protest.

Local politicians competing in Tuesday’s midterms have also used the topic as a wedge issue, to rally support among certain pockets of voters.

One of the most closely watched races in the Bay Area is for the seat left vacant by longtime Democratic leader Nancy Pelosi. After 39 years in the House of Representatives, Pelosi is retiring at the end of the year.

Two Democrats are competing in Tuesday’s election to fill her position in Congress: San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan and state Senator Scott Wiener.

Each one has staked out a different position on AI data centres. Wiener, for instance, opposes any ban on data centres.

“A blanket data centre moratorium could undermine AI regulation,” he told the publication Mission Local.

Chan, meanwhile, has pledged to seek a nationwide moratorium on data centres, at least until responsible AI regulation is put in place.

“Let’s start with a moratorium on data centres. Allow us to have that moment to regulate artificial intelligence,” she said at a debate in October.

Chan played a leading role in passing San Francisco’s moratorium in early October.

A poll from the University of Southern California showed Wiener leading Chan 47 percent to 41, as of mid-October.

Navigating public backlash

“Right now, data centre opposition is an issue that unifies the US public like no other,” said Shum Preston, a political analyst based in San Francisco.

So far, there has been relatively little opposition to the data centre moratoriums in local hearings. But he speculates that there may be several reasons for the lack of pushback to the bans.

Among them are the surveys indicating widespread public backlash to data centre creation.

An October CNBC poll found that 63 percent of registered US voters oppose building data centres within 16 kilometres, or 10 miles, of their homes.

“Data centres poll very poorly, and developers probably don’t want to put their supervisor friends in trouble ahead of elections. So they probably let this pass,” Preston said.

He also signalled that the short-term nature of the moratoriums may be a factor.

Certain Bay Area cities like San Francisco, Brisbane and Oakland paused construction on data centres for 45 days, with the option to extend the ban later.

Opponents of the moratoriums “will be more vocal when” the 45 days end, Preston said. By that time, the heat of the midterm election season will also have settled, he added.

“That’s when the hearings will get more contentious,” he said.

Not long enough?

Another hurdle facing the moratoriums is the lack of transparency surrounding data centre construction.

Supervisor Shamann Walton, who sponsored San Francisco’s moratorium ordinance, has argued that the city’s definition of “data centres” is outdated.

Created in 2001 — long before the AI boom — the city planning code defines data centres as “internet service exchanges”, a definition that may not accurately characterise the technology today.

Walton said the outdated language has made it hard for authorities to count how many data centres exist in the city.

Not being able to identify data centres can also prevent city officials from monitoring their power and water usage.

“We cannot use 2001 rules to regulate 2026 technology,” he said in a September 14 statement.

Another issue is the time it takes to carry out the necessary environmental assessments. The moratoriums may not offer enough time for a comprehensive review.

“Forty-five days is hardly enough time to document and study the impacts and then frame regulations,” said Roger Lin, senior attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity, a US environmental nonprofit.

He added that legal barriers limit access to such information from the data centres themselves.

“Data centres often have nondisclosure agreements, so even local air quality boards may not know the impact of data centres on air quality,” said Lin.

Supporters tout economic benefits

Still, AI industry supporters have touted the growth of the data centres as evidence of a flourishing industry, with positive downstream effects for US communities.

Anthropic, for instance, is preparing an initial public offering (IPO) that is likely to raise billions of dollars.

But critics warn that the company’s growth may not translate into an economic boom for the San Francisco Bay Area overall.

Instead, residents fear unequal economic growth that primarily benefits the wealthy. Already, San Francisco faces some of the highest and fastest-growing home rental prices in the country.

At a hearing at San Francisco City Hall, a resident vented their frustrations about the data centres to the supervisors.

“This city is less for humans and more for robots and billionaires,” the resident said.

title: Calls grow to include EV production tax credits, raising hopes for Hyundai Motor sales recovery
description:
If tax burdens are reduced based on the production performance of EVs manufactured domestically, domestic automakers, including Hyundai Motor, could build greater capacity to respond to price competition.
For Hyundai Motor, which is competing against Chinese-made EVs on its home turf, lowering vehicle prices or increasing discounts is one way to boost sales.
If a tax credit applies to domestically produced units, some of this burden can be alleviated.
To this end, industry officials point out that finished EVs must be included in the scope of the tax credit.
While battery makers can receive credits for batteries they manufacture and sell domestically, EVs produced by Hyundai Motor at its domestic plants were excluded.
text:
It is widely viewed that, to enhance the competitiveness of its electric vehicles (EVs), Hyundai Motor needs not only product improvements but also government support to back domestic production. In the domestic passenger EV market, the market share gap between domestically produced and Chinese-made vehicles has narrowed by a quarter in just one year.

This is the backdrop for the ruling and opposition parties’ unanimous call during this year’s national audit to include EVs in the scope of the domestic production tax credit. If tax burdens are reduced based on the production performance of EVs manufactured domestically, domestic automakers, including Hyundai Motor, could build greater capacity to respond to price competition.

According to data from the Korea Automobile Manufacturers Association (KAMA) and the Korea Importers’ Automobile Association (KAIDA), 112,417 Chinese-made passenger EVs were newly registered in South Korea from January to September this year, reaching 2.2 times the level of the same period last year.

The market share of Chinese-made vehicles rose from 35.1% in the same period last year to 43.5% this year, while the share of domestically produced vehicles fell from 54.9% to 48.7%. In other words, a gap that had been 19.8 percentage points (p) has narrowed to 5.2%p in just one year.

For Hyundai Motor, which is competing against Chinese-made EVs on its home turf, lowering vehicle prices or increasing discounts is one way to boost sales. However, the wider the discount, the lower the profit per unit sold.

If a tax credit applies to domestically produced units, some of this burden can be alleviated. Maintaining existing prices would help offset profitability, and redirecting part of the saved taxes into purchase incentives could lower consumers’ effective purchase price, thereby aiding sales recovery.

To this end, industry officials point out that finished EVs must be included in the scope of the tax credit. The tax reform plan announced by the government last August included a measure to reduce taxes based on performance for companies that produce and sell strategic items domestically.

However, it was limited to six sectors, including secondary batteries and semiconductors. While battery makers can receive credits for batteries they manufacture and sell domestically, EVs produced by Hyundai Motor at its domestic plants were excluded.

Unlike the government’s proposal, 24 bills introduced in the 22nd National Assembly include future vehicles such as EVs among the support targets. The scope of the tax credit under the government’s plan was also a key issue during last month’s national audit of the Ministry of Economy and Finance.

Democratic Party of Korea lawmaker Yoon Hoo-deok emphasized, “Chinese-made EVs are rapidly growing in the domestic market, so this must be included in the National Assembly’s tax discussions.” People Power Party lawmaker Ahn Sang-hoon also struck directly, stating, “In a situation where major countries are deploying even tariffs and tax benefits to protect their own auto industries, it seems there is virtually no country that has protected its market without an active response.”

In response, Lee Hyoung-il, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of the Ministry of Economy and Finance, stated during the national audit that he is reviewing with relevant ministries a plan to include EVs in the scope of the tax credit. Having also expressed his intention to actively participate in National Assembly discussions during an on-site visit on the 2nd, the review of the tax law amendment bill by the Tax Subcommittee of the National Assembly’s Committee on Finance and Economy this month is expected to become a venue where the government and the National Assembly will coordinate on the scope of the credit.

text:
As calls grow in the National Assembly, from both the ruling and opposition parties, to include electric vehicles among the products eligible for the domestic production tax credit, expectations are rising in the automotive industry. The program cuts taxes based on production performance for companies that produce and sell certain products domestically. Solar power and batteries are among the eligible products, but electric vehicles are not, and the industry has been arguing that they should be included.

Industry sources said on the 3rd that 24 bills have been introduced to extend the production tax credit to electric vehicles. Notably, last month, the only bill among them jointly introduced by lawmakers from both the ruling and opposition parties—with Yoon Hu-deok of the Democratic Party of Korea and Yoon Han-hong of the People Power Party among its lead sponsors—was put forward, further raising hopes that it would pass.

At last month’s parliamentary audit, lawmakers from both the ruling and opposition parties likewise called for the introduction of a production tax credit for electric vehicles.

At a meeting of the National Assembly’s Strategy and Finance Committee held on the 22nd of last month, lawmakers continued to criticize the Ministry of Finance and Economy, the ministry responsible for the matter, over the exclusion of electric vehicles from the eligible products.

People Power Party lawmaker Ahn Sang-hoon pointed out, “Looking at major advanced countries, they are deploying everything—tariffs, tax credits and subsidies—to protect their domestic electric vehicle industries, and it seems there are virtually no countries that have protected their markets without responding proactively.”

Bae Jun-young, the People Power Party’s ranking member on the Strategy and Finance Committee, stressed, “I believe support should be provided in areas facing difficulties in competing with other countries, such as through electric vehicle tax credits, or where support is needed to serve as a catalyst.”

When Democratic Party lawmaker Moon Jin-seok asked whether the ministry had discussed the program with the Ministry of Planning and Budget, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and Economy Lee Hyoung-il replied, “We discussed it at the previous meeting on economic issues with the minister of the Ministry of Planning and Budget, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy, and the Blue House, and it is currently under review.”

As lawmakers from both the ruling and opposition parties have repeatedly stressed the need to include electric vehicles among the products eligible for the production tax credit, whether to include them is expected to be discussed in earnest this month during the tax bill review by the Tax Subcommittee of the National Assembly’s Strategy and Finance Committee.

After review by the Tax Subcommittee, the production tax credit will go before the Strategy and Finance Committee’s full committee and the Legislation and Judiciary Committee. If deliberations in the National Assembly proceed smoothly, it is expected to receive final approval at a plenary session in early December. Since it is a tax-related measure, if designated as a budget-related bill, it will pass the plenary session together with next year’s budget bill.
