text:
The Rhodium Group released a new analysis this morning with the aim of modeling the bill’s effects on the energy system, particularly via provisions that would reduce barriers to building transmission infrastructure and protect ratepayers from shouldering the costs of the buildout of artificial intelligence. The review excludes other provisions regarding permit certainty, geothermal, and advanced transmission technologies.

Specifically, the research group found that the legislation as written would increase the construction of interregional transmission infrastructure to nearly three times the rate over the last decade.

It also estimated that it would drive up to an additional 249 gigawatts worth of clean energy resources to be built through 2040.

The Rhodium Group said it would also increase liquefied natural gas export levels by 8-15%, beyond the 76-145% increase already expected under current policies.

Still, the group forecast that BAAJA would lead a reduction in economy-wide greenhouse gas emissions by up to 148 million metric tons annually in 2040, and as much as 1.5 gigatons cumulatively.

You can read the full analysis here.

How much data centers could pay: Separately, consulting group Grid Strategies released a white paper this morning estimating how much data centers could be forced to pay for connecting to the grid if BAAJA is passed.

If you forgot, the legislation as written would force large-load facilities such as data centers to pay for the energy and transmission infrastructure needed for their operations, and would mandate that no incremental costs are passed on to other customers.

It also would order utilities to ensure that transmission costs are fully assigned to these large-load operators to “minimize or avoid cost burden on other customers.”

Under these provisions, Grid Strategies estimated BAAJA would result in $55 billion in transmission service charges to data centers over 10 years. The group said this represents an additional $35 billion over what data centers would otherwise pay to connect to the grid under current policies.

Biden alum split grows: As we explored a bit last week, there is a growing divide among former staffers of the Biden administration regarding support for the bill. There are several individuals who worked on climate issues under the last administration who have endorsed the bill – see Jane Flegal – and many others adamantly opposed.

Tracy Stone-Manning, director of the Bureau of Land Management under the Biden administration, joined the latter group today.

Stone-Manning currently serves as the president of The Wilderness Society, which released a statement of opposition this morning. The statement says the bill puts millions of acres of public lands and national monuments at risk of fossil fuel and data center development.

“A clean energy future is possible and necessary, but not at the expense of our country’s conservation heritage, the clean water our public lands deliver and the loss of cherished sacred sites and cultural histories,” Stone-Manning said.

All the rest:

OIL PRICES PLUNGE: Domestic and international oil prices plummeted today on the news a draft proposal for a peace deal between Washington and Tehran had been circulated after days of talks between Iran and Qatar.

An official briefed on the peace talks told Reuters that Iranian negotiators left Qatar on Sunday, and confirmed the draft proposal was being circulated.

Over the weekend, Axios also reported that President Donald Trump told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that he wished for negotiations to play out before striking Iran following the midterm elections.

The willingness to make a deal pushed domestic and international benchmarks for oil down today by more than 7%. Just after 2:30 p.m., Brent crude had fallen 7.79% and was selling at $104.59 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate also dropped 7.67% and was priced at $96.13 a barrel.

U.S. PUSHES TO RESTORE RUSSIAN GAS SALES TO EUROPE: The Trump administration is pushing to restore Russian natural gas sales to Europe via pipelines running through Ukraine.

The Wall Street Journal reported today that the idea is part of negotiations to secure an energy ceasefire ahead of the winter, citing U.S., European, and Ukrainian officials. The proposal came from Trump’s envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff and was floated during trips to Moscow and Kyiv in September.

The idea would include selling Russian gas via a U.S. intermediary to circumvent European sanctions, which could create a lucrative opportunity for investors, the WSJ said. Europe has been phasing out the purchases of Russian natural gas, with plans to completely phase it out by 2027.

The plan to restore natural gas sales was delayed last month because Ukraine stopped attacking Russian refineries, despite Russia continuing to attack Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. But attacks by Kyiv on key Russian energy infrastructure resumed last week.

IRAN WAR COULD ACCELERATE ENERGY TRANSITION: French oil major TotalEnergies suggested earlier today that the war in Iran could speed up the global transition to cleaner fuels, with demand for petroleum products peaking during the 2030s before seeing a slow decline.

The forecast comes one year after TotalEnergies estimated that oil demand would rise until 2040 before starting to fall.

This shift in predictions is directly connected to the war in Iran and the disruptions to the oil trade through the Strait of Hormuz, which the oil major said was “testing the resilience of the energy system.” TotalEnergies said the crisis has incentivized diversifying supply sources and developing available energies, such as renewables and biofuels.

The company then said the crisis “can also act as an accelerator of the energy transition,” pointing to increased sales of electric vehicles in Asia, Latin America, and Europe, as well as increased biofuel blending requirements.

You can find TotalEnergies’ full 2026 outlook here.

COMMENT PERIOD ENDS ON EPA’S PROPOSAL TO REPEAL ALL GREENHOUSE GAS LIMITS FOR POWER PLANS: Today is the final day to comment on the Environmental Protection Agency’s supplemental rule to remove all greenhouse gas requirements for fossil fuel power plants.

The supplemental rule was proposed in September as part of the agency’s final rule that repealed a set of Biden administration’s standards on new and existing power plants. Those standards were aimed at reducing pollution from power plants by using carbon capture, sequestration, and storage technology.

The supplemental rule asks the public to comment whether the agency should remove all greenhouse gas requirements for fossil fuel power plants, including the 2015 standards for new coal-fired power plants and the remaining aspects of the 2024 power plant rule.

The EPA argued that a full repeal of the remaining greenhouse gas emission standards would save an additional $370 million in compliance costs and for households across the country.

ICYMI – OFFSHORE WIND CRACKDOWN SPREADS TO BRITAIN: The United States isn’t the only place the offshore wind industry is facing hurdles, as the United Kingdom will be imposing new rules blocking some projects.

In an op-ed released Friday, U.K. Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey revealed that the government would not be supporting offshore wind projects that would not lower electricity bills.

“There’s no sense building power that can’t connect and then paying to switch it off,” he wrote in The Times. “We will take that approach into our next renewables auction, only buying projects that can lower bills while strengthening our energy security.”

The rules mark a significant shift from the Labour Party’s promise to have at least 95% of the UK’s electricity generated by clean sources of energy by 2030. As part of that pledge, the party said it would work to double onshore wind, triple solar power, and quadruple offshore wind.

Under the new rules, however, the government plans to be more selective about which offshore wind projects it will give contracts.

The shift in tone is primarily driven by concerns about wasted wind charges. The National Energy System Operator in the U.K. is required to pay wind turbines to shut off when there is not enough cabling capacity to transmit the electricity to consumers.

text:
Calls are growing across both ruling and opposition parties, as well as within the auto industry, to include electric vehicles in South Korea's domestic production tax credit, after Deputy Prime Minister and Finance and Economy Minister Lee Hyoung-il said he would unveil a plan to strengthen the competitiveness of the EV industry this month.

Newly registered Chinese-made electric passenger cars in South Korea totaled 112,417 units in the January-September period, 2.2 times the figure a year earlier, according to data from the Korea Automobile and Mobility Association and the Korea Automobile Importers and Distributors Association released on the 3rd. Their market share rose 8.4 percentage points to 43.5%. Domestic electric passenger cars, by contrast, saw their share fall 6.2 percentage points over the same period to 48.7%, dropping below the 50% mark.

Chinese EVs are rapidly encroaching on the domestic market. Industry officials say Chinese EV makers, backed by astronomical support from their own government, have built price competitiveness across the entire supply chain — from finished vehicles to materials, parts and batteries — and are swallowing up global markets.

The problem, industry officials say, is that competing with Chinese EVs has become all but impossible while government support falls far short. Given the impact of production bases and employment on the national economy, they argue, the domestic auto industry is an obvious candidate for protection, yet the absence of policy support has made South Korea a prime target for Chinese EV makers.

The domestic production tax credit, a key campaign pledge of President Lee Jae-myung, is designed to promote domestic manufacturing by granting tax credits to companies that produce and sell strategic items, based on their production volumes. But while the government's 2026 tax code revision plan announced on Aug. 3 included the creation of the credit, EVs were left off the list of eligible items.

As a result, momentum is building in the political arena to include EVs in the tax credit, which has been dubbed South Korea's version of the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act.

At a comprehensive audit of the Ministry of Finance and Economy held by the National Assembly's finance and economy committee on the 22nd of last month, Rep. Bae Joon-young of the People Power Party, who serves as the committee liaison for his party, said, "When our semiconductor industry was struggling in the past, the government served as a primer." He added, "Support should go to areas such as EV tax credits, where industries are struggling in competition with other countries or where a priming role is needed."

Earlier, at a parliamentary audit of the Ministry of Finance and Economy on the 6th of last month, Rep. Yoon Hu-duk of the Democratic Party of Korea said, "Chinese-made EVs are rapidly taking over the market both at home and abroad, leaving domestic EVs in a severe crisis." He stressed, "EVs were left out of the domestic production tax credit, and this needs to be included in the National Assembly's tax discussions."

Rep. Moon Jin-seok of the Democratic Party of Korea also said, "There are many gaps in the tax code revision bill submitted by the government," adding, "The current government proposal seems to be pushing domestic automakers, who must compete with price-competitive Chinese automakers, toward a cliff instead."

A total of 24 amendments to the Restriction of Special Taxation Act that would include EVs and other next-generation vehicles in the domestic production tax credit have been introduced since the 22nd National Assembly convened, according to the National Assembly's bill information system. Of those, 11 were introduced as lead sponsors by members of the finance and economy committee, which handles tax policy.

Even after the government's tax revision plan excluding EVs from the credit was made public, seven lawmakers from both parties — Yoon Han-hong, Lee Eon-ju, Moon Jin-seok, Ahn Sang-hoon, Yoon Hu-duk, Yoon Young-suk and Ahn Do-geol — introduced bills in succession to add EVs to the list of eligible items, underscoring the push for tax support for domestically produced EVs.

The deputy prime minister, who met with Hyundai Motor (005380.KS) Group Executive Chairman Euisun Chung the previous day to exchange views on expanding the domestic production tax credit, said at a subsequent meeting with auto industry officials, "On support through the EV production tax credit, the government will actively take part in the National Assembly's deliberations and discuss the matter in depth."

text:
Eugene voters will decide tomorrow whether to create a clean energy fund by charging certain large businesses a 2% fee, a proposal supporters say would help pay for climate and energy projects but opponents warn could raise costs for customers.

Measure 20-388 would create a clean energy fund to support climate and energy projects in Eugene. The money would come from a new fee on certain large businesses, though voters will decide on the measure before knowing exactly which businesses the fee would apply to.

Under the measure, the fee would apply to businesses with more than $1 billion in national gross profits and more than $500,000 in Eugene gross profits. The measure exempts most groceries, medicines, health care, and residential garbage and recycling services.

“The Eugene clean energy fund allows Eugene to do their part, make these investments, invest in their community directly and also reduce climate emissions, which will improve our health and our environment and create good-paying jobs along the way,” said Britney Vancitters, a steering committee member for the Eugene Clean Energy Fund.

If approved, the fund would allocate 60% to renewable energy and energy-efficiency programs, 25% to clean-energy job training and contractor support, 10% to green infrastructure and 5% to future innovation.

Stop the Hidden Tax, the opposition campaign, says it supports clean energy but argues the measure could hurt Eugene’s economy. “The tax is on gross profit which is calculated before rent wages or utilities,” opposition spokesperson Laura Sedwick said. “Small businesses buy their insurance supplies and equipment from these same companies a cost like that doesn't disappear. It shows up in prices that we all pay.”

Supporters dispute that the fee would lead to local price increases. “These big corporations are setting their prices at a regional or national level, and we have Portland to look at. Portland has not seen these types of price increases,” Vancitters said.

Portland’s clean energy fund was enacted in 2019 and is funded by a 1% surcharge on large retailers’ Portland sales.

In Eugene, the city would decide which businesses meet the measure’s definition of a “large retailer,” a process that could take up to six months. Potential businesses could include Walmart, Target and some banks.

The Oregon Bankers Association says the measure would put banks at a disadvantage to credit unions. In a statement, the association, which contributed $15,000 to the opposition, said: “We are concerned that the measure would impose a new tax on qualifying banks serving Eugene while specifically exempting competing credit unions – this would make the unfair tax gap separating banks and credit unions even larger.”

If the measure passes, a nine-member appointed committee would review funding proposals and recommend to the mayor and City Council how the money is spent. The measure could generate between $15 million and $40 million a year for the clean energy fund. If approved, the fee will take effect Jan. 1, 2029.

text:
Korea is weighing tax incentives for domestically produced electric vehicles (EVs) as Chinese rivals rapidly gain market share, fueling calls from automakers and lawmakers across party lines for government support to protect local production and jobs.

Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il said the government would announce measures to strengthen the EV industry's competitiveness this month, following talks with Hyundai Motor Group Executive Chair Chung Euisun on Monday.

Whether EVs should qualify for domestic production tax credits is expected to be a key focus of parliamentary debate over the government's tax reform plan.

Chinese-made passenger EVs accounted for 43.5 percent of new registrations in Korea from January to September, up 8.4 percentage points from a year earlier, according to the Korea Automobile and Mobility Association and the Korea Automobile Importers and Distributors Association. Registrations more than doubled to about 112,400 vehicles from 51,500 year-on-year.

Meanwhile, the share of domestically produced passenger EVs fell 6.2 percentage points to 48.7 percent, slipping below the 50 percent threshold for the first time.

Chinese automakers are stepping up their push into the Korean market, following BYD's entry last year and Zeekr's local sales launch this year.

Xpeng also appointed the first head of its new Korean unit on Tuesday, with former Volvo Car Korea executive Lee Man-sik set to take the post on Dec. 1. Chery Automobile and Great Wall Motor are also reportedly preparing to enter the market next year.

The competitive pressure has intensified demands to extend a domestic production tax credit to EVs.

The program, a key campaign pledge of President Lee Jae Myung, would provide tax credits based on production volumes to companies that manufacture and sell designated strategic products domestically. EVs were excluded from the government's tax reform proposal announced in August.

During parliamentary audits last month, lawmakers from both the ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK) and the main opposition People Power Party (PPP) urged the government to extend the tax credit to domestically produced EVs.

"The government stepped in to support our semiconductor industry when it was struggling. I believe we should provide support, including EV tax credits, to industries that are having difficulty competing with other countries and need a similar boost," Rep. Bae June-young of the PPP said during the audit.

Rep. Moon Jin-seog of the DPK also criticized the exclusion of EVs from the government's tax reform proposal, saying it appeared to be pushing domestic automakers "to the brink" as they compete with price-competitive Chinese manufacturers.

A total of 24 bills proposing to include EVs and other future mobility vehicles in the tax credit program have been introduced in the National Assembly. Seven more were submitted after the government unveiled its tax reform plan in August.

The issue is expected to be taken up by the National Assembly's tax subcommittee this month, ahead of a possible floor vote in December.

Meeting EV, autonomous-driving and parts industry executives on Monday, Lee signaled government engagement without committing to extending the credit.

“Regarding support through electric vehicle production tax credits, the government will actively participate in parliamentary discussions and engage in in-depth discussions on the matter,” he said.

He also said the government plans to announce a package of measures to strengthen the EV industry's competitiveness this month, incorporating industry feedback and support for autonomous driving technology and research and development of key components.

title: Duke's fixation on dirty energy is costing you - Salisbury Post
authors: Mikaela Curry and Tyson Slocum, Mikaela Curry, Tyson Slocum
description:

And the reason you’re being asked to live with less is Duke’s commitment to dirty energy.
Meanwhile, Duke is doubling down on dirty energy: Duke delayed three North Carolina coal plant retirements and has the second-most planned gas capacity nationally.
These decisions will make energy more expensive for North Carolina families and small businesses while Duke reaps the profits.
For the sake of affordable, reliable electricity, we must continue holding Duke accountable for its dirty, expensive energy agenda.
text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

By Mikaela Curry and Tyson Slocum

NC Newsline

When an unusual heat wave hit North Carolina on Sept. 18, millions of residents turned on the AC to escape the high temperatures. This unexpected demand strained the electric grid, jeopardizing the ability of homes and businesses to keep power on and stay safe. In a warming world with increasingly extreme weather, the lesson is clear: we need more affordable energy to ensure that everyone has year-round access to electricity.

But according to Duke Energy, the state’s largest utility, it’s ratepayers who have to fix this problem.

During the heat wave, Duke asked its 3.9 million North Carolina customers to reduce their electricity use from 2 – 8 p.m. to ease the strain on the electric grid. At the hottest point in the day, Duke wanted families to turn up the heat and limit oven use. Similarly, during Winter Storm Fern, Duke asked customers to set the thermostat to the coldest comfortable setting and avoid using appliances.

The point is not that we should never moderate our electricity use for the common good. The point is that this demand is coming from a monopoly utility that controls electricity for almost four million people. A utility that has abandoned renewable energy projects that would bring affordable, reliable power to our grid and prevent situations like these from happening. A utility that wants to raise electricity prices by 9.5 percent, lock North Carolina into decades of expensive, dirty energy projects, and shift your money into the pockets of its CEO and shareholders.

As it actively courts new power-hungry data centers, Duke is asking you to sacrifice your electricity needs, all while increasing your bills. And the reason you’re being asked to live with less is Duke’s commitment to dirty energy.

Last year, Duke slashed its planned solar capacity by over 50 percent (earlier this year, regulators froze the smaller plans entirely). In June, Duke accepted a $129 million buyout from the Trump administration to scrap an offshore wind project that could have powered 300,000 homes annually and sheltered customers from fossil fuel price volatility. Meanwhile, Duke is doubling down on dirty energy: Duke delayed three North Carolina coal plant retirements and has the second-most planned gas capacity nationally.

These decisions will make energy more expensive for North Carolina families and small businesses while Duke reaps the profits. A renewable-heavy energy portfolio would save North Carolinians between $4.5 and $8 billion. Solar and wind power are the cheapest ways to produce electricity and the quickest types of power to bring online, meaning they’re the best solutions to address rising energy needs. Coal and gas, meanwhile, are volatile fuel sources, subject to price shocks from external factors like geopolitical conflicts and extreme weather that send monthly bills soaring. Pipeline, storage and processing infrastructure make gas plants particularly expensive. Conveniently for Duke, this allows them to raise rates for customers and reward their shareholders and executives due to state-sanctioned return on capital investments.

These costs aren’t an oversight: locking North Carolina into decades of expensive fossil fuel projects allows Duke to justify endless rate hikes, all while they make record profits. It’s why they are demanding a 9.5-percent rate increase despite posting billions of dollars in profits already this year, and paying their CEOs $22 million last year.

By prioritizing profits over affordability, Duke is jeopardizing the safety and wellbeing of its customers. The biggest threat to reliable electricity isn’t keeping the thermostat too low on a hot day: it’s Duke. Last year, Duke disconnected customers 187,000 times, a 37-percent increase from 2024. One in five Duke customers in North Carolina are indebted to the utility, a number that could grow if they raise rates even higher.

Thankfully, people are fighting back. Duke initially proposed raising electricity rates by 18 percent, only to reduce the proposal after intense backlash (Attorney General Jackson continues to fight the 9.5 percent proposed increase). On Sept. 18, regulators rejected Duke’s proposal to build a new gas power plant over cost concerns. These decisions only happened because advocates and ratepayers sounded the alarm. For the sake of affordable, reliable electricity, we must continue holding Duke accountable for its dirty, expensive energy agenda.

Mikaela Curry is Sierra Club’s Beyond Coal Campaign Manager based in North Carolina. Tyson Slocum is the director of Public Citizen’s Energy Program.

title: $150 billion more paid by Americans for gas this year than last - CleanTechnica
description:
Since the beginning of America’s war against Iran, Americans have paid an additional $150+ billion for gas and diesel than they did last year during the same time period, according to a study from Brown University.
The industry seems not to have raised the full $1 billion, but oil interests still gave tens of millions to Trump-aligned committees.
They tried to eliminate Energy Star, a program that costs the government $32 million a year and saves Americans $14 billion a year.
They even tried to make it illegal for future legislators to improve energy efficiency legislation.
But the Iran War took it to a whole new level.
text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

Since the beginning of America’s war against Iran, Americans have paid an additional $150+ billion for gas and diesel than they did last year during the same time period, according to a study from Brown University. Global gas prices have risen because supply has been disrupted (Iran having one of the top oil reserves in the world). Americans are paying upwards of $6 a gallon even though American oil companies have not had their own supply chains disrupted the way crude from the Middle East has.

The result? Windfall profits for big oil at the expense of American citizens.

——————-

In the leadup to his election in 2024, Donald Trump asked about 20 oil executives at Mar-a-Lago to raise $1 billion for his campaign, promising to reverse dozens of Biden-era regulations if elected. The industry seems not to have raised the full $1 billion, but oil interests still gave tens of millions to Trump-aligned committees. The policies put in place by the Republican party, who has had control of congress and the White House since the last election, have been very pro oil & gas, whether they were anti-EV, anti-solar, anti-energy efficiency, anti-fuel efficiency, anti-wind, or just flat out subsidies to oil and gas.

They ended many of the Biden Administration’s clean energy policies. They ended the Solar For All Program (or tried to). They ended residential and commercial solar tax credits. They signed Executive Order 14315 to terminate wind and solar production and investment tax credits and impose additional restrictions. They made solar development on Federal lands more difficult. On his first day in office, Trump signed a memo withdrawing federal offshore areas from new and renewed wind leasing – but the rule didn’t apply to oil and gas. They ended wind tax credits. They kneecapped the federal standards for vehicle fuel efficiency. They tried to eliminate Energy Star, a program that costs the government $32 million a year and saves Americans $14 billion a year. They weakened Home Energy Rebate programs, SPECIFICALLY stipulating that they could not be used to replace polluting gas furnaces (that increase childhood asthma by more than 15%) with energy efficient electric options. They even tried to make it illegal for future legislators to improve energy efficiency legislation. Then, as if that wasn’t enough, they just gave our tax dollars to the fossil industries, allocating about $190 billion in tax breaks and subsidies over the next decade from the OBBBA.

If this isn’t quid pro quo, I guess I don’t understand what quid pro quo is. But the Iran War took it to a whole new level.

Since it began on February 28, as Americans have spent about $150 billion more on gasoline and diesel, U.S. oil and gas companies earned more than $130 billion in profit from April through September, nearly triple what they earned a year earlier, according to the New York Times.

We can’t say the war was fought for the industry. The president has said his focus is stopping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. But we can say who is paying at the pump and who is collecting.

Connect the dots however you like, but connect them before you vote. Add it to the roughly $50 billion that US taxpayers have directly spent on the war, and untold more that has percolated through the rest of our economy due to inflationary pressure from rising energy costs, and it’s safe to say it’s well over $200 billion that this war has cost us, alongside the unquantifiable cost in human lives and suffering.

Wars fought for oil are nothing new. But there are things about this conflict that are new.

The rest of the world isn’t waiting

Oil shocks focus the mind, and this week’s reporting shows how fast the world outside the US is moving to get away from oil dependency. CleanTechnica’s analysis argues that global oil demand is on track to fall by 2–3 million barrels a day this year, the first drop not caused by a recession or pandemic, as high prices push consumers away from fuel. You can see it in China, where gas-car sales fell 49% in September and EVs hit a record 67% share. Europe is also answering, with affordable small EVs like the Smart #2 and an electric Citroën 2 CV at about €15,000. In Australia, a Chinese-built electric semi is already hauling cement for about half the price of its rivals, and Africa’s e-mobility leaders are talking about building vehicles rather than just importing them. Drivers who’ve switched are happy too: 82% of XPeng owners in a 4,000-person European survey said they’d recommend the brand, versus a 53% average.

Every driver, trucker, and country that electrifies becomes less exposed to the next oil shock. The question for the U.S. is how fast it joins in. And this election will go a long way toward answering that question.

description:

text:
LG Energy Solution reported a 25.7 percent increase in third-quarter operating profit Tuesday, boosted by strong demand for energy storage systems in North America and recovering electric-vehicle battery sales, as the South Korean battery-maker raised its full-year revenue outlook.

The company posted an operating profit of 756 billion won ($564 million) for the July-September period, up 25.7 percent from a year earlier, according to its earnings release.

Excluding 416.9 billion won in US manufacturing tax credits under the Inflation Reduction Act, operating profit stood at 339.1 billion won, a sign that profitability in its core battery business is improving.

Revenue jumped 59 percent on-year and 27.6 percent from the previous quarter to a record 9.64 trillion won, driven by higher shipments of both energy storage and EV batteries.

“Third quarter revenue grew significantly on a sharp increase in ESS shipments, while both pouch type and cylindrical EV batteries recorded growth in their volume,” said Lee Chang-sil, chief financial officer of LG Energy Solution.

Lee also attributed the improved profitability to higher utilization rates at the company’s Polish plant, continued demand for cylindrical batteries and productivity gains at newly launched ESS manufacturing sites.

The results come as LG Energy Solution is focusing on energy storage batteries as AI data centers drive demand for reliable power, while its EV battery business continues to recover.

In the ESS segment, LG Energy Solution’s order backlog stood at approximately 160 gigawatt-hours at the end of September.

The company also secured its first direct battery energy storage system supply agreement with a major technology company, expanding its presence in the fast-growing AI data center market.

"We signed our first direct BESS supply agreement with a big tech company, strengthening our position in the AI data center market," said Lee during Tuesday's earnings conference call. "With discussions underway on new projects with multiple utilities and hyperscalers, we expect additional orders to continue into the fourth quarter.”

The company was also selected in September as the only South Korean battery manufacturer in Nvidia’s DSX Ready program, which supports the development of next-generation AI factories.

In EV batteries, the company secured another supply deal for its next-generation high-voltage mid-nickel batteries, strengthening its foothold in the European market.

Manufacturing operations also showed signs of recovery. In North America, LG Energy Solution launched additional ESS cell production lines and containerized system assembly facilities to boost local capacity.

Higher demand for cylindrical EV batteries and the resumption of operations at its joint venture with General Motors also helped lift overall factory utilization rates, the company said.

LG Energy Solution is stepping up efforts to localize its supply chain amid tighter US restrictions on battery materials linked to prohibited foreign entities, particularly Chinese suppliers.

In North America, LG Energy Solution plans to expand its ESS production capacity to more than 70 gigawatt-hours by the end of 2027, up from over 50 GWh targeted for the end of this year.

The expansion will include new prismatic battery production lines. The company also plans to complete final preparations for its Arizona plant, its first North American cylindrical battery manufacturing base, by the end of this year.

"Demand for locally produced ESS battery cells is rising rapidly in North America, driven by strong market growth and favorable policies for suppliers that meet non-prohibited foreign entity requirements," said Jung Jae-wook, executive in charge of ESS battery planning and management at LG Energy Solution.

"Most of our planned production capacity through 2028 has already been committed to customers," he added.

Buoyed by results that beat expectations, LG Energy Solution raised its 2026 revenue growth to 35-40 percent on-year. The revised outlook is sharply higher than its previous projection of growth in the mid-teens to around 20 percent announced earlier in the year.

LOS ANGELES (AP) — Millions of dollars of settlement money from the largest known methane leak in the United States are now available to affected residents to replace gas-powered appliances with electric ones.
In total, the program will make $40 million available to help people install heat pumps that cool and heat homes, electric stoves, water heaters and other appliances.
Evan Kamei is the director of TECH Clean California, a state program helping distribute the settlement money.
In 2021, thousands of families reached a settlement of up to $1.8 billion with the Southern California Gas Co. and its parent company, Sempra Energy.

text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Millions of dollars of settlement money from the largest known methane leak in the United States are now available to affected residents to replace gas-powered appliances with electric ones. Organizations involved in distributing the money say it will help create safer and cleaner homes.

The announcement makes available the first $20 million in incentive funding from the Aliso Canyon settlement to help home and building owners impacted by the 2015 Los Angeles-area blowout. In total, the program will make $40 million available to help people install heat pumps that cool and heat homes, electric stoves, water heaters and other appliances.

Evan Kamei is the director of TECH Clean California, a state program helping distribute the settlement money. He said the incentives “will help create healthier homes, lower energy costs, deliver cooling, and create local jobs by replacing aging gas appliances with efficient electric appliances.”

Anyone in the affected area with a single-family home will be eligible for the incentives, and certain income-qualifying residents will be eligible for extra funding. Access for multi-property owners will come later.

The Aliso Canyon gas leak took nearly four months to control, sickened thousands of families and forced them from their homes near the San Fernando Valley to escape a sulfurous stench and maladies including headaches, nausea and nose bleeds.

The natural gas storage well failed and uncontrollably released nearly 100,000 tons of methane and other substances into the atmosphere for more than 100 days. Methane is a potent, heat-trapping gas that contributes to extreme weather events worldwide through climate change. The natural gas facility involved in the blowout temporarily closed and later reopened at reduced capacity after being deemed safe to operate.

In 2021, thousands of families reached a settlement of up to $1.8 billion with the Southern California Gas Co. and its parent company, Sempra Energy. Some 35,000 plaintiffs were compensated after complaining of personal injury and property damage to their homes. SoCalGas spent more than $1 billion on the blowout, with most of the money going to temporarily relocate 8,000 families.

Weldon Kennedy is the co-founder and chief marketing officer of Copper, a California startup that sells electric induction stoves and ovens. He said his company got involved with the program to distribute settlement money after the group Energy Solutions highlighted how hard it would be to get people to switch their cooking appliances from gas to electric.

“People have a cultural attachment to gas when it comes to cooking,” Kennedy said. The kind of appliances Copper sells may help mitigate that attachment because they can be plugged into a regular outlet without the expense of rewiring that is usually associated with switching from gas-powered appliances to electric ones.

Cooking with electricity comes with health benefits. Gas stoves, which 47 million Americans use, release pollutants like nitrogen dioxide that’s been linked to asthma and cancer-causing benzene.

Products like electric appliances are one way to address the significant amount of pollution driving climate change that comes from cooking, heating and cooling living spaces and providing hot water in buildings.

Income-qualified residents affected by the Aliso leak are eligible for up to $31,800 worth of incentives to cover the cost of electric installations in their homes.

Switching from gas to electricity can save energy and lower bills.

Carol Kamei, Evan Kamei's 72-year-old mother, has lived for 46 years near the Aliso Canyon Natural Gas Facility and was one of the plaintiffs in the case against SoCal Gas. She remembers smelling gas and getting nose bleeds. When she read in the news that the leak was also spewing cancer-causing benzene, she knew it was time to go.

Carol Kamei said her nose bleeds went away after moving in with her sister in Hollywood for three months. She recently participated in a health study by the University of California, Los Angeles and found out she has diminished lung capacity, one of the health impacts researchers look for, she said.

“I do know some people that have died from blood-borne illnesses, cancer since then,” Carol Kamei said.

Kamei hopes to use the incentive funding to replace her oven with an electric one. “I’d rather not use gas,” she said.

September 23, 2026

The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) today announced awards for eight new bulk energy storage projects and 13 large-scale renewable energy projects. Combined, these projects are expected to provide 1.7 gigawatts (GW) of new large-scale energy resources, create more than 1,000 family-supporting jobs and generate over $3.7 billion in private investment. This reinforces New York’s commitment to the development of locally-produced clean energy, energy storage, grid resiliency and economic development.

NYSERDA President and CEO Doreen M. Harris said, “These newly-contracted large-scale energy projects not only further the growth of clean energy and more than double the utility-scale energy storage that exists currently statewide – but they contribute to New York’s comprehensive, all of the above energy strategy. This will help reduce costs for New York ratepayers while continuing to improve the reliability of our state’s grid.”

These newly contracted awards are the result of NYSERDA’S first Bulk Energy Storage solicitation and its 2025 Tier 1 Renewable Energy Standard solicitation. By producing and storing clean energy, these projects will provide public health benefits from reduced exposure to harmful pollutants and are expected to provide over $127 million in economic benefits to disadvantaged communities , as defined by the Climate Justice Working Group.

New York’s First Bulk Energy Storage Awards

Once operational, the eight contracted bulk energy storage projects will add 950 megawatts (MW) of new energy storage capacity. The projects represent a diverse portfolio ranging geographically from New York City and Long Island to Hudson Valley and Western New York. They were selected through a competitive process that included bid proposals from 46 projects totaling approximately 6 GW of capacity. The eight contracted projects range in duration from four to eight hours and will provide critical reliability benefits to the state’s electric grid. The awarded energy storage projects include:

Western New York

Lighthouse Energy Storage, Chautauqua County

Zenobe Burns, Allegany County

Finger Lakes

Eastwater Energy Storage, Monroe County

Hudson Valley

KCE NY 5, Ulster County

New York City

Blue Spruce Storage, Bronx County

Palladium Storage, Bronx County

Long Island

Holtsville Energy Storage, Suffolk County

KCE NY 37, Suffolk County

Payments under these contracts will not commence until projects have begun commercial operation, after having obtained all required permits and local approvals. All projects are expected to be placed in-service by the end of 2030 as required by the 2024 Public Service Commission’s Energy Storage Order.

The contracted projects will use lithium-ion technology and, as with all NYSERDA-supported energy storage projects, are contractually required to meet the new storage safety codes that became effective January 1, 2026, and reflect the work and recommendations of the New York State Inter-Agency Fire Safety Working Group – convened by Governor Hochul. These safety codes, which are among the most robust in the nation, ensure that first responders have the necessary training, facilities are sited safely, and that all sites have comprehensive emergency response plans.

NYSERDA will issue the second annual Bulk Energy Storage Request for Proposals by year-end to continue progress toward procuring 3 GW of bulk energy storage over three solicitations.

2025 Land-Based Renewable Energy Solicitation Awards

The 13 contracted large-scale land-based renewable energy projects will total more than 719 MW of renewable capacity – enough to power over 230,000 New York homes annually, once completed. Awarded projects include land-based wind, hydroelectric and solar:

Central New York

Finger Lakes

North Country

Diamond Island Hydroelectric Facility, Jefferson County

Ellenburg Windpark in Clinton County and Franklin County

Greens Corners Solar Park, Jefferson County

Rich Road Solar Energy Center, St. Lawrence County

Theresa Hydroelectric Project, Jefferson County

Southern Tier

Canisteo Wind Energy Center, Steuben County

The payments under the contracted projects will only begin once projects are constructed and begin delivering renewable energy to New York after obtaining all required permits and approvals. Several projects have already commenced construction activities. All projects are expected to be operational by 2030.

These projects will add to New York's robust portfolio of large-scale renewable energy projects, now comprised of 95 solar, land-based wind, hydroelectric and offshore wind projects currently operating or under development that are expected to deliver approximately 10.5 GW of clean power to the grid - enough to power over 4.6 million New York homes. Of these projects, over 3.2 GW of capacity are under construction, which, once completed, will add to the 36 operational projects currently delivering 2.7 GW of clean energy to the grid – now supplying enough clean energy to power nearly 2 million New York homes.

The State will continue to emphasize engagements with the projects’ host communities. NYSERDA offers resources and no-cost technical assistance to help local governments understand how to manage responsible clean energy development in their communities, including step-by-step instructions and tools to guide the coordination of new clean energy projects, permitting processes, property taxes, siting, zoning, and more.

title: EV Owners Need To Lend Out Their Cars If They Want Regular People To Go Electric
description:
Electric vehicles will probably never fully replace the internal combustion sports car, but mainstream daily drivers are living on borrowed time.
Which means EV owners need to start acting like they have an obligation to lend friends and family their cars.
A few days in an EV won't change anyone's mind if their lifestyle doesn't match what EVs currently offer, and that's fine.
So without the automakers, it falls on the EV owners who want to see EVs become more popular.
If you lend your car to someone who decides they probably shouldn't buy an EV, that's fine.
text:
Electric vehicles will probably never fully replace the internal combustion sports car, but mainstream daily drivers are living on borrowed time. It's not like anyone with no idea which wheels are powered or how many cylinders their car has cares about a missing exhaust note. But while EVs are taking off in the rest of the world, the U.S. lags behind, thanks in large part to pro-oil propaganda. People believe all sorts of myths about EVs, and I'm sorry, but short test drives won't fix it. Which means EV owners need to start acting like they have an obligation to lend friends and family their cars.

A few days in an EV won't change anyone's mind if their lifestyle doesn't match what EVs currently offer, and that's fine. But if they've been tricked by a bunch of pro-oil myths, you may find that a few days with your car is all it takes to convince them that EVs are the best thing ever. Because even an hour-long test drive doesn't show you the benefits of living with a gas station in your garage. It's the kind of thing that probably requires a three-day loan at a minimum, because they have to see how it fits into their regular lives.

Ideally, the automakers would take the lead here, but that's probably not happening anytime soon. I've discussed this idea with employees at several automakers, and so far, I don't think anyone wants to take on the cost and complexity of dealing with dealerships to make longer-term test drives happen. So without the automakers, it falls on the EV owners who want to see EVs become more popular. We need to be the ones pushing our cars on people like they're the supposed free samples that Deputy D. Diggity Dawg Dawson insisted drug dealers would force me to take.

At least anecdotally, I don't know of anything more powerful for changing minds about EVs than time spent with your butt in the seat. Most recently, a friend had to replace their beloved Mazda CX-5 after someone hit them; they asked me about EVs, and almost before I knew it, they were the proud new owners of a Hyundai Ioniq 5. So they were already open to a car that would save them money on gas, but even they quickly realized the things they were worried about weren't actually a big deal.

According to the friend, who I will call Bill, "driving them is super f—ing fun," and he did not think he "would enjoy trying to max out the mi/kWh using the regenerative braking... But [he does]." After only a few days of driving an EV, someone experiencing their first EV was already realizing how strong the oil propaganda is and how much better EVs are at things beyond saving money on gas.

An example of a borrowing experience changing minds is my brother — he borrowed my Fiat for a week while he was in the process of replacing his company truck. With three (soon to be four!) kids, he was never going to buy a two-door hatchback, but he loved being able to charge at home so much that he went out and bought a non-Fiat EV. All it took was a little time living with an electric car that he didn't even have any interest in owning, and it changed his mind about EV ownership before he'd even driven a competitive one.

I know it's scary letting other people borrow your car, and I certainly wouldn't want you handing the keys to someone you know is irresponsible. But without automaker or federal support, we're going to have to do this on our own, and the best way to get people to change their minds about EVs is to get some real time with the cars. And what better way to make that happen is there than trading cars with someone for a few days? Friends and family help each other out, after all.

If you lend your car to someone who decides they probably shouldn't buy an EV, that's fine. No harm, no foul. But just think how happy you'll be if a few days if your car convinces someone they've been wrong about EVs and should actually get one. It's pretty nice, I'm not going to lie, and definitely worth the risk of letting someone you know drive your car. They quite literally sell themselves.

text:
With Election Day less than 24 hours away, North Carolina voters will have a voice that reaches far beyond penciling in candidates on their ballots—as three proposed constitutional amendments could change voter requirements and how the state handles both income and property taxes.

During this midterm cycle, voters will decide whether these amendments are officially introduced into the state’s constitution.

“Getting an amendment on the ballot in North Carolina is not an easy thing to do. They’ve typically been tested in advance, and what tested means is typically somebody’s done some sort of survey or some kind of market research to get a sense of if they’re going to pass,” Dr. Jason Husser said. “I’ve done polling on the amendments. Generally, we found very high levels of support—in some cases, sort of three-to-one support to opposition.”

The first proposed amendment North Carolina voters will see on their ballots concerns expanding I.D. requirements for all types of voting—mainly targeting voter demographics that are casting absentee-by-mail ballots.

If approved, this requirement would be locked into the state's constitution and prevent future legislators from discussing changes.

Dr. Husser, who is a political science and public policy professor at Elon University and director of the Elon University Poll, describes how the controversy surrounding this debate has been ongoing for several years.

After being delayed by court proceedings and legal battles, this new voting-access measure could change the process for future elections.

"There's already statutory approval for voter ID for mail-in votes [and] what this constitutional amendment would do would basically be locking in those rules or a derivative of them into the North Carolina state constitution," Dr. Husser said. "What that means in practice is not necessarily any change for the next cycle, but it means that if the folks who support voter ID lose power and a new group of politicians come in, it's going to make it really hard for them to get rid of voter ID."

According to a research poll conducted by Elon University Poll in late August, approximately 65% of survey respondents voted in favor of the amendment—with about 24% standing in opposition.

Moving on to the next amendment, this proposal targets how state income tax is capped.

According to the North Carolina Department of Revenue, the state's current fixed rate of state income tax is listed at 3.99%—as state leaders are preparing to introduce a reduction plan that will lower this number in 2027.

Under the fine print of this proposed constitutional amendment, North Carolina voters can decide whether to set a hard limit on personal and corporate income taxes at 3.5%.

From the results of the Elon University Poll, 68% of respondents favor the income tax amendment—while 18% expressed their opposition.

"What this amendment would do is... even if political winds change [and] you have a different set of people running the General Assembly in Raleigh, they're not going to be able to raise income tax past this amount without going back to voters for permission," Dr. Husser said. "We may not see immediate terms or economic impacts of the amendment, but it is being done in a context in which there's a lot of competition between states, particularly for high net worth people and for businesses—trying to make sure that North Carolina remains a favorable business environment."

Opponents of this amendment argue that implementing this cap would directly constrain state officials if funds need to be designated in emergencies—such as natural disasters—or during a severe economic recession.

If these circumstances were to hypothetically play out, Dr. Husser notes that state legislators would have to explore alternative funding sources—ranging from sales taxes, excise taxes, fees for service, or borrowing—to address the situation appropriately and sufficiently.

"In the event that the state wants to say do things like dramatically raise teacher pay rates, if you have limits on your income tax ability, you've limited your entire budgetary power because much of the state budget is coming from these income tax amendments," Dr. Husser said. "The alternative in a world in which there's a constitutional amendment halving income tax is starting to look at the sales tax. People point out that's not necessarily the best solution, because sales tax—relative to income—hits poor people harder than wealthy people."

Lastly, for the third and final amendment, North Carolina voters will also have the opportunity to weigh in on how state officials approach limiting property taxes.

In simple terms, this proposed constitutional amendment would place a limit on how much local governing bodies can raise property taxes on a year-by-year basis.

However, the amendment's ballot language doesn't specify what this limit would cover—raising the idea that state lawmakers would decide after the election concludes.

"The General Assembly put this on the ballot, I think, to try to basically restrain the ability of any local government from exceeding a certain threshold of property tax rates," Dr. Husser said. "It's also worth noting that even if property tax rates don't go up, your property taxes can still go up simply because your house becomes more valuable over time. If the house goes up in value—even if the rates are the same—the bill is going to go up."

When it comes to the utilization of property taxes, state and local bodies of government use these funds to help pay the salaries of educators, support law enforcement, and ensure roads and parks are maintained across North Carolina—with opponents of this amendment citing how implementing a "blanket policy" could prove to be problematic over time.

Regarding the reception to this amendment capping property tax increases, a survey by Elon University Poll found 71% of respondents voted in favor of the proposal—with roughly 15% opposed.

Additionally, Dr. Husser found—during data collection for a separate survey—that nearly 84% of North Carolinians age 62 and older viewed this amendment favorably.

He adds that this demographic group expressed concerns about owning a house that continues to rise in value while their retirement savings remain the same.

CHARLOTTESVILLE, Va. (CBS19 NEWS) — Charlottesville is looking to expand its electric vehicle fleet over the next several years while addressing reliability concerns with some of its older public transit buses.

During a Charlottesville City Council work session on Monday, officials discussed an updated fleet and equipment replacement plan that projects the purchase of 24 additional electric vehicles between 2028 and 2030.

The city currently has 14 electric vehicles in its fleet, including vehicles used by several departments and electric buses operated by Charlottesville Area Transit.

Public Works Director Steven Hicks said the city is taking a phased approach to replacing vehicles based on their condition, reliability, safety and operational needs.

That includes addressing problems with older transit buses, which can leave riders waiting when vehicles break down. Garland Williams, director of transit, says that happens every day.

The city is also weighing the costs of transitioning to electric vehicles.

A city fleet electrification study estimates an electric passenger car could cost about $1,500 more than a comparable gas-powered vehicle. A larger electric SUV could cost about $18,000 more.

However, the study estimates replacing vehicles with electric models could save an average of $2,800 per vehicle over 10 years through lower fuel and maintenance costs.

"Just a year ago we were able to buy in bulk, diesel, for about $2.35. We're buying diesel now about $5.50 in bulk. That's unsustainable for us," said Williams.

Expanding the electric fleet also means investing in the infrastructure needed to keep those vehicles charged.

The city is requesting approximately $390,000 through its Capital Improvement Program for additional charging infrastructure. That includes about $225,000 for 17 Level 2 charging stations and $165,000 for one fast charger.

The proposed electric vehicle purchases and charging infrastructure would be considered through the city’s annual budget process. Officials say the timing of replacements will depend on vehicle conditions, department needs, available funding and whether electric options are needed.
