title: Finance Minister Signals Openness to Expanding Domestic Manufacturing Tax Credit to EVs
description:
Deputy Prime Minister and Finance and Economy Minister Lee Hyoung-il said the government will take an active part in parliamentary discussions on the auto industry's request for a domestic manufacturing tax credit for electric vehicles.
On the domestic manufacturing tax credit for EVs, he said, "The government will also take an active part in the National Assembly's discussions and pursue in-depth deliberations."
Industry officials called for the EV manufacturing tax credit at the meeting, saying swift government support is needed to respond to intensifying global competition.
The domestic manufacturing tax credit cuts part of a company's tax bill when it manufactures and sells products domestically.
Strengthening the industry's competitiveness is also seen as a task alongside tax support.
text:
Deputy Prime Minister and Finance and Economy Minister Lee Hyoung-il said the government will take an active part in parliamentary discussions on the auto industry's request for a domestic manufacturing tax credit for electric vehicles. The remarks followed his statement at a parliamentary audit that the government was reviewing whether to extend the credit to EVs, and he visited the Hyundai Motor and Kia research center to hear directly from the industry. With rival parties having jointly submitted related legislation, analysts say the chances have risen that EVs will be added to the list of eligible sectors during the National Assembly's review of tax bills.

Lee met Hyundai Motor Group Executive Chairman Euisun Chung at the Hyundai Motor and Kia research center in Hwaseong, Gyeonggi Province, on the 2nd, then held a roundtable with officials from the electric vehicle, self-driving car and auto parts industries. On the domestic manufacturing tax credit for EVs, he said, "The government will also take an active part in the National Assembly's discussions and pursue in-depth deliberations."

Industry officials called for the EV manufacturing tax credit at the meeting, saying swift government support is needed to respond to intensifying global competition. They also asked for expanded support for parts makers shifting to next-generation vehicles, a legal basis for introducing battery leasing, and more specialized staff at the agency overseeing self-driving cars.

The domestic manufacturing tax credit cuts part of a company's tax bill when it manufactures and sells products domestically. It takes effect next year, with companies claiming the credit from their corporate tax filings the following year. In this year's tax code revision, the government designated six sectors as eligible: solar power, wind power, secondary batteries, semiconductors, core materials and AI robot components. EVs were left out on the view that supporting core parts and materials, rather than finished products, better matches the purpose of the program.

The specific eligible items will be set by presidential decree, as will the size of the credit, which will take into account production costs and sales prices. If EVs are added, automakers that produce in South Korea and sell into the domestic market would see their tax burden fall.

In the National Assembly, lawmakers from both parties are pushing joint legislation to add EVs to the government's plan. On the 16th of last month, 19 lawmakers including Yun Hu-duk of the Democratic Party of Korea and Yoon Han-hong of the People Power Party jointly submitted an amendment to the Restriction of Special Taxation Act that would widen the credit from the government's six sectors to seven, including EVs. A sense of crisis is also growing in the domestic industry, with South Korean models accounting for 48.7% of newly registered electric passenger cars in the country from January through September this year, below half. With the joint legislation and the government's on-site consultations converging, whether to include EVs is expected to come up this month when the tax subcommittee of the National Assembly's finance and economy committee reviews the tax code revision bill.

Strengthening the industry's competitiveness is also seen as a task alongside tax support. Lee described EVs that day as "the next battleground for a rebound in the potential growth rate." He stressed corporate change and technological innovation, saying companies can survive only by securing technology on par with global leaders by 2028 or 2029.

The government is expected to call for self-help measures from the industry as it reviews applying the manufacturing tax credit to EVs, on the grounds that tax support alone will not be enough to counter China's price offensive and competition in self-driving technology. Lee's comments are read as meaning that efforts by companies themselves to raise competitiveness, such as securing autonomous driving technology and cutting costs, must proceed in parallel.

The government plans to announce measures to strengthen the competitiveness of the EV industry this month, reflecting views raised at the roundtable. The package is expected to include steps to upgrade self-driving technology and expand research and development on core parts and technologies.

name: EPA
title: EPA Proposes Revisions to Oil and Gas Methane Standards - The National Law Review
description:
The proposed rule follows previous Trump Administration rulemakings affecting the oil and gas methane regulations.
Associated Gas: EPA is proposing to rescind the requirement that all operators of oil wells with associated natural gas route the gas to a sales line.
As discussed in a prior VNF Alert, the history of the oil and gas methane regulations complicates EPA’s efforts to rescind CO2 emission standards for other facilities.
Like the CO2 emissions standards for power plants, the methane regulations arise under Section 111 and regulate a GHG.
Yet, EPA is proposing to revise the methane regulations rather than repeal them using the legal rationale it has proposed for the repeal of the power plant GHG standards.
text:
On October 29, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA or Agency) published a proposed rule that would modify several elements of the 2024 Clean Air Act methane regulations for new and existing facilities in the oil and gas sector. These are regulations are sometimes referred to as the “OOOOb” and “OOOOc” regulations because they are found at 40 C.F.R. Part 60 Subparts OOOOb and OOOOc, respectively. If finalized as proposed, EPA estimates that the changes to the OOOOb and OOOOc regulations would provide $45 billion in savings and result in an additional 210 million barrels of U.S. oil production and 1.41 trillion cubic feet of U.S. natural gas production. Comments on the proposed rule are due December 16.

The proposed rule follows previous Trump Administration rulemakings affecting the oil and gas methane regulations. In November 2025, EPA issued a final rule extending certain compliance deadlines under the 2024 regulations. Earlier this year, EPA finalized revisions to provisions addressing temporary flaring of associated gas and certain net heating value monitoring and performance-testing requirements.

Companies in the oil and natural gas sector should review EPA’s proposed rule because the scope of its potential impact is much broader than these previous actions. The rulemaking may also provide important insight into how EPA will reconcile its continued regulation of methane emissions with its proposed conclusion in a separate rulemaking that it lacks authority under Clean Air Act Section 111 to regulate power plant GHG emissions.

Key Changes in the Proposal

The Agency’s rulemaking is broad in scope and includes the following key proposed revisions:

Certain Well Sites: EPA is co-proposing two options to create separate categories and standards for well sites, which would relax or eliminate requirements on smaller wells. The first option would categorize well sites by production level (marginal or non-marginal). The second option would categorize well sites by resource type (conventional or unconventional).

Super Emitter Program: EPA is proposing to eliminate the Super Emitter Program, which authorizes certified third-party entities to notify the Agency, states, and operators about large emissions events (i.e., “super emitter” leak events). Currently, these notifications trigger obligations to investigate and take corrective actions.

Covers and Closed Vent Systems: EPA is proposing to split the “No Identifiable Emissions” aspect of covers and closed vent systems into design requirements and operational requirements. The proposed operational requirements would allow for repairs of identified defects rather than classifying detection of emissions as an immediate violation.

Associated Gas: EPA is proposing to rescind the requirement that all operators of oil wells with associated natural gas route the gas to a sales line. The proposal would restore the requirement that such operators can use 95% efficient flaring or other control devices to address the associated gas.

Control Devices: EPA is proposing several technical changes to the requirements for control devices to give flexibility for flame monitoring data deviations, control device alerts, and visible emissions test conditions where appropriate.

Interaction with EPA’s Proposed Repeal of Power Plant Greenhouse Gas Emissions Standards

This rulemaking has important interactions with EPA’s ongoing rulemaking concerning its authority to regulate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from power plants under Clean Air Act Section 111. In a September 2026 supplemental proposal, discussed in a previous VNF Alert, EPA proposed that Section 111 does not authorize the Agency to regulate power plant GHG emissions in response to global climate change concerns and, on that basis, proposed to repeal all remaining power plant GHG emissions standards. One of EPA’s proposed rationales for this conclusion is that Congress has not clearly authorized regulation of GHG emissions.

As discussed in a prior VNF Alert, the history of the oil and gas methane regulations complicates EPA’s efforts to rescind CO2 emission standards for other facilities. Like the CO2 emissions standards for power plants, the methane regulations arise under Section 111 and regulate a GHG. Yet, EPA is proposing to revise the methane regulations rather than repeal them using the legal rationale it has proposed for the repeal of the power plant GHG standards.

In the proposed revisions to the methane standards, EPA acknowledges the interaction with the power plant rulemaking but observes that the methane regulations “operate in a distinct manner, have their own regulatory history, and involve different and additional considerations.” EPA further states that, pending completion of the power plant rulemaking, the Agency might address in a future rulemaking the extent to which the conclusions in the power plant rulemaking require revisions to the methane regulations. The relationship between these different Section 111 regulatory programs will be an important issue to monitor as both rulemakings proceed.

title: Waiting on EPA '27 rule, Rush says it might not be soon - FreightWaves
description:

“There have been some things that have gone in the EPA that are going to delay it,” Rush said, without offering specifics.
“I’ve never seen an EPA law or decree where it wasn’t the same for everybody on one particular date,” Rush told the analysts.

text:
The initial proposed regulation and its amendments have numerous parts. But at the core, it will require about an 80% reduction in NoX emissions to get down to 0.035 g/bhp-hr, which represents grams of pollutant per brake horsepower-hour. There is no change in that basic part of the proposal.

“There have been some things that have gone in the EPA that are going to delay it,” Rush said, without offering specifics. “Possibly we’re going to be told to just work off a draft.”

EPA ‘27’s name is a reference to the model year engines where the tighter NoX rules will need to be met. And a truck retailer like Rush is going to be on the front end of whatever decisions are made by OEMs in how to meet the broader rule that is in place, either with some regulations that OEMs and others have not challenged, like the actual NoX limits, but others that are the subject of industry criticism, such as changes in warranty length.

Rush’s prediction in the earnings call: “We’ll get the final decree out in January or February, but it’s got to go on the first of January,” he said. “So it’s kind of up in the air exactly what is really going to stay the same.”

Wide backing for NCPs

The provision in the July amendments that garnered the most industry support were the noncompliance penalties (NCPs) that engine manufacturers can pay should they fail to meet the new standards. However, the NCPs are not a permanent change and will phase out.

Rush, from his perspective, is looking at OEMs that supply his retail outlets delivering NoX compliant or non-compliant vehicles on differing schedules, should the NCPs be adopted as an amendment to the original rule. “I’ve never seen an EPA law or decree where it wasn’t the same for everybody on one particular date,” Rush told the analysts. “Some will come in on January 1. Some may not do it until the following year.”

However, Rush added that “I don’t believe we’ve had time to truly test these engines.”

“So I think from a customer perspective, I would be leaning towards wanting to pay some NCPs, that’s my personal opinion, and roll in and test the new technology before I go all into the pool,” Rush said. “Let’s dive into the shallow end, not the deep end.”

‘Expiditiously’ at EPA

In a prepared statement sent to FreightWaves, a spokesman for EPA said the agency “recognizes the importance of timely action to provide regulatory certainty for manufacturers and the trucking industry. The agency is carefully reviewing the comments received and is working to finalize the rule as expeditiously as possible.”

Rush cited several OEMs by name, saying they were in favor of the NCPs. And their comments made to the EPA during the comment period on the amendments back that up.

For example, PACCAR (NASDAQ: PCAR), which Rush mentioned, said in its comments to EPA that it “strongly supports EPA’s proposal to establish nonconformance penalties for medium and heavy-heavy duty engines for the NOx standard.”

“The 2027 NOx standards meet the Clean Air Act’s criteria for nonconformance penalties, and they are critical to ensuring industry launches with robust and fully validated products rather than accelerating products to market before validation is complete,” PACCAR said in its comments.

Rush also mentioned engine manufacturer Cummins (NYSE: CMI).

Cummins, in its submission from late August, requested the EPA move quickly on the amendments, something Rush’s comments suggest is not going to occur.

“There is an urgent need for EPA to finalize some of the proposed amendments as soon as possible, for example, those related to emissions warranty, emissions useful life, and nonconformance penalties, so EPA can certify manufacturers’ model year 2027 engines to the revised provisions and manufacturers can introduce them into commerce by January 1, 2027,” Cummins said.

The reference by Cummins to other provisions under study by EPA include the questions of warranty and useful life, which are somewhat similar.

Warranty and useful life provisions

As Rush Truck Centers described it in their own Q&A on the EPA ‘27 rules, useful life “is a regulatory requirement that determines how long an engine must continue meeting federal emissions standards for certification purposes.”

As Rush Truck Centers added, the proposed amendment would not implement tighter useful-life standards until 2030, giving a three-year breather.

The warranty changes in the amendment would keep current requirements in place rather than the original changes, which would have forced OEMs to recognize longer warranties. It has been noted by several of the commenters on the amendments that this change alone is expected to have the greatest financial impact on restraining increases on the price of the cleaner trucks created by the EPA ‘27 rule.

Warranty table is from Rush Enterprises’ web page

Rush on the earnings call referred to the EPA sarcastically as “our great government that can’t seem to write a final decree.” But he softened that by saying that “I know there are a lot of legal ramifications. They have to be very careful with the changes. They have tried to make it easier for the customers.”

The NCPs, Rush said, will allow greater testing of the tighter NoX engines without actually adopting them in fleets.

“Most folks want to run this stuff for over a year before they roll it into their fleets, because we’ve seen through history that new technology does not always run right out of the gate,” Rush said.

The rollout of diesel exhaust fluid (DEF) in 2010, Rush said as an example, resulted in “clogged particulate filters all over the country.”

DEF gets some changes in the proposed amendments. Despite some online misinterpretation that the rule for diesel engines to use DEF is disappearing, what would change in the amendments would be the elimination of the “deratement,” where low DEF levels result in engines slowing the vehicle they are powering. Instead, audio alerts would replace them.

ATA reiterates NCP backing

In a coincidence, the American Trucking Associations had already made its views on the proposed amendments known during the comment period, but about the same time Rush was making its comments, the ATA used the group’s blog last week to reiterate its view on the changes in EPA ‘27.

The blog post was put up by ATA, according to a spokesman, “because the rule is up for interagency review in the coming weeks and it reiterates our stance on the rule. Congress left town, but this is content that speaks to important activity happening at the agencies.”

Like the OEMs made clear in their own comments, the ATA favors the NCPs as a key transition tool.

ATA said of the changes in general that they “lay out a responsible path forward, maintaining ambitious NOx emissions reduction targets while recognizing that manufacturers need sufficient time to test new technologies under real-world operating conditions.”

“NCPs preserve the incentive for manufacturers to meet the new standard as quickly as possible while preventing reliable engine models from becoming unavailable in the market,” the ATA said. “As EPA prepares to finalize its rulemaking, the NCP provisions must remain intact. Without them, the rule would lose a critical safeguard for truck availability, fleet reliability, and an orderly transition to the next generation of emissions technology.”

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is reviewing some aspects of Tesla's robotaxi service.
Still, CEO Elon Musk has seemed confident in Tesla's robotaxi service and market share lately.
text:
Tesla Inc. has expanded its robotaxi service to Fort Worth, adding another major Texas market after launching in Austin, Dallas and Houston.

Ahead of the launch, Tesla touted a geofence that extended west of downtown to include Texas Christian University and beyond to the suburb of White Settlement, and followed a jagged line along Interstate 820 to the edge of the northern suburb of Saginaw.

Tesla's robotaxis have been available in Austin since June 2025 with regular geofence expansions, in Dallas and Houston since April 2026 and San Antonio is expected to launch "soon," the Austin-based automaker says.

Rides in Fort Worth launched at 6 a.m. Monday, with cheers from Tesla fans and Railroad Commissioner candidate Bo French, formerly the Republican Party chairman in Fort Worth's Tarrant County.

Tesla's performance in the North Texas city, home to more than 1 million people, will be closely watched. The company has extended its service hours, with rides now available from 6 a.m. to 2 a.m. Tesla has also added new features, such as a rear-view camera feed and the ability to share trip details with a friend.

But it's been months since Tesla has added a new city to its robotaxi service. Its geofence claims, particularly a recent expansion to make Houston's resemble a rocket, have drawn questions about the boundaries Tesla is advertising. And its Cybercabs have only offered rides to customers in Austin, a point that analysts and investors raised with the company during its recent earnings call.

The service expansion to Fort Worth is the latest robotaxi activity in North Texas. Already, Tesla has shared plans to launch its purpose-built robotaxi, Cybercab, in Dallas this month. In December, Avride launched its robotaxi service in Dallas through a partnership with Uber. And Waymo opened rides to all in Dallas in early August.

Robotaxi and other autonomous vehicle services in Texas are called upon to report incidents and crashes. In the latest filings to federal regulators detailing incidents during the four weeks ending Sept. 15, Tesla reported eight crashes across Texas, three of which were in Austin. None of the crashes resulted in serious injuries.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is reviewing some aspects of Tesla's robotaxi service. Investigators are evaluating a complaint into both Model Y and Cybercab robotaxis, alleging that Tesla's automated driving system sped in school zones. Investigators are also examining the process and technical data Tesla relied on when certifying the Cybercab met vehicle safety standards.

Still, CEO Elon Musk has seemed confident in Tesla's robotaxi service and market share lately.

"I think Tesla will end up being a majority of all passenger miles on Earth in any country where it is allowed to operate freely," Musk said last month during an earnings call. "And you can come back and look at this prediction, but I feel confident about this prediction."

title: Share of Solar Generation with Co-Located Battery Storage is Increasing: EIA
description:
Utility-scale solar developers are increasingly co-locating battery storage with new solar photovoltaic capacity.
When operators co-locate battery storage with solar, they can direct solar electricity output to the grid or to the battery, depending on the wholesale prices, EIA noted.
Southwest states have higher-than-average solar capacity shares relative to their total generating capacity and also have higher levels of co-located utility-scale solar and battery capacity.
As of September, 13% of the total U.S. utility-scale generating capacity is solar photovoltaic, and 18% of that is co-located with battery storage, EIA reported.
The share of solar generation co-located with battery capacity in California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Nevada is more than double the national average.
text:
Utility-scale solar developers are increasingly co-locating battery storage with new solar photovoltaic capacity. As of September 2026, over 16% of new utility-scale solar capacity added this year is co-located with operable battery storage, compared with 2% in 2017, according to data reported to the U.S. Energy Information Administration by operators.

Reported plans for solar additions scheduled to come online in the last three months of this year show that the share with co-located battery storage could increase to 19% this year. Longer-term plans indicate that this trend will continue, with the portion increasing to more than 30% in plans submitted for 2027 and 2028, EIA said on Oct. 30.

When operators co-locate battery storage with solar, they can direct solar electricity output to the grid or to the battery, depending on the wholesale prices, EIA noted.

"Wholesale prices in regions with large solar participation tend to fall when solar contributions are high and rise as they decrease. Plants with both solar and battery storage can manage the combined output of their generating resources to maximize their value in a changing wholesale price environment," it said.

EIA publishes unit-level generator inventory data based on its annual and monthly data collections, including information on design attributes for all utility-scale plants.

Although battery storage and solar units at the same plant often enter commercial service at different times, the EIA-860 and EIA-860M data collection program tracks these developments and provides a monthly summary that can be used to identify co-located technologies.

Southwest states have higher-than-average solar capacity shares relative to their total generating capacity and also have higher levels of co-located utility-scale solar and battery capacity. As of September, 13% of the total U.S. utility-scale generating capacity is solar photovoltaic, and 18% of that is co-located with battery storage, EIA reported.

The share of solar generation co-located with battery capacity in California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Nevada is more than double the national average.

title: Antares, Last Energy, and Radiant hit DOE authorization milestones
description:
Launch Pad was created to extend and expand on the pathway established by the Reactor Pilot Program.
Last Energy milestone: On October 7, Last Energy announced the DOE’s approval of its DSA for its pilot reactor.
It is one of two companies whose Reactor Pilot Program project is centered on the campus—the other is Terrestrial Energy.
Radiant milestone: On October 29, Radiant announced the DOE’s approval of its DSA for its Kaleidos demonstration unit (KDU).
Radiant added that KDU “uses a similar reactor design and custom-designed fuel as the units Radiant plans to deliver to customers.” That design is a 1-MWe, helium-cooled, TRISO-fueled reactor.
text:
Approval breakdown: Companies working toward DOE authorization for the operation of their test and demonstration reactors through either the Reactor Pilot Program or the Nuclear Energy Launch Pad must pass through five milestones:

The OTA, or other transaction agreement, is the first step, marking the formal entrance into partnership between the DOE and a company.

The NSDA is the second step. It is generally described as the foundational safety framework on which future development rests.

The PDSA, or preliminary documented safety analysis, comes next. One participant, Oklo, has previously characterized this stage as a detailed review of a reactor’s design, covering “hazard analysis, accident analysis, safety controls, and design commitments.”

The DSA is the penultimate step. Last Energy has described this stage as “the final and most comprehensive safety analysis in the DOE authorization process,” documenting how a company’s reactor and facility will operate.

The readiness review is the final stage of DOE authorization. Radiant has said this last step is an assessment of whether the reactor and the team responsible for operating it are prepared to begin operations.

Antares milestone: On October 23, Antares announced that the DOE had approved the NSDA for Mark-1, which the company calls its first “electricity-producing reactor.” Mark-1 builds on the lessons learned by Mark-0, the company’s first reactor, which reached zero-power criticality at Idaho National Laboratory in June. Antares ultimately is pursuing a 100 kWe–1 MWe reactor design that uses TRISO fuel, sodium heat pipes for cooling, and a nitrogen-based Brayton cycle for power conversion. That reactor is called R1. Mark-1, according to the company, is the bridge between the demonstration work of Mark-0 and the deployment of R1.

Antares is planning to operate Mark-1 at full electrical power for six months in 2027 at INL. Beyond that, the company plans to deploy multiple R1 units at Fort Bragg, under the Army’s Janus Program, with the first unit planned for a 2028 deployment.

Stepping back from the company-specific details, this milestone also represents the first time a company has earned an NSDA for a second reactor design through this new DOE authorization framework.

While not explicitly confirmed by Antares, it is likely that the Mark-1 is progressing through the Nuclear Energy Launch Pad. Launch Pad was created to extend and expand on the pathway established by the Reactor Pilot Program. Antares was selected for the program in August.

Last Energy milestone: On October 7, Last Energy announced the DOE’s approval of its DSA for its pilot reactor. The company is ultimately pursuing a 20-MWe, LEU-fueled pressurized water reactor.

The company previously has called this pilot project the PWR-5 and described it as using “the same physical reactor geometry” of the PWR-20 with “reduced fuel enrichment scaled for 5 MW of electrical output.” This pilot reactor would demonstrate low-power criticality “before progressing to electricity generation.”

Notably, the name “PWR-5” does not appear in Last Energy’s newest announcement, but the company still said it is planning to use its pilot to “validate commercial-ready performance and advance into power generation.”

Last Energy’s pilot facility is located at Texas A&M University’s RELLIS campus. It is one of two companies whose Reactor Pilot Program project is centered on the campus—the other is Terrestrial Energy.

Radiant milestone: On October 29, Radiant announced the DOE’s approval of its DSA for its Kaleidos demonstration unit (KDU). The company is planning to test this pilot at full-power for 60 effective full-power days at INL’s Demonstration of Microreactor Experiments (DOME). This scheduled testing “will be the industry’s only full-power, extended-duration demonstration of a nuclear microreactor to date,” according to the company.

Radiant added that KDU “uses a similar reactor design and custom-designed fuel as the units Radiant plans to deliver to customers.” That design is a 1-MWe, helium-cooled, TRISO-fueled reactor.

The NSDA is the second step. It is generally described as the foundational safety framework on which future development rests.

The PDSA, or preliminary documented safety analysis, comes next. One participant, Oklo, has previously characterized this stage as a detailed review of a reactor’s design, covering “hazard analysis, accident analysis, safety controls, and design commitments.”

The DSA is the penultimate step. Last Energy has described this stage as “the final and most comprehensive safety analysis in the DOE authorization process,” documenting how a company’s reactor and facility will operate.

The readiness review is the final stage of DOE authorization. Radiant has said this last step is an assessment of whether the reactor and the team responsible for operating it are prepared to begin operations.

Antares milestone: On October 23, Antares announced that the DOE had approved the NSDA for Mark-1, which the company calls its first “electricity-producing reactor.” Mark-1 builds on the lessons learned by Mark-0, the company’s first reactor, which reached zero-power criticality at Idaho National Laboratory in June. Antares ultimately is pursuing a 100 kWe–1 MWe reactor design that uses TRISO fuel, sodium heat pipes for cooling, and a nitrogen-based Brayton cycle for power conversion. That reactor is called R1. Mark-1, according to the company, is the bridge between the demonstration work of Mark-0 and the deployment of R1.

Antares is planning to operate Mark-1 at full electrical power for six months in 2027 at INL. Beyond that, the company plans to deploy multiple R1 units at Fort Bragg, under the Army’s Janus Program, with the first unit planned for a 2028 deployment.

Stepping back from the company-specific details, this milestone also represents the first time a company has earned an NSDA for a second reactor design through this new DOE authorization framework.

While not explicitly confirmed by Antares, it is likely that the Mark-1 is progressing through the Nuclear Energy Launch Pad. Launch Pad was created to extend and expand on the pathway established by the Reactor Pilot Program. Antares was selected for the program in August.

Last Energy milestone: On October 7, Last Energy announced the DOE’s approval of its DSA for its pilot reactor. The company is ultimately pursuing a 20-MWe, LEU-fueled pressurized water reactor.

The company previously has called this pilot project the PWR-5 and described it as using “the same physical reactor geometry” of the PWR-20 with “reduced fuel enrichment scaled for 5 MW of electrical output.” This pilot reactor would demonstrate low-power criticality “before progressing to electricity generation.”

Notably, the name “PWR-5” does not appear in Last Energy’s newest announcement, but the company still said it is planning to use its pilot to “validate commercial-ready performance and advance into power generation.”

Last Energy’s pilot facility is located at Texas A&M University’s RELLIS campus. It is one of two companies whose Reactor Pilot Program project is centered on the campus—the other is Terrestrial Energy.

Radiant milestone: On October 29, Radiant announced the DOE’s approval of its DSA for its Kaleidos demonstration unit (KDU). The company is planning to test this pilot at full-power for 60 effective full-power days at INL’s Demonstration of Microreactor Experiments (DOME). This scheduled testing “will be the industry’s only full-power, extended-duration demonstration of a nuclear microreactor to date,” according to the company.

Radiant added that KDU “uses a similar reactor design and custom-designed fuel as the units Radiant plans to deliver to customers.” That design is a 1-MWe, helium-cooled, TRISO-fueled reactor.

text:
NEWPORT — Harvey Hanna & Associates has announced a deal that would install solar panels on more than 1.8 million square feet of rooftops on eight properties, including its future Scotts Run warehouse in Middletown.

The agreement is with King Energy, a venture-backed commercial solar company that builds, owns and operates rooftop solar on multi-tenant properties. It calls for more than 19 megawatts of direct current across the eight properties owned by Harvey Hanna, according to a press release. All eight projects are still in development and the entire portfolio is projected to represent more than 19 megawatts.

So far, these projects include the 1.3 million square-foot warehouse complex planned near Jamison Corner and Scotts Run, 750 Governor Lea Rd. in New Castle and 400 Ships Landing Way in New Castle, as well as five more unidentified properties.

The solar energy projected from the three named sites would be more than 14.7 million kilowatt-hours of electricity a year. That would be roughly enough to power 1,400 homes, based on a household average provided by the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

“At Harvey Hanna, we believe our buildings can do more than simply provide space for businesses. They can also contribute to the communities around them,” Harvey Hanna Managing Director Thomas Harvey said in a press release. “We have a significant portfolio of commercial rooftops, and this partnership with King Energy gives us an opportunity to put that existing infrastructure to work in a meaningful way. We’re excited about the long-term environmental and community benefits this program can provide.”

Harvey Hanna boasts of owning and managing nearly 4 million square feet of industrial and commercial space in Delaware and Maryland. The firm has undergone a major transition, with CEO E. Thomas Harvey III welcomed his three sons into the fold in top leadership positions.

The company reports it is developing 1.6 million square feet of industrial space, along with a mixed-use community. This summer, it acquired 103 acres of land prepped to build industrial and warehouse space in Middletown for $25 million.

The solar announcement offers a different approach to a Delaware challenge. The First State generates less electricity than it uses and imports a large share of its power through the regional grid run by PJM Interconnection. Delaware’s net generation was about 4.8 million megawatt-hours in 2024, among the lowest of any state, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. State law requires utilities to get 40% of their power from renewable energy by 2035 and utility providers typically comply by buying renewable energy credits or solar renewable energy credits.

Harvey Hanna and King Energy’s project would supply about 2.2% of the energy needed to meet that standard, according to Harvey Hanna officials.

King Energy CEO John Witchel said that Harvey Hanna “has been a terrific partner” because the company recognizes the opportunity at hand and takes a long-term view of the issue.

“By working together, we’re able to turn existing commercial buildings into sources of clean energy while expanding access to community solar for Delaware residents,” Witchel said in the release.

Gov. Matt Meyer’s office has accepted four King Energy solar projects into its JobsFirst Permitting Accelerator, a program meant to speed approvals around the state. That includes 400 Ships Landing Way, as well as others such as the Frankford Business Park in Sussex County and 1001 Lambson Lane and 10 Dock View Drive in New Castle.

Together, those projects account for 9.67 megawatts and $20.3 million in proposed private investment, according to the governor’s office.

description:
Fremont’s Director of Economic Development points to more jobs, increased city revenue, and improved city services as direct benefits of the city’s focus on rapid access to power.
A big part of its economic success is the alignment between Fremont’s city government, elected officials, and the city’s Office of Economic Development.
Along with that commitment to growth has come a need to understand the power grid so the city could ensure that industrial facilities have the power they need.

text:
Key takeaways:

Fremont, California has more than doubled its number of manufacturing jobs since 2018, from 30,000 to 70,000, while maintaining a very high quality of life for residents.

Ensuring rapid access to electric power has been crucial in attracting manufacturers to the city.

Bloom Energy provides fast time to power for Fremont-based manufacturers.

Fremont’s Director of Economic Development points to more jobs, increased city revenue, and improved city services as direct benefits of the city’s focus on rapid access to power.

On the edge of Silicon Valley, the city of Fremont is showing how enabling more rapid industrial growth goes hand-in-hand with improving quality of life. It’s got grassy, rolling hills, a wetland wildlife refuge, some of the most livable neighborhoods in the country—and one of the biggest manufacturing hubs in the state of California.

That’s not a coincidence, says Donovan Lazaro, Director of Economic Development for the city.

“You can draw a direct line between these manufacturing facilities that we’re standing up and Fremont’s ability to expand our parks, have better-maintained facilities and roads, and hire more firefighters, police, and city staff,” says Lazaro. “All of these different services that people want benefit significantly from the industrial growth that we’re seeing.”

Fremont has more than doubled the number of manufacturing jobs since 2018, from 30,000 to 70,000. It’s now home to more than 900 manufacturing sites of varying scale, including the country’s biggest Tesla factory, which produces more cars than any other automotive plant in the U.S, and Bloom Energy, the leader in on-site power.

A big part of its economic success is the alignment between Fremont’s city government, elected officials, and the city’s Office of Economic Development. That team, which Donovan likens to a “municipal startup,” works to ensure that companies setting up new plants in the city can get approvals in an efficient way. They also work with Bloom Energy to ensure rapid availability of electric power, which is a key constraint to industrial and commercial growth in many locales. If the grid capacity isn’t available right away, Bloom-powered microgrids can provide what they need. And that’s helped Fremont’s economic development team win again and again.

It’s a lesson that many other municipalities can learn from: Provide a streamlined path to approval, remove local regulatory uncertainties, and facilitate rapid time to power, and industrial growth will follow.

“If we can provide speed and certainty, we’re going to win disproportionately,” Lazaro says.

The happiest city in the U.S.

Fremont’s 230,000 citizens live in what a recent study called “the happiest city in the U.S.” The study ranked Fremont tops for emotional and physical well-being. It’s walkable, the weather is pleasant, and people are healthy.

One reason it’s so livable is thanks to a decades-long history of fostering industrial economic development. General Motors built an auto plant here in 1965, and it’s been operating since then. (It’s now the Tesla plant.) The manufacturing base grew from there, with years of thoughtful stewardship by the city.

Along with that commitment to growth has come a need to understand the power grid so the city could ensure that industrial facilities have the power they need.

To keep Fremont’s economy humming, the city is zoned to keep manufacturing facilities separate from residential and commercial areas. Within the industrial zones, getting approvals and permits for new facilities is a streamlined process.

Lazaro describes his job to manufacturers and developers like this: “Our job is to sit on your side of the table and be an advocate for your needs, to remove barriers and obstacles and to instill confidence in investing in Fremont.”

That approach makes Fremont stand out. “We’re really keen on retaining the innovation that is developed here in the Bay Area and giving it room to scale and thrive,” Lazaro says.

The time-to-power opportunity

Despite these advantages, it hasn’t always been smooth sailing. Many U.S. cities and counties have recently learned that the availability of electric power limits growth. Even with its robust grid, Fremont has faced this challenge, too. Lazaro’s team learned early on that fast time to power makes an enormous difference in being able to attract and grow industrial and commercial companies.

A big part of Fremont’s success is its ability to help deliver power rapidly, with a multi-pronged approach that includes a robust traditional grid allocation as well as microgrid capabilities from Bloom Energy. Fremont’s economic development team realized early on that they needed to become “grid literate” to help industrial customers set up in the city. They now act as facilitators, bridging conversations between companies and the local utility to help companies get the power they need.

The local utility provides hundreds of megawatts of power to Fremont’s many customers. But it also oversees an enormous and complex grid that covers much of the state. Wildfire-related costs and compliance with the state’s utilities commission challenge it even further. Getting a new connection to the grid can take years.

Fremont recognized that many commercial and industrial companies needed to supplement grid power if they wanted to get up and running quickly. They found the perfect partner in Bloom Energy, which has been operating a manufacturing plant in Fremont since July 2022. Bloom Energy Server® fuel cell systems can provide manufacturers and industrial customers with megawatts of generation capacity within a few weeks, rather than years. Plus, they’re climate-friendly, pocketbook-friendly, and neighborhood-friendly.

They’re compact, too. Bloom Energy Server systems are modular and can be stacked alongside a manufacturing facility. “Bloom not only bridges the time to energization but also supplements the grid allocation from the utility,” Lazaro says.

Fast time to power creates jobs

With a comprehensive approach to fostering industrial growth that combines intelligent zoning, streamlined permitting, “grid literacy,” and a compelling microgrid solution to supplement grid power, Fremont’s economic development strategy is paying off.

Bloom’s ability to provide fast time to power has helped Fremont win and keep several manufacturers who would otherwise have located their plants in Nevada, Texas, or Tennessee, Lazaro says.

Now, there are six manufacturers in the city actively using Bloom fuel cell systems.

“This has been really the closest thing to a silver bullet that we’ve had,” Lazaro says.

With more jobs and investment, the city has a bigger tax base, which enables it to invest in roads, parks, and more.

Education is a particular emphasis for Fremont—no surprise in a city where 63% of residents have a bachelor’s degree or higher. The city helped set up an “Earn to Learn” pipeline that helps students in the local community college learn trades and get jobs with local manufacturers. And it hosts a big “Manufacturing Week” event every year—one of the largest in the country—where high school and college students can visit factories and learn about the technologies and opportunities in manufacturing.

Bucking the manufacturing trends

Attracting and retaining manufacturing jobs is never easy, but Fremont has managed to grow its manufacturing base and add jobs.

“2026 has been a transformative year for our manufacturing sector. We’ve had the equivalent of nearly one new facility being announced every week,” Lazaro says.

Providing rapid access to grid and microgrid power has been essential to helping Fremont attract and retain manufacturers. With the rapid time to power afforded by Bloom’s Energy Server systems, other cities can do the same.

To find out more, contact Bloom.

title: Car Pro Commentary: DAMMIT, GM! Keep The Main Thing The Main Thing
authors: Jerry Reynolds, supporting the military, first responders
description:
General Motors is moving its stock listing to the Nasdaq, the exchange closely associated with technology companies, and apparently wants us to think of GM as a technology company.
But dammit, General Motors, the technology should serve the vehicle and its owner.
My concern is the thinking behind the message: whether being called a technology company has become more important to management than being an outstanding automobile company.
I want General Motors to succeed.
And remember what my daddy said before another executive gets carried away explaining what business GM supposedly wants to become.
text:
With apologies for language. The move by GM to the Nasdaq brought back bad memories for me and makes me extremely nervous about their future, and trust me, I want to be wrong here.

General Motors is moving its stock listing to the Nasdaq, the exchange closely associated with technology companies, and apparently wants us to think of GM as a technology company. My reaction? Bullshit. You can change the exchange where your shares trade, surround yourself with computer programmers, and talk about software until the batteries in your microphone die, but first and foremost, General Motors is an automaker. Somewhere inside the executive offices, somebody needs to put that on the wall in letters big enough to read without a subscription.

I have been down this road before, and that is why this gets under my skin. When I was Ford National Dealer Council chairman from 2000 to 2002, I fought then-CEO Jac Nasser tooth and nail over his desire to diversify Ford Motor Company. I believed Ford needed to concentrate on the business that put the blue oval on the building: making vehicles people wanted to buy, making them well, and taking care of the people who bought them. From where I sat, representing dealers who faced those customers every day, that was plenty of work to keep everybody occupied. Nasser bought dealerships, tech companies, body shops, and dot com company that he could find, even salvage yards.

I said it then, and I say it now: Technology is wonderful. I am thankful for it. Technology can make a vehicle safer, more dependable, more efficient, and more enjoyable to drive. It can help engineers solve problems that once seemed impossible. I spend enough time reviewing new vehicles to appreciate what good technology can do. But dammit, General Motors, the technology should serve the vehicle and its owner. When management becomes more excited about what else it can sell the customer than about the automobile it already sold them, I start getting nervous. Read the last line again and let it sink in.

My daddy had a way of cutting through this kind of nonsense. He told me, “Always make the main thing, the main thing.” There was no consultant’s invoice attached to that advice, no strategic presentation, and no committee needed to explain it. For General Motors, the main thing is building the best cars, trucks, and SUVs it possibly can, at prices customers will pay, with quality that gives them a reason to come back. Everything else ought to earn its place by helping accomplish that mission.

Consider the customer-data mess. GM agreed to pay $220 million to settle claims by more than three dozen states involving the sale of driving-behavior and location information associated with nearly 10.3 million drivers. The allegations involved third parties, including data brokers that passed information to insurers. Those are claims resolved through a settlement, and they should be described that way. But the business question practically asks itself: How did collecting and selling that information help GM build a better vehicle or earn a customer’s loyalty? It didn’t.

People walked into dealerships to buy transportation. Imagine finding out that information about how you used that transportation became a product somewhere along the way. There is a world of difference between using technology to warn a driver about a potential collision and finding another way to monetize the person behind the wheel. Customer trust takes years to build, and a corporate strategy that puts it at risk had better face some very hard questions.

Then there is the electric-vehicle strategy. I have no objection to GM building EVs for people who want them. Build a great one, price it competitively, and give the customer a reason to choose it. I’ve said on the show many times, my favorite EVs I’ve reviewed were made by GM. My objection is to executives getting so attached to their vision of the future that the customer’s preferences become an inconvenience. The showroom is where a corporate prediction meets somebody’s household budget, driving habits, and willingness to sign a contract. The customer gets the final vote, regardless of how enthusiastically Wall Street applauded the presentation.

GM has talented engineers, hardworking employees, extremely dedicated dealers, and customers who love its products. That is what makes this so aggravating. There is a tremendous business here worth protecting. A pickup that works hard for its owner, an SUV that serves a growing family, or a car that makes somebody smile every morning, like the C8 Corvette, can create loyalty that no corporate identity exercise or TV ad, will ever match. Give those customers dependable vehicles and stand behind them when something goes wrong. There is your business plan.

Could losing focus eventually mean the end of GM? Any company that repeatedly neglects the reasons customers choose it puts its future at risk. But moving a stock listing does not establish that GM is headed for collapse, and I am not predicting bankruptcy because somebody changed exchanges. My concern is the thinking behind the message: whether being called a technology company has become more important to management than being an outstanding automobile company.

I want General Motors to succeed. I want its dealers to prosper, its employees to have secure futures, and its customers to feel good about what they bought. That is exactly why I refuse to applaud every shiny new corporate direction as progress. Use the technology. Improve the vehicles. Listen to the people spending their money. And remember what my daddy said before another executive gets carried away explaining what business GM supposedly wants to become.

text:
Flaws Pervade EPA’s Repeal of Power Plant Greenhouse Gas Emissions Standards

Last month, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) eliminated key limits on greenhouse gas emissions from power plants. The agency doubled down, arguing in a separate proposed rule that it lacks authority to set any limits on these emissions because (a) the Clean Air Act doesn’t authorize the limits and (b) U.S. power plants’ contribution to climate change is so small that limits would be futile. This is wrong. The law, science, and economics all justify U.S. climate regulations, as we document in a new fact sheet. First, statutory text and relevant legislative history indicate Congress intended the Clean Air Act to extend to greenhouse gas emissions. Second, the Supreme Court has affirmed EPA’s authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions. Third, U.S. power plants cause enormous harm to U.S. health and welfare and are one of the largest contributors to U.S. greenhouse gas emissions. The sector’s greenhouse gas emissions annually cause thousands of U.S. deaths and hundreds of billions in economic damages. If the power sector were a country, it would be the world’s sixth-largest emitter. Read the fact sheet for the complete list of counterarguments and supporting resources.

New Piece in The Atlantic: EPA’s Repeal Is Nihilistic, and Wrong, Too

Although EPA repealed these key greenhouse gas emissions standards for power plants, the agency acknowledged that climate change is real and dangerous. EPA instead argues in its proposal that the U.S. government cannot do anything meaningful to avert harm. “This is utter nihilism,” writes our Richard Revesz in The Atlantic. EPA made a similar argument in its repeal of greenhouse gas emissions standards for motor vehicles, even though the power and transportation sectors account for almost half of U.S. emissions. “It follows from EPA’s logic that eliminating or substantially reducing the [emissions] of any other sector of the economy would be even more pointless,” writes Revesz. “And the same goes for the emissions of any sector of any country, anywhere in the world.” But U.S. greenhouse gas emissions are meaningful; they are deadly. One year of U.S. power-sector emissions roughly translates to 5,300 additional deaths from heat waves and wildfires in the United States alone. “Everyone will suffer the consequences” of this nihilistic national climate policy, writes Revesz.

Winding the Litigation Clock for Regulations

If a presidential administration issues a regulation in the first year of its term and the regulation is challenged in court, there is a 68% chance litigation will finish by the end of the term. Regulations issued in the second year have only a 42% chance of completing litigation, and a mere 7% chance in the fourth year. In a new article, our Bridget Pals discusses these findings—part of an original analysis on the timing of regulatory litigation that builds on our Major Rules in the Courts (MRITC) tracker—and their implications for agency rulemaking and prioritization. “An administration must prioritize speed if it wants to control the defense of its own regulations in court,” writes Pals. “Less than a quarter of challenged rules finalized during the first Trump Administration or Biden Administration finished litigation during the administration that issued the rule.” Pals’ analysis highlights the risk of a recent trend: The past two presidential administrations had an uptick in rulemaking in the final year of their terms. Future administrations should push through regulations early and fast if they want to ensure the rule is robustly defended throughout the entire litigation process. Learn more about litigation timing and our broader analysis of challenged major rules at our December 1 webinar.

Why Add Chaos to a Struggling Grid?

Data centers and electrification are swelling projections of electricity demand, and the White House has pressured PJM—the nation’s largest regional grid operator—to respond quickly. PJM proposed a one-time auction to procure nearly 7 gigawatts of additional electricity-generation capacity for the region. But the proposed backstop auction would “be putting an expensive Band-Aid on a gaping wound” and spill billions of dollars of data center costs onto ordinary customers, write our Jennifer Danis and Natalie Friedberg in RTO Insider. For now, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has paused the auction. But the Commission should more broadly reconsider whether the auction should proceed at all, especially given the opportunity for smarter reforms. “PJM and its member states must rise to meet the moment and use the data center buildout to enact meaningful reform,” write Danis and Friedberg, who with our Christoph Graf submitted feedback about PJM’s auction to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

Sixth Circuit Court Weighs Scope of Congressional Review Act with Federal Agencies’ Authority at Stake

The full U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit recently weighed arguments over an appeal of a 2025 panel ruling, with constraints on federal agencies’ rulemaking authority at stake. The Congressional Review Act empowers Congress within a limited time window to “disapprove,” or cancel, regulations promulgated by federal agencies. Afterward, an agency cannot reissue a regulation that is “substantially the same” as the disapproved regulation. The Sixth Circuit case considers how to apply the “substantially the same” test. In 2025, a panel from the Sixth Circuit held that agencies can reissue discrete provisions of a disapproved regulation. Our Max Sarinsky, Dena Adler, Adam Grogg, and former Legal Fellow Jack Jones defend the 2025 ruling in an amicus brief, explaining that a reading of “substantially the same” that prohibits reissuing discrete provisions is untenable. “The court should find that the ‘substantially the same’ test looks at the whole rule, not each part,” they write. As Sarinsky explains in an essay in the Yale Journal on Regulation’s Notice & Comment blog, whatever the Sixth Circuit decides will have significant implications for agency authority following the disapproval of a regulation through the Congressional Review Act.

A New Court Ruling Makes It Harder To Protect Americans from Dangerous Chemicals

Last month, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit issued an opinion rejecting limits on the use of methylene chloride, a hazardous chemical. The Fifth Circuit’s reasoning “will make it harder for EPA to put forth analytically sound rules that address unreasonable risks posed by toxic chemicals,” write our Katherine Welty and Martha Roberts in Bloomberg Law. The court ruled that under the Toxic Substances Control Act, the agency must evaluate the risk of methylene chloride and other hazardous chemicals on a use-by-use basis, an approach that will likely underestimate actual risk. If someone uses methylene chloride at work, and then at home, their total risk increases—but EPA now may be unable to address such aggregate risk. The Fifth Circuit also ruled that EPA must consider the use of personal protective equipment in its risk evaluations, despite evidence that workers don’t always use this equipment. EPA has recently proposed revising its procedures for risk evaluation in a way that largely tracks the Fifth Circuit’s ruling. If the rule is finalized, it is likely to provide an opportunity for another court to weigh in on these issues. “Meanwhile, methylene chloride will continue to pose risks to the millions of people exposed to it at work and at home,” say Welty and Roberts.

title: Tell Congress not to give free rein to fossil fuels - Southern Environmental Law Center
description:
We’ve seen local communities stand up to polluting power plants and pipelines to protect public health and safeguard our climate future.
But now, Congress has made a deal to trade away those environmental protections and the guarantee that communities have a voice.
Tell Congress not to give free rein to fossil fuels.
It would allow industries to short circuit environmental reviews and cut communities out of the decision-making process.
It would also cut off communities’ legal options to challenge the government when they are harmed.
text:
For decades, our country has set the standard for laws that preserve communities’ right to have a say in government decisions that affect our air and water. We’ve seen local communities stand up to polluting power plants and pipelines to protect public health and safeguard our climate future. And we’ve seen communities work collaboratively to make good projects better and more effective.

But now, Congress has made a deal to trade away those environmental protections and the guarantee that communities have a voice. The so-called “Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act” would weaken environmental protections, slash transparency requirements, and block opportunities for public participation at a time when the administration is also gutting environmental regulations across the board. The bill holds positive reforms to build more clean energy and transmission hostage to a host of pro-fossil fuel and anti-public participation rollbacks.

Tell Congress not to give free rein to fossil fuels.

But this backroom deal would do serious and lasting harm. It would allow industries to short circuit environmental reviews and cut communities out of the decision-making process. It would also cut off communities’ legal options to challenge the government when they are harmed.

As discussed in a prior VNF Alert, the history of the oil and gas methane regulations complicates EPA’s efforts to rescind CO2 emission standards for other facilities.

Yet, EPA is proposing to revise the methane regulations rather than repeal them using the legal rationale it has proposed for the repeal of the power plant GHG standards.
text:
On October 29, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA or Agency) published a proposed rule that would modify several elements of the 2024 Clean Air Act methane regulations for new and existing facilities in the oil and gas sector. These regulations are sometimes referred to as the “OOOOb” and “OOOOc” regulations because they are found at 40 C.F.R. Part 60 Subparts OOOOb and OOOOc, respectively. If finalized as proposed, EPA estimates that the changes to the OOOOb and OOOOc regulations would provide $45 billion in savings and result in an additional 210 million barrels of U.S. oil production and 1.41 trillion cubic feet of U.S. natural gas production. Comments on the proposed rule are due December 16.

The proposed rule follows previous Trump Administration rulemakings affecting the oil and gas methane regulations. In November 2025, EPA issued a final rule extending certain compliance deadlines under the 2024 regulations. Earlier this year, EPA finalized revisions to provisions addressing temporary flaring of associated gas and certain net heating value monitoring and performance-testing requirements.

Companies in the oil and natural gas sector should review EPA’s proposed rule because the scope of its potential impact is much broader than these previous actions. The rulemaking may also provide important insight into how EPA will reconcile its continued regulation of methane emissions with its proposed conclusion in a separate rulemaking that it lacks authority under Clean Air Act Section 111 to regulate power plant GHG emissions.

Key Changes in the Proposal

The Agency’s rulemaking is broad in scope and includes the following key proposed revisions:

Certain Well Sites: EPA is co-proposing two options to create separate categories and standards for well sites, which would relax or eliminate requirements on smaller wells. The first option would categorize well sites by production level (marginal or non-marginal). The second option would categorize well sites by resource type (conventional or unconventional).

Super Emitter Program: EPA is proposing to eliminate the Super Emitter Program, which authorizes certified third-party entities to notify the Agency, states, and operators about large emissions events (i.e., “super emitter” leak events). Currently, these notifications trigger obligations to investigate and take corrective actions.

Covers and Closed Vent Systems: EPA is proposing to split the “No Identifiable Emissions” aspect of covers and closed vent systems into design requirements and operational requirements. The proposed operational requirements would allow for repairs of identified defects rather than classifying detection of emissions as an immediate violation.

Associated Gas: EPA is proposing to rescind the requirement that all operators of oil wells with associated natural gas route the gas to a sales line. The proposal would restore the requirement that such operators can use 95% efficient flaring or other control devices to address the associated gas.

Control Devices: EPA is proposing several technical changes to the requirements for control devices to give flexibility for flame monitoring data deviations, control device alerts, and visible emissions test conditions where appropriate.

Interaction with EPA’s Proposed Repeal of Power Plant Greenhouse Gas Emissions Standards

This rulemaking has important interactions with EPA’s ongoing rulemaking concerning its authority to regulate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from power plants under Clean Air Act Section 111. In a September 2026 supplemental proposal, discussed in a previous VNF Alert, EPA proposed that Section 111 does not authorize the Agency to regulate power plant GHG emissions in response to global climate change concerns and, on that basis, proposed to repeal all remaining power plant GHG emissions standards. One of EPA’s proposed rationales for this conclusion is that Congress has not clearly authorized regulation of GHG emissions.

As discussed in a prior VNF Alert, the history of the oil and gas methane regulations complicates EPA’s efforts to rescind CO2 emission standards for other facilities. Like the CO2 emissions standards for power plants, the methane regulations arise under Section 111 and regulate a GHG. Yet, EPA is proposing to revise the methane regulations rather than repeal them using the legal rationale it has proposed for the repeal of the power plant GHG standards.

In the proposed revisions to the methane standards, EPA acknowledges the interaction with the power plant rulemaking but observes that the methane regulations “operate in a distinct manner, have their own regulatory history, and involve different and additional considerations.” EPA further states that, pending completion of the power plant rulemaking, the Agency might address in a future rulemaking the extent to which the conclusions in the power plant rulemaking require revisions to the methane regulations. The relationship between these different Section 111 regulatory programs will be an important issue to monitor as both rulemakings proceed.

title: Board adopts resolution setting pathway to decarbonizing County vehicle fleet
description:
“Electric vehicles cost significantly less to fuel and maintain, and those savings add up for taxpayers.
Transitioning to an electric fleet will benefit both the organization and the community.
It will also reduce air pollution locally,” said John Wasiutynski, the director of Multnomah County’s Office of Sustainability.
Four years later, the Board passed a resolution that solidified the County’s commitment to fossil fuel-free buildings and fleet electrification.
One of the strategies for reaching the plan’s “Clean Energy” goal is decarbonizing Multnomah County operations, including the County’s fleet.
text:
The Multnomah County Board of Commissioners on Thursday, Oct. 29, unanimously passed a resolution(link is external) to adopt the Fleet Decarbonization Strategy, which establishes the framework for fully transitioning the organization’s fleet from gasoline and diesel to electric vehicles by 2050. The resolution, along with an Oct. 15 briefing(link is external) on the matter, were advanced in response to a Fiscal Year 2027 budget note.

“Electric vehicles cost significantly less to fuel and maintain, and those savings add up for taxpayers. With difficult budget decisions ahead, this is an action we can take to reduce our long-term operating costs,” said Commissioner Julia Brim-Edwards, who co-sponsored the resolution with Commissioner Shannon Singleton, after the meeting. “This resolution moves us forward with a clear strategy and accountability for delivering results.”

“I know this might still be a controversial statement, but climate change is real… We see the impacts daily — the headlines continue to grow in the number and severity of incidents, and we're experiencing our driest October in 35 years,” said Commissioner Singleton. “So we have to take this issue seriously as a County.”

Multnomah County’s current fleet of more than 650 vehicles is used for a wide variety of purposes, including client visits, infrastructure maintenance, emergency management, law enforcement, health services and other needs. Transitioning to an electric fleet will benefit both the organization and the community.

“Moving from internal combustion engines to battery electric vehicles reduces County emissions. It will also reduce air pollution locally,” said John Wasiutynski, the director of Multnomah County’s Office of Sustainability. “We're seeing evidence that even the small increase in registered electric vehicles helps to improve local air quality.”

The initial costs of transitioning can be mitigated by partnerships with the state and utilities, and with other outside funding, Wasiutynski said, also noting that an electric County fleet will reduce longer-term maintenance costs and hedge against rising fuel prices.

The resolution represents the latest step in the County’s commitment to reducing the environmental impacts of its operations, particularly decreasing enterprise greenhouse gas emissions generated through County work — 35% of which is driven by County fleet vehicles.

In 2017, the Board adopted a resolution to put Multnomah County on track to meet 100% of community-wide energy needs with renewable energy — including the full decarbonization of the organization’s fleet — by 2050. Four years later, the Board passed a resolution that solidified the County’s commitment to fossil fuel-free buildings and fleet electrification.

Most recently, the Board adopted the 2026 Climate Justice Plan, a strategic 10-year roadmap for protecting residents from severe climate impacts and aggressively lowering carbon emissions. One of the strategies for reaching the plan’s “Clean Energy” goal is decarbonizing Multnomah County operations, including the County’s fleet.

The fleet decarbonization strategy(link is external), drafted by the Office of Sustainability, carries four main recommendations:

Establishing an "EV First" administrative rule that requires County departments to prioritize battery electric vehicles (BEVs) during procurement when possible

Establishing an interdepartmental BEV Task Force to make recommendations and work through implementation challenges

Establishing emissions reduction targets for 2035 and 2040 to track progress toward the 2050 goal.

Centralizing the funding for EV charging infrastructure, rather than making individual departments bear the cost

Commissioner Singleton introduced an amendment(link is external), approved unanimously, that adds interim fleet greenhouse gas reduction targets to the resolution — a 50% reduction from 2007 levels by 2035, and a 75% reduction by 2040 — rather than deferring the task of creating targets to a BEV Task Force that has yet to be formed.

“I don't think we need additional and long analysis on goals. (The Board) already has the role of setting ambitious but achievable goals, and that's what these goals will do — they're benchmarks that we can judge our progress by,” Commissioner Singleton said, pointing out that by 2024, the County’s 10-year cycle for replacing fleet vehicles will have turned over one and a half times. “We should be able to see substantial progress in this time frame.”

The amendment also added a commitment to “support the use of a skilled and trained local workforce,” along with contractors participating in apprenticeship programs and other employers that pay prevailing wages and benefits, through the County’s procurement choices regarding BEV charging infrastructure installation and maintenance.

With the resolution adopted, the County will take immediate steps to charter the Fleet Decarbonization Task Force and advance the “EV First” rule through the administrative procedure process, Wasiutynski said.

text:
Bruce Power began its Unit 5 Major Component Replacement (MCR) outage Nov. 1, taking another step forward in a privately funded refurbishment success story with the company, partners and skilled trades delivering strong planning and performance for the people of Ontario.

With Bruce Power’s renewed Units 6 and 3 operating with strong performance and Unit 4 setting records in its MCR outage, Unit 5 was taken off-line for its scheduled outage safely and successfully. This represents the second half of the company’s privately backed MCR Project that will see Units 3-8 renewed to provide clean, reliable energy for Ontario’s people, businesses and hospitals for decades to come, while also ensuring a dependable source of cancer-fighting medical isotopes for the world health-care community.

Ontario’s nuclear advantage has been on full display with its skilled tradespeople, vast supply chain and world-class innovation setting new standards for CANDU refurbishment. Bruce Power and its partners have leveraged lessons from each MCR and developed state-of-the-art technology to better their performance in each successive outage, bringing reliable units back online and passing savings on to ratepayers.

“Ontario’s nuclear advantage is powered by the best workers, engineers and skilled tradespeople in the world and the start of Unit 5’s refurbishment is yet another example of nuclear expertise that few jurisdictions can match,” said Stephen Lecce, Ontario Minister of Energy and Mines. “Extending the life of this critical asset will deliver reliable, affordable electricity, while strengthening Ontario’s position as a global energy superpower that can refurbish nuclear plants on time and on budget. With 95 per cent of Bruce Power’s spending staying in Canada, this work sustains 22,000 jobs and approximately $4 billion in economic benefits every year, supporting skilled trades, made-in-Ontario supply chains and communities across our province.”

Bruce Power’s first MCR outage in Unit 6 was completed ahead of schedule and cost in 2023 with $52 million delivered back to Ontario ratepayers. Since then, the renewed Unit 6 has shown excellent performance in powering the province.

Unit 3 was brought back online in June, more than seven months ahead of schedule, helping meet Ontario’s peak summer electricity demand, demonstrating strong post-refurbishment reliability while returning approximately $150 million to Ontario ratepayers through the Independent Electricity System Operator (IESO).

Unit 4’s MCR outage began in 2025 and is tracking ahead of the Unit 3 MCR, which was the first to employ innovative robotics on a nuclear reactor face for the first time.

“Our performance gets better with each MCR outage and we’re committed to delivering these projects safely with high quality and on time to return reliable units to power Ontario forward,” said Eric Chassard, Bruce Power’s President and Chief Executive Officer. “Along with our partners and skilled workforce, we are securing the future of the Bruce site, sustaining surrounding communities, driving the economy, and producing cancer-fighting medical isotopes for patients around the world.”

With the start of Unit 5, overlapping MCR outages will continue at the Bruce site until 2033, including a magnitude of work that no other utility in the world has faced. Unit 7’s MCR is scheduled to begin in 2028, with Unit 8 scheduled for 2030. Ontario is also evaluating a second MCR for Units 1 and 2, which were refurbished and returned to service in 2012 after being laid up in the late 1990s.

“The start of Unit 5’s Major Component Replacement outage is another important milestone for Bruce Power’s Life-Extension Program and for the thousands of skilled tradespeople, suppliers and businesses helping deliver this work,” said Lisa Thompson, MPP for Huron-Bruce. “As each refurbishment project is completed, we are seeing Ontario-made expertise and innovation produce real results for ratepayers while supporting good-paying jobs and strengthening communities across Bruce, Grey and Huron counties. This work is securing a reliable supply of clean electricity for decades to come and reinforcing our region’s role as a leader in Ontario’s nuclear success story.”

The Life-Extension Program and MCR Projects will extend the operational life of each reactor by 30 to 35 years, replacing key reactor components such as 480 Calandria Tubes and Fuel Channels (pressure tubes), 960 Feeder Tubes, and hulking Steam Generators.

The program and ongoing site operations create and sustain 22,000 direct and indirect jobs annually and contribute approximately $4 billion in annual economic benefits in communities throughout the province, particularly here in the Clean Energy Frontier region of Bruce, Grey and Huron counties. Ninety-five per cent of Bruce Power’s total spending is in Canada.

“The strong performance we’re seeing across our MCR program starts with the skill and experience of the tradespeople doing this work every day,” said Laurent Seigle, Bruce Power’s Executive Vice-President, Projects. “When you combine that expertise with Ontario’s robust nuclear supply chain and innovative technologies and processes, we have a powerful made-in-Ontario advantage that is helping us execute more efficiently with each successive MCR and deliver long-term value for ratepayers.”
