title: Hyundai Domestic Sales Fall 8.9% as Kia Surges 27.5%
description:
Hyundai Motor Company’s domestic sales last month decreased by 8.9% compared to the same period last year.
In contrast, Kia saw a 27.5% increase in domestic sales, showing a contrasting trend.
Domestic sales fell by 8.9% and overseas sales by 5.9% compared to last year, resulting in a 6.3% overall decline.
Domestic sales increased by 27.5% and overseas sales by 7.2%, boosting overall performance by 10.3%.
Hyundai’s ability to offset declining sales of existing models with the newly launched Tucson will be critical to recovering domestic sales by year-end.
text:
Hyundai Motor Company’s domestic sales last month decreased by 8.9% compared to the same period last year. In October 2025, sales had already declined compared to 2024 due to fewer business days caused by the Chuseok holiday, but this year’s sales were even lower. In contrast, Kia saw a 27.5% increase in domestic sales, showing a contrasting trend.

Hyundai sold 49,042 units domestically and 280,731 units overseas in October, recording total sales of 329,773 units, the company announced on the 2nd. Domestic sales fell by 8.9% and overseas sales by 5.9% compared to last year, resulting in a 6.3% overall decline. Kia sold 51,007 units domestically, 239,308 units overseas, and 904 special vehicles, totaling 291,219 units. Domestic sales increased by 27.5% and overseas sales by 7.2%, boosting overall performance by 10.3%.

Both companies saw growth in domestic eco-friendly vehicle sales. Hyundai’s electric vehicle (EV) sales rose by 48.9% to 6,779 units, while Kia’s surged by 86.5% to 13,169 units. Hyundai’s Ioniq 5 sales increased by 71.6% to 1,903 units, while Kia’s EV3 jumped by 119.5% to 3,124 units and EV5 by 209.4% to 3,558 units. Hybrid vehicle sales also grew: Hyundai by 3.9% to 15,207 units and Kia by 70.7% to 18,539 units.

However, recreational vehicle (RV) sales were the key factor in domestic performance. Hyundai’s Tucson sales dropped by 59.3% to 1,590 units, and Santa Fe by 49.2% to 2,469 units, leading to a 21.7% overall RV sales decline. The full model change Tucson, launched last month, had not yet impacted sales figures. Premium brand Genesis also fell by 34.4% to 5,942 units. Kia, meanwhile, saw Sportage sales surge by 90.1% to 7,708 units and Seltos by 43.1% to 4,816 units, driving a 43.7% increase in RV sales. The Sportage even outsold Hyundai’s top domestic model, the Grandeur (6,989 units).

Hyundai’s ability to offset declining sales of existing models with the newly launched Tucson will be critical to recovering domestic sales by year-end. Analysts note that Kia, which saw a rebound from last year’s Chuseok-related sales slump, must maintain strong sales of SUVs and eco-friendly vehicles through the end of the year to accelerate performance improvements.

text:
Deer Park-based United Way of Long Island was awarded a $250,000 grant through the Latinos United for Change (LUCHA) Equity Fund, an initiative of the New York State Legislature administered by Hispanic Federation. The funding will support United Way’s efforts to expand access to free, clean-energy and green-construction workforce training for Spanish-speaking Long Islanders through its Workforce Development Training Academy.

The grant will fund recruitment and training for 100 participants across Nassau and Suffolk counties. Delivered in Spanish, the program offers hands-on training in building science, renewable energy, solar, construction safety, tools and materials, and basic trade skills. Participants will have opportunities to earn industry credentials, including Occupational Safety and Health Administration certification.

“Access to training and meaningful employment can be a powerful pathway to financial stability,” Theresa Regnante, president and CEO of United Way of Long Island, said in a news release about the program.

“We are grateful to Hispanic Federation for investing in this program and helping us create more opportunities for Spanish-speaking Long Islanders to build skills, pursue careers and strengthen their futures,” she said.

Participants will also receive support with resumes, interview preparation, job searches and placement, connecting graduates to careers in clean energy; heating, ventilation and air-conditioning; solar; weatherization and green construction.

“The clean-energy transition is creating new jobs across New York, and Spanish-speaking Long Islanders deserve a fair shot at them,” Diana Caba, vice president for Community & Economic Development at Hispanic Federation, said in the news release.

“United Way’s Workforce Development Training Academy pairs hands-on training with real job-placement support, giving participants a clear path from the classroom to a career. We are proud to administer New York State’s LUCHA investment and to partner with United Way on a program that strengthens families and communities,” she said.

name: EPA
title: City responds to residents' questions on Chevron's long-awaited 'wet gas scrubber'
description:
The device, known as a “wet gas scrubber,” would use water to remove pollutants from gas exhaust that otherwise would be released directly into Richmond’s air.
What is a wet gas scrubber?
The company touts that its wet gas scrubber can easily be retrofitted into existing refining operations, such as Chevron Richmond.
This included a requirement that Chevron Richmond and the Martinez Refining Company install wet gas scrubbers.
In its response, the city said the wet gas scrubber would use 370,000 gallons of potable water per day from the East Bay Municipal Utility District.
text:
Richmond’s city council is scheduled to discuss the potential environmental impacts of a half-century-old technology that could drastically reduce toxic emissions at the Chevron oil refinery, at its meeting this week.

The device, known as a “wet gas scrubber,” would use water to remove pollutants from gas exhaust that otherwise would be released directly into Richmond’s air. The Bay Area Air District instructed Chevron to install a scrubber in 2021 to comply with its emissions targets, but the project has been delayed by lawsuits filed by the oil company and lengthy environmental reviews.

The debate over the wet gas scrubber is just the latest in a long, drawn out process to reduce oil refining emissions in Richmond and west Contra Costa County, which state regulators have identified as one of the most polluted areas in California.

Residents and environmental groups over the last few months have raised concerns over the project as it’s gone through an environmental review process mandated by the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), while also acknowledging the technology’s potential to drastically improve local air quality.

Chief among the concerns are the amount of water used in the scrubbing process, how Chevron will handle the highly contaminated soil where the scrubber is expected to be built, and the potential for increased light and noise pollution.

City officials are expected to address public comments submitted during the environmental review process at a public meeting in the Richmond city council chambers at 6:30 p.m. on Nov. 5. The city has also already done so in a document it released earlier this month.

What is a wet gas scrubber?

Wet gas scrubbing is a method developed in the 1970s by ExxonMobil that can be tailored to remove a host of pollutants during fluid catalytic cracking, a process used in oil refining. These pollutants include particulate matter, sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, according to Babcock & Wilcox Enterprises, which licenses the technology.

The scrubber uses a solution of water and sodium hydroxide, commonly known as lye, to remove sulfur compounds and particulates from the gas before it’s released into the air. The company touts that its wet gas scrubber can easily be retrofitted into existing refining operations, such as Chevron Richmond.

The liquid byproduct of the scrubbing process is a simple mix of water and sodium sulfate, an inorganic salt used in household detergents, paper manufacturing, and glass production, according to the company.

Most importantly, the wet gas scrubber is expected to reduce the refinery’s emissions of PM 2.5, a pollutant that is produced by the burning of fossil fuels, heavy industry and wildfires. Roughly 30 times smaller than the diameter of a human hair, the particles are particularly dangerous because they can permeate the blood-brain barrier and become embedded in the lungs and other vital organs.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency in 2024 lowered the annual exposure level of PM 2.5 — the highest number they consider safe for people’s health — to 9 micrograms per cubic meter. Recent testing of Richmond’s air has shown levels between 7.4 and 10 micrograms per year.

The Bay Area Air District has pinpointed Chevron’s refinery as Richmond’s single largest source of PM 2.5, and estimates that PM 2.5 emissions result in more than 11 premature deaths in the surrounding neighborhoods per year.

More recently, the air district has said that Point Richmond, the area south of the refinery, is exposed to emissions that are reportedly 3.5 times the level requiring correction, and pose an increased risk of cancer to people who live, work and go to school there.

Wet gas scrubbers are now required at Bay Area refineries

To start reducing the most harmful forms of air pollution, the Bay Area Air District adopted Rule 6-5 in July 2021, which set hard limits on the amount of particulate matter allowed on any given day by oil refineries. This included a requirement that Chevron Richmond and the Martinez Refining Company install wet gas scrubbers.

In expressing his support of Rule 6-5 in 2021, Benicia Mayor Steve Young wrote that the wet gas scrubber that Valero voluntarily installed at its refinery in 2010 had resulted in a “significant reduction in the overall emissions of criteria pollutants,” like PM 2.5.

Chevron and the Martinez Refining Company initially challenged Rule 6-5 by suing the air district. Chevron said the district’s rule-making process was “fundamentally broken” and that the ruling was “another example of how California policies have led to a hostile business environment for manufacturers.”

The companies eventually withdrew their lawsuits, settling with the air district for a combined $138 million in February 2024. The settlement included notices of violation the air district had levied against Chevron from 2019 to 2023, and established a Richmond-area Community Air Quality Fund. Residents and the city began deciding what local projects will be funded by that settlement earlier this year, including more parks, and projects to create safer streets and cleaner air.

The scrubber should vastly reduce pollution. But there’s disagreement over how quickly to proceed.

Last week, the city of Richmond released a report addressing questions and concerns brought up during the public comment period for the wet gas scrubber’s latest addendum to its environmental impact report, the first of which went up for review in 2018.

While CEQA doesn’t require public review for an addendum to an approved EIR, the city did it anyway.

In an email, Richmond resident Sally Tobin, a retired Stanford professor, inquired about the amount of potable water the scrubber would need and about the noise and light pollution it would cause.

In its response, the city said the wet gas scrubber would use 370,000 gallons of potable water per day from the East Bay Municipal Utility District. But if another proposed part of the project — the Isomax Cooling Water Tower — is approved, it said, Chevron can use recycled water instead of potable water for the scrubber.

The light and noise levels generated by the project are expected to be within permitted ranges, according to the city.

Michael Herz, an environmental activist and the founder of San Francisco Baykeeper, an environmental protection group, asked what will happen to the waste collected and created during the scrubbing process. The city replied that solids would either be disposed of in a landfill or recycled at a cement kiln, and liquid would be treated at the refinery’s wastewater treatment plant before being released into the adjacent San Pablo Bay.

The activist group Communities for a Better Environment has been among the most vocal critics of Chevron’s actions and pollution in Richmond, and its public comments during the environmental review focused on the project’s potential to have negative environmental consequences if rushed.

“Despite our position that this long overdue and life-saving technology should be installed, the environmental impacts of the construction and operation of the technology must be properly understood and adequately mitigated,” staff attorney Kerry Guerin and program director Shiva Mishek wrote on behalf of the group. “A good thing cannot be allowed to be done poorly.”

CBE asked how the scrubber would be powered, and whether Chevron planned to draw electricity from its Cogeneration Plant, which burns refinery fuel oil. CBE described the nearly 16,000 megawatt-hours per year that will be required to run the scrubber as “massive.”

Since Chevron’s Cogeneration Plant accounts for roughly 20% of the refinery’s PM emissions, the group said, an increase in power would also raise PM emissions. The city replied that the plant in question is already outputting at capacity and that any extra electricity needed would come from PG&E.

CBE also questioned what will happen to polluted groundwater at the site that’s disturbed during construction. “It is among the most contaminated sites in all of California, and the Project requires that the soil be excavated and transported through the rest of Richmond,” CBE wrote.

CBE suggested that the city should require Chevron to soil-test and report back monthly. “For the City to not impose this requirement would be to be willfully ignorant and put residents’ health and safety in danger,” CBE wrote.

In its response, the city said the soil would be “treated as contaminated unless laboratory testing confirms it to be non-hazardous” in accordance with state and federal law and be disposed of properly at places like the Buttonwillow Landfill in Kern County.

CBE, too, brought up noise concerns, particularly over what hours construction would be done. The city replied that it had given the project a waiver allowing construction to begin as early as 6 a.m., but that the loudest activities, like pile-driving, would be reserved for typical working hours.

Other public comments lauded the addition of the wet grass scrubber as a needed step forward.

Point Richmond resident Jeff Kilbreth, a former planning commissioner who sits on the steering committee for AB 617 — a state-funded program that aims to reduce air pollution in some of California’s most toxic communities, including the Richmond-San Pablo area — urged the city council, planning commission and air district to “do everything in your power to expedite rapid approval” of the scrubber.

In his written comment, he said the project “will result in the most significant single amount of pollution reduction in well over 30 years and very likely the most significant single pollution reduction possible in the future,” outside of the refinery cutting production by 40% or shutting down entirely.

In his letter to the city, Kilbreth also credited Chevron engineers for producing a high-quality project description. “Chevron often complains about the slowness of permit approvals,” he said, “so it is important to appreciate well done applications and to in response produce permits quickly when possible.”

“This project is an enormous regulatory success,” Kilbreth said.

text:
Utilizing waste carbon at scale, assessing public trust in artificial intelligence and data centers, and building a quantum toolkit for critical applications were among the topics energy experts explored at the MIT Energy Initiative (MITEI)’s annual research conference on Sept. 22-23.

The complexity of the energy transition demands “a truly interdisciplinary and international approach,” said Paula Hammond, Institute Professor and dean of the MIT School of Engineering, kicking off the conference, which was themed “Transitioning energy at a pivotal moment.”

More than 200 people attended Energizing@MIT: MITEI’s Annual Research Conference in person and online, including faculty, scientists, and researchers; representatives of global energy firms; nonprofit organizations; and academic institutions.

With the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence and data centers, the challenge of the energy transition grows ever greater, requiring “researchers who can pursue fundamental questions about materials, chemistry, and energy systems … engineers who can design new technologies and determine how they might function at scale … and experts in economics, policy, human behavior, and sociology who can help us understand how those technologies will interact with communities and with the world around us,” said Hammond.

From keynote speakers to panelists, seed grant innovators to startup entrepreneurs, the conference featured exemplars in all these categories.

Deploying today’s technologies

Eric Toone, chief technical officer and managing partner at Breakthrough Energy, set the tone for day one with a keynote address that was clear-eyed in his assessment. “If energy is prosperity,” he told the audience, “at least today, prosperity is emissions.” Yet, Toone was optimistic when he heralded examples of Breakthrough Energy-funded ventures, from iron-air batteries to vacuum-insulated glass windows, which can reduce the carbon costs of energy.

“We can absolutely develop new technologies that provide the exact same service, but at zero carbon,” he said.

The conference made Toone’s claim tangible as it spanned the full arc of decarbonization — from deploying what we know today to uncovering what may be possible tomorrow.

There are “projects that are actually being developed, companies that are putting steel in the ground now, electrons onto the grid to deliver capacity now, or in the very, very near term,” said John Parsons, deputy director for research at the MIT Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research. Parsons moderated a panel on the revival of nuclear fission power.

Highlights included Crane Clean Energy Center’s restoration of the Three Mile Island Unit 1 nuclear plant, set to restart in mid-2027; work by Électricité de France (EDF) to extend and modernize France’s 57-reactor nuclear fleet, adapting plants to climate impacts; and GE Vernova’s development of mature light-water reactor technology, with a new plant under construction in Ontario.

Carbon utilization offers another path to mitigating carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions. “The land and ocean are passively taking up almost 50 percent of anthropogenic CO2 emissions,” said Carolyn Ruppel, MITEI’s deputy director for science and technology, who moderated the panel. “The idea is to find uses for some of the rest of it.” The session showcased research exploring a host of technologies for making products with captured CO2.

Nicola Ferralis, a research scientist in the MIT Department of Materials Science and Engineering (DMSE), highlighted the importance of large-scale uses for carbon waste, such as structural carbon for vehicles and buildings. “We need to find applications that are actually able to match the supply by mass,” he said.

Admir Masic, an associate professor in the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering and DMSE, described self-heating concrete panels used in real-world conditions in Sapporo, Japan, as well as new concrete materials that can store energy.

“The pace of the transition to a renewable-energy economy will strongly rely on the availability of scalable, bulk energy-storage solutions,” said Masic.

Kripa K. Varanasi, a professor in the MIT Department of Mechanical Engineering, is working on ways to make technologies such as emissions-plume capture at power plants economically viable.

In a panel devoted to startups with links to MITEI or MITEI member companies, speakers described moving novel energy technologies from research to commercialization: Alfredo Rivela of Adaion has developed an AI tool for electrical utilities that optimizes their use of the grid; Eddie Obropta of Raptor Maps trains drones to inspect solar farms; Michele Guarnieri’s HiBot has created a robot that detects issues in power lines; and Michael Wang of Lithios is conducting field pilots that use electrochemistry to separate lithium from low-grade brines.

Successful ventures, the speakers agreed, begin with a clear customer problem that can be validated by industry users and that offers a path to scaled deployment. For industry users, “innovation is not a corporate virtue,” said Steve Hellman, managing partner at Alliance Partners. “It’s an existential requirement.”

Early-stage research and basic science

The conference also offered a bounty of promising early research on technologies and approaches for cutting carbon emissions. A panel on MITEI’s Seed Innovation Fund Program projects introduced MIT scientists who are separating and recycling rare earth elements; designing algorithms to decide which power plants should run to meet electricity demand; and modeling the impacts on human and natural systems of development and decarbonization.

A poster session revealed the next generation of energy researchers in such fields as chemistry, architecture, aeronautics and astronautics, and computer science. Graduate students are developing a wide array of technologies for carbon mitigation and new energy systems, such as a steam electrolysis process for hydrogen production; models of end-to-end decarbonization in buildings; and designs for hydrogen- and methane-fueled aircraft.

The conference highlighted the importance of fundamental science in feeding the pipeline of new energy technologies. Wednesday’s keynote speaker, Danna Freedman, the F. G. Keyes Professor of Chemistry at MIT and inaugural director of Quantum@MIT, traced scientists’ evolving capacity to harness quantum computing as a tool for solving a range of problems, including those in energy.

“What we want to do at Q-MIT is solve the hard problem, and the hard problem isn’t developing these ridiculously intricate and beautiful quantum tools,” said Freedman. “It is connecting the quantum tools with the applications that will change the world.”

A companion panel explored one such application: quantum sensing, which leverages fundamental physics to capture a nanoscale view of materials and their properties. For instance, Lukasz Zielinski, scientific advisor to the Integrated Sensing and Measurement Program at SLB, uses a lidar camera with single-photon detectors to identify methane plumes. Moderator Paola Cappellaro, the Ford Professor of Engineering in the MIT Department of Nuclear Science and Engineering, described her work using diamond-based sensors for detecting tiny magnetic fields from battery current, potentially helping measure battery conditions without disturbing the battery electrically. Such quantum sensors, Cappellaro said, can be “practical and impactful.”

Data centers and public trust

One critical challenge facing energy researchers and industry emerged in sessions throughout the two days: the explosive growth of AI and the energy-hungry data centers that fuel this technology. As Deepjyoti Deka, a MITEI principal research scientist, put it, “the big test for AI right now is whether AI can reduce energy usage, improve efficiency, as well as bring in innovation faster than the rate at which it is going to consume electricity to get trained and deployed.”

“New ‘hyperscale’ facilities built for artificial intelligence can use more power than entire cities,” said Steve Clemmer, director of energy research in the Climate and Energy Program at the Union of Concerned Scientists, sharing a recent analysis of data center proliferation. With new facilities being 10 to even 10,000 times larger than data centers built just a decade ago, he said, wholesale electricity costs will rise, and “increased reliance on fossil fuels will result in tens of billions of dollars in health damages, and trillions in climate damages.” He noted that decision-makers can mitigate these harmful impacts through clean energy development, strong ratepayer protections, and other safeguards.

Given mounting opposition to data centers, Kathryn Kline Tyndall, associate director of energy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, recommended that industry proponents provide early, accessible information about power, water, quality-of-life, land-use, environmental, and economic impacts, tailored to each community in which they hope to set up shop.

Larry Susskind, the Ford Professor of Urban and Environmental Planning in the MIT Department of Urban Studies and Planning, recommended that developers go further, and demonstrate credible benefits to communities. To achieve this, Susskind suggests a facilitated negotiation process between developers and local groups whose object is a community benefits agreement — a deal that might involve altering the data center design, and providing workforce development, infrastructure investment, and clean energy partnerships.

Ultimately, developers must accept that they can’t rush community acceptance; they have to earn it by giving residents a meaningful role in shaping projects and sharing their benefits.

“You’re going to have to proceed at the speed of trust,” said Susskind.

text:
Focus

BLM strengthens U.S. energy security with successful California geothermal lease sale

BLM – October 28

The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) accepted winning bids on 16 out of 17 parcels offered in California in a competitive geothermal lease sale held on October 27, 2026. Winning bidders, including Zanskar Geothermal, TLS Geothermics, and subsidiaries of Constellation Energy, California Resources Corporation (CRC), Quaise Energy, and Fervo Energy, will have the opportunity to enter into leases after BLM reviews the bids and receives payment. These leases will be the first step in the process to develop new federal geothermal resources on over 33,000 acres in Modoc, Sonoma, Lake, Mono, and Inyo counties. Before authorizing any surface-disturbing activities, the BLM will conduct additional environmental reviews based on applications for exploration or development plans, which include site-specific conditions in addition to the stipulations attached to the lease at the time of sale.

News

U.S. wind turbine orders hit three-year high

reNews – October 26

U.S. wind turbine orders reached 2.8 GW in the second quarter of 2026, their highest level since Q4 2023, as developers moved to meet tax credit deadlines. Wood Mackenzie said the surge in firm order intake was largely driven by developers placing turbine orders before July 4 to comply with start of construction requirements. The consultancy added that 5 GW of onshore wind capacity was installed during the quarter, driven primarily by the 3.65 GW SunZia project in New Mexico, the largest wind project built in the U.S. to date.

CAISO approves proposal to speed grid connections for large loads

Reuters – October 28

California Independent System Operator (CAISO) said on October 28 that its board has approved a proposal to establish new ‌procedures for connecting large loads, such as data centers and manufacturing operations, to the grid quickly and reliably. CAISO said it will file the proposal ⁠with the US Federal Energy Regulatory Commission by November 16. A key ‌element ⁠of the proposal would allow large loads to interconnect to the transmission system with flexibility until associated network upgrades are complete.

Morro Bay bans utility-scale battery storage plants after Moss Landing fire

The Tribune – October 28

On October 28, the Morro Bay City Council in San Luis Obispo County, California, voted unanimously to pass an ordinance banning the construction of utility-scale battery plants within city limits. However the ban, which goes into effect in 30 days, will not necessarily prohibit the development of new battery projects. Assembly Bill 205 allows developers to seek state approval for renewable energy projects, like battery energy storage systems, in lieu of local permits.

Projects

Critical Loop plans 25 MW industrial microgrid to bridge California grid delays

Microgrid Media – October 27

Critical Loop has announced plans for a 25 MW hybrid microgrid serving an SRG Commercial industrial campus in Southern California, where a planned utility upgrade will not arrive in time for a manufacturer’s anticipated operating schedule. The microgrid design includes 7 MW of firm grid capacity, 2 MW of flexible service, onsite generation, 3.5 MW of dedicated emergency backup generation, 12 MW of battery discharge power, and 60 MWh of stored energy that will be managed collectively to cover the gap between available supply and the tenant’s power requirements.

Solar farm developer offers Butte County $300K a year as residents raise concerns

NSPR – October 27

A 1,200-acre solar farm proposed by Cenergy Power outside of Chico, California, could bring hundreds of thousands of dollars a year to Butte County in addition to other one-time community benefits. But some residents say the benefits will not outweigh the environmental costs, including the loss of a significant number of blue oaks. Although they have not yet filed an application, in response to community feedback, Cenergy Power has already agreed to set aside nearly 600 acres of land as an ecological preserve for oak trees and will continue to take community input into consideration as the permitting process gets underway.

Copper Rays solar project wins key early Nye County approval

Las Vegas Review-Journal – October 23

A large-scale solar generation facility on 4,414 acres of Bureau of Land Management land just southeast of Pahrump, Nevada, won key early support from Nye County commissioners on October 20 despite continued community opposition. Commissioners voted 4 to 1 to grant the Copper Rays Solar Project a special use permit and approve a preliminary development plan. These approvals followed BLM’s publication of a final environmental impact statement for the project in August.

Neighborhood Sun acquires Meadow Energy and its NY community solar portfolio

Solar Power World – October 26

Community solar management service Neighborhood Sun has acquired Meadow Energy, a community solar aggregator with a substantial project portfolio in New York. The acquisition doubles Neighborhood Sun’s total project portfolio from approximately 300 MW to more than 600 MW, and quadruples its presence in New York state.

title: Vermont campuses, factories win Energy Leadership Awards
description:
Efficiency Vermont’s yearly event brings together the state’s largest commercial and industrial operations and businesses to share insights on energy efficiency and reducing energy costs.
Five Energy Leadership Awards honored projects and partners that demonstrated excellence in energy efficiency.
Efficiency Vermont Managing Director Peter Walke surveyed attendees about the biggest barriers they faced to completing energy projects.
Five Energy Leadership Awards were presented to individuals and organizations whose work exemplified industry-leading energy efficiency.
VTSU partnered with Efficiency Vermont on energy projects across its five campuses.
text:
KILLINGTON, Vt. – More than 190 people gathered at the Killington Grand Resort Hotel for the 15th annual Best Practices Exchange (BPX) on Sept. 23 and 24. Efficiency Vermont’s yearly event brings together the state’s largest commercial and industrial operations and businesses to share insights on energy efficiency and reducing energy costs.

Five Energy Leadership Awards honored projects and partners that demonstrated excellence in energy efficiency. The winners ranged from college campuses, to manufacturers, to innovative wood heating systems. The award-winning projects are among the commercial and industrial efficiency efforts in 2025 that will save Vermont businesses $78 million over their lifetimes.

This year’s event assembled leaders from industries like healthcare, manufacturing, education, agriculture, hospitality/tourism, and Vermont’s ski industry. Executives, facilities managers, and mechanical contractors met to discuss projects and share expertise. Presenters and installers shared energy-saving technologies and solutions, and 21 sponsors and vendors demonstrated equipment, industrial systems, and related technologies.

Efficiency Vermont Managing Director Peter Walke surveyed attendees about the biggest barriers they faced to completing energy projects. Many cited challenges like funding, costs, and inflation. Other barriers were operational constraints like staffing, labor, and time. Several said return on investment or changing federal policies created barriers. “This all means one thing: extend uncertainty,” Walke concluded. “That’s why investing in energy efficiency is always a good idea. Because efficiency gives you control – on costs, on runtimes, on fuel and energy use – when so many other things are out of your control.”

Jed Davis, Cabot Agri-Mark’s vice president of strategic engagement and sustainability, delivered a keynote about the co-op’s commitment to sustainability, including energy efficiency. “The farm family owners of our dairy cooperative know sustainability extends from farm to fridge,” Davis said. As a certified B Corporation, Davis told BPX attendees that commitment starts with Cabot’s people. “Our people identify projects that turn our values and strategy into savings. Working with Efficiency Vermont brings incentives and data-driven insights that help us invest in projects with measurable impact.”

The benefits of efficiency from Vermont’s commercial and industrial sector go beyond saving $78 million. In partnership with Efficiency Vermont, projects completed in 2025 will save 386 million kilowatt-hours (kWh) of electricity over their lifetimes. That’s enough to power 5,600 homes for a decade. The projects will also save enough fuel to heat more than 12,000 homes for a year.

Five Energy Leadership Awards were presented to individuals and organizations whose work exemplified industry-leading energy efficiency. The winners of the 2026 BPX Energy Leadership Awards are listed below.

– Impact Award: Vermont State University (VTSU). VTSU partnered with Efficiency Vermont on energy projects across its five campuses. The Castleton campus started with a “controls treasure hunt” that found numerous low- and no-cost improvements that reduced energy costs by $150,000. A campus-wide LED lighting upgrade will save Castleton an additional $168,000 annually. The Johnson campus completed a comprehensive controls optimization project, saving $250,000 a year. The Lyndon campus also upgraded to LEDs campus-wide, saving $64,500 annually. And the Randolph campus modernized its meat processing facility’s refrigeration system, saving more than $8,000 a year. Combined, these projects will save more than $600,000 annually, allowing VTSU to direct more resources to support students and academic programs.

– Changemaker Award: Vermont Glove in Randolph. Owner and President Sam Hooper made strategic investments in energy efficiency to reduce operating costs and strengthen his company’s future. A major energy improvement project at its 1920s manufacturing facility replaced an ancient coal boiler with an advanced wood pellet heating system. Adding insulation and air sealing cut the facility’s air leakage by 50%. A new addition was designed with a tight building envelope and high-efficiency heat pumps for heating and cooling. The company applied the same approach to workforce housing, weatherizing Randolph’s Windover House, and converting it from oil heat to wood pellet heating. These investments lowered operating costs while improving comfort, productivity, and sustainability.

– Innovation Award: Londonderry Village Market. Operated by Associated Grocers of New England, the Londonderry Village Market has taken a “continuous improvement” approach to reducing energy use and operating costs. Early efforts focused on refrigerant leak detection and repairs, followed by new high-efficiency refrigeration cases and an LED lighting retrofit. These efforts resulted in more than $40,000 in energy savings per year. The market then turned to its aging HVAC system and partnered with Efficiency Vermont, Turner Piping and Refrigeration, and Green Mountain Power. By installing a dual-fuel heat pump rooftop unit, the market electrified much of its heating and cooling needs while reducing fossil fuel use. Now, Londonderry Village Market is ready for future energy management solutions, and Associated Grocers of New England is evaluating similar upgrades at its other markets throughout Vermont.

– Energy Champion: Shawn Briggs with Vermont Composites in Bennington. Since 2024, Briggs has led companywide efforts to reduce energy costs through operational changes, employee engagement, and facility improvements. He championed a facility-wide “turn it off” campaign that increases awareness by encouraging employees to shut down ovens, lights, and production machinery when not in use. Briggs also led improvements in lighting, HVAC systems, refrigeration systems, and added programmable thermostats in office areas. By championing a compressed air leak audit and facility-wide submetering, Briggs now has energy usage data to inform future projects. These efforts help Vermont Composites save $107,000 annually while developing a culture of energy stewardship.

– Partner of the Year: Morton Bailey and Lyme Green Heat in Lyme, N.H. A member of Efficiency Vermont’s Efficiency Excellence Network (EEN) since 2017, Morton and his team have helped schools, municipalities, and businesses transition to high-performance, advanced wood heating systems with a focus on efficiency, performance, and reliability. The company has worked with Efficiency Vermont to support improvements to enhance wood heating system performance, simplify maintenance, and improve customer satisfaction. Lyme Green Heat is also strengthening regional wood fuel supplies by developing a pellet manufacturing facility at a former lumber mill. These efforts ensure a dependable, regional supply of pellet fuel, support local jobs and economic growth, and demonstrate leadership in advancing the region’s renewable energy future.

text:
As communities across North Carolina raise concerns about the rapid expansion of AI data centers, Republican U.S. Senate candidate Michael Whatley is defending the industry and questioning whether public opposition is genuine.

In Stokes County, residents of Walnut Cove are fighting a proposed data center development that would cover nearly three square miles of land. The project has sparked concerns about water consumption, electricity costs, pollution, and the impact on the rural community.

The opposition has crossed party lines. In a county where nearly 80% of voters supported Donald Trump in 2024, NPR found Republicans and Democrats alike questioning the development.

“We’re a little worried about it, yeah,” said Republican resident Chris Simpkins, citing concerns about water, noise, and air pollution.

Local hardware store owner Bill Petree, a Democrat who has organized opposition to the project, questioned whether the promised economic benefits would outweigh the costs.

“They fail to realize that this is not going to be an economic benefit to this area. It’s just going to be a detriment to everything else,” Petree said.

Despite community concerns, the all-Republican Stokes County Commission voted 3-2 to approve the development. A lawsuit forced commissioners to reverse their initial decision, but they subsequently voted in favor again. The project still requires state environmental approval and a major technology company to commit to the site.

As opposition grows, Whatley has dismissed the backlash as manufactured.

“This opposition to data centers is not organic,” Whatley said during an interview with Fox News host Brian Kilmeade. “This is being ginned up the same way that we saw opposition to energy projects around the country.”

Whatley also expressed support for tax breaks, though not direct subsidies, to encourage data center development. He has separately said communities should not be forced to accept projects they oppose.

His position has drawn scrutiny because of his financial ties to the industry. NBC News reported that Whatley, a former utility industry lobbyist, owns investments in companies that could benefit from data center expansion.

His disclosed holdings in companies connected to the data center industry, including Duke Energy, have been valued at close to a million dollars. Those investments raise questions about potential conflicts of interest as Whatley supports tax policies favorable to the industry, although the disclosures do not establish that he has personally profited from those policies.

Meanwhile, Democratic Senate candidate Roy Cooper has argued that data centers should bear the costs of their electricity needs rather than passing additional expenses on to residential customers.

With communities across North Carolina debating the future of data center development, the issue has become a point of disagreement in the Senate race over economic growth, local control, and who should pay for expanding energy infrastructure.

text:
FORT FRANCES – A local energy company is getting a funding boost for a project that will “increase energy security in Fort Frances,” according to the Ministry of Natural Resources.

With $92,500 from the provincial government, AUX Energy will develop plans for a biomass-powered generator project.

Although it lost its pulp and paper mill in 2014, Fort Frances is still surrounded by a lot of forestry, said the town's infrastructure and growth manager, Travis Rob.

“There are the treetops, the limbs, the unmarketable timber that's left. And it's largely, you know, in the bush. It's piled up and burned. But that's a wasted opportunity. There are other things that it can be used for,” said Rob.

“We need to look at what sort of opportunities those have … There isn't one big thing that's going to come in and take all of that biomass. It's going to be a number of smaller things. Looking at really diverse opportunities to use that wood as close to where it lies as possible, that keeps your costs low. That keeps your projects feasible,” he said.

“The upgrades will help increase the forest sector’s production and capacity, protecting over 700 direct jobs and more than 3,350 indirect jobs,” it said.

Further, Wanagekong Biiwega'iganan Clean Energy Corporation will receive $250,000 from the province "to study biomass supply, complete permitting and build partnerships to support a planned bio-refinery," according to a media release.

Fort Frances' mayor, Andrew Hallikas said that ever since they lost the mill, they've been trying to position themselves as a clean, green energy centre.

Along with the AUX Energy and Wanagekong Biiwega'iganan projects, the town will also see a 57.2 MW solar farm in the future.

"All of those are going to be generating clean sources of energy, and we're pretty darn excited about it," said Hallikas.

He added that the biomass projects have other benefits too, including the fact that it reduces fiber in the woods and lessens the risk of fires after "a horrific year for wildfires."

The Wanagekong Biiwega'iganan plant will also decarbonize the fuel created from the biomass, another environmental step forward, Hallikas said.

The funding for AUX Energy was announced in September by Thunder Bay–Atikokan MPP Kevin Holland, also the associate minister of forestry and forest products, at Thunder Bay Pulp and Paper last month where he also announced $2.5 million for that mill.

In the release, the province said the investment will “increase the industry’s use of mill byproducts and underused wood known as forest biomass.”

The Wanagekong Biiwega'iganan funding is part of a $1.1 million investment in a total of five Indigenous forestry projects, also announced by Holland.

text:
Campaigns are making their closing arguments to win over a shrinking pool of voters who haven’t decided how they will cast their ballots and persuade their supporters to show up on Election Day.

With control of Congress hanging in the balance, both parties are increasingly turning their focus to getting their supporters to vote with fewer undecided voters left to persuade and millions of ballots already cast.

Gloomy attitudes about the economy and voters increasingly blaming the war with Iran and widespread use of tariffs for higher prices have continued to climb are creating headwinds for Republicans trying to hang onto tight majorities.

President Donald Trump won the 2024 election promising to lower prices immediately upon retaking office with lower gas prices, cheaper groceries and creating a booming economy. But two years later, the GOP is struggling to convince many voters their economic policies have improved their situation as more Americans say they are struggling to get by.

Midterm elections typically serve a referendum on the president’s party that often lead to the loss of seats as Americans react to the first two years of the administration, adding to the difficult political environment for the incumbent Republican majorities.

“People have had 10 years of Donald Trump in one way, shape, or form, and that that's hard to maintain a positive momentum if you're Donald Trump or any president in their second term. You add on the external environment that we're seeing, and it produces a pretty plausible explanation why we're seeing such drastic changes,” said Rob Alexander, a political science professor at Bowling Green.

Multiple pollsters have found Democrats leading Republicans in which party voters would prefer to steer the economy, while other issues like healthcare and the war with Iran are a higher priority than concerns that have historically favored the GOP like immigration and crime.

Those frustrations are also adding to challenges for Republicans to hang onto voters who shifted toward the GOP in recent elections and making it harder to motivate parts of their base to vote in a race without Trump on the ballot.

Polling has found Democrats are significantly more voted to vote this year than their Republican counterparts. A Gallup survey released last week found 58% of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents said they were more enthusiastic than usual about voting, compared to 48% of Republicans and GOP-leaning independents.

Election forecasters are widely favoring Democrats to win control of the House, and odds of them taking the Senate have improved as Election Day gets closer as more polling finds Democrats with leads, though there are questions about the accuracy of the surveys amid issues capturing Republican voters in samples.

Republicans are banking on a strong showing on Election Day to offset those disadvantages, especially among people who backed Trump in 2024 but don’t consistently participate in midterm cycles. The party has voiced concerns about early voting trends in states with tight races for seats Republicans currently hold, raising the stakes of getting their voters to show up on Tuesday.

Republican National Committee chair Joe Gruters said on Sunday the party is facing challenges with voter turnout during an appearance on NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday.”

“If our voters turn out, we win. That’s what (Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas) is trying to communicate. You can’t sit back and think that we’re going to win if you don’t show up to the polls,” Gruters said in reference to a recent warning that large Democratic turnout could lead to a midterm wipeout for Republicans.

Trump, who has been a frequent presence on the campaign trail in GOP-leaning states over the last few weeks, has repeatedly asked voters to pretend he is on the ballot in hopes of getting low-propensity voters who have supported him during presidential years to come out and vote for Republicans. Vice President JD Vance, House Speaker Mike Johnson and other high-profile Republicans have also traveled to red states to rally their voters to show up on Tuesday.

It is a significant shift in the political dynamics from two years ago, when Trump and Republicans took control over Washington amid frustration over inflation and direction of the country. Democrats are now using many of those same issues against the GOP as more Americans question whether Trump and Republican majorities improved their financial situation.

Getting voters to turn out could decide which party controls the Senate after Election Day, where races have become increasingly competitive in traditionally Republican states like Kansas, Texas and Ohio, where the GOP has invested significant resources to rally support for their candidates.

“This is a particularly bad electorate for Republicans given the anxieties over the economy, Iran tariffs, and fuel prices. There's not a lot of areas that Republicans are emphasizing that get people excited in a positive way,” Alexander said. “It's a heavy lift because there's even some potential that their appearance may motivate some of those folks that typically sit midterm elections out to turn out and vote against them. That's just how angry the electorate appears to be.”

text:
Texas commuters facing construction along Interstate 35 have a new way to share the drive — and potentially earn money in the process.

Commuters can earn rewards for logging shared trips through a carpool program that helps people find travel partners between Kyle, Buda, and Austin, according to KXAN.

Here's what to know

CAMPO has launched We Ride I-35 in partnership with CTXGO to help people with compatible commutes find one another. A compatible match means heading toward similar destinations at similar times, so both the route and commuting schedule factor into the search.

Riding only as a passenger is an option; participants can instead drive or take on both roles. Meeting points and travel times are left to the commuters to choose after they have been matched.

More background

We Ride I-35 is available through the regional Transportation Demand Management initiative run by CAMPO as construction continues along the interstate connecting these communities.

The program also includes a backup option for eligible carpoolers through CTXGO's Guaranteed Ride Home feature. If an unexpected situation arises, the benefit provides a free ride home. For passengers, that backup can help if they need to leave outside the group's agreed-upon schedule.

Coverage is subject to eligibility requirements.

What can be done?

Travel times, intended destinations, preferred meeting places, and willingness to drive give CAMPO the information it needs to identify compatible carpool partners. Interested commuters submit those details through an online interest form, KXAN noted.

Pickup arrangements remain in commuters' hands. Matched participants coordinate the details of their shared commute rather than receiving an assigned arrangement. CAMPO handles the matching and helps new carpool groups get started.

Commuters may also be eligible for CTXGO Commute Rewards. The incentive is tied to logging carpool trips, with potential earnings of up to $5 per day. The CTXGO Commute Rewards incentive has a maximum payout of $150 for qualifying participants who log their carpool trips.

text:
The Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE) is opening a Request for Proposals for the MI Brightfields Pilot. The program is offering $10 million in grants to establish renewable energy and energy storage on environmentally contaminated properties, with $5 million available in this first round. A second round will open in spring 2027.

The MI Brightfields Pilot is primarily designed to support the development of solar and/or battery energy storage. However, all competitive projects that result in the deployment of renewable energy or energy storage technology on brownfield sites in Michigan are invited to apply. Eligible technologies may include, but are not limited to, ground-mounted solar, rooftop solar, carport solar, solar plus storage, standalone battery energy storage, wind, and geothermal.

Eligible applicants are local units of government, such as counties, cities, townships, villages, municipal electric utilities, brownfield redevelopment authorities, economic development corporations, or other public bodies created pursuant to state law. Governing bodies of federally recognized Indian tribes in Michigan are also eligible to apply. Applications must be for properties with known environmental contamination exceeding Part 201 criteria. Grant awards will be limited to $2 million per project and can be used for a variety of preapproved activities including:

Renewable energy and/or energy storage costs

Site preparation costs

Environmental assessment activities

Due care activities

Response activities beyond due care

Grant administration costs

EGLE will hold an informational webinar on Monday, November 9 at 11am to introduce the MI Brightfields Pilot, walk through the application process, and answer questions. Register for the webinar here.

title: Where does Britain need to reindustrialise? - Centre for Cities
description:
The reason is simple: jobs, and particularly higher-paid jobs, concentrate in cities.
Cities account for 73 per cent of Britain’s higher-paid jobs and, between 2014 and 2024, generated more than three quarters of all new jobs and 91 per cent of all new higher-paid jobs.
If they reached the national level, Britain would have around 100,000 additional higher-paid jobs, equivalent to more than a fifth of all the higher-paid jobs created nationally over the past decade.
Aberdeen experienced the largest decline, with 8.5 fewer higher-paid jobs per 100 working-age residents than a decade earlier.
York and Dundee are among the places where higher-paid employment has grown strongly, while Exeter and Oxford have moved in the opposite direction.
text:
The Government has put reindustrialisation at the centre of its plans for growth, with the aim of creating more good jobs across the country. As the Budget puts it, “Reindustrialisation means more good jobs around the country. It means more towns and cities making and innovating.” It goes on to link this to a stronger role for towns and cities in the national economy and more British-owned businesses exporting goods and services.

This is a goal Centre for Cities shares. Our recent Good growth briefing shows that delivering more good jobs around the country needs to start with getting more of Britain’s towns’ and cities’ economies firing.

The reason is simple: jobs, and particularly higher-paid jobs, concentrate in cities. Cities account for 73 per cent of Britain’s higher-paid jobs and, between 2014 and 2024, generated more than three quarters of all new jobs and 91 per cent of all new higher-paid jobs. This concentration is not accidental. Cities can both create and attract productive firms: deep labour markets, proximity to other businesses and the exchange of knowledge help new firms to emerge and existing firms to grow and become more productive.

Growing cities therefore matters for growth across the country, and not just within their boundaries. Their labour markets provide opportunities for people living in surrounding towns and rural areas, which in turn provide workers and skills to major employment centres. The result is that the benefits of stronger urban economies can extend into the hinterlands of urban areas.

Conversely, when large cities underperform, the effects are felt beyond them. Seven of Britain’s ten biggest cities have fewer higher-paid jobs per working-age resident than the national average. If they reached the national level, Britain would have around 100,000 additional higher-paid jobs, equivalent to more than a fifth of all the higher-paid jobs created nationally over the past decade.

Where are higher-paid jobs growing?

If reindustrialisation is to produce more good jobs around the country, an important question is where Britain’s towns and cities are already becoming more successful at generating them and where they are moving in the opposite direction.

As shown in Figure 1, over the past decade, some places have substantially increased the number of higher-paid jobs relative to their working-age populations. In 2024, Warrington had 3.7 more higher-paid jobs per 100 working-age residents than in 2014, Crawley had 3.3 more, Dundee and Reading each had 3.2 more, and York and Cambridge each had 3.0 more.

Elsewhere, higher-paid employment has become less concentrated. Aberdeen experienced the largest decline, with 8.5 fewer higher-paid jobs per 100 working-age residents than a decade earlier. Exeter fell by 3.8, Derby by 3.1, Ipswich by 2.9, and Oxford and Stoke by around 2.5.

Figure 1: Change in higher-paid jobs per 100 working-age residents, 2014–2024

Source: Business Register and Employment Survey (BRES), 2014-2024. Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings (ASHE), 2014-2024. Centre for Cities calculations.

The geography is not a straightforward north-south story. York and Dundee are among the places where higher-paid employment has grown strongly, while Exeter and Oxford have moved in the opposite direction. The picture among the biggest cities is mixed too: London, Leeds and Manchester have increased their density of higher-paid jobs, while Nottingham has seen a decline and Newcastle and Sheffield have changed little.

This is where the “re-” in reindustrialisation matters. In places where higher-paid job density has fallen, reindustrialisation means reversing that decline by strengthening the fundamentals that allow productive firms and good jobs to grow.

What reindustrialisation means in practice

Strengthening these fundamentals does not mean recreating the same industries everywhere. The Government’s own definition of reindustrialisation is broader than manufacturing alone. The Budget identifies sectors ranging from advanced manufacturing, defence and clean energy to digital and technology, life sciences, creative industries and financial and professional business services. It also says local growth plans should seek to maximise the agglomeration benefits that exist in their urban areas.

Different towns and cities will have different routes to creating more good jobs. But the national importance of improving their performance is the same. If more of the places where higher-paid employment has been falling can begin to reverse that trajectory, the benefits will extend beyond those cities themselves – to their wider hinterlands and to the British economy as a whole. In that sense, the success of reindustrialisation will depend in large part on whether Britain’s cities can become stronger engines of productive businesses and higher-paid job creation.
