title: Electric trucks hit 50% of China's heavy truck sales, diesel demand falls - Electrek
authors: Fred Lambert, Micah Toll, Jo Borrás
description:
Electric trucks made up 50.3% of all heavy trucks sold in China in September.
Electric is eating LNG, too For years, the alternative to diesel trucks in China was liquefied natural gas.
Diesel demand is falling China’s diesel consumption already peaked.
America has Tesla, a Semi factory in Nevada built for 50,000 trucks a year, and some of the best freight corridors in the world for electrification.
SANY and BYD already sell electric trucks in Europe, and CATL is building the swap network for them.
text:
Electric trucks made up 50.3% of all heavy trucks sold in China in September. That’s 33,100 electric big rigs in a single month, up 37% from a year ago, while the overall heavy-truck market shrank by 21%.

And it’s showing up in the oil data. China’s diesel demand is on track to fall by about 230,000 barrels per day this year, and trucks running on batteries and natural gas are doing most of the work.

From 14% to half in under two years

In 2024, new-energy vehicles accounted for 13.6% of heavy trucks (12 tonnes and up) sold in China. In 2025, sales nearly tripled to 231,100 units, up 182%, for a 28.9% share.

December 2025 hit 53.9%, but that was a rush. Buyers piled in before trade-in subsidies expired and new purchase tax costs kicked in, and the share dropped back to about 23% by March.

Advertisement - scroll for more content

Then it came right back. Through the first nine months of 2026, China sold 226,400 electric heavy trucks, up 64%, for a 38.1% share. That’s already almost as many as in all of 2025, with a quarter still to go. In tractors, the big rigs that pull long-haul trailers, the September share hit 64.5%.

That’s well ahead of Beijing’s own plan. This year, 11 government bodies set a target of 40% new-energy heavy-truck sales by 2030, along with 1.6 million of them on the road, 30,000 km of zero-carbon freight corridors and about 3,000 charging and swap stations. The market blew past that sales target four years early on a monthly basis, and CATL now says new-energy trucks will be half of China’s annual truck sales by 2028.

Why Chinese fleets are switching

It comes down to cost. In most uses, an electric heavy truck in China is now cheaper to own and run than a diesel one, and fleets run that math every day.

CATL claims savings of about 0.6 yuan per km. Independent numbers are more measured, but still favorable: a study by the ICCT and China’s CATARC found battery-electric trucks about 19% cheaper per tonne-km than diesel in good conditions, though they lose that edge at low annual mileage or when battery weight eats into payload.

Charging time is the other objection, and China’s answer is swapping. CATL’s Qiji brand operated about 300 heavy-truck swap stations at the end of 2025 and plans 900 by the end of this year and 2,000 in 2027. In August, it agreed to pay 2.56 billion yuan (about $370 million) for nearly 25% of Qiyuan Green Power, China’s largest heavy-truck swap operator with more than 1,600 charging and swap stations. Its new standardized packs hold 432 kWh and 513 kWh and swap in about five minutes.

CATL is already taking the swapping model to Europe with Octopus Energy.

The trucks themselves are domestic. XCMG led the segment in 2025 with a 15.4% share, ahead of SANY and FAW Jiefang, and the top three held 42.9% of the market. CATL supplied 60% of the batteries.

Electric is eating LNG, too

For years, the alternative to diesel trucks in China was liquefied natural gas. LNG trucks took nearly 30% of the market in 2024, when gas was much cheaper than diesel.

Now they’re losing to batteries. According to Kpler, LNG trucks had a 37% share of heavy-duty registrations in March, against 23% for electric. By July, electric was at 47% and LNG had collapsed to 11%. Monthly LNG truck registrations fell from more than 30,000 to about 6,200.

So China is skipping the “bridge fuel” phase for trucks almost as fast as it started it.

Diesel demand is falling

China’s diesel consumption already peaked. Rhodium Group found that diesel refinery runs topped out in April 2023, and apparent consumption dropped from 4.7 million barrels per day then to 4.0 million barrels per day in April 2025.

2026 is the steepest drop yet. Kpler estimates diesel demand fell about 420,000 barrels per day year-over-year in May, roughly 10%, and 460,000 in June. It expects a decline of about 230,000 barrels per day for the full year and only a 64,000 barrel-per-day rebound in 2027.

Kpler puts the gross diesel displacement from alternative trucks at about 680,000 barrels per day this year: roughly 450,000 from the LNG fleet built in recent years and 230,000 from electric trucks. Road freight still grew about 3% through July. China is moving more goods with less diesel.

There’s a catch. The fuel price spike this spring, tied to the Iran war, cut demand on its own and pushed more fleets toward electric. But that only explains part of it, and the fleet is still early: electric trucks will be only about 8% of China’s heavy trucks on the road by the end of 2026, according to Kpler. Every year of 40-50% sales shares compounds the diesel losses.

Meanwhile in Europe and the US

Europe is growing fast from a tiny base. ACEA data shows 5,120 heavy electric trucks (16 tonnes and up) registered in the EU through September, up 59.9%, for a 2.5% share. That’s up from 1.7% a year ago, but diesel still took 91.7% of all EU truck registrations.

A few countries stand out. Switzerland is at 24%, Norway 14.4%, the Netherlands 11.1% and Sweden 10.3%. Germany registered the most units at 1,722, but that’s only a 4.2% share.

The US doesn’t publish an official electric Class 8 sales figure, and that tells you something. The best indicator is the recent order for 2,500 Tesla Semis through ZET SCALE, which would roughly double the number of electric Class 8 trucks on US roads. Against about 230,000 Class 8 trucks sold per year, the electric share is well under 1%.

Price is the big difference. The ICCT puts the median electric Class 8 tractor in the US at $411,200, against $172,500 for diesel. Federal tax credits for commercial EVs ended in 2025, and California shelved the rule that would have required fleets to buy zero-emission trucks.

Electrek’s Take

This is the biggest under-covered story in the EV industry right now.

Everyone argued for years about whether electric semis could work. Range, weight, charging, cost. China settled it the boring way. It got the price of a battery-electric heavy truck close enough to diesel, built swap stations along freight routes, and let fleet operators do what fleet operators always do: pick the cheapest truck per kilometer.

And the result is showing up where it matters, in oil demand. Trucks are where diesel lives. Displacing a quarter of a million barrels a day in one year, with electric trucks still only around 8% of the fleet, means we’re still early on this curve.

The contrast with the US is hard to watch. America has Tesla, a Semi factory in Nevada built for 50,000 trucks a year, and some of the best freight corridors in the world for electrification. But electric Class 8 trucks cost 2.4 times as much as diesel here, the federal incentives are gone, and the market is under 1%. The ZET SCALE order is real progress. But it came from shippers pooling their demand, and twe have yet to see these trucks get delivered.

Europe at least has the regulation, and its best markets, at 10% to 24%, are roughly where China was in 2024 and 2025.

The question now is how long Chinese truck makers stay home. SANY and BYD already sell electric trucks in Europe, and CATL is building the swap network for them. If those trucks can come close to China’s pricing, how long can Western truck makers keep charging 2x diesel?

text:
This Energy Explained post represents the research and views of the author(s). It does not necessarily represent the views of the Center on Global Energy Policy. The piece may be subject to further revision. Contributions to SIPA for the benefit of CGEP are general use gifts, which gives the Center discretion in how it allocates these funds. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) could facilitate nuclear energy development through federal permitting reform, but nuclear-specific regulatory challenges involving licensing procedures, Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) capacity, and oversight would remain.

Six bills advanced unanimously by the House Energy and Commerce Committee in September 2026 seek to address these challenges through reforms to fuel-cycle licensing, mandatory hearings, independent technical review, NRC staffing, and transparency.

The effectiveness and durability of these reforms will depend on implementation that improves efficiency while preserving safety oversight and public confidence.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) could facilitate nuclear development by streamlining federal environmental reviews and providing greater certainty for permitted projects. But broad permitting reform alone may leave important nuclear-specific regulatory issues unresolved, including procedural requirements for Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) licensing, the agency’s capacity to conduct timely reviews, the predictability of licensing requirements for developers, and the durability of safety oversight and public accountability across administrations.

Six nuclear bills advanced unanimously by the House Energy and Commerce Committee on September 2, 2026, offer a window into additional reforms under consideration. Developed on a separate legislative track and advanced before BAAJA’s introduction, the bills address fuel-cycle licensing, the sequencing of construction and licensing, mandatory hearings, independent technical advice, senior NRC compensation, and transparency around Department of Energy (DOE) authorizations. Together, they illustrate the potential for nuclear-specific legislation to complement broader permitting reform by reducing regulatory delays and uncertainty while maintaining effective oversight, but also the importance of getting the details right to realize these benefits.

H.R. 3978 Nuclear REFUEL Act

This Act would amend the Atomic Energy Act’s definition of a “production facility” to exclude spent-fuel reprocessing equipment that does not isolate plutonium. This change would allow qualifying facilities to avoid associated statutory mandates that can cause delay, including a licensing hearing even when no party requests one, formal technical specifications, and the prescribed inspections, tests, analyses, and acceptance criteria associated with a combined license. It would also afford the NRC greater discretion to determine appropriate requirements through its regulations and license conditions.

The NRC’s June 2026 proposed rule states that reprocessing facilities could already be licensed under 10 CFR Part 50 or 10 CFR Part 70, but that neither framework fully addresses regulatory gaps related to the safety, security, and environmental considerations specific to these facilities. The rule would establish explicit Part 70 provisions to address some of these gaps and provide a more defined licensing pathway. The proposal illustrates the distinction between removing a statutory mandate and eliminating regulatory requirements altogether. If H.R. 3978 were to become law, the NRC proposed rule would retain existing requirements for operator licensing, restrictions on foreign ownership and control, and approval before construction even for reprocessing facilities that would fall outside the production facility classification. The NRC could also retain requirements it finds appropriate within its statutory authority and consider exemptions where available and justified.

The bill and the proposed rule thus address different aspects of reprocessing licensing: the bill would remove certain statutory requirements for qualifying facilities, while the NRC’s rulemaking would establish a regulatory framework for licensing reprocessing facilities more broadly. The NRC would still need to address technology-specific hazards, and policy questions surrounding reprocessing economics, proliferation concerns, and disposal of the resulting waste would remain.

H.R. 9612 American Enrichment Deployment Act

This Act would permit uranium enrichment facilities to begin construction before receiving an NRC license, under the same terms applicable to other fuel-cycle facilities and at the applicant’s own financial risk. Under current law, enrichment facilities must obtain a license before construction can begin.

The bill would allow limited construction and licensing review to proceed in parallel, though applicants would have to weigh the risks of starting construction before knowing whether a license would be granted and decide which construction activities to prioritize. The amendment expressly preserves environmental-review requirements, hearing rights, inspection authority, and the NRC’s authority to deny a license. The NRC would need to define which construction activities are permissible before issuing a license, as it has for other technologies.

H.R. 5549 Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act

This Act builds on earlier efforts to streamline the hearings process, including the NRC’s approval of simplified mandatory-hearing procedures in 2024. A recent CGEP report examining the history and purpose of mandatory hearings concluded that their costs and time demands were no longer justified by their contribution to regulatory oversight and public transparency. In line with this finding, the bill would eliminate mandatory uncontested hearings for covered reactor and enrichment licensing actions, while preserving affected parties’ right to request a hearing. For hearings held under the amended provision, it would also mandate the use of informal adjudicatory procedures.

Continued support may depend on demonstrating increased efficiency while maintaining a record of transparency in licensing decisions and meaningful opportunities for affected parties to raise concerns.

H.R. 9613 Nuclear Advisory Committee Reform Act

This Act would allow the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards (ACRS) to decline to review an application if it determines the application contains no unique, novel, or noteworthy issues and raises no other issues warranting review. Where practicable, it would direct the committee to focus on safety-significant facility-design issues that are unique, novel, or noteworthy and that ACRS has not previously acted on.

The proposal revisits the question of when outside technical review adds value beyond what NRC staff can provide. It also requires diverse technical expertise and timely staff coordination, generally limits members appointed after enactment to two four-year terms, and gives the Commission responsibility for selecting the chair.

As initially introduced, the bill would have required ACRS advisory activities to begin at NRC request. The substitute amendment that was passed out of committee instead preserved existing automatic advisory reviews. Representative Frank Pallone (D) identified that change as important to his support.

The bill retains automatic review as the statutory default, allowing ACRS to decline reviews only when it determines that an application contains no unique, novel, noteworthy, or otherwise review-worthy issues. As discussed in an earlier CGEP blog, making that determination and documenting it could require substantial technical work, limiting potential efficiency gains. An alternative would be to allow ACRS to select applications for review using its own publicly explained screening approach, while preserving its authority to initiate reviews and the Commission’s ability to request advice.

H.R. 9614 NRC Staff Pay Alignment Act

This Act builds on workforce and compensation authorities established by the bipartisan ADVANCE Act of 2024. The bill would authorize the NRC chair to set basic pay for career senior executives at up to 110 percent of the maximum Senior Executive Service rate within the Commission. This expanded compensation flexibility could help the NRC recruit and retain experienced senior personnel without requiring an across-the-board increase, sustaining technical expertise and consistent implementation across administrations.

H.R. 9084 Department of Energy Nuclear Transparency Act

This Act would require DOE to publish announcements within 72 hours of specified actions involving covered nuclear facilities, including authorizations, issuance of safety analyses, and changes to directives or safety standards. It would also require annual congressional reporting, with protections for commercially sensitive, classified, and other controlled information. By making DOE oversight more visible to the public, the bill may help build public confidence in DOE’s authorization of nuclear energy technology demonstrations and strengthen the durability of those authorizations across administrations.

title: Will 'Gina' Break Texas's Corporate Welfare Consensus? - The American Prospect
description:
MISSOURI CITY, TEXAS – Her full name is Regina Inez Hinojosa, but almost nobody in Texas calls her that.
In Fort Bend County, Kamala Harris defeated Trump by less than two percentage points and lost Texas by roughly 14.
Hinojosa’s message about cutting corporate welfare is gaining popularity among young families, Prestage said, partly because workers increasingly feel they are not benefiting from the subsidies while still paying their own property taxes.
Uphill Battle The latest polls show that Hinojosa’s path to becoming Texas’s first Democratic governor in more than three decades remains complicated.
However, the state’s electoral history over the past 30 years helps explain why Hinojosa’s message appears more promising today.
text:
MISSOURI CITY, TEXAS – Her full name is Regina Inez Hinojosa, but almost nobody in Texas calls her that. From the people she met on the streets during the final stretch of her campaign to her own staff, Hinojosa is simply “Gina.” Her hope, and that of the Democratic Party, is that her nickname will soon become “Governor Gina,” as volunteers and supporters chanted while welcoming her to Fort Bend County ahead of a canvassing event this weekend.

A civil rights lawyer by training and a former Austin school board president, Hinojosa challenged incumbent Greg Abbott for Texas governor with a message that goes beyond the usual Democratic arguments about Republican extremism. Unlike many of her predecessors, she has explicitly focused her campaign on reining in corporate welfare, while supporting public education and expanding the safety net for middle-class families.

“Texas has always been a pro-business state, but we need to first and foremost make sure it is a pro-Texan state, and so that’s what needs to be rightsized,” Hinojosa told the Prospect after kicking off the door-knocking event in Missouri City, a major Houston suburb, on Saturday morning. “I’m running to be the governor for the people of Texas, not the billionaire CEOs. And that’s the difference between me and Greg Abbott. People see it, people know it, and people are voting for change.”

Until recently, most advisers in Texas would likely have warned her against building a gubernatorial campaign around this economic message in a state where corporations benefit from a wide range of tax breaks and subsidies, including property-tax incentives for major industrial projects, sales-tax exemptions for data centers, and grants to major technology and energy companies.

Yet despite polls continuing to narrowly favor Abbott for a fourth term, Hinojosa’s economic message is picking up steam as wealth inequality and affordability become increasingly prime concerns among middle-class and independent voters.

Among her most significant proposals, Hinojosa promised to end sales tax exemptions for large data centers and review incentives awarded to companies such as Elon Musk’s, including the property tax savings tied to his Terafab project, which are estimated at $1.6 billion. She also wants to audit government contracts, scrutinize privatization deals, and make sure companies meet job-creation commitments before receiving public incentives.

“We are at a time in history where the crony capitalism and the corruption are in our face, it is blatant, right?” Hinojosa told the Prospect. “We know that wealth is built on the backs of our government with our taxpayer dollars, and so there is anger and frustration about that. It is out of hand. It is so imbalanced.”

The volunteers who welcomed her on Saturday knocked on doors in Fort Bend County, one of the fastest-growing and most diverse parts of the state, where roughly 70 percent of the population is non-white. Democrats are still fighting to regain Latino voters’ trust after many backed Donald Trump in 2024, hoping it would help defeat inflation. In Fort Bend County, Kamala Harris defeated Trump by less than two percentage points and lost Texas by roughly 14.

“People invoke their pocketbook—they’re concerned about the quality of life and how the families are faring, whether the next generation is going to be able to buy a home [and] have a decent quality of life,” said Grady Prestage, a longtime county commissioner for Precinct 2 on the Fort Bend County Commissioners Court. Hinojosa’s message about cutting corporate welfare is gaining popularity among young families, Prestage said, partly because workers increasingly feel they are not benefiting from the subsidies while still paying their own property taxes.

Meanwhile, more voters are realizing that Texas missed a major opportunity by continuing to reject the Biden-era health coverage expansion under the Affordable Care Act, Prestage said. The GOP state legislature convinced “constituents that it was not in their best interest to do this, which is ridiculous,” he said.

Uphill Battle

The latest polls show that Hinojosa’s path to becoming Texas’s first Democratic governor in more than three decades remains complicated. A Texas Politics Project tracker showed Abbott ahead by two to five percentage points in several surveys conducted in the second half of October, while RealClearPolitics’ polling average placed his lead at 3.7 points.

However, the state’s electoral history over the past 30 years helps explain why Hinojosa’s message appears more promising today.

The last Democrat to win a gubernatorial race in Texas was Ann Richards in 1991, a charismatic and popular former state treasurer who championed public education and economic renovation. Richards is also remembered for appointing unprecedented numbers of women and minorities to state leadership positions at a time when Texas politics was heavily dominated by white men, even more so than today. Democratic gubernatorial candidates have suffered heavy defeats in every election ever since, sometimes struggling to reach even 30 percent of the vote.

Hinojosa hasn’t quite soared as high as fellow Democrat James Talarico, who is running for the U.S. Senate against Republican Ken Paxton. Recent polls have given Talarico a narrow lead, with most polling averages putting him ahead by a few points. However, an October 26–28 survey by Quantus Insights, a pollster with one of the most accurate records in forecasting the 2024 presidential elections, found Paxton slightly ahead, 48.7 percent to 47.6 percent.

Rep. Joaquin Castro, who introduced Hinojosa at a canvassing event in San Antonio over the weekend, said that Texans are “standing up and finally going to vote” after “thirty years of increasingly right-wing government.”

“There’s no guarantee that we’ll win, but I think we’re right there,” he told the Prospect in an interview, adding that Hinojosa’s message can potentially resonate with “anybody who is feeling the pinch of money.”

Young people and middle-class families are seeing “tax breaks going to corporations that are already very wealthy,” he said. “And so they ask themselves, ‘Well, wait a minute, why are these big, wealthy, profitable corporations getting free money and here I am struggling to pay for my groceries?’”

Talarico and Hinojosa appeared side-by-side at rallies in Houston and San Antonio over the weekend. Hinojosa’s closing remarks onstage Saturday echoed the arguments she had made in Missouri City earlier that morning.

“Just this summer [Abbott] redirected a $100-million-dollar broadband contract to Elon Musk, an act so corrupt that even Republicans in Austin said, ‘This stinks,’ and shut the whole broadband program down,” she said, referring to the $108.8 million in federal Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment, or BEAD, funding allocated to Musk’s Starlink. The allegations of preferential treatment in the awarding process prompted Republican lawmakers to demand an audit of the broadband program, as reported by KUT Radio and the Texas Tribune.

“I will ensure every Texas child has quality health care [instead],” she said during the rally. “We are a wealthy state. We have enough to make sure our kids get the health care they need.”

Message Resonating

Early voting ended Friday with record turnout. Texas recorded more than 7.4 million early votes, the highest total ever for a midterm election, with roughly 39 percent of registered voters casting ballots. Participation was particularly strong in bluer urban counties, including Harris, Dallas, and Tarrant. But Republicans could still benefit from their base’s habit of showing up on Election Day.

Voters attending rallies and waiting in line to cast their ballots expressed that Talarico can win the Senate seat only if Hinojosa avoids losing to Abbott by more than five percentage points. The spotlight is now on Republican voters who may finally break with their party.

For his part, Abbott—whose campaign reportedly raised $26 million during this past month, including a $5 million contribution from Musk—made stops in El Paso, Lubbock, Amarillo and Laredo in the past few days, pitching his re-election bid as a choice between “common sense and chaos” and warning voters that Hinojosa would be “wrong for Texas.”

Read more election coverage from The American Prospect

In Laredo, Abbott focused on property taxes, telling supporters that “your property taxes should never go up without you having a vote on it,” while promoting proposals to expand homestead exemptions. In El Paso, he defended his administration’s approach to data centers, saying he had “put a total halt on any data centers” until the state completed an audit of their electricity and water use.

Meanwhile, in Houston, drivers can hardly go thirty minutes without running into an Abbott radio ad warning that Hinojosa would “open the border” to undocumented immigrants and hurt the local economy.

Emanuel, a 48-year-old conservative Latino voter who works as a handyman in Northeast Houston, said he couldn’t wait for Tuesday because he was tired of being bombarded by advertising. “I want to go to work and just listen to my music,” he joked right after voting.

Yet he picked both Abbott and Paxton because he believes the economy performs better in Texas than in most states run by Democrats. “I don’t want to make this place like New York, and I believe a majority agrees with me,” he said.

Not everyone, however, is so sure of the results.

Snacking on nachos at a karaoke event featuring local candidates at the Eldorado Ballroom, a historic venue opened in Houston by Black entrepreneurs Anna Johnson and Clarence Dupree in 1939, Xanté Wallace said Hinojosa’s message has everything it needs to “resonate with younger people” in today’s economy.

Unlike Manuel, Wallace, a 30-year-old firefighter born and raised in Houston, said it is impossible to predict whether the economic message alone will be enough to turn Hinojosa’s campaign into a winning one.

“A lot of corporations have interceded with politics and are not paying their fair share of taxes,” he says. “That is creating too much inequality and needs to be addressed.”

text:
Louisiana has no shortage of energy expertise, industrial assets or promising research. The harder challenge has been connecting them—turning discoveries in the lab into commercial technologies, preparing workers for the jobs those technologies create and giving emerging companies a place to prove they can operate at industrial scale.

FUEL is positioning itself as the connective tissue.

Since securing a $160 million, 10-year award from the National Science Foundation in 2024, the LSU-based organization has evolved into far more than a source of early-stage capital. It is investing in workforce development, building specialized innovation infrastructure and creating pathways for Louisiana scientists and engineers to move their research from the university into the marketplace.

The broader reach is not a departure from FUEL’s original mission. It is the execution of a five-year strategic plan built around 12 goals and overseen by a governing board that includes industry representatives, investors, academic leaders and state officials.

“If I were a preacher, FUEL’s strategic implementation plan would be my Bible,” says Mike Mazzola, executive director of Future Use of Energy in Louisiana. “Our board maintains that plan to ensure we’re achieving our purpose.”

That purpose is ambitious: Capitalize on Louisiana’s existing industrial strengths and position the state as a leader in energy innovation, carbon management and industrial decarbonization.

For energy executives, the potential payoff extends beyond promising technology. FUEL is attempting to assemble the talent, facilities, capital and industry partnerships needed to move new ideas toward commercial deployment—and encourage more Louisiana researchers to build companies in the state.

“We want to take advantage of the resources we already have here,” Mazzola says. “Rather than chasing what the Joneses are doing someplace else, we’re focusing on what our core strengths are right here.”

Increasingly, that means connecting workforce training, research, startup support and industrial deployment as parts of a larger strategy.

FUEL is supporting technical education, helping researchers become entrepreneurs, giving startups access to specialized facilities and pairing emerging technologies with industrial sites capable of testing and deploying them.

Its latest initiatives offer a clearer picture of how those pieces are beginning to come together.

Building the workforce pipeline

One of the clearest examples is FUEL’s growing investment in the workers who will be needed to support Louisiana’s evolving energy sector.

In August, the organization announced a one-year, $800,000 investment in the Louisiana Community and Technical Colleges system to enhance and expand energy-related programs at community colleges across the state. It is the first installment in what is expected to become a multiyear commitment.

Through the partnership, FUEL and LCTC plan to build on established best practices and advance energy education and workforce development statewide.

The initiative follows earlier FUEL investments in the field, including a $100,000 FUEL Scale award to River Parishes Community College in 2025.

The latest funding is intended in part to strengthen programs serving nontraditional learners pursuing degrees or certifications relevant to the energy industry.

“Louisiana’s energy sector supports a wide range of middle-skill jobs and career paths that create wealth-building opportunities for Louisiana residents,” Lacy McManus, FUEL’s director of workforce development, said in a press release. “These in-demand roles, however, require advanced technical training and programs aligned with industry needs.”

The innovation infrastructure

A trained workforce is only one piece of the equation.

Emerging energy companies also need specialized facilities where they can develop, test and scale capital-intensive technologies in real-world environments.

FUEL moved to address that need in 2025 by investing in Newlab, a New Orleans innovation hub designed to help startups scale technologies focused on clean energy, carbon management and maritime innovation.

Newlab currently operates from temporary facilities in the Garden District. In March 2027, it is expected to move into a $50 million permanent facility at the Bywater redevelopment site, funded by the city of New Orleans, Louisiana Economic Development, Greater New Orleans Inc. and FUEL.

“FUEL is more than a funding source for us,” says Cameron Poole, Newlab New Orleans’ director of strategy. “We’re meeting with them almost every week, since a lot of their programs sync with our needs.”

The Newlab facilities are intended to provide a platform for technologies that could potentially transform some of Louisiana’s key industries. That makes the hub’s work a natural fit with FUEL’s broader strategy.

“FUEL’s North Star is carbon management and utilization, and that’s a huge focus of ours,” Poole says. “We’re aligning these programs so our startups can meaningfully leverage their initiatives.”

Much of Newlab’s work so far has centered on carbon management and energy production. The organization is building the specialized laboratory infrastructure startups need to prototype, construct and deploy their technologies in real-world environments.

Some of those connections are already taking shape. Shell and Japan-based JERA Co. Inc. are each using Newlab to landscape, validate and deploy emerging technologies.

“A lot of these technologies are very capital intensive, and we have a global network of investors and regional partners that can help,” Poole says. “What’s exciting is that we’re starting to see some of the startups already receive startup equity.”

FUEL is also creating a pathway for Louisiana scientists and engineers to develop and commercialize their research without leaving the state.

In May, the organization announced the Louisiana Science Innovator BRIDGE program, a joint initiative with Washington, D.C.-based Activate. The program aims to build a connected hard-tech and carbon-tech innovation workforce across Louisiana by providing the entrepreneurial infrastructure needed to turn research into new energy companies.

“It’s a super important component to our plan,” Mazzola says. “We’ll be encouraging many of our graduates to use their research to start a company here rather than elsewhere.”

FUEL is currently searching for a coordinator to run the program.

Creating an ecosystem of startups

The growing network of early-stage companies in FUEL’s orbit offers one of the most tangible measures of the strategy’s progress. Its startup ecosystem currently includes 14 companies.

In May, FUEL announced a second round of proof-of-concept funding, awarding a combined $1.2 million to seven early-stage companies. The funding is intended to help close the gap between early research and market entry.

One recipient, Tickfaw-based Waste to Energy Systems, is using its $200,000 award to move a gasification technology beyond the research-and-development phase. The system converts biomass into heat and electricity using a single piece of equipment.

But the funding also comes with an additional objective: FUEL wants Waste to Energy to determine whether the technology can produce hydrogen from the resulting gas.

“They want us to see if we can strip hydrogen out of the gas,” says Alissa Mahoney, the company’s chief operating officer. “It’s a better option than pulling hydrogen out of air or water, and we’re not using any natural resources in the process.”

The idea originated more than a decade ago with Mahoney’s father, Albany Woodworks founder Richard Woods.His sawmill reclaims heart pine and cypress and remills the wood into a variety of products.

The operation also generated a recurring challenge: a pile of sawdust.

“We’d always had a pile of sawdust sitting around and he has always been a bit of an environmentalist, so he started thinking of ways to put it to use,” Mahoney says.

Woods built a small gasification system in 2010 and gradually increased its size over the years that followed. Mahoney now hopes the FUEL award will help move the technology out of R&D and into a real-world application.

Waste to Energy has purchased a syngas analyzer, enabling the company to optimize its processes. Initial testing indicates that the system has successfully stripped hydrogen from the gas, and the company is seeking third-party validation of the results.

“With any new technology, convincing people to change the way they think about things is the biggest challenge,” Mahoney says. “This funding has significantly helped us go down that path. We hope to walk away from this with a third-party validated sales package that gives customers reliable data.”

FUEL’s support has extended beyond the financial award. It also connected Waste to Energy with StartUP Northshore in Covington and Scale Up! Louisiana for assistance with business development.

“We realized there was some room for improvement on the business side, and that we needed to shift our thinking and how we approached things,” Mahoney says.

Connecting innovation with industry

Perhaps the clearest illustration of FUEL’s connective role can be found at Cornerstone Energy Park in Waggaman, where an established industrial site could provide emerging technologies with the assets and feedstocks needed to move toward commercialization.

Jacques Byrd, vice president of site development at Cornerstone Chemical Co., which owns the park, says FUEL’s emphasis on carbon utilization aligns with Cornerstone’s long-term vision. The company wants the park to become an integrated, sustainable industrial hub that advances green energy innovation while strengthening domestic manufacturing supply chains.

The 800-acre industrial park has 180 available acres, excess utility capacity and access to rail and water.

“We plug in nicely with their model,” Byrd says. “Our ammonia plant provides an abundant source of pure CO2,” he says, “and we already utilize some of it in our urea and melamine manufacturing.”

“FUEL was happy to see carbon utilization already happening in their backyard.”

FUEL is now connecting Cornerstone with developers of late-stage technologies seeking to commercialize their work and needing access to carbon or other industrial feedstocks.

“We’re also the primary recipients of FUEL funding for a study into utilizing carbon to make syngas,” Byrd says. “We’ll disburse a portion of that funding to a technology provider to build out a syngas facility at our plant, and from there we could go in any number of directions.”

It is the kind of connection FUEL’s strategy is designed to create: pairing an emerging technology with funding, an industrial partner, essential feedstocks and a site where it can be put to work. Taken together, those efforts reveal the larger ambition behind FUEL’s expanding portfolio—not simply to fund energy innovation, but to build the Louisiana ecosystem needed to carry it from research to commercial reality.

title: APAC EV Supply Chain Investment: Thailand's $4.1B [2026] - Tech Insider
description:
That is the clearest sign yet that APAC EV supply chain investment is moving from the assembly line to the component bin.
Why Components Matter More Than Assembly Now Final assembly is the easiest part of an EV supply chain to relocate.
Five Predictions for APAC EV Component Investment These are our analysis, not reported facts, and they rest on the confirmed figures above.
The Bottom Line on APAC EV Supply Chain Investment The takeaway: the money is following the parts.
Those are the indicators that will show whether APAC EV supply chain investment is building durable industrial capacity or just a strong set of announcements.
text:
Thailand’s Board of Investment (BOI) now counts more than US$4.1 billion in EV-supply-chain investment pledges across 198 projects, EV Infrastructure News reported, and the split inside that headline number tells the real story. Vehicle plants still take the largest single slice. But batteries, energy storage and the parts between them now pull in hundreds of millions of dollars each. That is the clearest sign yet that APAC EV supply chain investment is moving from the assembly line to the component bin.

TNGlobal is among the outlets reporting the shift as the top regional automotive story. BMI, which sits inside Fitch Solutions, made a related case in a July 2026 autos investment roundup on APAC value chains deepening as the EV transition continues. Across these reports the pattern is the same. Money is moving toward battery materials, electric powertrains, recycling and component localisation, and away from simply bolting kits together.

For hardware readers this matters because drive motors, battery management systems and power control units decide what an EV costs and where it can be built. We saw a version of this in India, where Sona Comstar posted a 129% jump in EV sales as a supplier rather than a carmaker. More device and component coverage lives in our hardware section. This article walks through the numbers, the Malaysian test case, the local-content gap and what could change next.

Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions.

Add Now

Thailand’s US$4.1 Billion Pledge Book, Line by Line

The BOI’s own release is the primary document here, and its structure is worth reading slowly. The agency groups pledges by product category, and three of those categories carry figures that anyone tracking the supply chain should memorize. Battery electric vehicles (BEVs) account for US$1.18 billion across 18 projects. Batteries and energy storage systems (ESS) account for US$1.00 billion across 57 projects. Critical components, meaning drive motors, battery management systems (BMS) and power control units, account for US$373 million across 49 projects.

Those three lines add up to roughly US$2.55 billion, or about 62% of the headline total. The remaining US$1.5 billion or so sits across 74 projects in categories this article does not break out, because the verified figures we hold do not itemize them. The table below lays out what is confirmed and the shares are our own arithmetic against the more-than-US$4.1-billion total, so treat them as approximate.

Look at the project counts before the dollar figures. BEVs draw the most money from the fewest projects (18), which is what you expect from vehicle plants. Components draw the least money from nearly three times as many projects (49). Batteries and ESS sit in between. A pledge book with that shape signals a broad base of mid-sized and smaller component investors rather than a handful of mega-factories.

Why Components Matter More Than Assembly Now

Final assembly is the easiest part of an EV supply chain to relocate. A plant needs land, power, permits and a labor pool. The value-added content is thin if most of the vehicle arrives as imported subassemblies. Components work the other way. A drive motor line, a BMS board or a power control unit requires process know-how, qualified suppliers and long-term volume commitments. Once those exist, they tend to stay put.

That logic explains why governments and investment agencies now brag about parts. A country that hosts only assembly captures wages and a slice of tax revenue. A country that hosts motors, battery management and power electronics captures engineering jobs, supplier ecosystems and some resilience when tariffs or export rules change. The same instinct shows up in the trade fights that Tesla and Samsung are contesting over a US tariff probe tied to Vietnam ahead of a November 29 deadline, where goods are made carries real price consequences.

What the Per-Project Math Shows

Dividing each category’s pledge by its project count gives a rough sense of ticket size. This is our own calculation from the BOI figures, and it is a floor, because the total is stated as more than US$4.1 billion. Averages also hide big outliers, so read the numbers as a texture check rather than a ruling.

A BEV project averages close to nine times the size of a component project. That gap is normal. A vehicle plant needs a stamping, body and paint footprint that a motor or BMS line does not. What matters is the direction of travel. Components are no longer a rounding error in the pledge book. At about US$7.6 million per project, they are the kind of ticket that mid-sized tier-two suppliers can write, which widens the pool of who can participate.

Critical Components: Drive Motors, BMS and Power Control Units

The BOI specifically names drive motors, battery management systems and power control units inside its critical-components bucket, and the choice is telling. These three parts sit at the heart of an EV’s electrical architecture. The drive motor turns stored energy into motion. The BMS watches cell voltage, temperature and state of charge, and it is the main safeguard against thermal problems. The power control unit manages how electricity flows between the battery, the motor and the vehicle’s other systems.

None of these is a commodity bolt-on. Each combines mechanical, electrical and software work, and each carries safety and warranty exposure for the carmaker. Localizing them means a supplier must pass automaker quality audits, run production at predictable volumes and support software updates over a vehicle’s life. That is a higher bar than stamping brackets, which is partly why the US$373 million pledge is smaller than the batteries line today.

It is also why the 49-project count deserves attention. Forty-nine separate commitments in a category this technical suggests that suppliers see durable demand and are willing to commit capital before every volume target is locked. Whether those projects ship on schedule is the open question, and we cover the execution risks further down.

Batteries and Energy Storage: US$1.00 Billion Across 57 Projects

The batteries and ESS line is the second-largest confirmed category, and its pairing is deliberate. Battery factories built for EVs can also serve stationary storage, which gives investors a second revenue stream if vehicle demand swings. A plant that makes cells or packs for BEVs can, with tooling changes, supply grid and commercial storage customers. Fifty-seven projects is the highest count in any of the three confirmed categories.

The energy side of the story is moving in parallel across the region. When we covered VinEnergo’s 22 MWp solar and 45 MWh battery system for three Vietnam EV plants, the point was that factories now plan their power alongside their production lines. Thailand’s pairing of batteries with energy storage in one pledge category reflects the same thinking.

One more detail from the BOI figures: the planned annual domestic production capacity for BEVs exceeds 370,000 units. Set that next to the US$1.00 billion batteries pledge and the US$373 million components pledge, and you get a crude ratio. The component pledge works out to roughly US$1,000 of investment per unit of planned BEV capacity, and the batteries pledge to roughly US$2,700. These ratios are our arithmetic and mix different project timelines, so they only suggest scale. They do show that the supporting industry is being funded at a level that could plausibly serve the planned vehicle output.

Malaysia’s Chery Matchmaking: 35 Suppliers, 4 Agreements

Thailand shows what a pledge book looks like. Malaysia shows what it takes to build one from a thin base. In May 2025, the Malaysian Investment Development Authority (MIDA) brought together 23 domestic parts suppliers and 12 technology suppliers with Chery. The session produced four commercial agreements covering components, technology transfer and joint investment, according to the reports we reviewed.

Four agreements out of a 35-supplier room is a modest tally, and nobody should oversell it. But the format is the point. Instead of waiting for a foreign automaker to find local vendors on its own, the investment agency put both groups at one table and pushed for contracts. That is a deliberate industrial-policy tool, and it targets the exact weakness that critics raise about Chinese EV investment in Southeast Asia: foreign brands arrive with their own supplier networks and leave local firms on the sideline.

The session happened roughly 18 months before this article. That is long enough that readers should ask what happened next, and the reports we reviewed do not detail follow-on contracts or volumes. We will not guess. The honest read is that matchmaking opened a door and the proof will come when those four agreements show up as shipping parts.

The Local Content Gap: 20%-30% vs Up to 70%

The sharpest statistic in the Malaysian reporting is a comparison of local content. Domestically assembled EVs reportedly carry 20% to 30% local content. Foreign-branded conventional-engine vehicles assembled in the same market carry up to 70%. That is a gap of 40 to 50 percentage points, and it is the plainest measure of how much work localization still has to do.

Why does the gap exist? Conventional-engine supply chains in the region took decades to build. Local firms learned to make seats, wiring, brake parts, exhaust systems and stampings to the exacting specs of established carmakers. An EV removes much of that content. There is no exhaust, no conventional transmission and far less engine-related machining. What replaces it is a battery pack, an electric drive unit and power electronics, which are exactly the items local suppliers have not yet had time to master.

For perspective, El Nasr’s MAGE EV output in Egypt was reported with 45% local content, which sits above Malaysia’s reported 20% to 30% range for EV assembly. Different countries use different measurement rules, so the comparison is loose. Still, it shows that localization targets in the mid-40s are being set elsewhere for early-stage EV programs in other emerging markets.

What Analysts and Suppliers Are Saying

The South China Morning Post’s Week in Asia section ran a piece under the headline “Southeast Asia’s EV boom sidelines local car parts suppliers.” In it, Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara, Executive Director of the Centre of Economic and Law Studies, told the paper: “The supply chain is very different between Japanese autos and Chinese EVs.” His remark addresses Chinese EV investment in Southeast Asia and its limited integration with established local automotive-component suppliers.

In the same SCMP coverage, Adhinegara described the obstacles facing local parts makers who want a place in Chinese EV supply chains: “The biggest barriers are financing, technology and access to manufacturers.” Those three barriers map neatly onto the policy responses we are now seeing. Pledge incentives address financing. Technology-transfer clauses address know-how. Matchmaking sessions like the MIDA-Chery event address access.

On the investor side, BNP Paribas has published an APAC electric-vehicle discussion with several of its executives. Jean-Christophe Vallat, Managing Director and Head of Industrials and Consumer at BNP Paribas, said: “Supply chain considerations are of key importance to the development of the EV market, with significant growth opportunities and geopolitical challenges that will influence the entire industry’s value chain.” In the same BNP Paribas discussion, Giulio Pescatore, Director of Automotive Research at BNP Paribas Exane, said: “The automotive industry is going through one of the most disruptive and transformative periods in its history.”

Read together, the quotes frame a tension. Bankers see opportunity and geopolitical risk in the value chain. Local economists see a risk that the opportunity bypasses domestic firms. The pledge data from Thailand suggests that at least one government is trying to keep the opportunity at home by funding the middle of the chain.

Market Impact: Who Wins and Who Gets Squeezed

Likely Winners

Component makers with existing automotive quality certifications hold the best position. A firm that already supplies motors or electronic modules to conventional-engine programs can pivot faster than a startup. Battery-pack assemblers also benefit, since the 57 batteries and ESS projects create demand for cell handling, thermal management and testing equipment. Suppliers of those tools and materials gain a regional customer base.

Investment agencies that run structured matchmaking also come out ahead. MIDA’s Chery session gave Malaysia a template it can repeat with other automakers. Agencies that simply publish incentive schedules without brokering introductions risk watching foreign automakers import their own supplier base.

Likely Losers

Suppliers tied to engine and exhaust content face the hardest road. As EV share rises, demand for those parts shrinks, and the 70% local content that conventional-engine vehicles reportedly achieve in Malaysia will not transfer automatically to EVs. Firms in that group need to retool toward electric drive components or lose volume.

Consumers and fleets also feel indirect effects. Demand for EVs depends partly on price and incentives. Our earlier look at EV sales falling 23.8% without tax credits showed how sensitive buyers are when subsidies disappear. Localized supply chains can lower costs over time, but they do not remove the need for demand support in the near term.

Competitive Comparison: Thailand’s Pledges vs Malaysia’s Matchmaking

Thailand and Malaysia are pursuing the same goal with different tools. Thailand leads with a large, categorized pledge book. Malaysia leads with brokered introductions to a single automaker. The table compares what each approach has produced based on the confirmed figures.

Neither model is clearly better. Pledges generate attention and signal confidence, but they are intentions and not factory output. Matchmaking produces signed contracts but at small scale. The most credible path combines both: a visible investment pipeline plus structured introductions that turn pledges into purchase orders. Other markets across APAC, including Indonesia, Vietnam and India, are working through their own versions, and the reports we reviewed describe battery materials, powertrains, recycling and localisation as the common themes. We have not itemized their figures here because the numbers were not part of our verified set.

Historical Context: From Assembly Hub to Parts Race

Southeast Asia built its auto industry on an assembly-first model. Foreign carmakers, many of them Japanese, set up plants, brought their own tier-one suppliers and gradually pulled local firms into the chain. Over time that produced the high local-content ratios seen in conventional-engine production today. It took years, and it rewarded patient partnerships between automakers and domestic vendors.

The EV transition scrambles that arrangement. As Adhinegara noted, the supply chain for Japanese autos differs sharply from the one Chinese EV makers use. New entrants bring different supplier relationships, different component architectures and often their own battery partners. Local firms that spent a generation qualifying with Japanese programs find the rules reset.

That is the backdrop for the policy shift now underway. Governments learned from the first wave that landing the assembly plant is not enough. If they want the second wave to leave more value behind, they need to fund motors, battery management, power electronics and recycling early, while sourcing decisions are still being made. The Thai pledge book and the Malaysian matchmaking session are two early attempts at that.

What It Means for Hardware Makers and Buyers

For hardware companies, the component pledges open a real market. Drive motors, BMS boards and power control units are electronics and electromechanical products with long design cycles. Firms that sell sensors, power semiconductors, connectors, thermal materials and test systems to automotive customers will see requests for quotations tied to these projects. The 49 component projects in Thailand alone represent dozens of separate sourcing decisions.

For EV buyers, the effect is slower and less direct. Local component production can trim logistics costs and shorten repair-part lead times. It may also improve warranty service in the home market. But those benefits arrive after factories ramp, and vehicle prices in the next year or two will still track incentives, currency and competition more than localization. Demand for EVs in India shows the same dynamic, as we saw when Mahindra eyed 12,000 EVs a month as demand ran into capacity limits: factory capacity, not just buyer interest, shaped what customers could get.

Risks and What to Watch

The main risk is conversion. A pledge is a statement of intent, and the gap between a BOI-recorded commitment and a running production line can be wide. Delays, changes in demand, shifts in automaker strategy or financing trouble can all stall a project. Anyone using the US$4.1 billion figure should remember it describes commitments, not delivered capacity.

A second risk is concentration. If a handful of foreign automakers anchor most demand, suppliers depend on their decisions. A strategy change at one automaker could ripple through dozens of component projects. That is one reason matchmaking with several carmakers matters more than a single marquee deal.

Third, technology can move faster than factory plans. Battery chemistries, motor designs and power electronics evolve quickly. A line built around today’s design might need retooling before it pays back. Suppliers that invest in flexible tooling and software capability will handle that better than those locked to one spec.

Five Predictions for APAC EV Component Investment

These are our analysis, not reported facts, and they rest on the confirmed figures above.

Matchmaking spreads. Expect more investment agencies to copy the MIDA-Chery format with other automakers within the next 12 to 18 months, since it targets the access barrier that local economists keep naming.

Component share rises. Critical components sit at about 9% of Thailand’s pledge total today. As tier-one suppliers follow vehicle and battery plants, we expect that share to grow in future BOI updates.

Local content for EVs inches up. Malaysia’s reported 20% to 30% range for assembled EVs should move toward the upper end first, because that requires only a few additional localized items rather than a full powertrain.

Recycling enters the headline. With investment emphasis already shifting toward recycling per regional reports, expect recycling and battery-materials announcements to appear beside component pledges in the next round of investment roundups.

Execution becomes the story. Within two years the question will shift from how much was pledged to how much is shipping. Watch for BOI or MIDA data on realized investment and production, which would be a sharper signal than pledge totals.

The Bottom Line on APAC EV Supply Chain Investment

The takeaway: the money is following the parts. Thailand’s more than US$4.1 billion across 198 projects, including US$373 million for motors, BMS and power control units, shows an investment base that goes well beyond vehicle assembly. Malaysia’s 35-supplier session with Chery shows a smaller economy building supplier depth one contract at a time. Both point the same way, toward component localisation as the next phase of the region’s EV build-out.

The numbers still need to turn into factories. Readers tracking this story should watch for realized investment data, follow-on agreements from the Chery session and any change in local-content figures for EVs. Those are the indicators that will show whether APAC EV supply chain investment is building durable industrial capacity or just a strong set of announcements.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much has Thailand attracted in EV supply chain investment?

The Thailand Board of Investment reports more than US$4.1 billion in EV-supply-chain pledges across 198 projects. BEVs account for US$1.18 billion across 18 projects, batteries and energy storage for US$1.00 billion across 57 projects, and critical components for US$373 million across 49 projects.

What counts as a critical component in the BOI figures?

The BOI’s critical-components category covers drive motors, battery management systems and power control units. These are the electrical and electromechanical parts at the core of an EV’s drivetrain and battery safety.

What did Malaysia and Chery agree in May 2025?

The Malaysian Investment Development Authority brought together 23 domestic parts suppliers and 12 technology suppliers with Chery. The initiative produced four commercial agreements covering components, technology transfer and joint investment.

How much local content do Malaysian-assembled EVs have?

Reports put local content for domestically assembled EVs at 20% to 30%. Foreign-branded conventional-engine vehicles reportedly reach up to 70%, which leaves a gap of 40 to 50 percentage points.

Why is investment shifting from assembly to components?

Regional reporting describes investment emphasis moving toward battery materials, electric powertrains, recycling and component localisation. Components are harder to relocate than assembly, create engineering jobs and give countries more control over their supply chains.

Are the pledges the same as built factories?

No. A pledge is a recorded commitment, and the time between pledge and production can be long. Realized investment and output data will be a better test than the headline total.

What do local suppliers say holds them back?

Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara of the Centre of Economic and Law Studies told the South China Morning Post that the biggest barriers are financing, technology and access to manufacturers.

Which sources back the shift to components?

TNGlobal and other outlets report it as the leading regional automotive story. The Thailand BOI figures, the Malaysia-Chery reporting and BMI’s July 2026 APAC autos investment roundup all point in the same direction.

text:
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recently announced two negotiated rulemakings to update federal safety standards for vehicle headlights and tires. Negotiated rulemaking is a rarely used regulatory process that gives nongovernmental stakeholders a direct role in shaping regulations. NHTSA appears to be turning to this approach to accelerate long-awaited updates to its safety standards.

Negotiated Rulemaking as a Regulatory Tool

Negotiated rulemaking is a process in which a federal agency convenes a committee of affected stakeholders to try to reach consensus on a proposed rule before it is published for public comment.

Negotiated federal rulemakings emerged in the 1980s, and Congress formalized the process with the Negotiated Rulemaking Act of 1990 (the “Act”). Under the Act, an agency may establish a negotiated rulemaking committee to negotiate and develop a rule if the agency determines that doing so would be in the public interest. That determination in turn considers a number of factors, including whether “there are a limited number of identifiable interests that will be significantly affected by the rule,” and “there is a reasonable likelihood that a committee can be convened with a balanced representation of persons who … can adequately represent” those interests.

Once established, the rulemaking committee “shall consider the matter proposed by the agency for consideration and shall attempt to reach a consensus concerning a proposed rule.” If it does reach a consensus, the committee transmits to the agency a report with the proposed rule. If it cannot reach a consensus, the committee may issue a report “specifying any areas in which the committee reached a consensus,” as well as any other “information, recommendations, or materials that the committee considers appropriate.” Individual committee members may also “include as an addendum to the report additional information, recommendations, or materials.”

Importantly, the use of a negotiated rulemaking committee does not obviate the requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act. A proposed rule that comes out of a negotiated rulemaking committee still must undergo the standard notice-and-comment process and is still subject to judicial review.

Though not a common process in the federal government, especially in the last quarter century, negotiated rulemaking has been occasionally employed by other federal agencies, including the Departments of Education, Energy, Health and Human Services, Agriculture, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)—sometimes in response to statutory mandates specifically requiring it.

Negotiated rulemaking has several potential benefits: it gives affected stakeholders up-front involvement in the conception and drafting of the rule; it can help build consensus at the outset of the rulemaking process; it may encourage creative solutions through group interaction; and it can potentially do more to address and resolve objections to a rulemaking early in the process. But the evidence on whether the promises of negotiated rulemaking are borne out in practice is mixed: one study found that the EPA negotiated rulemakings took at least as long as conventional rulemakings, despite the extensive up-front efforts, and that negotiated rules were not less likely to be challenged in court. Other scholarship has challenged these conclusions.

The NHTSA Proposals

In a speech in January 2026, NHTSA’s Administrator previewed that the agency was considering using negotiated rulemaking.

On October 8, NHTSA released a notice of intent to establish a Negotiated Rulemaking Advisory Committee for Vehicle Lighting. NHTSA’s lighting standards, set forth in Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard (FMVSS) No. 108, have not kept pace with recent advances in automotive lighting technology. Headlight glare is a common complaint, as modern vehicles increasingly employ LED and xenon headlights that are brighter than the halogen lights used in older models. Glare has been cited as a factor in at least some crashes, although the magnitude of its effects is less evident.

On October 27, NHTSA followed up with a notice of intent to establish a Negotiated Rulemaking Advisory Committee for Tire Safety. Several existing FMVSS set tire safety standards. NHTSA explained that the agency has been considering updates to those tire standards since 2018, and that this would be the “first major overhaul in more than 20 years.” In particular, the rulemaking would consider updating testing methods and setting rules for new designs such as airless tires.

Both negotiated rulemaking announcements proposed similar committee memberships:

Four representatives from equipment manufacturers or retailers;

Two representatives from national motor vehicle manufacturers;

Four representatives from national motor vehicle or motor vehicle equipment manufacturing associations;

Two representatives from national motor vehicle or motor vehicle equipment safety organizations;

Three representatives from educational or research institutions, or testing organizations within the United States; and

Three representatives from national professional engineering associations or standard-setting associations.

The two announcements also provided for similar procedures. Committee members would be nominated and appointed in accordance with the Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA). The rulemaking committee would meet publicly approximately four times per year. The committee would be tasked with “developing a detailed term sheet consisting of consensus recommendations to inform the agency’s rulemaking proposal.” NHTSA then would publish a notice of proposed rulemaking “promptly after the committee submits its consensus recommendations, the Secretary approves them either as submitted or in modified form, and after appropriate consultation with the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs.” Each committee’s charter would expire after two years, unless the Secretary of Transportation renews it.

Takeaways:

As the saying goes, if you’re not at the table, you’re on the menu. Parties interested in the outcome of these proposals should make every effort to have a voice in the negotiated rulemaking process, either directly or through trade associations or other representatives. Stakeholders not represented on the committee would still have an opportunity to comment on the proposed rules, although committee members would likely have considerably greater influence over their development.

These negotiated rulemakings amount to something of an experiment for an agency that has not deployed the method in decades. In some ways, the subject matter of the proposed actions may be well suited to negotiated rulemaking: the lighting and tire standards are highly technical rules that would benefit from outside expertise and the number of regulated parties—primarily manufacturers of vehicles and equipment—is limited.

The timeline for these rulemakings is unclear. Both proposals indicated that NHTSA expects the committee to “finalize its deliberations and provide its detailed term sheet within the active period of its charter”—namely, two years, though in principle the committees could complete their work more quickly. But following the completion of the term sheet, the agency would then need to draft and publish the actual notice of proposed rulemaking, followed by a public comment period and then completion of the final rule. And there is normally substantial lead time between the publication of an updated FMVSS and the actual compliance date for manufacturers.

text:
Construction is progressing well at the 3.0-GW North Carolina facility as it moves into the equipment installation phase

GREENVILLE, N.C., Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Inox Solar Americas LLC, a U.S.-based solar technology and manufacturing company specializing in advanced PV cells and high-performance PV modules, today announced that its planned PV cell manufacturing facility in Greenville, North Carolina, with an annual production capacity of 3.0 GW, remains on schedule to begin production in the second quarter of 2027.

The 515,460-square-foot facility is a key part of Inox Solar Americas' strategy to build a more vertically integrated U.S. solar manufacturing platform. Once operational, domestic advanced PV cell production will complement the company's existing U.S. PV module manufacturing capabilities, providing customers with greater access to U.S.-manufactured solar technology and a more transparent, resilient, and reliable domestic supply chain.

Domestic Manufacturing & Regulatory Compliance

Inox Solar Americas' vertically integrated U.S. manufacturing strategy is designed to provide customers with greater access to domestically manufactured PV cells and PV modules while increasing domestic content across the company's product portfolio. The addition of U.S. PV cell manufacturing will further support customers addressing evolving U.S. domestic-content requirements, Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) and Prohibited Foreign Entity (PFE) considerations, applicable trade requirements, and federal energy-policy provisions. The company's approach emphasizes qualified sourcing, documented manufacturing processes, and compliance readiness to help customers manage increasingly complex procurement and project requirements.

Supply-Chain Security, Transparency & Traceability

Integrating U.S. PV cell and PV module manufacturing will provide greater visibility and control across critical stages of the solar supply chain. Inox Solar Americas is strengthening supplier qualification, component-origin documentation, material traceability, production records, and supply-chain due diligence to support customers seeking greater transparency regarding where and how their products are manufactured. Increased domestic production is also designed to reduce dependence on imported PV cells, mitigate exposure to global supply disruptions and trade-related risks, and provide more reliable product availability for U.S. project pipelines.

Advanced Technology, Quality & Performance

The Greenville manufacturing platform will integrate advanced Galaxion™ monocrystalline PV cell technologies with Inox Solar Americas' U.S.-manufactured Gamma Series™ monofacial and Vega Series™ bifacial PV modules. Advanced automation, precision cell processing, integrated inspection and testing, process controls, documented quality procedures, and production traceability are designed to provide greater manufacturing control from PV cell production through finished-module assembly. This integrated approach will support consistent product quality, high efficiency and energy yield, durability, and dependable performance across demanding U.S. solar applications.

Bankability, Supply Reliability & Customer Confidence

Expanding from U.S. PV module manufacturing into domestic PV cell production further strengthens Inox Solar Americas' manufacturing capabilities and ability to support large-scale, multiyear customer requirements. The company is building greater manufacturing scale, supply continuity, domestic-content capability, traceability, compliance readiness, and product support. Together with product performance, quality systems, warranty support, and a commitment to the U.S. market, these capabilities are designed to strengthen customer, developer, investor, and lender confidence in Inox Solar Americas and the projects its products support.

"Our continued progress on U.S. PV cell manufacturing represents an important step in building a more integrated and resilient domestic solar supply chain," said Ashok Nair, President & CEO of Inox Solar Americas. "By bringing advanced cell technology, high-performance module manufacturing, and rigorous quality control together within our U.S. manufacturing platform, we are strengthening our ability to support customers with reliable supply and the bankability required for their project pipelines."

INOX SOLAR AMERICAS

Inox Solar Americas, founded in 2026 in the United States, is a leading solar technology and manufacturing company specializing in advanced monocrystalline PV cells and high-performance Gamma Series™ monofacial and Vega Series™ bifacial PV modules. Inox Solar Americas' photovoltaic solutions are engineered to meet the needs of residential, commercial, industrial, community solar, and utility-scale applications, delivering exceptional efficiency, reliability, and long-term value.

Inox Solar Americas acquired Boviet Solar's U.S. PV manufacturing assets in Greenville, North Carolina, USA, including 3.0 GW of annual PV module manufacturing capacity and 3.0 GW of planned annual PV cell manufacturing capacity, expected to come online in 2027. Through localized manufacturing, resilient supply chains, operational excellence, and efficient logistics, Inox Solar Americas is helping strengthen the U.S. solar supply chain and meet growing domestic demand.

Inox Solar Americas is part of the broader renewable energy platform of Inox Clean Energy and the INOXGFL Group, headquartered in India. Backed by the group's financial strength, business stability, manufacturing capabilities, technological innovation, and industry expertise, Inox Solar Americas is committed to delivering high-quality, reliable, and sustainable solar solutions to customers across the U.S. solar energy market.

For more information, visit: inoxsolar.us, inoxclean.com and inoxgfl.com.
