text:
Heriot-Watt University helps launch £1.4m network to turn UK clean energy research into commercial success

Heriot-Watt University is helping drive a new £1.4 million UK-wide initiative designed to support researchers in transforming cutting-edge clean energy technologies into commercial products and spin-out companies.

The Electrochemical Entrepreneurship Network Plus (EENet+), led by the University of Surrey and funded by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC) through the National Materials Innovation Programme, aims to bridge the gap between promising laboratory research and real-world commercial deployment.

Bringing together universities, industry experts, entrepreneurs and investors from across the UK, the network will support innovation in electrochemical and energy materials technologies, including fuel cells, energy storage systems and technologies that can convert captured carbon dioxide into valuable products.

Heriot-Watt is one of the network's partner institutions, represented by Professor Bing Xu from the University’s Edinburgh Business School. Unlike a traditional research grant, EENet+ is designed to build a national innovation community, supporting researchers through networking opportunities, commercialisation training, funding calls and connections with industry and investors.

Led by the University of Surrey, this network project is being worked on by Imperial College London, Loughborough University, University of Glasgow, University of Liverpool, University of Oxford and Heriot-Watt University.

A £460,000 flexible funding pot managed through the network will support proof-of-concept projects, mobility placements and community-led initiatives across the UK, with the first funding call expected to open in early 2027. Researchers based in Scotland will be eligible to apply.

Professor Bing Xu, Director of the Centre for Sustainable Finance at the University's Edinburgh Business School, said: "The UK has world-leading research in electrochemical technologies and energy materials, but too often there remains a gap between a promising idea and a solution that can make a real-world impact.

"This network is about helping researchers translate their research into practical technologies, supporting them as they move towards commercialisation. That is where we can create real impact.

"If we can help turn a great idea into a new technology, a spin-out company or a product that contributes to the net-zero transition, that is exactly what this initiative is designed to achieve."

Professor Angus Laing, Executive Dean of Edinburgh Business School, said: “At Edinburgh Business School, we are committed to supporting research that promotes responsible business and creates a more sustainable future. EENet+ reflects these ambitions, bringing researchers, industry, and investors together to turn promising ideas into practical solutions. Building on our expertise in sustainable finance, this network offers an exciting opportunity to support innovation, drive sustainable economic growth and make a meaningful difference to societies around the world.”

The network will also provide entrepreneurship and commercialisation training for early-career researchers, helping them develop the skills and connections needed to bring innovative technologies to market.

EENet+ brings together expertise from universities across the UK, creating opportunities for researchers to collaborate, access specialist facilities and engage with investors and industrial partners who can help accelerate commercial development.

By 2030, the network aims to strengthen the UK's pipeline of clean energy technologies and increase the number of electrochemical innovations progressing towards commercial deployment, supporting economic growth and the country's net-zero ambitions.

How researchers can get involved

Researchers based in Scotland who are developing electrochemical or energy materials technologies are encouraged to engage with EENet+ and monitor upcoming funding opportunities, training programmes and networking events.

Further information on the first funding call will be shared through the network in 2027.

FILE PHOTO: The logo of Tesla is seen on a Tesla car in Brussels, Belgium April 24, 2025. REUTERS/Yves Herman/File Photo

By Amir Orusov

Nov 2 (Reuters) - Registrations of new Tesla cars rose across several Northern European markets in October, as the US electric vehicle maker extended its regional sales recovery despite growing competition from Chinese automakers.

Tesla registrations soared 248% in Sweden, 131% in Norway and 34% in Denmark, data from Mobility Sweden, Norway's OFV and Denmark's bilstatistik.dk showed.

The rebound has been aided by easier year-ago comparisons, higher fuel prices, government incentives and continued growth in EV demand.

Performance, however, varied across the region. Tesla saw strong gains in Norway and Sweden, but trailed several Chinese rivals in Denmark, which highlights the increasingly fragmented competitive landscape in Europe.

In Norway, Tesla recorded its best October on record and was the country's top-selling car brand with a 9.8% market share, according to OFV. Chinese brands continued to expand their footprint, accounting for 22.5% of new passenger car registrations, their highest monthly share on record.

"Especially in Norway people are generally more affluent than elsewhere in Europe, people are less seeking the lower offerings of Chinese brands than in other European countries," Rico Luman, senior economist at ING Research, said.

By contrast, Tesla's market share in Denmark was only 0.73%, behind BYD, Leapmotor, Xpeng and SAIC-owned MG, which captured between 1.6% and 5.5% of the market each.

"Northern Europe is quite open to the new players as long as they are efficient EVs. That's what allowed Tesla to get to a leading position and it’s what is allowing the Chinese to gain ground fast," industry analyst Felipe Munoz, who runs the Car Industry Analysis platform, told Reuters.

Tesla remains one of Europe's strongest EV brands, though its reliance on the Model 3 and Model Y has left it facing growing competition from rivals with broader line-ups.

The automaker said in October it had ended the third quarter with its largest passenger vehicle order backlog in four years.

(Reporting by Amir Orusov in Gdansk, additional reporting by Anastasiia Kozlova; editing by Milla Nissi-Prussak)

name: Clean Energy
title: Will a Proposed Law Let Trump Handcuff His Successors to Fossil Fuels?
authors: Kainoa Lowman, Bruno V. Manno, Jon Marcus, Michael T. Nietzel
description:
If that happens, they argue, BAAJA would be a climate disaster no matter how much it boosts clean energy.
The environmentalists’ fear: Codifying the second Trump administration’s record of fossil fuel permit approvals as a standard that future administrations must follow.
First, the argument that the bill compels future administrations to match Trump’s frenzied approval of fossil fuel permits is misguided.
“The constraint is not on the regulatory front.” Coal provides the starkest example of the limits of Trump’s ability to spur fossil fuel development.
On the other side of the ledger, BAAJA would unleash clean energy projects and electrical transmission infrastructure, which are generally much more permit-constrained than fossil fuel projects.
text:
After Election Day, when Congress returns for its post-election session, the Senate will consider a sweeping bipartisan bill to ease regulatory constraints on energy projects. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, supercharges clean-energy development by cutting red tape and curbing utilities’ ability to block competition, but it would also make it easier to build fossil fuel infrastructure and weaken longstanding environmental protections. That trade-off has divided Democrats and the environmental community. Some see the bill as a rare opportunity to accelerate the clean energy transition; others fear it would give President Donald Trump license to harm the environment in the remaining two years of his term.

The controversy largely centers on one section, “Project Certainty,” which limits presidential administrations from using the federal permitting process to fight energy sources they dislike. Democratic Senate negotiators Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich backed the provisions, wanting to guard against future GOP attempts to sabotage clean energy projects, as the Trump administration has done with offshore wind. But a number of environmental groups warn that this part of the bill could backfire by locking in an unsustainable rate of fossil fuel development in perpetuity. If that happens, they argue, BAAJA would be a climate disaster no matter how much it boosts clean energy.

BAAJA could indeed make it harder for future administrations to reverse environmentally damaging projects. But sweeping claims that the bill could lock in “fossil fuel dominance” rest on dubious interpretations of the legislative text and flawed assumptions about how energy companies operate. Market conditions constrain oil, gas, and coal production far more than federal permits. Clean energy developers, by contrast, enjoy enormous demand for their power but face maddening permitting delays and grid bottlenecks that prevent them from meeting it. That makes it difficult to argue that passing BAAJA—which Congress could do during the lame-duck session beginning November 9—would be worse for the climate than rejecting it.

The Nightmare Scenario

BAAJA’s “Project Certainty” section contains two key provisions. The first bars federal agencies from rescinding, terminating, or altering permits granted to energy projects—with limited exceptions, such as when a court finds a permit was issued illegally. Some critics fear this could allow Trump to crank out “forever permits” for dirty energy that a Democratic administration couldn’t undo. “There’s an incentive for developers to come up with any idea they can, and get it rubber-stamped before Trump leaves office,” says Jeremy Symons, the president of the Center for Energy and Environmental Analysis think tank.

This provision also prohibits federal agencies from taking any action that interferes with the “operation at full capacity” of permitted projects, which worries some environmentalists. A group of former Environmental Protection Agency lawyers warns that this language could prevent agencies from issuing broadly applicable regulations under laws like the Clean Air Act, if they impose costs on existing power plants.

The second provision allows companies to sue the federal government if they can prove it discriminated against a certain type of energy project in the permitting process. Such discrimination might take the form of a “substantial increase” in permitting delays for a project type compared to the previous five years. The environmentalists’ fear: Codifying the second Trump administration’s record of fossil fuel permit approvals as a standard that future administrations must follow. According to the environmental litigation group Earthjustice, fossil fuel developers “may be more able to show discriminatory treatment from a baseline of rapid permitting during the Trump administration” than clean energy developers, “who will be operating from a baseline of slow permitting.”

These interpretations of the bill paint a scary picture. They suggest Trump could dictate the trajectory of fossil fuel development forever by locking in a flood of projects now, and then forcing future administrations to maintain his pace. Symons, a veteran of energy legislation fights on Capitol Hill, called BAAJA’s project certainty provisions “the single most dangerous legislative provisions that I have ever seen this close to a finish line in Congress.”

What Trump Can—And Can’t—Actually Do Under BAAJA

BAAJA likely would allow Trump to lock in certain projects that a future Democratic administration might be inclined to reverse—for example, mining roads through national parks, or drilling leases in the Alaskan Arctic. By the same token, Trump would have to end his blockade of offshore wind projects that could power millions of homes. Still, for advocates of nature conservation and historical preservation, this may be an intolerable tradeoff, as John Podesta, the climate czar in Joe Biden’s White House, has argued.

And while legal experts can only guess how courts would interpret BAAJA’s prohibition on federal actions that interfere with the “operation at full capacity” of permitted projects, even supporters of the bill told me they hope Congress clarifies this language to ensure it does not deter agencies from issuing health, safety, or environmental regulations. “This is a provision that Democrats sought, so if there is a technical fix to better correspond with their intent, ideally [Senate negotiators] would take advantage of the intervening period before the floor vote to fix it,” says Marc Levitt, a former EPA official and now director of environmental regulatory reform at the Breakthrough Institute, an “Abundance”-aligned, pro-technology environmental group.

On a macro level, however, BAAJA would be unlikely to lock in a Trumpian vision of unbridled fossil fuel development, for two reasons.

First, the argument that the bill compels future administrations to match Trump’s frenzied approval of fossil fuel permits is misguided. While agencies could face lawsuits for a “substantial increase” in permitting delays, delays count as such only if they exceed years-long timelines laid out in the bill, preserving flexibility for agencies to take their time evaluating permit applications. Crucially, litigants must also prove government intent to discriminate against their project type, a high bar. In short, this provision is much less restrictive than critics have made it out to be. “If the Trump administration gets a bunch of fossil fuel projects permitted really quickly, that average time has no bearing on what the next administration does,” says Aidan Mackenzie, an infrastructure fellow at the Institute for Progress think tank.

A more fundamental problem with the “lock in” argument is that federal permits alone don’t set the trajectory of fossil fuel development. Energy market conditions matter far more.

Take oil drilling. Exploration and production companies are currently sitting on over 10,000 unused Bureau of Land Management drilling permits, a fairly typical surplus. In other words, permitting is not the constraint on drilling activity. Rather, the constraint is the capital discipline of the companies themselves, who face shareholder pressure to be cautious about making the expensive investments required to expand production. Indeed, even as the Iran war has sent global oil prices soaring, U.S. producers have barely expanded production. Reaping the benefits of scarcity, it seems, beats heeding Trump’s exhortations to drill, baby, drill. “These are mature manufacturing businesses,” says Amy McCullagh, an independent analyst and author of the Measured Depth Substack. “They attract the capital they do by generating strong free cash flow and returning those profits to investors via buybacks and dividends.”

Moreover, most American drilling activity happens on state and private lands, while BAAJA’s permitting certainty provisions cover only federal permits. Federal permitting is thus “not a lever that would likely change [drilling] activity in the U.S. at a macro level,” McCullagh said.

Market conditions also determine the development of natural gas pipelines. Developers only build them after securing long-term capacity commitments from shippers (often producers or utilities). When demand is strong, BAAJA could help projects with secured commitments build faster—mainly through a provision that would limit states’ ability to block interstate pipelines under the Clean Water Act. But even with new project-certainty powers, the Trump administration couldn’t accelerate development by permitting a barrage of speculative projects, as some BAAJA critics charge. Developers “are not going to just build these pipes out of nowhere,” says Dulles Wang, a director of Americas gas research at consultancy Wood Mackenzie. “Somebody has to hold the bag.”

The same story applies to liquefied natural gas (LNG) export terminals. These facilities cost billions to build, and lenders want to see guaranteed revenue in the form of long-term purchase agreements with buyers. But buyers are currently hesitant to commit amid concerns about a looming global supply glut, and several LNG terminals that secured permits have stalled out in the pre-construction phase. “We’re waiting on commercial momentum to pick up to support the build-out of these projects,” Wang said. “The constraint is not on the regulatory front.”

Coal provides the starkest example of the limits of Trump’s ability to spur fossil fuel development. The administration has done what it can to boost coal production: Expediting permitting, making millions of acres of federal lands available for mining leases, and handing out over $100 million to subsidize proposed coal plants in West Virginia and Alaska. But amid weak demand for expensive coal power, these efforts have overwhelmingly flopped. After lease sales on federal lands in Montana and Utah attracted only lowball offers, BLM had to reject them and postpone other planned sales. And analysts doubt that the West Virginia and Alaska plants will ever be built, despite the subsidies Trump lavished on them, given their astronomical costs and a lack of interest from buyers.

The Big Picture on Emissions

While nobody can be 100 percent certain of the BAAJA’s effects, two preliminary modeling efforts released last week (one from a solar industry trade group) find that the bill would lower net emissions compared to a baseline scenario where it doesn’t pass. This makes sense given the bill’s likely impact on specific project types. As discussed previously, BAAJA probably wouldn’t significantly affect oil production, LNG exports, or coal power plants. It would likely speed the gas pipeline build-out—particularly in the Northeast, where states have blocked pipelines using a permitting authority that BAAJA restricts—although this would not be the clear-cut climate harm that some make it out to be. More pipeline capacity into the Northeast could deliver a short-term emissions reduction by displacing dirtier, higher-cost shipped gas and oil. Nevertheless, it would likely drive up emissions over the long run by enabling greater gas consumption and weakening the investment case for renewables.

On the other side of the ledger, BAAJA would unleash clean energy projects and electrical transmission infrastructure, which are generally much more permit-constrained than fossil fuel projects. It could also curb a major driver of skyrocketing gas use—private, on-site power plants for data centers—by making it easier for them to connect to the electrical grid. The bill would make data centers pay more than their fair share for grid upgrades and energy costs, but analysts expect operators would prefer this arrangement to building more expensive, less reliable on-site plants, as long as they can connect quickly. “Broadly speaking, [data center operators] would prefer to have a grid connection,” says Dan O’Bierne, a researcher at Global Energy Monitor, noting that shortages of fuel-efficient turbines and the need for backup capacity raise the costs of on-site gas generation.

To be sure, BAAJA is no substitute for a comprehensive climate policy. But the bill’s supporters argue that its reforms are a necessary precondition for any such policy to be effective, whether that be new clean energy subsidies, a carbon tax, or a national clean electricity standard. “If you haven’t done permitting first, that future bill is not going to work well because it’s going to be so hard to build the clean stuff,” says Xan Fishman, executive vice president of the Bipartisan Policy Center’s energy program.

In other words, environmentalists might be worried about the wrong “lock-in” scenario. If Congress muffs a generational opportunity to pass durable, bipartisan permitting reform, it could lock in a regulatory status quo far more favorable to fossil fuels than renewables.

text:
Every year, Kotzebue, a small city in northwest Alaska, has a three-month window to receive all the diesel fuel it will use throughout the following year. It sits on a gravel spit that juts into Kotzebue Sound just north of the Arctic Circle, and is accessible only by air and sea. Ice keeps freight barges from reaching it for most of the year.

The community relies on diesel for 75 percent of its power, and residents put about 20 percent of their income toward buying it. That’s more than three times the average energy burden for low-income households nationwide.

“We’re pretty much at the mercy of world markets,” Chad Nordlum, who is the energy project manager for the Native Village of Kotzebue, told Grist. “Right now, with the Iran war going on, the diesel prices are very high and we’re locked in to much higher prices than we’ve had in the past. There’s really nothing the community can do about diesel prices, but what we can do is produce our own energy.”

That’s why Nordlum was so excited about a $20 million grant from the Environmental Protection Agency to support a wind energy project. The funding, announced in 2024, was part of a larger $150 million allocation for tribal infrastructure in Alaska. Nordlum says it would have lowered the community’s reliance on diesel to about 40 percent to 50 percent and given the tribe more control over energy and economic decisions.

But the Trump administration canceled the grant in May 2025. More than a year later, the project remains paused.

That cut was among hundreds of millions of dollars the Department of Government Efficiency pulled from Indian Country, and part of a broader pattern of funding rollbacks and underinvestment in Indigenous communities. Two new reports from the Brookings Institution show that the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act killed many of the funding streams established by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, while DOGE eliminated another $468 million, about half of which was allocated for environmental and natural resources. Another 11 percent targeted agriculture. Those projects include climate resiliency plans, renewable energy projects, and jobs programs.

According to Brookings, despite historic investments flowing into Indian Country after the pandemic, a massive underinvestment in Indigenous communities continues. Not only is that a violation of the federal government’s trust and treaty obligations to tribes, it is hindering Indigenous efforts to protect the environment and address climate change. The report authors are calling for policy changes that would ensure tribes receive funding, regardless of political winds.

Rob Maxim, who is Mashpee Wampanoag and a fellow at Brookings Metro, said climate and environmental funding is especially crucial for Indigenous communities because they are often the most severely impacted by climate change, especially after years of underinvestment.

“The actions that the Trump administration is taking are particularly significant, but it’s not totally out of trend with previous administrations,” he said. “And what we wanted to show was that actually this underinvestment is kind of the default for the U.S. rather than a blip.”

The true aberration was the unprecedented levels of funding after the pandemic. That funding, which came under the Biden administration, included over $700 million in climate, energy, and infrastructure funding for tribes. It covered projects like development of climate action plans, food systems analysis, and more. For example, the Hopi Tribe was to receive a $25 million grant to install solar panels for 600 homes. That grant, and the entire $7 billion Solar for All program, were cut.

Maxim says that funding for Indigenous communities is a federal obligation based on treaties and other agreements with tribes and should be standard and irrevocable. “The funding that was flowing to Indian Country was not being done on the basis of race or DEI, and it was absolutely not illegal,” he said. “It was aimed at the promotion of tribal sovereignty and the well-being of tribal citizens and tribal communities, and so that is, you know, an obligation that the U.S. government maintains.”

The White House and the EPA did respond to requests for comment.

Glencora Haskins, a senior research associate and applied research manager at Brookings Metro, said that the administration had targeted funding to tribes, with “tribal” being the most frequently flagged term. “I think that there was a very surface-level view of what a lot of these programs were doing, rather than any deep interrogation of the types of systemic infrastructure deficits that programs were trying to fix,” Haskins said.

In Native communities throughout Alaska, and around the country, energy and infrastructure needs are especially acute because of increasingly frequent and destructive storms, wildfires, and other climate-driven disasters.

Haskins and Maxim recommend that Congress pass legislation that bars the cancellation of grants and contracts for tribes, and stipulates that all funding for Indigenous nations and communities is in service of trust and treaty obligations even if it is from a program with a different stated purpose. They also call for a statutory requirement that money should flow directly to tribes rather than having them seek reimbursement from the U.S. Treasury.

In Kotzebue, Chad Nordlum hopes the political tide will turn enough to get the funding for the wind project moving. In the meantime, he is working on a smaller solar project that he hopes will help alleviate the community’s energy challenges.

“Our main goals are energy security and economic development for the tribe, which is ultimately being able to invest in our own community, help make the lives of people here a little more sustainable,” Nordlum said. “We want our community to continue on into the future. We have to get a handle on our energy prices and availability.”

title: Boise plans to tap its geothermal network to heat 300 affordable homes - Canary Media
description:
The cash fills a funding gap to extend the geothermal system to a planned affordable housing development with more than 300 units.
Already, the city’s geothermal network cuts thousands of tons of carbon emissions every year, the equivalent of taking more than 2,000 gas-powered cars off the road.
The tiny rural town of Enfield, North Carolina, secured seed funding earlier this year for a geothermal network to lower residents’ energy costs.
Because renewable geothermal energy itself is free, the network could save residents up to 80% on utility bills, according to the city.
​“Thanks to Micron’s investment, we are one step closer to bringing clean geothermal heat to hundreds of affordable homes in Boise.”
text:
Boise already knows how to tap the carbon-free heat beneath our feet. The city operates the country’s largest geothermal heating system, which pipes naturally warmed, 177-degree-Fahrenheit water from underground to about 100 buildings — including the Idaho State Capitol.

Last week, semiconductor multinational Micron Technology gave Boise $2.5 million to build on that expertise. The cash fills a funding gap to extend the geothermal system to a planned affordable housing development with more than 300 units. In total, the project price tag is about $140 million, according to the city.

“Boise has been Micron’s headquarters for 48 years, and investing in this community means investing in the people who call it home,” April Arnzen, executive vice president and chief people officer at Micron and president of its philanthropic arm, the Micron Foundation, said in a statement.

In February, the Bloomberg Philanthropies Mayors Challenge awarded Boise $1 million to upgrade its geothermal system for affordable housing, as well as to explore a new use for the network: Some early-stage technologies exist that could potentially harness the hot water from Boise’s system to provide cooling, according to Maria Ortega, the city’s communications senior manager.

The clean-heat expansion will help Boise get closer to its goal of becoming carbon-neutral by 2050. Already, the city’s geothermal network cuts thousands of tons of carbon emissions every year, the equivalent of taking more than 2,000 gas-powered cars off the road.

Geothermal networks like Boise’s are gaining traction across the country, with 33 scattered projects planned, in construction, or completed, according to the nonprofit Building Decarbonization Coalition. These systems, which rely on bore holes, can form a part of thermal energy networks that move heat among buildings and serve as a climate-compatible business model for gas utilities.

Denver is planning to harvest heat from the earth and sewage to keep downtown buildings comfy. The tiny rural town of Enfield, North Carolina, secured seed funding earlier this year for a geothermal network to lower residents’ energy costs. And in Framingham, Massachusetts, about 140 customers are the first in the U.S. to be heated and cooled with a geothermal network owned by a gas and electric utility, Eversource Energy. Last December, that project got an $8.6 million federal grant to double in size.

Back in Boise, the Housing Land Trust Program has partnered with J. Fisher Cos. to develop the affordable multifamily housing project in the Lusk District. It’s expected to break ground in spring 2027 and be ready for residents in 2028. Because renewable geothermal energy itself is free, the network could save residents up to 80% on utility bills, according to the city.

“Building more homes that Boiseans can afford takes partners who are willing to roll up their sleeves and invest in solutions,” Mayor Lauren McLean said. ​“Thanks to Micron’s investment, we are one step closer to bringing clean geothermal heat to hundreds of affordable homes in Boise.”

text:
President Donald Trump's administration has gutted US climate policy. Yet even as wildfires, record heat waves and flooding hit communities across the country, Democrats are keeping quiet about global warming on the midterm campaign trail.

Instead, candidates are packaging climate policy as an affordability issue, stressing how Americans are struggling to afford gas, groceries and to insure their homes against climate-fueled weather extremes.

Take Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico in Texas, who represents the party's best chance at winning the race in the Republican stronghold in nearly 40 years. Though he makes some mention of climate change on his campaign's "energy and environment" page, that is not his focus.

His pledges center around lowering energy costs, providing emergency relief for spiking utility bills, making data centers pay for their own grid upgrades and growing energy sector jobs.

This aligns with analysis from nonprofit news organization Inside Climate News showing that the Democrats have dramatically reduced mentions of climate change in their press releases and campaign messaging.

"We've entered an interesting space where climate policy doesn't need to be called climate policy to be climate policy," Max Frankel, executive director of the SEEC Institute, a nonprofit that helps guide climate policy in Congress, told DW.

What would a Democratic win mean for climate policy?

Most forecasts project Democrats winning the House and a narrow majority in the Senate in the November 3 election. But without control of the White House, passing any legislation will be difficult and almost any climate policy will have to be a bipartisan endeavor, say analysts.

Given that and the Democrats' messaging-shift to affordability over climate, few experts expect a fully resurrected Inflation Reduction Act. Introduced under the Democrats to create incentives for building clean energy projects, the legislation was largely decimated by President Trump's major tax law.

But Democrats may try to bring back some climate-friendly IRA provisions, particularly measures aimed at lowering household energy costs, analysts told DW. Those include incentives for home energy-efficiency upgrades and appliances like heat pumps to replace oil and gas heaters that typically help bring down household energy bills.

Politicians could also expand an IRA manufacturing tax credit for solar, batteries, and critical minerals that largely survived. One bipartisan bill proposes extending it to include nuclear fusion components.

"It's not going to be anything at the scale of the IRA," Adrian Deveny, founder of Climate Vision, a policy firm dedicated to decarbonization, told DW. "It's like singles and doubles as opposed to a home run, which is still worth doing."

A first bipartisan test over building infrastructure

In a rare area of agreement between the parties, some Democrats and Republicans are already backing a reform bill they're hoping to pass before a new Congress is sworn in January.

If enacted, the bill could make it significantly easier to build major infrastructure projects in the US, including long-distance transmission lines that carry electricity between regions but that currently take years to build because of complex permitting rules.

"The biggest beneficiary of building more transmission will be wind and solar power, because the best and cheapest way to generate wind and solar energy tends to be far away from cities," said David Spence, a political scientist at the University of Texas who researches the politics of energy regulation. "And so, they need transmission to get their product to market."

But environmental groups say the bill could also speed up the approval of fossil fuel projects.

If Democrats win big in the midterms there might be some "peeling off their support for that bill because they think they can do better in the next Congress," said Spence.

Looking to the 2028 presidential elections

Major new federal climate legislation is a long shot before the 2028 presidential election. And afterwards it would likely require Democrats winning the White House, the Senate and the House. While no 2028 platforms have been released yet, policy experts expect a few ideas to feature prominently.

One is data centers. Opposition to the energy-guzzling infrastructure being built en masse to power the AI boom is mounting across the country. Half of Americans are now against data centers being built close to their homes, according to a pollfrom news outlet Politico.

"I'm sure every candidate is going to have a platform with a focus on data center constraints on some level, as a way to address affordability," Deveny, who led negotiations on the IRA, said. "And that's the entry point for climate policy."

There are several ideas currently circulating — including a proposal by Democrats Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to pause data center construction — as well as ending tax breaks for data centers and imposing new taxes on their electricity use.

Democrats may also seek to restore the IRA's clean energy tax incentives. This year, more than 150 legislators co-sponsored the so-called Energy Bills Relief Act designed to reinstate IRA clean energy tax incentives, reform how transmission permits are granted, and make data centers pay for the grid upgrades they need. The bill is unlikely to pass anytime soon but offers a window into what Democrats might support.

"By far, the biggest consensus — to the extent there's anything remotely resembling a consensus — is restoring a lot of the clean energy tax incentives from the IRA," Deveny said. "Not everybody supports that but it is a highly supported idea amongst most congressional Democrats."

Support for other proposals include a new federal program to help insurers cover climate-driven disasters and bring down hefty premiums, as well as so-called climate superfunds. This would require fossil fuel companies to contribute to the costs of damage caused by extreme weather and adapting to the risks of climate change.

Vermont and New York both passed legislation to create funds, although a federal judge blocked New York's.

The 2028 presidential race is expected to begin a few weeks after the midterms end, bringing a fresh round of policy ideas and debates. A new president typically gets to drive the legislative agenda in the beginning of their term if their party also wins Congress.

"As long as the consensus is that clean energy is the cheaper source of energy, and it's going to provide stability over the long term for high energy costs — there's a million ways you can propose solutions through that lens," Deveny said.

text:
China has seen a significant achievement in its legislative activity over the past 15 years, with a focus on strengthening laws in key, emerging, and international areas, thereby enriching the nation's legal framework, an official said on Friday.

Huang Huaihua, the spokesperson for the Legislative Affairs Commission of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, China's top legislative body, shared at a news conference that the number of active laws in China has grown from 236 in March 2011 — when the socialist legal system with Chinese characteristics was formally established — to 303 today.

Since 2021, Huang specified, the 14th NPC and its standing committee have developed an Ecological and Environmental Code, enacted 23 new laws, and amended 45 existing ones.

He highlighted that legislation has been consistently enhanced in critical, emerging, and international fields, fostering comprehensive legal development in areas such as the market economy, cultural growth, social welfare, environmental protection, national security, international relations, and anti-corruption efforts.

"For instance, we have bolstered foreign-related legal frameworks by formulating or revising laws concerning foreign relations, state immunity, foreign trade, maritime commerce, arbitration, and more," he said, revealing that draft laws targeting cross-border corruption and Antarctic activities and environmental protection are set for further review by lawmakers next week.

"These legislative items have played a big role in safeguarding national sovereignty, security, and developmental interests while promoting high-level opening-up," Huang added.

Moreover, he noted that the 14th NPC and its standing committee have crafted or revised laws centered on ecological conservation of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, national parks, marine environmental protection, and other sectors, striving to enhance China's ecology and environment through legislation.

"All these legislative actions in the fields have enriched our country's legal frameworks and optimized the socialist legal system with Chinese characteristics," Huang added.

To ensure high-quality legislation and embody the concept of whole-process people's democracy, Huang emphasized that the 14th NPC and its standing committee have established outreach offices across the country to widely gather public legislative opinions, actively introduce legislative initiatives, and effectively address public concerns through lawmaking or amendments.

Additionally, in the past decade or so, the authority, principles, and spirit of the Constitution, China's fundamental law, have been further upheld, with over 8,800 normative documents — such as administrative rules and judicial interpretations — reviewed for constitutional consistency since 2021, he said.

Apart from the draft laws on Antarctic activities and cross-border anti-corruption, the 14th NPC Standing Committee will review draft laws on public interest litigation by procuratorates, State-owned assets and finance, and a proposed revision to the Water Law during its upcoming session from Monday to Friday.

Other draft items, including amendments to the Criminal Procedure Law and revisions to the Renewable Energy Law and the Tax Collection Administration Law, are also slated for discussion at the session.

[Financial News] NH Investment & Securities cut its target price for Kia Corporation by 21.1%, from 190,000 won to 150,000 won.

The decision reflects its view that profitability improvements are being constrained despite growth in automobile sales, due to rising raw material prices, conflict in the Middle East, and the burden of incentives and price cuts as electric vehicle (EV) sales expand. It maintained its Buy recommendation but lowered both its earnings estimates and valuation.

Haneul, an analyst at NH Investment & Securities, said on the 2nd, “With global EV price competition continuing, a cautious approach to profitability recovery is needed until reduced incentives and the results of cost-cutting efforts become visible.”

Kia Corporation’s consolidated third-quarter revenue rose 10.1% year over year to 31.597 trillion won, but operating profit came in at 1.8183 trillion won, below the market consensus of 2.357 trillion won.

The operating margin was just 5.8%. The burden from rising raw material prices was estimated at 368 billion won, while the impact of the prolonged conflict in the Middle East was estimated at 209 billion won. Higher incentives and price-cut burdens associated with expanding EV sales also amounted to 727 billion won.

NH Investment & Securities cut its 2027 operating profit forecast by 17.3%, from 10.807 trillion won to 8.938 trillion won. It also lowered its forecast for this year by 12.2%, from 9.483 trillion won to 8.33 trillion won. The target price-to-earnings ratio (PER) used to calculate the target price was also reduced, from 8.4 times to 8.1 times.

Weaker expectations for new businesses were also reflected in the lower target price. Analyst Ha said this “reflects a reduced valuation premium due to the prolonged absence of momentum from new businesses.”

The analysis said expectations for Kia Corporation’s level of participation and role in new businesses had declined relative to those for Hyundai Motor Company, which is leading Hyundai Motor Group’s strategy for new businesses such as robotics.

Kia Corporation’s electrification strategy, however, remains in place. It plans to expand sales of hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) in the United States and focus on EVs in Europe, while cutting the cost of key components by about 10% annually for three years to improve EV profitability.

Analyst Ha said the goal was to “normalize EV profitability by securing cost competitiveness within the next two to three years.”

NH Investment & Securities left open the possibility of a recovery in profitability next year, supported by increased hybrid sales in the United States and easing external pressures. However, it maintained a cautious view until cost cuts and reduced incentives are reflected in actual results.

text:
Input

[Financial News] Despite slowing demand in the global auto market, Kia Corporation is increasing both sales and market share, expanding its growth base. Sales of electric vehicles (EVs) and hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) have risen sharply in particular, accelerating the company’s shift toward eco-friendly vehicles. While higher raw material prices and sales incentives continue to weigh on it in the short term, the company plans to pursue a recovery in profitability starting next year by cutting EV costs and expanding its hybrid lineup.

According to a corporate analysis report on Kia Corporation released by Hana Securities on the 2nd, the company’s global wholesale sales in the third quarter of this year rose 7.9% year over year to 847,000 vehicles. Sales in global markets also increased 6.9% to 829,000 vehicles. Its share of the global market climbed from 3.5% to 4.0%, an all-time high. Excluding China, its market share reached 5.0%.

By region, Kia Corporation’s market share in the U.S. reached 5.8%, a quarterly record. Its share in South Korea also rose 4.6 percentage points to 36.8%, while it stood at 4.0% in Western Europe. In India, wholesale sales surged 38.5%, driven by increased sales of the Kia Seltos and Kia Sonet.

Growth in eco-friendly vehicles was also notable. Sales of these vehicles in the third quarter totaled 300,000, up 47.0% year over year. Hybrids accounted for 172,000, up 46.0%, while EVs totaled 123,000, up 75.4%. The 118% increase in U.S. hybrid sales and 163% rise in Western European EV sales also stand out.

Buoyed by higher sales, revenue in the third quarter rose 10.1% to 31.597 trillion won. Operating profit also increased 24.3% to 1.818 trillion won. However, amid higher raw material prices, the conflict in the Middle East and increased EV sales incentives, the operating margin fell 2.2 percentage points from the previous quarter to 5.8%.

Kia Corporation plans to maintain its strategy of expanding EV sales despite short-term pressure on profitability. The company believes it is important to secure market share early, as Europe’s auto market is rapidly shifting toward EVs.

To that end, the company plans to cut the costs of batteries, motors, thermal management and power electronics (PE) systems by around 10% annually over the next three years. Its plan is to bring EVs’ total cost of ownership competitiveness up to the level of internal combustion engine vehicles in 2027–2028, and to improve profitability by achieving economies of scale.

Hybrids are also a key pillar of earnings resilience. Expanding the hybrid lineup with models such as the Kia Telluride, Kia Sportage, Kia Seltos and Kia Sorento is expected to improve the sales mix and profitability.

Hana Securities said the pressure from the conflict in the Middle East and rising raw material prices could continue through year-end, but Kia Corporation’s profitability may return to normal next year as external headwinds ease, sales increase and hybrids make up a larger share.

text:

[Financial News] As the government prepares to unveil measures to strengthen the competitiveness of the EV industry this month, Vice Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyeong-il visited Namyang Research Institute, Hyundai Motor Company and Kia Corporation's R&D hub, on the 2nd to hear the industry's requests. Attention is focused on whether domestic production tax credits for EVs, excluded from the tax reform plan in August, will return to the discussion table.

According to the Ministry of Economy and Finance, Lee chaired a meeting with industry representatives on strengthening the competitiveness of the EV industry that day at Hyundai Motor Company and Kia Corporation's Technical Research Institute in Hwaseong City, Gyeonggi Province. Government attendees included the vice minister of the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy, the second vice minister of the Ministry of Climate, and the second vice minister of the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport.

“The next battleground for a rebound in the potential growth rate is EVs,” Lee said. He explained that businesses urgently need to change quickly and innovate technologically, as they must secure technological capabilities on par with those of leading global countries within the next two to three years to survive.

Business leaders called for support through production tax credits for EVs to survive intensifying global competition. In the 2026 Tax Reform Plan announced in August, the government decided to establish a domestic production tax credit that reduces taxes in proportion to domestic output. However, support is limited to six sectors: semiconductors, secondary batteries, solar power, wind power, key materials, and AI robotics components. The scheme excludes fully assembled EVs and supports only secondary batteries, a key component.

Industry demands have continued. The Korea Automobile & Mobility Association (KAMA) argued at a National Assembly forum on the 26th of last month that fully assembled EVs should also be eligible for support, citing the cost burden on domestic manufacturers competing with Chinese-made EVs. The government discussed possible supplementary measures at a recent economic issues meeting, but whether to add EVs remains under review.

Hyundai Motor Group is expanding its domestic production base for vehicle electrification. Hyundai Motor Company invested about 2 trillion won to build the Ulsan Electric Vehicle Dedicated Plant, with annual capacity of 200,000 vehicles. It is the first new plant built in Korea in 29 years, since the Hyundai Motor Asan Plant opened in 1996. The group also announced plans to invest 125.2 trillion won in Korea from this year through 2030.

“Regarding support through production tax credits for EVs, the government will actively participate in the National Assembly's discussions and engage in in-depth discussions,” Lee said. He added that, reflecting industry feedback, the government would announce competitiveness measures this month that include strengthening autonomous-driving technology and expanding R&D in core parts and technologies. eastcold@fnnews.com Reporter Kim Dong-chan

One quarter of the 176 wind turbines that will spin at the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind (CVOW) site have been installed, with the installation of the 45th turbine underway.

This is according to an update shared by Dominion Energy in its Q3 2026 results on 30 October, when the company also said CVOW’s levelized cost of energy (LCoE) dropped from USD 83/MWh (around EUR 74.10/MWh) reported in the prior update to USD 62/MWh (around EUR 55.40/MWh) because higher Renewable Energy Certificate (REC) revenues offset a flat gross generation cost of USD 100/MWh (around EUR 89.30/MWh).

The first of CVOW’s 176 Siemens Gamesa 14 MW wind turbines was installed in January 2026, and the project delivered first power to the grid in March 2026, with each completed turbine becoming operational as installation progresses.

The wind turbines are being installed by Charybdis, the first Jones Act-compliant wind turbine installation vessel (WTIV), commissioned by Dominion Energy and built at Seatrium’s AmFELS shipyard in Brownsville, Texas.

Earlier this year, Dominion revised the completion timeline for its 2.6 GW offshore wind project, according to which the installation of the 176th and final wind turbine is expected by the end of next year. The company had previously targeted full project completion in early 2027.

Dominion said the updated schedule reflected additional contingency for weather, vessel maintenance, loadout operations and extended jacking activities, rather than changes to the base turbine installation rate, which had been two days per turbine, excluding load-out and transit, weather, and maintenance.

According to Dominion’s update on 30 October, the installation rate has remained the same so far, and the company still expects the 176th turbine to be installed at the end of 2027.

The first two offshore substations are already commissioned, and the third and final substation is expected to be energised by the end of 2026.

Once fully commissioned, the 2.6 GW CVOW will become the biggest US offshore wind farm and, with an installed capacity of 2.6 GW, one of the biggest in the world today.

description:

The government expects to commission the 445-MW Bilasuvar solar power plant and the 25-megawatt Shams 1 solar power plant by the end of the year.
Meanwhile, several more renewable energy projects are expected to be completed next year, including the 315-MW Neftchala, 240-MW Shafag, 50-MW Shams, 50-MW Ufug, and 25-MW Western Ufug solar power plants.
The country’s Energy Minister, Parviz Shahbazov, said that renewable energy auctions are expected to commence in 2028 to spur further development.
Azerbaijan is accelerating the deployment of new renewable energy capacity and strengthening supporting infrastructure to ensure its energy system is both flexible and reliable.
text:
Azerbaijan, long known as a major oil and gas power, has ventured into renewable energy in recent years and is rapidly ramping up its capacity. As host of COP29, Azerbaijan’s government announced an ambitious climate target and encouraged other governments to do the same.

Renewable energy contributed 20 per cent of Azerbaijan’s total electricity production in the first nine months of the year, an increase from 13.4 per cent in 2025, marking a significant achievement in capacity growth. Azerbaijan produced 21.2 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity between January and September 2026, compared with 28.7 billion kilowatt-hours for the whole of 2025, according to official figures.

The government plans to increase the share of renewables in its total installed electricity generation capacity to 33.3 per cent by 2027. Azerbaijan has an estimated technical renewable energy potential of 135 GW onshore and 157 GW of offshore wind capacity in the Caspian Sea, providing substantial opportunities for solar and wind development. The government aims to develop 8 GW of renewable energy generation capacity by 2032, with 2 GW expected to be completed by 2027.

Some regions of the country are transitioning to green energy far more quickly than others, with the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic meeting 100 per cent of its electricity demand from renewable sources between 21st April and 2nd July, according to Azerbaijan’s Energy Minister Parviz Shahbazov.

ADVERTISEMENT

The growth of the country’s renewable energy capacity, mainly driven by the expansion of solar and wind projects, enabled Azerbaijan to avoid using an estimated 840 million cubic meters of natural gas during the first nine months of the year, thereby helping reduce the country’s carbon emissions from fossil fuels.

Azerbaijan is accelerating the development of solar and wind farms to meet its ambitious clean energy targets, with plans to commission 11 solar and wind power plants totalling 2 gigawatts of capacity. Three facilities, with a combined capacity of 570 MW, have already come online. The government expects to commission the 445-MW Bilasuvar solar power plant and the 25-megawatt Shams 1 solar power plant by the end of the year.

Work is already well underway on UAE-based Masdar’s 200-MW wind power project. Meanwhile, several more renewable energy projects are expected to be completed next year, including the 315-MW Neftchala, 240-MW Shafag, 50-MW Shams, 50-MW Ufug, and 25-MW Western Ufug solar power plants. The planned projects are expected to produce a combined 5 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity a year, which could reduce gas use by more than 1.1 billion cubic meters a year and cut carbon emissions by 2.4 million metric tonnes.

The accelerated deployment of renewable energy in Azerbaijan has been largely driven by high levels of foreign direct investment, which have surpassed $500 million. Companies from the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and China all have large-scale green energy projects in Azerbaijan. The country’s Energy Minister, Parviz Shahbazov, said that renewable energy auctions are expected to commence in 2028 to spur further development.

In October, the European Union’s Business Climate Report Azerbaijan 2025/26 highlighted the progress that the country has made in expanding its renewable energy sector in recent years. It states, “According to European companies participating in the survey, Azerbaijan has made significant progress in developing its renewable energy sector and is actively engaging international project developers to implement large-scale projects.”

The government is also supporting significant investment in Azerbaijan’s battery energy storage systems and electricity grid upgrades, including the AZURE project, the Navoi substation and new 500-kilovolt transmission lines. Azerbaijan plans to invest around $2.6 billion in renewable energy projects and power grid development by 2027, including $600 million to strengthen the grid infrastructure, according to Shahbazov.

These projects will help improve the flexibility of Azerbaijan’s power system, according to the report. The government also plans to develop domestic manufacturing capabilities in green energy, with a solar panel manufacturing project underway and plans for wind turbine blade and tower manufacturing projects in the Alat Free Economic Zone.

While Azerbaijan does not currently have a nuclear power programme, the government is also considering eventually developing the sector. In April, Shahbazov announced, “We are moving to a new model and will ensure energy security not only through hydrocarbons, but also through electricity, including renewable sources. In addition, we have decided to include nuclear energy in our energy balance, as we consider it a clean energy source and an important component of the future energy balance,” during an energy panel session at the Antalya Diplomacy Forum.

To support these efforts, the International Atomic Energy Agency conducted a legislative assistance mission to Azerbaijan in late 2025, in cooperation with the State Agency for Regulation of Nuclear and Radiological Activity. The aim was to raise awareness of the importance of adhering to the relevant international legal instruments and the elements of comprehensive national nuclear legislation.

Azerbaijan is accelerating the deployment of new renewable energy capacity and strengthening supporting infrastructure to ensure its energy system is both flexible and reliable. This is expected to help the country decrease dependence on oil and gas in the coming years. text:
The global renewable energy boom is running into an increasingly expensive obstacle: electricity grids that cannot always absorb, transmit or store the power being generated. The consequences range from wasted clean electricity to delayed projects and growing pressure on governments to upgrade infrastructure.

Advertisment

Here are five reasons why the scale of the problem if massive, and needs urgent intervention.

1. 360 TWh — China's renewable electricity wastage

China curtailed an estimated 360 TWh of wind and solar electricity in the first half of 2026, according to Global Energy Monitor and the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). This was 49% higher than a year earlier and enough electricity to power Mexico for a year. The estimate includes unreported curtailment, making it substantially higher than official figures.

2. 14% — India's solar curtailment

India curtailed 14% of its solar output in the June quarter of 2026, according to the same analysis. The problem is particularly acute in regions where renewable generation is expanding faster than transmission capacity, like Rajasthan and Gujarat.

3. 15.1% — Chile's renewable energy curtailment

Chile curtailed 15.1% of its wind and solar generation in 2024. The country is responding with grid expansion and battery storage, including projects that can absorb excess daytime generation and release electricity during evening peaks.

4. Four million units daily — Sri Lanka's solar problem

Sri Lanka's solar industry reported daily losses of around four million units of electricity due to curtailment in January 2026, despite a tight power situation. The country has since moved to strengthen grid management, including remotely controlling larger rooftop solar systems and accelerating battery storage deployment. A 5 hour blackout in October however has seen a temporary switch off when it comes to solar rooftop systems, as the grid operator grapples with stability issues.

5. 692 GW — Global renewable capacity added in 2025

The world added a record 692 GW of renewable capacity in 2025. Yet the International Renewable Energy Agency expects global clean energy additions to decline in 2026, partly because transmission and distribution infrastructure cannot keep pace.

The takeaway is clear: renewable energy growth is no longer just about building more solar and wind farms. Transmission, storage and grid flexibility will increasingly determine how much of that capacity actually delivers electricity.

text:
Amid voices calling for supplementation of the exclusion of electric vehicles from industries subject to domestic production tax credits, which are at the heart of this year's tax reform plan, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and Economy Lee Hyung-il visited Hyundai Motor and Kia Technology Research Institute in a surprise move to listen to industry opinions.

The ministry said it initially excluded electric vehicles from the list of industries, citing trade risks and careful consideration of financial support policy directions. However, considering the severe situation inside and outside the industry, the deputy prime minister visited to take a look at the site himself. As a result, expectations are growing that the tax subcommittee of the National Assembly's Finance and Economic Planning Committee will supplement it. In fact, Deputy Prime Minister Lee said, "We will prepare and announce a plan to strengthen the competitiveness of the electric vehicle industry within November."

The Ministry of Finance and Economy said on the 2nd that Deputy Prime Minister Lee visited the Hyundai Motor and Kia Technology Research Institute in Hwaseong, Gyeonggi Province, and held an industry meeting to strengthen the competitiveness of the electric vehicle industry. The ministry explained that the meeting was held to examine the current state of electric vehicle industry and autonomous vehicle technology development and to listen to industry opinions on corporate difficulties and government support. Deputy Prime Minister Lee, who visited the Hyundai Motor and Kia Technology Research Institute, also met with Hyundai Motor Group Chairman Chung Eui-sun.

On this day, Deputy Prime Minister Lee personally checked the self-driving demonstration vehicle, which is scheduled to be put into the Gwangju self-driving demonstration city from this month, and checked the vehicle production and technology development status. The demonstration vehicle is a vehicle for verifying electric vehicle-based autonomous driving technology, and 200 vehicles will be used at the end of this year and 3,000 cumulative vehicles next year. Lee also listened to Hyundai Motor and other local companies' plans to develop next-generation electric and self-driving cars.

In a meeting that took place immediately, Deputy Prime Minister Lee said, "The next battleground for a rebound in potential growth is electric vehicles," and stressed, "As we can survive only with technology that is the level of a global leader within the next two to three years, rapid change and technological innovation of our companies are more urgent than ever."

Businessmen in the electric vehicle, autonomous vehicle and parts industries officially requested support for production tax credits for electric vehicles, saying, "We need quick support from the government to help our companies survive the intensifying global competition." He then proposed expanding support for the future transformation of the parts industry, establishing a legal basis for introducing a battery lease system, and expanding professional manpower at institutions dedicated to autonomous vehicles.

Deputy Prime Minister Lee responded, "The government will also do its best with companies." He continued, "We will closely review the industry's recommendations with related ministries and improve them quickly." In particular, he stressed that "the government will actively participate in the discussion process of the National Assembly and discuss in-depth" on support for the tax credit for electric vehicle production. In addition, he announced that he would prepare and announce "measures to strengthen the competitiveness of the electric vehicle industry" by November, including enhancing autonomous driving technology and expanding core components and technology R&D.

description:
VinEnergo Energy Joint Stock Company switched on a rooftop solar and battery storage system in the Vung Ang Economic Zone of Ha Tinh province on October 28, 2026.

A rooftop solar system combined with a battery energy storage system in the Vung Ang Economic Zone, Ha Tinh province, Vietnam.
It went into operation on October 28, 2026, at 22 MWp of solar and 45 MWh of storage, according to Vietnam.vn.
text:
VinEnergo Energy Joint Stock Company switched on a rooftop solar and battery storage system in the Vung Ang Economic Zone of Ha Tinh province on October 28, 2026. Vietnam.vn, republishing a Tien Phong report, says the system runs at 22 MWp of solar and 45 MWh of battery energy storage (BESS). It feeds three factories: the VinFast electric-car plant, the VinES battery plant and the VG battery-manufacturing joint venture.

The project is VinEnergo’s first to run under a Direct Power Purchase Agreement (DPPA). That matters well beyond one industrial zone. Vietnam is trying to pull export manufacturing, much of it exposed to US tariff scrutiny that Tesla and Samsung are now fighting, onto cleaner and more predictable power. A battery-backed rooftop array that sells straight to the factory floor is one concrete way to do it.

This analysis covers what was commissioned, which numbers hold up and which do not, how the hardware likely works, and what the project signals for Vietnam’s battery and EV supply chain. It also offers five predictions. Where the public reports leave gaps, such as battery supplier, panel models and project cost, we say so rather than guess.
