What VinEnergo Switched On in Vung Ang

The commissioning report describes a rooftop solar system combined with a Battery Energy Storage System, installed on factory buildings in the Vung Ang Economic Zone. VinEnergo invests in, installs and operates the assets. The factories buy the electricity. That split keeps capital spending off the customers’ books, which is a pitch VinEnergo repeats on its own project page, where it lists zero upfront capital investment for customers among its selling points.

The reported commissioning date is October 28, 2026, which makes this a five-day-old story as of today, November 2. The confirmed operating capacity is 22 MWp of photovoltaics and 45 MWh of storage. The reports do not name a battery cell supplier, an inverter vendor, a panel model or a project price. Anyone quoting those details today is guessing.

The recipient list is the interesting part. VinFast builds electric cars. VinES builds battery packs and energy storage products. The VG joint venture makes batteries. All three sit in the same industrial complex, so the power travels a short distance and the load profile is predictable: three-shift manufacturing with large, steady daytime demand.

Confirmed Numbers Versus Earlier Plans

Two sets of figures circulate for this project, and they do not match. The commissioning coverage gives 22 MWp. Reports from August 2025, when VinEnergo signed memoranda of understanding for the three plants, described a larger rollout. VOV reported a plan for 43 MWp of rooftop solar and 45 MWh of BESS across the three sites, producing nearly 50 million kWh a year and cutting more than 33,000 tonnes of CO2 annually.

The safest reading is that 22 MWp is what runs today and 43 MWp was the plan, with further phases still to come. The commissioning coverage itself points to later phases. We treat the 43 MWp, 50 million kWh and 33,000 tonnes figures as earlier plan numbers, not as current operating data.

Notice that the storage figure stayed at 45 MWh in both versions while solar capacity dropped from 43 to 22 MWp. Either the battery arrived first and solar will catch up, or the first phase carries more storage per watt of solar than the original design. The reports do not say which.

The Three Factories Taking the Power

The customers are not random. They form a vertical chain. VinES and the VG joint venture make batteries, and VinFast puts batteries into vehicles. Powering all three from one local source means the carbon intensity of the final car depends partly on the electricity used to make its cells.

That link is getting more attention from buyers and regulators. Our earlier analysis of whether a new EV beats an old car on emissions, with a roughly three-year payback claim, showed how much of an EV’s lifetime footprint is locked in during manufacturing. Cleaner factory power attacks that upfront carbon directly.

The reports also say the system helps ease pressure on the national grid and raises the factories’ self-sufficiency. Both are outcomes of generating and storing power on site. A plant that draws less from the grid at midday and shifts storage output into the evening cuts the load it places on the local network at the times that matter most.

How the Rooftop Solar and BESS Hardware Fits Together

Public reports do not publish a single-line diagram, so what follows is general engineering context, not a description of VinEnergo’s specific design. A behind-the-meter system like this normally has three layers: photovoltaic arrays on roofs, inverters that convert DC to AC, and a battery bank with its own power conversion and controls. A site controller decides each moment whether solar output goes to the factory, to the battery, or to the grid.

The solar side

Rooftop arrays on industrial sheds have a structural advantage. The roof already exists, the land cost is zero, and the generation sits right next to the load. Their limit is surface area. A 22 MWp array needs a very large amount of roof, which helps explain why VinEnergo spread the work across three buildings.

The storage side

The 45 MWh figure describes energy capacity. It says nothing about power rating, so we cannot say how fast the system discharges. The pairing still tells a story. Solar peaks around midday, while factories run through the evening and night. Storage moves some of the midday surplus into the hours when the sun is gone. VinEnergo’s project page describes cabinet-type industrial storage solutions designed to integrate with rooftop renewables, though it does not tie that product line to this site.

Power-electronics design is also getting tighter at the other end of the storage market. Our report on the DSX Flex approach to cutting AI data-center power draw by 25% for three hours shows the same logic at work: buffer fast-changing loads with local storage so the grid sees a flatter profile.

What the Output Math Says

The reports give three numbers that can be cross-checked: 22 MWp, 45 MWh and roughly 39 million kWh in the first year. Running simple arithmetic on them (our calculations, not figures from the sources) produces some useful ratios. They also expose a gap in the public data.

The yield figure deserves a flag. The earlier plan implies about 1,160 kWh per kWp (nearly 50 million kWh from 43 MWp). The commissioning numbers imply about 1,770. That is a 50% jump between two company-linked estimates for similar roofs in the same province. Either the 39 million kWh figure assumes more installed capacity than 22 MWp, or it is optimistic, or the first-year estimate counts something the reports did not describe. We cannot resolve this from public sources.

The storage ratio is cleaner. A battery holding about 42% of an average day’s solar output can shift a meaningful share of generation into evening hours without being oversized. That fits a plant with round-the-clock demand.

Why the DPPA Model Matters

A Direct Power Purchase Agreement lets a generator sell electricity straight to a large consumer rather than routing every kilowatt-hour through the state utility. Vietnam updated its DPPA rules in 2025. Reports on the framework say eligible renewable producers, including rooftop operators unless restricted by contract, can sell directly to large users. They also describe limits on surplus power sold back to the grid and extra incentives for projects that include storage.

For VinEnergo, this project is the first test of that model in its own portfolio. The company says it wants to build a full energy chain: generation, storage, DPPA contracting, distribution and retail. Its project page lists retail electricity sales and grid operation services for industrial parks and urban areas as a core business line, alongside a stated pipeline across Vietnam, Laos, India, Indonesia and the Philippines.

Storage helps under DPPA because the buyer wants firm supply, not just midday supply. A factory cannot tell its production line to wait for sunshine. Adding batteries turns an intermittent source into something closer to a scheduled one, which makes a long-term contract easier to sign and to finance.

Historical Context: From MoU to Commissioning in About 14 Months

VOV reported on August 9, 2025 that VinEnergo signed memoranda of understanding with the VinFast plant and two battery factories in Ha Tinh. SolarQuarter covered the same MoU on August 18, 2025. The first phase went live on October 28, 2026, roughly 14 months later.

That is a quick turn for an industrial project that includes a new contracting model. It suggests the buildings, grid connection points and customer approvals were largely in place before work started. It also supports the view that this is a phased program, with the first phase delivered at about half of the planned solar capacity.

The timing also fits a broader pattern. Vietnam has been building a legal path for corporate renewable procurement, and projects that pair generation with storage behind the customer’s meter sidestep many grid-connection bottlenecks.

Competitive Comparison: Four Ways a Factory Can Buy Green Power

VinEnergo’s design is one of several routes open to a large Vietnamese manufacturer. The table below compares them qualitatively. We deliberately avoid cost figures because none were published for this project.

VinEnergo’s own materials list guaranteed renewable supply with REC or I-REC certificates among customer benefits, so the company can stack certificates on top of physical supply. That combination is hard for a pure certificate seller to match.

Market Impact for Vietnam’s Storage and EV Supply Chain

Vietnam’s storage market is young. Local reporting on the sector points to missing pricing and payment mechanisms, incomplete technical standards, tight financing and thin domestic manufacturing as the main obstacles. A 45 MWh project that runs commercially under a DPPA is a rare working example, and it carries more weight than another pilot or a pipeline announcement.

The captive-supply angle is just as important. The same corporate family appears to sit on both sides of the transaction, with VinES and the VG joint venture making batteries and VinEnergo deploying storage. That gives local battery makers a flagship reference site in their home market. Other countries are chasing the same goal. We covered how Egypt’s El Nasr aims for 45% local content in its MAGE EV, and India’s Sona Comstar tied a 129% EV revenue jump to a domestic supply chain. Vietnam is pursuing a similar play, with energy infrastructure bundled in.

The wider hardware picture is shifting too. Memory, power electronics and grid equipment all compete for the same capital as AI data centers. If you track those trends, our hardware coverage hub collects the related stories.

Why Factory Roofs Work Where Car Roofs Do Not

A story published November 1, 2026 by Engadget on the limits of solar roofs for EVs makes a useful contrast. Engadget’s Husain Parvez runs the numbers on a car roof. Using the EPA’s estimate that a median model-year 2025 EV consumes 39 kWh per 100 miles, he assumes a 400 W array on about 22 square feet and four hours of full output. That yields 1.6 kWh before charging losses, enough for roughly 4 miles.

Scale changes the answer. A car roof is tiny and moves around, parks in shade and carries the weight of every panel. A factory roof is enormous, fixed and unshaded, and it feeds a load that never leaves. Vung Ang takes the same energy source and puts it where the geometry works. The cars made at VinFast do not need solar roofs if the plant that builds them runs on solar roofs.

The practical lesson for EV makers is that decarbonizing the supply chain may deliver more per dollar than adding panels to the vehicle. It also gives buyers a story they can verify, since factory electricity can be metered.

Risks and Open Questions

Several things remain unconfirmed. The reports do not name the battery chemistry or supplier, the contract term, the electricity price, the project cost or the financing structure. The gap between the 22 MWp and 43 MWp figures needs an official explanation, and so does the 39 million kWh estimate. VinEnergo has not published a schedule for the next phases in the sources we reviewed.

Operational risks are the usual ones for rooftop solar plus storage. Roof structures must carry the load for decades. Batteries degrade with cycling and heat, and central Vietnam is hot and humid. Cybersecurity of the site controller matters too, since a system that talks to the grid and to a factory network is a juicy target. None of these is unique to this project, but none is addressed in the public reports either.

There is also policy risk. DPPA rules are young. If the rules on grid exports, wheeling charges or storage incentives shift, contracts written today could look different in three years.

What It Means for Hardware Buyers and Integrators

For equipment makers, the template is what counts. Buyers get power without capex. The developer owns the assets and earns from the electricity contract. That model favors suppliers who can offer bankable warranties and remote monitoring, since the developer carries the performance risk for years.

For factory operators outside Vietnam, the project is a reference design. Any plant with heavy daytime load, a large roof and an unreliable or carbon-heavy grid can ask the same question: why not let a third party build solar and storage on my roof and sell me the output?

The wider power-demand story cuts the other way. As hyperscalers pour money into compute, the $720 billion data center bet is competing for transformers, switchgear and grid connections. Industrial sites that generate and store their own power ease that squeeze on the local grid, and they get to keep running when connections stall.

Five Predictions for Vung Ang and Beyond

These are our expectations, not reported facts.

Phase two adds solar, not storage. The 45 MWh figure appears in both the plan and the commissioned system, while solar sits at roughly half the planned capacity. The next announcement is likely to add MWp.

Customer numbers go up. With three anchor customers live, VinEnergo has a reference for other tenants in the Vung Ang zone and in other industrial parks.

Disclosure improves. Investors and ESG auditors will push for the battery supplier, contract term and metered output. Expect a fuller technical release within a few quarters.

Rivals copy the template. Other Vietnamese developers will pitch rooftop plus BESS DPPAs to export manufacturers who face carbon scrutiny from buyers.

Storage standards tighten. Early commercial projects like this one tend to expose gaps in technical standards and payment rules, which regulators then close.

The first prediction is the most testable. If the next VinEnergo update lists solar capacity near 43 MWp with storage unchanged, the August 2025 plan is still the roadmap.

FAQ

What did VinEnergo commission? A rooftop solar system combined with a battery energy storage system in the Vung Ang Economic Zone, Ha Tinh province, Vietnam. It went into operation on October 28, 2026, at 22 MWp of solar and 45 MWh of storage, according to Vietnam.vn.

Who receives the electricity? The VinFast electric-car manufacturing plant, the VinES battery manufacturing plant and the VG battery-manufacturing joint venture.

What is a DPPA? A Direct Power Purchase Agreement lets a generator sell electricity directly to a large consumer. This is VinEnergo’s first project operating under that model.

How much clean power will it produce? The commissioning report estimates about 39 million kWh in the first year and more than 25,000 tonnes of CO2 avoided. Earlier plans cited nearly 50 million kWh and more than 33,000 tonnes, which the commissioning coverage does not repeat.

Why do the capacity figures differ? The August 2025 MoU coverage described 43 MWp of solar across the three plants. The commissioned system is 22 MWp. The reports do not explain the gap, though phased delivery is the likeliest reading.

Who supplied the batteries and panels? The available reports do not say. No product models, battery manufacturer or project price were identified.

title: Why green jobs are resilient to AI substitution - Trellis Group
description:
Green jobs should be an extremely compelling proposition.
The conclusions of the report — Green Advantage: Employment in an AI-Enabled Economy — are clear: green jobs are more resilient to AI substitution.
Across the wider green economy, more than four in five green jobs are in roles less exposed to AI substitution, compared with around three in four across the U.K. workforce.
Use this analysis in your decks and conversation to make the point that momentum is growing again for corporate sustainability.
Keep going For the corporate sustainability community, my main conclusion from the report is that we truly are in the decade of delivery.
text:
Last month, I had a conversation with my daughter about what she wanted to do with her life. She likes the idea of being a lawyer, but isn’t sure whether that job will still be around by the time she leaves school.

She is not alone in being nervous about her livelihood. But advances in artificial intelligence are happening alongside the energy transition. To understand the intersection of these two mega-trends, my colleagues and I at the Futerra Solutions Union, an independent nonprofit that exists to push the cultural narrative on climate and nature toward solutions, commissioned a report that examines how green jobs will be impacted by AI.

Green jobs should be an extremely compelling proposition. We already know that they pay more than the national average and that green skills are in high demand. To examine the impact of AI on these roles, our partners at the consultancy CBI Economics and the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, a nonprofit, asked whether the occupations supporting green activity today, and those expected to grow as the energy transition progresses, have lower or higher potential to be carried out by AI.

There is no single definition of green employment, so the analysis covers parts of the green labor market, including the renewable energy and low-carbon transport sectors, as well as green apprenticeships offering roles such as horticulture operative and crop technician. And while this is U.K.-focused research, it’s applicable to other markets. These occupations are found, to a greater or lesser extent, across the world’s major economies.

The conclusions of the report — Green Advantage: Employment in an AI-Enabled Economy — are clear: green jobs are more resilient to AI substitution.

Nearly all green apprenticeships in England (96 percent) lead to jobs that are harder for AI to replace, compared with around three-quarters of all apprenticeships.

Ninety-four percent of the additional clean energy workers the U.K. government says are needed by 2030, such as wind turbine engineers, are in roles where AI is more likely to support the work than take it over.

Across the wider green economy, more than four in five green jobs are in roles less exposed to AI substitution, compared with around three in four across the U.K. workforce.

What does this mean for those of us working in corporate sustainability?

Selling sustainability

It can be hard selling sustainability in a downturn. Use this analysis in your decks and conversation to make the point that momentum is growing again for corporate sustainability. The anecdotes it contains can help whether you are pitching internally for more resources, persuading your board to stay the course or motivating your team.

Talent attraction and retention

Use this frame if you are hiring, particularly for trades and technical teams. Attract the best talent by making your employer proposition one of resilience and long-term stability. We also need to help existing workers update their skills as AI and green technologies develop. Make this part of your talent retention program.

Future-proof your own career

First the bad news: “Corporate responsibility and sustainability practitioner” has a large proportion of research, reporting, communications and information-processing tasks, which generative AI is increasingly able to support or perform. That means it has a higher potential for AI substitution.

But ask yourself if your job also meets the components of “AI complementarity,” meaning the role can benefit from AI rather than being replaced by it. These include the level of responsibility, consequences of error, importance of interpersonal interaction, level of human judgment, as well as the training and expertise required to perform the work.

Share the findings with younger generations

As the mother of two school-age children, this research has made me think completely differently about what constitutes a good job for them. I now counsel my kids to think about trades, technical, operative or installation occupations. Roles that involve doing and building things while exercising human judgment.

Keep going

For the corporate sustainability community, my main conclusion from the report is that we truly are in the decade of delivery. The most resilient roles, highly in demand, are those in clean energy, low carbon transport and other roles that support the transition. Renewable energy employment in the U.K. grew almost two-thirds between 2014 and 2024, while low-carbon transport jobs increased almost three-fold — evidence of a changing economy that needs people with the skills to make it happen. This is a genuinely exciting proposition.

text:
China is exporting a record amount of clean energy technology and equipment as the energy crisis from the Iran war drives surging demand for renewables. This will help reduce global emissions, according to a report released on 29 October.

Once installed or deployed, these 2026 exports will likely avert emissions of about 450 million tonnes of carbon dioxide per year, roughly equal to Brazil’s annual emissions, says the analysis by the Finland-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).

It's a small sign of progress as global efforts to curb climate change fall short. In November, Türkiye will host annual UN climate talks where electrification is expected to be a leading topic.

"This is a pivot point for the outlook of global energy and global emissions," says Lauri Myllyvirta, with CREA. “We’re seeing growth in clean energy that is much, much faster than anyone predicted just a few years ago.”

Related

Record-breaking year for Chinese exports

China is by far the largest global supplier of renewable energy equipment, from solar panels and wind turbines to electric vehicles and batteries. Most of what it makes is sold domestically, but a sizeable share is exported.

In the first nine months of 2026, CREA tracked a 61 per cent increase in exports of electric vehicles, a 45 per cent jump in shipments of wind turbines, a 39 per cent spike in battery exports and 22 per cent growth in overseas sales of solar equipment, compared to the same period last year.

Southeast Asia was a major destination. China's clean energy exports to the region jumped nearly 160 per cent from last year to this September, according to Ember, an independent global energy think tank.

The value of China's electric vehicle exports hit $72.8 billion (€65bn) in the first nine months of this year, up from $39.7 billion (€35.5bn) last year, according to the research firm Atlas Public Policy.

Chinese clean tech dents emissions

If these export trends continue for the rest of 2026, about 8,400 million tonnes of carbon dioxide will be averted over the lifetime of all the clean tech China exported this year, CREA estimates.

That's about 24 per cent of annual global emissions, more than the United States' and India's emissions combined.

The analysis by CREA is based on export data, the electricity systems in destination countries and Chinese emissions during manufacturing. Independent experts said the estimate was in line with the scale of China's exports, but were unable to validate the data.

Despite President Donald Trump's higher tariffs, Chinese clean tech exports to the US rose 13 per cent in January-September compared to a year earlier.

“The demand is much stronger than I expected,” Myllyvirta says. “That’s certainly noteworthy.”

China is both the world's biggest provider of clean tech equipment and the largest global source of carbon emissions.

Muyi Yang, a senior policy analyst at Ember, likens China's energy transition to replacing the engine of a ship while it's still at sea.

Interest in renewables likely to persist, experts say

The drastic war-related disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, usually the source for a fifth of the world’s oil and gas, hit import-dependent Asian countries first and hardest.

Renewed interest in clean energy options is likely to persist even after the war, says Yu Sun Chin, with the research group Zero Carbon Analytics.

Consumers in Southeast Asia are paying more for their electricity and fuel and opting for renewable alternatives such as rooftop solar.

Laos, Thailand and Vietnam have offered various incentives for installing solar and purchasing electric vehicles to help reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels.

The Philippines implemented similar policies and became the second-largest destination for Chinese solar exports in the first quarter of 2026. Indonesia has pledged to install 100 gigawatts of solar power by 2029.

text:
The Environmental Protection Agency discarded a report warning of the risks that "forever chemicals" pose in sewage-based fertilizer despite evidence of contamination on farms.

On one Texas ranch, more than 80 cattle died as investigators examined pollution believed to have come from fertilizer stored nearby, WJLA reported.

Here's what to know

A proposed national survey awaiting action at the White House's Office of Management and Budget was designed to map PFAS contamination and identify its sources.

A WJLA investigation found that the EPA left the survey unused while citing a lack of data.

Former EPA scientist Betsy Southerland spent 33 years at the agency and led water-related work in its science and technology office.

"That has been ready to go since November of 2024, and the current administration never mentions the survey and has never taken any steps to put that survey out," Southerland told WJLA. Her team produced the nearly 300-page risk report that the EPA discarded.

According to the findings WJLA reviewed, even biosolids containing small amounts of certain PFAS could pose serious risks to people, livestock, and the environment.

More background

At Tony Coleman's family ranch in Johnson County, Texas, Dana Ames examined contamination in her role as an environmental crimes investigator.

Investigators suspected that biosolid fertilizer made from human waste and stored beside the property was the source of the contamination. Tests detected high PFAS levels in the ranch's animals, soil, and water.

Ames' work included collecting samples for analysis while Coleman watched his cattle die.

State regulators from Maine to Michigan have linked damaged land and sick farm animals to sludge contamination. PFAS exposure is linked to cancer, thyroid conditions, and developmental difficulties in both people and animals.

Sewage-based fertilizer is applied annually to roughly 70 million acres of agricultural land.

What's being done?

Asked why the survey hadn't been sent out, EPA Deputy Administrator David Fotouhi claimed PFAS contamination was a priority for EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin and the agency.

Fotouhi said the EPA wanted water systems and biosolids users to have information and technical support for treatment where necessary, but he didn't explain why the survey remained unused.

Instead, Fotouhi pointed to nine pages of voluntary suggestions that acknowledge the benefits of biosolids but advise against applying the fertilizer near children or to particular crops.

Southerland called for conducting the survey to identify the specific industries discharging PFAS into wastewater. Without that information, efforts to trace contamination before it reaches farms remain incomplete, leaving agricultural communities without answers about its sources.

For Ames, those concerns extend to the food she serves her own family.

"As a mother and a grandmother, knowing that the food, the very food that I feed my family, could be tainted with toxic chemicals that our government's aware of and refuses to respond to. That is not OK," she told WJLA.

Where can I learn more?

Concerns about PFAS in soil and water reach far beyond one Texas ranch. These stories examine the chemicals' industrial ties, opposition to wastewater expansion, and lawsuits over forever chemicals.

• North Carolina's PFAS fight exposed an industry trail spanning Texas, Europe, and India.

• Maryland residents are pushing back against Perdue's proposed fivefold wastewater increase amid PFAS concerns.

• North Carolina residents sued over PFAS contamination in their well water and soil.

• Vermont well owners filed a federal class action against Saint-Gobain, 3M, and DuPont over PFOA.

Two Point O Capital (TW.O), an AI-powered clean energy deployment platform for commercial and industrial (C&I) businesses, has raised $10 million in a funding round led by Transition Venture Capital. Existing investor Omnivore and angel investors Chiranjeev Singh Saluja and Sudhir M Reddy also participated in the round.

The proceeds will be used to expand into battery energy storage systems (BESS) and strengthen its presence in solar energy, energy efficiency and wastewater treatment, the company said in a press release.

Founded in 2024 by Archit Mehrotra, Karan Bhutani, Manya Ranjan and Shashidhar Reddy, TW.O provides sustainable infrastructure solutions to businesses through flexible financing, project ownership, transparent measurement and guaranteed outcomes.

The company works with original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) firms across India. Its clientele includes Premier Energies, Godrej, JK Tyre, Morepen Pharma, Wipro and Phoenix Mills.

TW.O said its assets under management (AUM) have grown 1.5 times every quarter over the past three quarters. The company uses a proprietary artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning platform for solutioning, underwriting and asset monitoring. The platform enables predictive maintenance, risk mitigation and performance optimisation.

According to the company, the C&I segment presents an annual opportunity of $100 billion to $150 billion for customised capital and asset solutions that address clean energy and utility requirements. Such solutions can help businesses reduce operating costs, improve operational resilience and access markets such as the European Union.

TW.O also plans to deepen its presence in energy- and water-intensive sectors, including data centres, automotive, pharmaceuticals, manufacturing and healthcare.

The company aims to help factories, hospitals, data centres and manufacturing facilities adopt cleaner energy and more efficient water management solutions.

text:
Headlines report falling battery prices, LFPs dominating stationary storage, and sodium-ion edging into utility tenders. These market swings point to the chemistry likely to dominate the global storage race and what it could mean for grid operators, end users and investors.

Battery cell manufacturing overcapacity and fierce competition drove lithium-ion (Li-ion) prices down over the past decade, and they continue to fall.

In its 2025 Lithium-Ion Battery Price Survey, BloombergNEF puts the average global battery pack price at $108/kWh in 2025, down 8% from 2024. Stationary storage packs fell further, to around $70/kWh, down 45% year-on-year, while China’s average pack price dropped to $84/kWh.

Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) drove much of that price decline. The IEA reports that LFP packs were more than 40% cheaper per kWh than nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) packs in 2025. Part of that gap reflects LFP’s grip on stationary storage, where it accounted for more than 90% of global installations that year.

However, while batteries keep getting cheaper to manufacture, the risks from commodity prices, supply-chain constraints and overcapacity cycles can sharply reverse the trend in the short term.

DID YOU KNOW? Africa is pursuing battery value-chain growth through DRC precursor manufacturing and South African gigafactory plans, while evolving chemistries threaten demand for its cobalt, lithium and nickel resources.

The markets where LFPs and NMCs dominate

Low cost, long cycle life and strong thermal stability make LFPs very difficult to beat on grid-scale BESS installations. The same holds for C&I storage, where space is usually available and, for ROI, daily cycling matters more than achieving maximum energy density.

title: VinEnergo Solar-BESS Powers 3 Factories: 39M kWh [2026] - shattered.io
description:
VinEnergo has switched on a rooftop solar and battery energy storage system (BESS) that feeds three factories in Vietnam’s Vung Ang Economic Zone.
The report does not publish a solar capacity in MWp or a storage capacity in MWh, and it names no equipment suppliers.
Why Pair Rooftop Solar With Battery Storage Solar alone produces power in a bell curve that peaks near midday.
CleanTechnica reported that installed solar capacity grew from 86 MW in 2018 to nearly 18,000 MW by April 2025.
SolarQuarter reported on November 2, 2026 that it supplies the VinFast EV plant, the VinES battery plant and the VG battery joint venture.
text:
VinEnergo has switched on a rooftop solar and battery energy storage system (BESS) that feeds three factories in Vietnam’s Vung Ang Economic Zone. SolarQuarter reported the commissioning on November 2, 2026, and said the system supplies the VinFast electric vehicle plant, the VinES battery plant and the VG battery manufacturing joint venture in Ha Tinh province. The same report puts annual output at about 39 million kWh.

That makes this a hardware story as much as an energy story. Battery cells are the costliest part of any EV, and the plants that make them draw heavy, steady power. As our tracker of global EV battery market share shows, the cell race is already fierce, and cheap clean power is becoming a lever in it.

This analysis covers what was commissioned, which numbers hold up, how the direct power purchase model works, and what it could mean for EV and battery makers in Southeast Asia. It also flags where the public record disagrees with itself. Every figure below comes from named outlets, and anything that is our own arithmetic is labeled that way.

·

Don't miss new tech stories on Google

Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.

Add now

What VinEnergo Commissioned at Vung Ang

VinEnergo Energy Joint Stock Company built a rooftop solar array paired with battery storage inside the Vung Ang Economic Zone in Ha Tinh, a central Vietnamese province. SolarQuarter says the system now supplies green electricity to the VinFast EV manufacturing plant, the VinES battery manufacturing facility and the VG battery joint venture. The operators named in that report are the Future Production, Investment and Development Joint Stock Company, which runs the VinFast side, and VinES Ha Tinh Energy Solutions Joint Stock Company.

The report describes the installation as the first operational renewable project under Vietnam’s direct power purchase agreement (DPPA) mechanism. That label matters more than the megawatts. A DPPA lets a generator sell electricity straight to a large consumer instead of routing every kilowatt-hour through the state utility’s pricing. For an industrial park with three big power users in one place, the model fits naturally.

Roofs make sense here for a plain reason. Car and battery plants have enormous flat roofs, the land is already paid for, and the generation sits next to the load. No new transmission corridor is needed. The battery then smooths the gap between when the sun shines and when the lines run.

One timing detail needs care. SolarQuarter dated its commissioning story November 2, 2026. A Vietnamese outlet’s English edition, surfaced in our search, reportedly dated the start of operation to October 28. We treat the system as commissioned in the final days of October or on the first days of November, and we do not pin a single go-live day on it.

The Numbers Reported on Commissioning Day

SolarQuarter lists four headline performance figures. The system should generate roughly 39 million kWh a year, cut carbon dioxide emissions by more than 25,000 tonnes a year, offset the equivalent of over 1.13 million trees annually and save close to VND 3.5 billion a year. The report does not publish a solar capacity in MWp or a storage capacity in MWh, and it names no equipment suppliers.

We can do some simple math on those figures, and we flag it as our own calculation. Spread across 8,760 hours, 39 million kWh equals an average draw of about 4.5 MW. The CO2 figure implies roughly 0.64 kg of avoided emissions per kWh, which fits a grid still leaning on fossil generation. The savings figure implies about VND 90 per kWh, though SolarQuarter does not say how it computed the saving.

Those ratios are useful as sanity checks. They show the three claims hang together, which is not guaranteed in press releases. An average 4.5 MW is a modest slice of what an EV plant plus two battery lines might consume, so the system cuts the bill and the emissions without making the plants energy-independent. Treat it as a hedge, not a replacement for grid supply.

Planned Versus Reported: Why the Figures Differ

The project was announced well before it went live. In August 2025, The Investor, VietnamPlus and Bao Quoc Te all covered the launch of a plan combining 43 MWp of rooftop solar with 45 MWh of battery storage. Those reports projected nearly 50 million kWh a year and more than 33,000 tonnes of avoided CO2.

Set those side by side with the commissioning-day numbers and a gap appears. The 39 million kWh figure sits about 22% below the 50 million kWh plan, and the 25,000-tonne CO2 figure sits about 24% below the 33,000-tonne plan. Those percentages are our arithmetic. They suggest the commissioned scope may be smaller than the original plan, or phased, or measured on a different basis.

The English edition of a Vietnamese outlet, found in our search, reportedly describes the operating system as up to 22 MWp of solar plus 45 MWh of storage. We could not retrieve that page in full, so we flag the number as unconfirmed. If it holds, it would explain the lower generation, since a 22 MWp array cannot produce what a 43 MWp one would. We have not seen an official statement that reconciles the two capacity figures.

How to read conflicting project figures

Large solar projects often change between announcement and energization. Roof space gets re-surveyed, phases get split and early output estimates get trimmed once real irradiance data arrives. Our rule here is the conservative one. When two sources disagree, we quote the lower, later figure for what is running today and the earlier figure only as the plan.

Which Factories Draw the Power

Three industrial users share the system. The first is the VinFast automobile plant, which assembles Vietnam’s homegrown electric vehicles. The second is VinES, which makes battery packs and energy storage products. The third is the V-G High-Tech Energy Solutions battery plant, described in the 2025 launch coverage as a battery manufacturing joint venture.

Clustering the load matters. A DPPA works best when a few creditworthy buyers sit close to the generation, because the contract is simpler and the line losses are tiny. Vung Ang is effectively a purpose-built customer base. It also ties the clean power to a specific product claim, since a battery cell made on solar-backed electricity carries a lower embedded carbon number than one made on the average grid mix.

That embedded carbon figure is rising in importance for exporters. Buyers in Europe increasingly ask for battery carbon footprints, and plants in Asia that can document cleaner power gain a negotiating edge. Neither SolarQuarter nor the Vietnamese outlets say VinFast plans to market its cells that way, so this stays our reading of the incentives and not a reported strategy.

The Investor reported that the project supports Vingroup’s net-zero emissions target for 2040 and aims to turn Vung Ang into a green industrial hub. Nguyen Huong Giang, VinEnergo’s deputy general director, framed it as a showcase of Vietnamese enterprises’ determination and pioneering use of new technology to advance the country’s net-zero goal. We paraphrase her remarks here because they did not reach us through our verified-quotes process.

How a DPPA Works and Why It Matters Here

A direct power purchase agreement is a contract between a generator and a large buyer. In Vietnam, the mechanism was designed to let industrial customers source renewable electricity without buying it all through the utility’s standard tariff. SolarQuarter calls the Vung Ang system the first operational renewable installation under that mechanism, and The Investor said the 2025 plan was the first in Vietnam to combine rooftop solar and BESS under a DPPA.

CleanTechnica, writing in September 2025, called the DPPA model relatively untested locally for combined solar and battery projects. It also noted that selling directly to corporate customers lets a project sidestep some grid bottlenecks. Both points cut the same way. The structure has real appeal, and the track record is thin.

For buyers, the draw is price certainty and a credible sustainability claim. For developers, it is a bankable offtaker. For regulators, a working example shows whether contract terms, grid fees and metering rules hold up under daily use. The first commissioned project becomes the template, and every clause that causes friction gets copied or fixed by the next deal.

What we do not know about the contract

None of the sources we reviewed disclose the tariff, the contract length or the investment cost. CleanTechnica estimated a cost of $35 million to $50 million for the 43 MWp plan, based on industry per-kilowatt rates, and stressed that the actual terms were not disclosed. That is an outside estimate for a plan that may have been scaled down, so we do not use it as a project cost.

Why Pair Rooftop Solar With Battery Storage

Solar alone produces power in a bell curve that peaks near midday. A factory that runs multiple shifts needs power at 3 a.m. too. A battery shifts some of the midday surplus into the evening and overnight hours, and it can also shave the sharp demand spikes that raise bills under peak-based tariffs.

Storage plays a second role that matters in Vietnam, which is grid relief. SolarQuarter says the project contributes to reducing pressure on the national grid. Batteries at the point of use let a plant draw less from the grid during stressed hours. They also keep solar output from being wasted when the local network cannot absorb it.

There is a quality angle for battery plants as well. Cell formation and drying rooms are sensitive to power interruptions. A storage system can ride through short dips, though SolarQuarter does not say this system is configured as backup power, so we do not claim it. The same logic is playing out at other power-hungry sites. Our look at the AI power problem and 800V DC designs shows data centers chasing the same mix of on-site generation, storage and tighter power electronics.

Vietnam’s Grid Context: A Solar Boom Meets Congestion

Vietnam’s solar build-out has been rapid. CleanTechnica reported that installed solar capacity grew from 86 MW in 2018 to nearly 18,000 MW by April 2025. It also reported a government target of 46 to 73 GW of solar by 2030, coal at 45% of electricity generation as of 2021, and a 10.9% rise in energy demand in the first nine months of 2024.

Growth that fast strains wires. CleanTechnica said grid congestion and renewable curtailment persist, particularly in southern provinces, because transmission infrastructure lags behind generation capacity. Curtailment means a working solar farm gets told to switch off because the network cannot take its power. Developers hate it, because every curtailed kilowatt-hour is lost revenue.

Behind-the-meter systems like the Vung Ang one dodge much of that problem. Power generated on a factory roof and used on site never needs to cross a congested line. The battery adds a buffer, so a sunny midday does not force a shutdown. In a market where the wires are the bottleneck, that design advantage may count for more than raw panel efficiency.

The Hardware Angle for EV and Battery Supply Chains

Battery manufacturing is energy-hungry, and electricity is a meaningful slice of cell cost. That is why cleaner, steadier supply is turning into a competitive tool. Makers that lock in long-term power through contracts like a DPPA can plan margins more precisely than those exposed to retail tariffs.

Capacity race news elsewhere shows the same pressure. Group14 recently drew attention for a $169 million raise tied to a 10 GWh plant in Spain, a reminder that new battery material capacity is arriving in several regions at once. Plants in each region will compete on cell price, quality and, increasingly, the carbon footprint of the power behind them.

For VinFast, the picture is mixed. The company is a young carmaker, and EV makers across Asia are fighting for volume. Our report on Xiaomi topping 50,000 EV deliveries in October shows how fast a new entrant can scale when supply chains line up. Cutting energy costs at the plant will not decide that contest, but every point of cost matters when rivals sell at thin margins.

Market Impact: Costs, Carbon and Contract Templates

The cleanest read of the reported savings is that they are real but small. Nearly VND 3.5 billion a year is a rounding error against the revenue of an automotive plant. The value lies elsewhere, in the contract template, the carbon claim and the proof that a DPPA with storage can run in practice.

Investors in Vietnamese industrial real estate will watch this closely. If Vung Ang demonstrates a lower power bill and a cleaner footprint, other zones will pitch the same package to tenants. Foreign manufacturers weighing a Vietnam site often ask about renewable access, and a working example answers that question better than a policy paper.

On the utility side, large industrial buyers moving to direct contracts shift some demand off the standard tariff. Grid companies will want clarity on fees for using their wires and on backup supply. The commissioning gives them a live case to study. It mirrors fights seen in other markets, such as the U.S. debate we covered in power bills, data centers and the midterms, where big loads and household customers argue over who pays for the grid.

Competitive Comparison: Three Ways to Power a Plant

Factories and vehicles chase clean power in different ways, and the contrast helps explain why VinEnergo chose rooftops. Engadget examined the other end of the spectrum, putting solar on the car itself. It found that a 400W roof array yields only about 4 miles of range worth of energy, and that extra panels add weight and drag. Read that piece on the limits of solar roofs on EVs for the vehicle side of the story. A factory roof has the opposite profile, with huge area, no weight limit and no aerodynamics to worry about.

Fast charging sites follow a third path. The Tesla site in our 164-stall Supercharger walkthrough pairs charging with an 11 MW solar installation, according to the title of that report. It shows on-site generation working at the charging end, while Vung Ang shows it at the manufacturing end.

Historical Context: From MoU to Commissioning

The path started in the summer of 2025. SolarQuarter reported on August 18, 2025 that VinEnergo signed a memorandum of understanding to deploy solar and energy storage at VinFast, VinES and V-G plants. Days earlier, on August 9, 2025, Vietnamese outlets covered the launch of the rooftop solar and BESS initiative itself.

CleanTechnica followed in September 2025 with a skeptical angle, asking whether Vietnam’s strained grid could carry the ambition. At that point it found no operational date, and it noted that comparable projects typically take 12 to 18 months. Commissioning arrived roughly 14 to 15 months after the August 2025 launch, which lands inside that range.

That timeline is worth stating plainly. From announcement to first output took about a year and a quarter, with no reported public delay. Developers elsewhere would welcome that pace, though the scope may have shrunk along the way, as the gap in reported numbers suggests.

VinEnergo’s Wider Ambitions

The Vung Ang system is not VinEnergo’s only play. SolarQuarter reports the company is supplying BESS solutions for several major projects of Hanoi Power Corporation and Northern Power Corporation, with a combined capacity above 1.1 GWh. That makes the factory installation a small part of its storage business by capacity.

The same report cites a much larger goal. VinEnergo’s portfolio currently stands at 10 GW, and the company aims to expand to 100 GW within three years, with projects planned in Asia and Europe. We treat that as a stated ambition from a company announcement. A tenfold jump in three years would require financing, equipment supply and permitting on a scale that few developers have ever managed.

Why would a Vingroup-linked energy firm chase such a target? A plausible reading, which is our analysis and not a reported fact, is that captive demand from group companies gives it a base load of customers, while storage skills carry over to utility clients. Whether the strategy works abroad depends on execution that the Vung Ang project only begins to test.

Risks and Open Questions

Five questions remain open. First, what is the real installed capacity, 43 MWp, 22 MWp or something else? Second, what are the tariff and contract length under the DPPA? Third, which suppliers provided the panels, inverters and battery cells? Fourth, how does the system perform over a full year, including Vietnam’s rainy season? Fifth, how will grid operators price the use of their network for such contracts?

There is also a measurement risk in the headline metrics. The tree-equivalent figure is a communications device, not an engineering result, and conversion factors vary. The CO2 number depends on which grid emissions factor the company applied. Readers should lean on the kWh figure, which is the most direct output of the system, and treat the rest as derived claims.

Finally, the press picture is thin. Our verified-quotes search returned nothing, and the single source URL our pipeline vetted for this story was an unrelated Engadget piece on car-roof solar. SolarQuarter, The Investor and VietnamPlus carry the core facts, and we attribute accordingly. A statement from VinEnergo or VinFast with full specs would settle most of these points.

Five Predictions for Rooftop Solar and BESS in Vietnam

These are our forecasts, not reported facts.

More DPPA deals will follow within 12 months. A working template lowers the risk for the next buyer, and other industrial zones will want the same package.

Storage will become a standard add-on. With curtailment a known problem, new rooftop projects will bundle batteries from day one.

Disclosure will improve. Once buyers ask for carbon data, VinEnergo and its customers will publish clearer capacity and supplier details.

Carbon labels will reach Vietnamese cells. Exporters facing European buyers will cite on-site clean power in their pitch.

The 100 GW goal will slip or shrink. The ambition is real, but a tenfold expansion in three years collides with financing and supply limits.

The takeaway: the Vung Ang commissioning is a modest system with an outsized signal. It shows a DPPA with storage can move from announcement to operation in roughly 14 months, and it hands Vietnam’s EV and battery makers a cleaner power model to copy. What it does not yet show is the full capacity, price or supplier list. Watch for those disclosures, because they will decide whether this is a template or a one-off.

FAQ

What did VinEnergo commission?

VinEnergo commissioned a rooftop solar system with battery energy storage in the Vung Ang Economic Zone in Ha Tinh, Vietnam. SolarQuarter reported on November 2, 2026 that it supplies the VinFast EV plant, the VinES battery plant and the VG battery joint venture.

How much power will it generate?

SolarQuarter reports about 39 million kWh a year. The August 2025 launch coverage projected nearly 50 million kWh, so the commissioning figure is the lower and later one.

What is a DPPA?

A direct power purchase agreement lets a generator sell electricity directly to a large consumer. SolarQuarter calls this the first operational renewable installation under Vietnam’s DPPA mechanism.

How much CO2 and money does it save?

SolarQuarter cites more than 25,000 tonnes of CO2 avoided a year and nearly VND 3.5 billion in annual savings. It does not explain how either number was calculated.

Why do the capacity numbers differ between reports?

The 2025 launch coverage cited 43 MWp of solar and 45 MWh of storage. A Vietnamese outlet’s English edition reportedly cites up to 22 MWp for the operating system. No official statement we found reconciles the two, so the capacity remains unconfirmed.

Does this make the factories fully solar-powered?

No. By our arithmetic, 39 million kWh a year averages about 4.5 MW, which covers part of the demand of three large plants. The factories still depend on the grid for the rest.

What else is VinEnergo building?

SolarQuarter reports BESS work for Hanoi Power Corporation and Northern Power Corporation totaling more than 1.1 GWh. It also cites a 10 GW portfolio and a goal of 100 GW within three years, with projects planned in Asia and Europe.

text:
VinEnergo has commissioned a rooftop solar power system integrated with a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in the Vung Ang Economic Zone in Ha Tinh, Vietnam. The project will supply clean electricity to the VinFast electric vehicle manufacturing plant, the VinES battery manufacturing facility and the VG battery manufacturing joint venture.

The project marks VinEnergo’s first operational renewable energy installation under the Direct Power Purchase Agreement (DPPA) mechanism. It is designed to support the electricity requirements of major industrial facilities while reducing dependence on conventional grid power.

The initial beneficiaries include Future Production, Investment and Development Joint Stock Company, which owns and operates the VinFast electric car and motorcycle manufacturing plant in Ha Tinh, and VinES Ha Tinh Energy Solutions Joint Stock Company, the operator of the VinES battery manufacturing facility. The rooftop solar installation will also supply electricity to the VG joint venture battery factory within the same electric vehicle and battery manufacturing complex.

According to company estimates, the integrated solar and storage system is expected to generate approximately 39 million kWh of clean electricity during its first year of operation. The project is projected to reduce carbon dioxide emissions by more than 25,000 tonnes annually, equivalent to the estimated annual carbon absorption of over 1.13 million trees.

The transition to renewable electricity is also expected to ease pressure on the regional power grid, improve energy self-sufficiency for participating factories and deliver annual cost savings of nearly VND 3.5 billion.

The successful commissioning and initial stable supply to the three industrial facilities provide a foundation for VinEnergo to expand its green energy activities in subsequent phases. The company aims to develop an integrated energy model combining renewable generation, large-scale battery storage, electricity distribution and retail infrastructure to support growing industrial demand in the Vung Ang Economic Zone.

Nguyen Huong Giang, Deputy General Director of VinEnergo, said the project represents an important step towards developing a comprehensive energy ecosystem covering renewable generation, storage, DPPA mechanisms and electricity distribution. She highlighted the company’s focus on applying Vietnamese-developed products, manufacturing capabilities and technology to address the energy requirements of industrial customers.

Beyond this project, VinEnergo is providing BESS solutions for several major projects of Hanoi Power Corporation and Northern Power Corporation, with a combined capacity exceeding 1.1 GWh.

Internationally, the company has announced a renewable energy project portfolio totalling 10 GW and is implementing its first projects in Asia and Europe. VinEnergo aims to expand its project portfolio to 100 GW within the next three years, positioning itself among the world’s leading renewable energy companies.

title: Massive AI Data Center Sparks Backlash Despite Clean Energy Promises | OilPrice.com
description:
Google has proposed an agreement with Xcel Energy to support significant wind, solar and battery storage development alongside its new 780-MW Project Skyway data centre.
Xcel Energy says the new energy resources will serve the wider grid, benefiting other customers as well as the data centre.
This is driving demand for new clean energy capacity to ensure that data centres are not powered by fossil fuels – although several companies still depend on gas-powered plants.
In addition, the use of clean power in data centre operations is not the only sustainability concern.
So, while Google may be attempting to develop a more “sustainable” data centre, it is failing to win over local residents, who remain concerned about the long-term implications of building a giant AI data centre.
text:
As more governments put increasing pressure on tech companies to develop more sustainable data centres, to ensure they do not place a further burden on the grid, several tech firms are investing in developing new energy capacity and incorporating other innovative ideas into their facility development. This has led Google to suggest that the development of its new U.S. data centre in Minnesota, and associated energy development, will have a positive benefit on the region’s transmission network.

Google has proposed an agreement with Xcel Energy to support significant wind, solar and battery storage development alongside its new 780-MW Project Skyway data centre. The tech giant plans to finance Xcel's addition of 1.4 GW of wind, 200 MW of solar power and 300 MW of battery storage to the grid. While the combined capacity of these projects exceeds the data centre's projected electricity demand, wind and solar generation fluctuate depending on weather conditions, and battery storage does not generate additional electricity. Xcel Energy says the new energy resources will serve the wider grid, benefiting other customers as well as the data centre. Google plans to cover the associated costs under the proposed agreement, including payments for capacity it does not fully use.

The aim is to get the residents of Pine Island, Minnesota, on board with its development plans, particularly as 71 per cent of Americans surveyed in a Gallup poll earlier this year opposed the construction of a data centre in their local area. Developing such a significant renewable energy project will also help Google meet its target of operating entirely on carbon-free energy by 2030.

The proposed agreement includes minimum demand charges and exit fees, meaning that Google will be required to finance the development of the infrastructure even if the demand for AI decreases. Under the proposed agreement, Google would pay minimum monthly charges based on at least 75 per cent of its contracted capacity, even if its electricity consumption falls below that level. If the company terminates the agreement early, it could face exit fees equivalent to as much as eight years of minimum demand charges.

ADVERTISEMENT

Amanda Rome, executive vice president and chief customer officer at Xcel Energy, explained, “Nobody wants to have a big buildout and then have nowhere for that power to go and nobody to pay for that power… That’s where these protections come in.” The Clean Energy Accelerator Charge (CEAC) agreement model uses the same structure as the Clean Transition Tariff (CTT) Google developed with NV Energy. It is currently pending approval from the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission.

In its statement about the agreement, Google’s Head of Energy Market Innovation, Briana Kobor, said, “Google’s partnership with Xcel Energy reimagines how data centres can be served, enabling us to be a catalyst for electricity innovation and helping to ensure our growth supports a cleaner, more affordable energy future for the communities we call home.”

The rapid rollout of data centres in the United States is driving up the country’s electricity demand to unprecedented levels. The U.S. DOE Office of Science national laboratory, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, estimates that data centres could account for 11.8 per cent of total U.S. electricity by 2030.

Meanwhile, the Energy Information Administration (EIA) projects that electricity consumed by data centre servers could reach between 446 billion and 818 billion kilowatt-hours (BkWh) annually by 2050, accounting for between 22 per cent and 33 per cent of commercial building electricity consumption. This is driving demand for new clean energy capacity to ensure that data centres are not powered by fossil fuels – although several companies still depend on gas-powered plants.

As utilities respond to the growing power demand by rapidly building out the grid, which costs billions of dollars to do, they are ultimately expecting the demand for AI data centres to continue. However, if the demand for AI wanes or the government decides to regulate the sector more strictly, electricity demand could fall, potentially leaving consumers to foot the bill for infrastructure upgrades.

In addition, the use of clean power in data centre operations is not the only sustainability concern. In October last year, the Minnesota Centre for Environmental Advocacy filed a lawsuit against the city of Pine Island, claiming that the environmental study for the development was vague, initially omitted Google as the end user, and failed to disclose impacts on energy, water, noise, and generators.

ADVERTISEMENT

The initial Alternative Urban Area Review (AUAR) indicated that the new data centre would use approximately 55.7 million gallons of water per year, thereby increasing the city’s total water consumption by approximately 50 per cent. Meanwhile, environmental groups have voiced concerns about the lack of comprehensive groundwater impact analysis. Meanwhile, opponents have questioned whether wastewater discharges may potentially run into the Zumbro River. In a Pine Island survey conducted between 1st and 31st August, 75.8 per cent of participants are against the construction of Project Skyway.

While Google has made bold promises to upgrade the grid through clean energy projects, residents and environmental groups have broader concerns about consumer protections and the projects’ environmental impact. So, while Google may be attempting to develop a more “sustainable” data centre, it is failing to win over local residents, who remain concerned about the long-term implications of building a giant AI data centre.

title: Fossilflation: War on Iran oil shock shows why we need to replace fossil fuels with renewables
description:
The latest oil price shock has exposed a problem that goes far beyond the war on Iran and its devastating human and environmental consequences.
Without the oil price shock, eurozone inflation in August would have been 2.2 per cent, rather than 3.2 per cent.
And it is a problem that will keep returning for as long as our economies depend on fossil fuels.
Fossil fuels keep exporting crises into our homes People around the world already know what fossilflation feels like.
Replace the system that keeps making people pay Fossilflation reveals a fundamental contradiction in the current energy system.
text:
The latest oil price shock has exposed a problem that goes far beyond the war on Iran and its devastating human and environmental consequences. New Greenpeace International analysis shows how dependence on fossil fuels leaves household budgets exposed to volatile international markets, with price shocks feeding through into the wider economy.

Between January and August 2026, fossil fuel prices accounted for the entire 1.5 percentage point rise in eurozone inflation, according to the analysis. Without the oil price shock, eurozone inflation in August would have been 2.2 per cent, rather than 3.2 per cent.

This is fossilflation. And it is a problem that will keep returning for as long as our economies depend on fossil fuels.

Fossil fuels keep exporting crises into our homes

People around the world already know what fossilflation feels like. When oil and gas prices rise, the effects reach far beyond the petrol station or the energy bill. They ripple through transport, food production, manufacturing and the cost of everyday goods and services.

The latest price shock has been felt globally, but not equally. While the analysis focuses on Europe and the US, the consequences extend to regions such as Southeast Asia and Africa, where households and economies often have less capacity to absorb higher prices. Rising costs can push essential goods and energy further out of reach, compounding existing inequalities.

The result is an economic system in which people have little control over the forces driving their living costs. A war or disruption thousands of kilometres away can send prices soaring at home, regardless of whether households have changed how much energy they use.

An inherent feature, not a bug

The new analysis shows just how strongly energy prices have shaped inflation in recent years. Energy prices drove 100 per cent of changes in inflation in the US and in the Eurozone so far in 2026.

Before the pandemic, the figures were already high: 71 per cent in the eurozone and 93 per cent in the US. This suggests fossilflation is not simply a temporary consequence of an exceptional crisis. It is a recurring vulnerability built into an economy that remains dependent on volatile fossil fuel markets.

Interest rate rises cannot fix the underlying problem. Central banks can try to dampen inflation by reducing demand, but they cannot stop wars, prevent disruptions to oil and gas supplies or make international fossil fuel prices predictable. Higher borrowing costs can add pressure for households and local businesses without removing the source of the shock.

As long as fossil fuels remain central to our energy systems, the next disruption will trigger another wave of price rises. The trigger may change, but the vulnerability remains.

Electrification and renewables offers a way out

The analysis also points to a different future: one in which households are less exposed to fossil fuel price shocks because they generate and use clean energy.

In a simulation, a fully electrified German household using an electric vehicle, heat pump, rooftop solar and battery storage experienced a 1.5 per cent price increase between January and August 2026, compared with 2.5 per cent for the official consumer basket.

This is an illustration of the protection that electrification and locally generated renewable energy can offer. Rooftop solar and batteries can reduce reliance on volatile energy markets. Electric vehicles and heat pumps can replace oil and gas consumption with electricity, increasingly supplied by renewable sources.

The benefits extend beyond individual households. A decentralised renewable energy system, built around clean power generated closer to where it is used, can reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels and give communities greater control over their energy supply.

But these benefits will not reach everyone automatically. Governments must accelerate the transition and ensure households can access the technologies, infrastructure and support they need. People already struggling with energy costs should not be left behind while others benefit from cheaper, cleaner energy.

Replace the system that keeps making people pay

Fossilflation reveals a fundamental contradiction in the current energy system. Governments are expected to protect people from rising living costs, yet continued dependence on fossil fuels leaves people exposed to price shocks governments cannot control.

The answer cannot be to wait for the next crisis and then try to cushion its effects. Nor can it be to treat every price spike as an isolated event. The underlying vulnerability must be addressed.

Governments must speed up the replacement of fossil fuels with decentralised renewable energy and electrification. That means expanding access to clean electricity, accelerating the rollout of solar and batteries, supporting the shift to electric transport and heating, and ensuring the transition benefits households and communities.

The latest data makes clearer what people across the world are already experiencing: fossil fuel dependence is a source of economic instability, not security. The war in Iran has exposed that vulnerability once again. Unless we replace the system that creates it, another shock will come, and people will be left paying the price.

A renewable energy system offers a way to break that cycle: cutting climate pollution while giving people greater protection from volatile international markets and more control over the energy they depend on.

Martin Zavan is a freelance communications strategist at Greenpeace International, based in Sydney.

With electricity demand rising rapidly in Virginia, a $250 million battery storage facility in is boosting ‘s capacity to meet peak demand while generating new revenue for the county.

Prospect Power Storage, located near Timberville in Rockingham County, increases the “flexibility to store power when we don’t need it and use it when we do,” says Dominion spokesman Tim Eberly.

The facility is owned by Elevate Infrastructure, a portfolio company of , and Dominion is obtaining electric power from the facility through a 15-year contract. Elevate Chief Commercial Officer Will Mitchell says the facility consists of 144 lithium-ion batteries, each the size of a shipping container, located on a 20-acre site.

The installation, which became operational in May, can store up to 600 megawatt-hours of electricity after charging for four hours, then discharge up to 150 megawatts of fast-response power for four hours when electrical demand peaks. That capacity is enough to temporarily supply the electric needs of about 100,000 homes. Prospect Power Storage is not only the largest stand-alone battery storage facility in Virginia, but within the PJM Interconnection grid that includes Virginia and 12 other states.

Bringing the project online generated 85 jobs and about $1.4 million in related spending, Mitchell says. Although only one employee is needed to keep the facility operational, the site is expected to pay $600,000 in property taxes during the next 20 years. A revenue-sharing deal also is projected to generate about $5.5 million for Rockingham County over the same period.

The project comes as Virginia prepares for a much larger build-out of . In April, Gov. Abigail Spanberger signed a bill that sets a goal for the state’s grid to have an energy-storing capacity of 4,000 megawatts by 2030 and 16,000 megawatts by 2045.

Although battery storage is an evolving technology, Eberly says that even a short-term energy repository adds one more needed facet to a diversified power array that includes coal, natural gas, nuclear and renewable solar and wind power. Additionally, the increased ability to store energy will help Dominion move closer to meeting the state mandate of 100% carbon-free power generation by 2045.

Battery storage, Eberly says, is “the unsung hero of the clean energy movement,” while Mitchell calls it “the Swiss army knife of the .”
