text:
Green Advantage

02 Nov. 2026

Employment in an AI-Enabled Economy

Last updated: 01 Nov. 2026

Full report

Download PDF - 3.94 MB

Technical annex

Download PDF - 1.234 MB

Across all measures examined, green jobs have less potential for AI substitution than jobs in the UK economy as a whole. This pattern reflects two groups of occupations.

In the first, exposure to AI is low because its capabilities overlap with relatively few of the abilities required, leaving limited scope for current AI systems to perform the core work. In the second, AI capabilities align more closely with the work, but requirements such as responsibility, judgement and interpersonal interaction make AI more likely to complement workers’ expertise than replace it.

AI and green apprenticeship routes for young people •

Around 96% of young people on green apprenticeships in England are training for occupations with lower potential for AI substitution, compared with around three quarters (73%) across apprenticeships as a whole. This reflects the concentration of green apprenticeships in trades and technical roles, where AI overlaps with relatively few of the abilities the work requires.

This profile is driven by trades. Green apprenticeships cover two broad groups: roles that directly deliver environmental outcomes, such as horticulture and environmental practice, and established trades whose skills are changing with the transition, such as electricians and plumbers. All ten of the largest apprenticeships in the second group lead into occupations with low AI exposure, led by installation and maintenance electricians, motor vehicle service and maintenance technicians, and plumbing and domestic heating technicians. Nine of the ten largest in the first group also lead into occupations with lower substitution potential. Overall, around 86% of young people on green apprenticeships are training for low-exposure occupations.

Green apprenticeships already operate at scale, accounting for around 32% of all apprenticeship participation among 16- to 24-year-olds in England. Around two thirds of this is at Level 3, broadly equivalent to A levels. Green standards make up only around one in five (19%) apprenticeships at Level 2, broadly equivalent to GCSEs, which is an important entry point for young people with few or no qualifications.

AI and the current green workforce •

More than four in five green jobs are in occupations with lower substitution potential. The figure is around 82% and 84% respectively on the ONS-defined Low Carbon and Renewable Energy Economy (LCREE) and Environmental Goods and Services Sector (EGSS) measures, compared with around 74% across the UK workforce.

The share of green jobs in the occupations with the highest substitution potential is around a third lower than across the UK on the LCREE measure (18% against 26%) and nearly two fifths lower on the EGSS measure (16%).

The difference is driven by low-exposure work, which accounts for half of LCREE employment and 58% of EGSS employment, against 41% across the UK. The largest green occupations are practical trades and operative roles, including construction trades, carpenters and joiners, plumbers, electricians and water and sewerage plant operatives.

AI and future clean energy workforce demand

Clean energy employment is expected to almost double, from around 440,000 in 2023 to 860,000 by 2030, according to the government's Clean Energy Jobs Plan. Every UK region will need additional workers, with the largest requirements in Scotland and the East of England, at around 55,000 to 60,000 each.

The large majority of additional workers needed in priority occupations by 2030, around 94%, are in occupations with lower substitution potential. Two thirds (66%) are in low-exposure occupations, and a further 28% are in occupations where AI is more likely to support the worker.

Demand is concentrated in established trades. Plumbers and heating and ventilating installers have the largest projected increase, at 8,500 to 10,000 additional workers. Electricians and carpenters and joiners each need a further 7,000 to 8,499.

Many of these roles are accessible without a degree. Skills England estimates that 59% of projected additional employment in key priority occupations will require qualifications at Level 2 or 3, making clean energy one of only three sectors, alongside adult social care and construction, where most expected demand sits at these levels.

AI in renewable energy and low-carbon transport

These are among the fastest-growing parts of the green economy. Between 2014 and 2024, renewable energy employment grew by around 64% to 70,600 full-time equivalents. Low-carbon transport employment grew by around 260% to 33,400.

Around four in five jobs in each sector are in occupations with lower substitution potential. The share in the category with the highest substitution potential is 19% in renewable energy and 20% in low-carbon transport, against 26% across the UK, which is around a quarter lower.

Both sectors are close to the UK average for occupations where AI is more likely to support workers, at 34% and 33% against 34% nationally, standing to gain from AI-driven productivity improvements to a similar degree as the wider economy.

Most of the largest occupations in both sectors combine lower substitution potential with an established apprenticeship pathway. This applies to eight of the ten largest occupations in renewable energy and six of the ten largest in low-carbon transport.

text:
Japan, the United States, and South Korea are considering Indonesia a leading candidate for deploying small modular reactors (SMRs), a next-generation nuclear technology the three countries are jointly developing.

The initiative aims to counter the growing influence of China and Russia, both of which are seeking to strengthen their foothold in the Indo-Pacific through nuclear power plant exports, multiple government sources said on October 25.

SMR Interest Grows in Southeast Asia

Interest in SMRs is growing across Southeast Asia as electricity demand rises, driven in part by the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI). The three countries hope to establish a foothold in Indonesia before expanding into other markets, including Malaysia and the Philippines.

Leveraging Each Country's Strengths

The three countries bring complementary strengths to the initiative. The United States leads in reactor design, South Korea specializes in nuclear power plant construction, and Japan excels in manufacturing critical components. They are also considering establishing a joint venture involving companies from all three countries.

Competition With Russia Intensifies

Indonesia has already reached an agreement with a Russian state-owned nuclear company to introduce floating nuclear power plants.

Meanwhile, Japanese and American companies are conducting feasibility studies on deploying their own reactors, intensifying competition in the country's nuclear energy market.

Nuclear power plant exports create long-term ties between supplier and recipient countries, as fuel supplies and maintenance services remain necessary long after construction is complete. These relationships can help exporting countries maintain their economic and security influence.

text:
It’s been a big year for anti-data center activism in North Carolina. WFDD’s April Laissle has had a front-row seat, attending packed public meetings across the Piedmont and listening to hours of testimony from concerned residents. With Election Day imminent, she wanted to know: how is the debate carrying over to the midterms?

For this week’s Carolina Curious, we brought the question to Western Carolina University political science professor Chris Cooper.

Interview Highlights

On the debate becoming a major campaign issue:

“I think we could have predicted that the economy would matter. We could have predicted that prices and affordability and all that would matter. Healthcare, sure, but I think the data centers issue is really the one new one that seems to be defining this election season.”

On politicians following the public's lead:

“It's very clear that candidates want to make known their stance on data centers, their stance that they are against data centers, or at least for more restrictions on data centers. So I think this is definitely a case where the leaders are following the people. Some folks in office, particularly some Republicans, might have seen this as economic development just six months ago, but now the way public opinion has changed, they are a bit on their heels.”

On the role the issue could play in future elections:

“I expect this cycle the data center issue is going to probably be the number one issue for some of these municipal off-year elections coming up in 2027. So after this election, don't feel like we're done with this issue for two more years."

description:

It lost about 12,575 people, a drop of less than half a percent from 2024, when the state marked two years of estimated population growth.

text:
This story was originally published by Bridge Michigan, a nonprofit and nonpartisan news organization. Visit the newsroom online at bridgemi.com.

US Census Bureau data released this week shows a tiny decrease in state population

Median household income increased, but trails the nation

Among other takeaways: Electric vehicle ownership in Michigan is also below the national average, with about 148,000 households owning an EV

Michigan’s population held steady last year, while four of the state’s 17 largest cities saw modest increases, according to data released by the US Census Bureau this week.

The Census Bureau estimated that Michigan had about 10.1 million residents in 2025. It lost about 12,575 people, a drop of less than half a percent from 2024, when the state marked two years of estimated population growth.

Michigan’s two largest cities, Detroit and Grand Rapids, both inched up 0.5% in population — adding 3,413 and 1,049 people respectively. But Lansing saw the biggest gain among large cities. It added 1,317 new residents, boosting its population by about 1.2% from 2024.

Detroit’s estimated population last year was 649,115. Grand Rapids remained the second largest city in the state with its 201,180 estimated population, and Lansing’s increase took it to 114,783, the sixth largest in Michigan.

Dearborn, Southfield, Rochester Hills and Farmington Hills each lost around 800 residents, but their estimated populations all remain larger than 75,000.

The annual American Community Survey looks at a wide variety of characteristics – from educational attainment to income to transportation – to provide national and statewide estimates as well as estimates for areas with more than 65,000 residents.

Here are some key takeaways:

Income

While the median household income in Michigan increased from $72,389 in 2024 to $75,832 in 2025, the state still trails the national median household income of $84,780, according to Census data.

EVs and solar panels

The survey, for the first time, included data on households that have an electric vehicle or solar panels. In Michigan, an estimated 148,819 households, or about 4%, had an electric vehicle last year, a rate that came below the 5.5% national estimate.

Among nearby states, Michigan trailed Illinois and Minnesota in the percentage of households with an electric vehicle.

“Western states have led the way in switching to electric vehicles,” Tricia Holley, a survey statistician at the Census Bureau, said in a news release.

“California overall had the highest rate of EV adoption per household, followed by Washington, Hawaii and Nevada.”

The Census estimated that 65,918 Michigan households were equipped with solar panels in 2025, which trailed Illinois and Ohio, which had 177,113 and 72,125, respectively.

Education

Michiganders with a high school diploma or equivalent stood at 92.7% in 2025, higher than the 90.6% national estimate. However, when it comes to the portion of the population to earn a bachelor’s degree or higher, Michigan’s 33.9% estimate was below the 37.4% seen across the country.

Michigan’s struggles with postsecondary degrees have persisted for nearly a decade. According to data on SAT scores released earlier this year, only a fourth of 11th graders in the state are college ready, a slight dip from 26.6% the year prior. A decade ago, it was 35%.

Matt Mencarini is a Report for America corps member who covers data and accountability for Bridge Michigan.

name: American Energy
title: A California hillside water battery is designed to hold 5 million gallons in its upper tank that ...
description:
The Lake County version uses no dam at all.
Five million gallons the turbines never get The fire angle is where this gets interesting, and it’s also where the name comes from.
Is 5 million gallons a lot?
A battery pack can’t put out a wildfire, and a battery pack doesn’t refill itself from the sun every morning the way a solar-fed water tank does.
It’s arguably the most Lake County idea anyone’s had.
text:
If you live anywhere PG&E strings a wire, you already know the drill. The forecast calls for wind, the humidity drops, and the utility announces a Public Safety Power Shutoff, which is the polite name for switching off your neighborhood so a power line can’t start a fire. On Thursday, October 15, that meant 3,601 customers in Lake County, California, sitting in the dark under a red flag warning, part of what the Press Democrat described as the utility’s biggest planned outage since 2021.

That same Thursday, in the same county, a drilling rig run by an outfit from Forestville was pulling core samples out of a hillside in Hidden Valley Lake for a battery made of water. The kind of battery that, if it ever gets built, is supposed to keep the lights on through exactly that sort of shutoff. And its top tank is designed to double as the fire department’s emergency reserve.

I had to read the acronym three times. The project is called FLASHES, which stands for Firemain Linked Auxiliary Supply/Hydraulic Energy Storage.

The developer is Trane Energy Services, which is the part of Trane Technologies that does energy projects rather than air conditioners, and the money for the study is coming from PG&E’s Microgrid Incentive Program. So the utility that cut the power is paying to find out whether a hill full of water can stop that from mattering next time.

So what is a water battery, exactly?

Pumped hydro is about the oldest trick in the energy storage book. You pump water uphill when electricity is cheap and plentiful, you let it run back down through a turbine when it isn’t, and the hill does the storing. The big ones use dams and whole valleys.

The Lake County version uses no dam at all. As Microgrid Knowledge put it, there’s “just two tanks and a hill.”

Here’s the loop. A solar field covering more than 100 acres makes power during the day. That power runs pumps that push water from a tank at the bottom of the slope up to roofed tanks at the top.

In the evening, or during an outage, the water drops back down through a turbine and comes out as electricity again. The tanks are covered, which keeps the water from evaporating in a county that bakes all summer, and the water itself is supposed to come from a dedicated well that developers told the Press Democrat could reach more than 1,000 feet down.

That well is, frankly, the whole ballgame. Trane’s Michael Day told Lake County supervisors back in June that the project has to prove it’s pulling water from somewhere other than the local supply everyone else is drinking from. If the geology down there doesn’t cooperate, none of the rest matters.

Five million gallons the turbines never get

The fire angle is where this gets interesting, and it’s also where the name comes from. “Firemain Linked” means the upper tank is plumbed into the firefighting water system, and part of it gets walled off from the energy side entirely. Day told the Press Democrat the upper tank would always hold 5 million gallons as a “never-touch-it emergency fire reserve.” Those 5 million gallons sit above the turbines and are meant to go to firefighters without ever being spun into electricity first.

Is 5 million gallons a lot? For a fire crew it’s a pretty big deal.

A typical engine tank holds a few hundred gallons, and a rural water district’s whole storage tank can be well under a million. Having 5 million gallons parked on a hill above your subdivision, pressurized by gravity, is the sort of thing Lake County has wanted for a while now, given that the place has burned repeatedly over the past decade.

You might be asking why anyone would build a giant hydro battery just to get a fire tank, and the answer is you wouldn’t. Day calls these triple-threat facilities, and his pitch to Microgrid Knowledge was that their day job is making solar power, storing it and selling it back to the California grid during peak hours. The fire reserve is a bonus bolted onto a machine that’s supposed to pay for itself. Whether it actually does is what the next year and a half is for.

Three plants, two hills, one feasibility study

PG&E’s project manager Madison Hoffacker laid out the design figures for the study: one facility at 10 megawatts of solar with 40 megawatt-hours of storage, and two at 20 megawatts of solar with 80 megawatt-hours each. Those are paper numbers for a project that is still at the feasibility stage, not a built plant. If you’re not used to those units, megawatts are how fast the thing can deliver power and megawatt-hours are how much it has in the tank.

An 80 megawatt-hour plant running flat out at 20 megawatts would last about four hours, give or take. At half output it’d go roughly twice as long.

The Hidden Valley Lake unit is one of the 80 megawatt-hour plants. The other two, serving the Hartley and Lucerne areas on Clear Lake’s northwest side, are being developed together as one project near North Lakeport.

Day sketched that northern setup for the Press Democrat as design figures, not as something poured in concrete: a pair of upper tanks in the 45 million gallon range apiece, one lower tank roughly twice that size at about 90 million gallons, and three pipelines running down to generators rated at 10 megawatts each. For comparison, Hidden Valley Lake itself, the reservoir the town is named after, holds about 3,500 acre-feet, which is north of a billion gallons. So we’re talking tanks, not lakes, but very large tanks.

I couldn’t find a published height for any of those tanks, and height is what decides how hard the water hits the turbine, so I can’t tell you how the gallons translate into the megawatt-hours. That math stays inside Trane’s spreadsheets until the study comes out.

Why not just buy lithium batteries, like everyone else on the planet? Two reasons, as far as I can tell. A battery pack can’t put out a wildfire, and a battery pack doesn’t refill itself from the sun every morning the way a solar-fed water tank does.

PG&E’s own release talks about “multi-day resilience” during outages, which is a bigger claim than the four hours of storage suggests, and it only works if the panels keep pumping water back up each day while the grid is down. That’s the utility’s framing, so take it as a goal rather than a spec.

What actually started on October 15

Here’s what I’d want you to hold onto. Nothing has been built yet, and the well everything depends on hasn’t been drilled.

The rig at Hidden Valley Lake was doing geotechnical core boring, which is a fancy way of saying it drilled holes to see what the hill is made of. PG&E’s September 17 announcement spells out what the grant pays for: the core boring, some early test wells, and the environmental and financial studies.

Day was pretty blunt about it on camera, telling the Press Democrat that what began on October 15 was a feasibility study and nothing resembling construction. Trane expects to know whether the projects pencil out by May or June 2027, and the Press Democrat put the overall proposal at about $300 million, a developer estimate rather than a signed construction contract. Lake County hasn’t even decided whether it wants to own the plants itself or hand them off to an investor, according to Day, and the study is supposed to settle that too.

The Microgrid Incentive Program behind this is a $200 million statewide pot approved by the California Public Utilities Commission, with $79.2 million allocated to PG&E and a cap of $14 million per project. PG&E told Microgrid Knowledge that developers in the program expect to find about $6 from other sources for every dollar the utility puts in.

So the grant gets you drilling and paperwork. It doesn’t get you a hill full of water.

I’ll admit a soft spot for this one. Lake County is a place where the lights go off on purpose every fall and the hills catch fire anyway, and somebody looked at that and designed a machine that stores sunlight in a tank the fire department can also drink from.

It’s arguably the most Lake County idea anyone’s had. Whether wells 1,000 feet down can keep tanks holding tens of millions of gallons topped up without draining someone’s aquifer is a fairly big if, and that’s what the drill rig was there to answer.

Trane’s Johnny Brown said the company has spent seven years working on this with the county. The drilling at Hidden Valley Lake started on October 15, 2026, with Pearson Drilling of Forestville operating the rig, and the viability call is due in May or June of 2027.

title: Why Is This Rare Earth Metal 346 Times More Expensive In America Than in China? | OilPrice.com
description:
The arrangement protects MP Materials against the price collapses that have historically threatened Western rare earth producers.
American manufacturers buy about 48,000 tonnes of rare earth magnets a year, and in 2025 the U.S. made just 300 tonnes.
REalloys already operates a facility in Euclid, Ohio, producing rare earth metals, alloys and magnet materials.
The company says it has the only operating heavy rare earth metallization capability in North America, giving it an early position in the industrial process that Canaccord expects to become increasingly scarce.
The Next Wave of Rare Earth Demand Could Dwarf the Last By 2035, the world could need 365,000 tonnes of rare earth magnets a year.
text:
Samarium sells for as much as 346 times more in North America than in China, and that price is just a preview of what American industry would pay the day Beijing stops exporting.

Jet engines, industrial motors, EVs, wind turbines and medical scanners all run on rare earth magnets, and most U.S. manufacturers still buy theirs from China, at Chinese prices.

Outside China, dysprosium costs five times as much and yttrium more than 100 times as much. Japan has already learned what happens when the Chinese supply slows: its government is asking Washington for help before its yttrium runs out at year-end.

REalloys (NASDAQ: ALOY) is positioning itself to profit from one of the most serious shortages developing in America's rare earth supply chain, and it's a shortage that billions of dollars in new mining and magnet manufacturing investments won't solve on their own.

Washington has begun intervening to protect domestic production from Chinese price competition. Under its 10-year agreement with MP Materials, the Pentagon guarantees a minimum price of $110 per kilogram for NdPr, making up the difference when benchmark prices fall below that level. The arrangement protects MP Materials against the price collapses that have historically threatened Western rare earth producers.

But in the meantime, investment in new mines and magnet factories is accelerating, creating an increasingly urgent question: who will supply the rare earth metals and alloys needed to connect the two?

That's where REalloys is concentrating its efforts. For magnet manufacturers, rare earth oxides first have to be reduced to metal, then melted with other materials and cast into the alloy strip that feeds the magnet line.

China controls more than 90% of the world's 210,000 tonnes of capacity for that step, according to Canaccord Genuity, whose analysts call metallization "a major blind spot in western supply chain development." The strip casters that make the alloy now take up to two years to deliver, and Canaccord's channel checks found that buying them from China is "impossible under current export controls."

Canaccord expects magnet plant capacity outside China to more than triple to about 70,000 tonnes by 2030. Non-Chinese metal and alloy capacity, however, is expected to reach just 38,000 tonnes over the same period, roughly half of what those new magnet plants will need.

Every Western magnet line that opens without its own metal supply will have to buy from China or compete with other Western plants for limited alternative supplies.

ING has warned that China's grip may outlast this decade because the bottleneck is "industrial rather than geological." American manufacturers buy about 48,000 tonnes of rare earth magnets a year, and in 2025 the U.S. made just 300 tonnes.

REalloys already operates a facility in Euclid, Ohio, producing rare earth metals, alloys and magnet materials. The company says it has the only operating heavy rare earth metallization capability in North America, giving it an early position in the industrial process that Canaccord expects to become increasingly scarce.

The company has also secured non-Chinese feedstock to support its expansion. It holds rights to approximately 80% of the Saskatchewan Research Council's expanded output, including roughly 525 tonnes of NdPr metal annually, alongside dysprosium and terbium products. It also has a 15-year offtake agreement covering 15% of Phase 1 production from Critical Metals Corp.'s (NASDAQ: CRML) Tanbreez project in Greenland.

Under a Defense Logistics Agency contract, it is designing a 300-tonne-per-year facility for samarium and gadolinium metal, two materials with no established commercial production in the United States. Samarium currently commands a price premium of as much as 346 times its Chinese price in North America, illustrating the extraordinary economics of supply outside Beijing's control.

REalloys reported $122.4 million in cash at the end of June and says its Saskatchewan and metallization expansions are fully funded. With Western magnet manufacturing capacity projected to grow far faster than non-Chinese metal production, REalloys is building capacity in the part of the supply chain where manufacturers could face some of their toughest shortages.

The Next Wave of Rare Earth Demand Could Dwarf the Last

By 2035, the world could need 365,000 tonnes of rare earth magnets a year. And Canaccord Genuity has just raised that forecast by another 15%, as EVs, data centers, drones and humanoid robots push demand beyond its earlier projections.

The bank expects global NdFeB magnet demand to grow 7.3% annually, with EV sales more than doubling from 23.5 million this year to 52 million in 2035.

Canaccord analyst Reg Spencer has also pointed to the growing demand from data centers, e-bikes, scooters and drones. Drones account for only about 1% of forecast demand, but Ukraine and Russia alone were estimated to produce some 9 million military drones, and Canaccord acknowledges that its estimates may prove conservative.

And Canaccord may still be underestimating one of the biggest emerging sources of demand: humanoid robots. Canaccord models humanoid robot deliveries growing 45% annually to 2.5 million units by 2035, while Tesla is reportedly preparing an Optimus production line designed for 1 million robots a year. Global EV sales rose more than 4,600% between 2014 and 2024, demonstrating how quickly a new source of magnet demand can expand.

If robots follow anything close to that trajectory, today's magnet forecasts could prompt another major upward revision.

Independent McKinsey research also projects annual demand growth of approximately 8.8% for dysprosium and terbium, two heavy rare earths essential to high-performance magnets.

Canaccord expects the NdPr market to run a roughly 7% deficit this year, with shortages continuing through 2028. New mines and refineries in Australia, Malawi, Brazil and Utah, alongside Lynas' expansions, could bring the market roughly into balance between 2029 and 2031. But the deficit is projected to return and widen to 10% by 2035, while dysprosium and terbium face a projected 12% shortfall.

The International Energy Agency independently projects a 50% increase in demand for magnet rare earths outside China by 2035 and warns that non-Chinese metallization and magnet manufacturing capacity will remain severely inadequate even if all announced projects proceed. Every new magnet factory will need a reliable source of rare earth metals and alloys, and the companies capable of supplying those materials outside China are entering a market where demand is expected to outgrow available production.

The broader race to secure critical minerals is already reshaping the world's largest mining companies. Copper and lithium producers are expanding operations and investing in supply chains essential to electrification, batteries and advanced manufacturing. Although these materials serve different purposes from rare earth magnets, the investments demonstrate just how much industrial capacity the West is trying to build as demand accelerates.

BHP Group (NYSE: BHP) is one of the largest beneficiaries of the global push for electrification, with its copper operations spanning Chile, Australia and Peru. The mining giant produced approximately 1.95 million tonnes of copper in fiscal 2026, while its copper division generated $18.2 billion in underlying EBITDA, up nearly 48% from the previous year. Its Escondida operation in Chile remains one of the world's most important copper mines, supplying a metal essential to electricity grids, industrial motors and data center infrastructure. With BHP anticipating continued long-term growth in copper demand, its expanding focus on the metal reflects the scale of investment required to support an increasingly electrified global economy.

Teck Resources (NYSE: TECK) is another major player strengthening its position in critical minerals, particularly copper and zinc. The Canadian miner operates the Quebrada Blanca mine in Chile, Highland Valley Copper in Canada, and holds an interest in Peru's Antamina mine. In its latest third-quarter results, Teck reported C$2.3 billion in adjusted EBITDA, nearly double the previous year's level, supported by record copper prices and stronger operational performance. Copper production increased 11% year-over-year to 115,700 tonnes. The company is also pursuing a merger with Anglo American, a transaction designed to create one of the world's leading copper producers and significantly expand its presence in the global critical-minerals market.

Freeport-McMoRan (NYSE: FCX) sits at the center of America's copper supply chain, with major mining operations across the United States, South America and Indonesia. Its Morenci operation in Arizona and Grasberg mining complex in Indonesia are among the industry's most significant assets. Freeport produced 832 million pounds of copper during the third quarter of 2026, alongside 234,000 ounces of gold and 22 million pounds of molybdenum. The company is also advancing copper recovery technologies and potential expansions in the Americas as demand grows from electricity infrastructure, data centers and industrial manufacturing. Its scale demonstrates the importance of securing reliable domestic and allied supplies of materials critical to modern industry.

Albemarle Corporation (NYSE: ALB) provides another perspective on the critical-minerals race through its position in the global lithium industry. The company operates lithium resources and processing facilities across Chile, Australia and the United States, supplying materials used in electric vehicle batteries and energy storage systems. Albemarle reported second-quarter 2026 revenue of $1.7 billion, up 31% year-over-year, while adjusted EBITDA climbed 155% to $858 million, supported by stronger lithium pricing and improved operating performance. Its operations at Chile's Salar de Atacama and Australia's Greenbushes and Wodgina projects illustrate the geographical reach of the global battery supply chain and the importance of securing both mineral resources and processing capabilities.

For REalloys (NASDAQ: ALOY), the opportunity grows with every new magnet factory that comes online outside China. Those factories will need a dependable supply of rare earth metals and alloys, and Canaccord's forecasts suggest there won't be nearly enough to go around.

REalloys has an operating facility in Ohio, has secured feedstock for expansion, and has the financing to pursue what it says will be the largest heavy rare earth metallization facility outside China and the first commercial-scale heavy rare earth metallization platform in the Western Hemisphere. If Canaccord's demand forecasts prove accurate, REalloys is building capacity in exactly the part of the supply chain where the next decade's shortages could be most severe.

text:
Breckenridge is joining a legal effort to challenge the federal government’s repeal of longstanding greenhouse gas regulations , citing concerns about the potential impacts of climate change on the town’s ski-dependent economy and mountain environment.

Breckenridge Town Council unanimously agreed Tuesday, Oct. 27, to sign onto a legal brief supporting a multistate lawsuit objecting to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s decision to rescind a 2009 scientific finding that greenhouse gas emissions threaten public health and welfare.

The Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding established the legal basis for federal regulations limiting greenhouse gas emissions from motor vehicles under the Clean Air Act. The EPA effectively axed the finding in February, eliminating federal emission standards for cars and trucks.

Colorado Attorney General and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Phil Weiser has joined attorneys general from 22 other states in challenging the decision , arguing that the rollback undermines efforts to combat climate change and protect public health.

In a legislative committee memo presented to Breckenridge council members, sustainability director Jessie Burley outlined several ways the federal ruling could affect the town, referencing increasingly volatile winters, heightened wildfire risks and additional costs for local governments.

“Climate change is already producing shorter, warmer and less predictable winters, directly threatening Breckenridge’s ski-dependent economy, local businesses and tax base,” the memo states.

The memo also warns that reduced snowpack and earlier spring snowmelt could lengthen wildfire seasons, driving up costs for emergency preparedness, insurance and infrastructure protection.

Town officials additionally expressed concern that the rollback could undermine investments in clean energy , electrification and climate resilience made under longstanding federal protections.

Breckenridge will participate by signing an amicus curiae , or “friend of the court,” brief, which allows organizations and municipalities to submit arguments supporting a legal challenge without becoming plaintiffs.

The law firm WilmerHale is preparing the brief on behalf of Aspen Skiing Company and a coalition of ski industry representatives and mountain communities, according to the memo.

text:
The proposal has divided clean energy and environmental groups, while a new report shows potential emissions benefits.

In less than two weeks, U.S. Senate leaders plan to take an initial vote on the divisive permitting reform bill aimed at easing regulatory barriers that can delay energy projects. As the date nears, some of the country’s leading environmental groups are ramping up their opposition, arguing that the measure would do more harm than good.

A new report from Resources for the Future, a research nonprofit, projects that the bill’s power-sector provisions would cut carbon emissions by 1.8 gigatons by 2041 and reduce annual electricity-system costs by an average of 3.5 percent to 7 percent compared to a scenario without the bill.

But the projected benefits are unlikely to convince the bill’s critics, partly because the analysis doesn’t address the provisions that have drawn the most opposition, including changes to the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.

The debate over the bill, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, has divided environmental and clean energy advocates and threatens to unravel a compromise between the bill’s Democratic and Republican co-sponsors.

On one side, clean energy business groups and advocacy organizations praise the bill’s approach to accelerating timelines for building transmission lines and renewable energy projects. On the other side, key environmental advocacy groups say the proposal would speed up fossil fuel infrastructure buildout and remove current tools to oppose projects.

“Over the next two years, BAAJA would create more legal runway for this president to make corrupt deals and greenlight harmful projects of all kinds, and it would constrain any future president from repairing the damage,” said Abigail Dillen, president of Earthjustice, an environmental law nonprofit, in a commentary posted on Tuesday.

The same day, four Senate Democrats sent a letter to the bill’s co-sponsors saying they have concerns that President Donald Trump’s administration cannot be trusted to follow through on promises that were made during negotiations.

“Beyond consideration of the actual text, the promise of BAAJA will only succeed if President Trump takes care that it is faithfully executed,” reads the letter from Democratic Sens. Tammy Duckworth of Illinois, Ed Markey of Massachusetts and Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden, both of Oregon. “The Trump administration’s record gives us no basis to assume that he will.”

The senators cite the Trump administration’s cancellation of already-approved clean energy grants and loans and evidence that decisions were made with intent to harm states that voted for Democrats. They said the administration should reinstate all canceled awards and commit in writing to no longer basing grant decisions on the political affiliation of a state’s elected officials.

If the administration doesn’t comply, the senators have threatened to oppose a motion to proceed to debate on the bill at a vote scheduled for Nov. 9. Losing the support of four senators who have been vocal advocates for environmental protection could make it harder to secure the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster.

In a statement, a Trump administration spokesperson said the White House supports the bill because it will deliver jobs and investment.

“The text of the legislation has been published, and all that is left to do is vote,” the spokesperson said. “We are in direct conversations with the lead negotiators in the Senate and are looking forward to action on this historic legislation to unleash more energy in the United States.”

A co-sponsor of the bill, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-Rhode Island, has also expressed concerns that the Trump administration will go to extraordinary lengths to oppose renewable energy even if the bill becomes law.

“We await real signs of regulatory good faith,” he said in a post on X, along with a link to a Bloomberg article about the administration’s recent contradictory actions on wind power.

Meanwhile, a coalition of conservative groups, many funded by the petrochemical billionaire Koch family’s network, urged the Senate this week to pass the bill to “protect property rights, promote energy abundance, and restore America’s ability to build.”

Emissions Cuts, But an Incomplete Picture

The new analysis by Resources for the Future follows several by other organizations that also show substantial cuts in emissions resulting from the power-sector provisions of the bill.

Resources for the Future is a leader using economic models to estimate the effects of complex legislation. Among the findings:

The bill would increase the country’s transmission line capacity by 30 percent by 2041, meaning more power can be transported on interstate power lines. A lack of transmission capacity is one of the main factors impeding construction of new wind, solar and battery projects and more lines would allow more of those systems to be built.

Building new, cleaner power sources would help displace some of the older, more polluting sources on the grid, adding 60 gigawatts of clean power capacity compared with a baseline scenario without the bill. The analysis also found that removing existing constraints would lead to a small increase in combined-cycle natural gas plants, though that effect would diminish over time.

Power-sector carbon dioxide emissions would be lower under the bill than without the bill, although both scenarios show emissions growth over the study period. Adopting the bill would reduce cumulative carbon emissions by 1.83 gigatons through 2041. In the final year, emissions would be 6 percent less than the baseline level.

Kevin Rennert, a research fellow at Resources for the Future and co-author of the report, acknowledged the limitations of focusing only on the power sector.

“Anybody that is making up their mind about this bill should look across a fulsome set of analyses to inform their overall take on what the bill would do,” he said.

Rennert was not aware of any report that attempts to estimate the emissions effects of the entire bill. One reason may be that some parts are challenging to analyze because of uncertainty about their potential effects.

Kevin Kircher, a mechanical engineering professor at Purdue University, has criticized the use of the economic models in the debate over the bill. He said models that examine only the power sector overlook potentially huge issues, such as methane leakage from increased gas use and emissions from fossil fuel exports, among others. He had no comment about the Resources for the Future report, which he had not yet read.

“I think hyper-focusing on the [power sector] is sort of missing the forest for the trees,” he said.

Kircher has concerns about the bill, including about the “project certainty” section, which would allow developers to sue the federal government for permit denials or delays. The change would let the Trump administration set implementation parameters, leaving future presidents little leeway to change course.

He has written that streamlining the permit process would largely benefit natural gas, based on the queue of projects in the PJM Interconnection and Midcontinent Independent System Operator regions.

Kircher also expressed dismay that the bill has divided groups that are usually allies.

“It’s really telling that so many people formed strong opinions before they would have had any time even to read [the bill], let alone to kind of think carefully about it,” Kircher said.

Marianne Lavelle contributed to this story.

The $100 Flight

| Joby Aviation's recent electric air taxi flight across Tampa Bay retraced the route of the world's first scheduled airline service, highlighting the promise of eVTOL aviation. Yet the real challenge is economic, not technical. With four seats, pilot costs, insurance, maintenance and infrastructure expenses, fares near $100 may be necessary initially. Long-term success will depend on aircraft utilization, network growth, passenger demand and eventually automation.

Read Full Story

The Second Life of EV Batteries: A Billion-Dollar Opportunity Meets a Reality Check

| Millions of EV batteries will eventually retire from automotive service, creating an opportunity for a second life in solar storage, grid support and commercial backup power. But reusing old batteries isn't as simple as connecting them to a new application. Testing, refurbishment, safety certification and falling prices for new batteries are challenging the economics. The emerging industry must prove that reuse can compete with recycling and newly manufactured storage systems.

Electric School Buses Didn't Fail. Washington's Rollout Did

| The $5 billion federal Clean School Bus Program has encountered delivery delays, manufacturer bankruptcies, reliability concerns and serious EPA oversight failures. But these shortcomings do not establish that electric school buses are a failed technology. They expose Washington's inability to manage a complex transportation transition. The real lessons involve procurement, infrastructure, manufacturer accountability and the need to measure actual results rather than simply announce ambitious spending targets.

text:
Joby Aviation has been working to bring its electric air taxis to Texas, and, in September, the company started flying them around Dallas-Fort Worth. The flights started at Perot Field Fort Worth Alliance Airport on September 10 and went on for about a week. During that time, Joby flew its air taxis into DFW Airport, as well as out to Arlington and along a route to Toyota's North American headquarters in Plano.

None of the flights carried any passengers, though. Instead, Joby says the test flights are designed to give the FAA the real-world data it needs to build safety rules for commercial air taxi service. However, Joby's CEO JoeBen Bevirt says the flights are "just the beginning of what Texas and Joby can build together," and it does seem like the company is planning to stick around in Texas.

Back in August, Joby signed a lease at Alliance Air Trade Center, which is part of Perot Field. The company says it will use the space as a base for its air taxi operations in Dallas-Fort Worth. That was about a month before Tesla launched its self-driving Cybercab in Austin, so there has been a lot going on in Texas when it comes to innovative ways to travel.

The flights Joby made in Dallas-Fort Worth are part of Project Nexus, which is TxDOT's piece of the FAA's eVTOL Integration Pilot Program. The FAA's program is set to run for three years, and Texas isn't the only state involved. TxDOT is working with Oklahoma, Louisiana, and the Choctaw Nation on the project, so the FAA will be able to test air taxis in cities as well as in rural areas.

The long-term goal of Project Nexus is to have air taxis make regional flights between Dallas, Austin, San Antonio, and eventually Houston. There's no date specified for when that could happen yet, though. Project Nexus isn't just about passenger flights, either. TxDOT also wants to test medical and cargo flights with these aircraft, and we've already seen a medical flight happen in another part of the FAA's program. In July, BETA Technologies and United Therapeutics flew a genetically modified pig heart between airports in Virginia and Maryland using BETA's electric aircraft, and that flight was actually the first one in the FAA's entire program. Getting an organ where it needs to go is highly impactful.

Joby still needs the FAA to certify its air taxi before it can start flying passengers. The company says it is currently in the fifth and final stage of the FAA's type certification process, but Joby hasn't revealed when people in Texas will be able to actually book a flight.

Getting to an air taxi might also be a problem for some people. The FAA says that early air taxis will use existing helipads where they can, and that they will operate a lot like helicopter services do today. The system will operate very differently from a robotaxi service like Waymo, where the car comes to pick you up. Even if air taxis were to expand the same way that Waymo has been to major U.S. cities like Las Vegas and San Diego, you wouldn't be able to call an air taxi as easily. Instead, you'd have to go to a helipad or landing site to catch your flight.

Air traffic at DFW is another thing that Joby and the FAA will have to deal with, too. DFW had the third-most takeoffs and landings of any airport in the world in 2025. NASA and Joby ran simulations of air taxi flights at DFW and Dallas Love Field back in 2023 to test procedures that could help reduce the workload on air traffic controllers. NASA researcher Ken Freeman said the simulation "validates the idea that we can find a way to safely integrate these vehicles into the airspace at scale." Still, a simulation isn't the same as flying real passengers over Dallas, and Joby hasn't done that yet.

text:
Companies should understand the significance of a June 21, 2021 U.S. Environmental Protection Agency ("EPA" or "Agency") memorandum entitled "Strengthening Environmental Justice Through Criminal Enforcement." Addressed to EPA personnel, including Senior Management and Special Agents with EPA's Office of Criminal Enforcement, Forensics and Training, and Regional Criminal Enforcement Counsel with EPA's Office of Regional Counsel, the memorandum outlines how EPA will work with the U.S. Department of Justice ("DOJ") and use existing resources to more aggressively identify and prosecute environmental crimes committed in "overburdened communities." A directive to focus investigative resources on particular communities and affirmatively consider criminal enforcement is unprecedented. Companies need to understand both their environmental justice risk profiles and the unique challenges associated with criminal investigations.

EPA's most recent memorandum should be seen in the context of the Administration's "whole of government" approach to environmental justice and also in conjunction with Attorney General Garland's statements regarding environmental crime victims. EPA makes clear that while the Department of Justice ("DOJ") retains prosecutorial discretion over environmental crimes, the Agency is taking steps to achieve environmental justice in criminal cases by strengthening tools for the detection of environmental crimes in overburdened communities, enhancing outreach to the victims of environmental crimes; and ensuring that EPA investigations are structured to maximally support the DOJ.

Enhanced Communication between EPA Civil and Criminal Staff - EPA recommends that civil and criminal staff maintain regular and open communication regarding increased facility inspections in overburdened communities. Historically, communication between the civil and criminal components of EPA has been discouraged, and it was rare for a civil case to "turn" criminal. This directive will increase the likelihood that civil enforcement matters in overburdened communities will be referred for criminal investigation.

Impact of Early Outreach to Environmental Crime Victims - EPA advises case teams to use crime victim data and other relevant information to ensure the proper identification of individuals harmed by purported environmental crimes in overburdened communities.EPA is also considering creative avenues for directly communicating with environmental crimes victims, such as use of social media platforms, with the intent, in part, to integrate environmental crime victim concerns into every investigation and prosecution and identify first-person testimony of harm to bolster enforcement outcomes.

Cross-Training of EPA and DOJ Staff on EJSCREEN and Other Tools - EPA will form an Environmental Justice Workgroup for EPA and DOJ staff focusing on the use of EPA's EJSCREEN mapping tool and the identification of crime victims. Training will be provided to EPA environmental justice staff on the criminal enforcement process to enhance cross-referrals. Historically, environmental criminal investigations have arisen in the context of catastrophic events, or in the face of blatant violations of the law. The use geospatial mapping tools in conjunction with criminal enforcement training of EPA civil personnel will almost certainly lead to broader categories of conduct being at risk for criminal investigation.

Focus on Environmental Justice Remedies - EPA has directed that investigations be conducted in a manner that facilitates the identification of remedies that meaningfully protect overburdened communities and victims of environmental crimes.Notably, the memorandum emphasizes that "EPA recognizes that punishment for environmental crimes must be sufficient to achieve the goal of deterrence." Further, EPA's Environmental Justice Workgroup will develop guidance for agency attorneys and prosecutors to ensure restitution, community service payments, and other court-ordered projects supporting overburdened communities are considered in all cases identified as having environmental justice concerns.Historically, investigations have focused primarily on identifying misconduct and proving the elements of the alleged crime. Expanding the scope of the investigation to include information relevant to potential remedies may significantly increase the duration of the investigation and make it even more difficult to discern the potential charges at issue.

Now, more than ever, it is important for companies to understand their risk profile with regard to environmental justice issues. We urge you to consider the ACELAS environmental justice resource, which provides a convenient framework for analysis. Equally important is understanding the unique risks associated with criminal enforcement and importance of having a crisis response plan in place.

The content of this article is intended to provide a general guide to the subject matter. Specialist advice should be sought about your specific circumstances.

text:
In autonomous and self-driving vehicle news are Waymo, Toyota, Baidu, Lyft, Freenow, WeRide, Allianz, Ping An, Marti, CalmCar, TIER IV, NTRO, May Mobility, Rivian, Aurora, Roush, , Kodiak, Hyundai and Innoviz.

Waymo Scales Toward 20,000 Vehicles as Witherite Law Group Flags Stalled First-Responder Bill

Witherite Law Group founder Amy Witherite has pointed to safety vulnerabilities in autonomous vehicle operations as federal legislation addressing first-responder interactions remains stalled in committee without cosponsors. The delay coincides with Waymo advancing plans to scale its commercial robotaxi deployment to a 20,000-vehicle fleet while conducting active roadway testing across Philadelphia.

The push follows incidents involving autonomous fleets and emergency personnel, including a May 28, 2025 event in Dallas in which a stalled, unoccupied Waymo obstructed fire apparatus responding to a fatal gas explosion. Rep. Kevin Mullin introduced H.R. 10033, the AV Emergency Response Coordination Act, which would mandate 30-second hotline response thresholds for commercial operators, two-minute scene clearance timelines, and explicit manual-override protocols for emergency responders. Oversight remains contested at the state and local level, with PennDOT maintaining preemptive regulatory authority over autonomous deployments and thereby restricting municipal intervention in Philadelphia. Safety advocates and NHTSA leadership have emphasized that autonomous vehicle integration cannot compromise emergency response corridors, and have urged congressional delegations to establish enforceable federal operating mandates.

Waymo Adds Nearly 250 Square Miles Across Five U.S. Metros

Waymo announced an expansion across five commercial deployment zones that adds nearly 250 square miles of operational design domain coverage over the coming week. The additions extend commercial ride-hailing deeper into existing territories in Los Angeles, Nashville, Orlando, San Diego, and the San Francisco Bay Area.

The new perimeters add suburban and intermodal connectivity, including a coastal push south to Torrance in Los Angeles County and southern coverage to the Berryessa BART transit hub in the Bay Area. Service also extends north to La Jolla in San Diego, with expanded southern corridors in Nashville and doubled service density across eastern sectors and downtown Orlando.

Toyota and Waymo Move From Memorandum to Factory Production of Level 4 bZ4X

Toyota Motor Corporation and Alphabet subsidiary Waymo have expanded their autonomous mobility collaboration from an exploratory memorandum of understanding to factory-level production and deployment. Toyota will build purpose-built bZ4X electric vehicles at its Takaoka plant in Toyota City, integrating Waymo’s Level 4 sensor and compute hardware on the assembly line rather than through post-production retrofitting. Initial validation operations begin in Japan in 2027 and are intended to form the foundation for high-volume driverless ride-hailing before expansion to the United Kingdom and other territories.

The right-hand-drive bZ4X platform includes power-actuated doors, an automated liftgate, optimized rear-seat legroom, and integrated ambient interior lighting. In parallel with commercial robotaxi operations, Toyota, Waymo, and Toyota software subsidiary Woven by Toyota will use operational telemetry and real-world edge cases to develop safety-critical driver assistance architectures for privately owned vehicles and vehicle-to-infrastructure safety networks.

Baidu and Lyft’s Freenow Debut Apollo RT6 Robotaxi in London

Baidu’s autonomous driving division, Apollo Go, and Lyft subsidiary Freenow have publicly debuted the sixth-generation Apollo RT6 electric robotaxi in London, targeting driverless testing in 2027 ahead of full commercial deployment. Closed and safety-operator trials began in the London Borough of Brent in July, and the partnership plans to scale to tens of vehicles over the next 24 months. The RT6 features a purpose-built passenger cabin with a detachable steer-by-wire assembly and a manufacturing cost of approximately $37,000.

The deployment places London among the Western testbeds for Chinese autonomous vehicle stacks at a time of regulatory scrutiny and proposed vehicle hardware and software bans in the United States. Operating amid 20 mph municipal zones and traffic-calming infrastructure, the Baidu-Freenow service enters a competitive field that includes Wayve and Uber, Waymo, and Pony.ai. Beyond Transport for London licensing and Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency driverless permits, long-term commercial scaling remains contingent on international trade policy, specifically whether upcoming UK electric vehicle tariff structures will impose penalties on China-assembled automated vehicle hardware.

WeRide Builds a Global Insurance Program With Allianz and Ping An

WeRide has launched a global insurance partnership program with Allianz Insurance Singapore and Ping An Property & Casualty Insurance as founding underwriters. The program is designed to support the commercial rollout of tens of thousands of Level 4 vehicles across East Asia, the Middle East, and Europe, and establishes standardized underwriting frameworks covering motor liability, commercial general and product liability, data privacy, and vehicle cybersecurity risks. Through centralized risk pooling and long-term contracts across high-volume deployments, the framework aims to lower per-mile insurance premiums and improve unit economics as driverless operations grow.

The program builds on existing deployments with each carrier. In Singapore, Allianz underwrote WeRide’s Sentosa Robobus service and its Ai.R robotaxi fleet operated with Grab in Punggol, which has surpassed 135,000 autonomous kilometers and 13,000 unique passenger trips. Ping An covers commercial robotaxi operations across Guangzhou, Beijing, Abu Dhabi, and Dubai, with trips dispatched through both the WeRide Go app and Uber’s platform. WeRide’s active global fleet totals approximately 3,600 automated vehicles, including more than 1,800 robotaxis.

Marti Partners With CalmCar on Level 4 Deployment in Türkiye

Marti Technologies has partnered with China-based autonomous driving software developer CalmCar to bring automated driving to its Turkish mobility platform. The first test vehicle running CalmCar software has arrived in Türkiye to begin closed-course validation and local operational testing in Istanbul, pending regulatory test permits. After track validation, Marti plans to offer autonomous vehicle hailing through its core application across a ride-hailing footprint spanning 40 cities.

CalmCar supplies L2 to L2+ advanced driver assistance stacks, Level 4 software, driver monitoring systems, and integrated smart cockpit solutions, and currently powers commercial robobus operations in Chongqing and Chengdu. The agreement supports Marti’s multi-partner autonomous driving strategy, which evaluates perception models, sensor suites, and drive-by-wire software under local infrastructure and operating conditions.

TIER IV and NTRO Bring an Autonomous Electric Bus to Australia and New Zealand Trials

Australia’s National Transport Research Organisation has procured a mid-sized autonomous electric bus from open-source autonomous driving software developer TIER IV to accelerate automated transit deployments across Australia and New Zealand. The 15-passenger vehicle, designated Rita, carries a TIER IV automated driving system calibrated for regional operating domains on a dedicated test track. It is built to support conditional automation with onboard safety operators as well as fully driverless operation, and is intended to progress to public road demonstrations and revenue-service trials with municipal councils, airport authorities, transit agencies, and fleet operators.

The deployment responds to projected driver shortages driven by late-2020s workforce retirements and to safety mandates aligned with Australia’s National Road Safety Strategy, which targets zero roadway fatalities by 2050. Drawing on deployment architectures established in TIER IV’s Japanese pilots, NTRO plans to validate the low-floor electric platform for first- and last-mile connectivity, specialized routes for riders with mobility impairments, and high-frequency off-peak circulators to replace underused heavy fleet assets.

May Mobility Adds Third-Party Safety Review With Edge Case

May Mobility has made third-party safety validation a mandatory gate for driverless deployment following an initial safety case assessment by safety assurance consultancy Edge Case. The milestone extends a technical evaluation partnership begun in 2022 and measures May Mobility’s end-to-end safety argumentation against recognized assurance standards, including UL 4600 and the Open Autonomy Safety Case framework. Edge Case applied its proprietary DevSafeOps methodology to audit the logical hierarchy, structural completeness, and clarity of the operator’s safety claims before commercial expansion.

Following the findings, May Mobility is streamlining its safety case architecture to keep it manageable as driverless transit fleets grow across municipal networks. The operator is benchmarking safety metrics against verified human-driving performance and expanding automated telemetry processing to resolve edge-case fleet anomalies. The next phase of the assessment will move from structural review to empirical verification, with individual autonomy and behavior-planning claims subjected to evidentiary auditing.

Rivian’s Scaringe Frames Autonomy as a Market Share Driver

Rivian Automotive CEO RJ Scaringe described autonomous driving technology as an industry inflection point during the company’s third-quarter 2026 earnings briefing, projecting that automated driving capabilities will reshape automotive market share. Addressing analysts, Scaringe positioned self-driving features not only as optional subscriptions but as core system software whose development costs will increasingly be built into base vehicle pricing to drive competitive volume.

The emphasis aligns with Rivian’s vertically integrated, software-defined vehicle strategy, which includes a proprietary zonal electrical architecture, in-house compute hardware, and a vision-centric Large Driving Model foundation stack. Rivian reported higher-than-expected adoption of its Autonomy+ package on the newly launched R2 platform and recently acquired Third Dimension AI to scale closed-loop neural network simulation ahead of its scheduled Autonomy and AI Day. The autonomy program serves as a foundational layer across consumer vehicle lines and commercial fleet integrations, including a multi-year fleet supply agreement with Uber.

Aurora Targets 20 Trucks Weekly Through Roush as FMCSA Approves Beacon Exemption

Aurora Innovation announced plans to scale production of its autonomous driving system to 20 Class 8 trucks per week beginning in early December through contract upfitting partner Roush. The run rate implies annualized build capacity above 1,000 Level 4 commercial vehicles and positions the company to surpass 200 operational driverless trucks by February 2027 and to target more than 1,000 deployed trucks by the end of 2027. The ramp bridges near-term carrier delivery timelines ahead of factory-integrated assembly with Volvo Trucks and PACCAR.

The scaling follows a five-year Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration exemption that allows Level 4 commercial vehicles to use cab-mounted, flashing amber warning beacons rather than physical roadside warning triangles or flares during highway stops, resolving a key operating constraint for driver-out interstate freight. Supported by cash reserves above $1 billion, Aurora also signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding with asset-based carrier Charger Logistics covering up to 500 autonomous Class 8 trucks powered by the Aurora Driver, with deliveries slated for 2027 and 2028. The agreement expands on an initial operational contract begun in July 2026 across Texas cross-border corridors.

Aurora and Charger Logistics Outline Ownership and Software Model

Under the proposed structure, Charger Logistics will purchase and retain ownership of the autonomous trucks while subscribing to Aurora’s Driver as a Service software model. The framework is designed to optimize total cost of ownership for fleet operators and supports Aurora’s capital-light path toward a targeted 30,000-truck footprint by 2030.

Charger plans to deploy the second-generation hardware platforms across domestic long-haul corridors and high-volume cross-border freight routes linking the United States and Mexico. The deployment connects the Aurora system directly to Charger’s internal transportation management system to scale unmanned middle-mile capacity across key commercial lanes.

DTL Transport Signs Binding Agreement for 75 Driverless Kodiak Trucks

California-based refrigerated long-haul carrier DTL Transport has entered a binding commercial agreement to deploy 75 driverless Class 8 trucks running the Kodiak Driver autonomous platform. Under a recurring Driver-as-a-Service framework, DTL retains ownership of the tractors and pays Kodiak AI a per-mile software utilization fee. The deployment is described as the first publicly announced, binding driverless fleet commitment by an interstate long-haul carrier. Initial rollouts target Sun Belt corridors, specifically Interstate 10 between Dallas and El Paso, Texas, and Interstate 20 between Dallas and Atlanta, Georgia, designed to bypass Hours of Service constraints in high-tempo refrigerated grocery distribution.

The contract expands on a September 2026 commercial pilot in which Kodiak-equipped trucks hauled temperature-sensitive produce 225 miles on California State Route 99 and Interstate 5 between Fresno and Los Angeles under state autonomous vehicle testing permits. It also extends Kodiak’s Driver-as-a-Service model beyond industrial energy transport, where partner Atlas Energy Solutions operated 35 driverless trucks in the Permian Basin as of mid-2026 toward an objective of 100 autonomous units by mid-2027.

Stoneridge and Kodiak AI Integrate MirrorEye Into Autonomous Trucks

Stoneridge and Kodiak AI have established a technology collaboration to integrate Stoneridge’s MirrorEye Camera Monitor System into commercial vehicles running the Kodiak Driver. Newly deployed Kodiak trucks feature the digital vision system, and both engineering teams are evaluating deeper integration of Stoneridge hardware and onboard edge processing to support autonomous operations.

The integration relies on Stoneridge’s Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration exemption, renewed in 2024 for a five-year term, which authorizes commercial vehicles to operate without conventional rear-vision mirrors. Kodiak’s proprietary SensorPods previously retained standard glass mirror assemblies to meet regulatory requirements alongside perception sensors. The compact, door-frame-mounted MirrorEye camera wing allows Kodiak to develop next-generation SensorPods with reduced mass, optimized aerodynamic drag, and simplified modular field serviceability. Stoneridge reports cumulative production above 200,000 MirrorEye units across six global commercial OEM platforms and more than 40 North American retrofit fleets.

Hyundai Motor Group Demonstrates Residential Parking Robots in South Korea

Hyundai Motor Group, through a consortium including Hyundai Motor Company, Hyundai WIA, and Hyundai Engineering & Construction, has demonstrated autonomous parking robot technology at the Hillstate The Wave City apartment complex in Siheung, Gyeonggi Province. Operating under South Korea’s Smart City Regulatory Sandbox, the pilot marks the country’s first residential deployment at a facility with more than 50 vehicle spaces. The demonstration covered simultaneous vehicle intake and dispatch, temporary retrieval, and automated double-parking relocation, with robots moving vehicles to designated staging zones within three minutes of a request from an in-home wall terminal.

The system combines facility access barriers, in-unit smart wall pads, and an AI-based automated vehicle inspection system with Hyundai’s Smart Parking Control System 2.0, which plans trajectories for up to 200 robots at once. Hyundai plans to use data from the Siheung pilot to establish safety and operational benchmarks, while consulting the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport on regulatory revisions to extend automated valet robotics to commercial office towers, airports, and public transit nodes.

Innoviz Positions Perciz LiDAR for Counter-UAS Defense Work

Innoviz Technologies reported rising engagement for its defense-focused Perciz brand following the Association of the United States Army Annual Meeting and Exposition. System integrators and defense prime contractors are prioritizing high-resolution 3D spatial sensing to counter low-cost first-person-view and fiber-optic tethered uncrewed aircraft. According to the company, legacy radio-frequency detection and jamming suites struggle against non-emitting guidance, while active optical point-cloud data provides the centimeter-level localization needed for kinetic and directed-energy interception.

The Perciz platform adapts Innoviz’s automotive-grade solid-state LiDAR, currently deployed with Tier 1 automotive programs including BMW and Volkswagen, to defense and perimeter security applications. Combining hardware returns resilient to environmental occlusion with perception software for positive target identification, the system is meant to address effector cueing gaps in heavy clutter. Innoviz aims to convert recent pipeline engagements into formal system-level evaluations ahead of C-UAS Technology USA in late 2026.

text:
HIROSHIMA, Japan, Nov 1, 2026 - (JCN Newswire) - Mazda Motor Corporation (Mazda) is advancing initiatives based on three pillars-energy conservation, shifting to renewable energy, and introducing carbon-neutral fuels-with the goal of achieving carbon neutrality at its global manufacturing facilities by 2035. As part of its renewable energy initiative, Mazda will expand the use of on-site power purchase agreements (PPA)(*1) to the Mazda KD Center, scheduled for completion in November, and to the Miyoshi Plant, which includes an battery energy storage system.(*2)

At the Miyoshi Plant, ORIX Corporation (ORIX) will install solar power generation equipment as the PPA provider. The generated electricity will be consumed on-site, and any excess solar power will be stored in a battery energy storage system that uses new automotive lithium-ion batteries. This will allow Mazda to effectively utilize surplus solar power and reduce peak electricity demand.

At the Mazda KD Center, ORIX will also install solar power generation equipment as the PPA provider. Toyo Kohan Co., Ltd., a steel sheet product manufacturer, will utilize the environmental value(*3) associated with surplus electricity. These efforts will contribute to the increased use of renewable energy throughout the region's total supply chain.

Mazda aims to contribute to the region's sustainable development and enhancement of the industrial competitiveness by working with its partners to demonstrate and implement a range of carbon-neutral technologies, drawing on their respective strengths.

Mazda will continue to collaborate with like-minded partner companies to advance initiatives toward carbon neutrality. These initiatives include expanding the use of renewable energy and creating a positive impact on communities, the environment, and society.

(*1) A system in which a power producer installs solar power generation equipment on a customer's premises and supplies them with electricity generated from renewable energy, along with associated environmental value.

(*2) A system that stores surplus solar power and other electricity in batteries for use during periods of high electricity demand, thereby enabling the effective use of renewable energy and reducing peak electricity demand.

(*3) The environmental value of electricity generated from renewable energy sources, such as solar power, including the value of reducing CO2 emissions.

(*4) A system in which the environmental value of electricity generated from renewable energy sources, such as solar power, is traded separately from the electricity itself.
