WEST PALM BEACH, FL / ACCESS Newswire / October 31, 2026 / Elektros, Inc.

Keeping the Focus on North American Supply

Lithium plays an important role in the rechargeable battery systems used in electric vehicles and stationary energy storage. With manufacturers and markets focused on dependable sources of supply, opportunities within the United States continue to attract attention.

ELEKTROS Inc. ELEK, a publicly traded OTC-market company, is studying a potential hard-rock lithium opportunity in northern New York, close to the Canadian border but located on the U.S. side. This is an early-stage evaluation only. ELEKTROS has not completed an acquisition and has not announced an independently verified mineral resource or reserve.

Why Geography May Be Relevant

A potential U.S. lithium project could, if the geology and economics support development, create an opportunity to serve domestic processing channels with a more direct transportation route. Depending on the eventual project design, domestic sourcing could potentially lessen exposure to overseas shipping and some cross-border import procedures.

Those possibilities remain unproven. The property must be evaluated for mineral potential, ownership and rights, permitting, infrastructure, processing access, costs and overall commercial viability before any development conclusions can be reached.

Demand Projections Put Supply in the Spotlight

An October 22, 2026 Benzinga report, "Lithium's $100 Billion Supply Gap Hands Albemarle a Domestic Moat," cited a Benchmark Mineral Intelligence outlook projecting that global lithium demand could more than triple by 2050. The report referenced a possible requirement for 134 additional mines and over $100 billion in investment, reflecting demand from electric vehicles and stationary battery storage.

The figures describe a global industry outlook and should not be interpreted as a forecast of ELEKTROS performance, a valuation of the New York opportunity or evidence of a mineral discovery.

EV Charging Patent Remains an Area of Interest

Alongside its review of lithium-related opportunities, ELEKTROS continues to explore potential development relationships concerning its multi-port EV charging patent, U.S. Patent No. 12,522,100 B1. The company sees potential relevance in both the materials supporting electrification and the infrastructure that serves electric vehicles.

No commercial charging prototype, patent license, customer deployment or related revenue is being announced at this time.

A Measured Path Forward

ELEKTROS expects that any further assessment of the northern New York possibility would require a sequence of practical diligence steps: verification of property and mineral rights; independent geological work and sampling; review of environmental and permitting obligations; evaluation of processing, transport and infrastructure; and analysis of financing and potential transaction terms.

The company believes that a disciplined process is essential. The opportunity remains preliminary, and there can be no assurance that due diligence will support an acquisition or commercial development.

Appreciation for Shareholder Interest

The company thanks its shareholders and those monitoring the evolving U.S. lithium landscape for their continued attention. ELEKTROS remains focused on examining opportunities carefully and pursuing progress that can be supported by facts, technical review and responsible business planning.

Management expresses gratitude to Almighty God. This release is not an offer to sell securities or a solicitation or recommendation to buy ELEK shares.

text:
A protest challenging energy demands linked to artificial intelligence targeted technology leaders and state officials during Seattle AI Week's opening panel.

The opening panel focused on AI and economic growth. Climate activists interrupted the discussion while kayakers on Elliott Bay displayed a banner reading "Power for People, Not for Tech."

Here's what to know

Members of Seattle climate activism group Troublemakers disrupted the Washington Technology Industry Association's third annual event several times before security escorted them out, GeekWire reported.

According to the tech news outlet, Troublemakers members want green jobs and clean energy to be Washington's investment priorities. They described the expansion of data centers and the deployment of AI as threats to the state's environment, jobs, and communities.

The panel included Beau Perschbacher, senior policy advisor to Gov. Bob Ferguson; Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce leader Joe Nguyen; and OpenAI community programs global head Mattie Zazueta. OpenAI also served as the event's presenting sponsor.

The demonstrations were only the latest of the group's efforts to challenge data center expansion. In 2024, Troublemakers blocked access to Amazon's Seattle headquarters to oppose its plan to use natural gas for Oregon data centers.

More background

AI relies on electricity-powered computing in data centers, tying its expansion directly to energy-grid demand.

Perschbacher acknowledged that these facilities "use a really significant amount of electricity," according to GeekWire. With demand from electric vehicles and heat pumps also growing, he said ensuring an adequate power supply is a major challenge.

Water use is another concern. Perschbacher said, however, that the state's review found data centers' consumption was "not out of line with a typical industrial user."

What's being done?

Washington AI Resistance coordinated 19 or more demonstrations across Washington in October to seek a statewide moratorium. Seattle's City Council unanimously approved a yearlong halt on new large data centers in June, according to GeekWire.

Ferguson's administration established a working group to examine data centers' effects. Perschbacher said Washington won't allow the facilities to operate diesel generators continuously and that lawmakers would likely reconsider legislation addressing ratepayer protections.

During a later panel, State Sen. Marko Liias, who sponsored legislation on high-risk AI uses, outlined expectations for facilities seeking to locate in Washington.

"When energy becomes scarce," Liias said, per GeekWire, "I do think we need to be clear that our communities deserve access to that energy before the data centers do."

The tech outlet described the lawmaker's other data center expectations as including: supplying the grid with additional clean energy, reusing water, and abandoning nondisclosure agreements that leave communities uninformed.

Where can I learn more?

These stories examine how concerns about data centers' energy and water use have sparked opposition well beyond Seattle:

• New York activists rallied at Tesla, demanding a data center moratorium over Musk's Dojo plans.

• Texas residents pressed candidates on power and water concerns during an acrimonious data-center forum.

• India's data center expansion has sparked land and water backlash, with communities demanding consultation.

text:
The UAW Needs a Strategy for the Future of Manufacturing

Labour • November 1, 2026 • Toly Rinberg

The United Auto Workers (UAW) has a problem: the future of the auto industry. The crisis facing autoworkers is unfolding on many fronts. Beyond the chaotic corporate-led electric vehicle (EV) transition, there is also the ongoing restructuring toward non-union manufacturing in the South, continued labor-replacing reorganization, and growing international competition. Workers bear the brunt on every front, most recently weathering plant closures, mass layoffs, and cross-border supply chain shocks.

UAW President Shawn Fain – whose entire slate swept the recent election for top office – has rhetorically distanced himself from UAW’s legacy of concessions. “Keep in mind how far we’ve come in the last four years,” Fain said at the June UAW Constitutional Convention. “We’ve gone from defense to offense.”

In reality, after decades of managed decline, the UAW has only just started to play defense. Fain’s administration, which came to power in 2023 through the organizing of Unite All Workers for Democracy (UAWD), has revived splashy, agitational contract campaigns. Yet the long-standing culture of union-management collaboration has left the UAW unable to resist the harm from the EV rollbacks. Moreover, the corporations are restructuring the industry faster than the union can build power.

Organizing the South

Non-union production is nearing two-thirds of the market share as UAW’s renewed push to organize the South faces setbacks, including its loss at Mercedes and its withdrawal from some campaigns. There is still no plan for the heavily non-union parts sector. If a 2028 strike against the Big Three wins back the retirement benefits Fain campaigned on, it would essentially bring unionized assembly work to pre-2008 standards. But it would cover fewer workers, and inflation-adjusted wages would likely still be lower (Figure 1).

The situation is grim. Even with its renewed dynamism, the UAW’s current trajectory is a continued loss of leverage on an industry-wide scale. If the next administration tries to accelerate EV development again, corporations will cite the Trump-era rollback as a reason to demand more federal guarantees at labor’s expense. If protectionist policies prevail, a zero-sum market dynamic will force competition over jobs and devastate solidarity among North American workers, trapping the union into tailing corporations as they jolt back toward fossil fuels. The United States will continue to produce overpriced trucks to sell at home while Chinese companies sell better and cheaper EVs around the world. The result will be a weakening union presiding over a slow decline.

But there is an opening for workers: the recent pivot away from EVs reveals the corporate-led transition’s fundamental inability to deliver clean and safe transportation for the working class. This impasse is an opportunity to introduce political solutions that long seemed out of reach. If workers are serious about going on offense, they must look to UAW’s roots: a strategy of class struggle unionism that breaks with union-management collaboration, invests in militant shopfloor leaders, and fights for worker control alongside bread-and-butter demands.

Shopfloor militancy is necessary, but not enough on its own. The deeper problem is capitalist competition and workers face too many threats at once to beat them with one-off bargaining pushes. The way out is to chart a path toward collectively controlled manufacturing that serves the working class. This could look like building affordable EVs and public transit needed to improve working people’s lives and addressing the climate crisis, with public procurement enabling planning for decades to come. Such an approach would both break the zero-sum market trap and enable the rebuilding of worker-led solidarity at home and abroad.

How Workers Experience the Corporate-led EV Transition

Between the EV restructuring and uncertainty from the trade war, plant shutdowns, mass layoffs, and production pivots have roiled the industry over the last three years. Employment in the entire US auto sector decreased by over sixty-five thousand jobs, though the decline has recently plateaued and is slowly recovering. This number represents an expansive picture of the sector that includes parts and assembly subsectors, union and non-union jobs, and production workers and supervisors.

In the Midwest, thousands of workers face temporary or indefinite layoffs as EV production at several factories is spooling down and multiple plants are being re-retooled from EV assembly back to combustion engine vehicles. GM laid off over one thousand workers at one Ultium Cells battery facility, closed another to retool for energy storage, and sold off a third. Reneging on its 2023 agreement with the UAW, Stellantis canceled plans for their EV assembly lines and battery plant in Belvidere, IL, eventually leading to the UAW’s “Keep the Promise” campaign.

Perhaps most illustrative of the current moment is the recent closure of the Kentucky BlueOval electric-vehicle battery facility co-owned by Ford and a South Korean company. The 1,600 workers who were fired had previously voted to unionize with the UAW in the face of rabid anti-union corporate tactics. But now, Ford is using the closure as an opportunity to bust the union, claiming it will reopen the facility in 2027 for battery storage manufacturing, in part supplying data center construction driven by AI speculation. Workers from the plant held a rally with the help of the UAW, but other Ford Locals have not mobilized in solidarity, leaving the fired workers with little leverage.

When I worked at General Motors Factory Zero, which produces gigantic luxury EVs like the $100,000 Electric Hummer, I experienced the plant shifting from mandatory overtime in 2024 to mass layoffs in 2025. The company used a loophole in the contract, which allows for waiving overtime restrictions when launching new vehicles – forcing workers to work six days a week for 12.5 hour shifts (including a half hour of unpaid lunch) for almost a year. GM also relied on the inability of over a thousand new hires to get relief through the federally protected Family Medical Leave Act (FMLA), which only kicks in a year into employment.

Local 22 union officials were uninterested in organizing against the brutal mandatory overtime, even when the death of one of our union siblings while driving home after a long shift galvanized anger on the shopfloor. The rank-and-file formation I was a part of, anchored by UAWD members, put out a petition demanding easing of the mandatory overtime schedule and raising striking as a threat. Local officials quashed the organizing despite more than seven hundred workers signing the petition. Officials pushed through a vote to adjourn during one membership meeting to avoid discussing the matter. In the monthly newsletter, the Local president claimed that signing the petition may result in workers getting fired. Regional leadership was made aware of these actions and the conditions the workers faced, but did not support the campaign either.

After Trump’s EV policy reversals came into effect, management at the plant started to ramp up layoffs in 2025, ultimately impacting over a thousand workers. In union newsletters and from the front of the room during membership meetings, Local union officials blamed the downsizing on so-called “absenteeism” rather than fighting to keep workers in the plant. Many workers were finally able to take time off with FMLA after a brutal year of mandatory overtime. This boom-and-bust dynamic over the span of just two years revealed deep cultural challenges at the Local level: instead of the corporations’ decision to make luxury EVs with limited market appeal or the Trump administration’s anti-EV policies, workers were being blamed for their own layoffs, weakening solidarity and pitting the union against itself.

A union that put the blame where it belonged and oriented around expanding worker control would have fought for strong work-sharing provisions to spread the downturn’s burden across the workforce, and over the longer term, for a say in the product decisions that caused the bust in the first place.

At the Local level, organizers face the profound challenge of breaking with business unionism – the ideology that seeks labor peace with the boss and narrowly confines the union to bargaining better deals for its own members. Some of our strongest opposition came from proud union members who have been in the Local for decades, and many come from UAW families. Their positions on the Local Executive Board or as union stewards kept them from grueling work on the shop floor, which in turn made them worried about losing their union role. This reinforced the conservative belief that fighting management is more destabilizing than smoothing over conflict.

Such was the reality on the ground, despite UAW’s claim that a “just transition” was won. The 2023 national agreements gave the UAW little contractual standing to resist the EV-related mass layoffs and plant closures, as the companies used “market condition” exception clauses to explain their restructuring. UAW’s current focus on contracts ultimately obscures that management’s control over workers is a question of power, not legalism.

The biggest experiment in resistance was UAW’s aforementioned Stellantis Keep the Promise campaign. After the Stand Up strike, Stellantis began a wave of layoffs, reversed its decision to reopen the Belvidere Assembly Plant, and dropped other product commitments. Fain tried to unite Local presidents around escalating strike threats in solidarity, and the UAW reported that 28 Locals passed resolutions that put them on track to strike over violations of the contract’s product commitment provisions. Two Locals of parts-distribution workers cleared the strike authorization threshold, but assembly-plant workers were more conflicted.

As a co-chair of UAWD’s Organizing Committee at the time, I worked with others to support rank-and-file workers in launching a small bottom-up campaign across assembly plants to build support for Fain’s strategy – convening meetings, handing out flyers, and intervening at membership meetings. While some in the rank and file grasped the importance of cross-Local solidarity, many were resistant and skeptical, especially as officials fear-mongered about further layoffs. Decades of business unionism had atrophied the muscles for bottom-up deliberation. Without a meaningful democratic process, the campaign felt like an imposition, and the chance for political education and buy-in was lost. UAW’s top leadership cut it short after Stellantis agreed to some demands, while cancelling plans for a battery plant and parts megahub in Belvidere.

The inability to resist the corporate-led EV restructuring while the Big Three continue to profit reveals the overall weakness of the UAW, especially between contract negotiations. The ideology internalized across UAW workers, staff, and union officialdom is that management has a right to do what it wants, and workers can only ride the boom and bust cycle of the industry and hope they make it out on the other side.

Organizing Setbacks and the Way Forward?

UAW’s organizing drive in the South is one of the most ambitious and important endeavors in the labor movement today. Coming out of the recent Constitutional Convention, in June 2026, where delegates approved an increase in the organizing budget from $60 to $100-million over four years, UAW’s current organizing approach should be critically evaluated.

In 2024, UAW homed in on new organizing, claiming to focus on more than a dozen non-union assembly and battery plants, mostly in the South. As multiple analyses have revealed, this increased funding also came with a pivot in strategy emphasizing worker-led organizing, leadership identification, workplace mapping, public pressure campaigns, and the use of experienced staff (primarily coming from the higher education sector).

The big breakthrough has been the Volkswagen plant in Chattanooga, Tennessee, where workers recently settled a contract after nearly two years of bargaining with the company. A parts plant down the road from the Volkswagen facility also unionized with the UAW, showing the possible ripple effect of southern organizing wins. Workers at Daimler Truck plants in North Carolina and elsewhere in the South ran an animated contract campaign that secured significant wins. The unionization victory at BlueOval, mentioned above, was eked out with an 11-vote margin, and would have continued the pattern if the company did not deliberately shut down the factory for retooling.

Yet, in the face of unrelenting union busting, the UAW appears to have reassessed its strategy and pulled resources from certain organizing drives. A UAWD member leading an organizing drive at an Alabama plant recently told Daily Struggle, “I feel there was a ton of enthusiasm from International at the start, but when things got hard, like they inevitably do in new campaigns, they kind of folded to the adversity. We don’t dislike our staff, they’ve just been hard to reach for months, they’re managing multiple campaigns across the South and they’re not down here that much. They sometimes have advice for us when we get them on the phone, but, beyond that, there aren’t organizing resources flowing to us as workers.”

A similar pattern is playing out at a Rivian electric vehicle plant in Normal, IL. The UAW has pulled back support for the organizing drive, after establishing a neutrality agreement that will only kick in once the company reaches a threshold of profitability. Certain Rivian workers publicly disagreed with this strategy, telling WGLT: “Money’s not in the Top 5. I want a say in what goes on in my work life and my home life. Right now, I don’t have any of that. They can change your schedule. They can do whatever they want because I don’t have a seat at the table.”

The Mercedes unionization drive in 2024, which failed by a margin of about six hundred votes out of five thousand voters, is an important recent case study. There have been many insightful analyses by workers and labor researchers assessing the loss. As the campaign is regrouping for another push, the organizing demands are worth analyzing more deeply.

Mercedes organizers picked eliminating the wage and healthcare tier that was instituted in 2020 – or what they dubbed the “Alabama discount” – as a key target of their campaign. Under pressure from the organizing drive, the company eliminated the tiers and went on a charm offensive after replacing their CEO. According to organizers, who were able to secure a large majority of “yes” commitments, the company’s pivot swung many voters to “no” in the weeks leading up to the election. Then, months after the election, the company reasserted its control by, for example, forcing excessive Saturday work and dragging its feet on addressing shopfloor issues. The defeat at Mercedes closed the chapter on what organizing leaders in the Fain administration had previously called a “movement moment,” raising questions about the way forward.

One aspect of the way forward would include parts plants. Briefly, the 2008 crash and subsequent restructuring drove a wave of closures and mergers, leaving a more centralized parts sector with fewer but larger facilities across the Midwest and South. Yet, despite the organizing advantage of a more concentrated supply chain and recent signals of rank-and-file militancy, the UAW has not pursued a sectoral effort to organize parts plants.

While not mutually exclusive, these setbacks and missed opportunities point to an underlying weakness of more narrowly targeting “bread-and-butter” demands (like wages and benefits), rather than issues of workplace conditions and control (like maintaining production standards, protections from new technology and outsourcing, union control over training, immigrant protections, product decisions and commitment, and so on). It is a lot easier for the company to shift its finances to take the wind out of the sails of an organizing drive than to fundamentally relinquish control over its operation. Campaigns like these take longer because they depend on developing ideological worker-leaders, but that work is essential to waging class struggle on a larger scale.

The Zero-Sum Trap

Given the challenges posed to organizing and by the EV transition, the UAW has turned to supporting protectionist trade policies in hopes of tipping the balance in its favor. But in doing so it has accepted a false premise: that North American autoworkers are locked in a zero-sum competition for jobs.

In a comprehensive policy paper, the UAW argues that, “If the production-to-sales ratio in the United States were 1-to-1, we would manufacture nearly 6 million more cars per year.” But because most of the current imbalance comes from a highly integrated supply chain across North America, they are essentially saying that Mexican and Canadian workers should give up their jobs to American workers.

Shawn Fain’s administration, aligning with past UAW presidents Bob King and Ron Gettlefinger, is right to blame NAFTA and other pro-business trade policies for undermining labor’s strength. But it is actually UAW’s lack of international solidarity and inability to avoid harms to workers from technological advancement and industry restructuring that led Fain to cheer on Trump’s tariffs.

Even if we accept the UAW’s reshoring premise, corporations would need billions of dollars of investment to ramp up domestic production (as was the case when investment flowed for Mexican auto industry expansion). But the automakers have already been burned by whiplash from Biden to Trump. The rollback of the Inflation Reduction Act and tariffs have cost them billions in their scramble to restructure under Trump’s new policies. If the state makes an onshoring push or attempts to accelerate EVs again, corporations will extract concessions from the federal government and demand strong assurances before moving forward. Such state-capital alignment premised on appeasing corporations would surely further undermine labor.

The scant evidence of reshoring under the current 25 percent tariffs on Mexican and Canadian vehicles and Trump’s inability to push his nationalist agenda further are signs of capitalism’s strength and inertia. The conditions that limit a Mexican autoworker’s daily pay to what a Michigan autoworker makes in an hour cannot be undone without class struggle. And, in any case, to bankroll such a massive pivot in a short period would require either increasing vehicle prices or massive amounts of federal subsidies and loans, or both.

Why accept this zero-sum framing? And if the federal government is going to cough up billions, why let them give it to corporations again and not workers?

Beyond Protectionism and Competition

The recent uptick in protectionist policies is already eroding the possibility of cross-border solidarity, perpetuating the downward spiral of union power. The impact on the United States’s “most loyal ally” has led former research director of the Canadian Auto Workers, Sam Gindin, to conclude that “Canadian auto isn’t in ‘crisis’, it’s in danger of extinction.” With pressure from Trump’s tariffs, GM’s CAMI and Stellantis Brampton plants each recently shuttered. The same month as Canadian workers rallied against these shutdowns, UAW cheered the move of these jobs from Canada to the United States, enabling cross-border whipsawing. At the same time, US trade policy has already led many Mexican parts plants at the border to close, impacting tens of thousands of workers. Lear Corporation is relocating a Juarez plant to find cheaper labor in Honduras, threatening the possibility of bigger capital flight.

If a substantial increase in domestic production does occur, it will likely happen at non-union plants in the South, like Toyota’s recent expansion in Texas or Hyundai’s in Georgia. This will continue to erode unionized market share if organizing drives do not pick up, and corporations will continue to use every restructuring period to advance their technological frontier, which arcs toward requiring fewer work-hours to produce a single vehicle.

What’s more, a protectionist orientation subordinates the union to state interests. At a Rutgers University bargaining training in November 2025, Chris Brooks (Fain’s former Chief of Staff) revealed that the Trump trade officials the UAW was negotiating with would stop responding whenever Fain said something that the Trump administration did not approve of. This kind of engagement belies the misguided view that the ‘antiworker’ Trump administration will be swayed through lobbying and that the union’s strength can grow through alignment with whichever party is in power.

But the backdrop to Trump’s and UAW’s turn to protectionism are the deeper forces of capitalist competition that continue to shift control away from workers toward management. As Kim Moody convincingly argues in On New Terrain, the lion’s share of the decrease in the manufacturing workforce over the last few decades is due to increasing work intensification, new management tools to control workers, and the continued rise in “productivity,” rather than offshoring or increased imports. Even through waves of offshoring, the US light-vehicle annual production rate trends modestly upward (if you smooth out the ups and downs of the market).

Today, the evolving technological frontier entails a combination of cobots (collaborative robots), humanoid robots, AI-modified manufacturing processes, and new assembly platforms like the one Ford is launching, all of which are already displacing or on track to displacing future work. I witnessed the leading edge of automation when I worked in the “Body” department at Factory Zero. My work involved aligning and staging stamped sheets of metal for robots to pick up and weld. In so-called “dark factories” in China, this part of the process has been essentially fully automated, meaning workers are not needed and the lights can be turned off.

Neither US automakers nor the UAW has an answer to increasing competition from Chinese corporations, which now build three out of every four EVs produced globally. Without a secure plan for workers, if the United States were to suddenly drop its auto tariffs against Chinese vehicles, or let Chinese companies enter the United States (as Trump recently toyed with), conditions for US workers would enter a tailspin. For the labor movement, solidarity with Chinese autoworkers is a true puzzle, but a necessary one to solve.

To make headway on these questions, workers must realize their power actually lies in class independence and solidarity with their working-class allies internationally. So far, however, the UAW has sided with short-term gains over long-term power building. The UAW must rethink its zero-sum assumptions and understand that the way to break the false choice between protectionism and international competition is through a commitment to fighting over workplace and industry control with a path toward collectively controlled manufacturing that meets working-class needs.

Of course, these ideas are not new. Through the late 1940s, workers set their own pace on machines, which allowed them to establish simple forms of workers’ control over the speed of work. In the 1960s, the UAW helped organize World Auto Councils to unite workers across countries in shared fights against multinational corporations. French and German autoworkers have made progress on reducing their workweek. And workers around the world, like in the UK, Canada, Italy, Argentina, and elsewhere have long fought for collectively controlled manufacturing.

Some starting points for such a program within the UAW could include political education campaigns, preparing stewards and rank-and-file members to take over plants threatened with closure, or pressure against the next administration to launch manufacturing facilities controlled by UAW workers. While the specific implementation lies beyond the scope of this analysis, such an effort must expand capacity for worker self-organization rather than simply replace a capitalist boss with a state technocrat. Even one success would be significant, as it would demonstrate how public funding enables planning of socially useful manufacturing, while shifting the paradigm away from both business unionism and protectionist cooperation. Paired with winning policies like a shorter workweek, this path would build working-class power and could secure millions of jobs for decades to come.

Live to Fight Another Day?

“We did what we had to do to get to tomorrow,” said Ron Gettlefinger, UAW president who oversaw the negotiations of the concessionary contracts following the 2008 crash. Tomorrow has now arrived, and the depth of the well-documented UAW decline should be an alarming call to action. The union had 1.5 million active members primarily in the auto industry in 1979, but today has roughly 400,000, with only about 150,000 in the Big Three.

Over the last twenty years, unionized US plants have dropped dramatically from around forty-five down to below twenty-five, with non-union plants in Mexico and the US South increasing to fill the gap (Figure 2).

This restructuring is easily seen by comparing auto employment in a few major states in the Midwest and the South (Figure 1, bottom-left panel). The Midwest workforce dramatically decreased leading up to and during the 2008 crash. Southern states, like Alabama, Kentucky, and Texas, now surpass Ohio and Missouri in assembly worker counts.

With the exception of the recent expansion into the Volkswagen plant, the union foothold has been set by the number of Big Three assembly workers, as well as some parts plants. In 1990, over half a million workers across the entire sector were unionized, including assembly and parts plants. Today, that number is below two hundred thousand.

Average real wages across the entire assembly subsector, accounting for inflation, were relatively flat at around $25 per hour from 1990 until the 2008 crash; after the collapse, wages dipped below $20 per hour (in 2000 dollars; Figure 1, upper-right panel). They have still not recovered, and even the top rate from the UAW-GM contract in 2028 will be below the pre-crash inflation-adjusted average.

Meanwhile, although more challenging to interpret due to periodic economic fluctuations, the productivity rate increase (or the decrease in the number of work-hours required to produce a vehicle) since 1990 outpaces sales growth roughly by a factor of three – 1.7 percent to 0.6 percent per year (Figure 1, bottom-right panel). The decrease in productivity over the last decade – likely due to the launch of new EV manufacturing – is becoming less of a factor, especially with the recent EV reversals. This is further evidence that with each restructuring, corporations continue to need fewer workers.

Labor Peace and the Seeds it Buried

To best respond to the shifting terrain, the UAW would do well to tend to seeds planted about a century ago.

The GM sit-down strike of 1936 took place during a time when industry-wide wins were born from class struggle waged by ideologically-minded militant workers willing to take collective risks and execute aggressive tactics during upsurges. This layer of worker-leaders was made up of organized socialists and other militant trade unionists ready to build fighting strategies. Studying history shows that such working-class breakthroughs did not rely solely on spontaneity but rather required years of organization building, political education, and deep connections to the surrounding community.

But the union-management collaboration that grew during this period of class struggle now has a stranglehold over the UAW. This tendency finally won out when UAW President Walter Reuther signed the Treaty of Detroit in 1950, codifying a regime of labor peace in exchange for a bigger cut of capital’s growth. The UAW agreed to longer contract durations, “no strike” clauses during the life of the contract, stronger management-rights provisions, and an increasingly bureaucratic grievance procedure. Decades later, this ideology of labor peace was eventually institutionalized through joint programs, the system of co-governance between the UAW and management that became the vehicle for union corruption and led to further co-optation of the union bureaucracy.

At my UAW-GM orientation, the joint programs official said nothing about the grievance procedure or shopfloor fights, but repeated the following phrase for what felt like a hundred times: “Don’t be late, be on time, do your job.” The lesson he imparted to hundreds of new UAW members, many of whom were young Detroiters who had never been in a union before, was simple: management is in charge.

Even as individual workers stayed relatively well-off, labor’s aggregate share of capital’s gains plummeted along with UAW membership count after its 1970s peak. Worse, over the last two decades, the average share per worker has declined (Figure 1; top-right panel). Yet, throughout this decline, the union’s culture of collaboration and business unionism has prevailed. This perspective has resulted in the UAW focusing narrowly on wage and benefit fights, rather than control over jobs or production decisions.

Under the current UAW administration, the lack of a plan for the future of auto manufacturing is concomitant with Fain’s political approach: a form of progressive bureaucratic unionism that, despite its militant rhetoric, has ultimately been captured by the top-down bureaucracy he previously ran against. This limitation stems largely from Fain’s orientation toward internal union maneuvering rather than the rank and file – an approach that quickly ran into political headwinds. The fact that only about 7 percent of the UAW membership voted for him in the recent election with 90 percent not voting at all, shows the deep disconnection between the membership and his slate’s program. More importantly, Fain’s perspective – as well as recent proposed strategies from UAW organizers – does not grapple with labor’s key barrier: the continued avoidance of fighting for worker control over capital’s decision-making power.

In this period of limited class struggle, what does it mean for workers to organize themselves with a goal of developing class struggle?

Seeds of Class Struggle Strategy

Workers looking to go on the offense for the long haul ought to revive the class struggle unionism of the further past. Key to this work is continuously identifying where workers have been organizing themselves to fight collectively over their material conditions. Even in a time when the organized left is weak, workers in non-union Toyota plants in the South have been staging walkouts against mandatory overtime, GM workers fought job mergers through work-to-rule campaigns, and parts workers voted down three contracts, to name a few examples.

In the absence of either a working-class party or a socialist party with a broad working-class character, building independent left organization within industrial workplaces is a way to develop worker-leaders who see both the possibilities and limitations of shop-floor struggles. Shop-floor militancy can improve conditions and win reforms but will not challenge capital’s exploitation at scale on its own. Coming up against those limits advances the conclusion that the fight is not against a single boss but rather the system that every boss answers to, and that winning it requires a revolutionary rupture with capitalism.

Independent self-organized working-class formations anchored by socialists and radicals take years to build and are important both to resist the coercive forces of the union bureaucracy and the ruling class parties and to introduce bold class-struggle strategies to fight for the working class’s future.

Worker-led formations like Unite All Workers for Democracy and the Southern Workers Assembly (SWA) are putting such class-struggle strategies to the test. At their core, these strategies begin by recognizing that the working class and capitalist class are fundamentally at odds and focusing on bottom-up militant approaches to expand worker control. Vying for control starts small – for example, resisting unilateral management decisions on the shop floor or winning job security during downturns – but it must expand to decisions over production, the industry, and ultimately, over society as a whole. This control concerns political questions about the movement of people and wars abroad as much as economic organization.

UAWD is committed to a “vision of class struggle unionism and fighting to build a militant, democratic UAW.” Rather than focusing on reforming the UAW, it has prioritized developing worker-leaders who can draw their coworkers into shop-floor struggles over working conditions and workplace control. That means running work-to-rule campaigns, resisting mandatory overtime, fighting layoffs, and preparing members to strike over economic and political issues like ICE escalations. It also laid out a long-sighted vision for a worker-led transition to EVs and public transit. UAWD pursues this program in three ways: it supports worker-leaders in building chapters in UAW Locals that are rooted in shop-floor action; it runs trainings on class-struggle unionism; and it carries out a political education program by producing and distributing its publication, Daily Struggle, online and to more than one hundred UAW workplaces.

There is a fundamental difference between class-struggle unionism and reform-based strategies – like that of a group of leaders who split from UAWD in April 2025 to form UAW Member Action, a Labor Notes-backed project. Reform strategies focus on installing better leaders, improving grievance handling, or making the union more democratic: on their own, these strategies cannot challenge the paradigm of labor peace or address the crisis facing working people. Class struggle strategies seek to transform relations between capital and labor in the workplace and beyond.

SWA’s scope is broader than the UAW, but some of its main organizing targets are non-union auto plants in the South, emphasizing that fights must be anchored in communities and expand beyond the contours of existing labor law if workers are to win. One of its core efforts is its rank-and-file project, helping militants secure jobs in strategic workplaces – like EV plants – to build power.

Finally, it is crucial to see the strategy of class-struggle unionism and the vision of collectively controlled manufacturing as parts of the same whole. Without an internationalist worker-led program, a zero-sum trade logic will short circuit the possibility of expanding solidarity and will trap workers into competing against each other as new technology and industry restructuring continues to erode jobs. On the other hand, these goals cannot be achieved by simply asking nicely. They can only be won through militancy, self-organized working-class formations, and a cohesive vision for the future of manufacturing shared by rank-and-file workers. Ultimately, these efforts build toward a socialist horizon: transforming the entire industry to be run for social benefit rather than private profit.

For the UAW and the entire working class, it will be impossible to reverse the decline of the labor movement, let alone go on the offense, through piecemeal reforms or tinkering with organizing tactics. As we approach the 2030s, a new layer of committed worker-leaders with a political vision is direly needed to lead their coworkers in the fight for control over the future of manufacturing. •

text:
Sona Comstar told investors on November 1, 2026 that its annual spending will climb from the current range of INR 500-600 crore, according to a Business Standard report quoting Managing Director and Group CEO Vivek Vikram Singh. The money goes to R&D, capacity and new capabilities, and it arrives just days after the Indian drivetrain supplier posted a quarter in which EV revenue grew 129% and reached 51% of automotive product sales, per an Investing.com summary of the October 26 earnings call.

The pairing matters for anyone tracking hardware supply chains. A company that makes differentials, reduction gears, e-axles and motor controllers is telling the market that India’s EV demand is running ahead of plan, and that the country could win business as global carmakers look beyond China. Singh added a condition: Indian suppliers must build the design and manufacturing depth to earn it.

This analysis walks through the numbers, the hardware behind them, and the competitive context. It also separates what the companies have confirmed from what still sits in the reported-only bucket. The US backdrop is worth keeping in view, since EV sales fell 23.8% without tax credits while Indian demand moved the other way.

The November 1 Investment Signal

Business Standard reported that Singh expects Sona Comstar’s annual investments to rise as the business grows. The current run rate sits at INR 500-600 crore a year. He pointed to three destinations for the extra spending: R&D, capacity expansion and new capabilities. The company has not published a new capex figure or a project list alongside the comment, so the signal is directional rather than a budget.

The same report carried Singh’s view that EV adoption in India has moved faster than the company expected. He called India the fastest-growing EV market in the world, and said orders already won will begin to convert into revenue. That framing explains why a supplier with a big order book still talks about spending more. Orders on paper need tooling, lines and engineers before they turn into shipped gearboxes.

Compare the INR 500-600 crore figure with the cash-flow data from the October 26 call. Investing.com’s summary shows H1 FY27 capex of INR 148 crore, which would put the first half well below an annual pace of INR 500-600 crore. Two readings are possible. Either spending is back-loaded into the second half, or the annual investments figure counts items beyond plant and machinery, such as R&D. The reports do not settle it, so treat the second half as the test.

Q2 FY27 Results: The Numbers Behind the Signal

Sona Comstar’s Q2 FY27 revenue reached INR 1,546 crore, up 35% from a year earlier and 18% from the prior quarter. Profit after tax hit INR 223 crore, up 29%. The company ran an EBITDA margin of 23.0%, which is 230 basis points lower than a year earlier. It sits at the bottom of the 23%-25% guidance band that management kept in place.

Source: Investing.com summary of the October 26, 2026 earnings call.

Revenue grew faster than profit, and margins slipped. That pattern fits a business ramping new EV programmes, where early volumes carry heavier start-up costs. Management still guides to 23%-25%, and it describes a medium-term aspiration of 25% revenue CAGR. Cash conversion of 90% of EBITDA gives the company room to fund the higher spending Singh described without leaning on debt.

EVs Now Make Up Over Half of Automotive Sales

The headline shift sits in the product mix. EV revenue grew 129% year over year in Q2 FY27 and made up 51% of automotive product sales. For the first half, the share was 48%, and H1 battery-EV revenue topped INR 1,042 crore. Autocar Pro’s April 30 report put the Q4 FY26 battery-EV share at 39% and the full-year FY26 share near 35%. So the share climbed roughly 12 points in two quarters.

Why the mix shift matters for a gear maker

An EV drivetrain cuts the part count of a combustion powertrain but raises the content value of what remains. A single-speed reduction gear, a differential assembly and an e-axle replace a multi-speed transmission. Suppliers that already cut precision gears can capture more rupees per vehicle if they move up to assembled systems. Autocar Pro described exactly that goal, saying Sona Comstar is moving from component supplier to integrated-systems provider.

What the crossover point says

Crossing 50% marks the point where the legacy business stops defining the company. Combustion-linked lines still generate cash, but the growth, the new customers and the capital all point at electric programmes. Investors who valued the stock as an auto-parts maker now have to price it as an EV hardware supplier.

Order Book Growth: From a 2022 Capex Plan to INR 251 Billion

The order book gives the clearest read on how far the company has come. In March 2022, S&P Global’s AutoTechInsight, citing ET Auto, reported a plan to spend up to INR 9.5 billion (about USD 123.7 million) on EV capacity over fiscal 2022 to 2024, funded through debt and equity. By the October 2026 call, the net order book stood at INR 251 billion, with INR 36 billion of new orders added in Q2 alone.

The 31 programmes yet to start deserve attention. They represent revenue the company has won but not yet shipped, which is the pipeline that justifies the higher investment Singh described. Robotics accounted for 4% of the order book, a small slice that shows management’s push beyond passenger cars into other applications.

The Hardware Inside: Differentials, E-Axles and Controllers

Sona Comstar’s core products are differential gears and assemblies, starter motors, and EV traction components. Autocar Pro cited a global share of 8.7% in differential gears, with a double-digit share in EV differential assemblies. In Q2 FY27 the company commercialised three new products: a helical limited slip differential, air springs and rear radar sensors. None of the three belongs to a classic gear shop’s catalogue, which shows how far the portfolio has stretched.

Autocar Pro’s April report listed motor controllers, radar sensors, e-axles and propulsion systems for eVTOL aircraft and autonomous mobile robots as areas of expansion. The company frames its future under the term EPIC mobility, short for electric, personalized, intelligent and connected. For a hardware reader, the useful takeaway is that the company is buying its way into electronics and sensing, not just gear cutting.

Its operating model leans on what Singh calls fungible capacity. Production lines serve multiple customers and programmes, so equipment and floor space can shift as demand moves. Competitors tied to a single customer or vehicle programme lack that flexibility. When a programme slips, a fungible plant reassigns the line. A dedicated plant sits idle.

The C-Motive Electrostatic Motor Bet

One partnership shows where the R&D money may flow. In May 2022, S&P Global’s AutoTechInsight reported that Sona Comstar partnered with C-Motive Technologies to develop electrostatic drive motors for EV applications, with serial production expected in 2026. The accessible portion of that report did not detail performance claims, and nothing in the current reporting confirms whether the 2026 target has been met.

The idea matters because conventional EV motors depend on magnets and copper windings, and magnet supply chains concentrate in China. An electrostatic design takes a different physical route to torque. Whether it reaches commercial volume is unconfirmed, so treat it as an option on a supply-chain shift rather than a proven product. If Singh’s call for deeper Indian design capability has a concrete example, this is a candidate.

India’s EV Demand Outruns the Plan

Singh told Business Standard that India’s EV adoption has moved faster than Sona Comstar anticipated. The data on the supplier side backs this up, though it cannot isolate India from other markets. The Investing.com summary says Eastern markets contribute about two-thirds of total revenue, which reflects the company’s reorientation toward Asia. An earlier Finimize report, undated in the version retrieved, had North America and Europe at 66% of revenue and India at 28%.

Read together, those two snapshots suggest a flip in the revenue map, with the caveat that the sources use different category definitions and dates. Indian demand now matters for the supplier base in a way it did not three years ago. For a wider view of how the country is building its tech base, see India’s sovereign AI push of 20 models and 38,000 GPUs, which shows the same pattern of domestic capability building in a different sector.

The China Diversification Question

Business Standard reported that Singh sees India gaining as global companies diversify supply chains away from China, provided domestic suppliers develop the design and manufacturing capabilities required. He also said a broader lift in manufacturing standards across Indian suppliers would help pull more volume to the country. This is a conditional statement from a company executive, not a forecast of lost Chinese share.

The scale gap shows why the condition matters. China’s EV industry operates at volumes that few markets match. Xiaomi alone delivered more than 50,000 EVs in October, and that is a single newer entrant. Winning business from China-centred supply chains means matching cost, quality and delivery timing against a mature ecosystem.

Sona Comstar itself keeps a foot in China. Convergence Now and Acko Drive reported a joint venture with China’s Jinnaite Machinery, based in Shandong province, to make differential assemblies and reduction gears for global EV makers. Acko Drive’s headline put the venture at INR 167 crore. So the company hedges: it invests in India while building inside the Chinese cost base.

Asia Pivot and the Joint-Venture Calendar

Finimize reported that Sona Comstar wants Asian markets to deliver more than half of revenue within five years, with China, Japan and South Korea as the focus. The same report noted Western light-vehicle sales falling from 37 million units in 2015 to 34 million in the year it covered, and China’s electric and hybrid sales rising 50% in 2024. It also mentioned a pursuit of acquisitions, including Escorts Kubota’s railway unit.

The October 26 call added dates. The Investing.com summary lists a first joint-venture carve-out targeted to close by the end of December 2026 and a second targeted for the first half of calendar 2027. The summary does not name the counterparties for those two deals, so readers should not assume they match the Jinnaite venture. Those closings are the nearest hard checkpoints for the Asia strategy.

Competitive Picture: Europe’s Supplier Shakeout

Singh used an Autocar Pro interview to describe Sona Comstar’s position after European supplier failures. Autocar Pro named Neapco Europe and AIMS as regional competitors that went bankrupt. Singh argued that the distress came from the timing of legacy investments, not from weak EV demand, and he cited EV sales in Europe jumping around 50% in certain recent periods.

He split the growth strategy into three axes. Axis X means more share with existing products. Axis Y covers new product development. Axis Z targets new applications beyond passenger vehicles, including off-highway, robotics, aerospace, electric two-wheelers and heavy-duty buses. Fungible capacity gives the company a way to fund all three without stranding assets.

Rivals in the US and Europe face a different cost of capital and a different demand picture. For a US read on how EV makers are holding up, Rivian’s Q3 delivered 19,248 vehicles and $2.155 billion in revenue. Sona Comstar sells into that kind of customer base, among others, which is why its order book spans 37 customers.

Market Impact for Investors, OEMs and Suppliers

For investors, the data points to a supplier whose growth is real and whose margin is under mild pressure. Revenue climbed 43% in the first half, yet the Q2 margin hit the low end of guidance. The order book equals roughly five times annual revenue by Autocar Pro’s April math, which gives long visibility. The risk lies in execution, since 31 programmes still have not started production.

For automakers, the message is that a credible non-Chinese drivetrain source is scaling up. For Indian suppliers, the message carries a harder edge. Singh tied India’s chance to design and manufacturing capability, which means smaller firms that cannot meet quality and engineering standards will not share in any diversification gains. Component bottlenecks elsewhere in the stack add pressure too, as shown by SK Hynix’s sellout through 2029, a reminder that electronics supply can constrain vehicles as much as gears do.

Historical Context: Four Years of Repositioning

In March 2022 the company planned up to INR 9.5 billion of EV capex across three fiscal years. By April 2026 the order book was INR 23,700 crore, with nearly 70% tied to EV programmes. By October 2026 it reached INR 251 billion with EV revenue above half of automotive product sales. FY26 itself brought 26% revenue growth to INR 44,751 million and 13% EBITDA growth to INR 11,069 million, at a 24.7% margin, per Autocar Pro.

The arc runs from a gear maker with an EV plan to an EV systems supplier with a combustion legacy. Each step added products: motors, controllers, sensors, air springs. Margins eased from 24.7% in FY26 to 23.0% in Q2 FY27 as the mix changed. That trade-off, more revenue and more content in exchange for slightly thinner margins, is the cost of the transition. A parallel consumer-side view appears in our look at the three-year payback claim for a new EV.

Predictions: What to Watch Through 2027

Capex steps up in H2 FY27. If the INR 500-600 crore annual figure is a capex guide, H1’s INR 148 crore implies a heavier second half. Watch the Q3 call for the number.

The first joint-venture closes on schedule or slips. Management targeted end-December 2026. A delay would hint at regulatory or counterparty friction.

EV share stays above 50%. With 31 EPIC programmes not yet in production, the mix should hold or rise as they start, though a margin dip toward the bottom of guidance is plausible.

More integrated-system wins. Expect announcements around e-axles and controllers, where content per vehicle rises fastest.

Indian supplier consolidation. Singh’s capability condition favours larger, better-capitalised firms, so smaller suppliers may seek partners.

These are analytical expectations, not company guidance. The only guidance on record is the 23%-25% EBITDA margin band and the 25% medium-term revenue growth aspiration. For more hardware coverage, browse the hardware section.

FAQ: Sona Comstar and India’s EV Supply Chain

What did Sona Comstar announce on November 1, 2026?

Business Standard reported that Managing Director and Group CEO Vivek Vikram Singh expects annual investments, now INR 500-600 crore, to rise as the business grows. The company has not published a specific new capex amount.

How big is Sona Comstar’s EV business?

EV revenue grew 129% year over year in Q2 FY27 and made up 51% of automotive product sales, according to the Investing.com summary of the October 26 call. H1 battery-EV revenue exceeded INR 1,042 crore.

What is the company’s order book?

The net order book stood at INR 251 billion at the Q2 FY27 call, with INR 36 billion added in the quarter. It covers 75 EPIC programmes across 37 customers, of which 44 are in production.

Will India replace China in EV supply chains?

No source says so. Singh said India could gain from supply-chain diversification away from China if Indian suppliers build the needed design and manufacturing capability. The company also runs a reported joint venture in China’s Shandong province.

What is the profit and margin picture?

Q2 FY27 PAT reached INR 223 crore, up 29%, on a 23.0% EBITDA margin. Management kept its 23%-25% margin guidance and a 25% medium-term revenue CAGR aspiration.

What products drive the shift beyond gears?

Q2 brought a helical limited slip differential, air springs and rear radar sensors. Autocar Pro also lists motor controllers, e-axles and propulsion for eVTOL aircraft and autonomous mobile robots as expansion areas.

When do the joint ventures close?

The earnings-call summary targets the first carve-out by the end of December 2026 and the second in the first half of calendar 2027. Counterparties were not named in the summary.

text:
Ford's Escape SUV may be getting a second chance as an electric vehicle after the automaker ended production of the gas-powered model.

A new report points to 2029 as a possible return date for the SUV, whose gas-powered run lasted 25 years. Ford has left the door open, saying the "SUV may be taking a breather for now," after ending production.

Here's what to know

Louisville Assembly Plant is the proposed production site for the electric Escape, with manufacturing expected to begin in 2029, Electrek reported. The crossover would use Ford's Universal Electric Vehicle platform, per Ford Authority.

With the Fathom electric pickup scheduled to launch in 2027, the Escape could be next in line to use the platform.

The electric model is expected to have dimensions similar to the outgoing Escape, which Electrek lists as having a 106.7-inch wheelbase, a length of 180.1 inches, a width of 74.1 inches without mirrors, and a height of 66.1 inches.

Hyundai's Tucson and Toyota's RAV4 would therefore remain compact-SUV peers for an Escape of that size.

More background

Shoppers visiting the Escape's page on Ford's website are currently directed to other Ford vehicles. The Edge's page, by contrast, describes that model's run as over.

The reported Escape revival would give Louisville another EV to build after the Fathom pickup. Electrek says the factory's conversion for Fathom manufacturing coincided with the end of gasoline Escape production.

For Escape shoppers considering an EV as their next car, potential benefits include lower fuel costs and reduced routine maintenance. However, the report provides no Escape EV price, driving range, or charging specifications.

What's being done?

Ford's more immediate effort to offer an affordable electric vehicle centers on the Fathom.

A $1,595 delivery fee brings the starting cost to $29,945, keeping it below $30,000. Preorders are scheduled to open in early 2027, with the standard-range version starting at $28,350.

The pickup's standard equipment will include Apple CarPlay, Android Auto, and bidirectional charging. Electrek also says the vehicle will be BlueCruise-capable for hands-free driving and will debut Apple Maps integration in its navigation system.

During Ford's third-quarter earnings call, CEO Jim Farley described the pickup as "a breakthrough product."

Where can I learn more?

title: Roadmap outlines plastics industry emissions cuts - American Recycler
description:
The roadmap identifies practical strategies that could significantly reduce emissions associated with predominant U.S. PET beverage bottle systems through 2050.
The roadmap finds that, by 2050, the PET industry can reduce the life cycle greenhouse gas emissions intensity of the PET beverage bottle systems studied by approximately 57 percent.
The roadmap demonstrates how the industry can reduce emissions from PET beverage bottles even further.
More efficient production, expanded collection and processing, greater availability of recycled PET, and continued packaging innovation can strengthen domestic supply chains while reducing environmental impacts.
“Efficiency gains matter, but deeper reductions require reliable access to high-quality recycled PET.
text:
The National Association for PET Container Resources (NAPCOR) released PET Forward: A Decarbonization Roadmap for the PET Packaging Value Chain, a new analysis developed by independent environmental consulting firm Eastern Research Group, Inc. (ERG). The roadmap identifies practical strategies that could significantly reduce emissions associated with predominant U.S. PET beverage bottle systems through 2050. PET (polyethylene terephthalate), widely identified by the #1 inside the triangle, is the most recycled plastic in the world.

The roadmap finds that, by 2050, the PET industry can reduce the life cycle greenhouse gas emissions intensity of the PET beverage bottle systems studied by approximately 57 percent. In practical terms, this means significantly reducing the greenhouse gas emissions associated with each bottle across its full life cycle, from the materials used to make it through its eventual disposal or recycling. Even as production grows, total annual emissions associated with the systems studied could decline by about 42 percent, the equivalent to taking 323,000 gas-powered passenger vehicles off the road.

NAPCOR’s new research builds on its comparative life cycle assessment, which found that a typical PET soda bottle has less than half the total greenhouse gas footprint of an aluminum can and approximately one-fifth that of a glass bottle. The roadmap demonstrates how the industry can reduce emissions from PET beverage bottles even further.

Meaningful progress does not depend solely on future breakthroughs. Many of the strategies driving the modeled reductions are already available across the PET value chain, including lightweighting, renewable energy, and improvements in manufacturing efficiency. Over time, stronger collection systems, increased recycling and recycled content, and continued investment in infrastructure and innovation can drive further progress.

“PET is already starting from a position of strength,” said Laura Stewart, executive director of NAPCOR. “It has a lower greenhouse gas footprint than common beverage packaging alternatives, is the most recycled plastic in the world, and is supported by an established bottle-to-bottle recycling system operating at scale. This roadmap shows that we don’t have to choose between meeting growing consumer demand and continuing to improve environmental performance; we can do both.”

A practical pathway to lower emissions

The ISO-compliant roadmap builds on NAPCOR’s 2023 peer-reviewed, ISO-compliant life cycle assessment and examines four of the predominant PET beverage bottle systems sold in the U.S.– 16.9 ounce water bottles and 16.9 ounce, 20 ounce, and 2 liter carbonated soft drink bottles. The PET Forward Roadmap evaluates emissions across the bottle life cycle, from raw material production and manufacturing through transportation and end-of-life management, and models how that footprint could change through 2050. An independent third-party expert peer-reviewed the final report.

The analysis shows that substantial progress can happen well before 2050. Under the modeled pathway, the emissions intensity of a 16.9 ounce PET water bottle system, measured per 1,000 gallons of beverage delivered, could decline approximately 44 percent by 2035 compared with the 2023 baseline. The three carbonated soft drink bottle systems studied could achieve emissions intensity reductions of approximately 35 to 43 percent over the same period.

The roadmap also distinguishes between actions the PET industry can advance directly, and the broader conditions needed to unlock additional progress. Manufacturers can continue improving bottle design, energy efficiency, and production processes, while deeper long-term gains depend on factors across the wider system, including reliable supplies of high-quality recycled PET, stronger collection and sorting infrastructure, recycling capacity, and supportive policy.

“The analysis is designed as a roadmap. It models the cumulative impact of multiple strategies over time and includes sensitivity analyses to account for variables such as future production growth and different approaches to measuring the benefits of recycling. The result is a framework for identifying where the PET industry can act today and where collaboration across the value chain will be necessary to achieve further progress,” said Dr. Mariya Absar, senior LCA expert at ERG.

Decarbonization and American manufacturing

The roadmap also demonstrates that reducing emissions and supporting economic growth do not have to be competing objectives.

“Recycling strengthens American manufacturing,” added Stewart. “When we collect more PET and recycle it here in the United States, we create a stronger domestic supply of valuable material for manufacturers. Policies that improve collection and encourage investment in recycling infrastructure can help accelerate environmental progress while also strengthening American manufacturing and supply chain resilience.”

Many of the investments needed to advance PET decarbonization are also investments in U.S. manufacturing and recycling capacity. More efficient production, expanded collection and processing, greater availability of recycled PET, and continued packaging innovation can strengthen domestic supply chains while reducing environmental impacts.

“Decarbonization depends on connecting manufacturing with the recycling system,” stated Tom Busard, NAPCOR board chair, chief polymers and recycling officer for Plastipak Packaging, Inc., and president of Clean Tech, Plastipak’s recycling affiliate. “Efficiency gains matter, but deeper reductions require reliable access to high-quality recycled PET. That makes stronger collection and domestic recycling capacity essential to delivering lower carbon packaging at scale.”
