title: Colorado firm seeks to challenge China's grip on rare-earth production - Denver Gazette
description:
Energy Fuels is investing in additional equipment and acquiring overseas manufacturers to extend that capability from raw minerals to finished magnets.
Its Lakewood headquarters directs a strategy spanning mines, processing plants and manufacturing facilities in several countries.
Its owners maintained the facility and its operating capabilities through periods when conventional uranium production was financially unattractive.
Energy Fuels’ 2025 annual report listed 1,069 employees, including 252 in the United States, before the Australian acquisition.
Those disputes are part of the industrial history Energy Fuels is carrying into its new business.
text:
Industrial capabilities preserved through decades of uranium market decline have given a Lakewood company a starting point in the national effort to establish rare-earth production outside China.

China dominates global production of the rare-earth permanent magnets used in electric vehicles, wind turbines and weapons systems. The International Energy Agency estimates that China produced 94% of the world’s sintered permanent magnets in 2024.

Recommended Stories

▶

Lakewood-headquartered Energy Fuels Inc. is attempting to challenge that dominance using an unlikely foundation: the last operating conventional uranium mill in the United States.

Energy Fuels Inc. is building a rare-earth processing and magnet-manufacturing business around its White Mesa Mill in southeastern Utah, a facility that survived decades of uranium-industry decline while other conventional mills across the Colorado Plateau shut down.

White Mesa’s existing permits, specialized workforce, processing equipment and experience handling radioactive materials provided a foundation for separating rare-earth elements without building an entirely new processing complex, according to company officials.

Energy Fuels is investing in additional equipment and acquiring overseas manufacturers to extend that capability from raw minerals to finished magnets. Its Lakewood headquarters directs a strategy spanning mines, processing plants and manufacturing facilities in several countries.

The transformation illustrates how infrastructure developed for America’s nuclear industry has acquired new importance, as the federal government seeks to reduce dependence on China for critical minerals.

The strategy also depends on an industry with a complicated history in Western Colorado, Utah and Arizona, where environmental opposition continues over abandoned mines, contaminated processing sites and potential groundwater impacts.

A mill that survived

White Mesa began operating in 1980, near the end of the uranium boom that transformed communities across the Colorado Plateau.

During World War II and the Cold War, uranium mills processed ore from mines throughout Western Colorado and neighboring states. When demand weakened and prices fell, most mines and mills closed, according to federal uranium-industry histories.

White Mesa survived successive downturns. Its owners maintained the facility and its operating capabilities through periods when conventional uranium production was financially unattractive.

The present Energy Fuels Inc. acquired White Mesa from Denison Mines in 2012. Earlier owners were responsible for preserving the facility before that acquisition, although Energy Fuels has described longstanding connections between some of its leadership and the uranium industry.

Energy Fuels subsequently retained the mill as a central part of its business, maintaining the capability to process uranium even when market conditions limited production.

“We’ve kept the mill running through periods when uranium prices were very low. That is what allows us to do the rare earth work now,” said Curtis Moore, senior vice president of marketing and corporate development. “The White Mesa Mill is the only conventional uranium mill operating in the United States.”

That continuity matters because rare-earth production requires more than access to mineral deposits. Companies must chemically separate the elements, refine them to industrial specifications and convert them into metals, alloys and magnets.

Monazite, a mineral Energy Fuels intends to process, can contain naturally occurring uranium and thorium. The company says White Mesa’s existing capabilities for handling radioactive materials give it an advantage in processing feedstocks that present additional technical and regulatory challenges.

The mill is not simply switching businesses. Energy Fuels officials said the company intends to maintain uranium production while expanding rare-earth processing.

According to the company’s 2025 production results, White Mesa produced more than 1 million pounds of finished uranium oxide, commonly called yellowcake, that year. Industry analyses of U.S. Energy Information Administration data identified Energy Fuels as the leading domestic uranium producer.

From uranium to magnets

Energy Fuels has installed equipment at White Mesa to separate light rare-earth elements, including neodymium and praseodymium, used in powerful permanent magnets.

In July, the company announced construction of a commercial-scale expansion to separate heavy rare-earth elements, including dysprosium and terbium, which improve magnet performance under high-temperature conditions.

Energy Fuels estimated that the expansion will cost $104 million and targets commissioning in late 2027.

The company is extending that processing capability into an international manufacturing business.

Energy Fuels completed its acquisition of Australian Strategic Materials, according to an August filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, gaining existing rare-earth metals and alloys production at a plant in South Korea.

It also has an agreement to acquire Vacuumschmelze, a German permanent-magnet manufacturer with operations in Europe and South Carolina. Company disclosures assigned the transaction an implied equity value of about $1.9 billion when announced.

Energy Fuels expects completion in early 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and other conditions.

The acquisitions would establish corporate control over successive production stages, from refining rare-earth minerals to manufacturing finished magnets, according to Energy Fuels.

“We will have the ability to go from the mine to the magnet, which is something that no other company outside of China can currently do,” Moore said. “Energy Fuels will be the only fully integrated mined magnet rare earth manufacturer in the world outside of China.”

That is the company’s competitive claim, not a description of its current capabilities. Some stages are operating, others are under construction and the proposed magnet business depends on acquisitions that have yet to close.

Other companies are also developing rare-earth supply chains outside China. Energy Fuels identifies its proposed distinction as corporate control over every major production stage.

In June, the U.S. Office of Strategic Capital announced a conditional loan commitment of up to $725 million to support expanded rare-earth processing at White Mesa and development of a U.S. metals and alloys plant.

The Department of Defense described the financing as part of its effort to expand domestic permanent-magnet production and reduce reliance on Chinese processing. The loan remains subject to final reviews and closing requirements.

Energy Fuels said much of its rare-earth feedstock will come from heavy-mineral-sand projects outside Colorado, including operations or proposed developments in Australia, Madagascar and Brazil.

Moore has projected that the expanded rare-earth and magnet business could eventually employ about 2,500 people worldwide. Energy Fuels’ 2025 annual report listed 1,069 employees, including 252 in the United States, before the Australian acquisition.

The company has not publicly quantified how many additional jobs the strategy would create in Colorado. Most identified processing and manufacturing facilities are outside the state.

The mines behind the mill

Energy Fuels’ expansion into rare earths does not mean it is abandoning uranium.

According to company production reports, its Pinyon Plain mine in Northern Arizona supplies high-grade uranium ore to White Mesa, sustaining the processing business that helped make the rare-earth expansion possible.

Pinyon Plain, south of Grand Canyon National Park, demonstrates that uranium mining remains an active part of Energy Fuels’ operations, rather than merely its industrial history.

The Navajo Nation opposed transporting uranium ore across tribal lands, citing historical contamination and the legacy of hundreds of abandoned mines.

In 2025, Energy Fuels and the Navajo Nation announced an agreement allowing limited shipments under inspection and decontamination protocols, accompanied by company commitments to assist with cleanup of abandoned uranium mines.

Navajo Nation President Buu Nygren has said the nation supplied more than half the uranium mined in the United States during an earlier era and was left with more than 500 abandoned mines.

“We’ve got people that live close to a lot of these mines, and it’s continuing to affect our land, our environment,” he said.

The Navajo Nation banned new uranium mining on its lands in 2005.

For Energy Fuels, Pinyon Plain supports the uranium business that helps sustain White Mesa. For tribal opponents, the operation remains connected to an industry whose earlier environmental consequences have not been fully resolved.

Western Colorado’s uranium revival

The uranium industry is also moving toward renewed production in the historic mining districts of Western Colorado.

Energy Fuels reported that it began dewatering and rehabilitating the access tunnel at its permitted Whirlwind uranium mine on the Colorado-Utah border near Gateway.

According to the company’s operating updates, rehabilitation is expected to finish in 2026, with production potentially beginning in 2027 if market conditions justify it.

Other operators are pursuing production in the same mineral belt.

Western Uranium & Vanadium has reported shipping ore from its Sunday Mine Complex above the Dolores River to White Mesa under a purchase agreement. The company is also pursuing its proposed Mustang processing plant at the former Piñon Ridge site in Montrose County.

Anfield Energy has advanced permitting to restart its past-producing JD-8 mine in Montrose County. State regulatory records and company disclosures show that the project progressed beyond its initial application-completeness review, although financial warranties and other conditions remain relevant.

The renewed activity is taking place in the Uravan Mineral Belt, whose uranium and vanadium deposits supplied wartime and Cold War industries, according to federal mining histories.

Its history also includes extensive federal and state reclamation projects.

Along the Dolores River corridor, government agencies have reclaimed abandoned mine portals, waste-rock piles and processing sites.

The Department of Energy’s Office of Legacy Management reports completing reclamation at the Burro Mines Complex in San Miguel County to address erosion and waste-rock sedimentation affecting the Dolores River.

At Slick Rock, former uranium-processing sites beside the river remain subject to groundwater monitoring. Federal monitoring records identify residual uranium contamination in some shallow groundwater, although those findings do not by themselves establish that river water exceeds applicable standards.

The former Uravan mill town on the San Miguel River was evacuated, demolished and remediated under the federal Superfund program.

In January, San Miguel County commissioners adopted updated mining and mineral-processing regulations, according to county records.

The Colorado Mining Association and Western Uranium & Vanadium argued that the requirements duplicate state regulations and could give the county effective veto authority over projects holding state permits.

County officials maintained that the rules address local impacts, recognize qualifying state and federal permitting documents and do not prohibit mining.

Mining companies emphasized modern reclamation requirements, financial assurances and environmental controls that differ from those governing the industry during the Cold War. Local governments, tribal communities and environmental opponents continue to question whether those measures adequately address groundwater contamination, waste handling and long-term impacts.

Those disputes are part of the industrial history Energy Fuels is carrying into its new business.

Survival means capabilities, company says

Energy Fuels said White Mesa’s continued operation gives it capabilities that would be difficult to reproduce quickly by acquiring mineral rights or announcing a manufacturing plant.

The company already possesses a permitted uranium-processing facility, experienced workers, established infrastructure and the ability to handle mineral feedstocks containing radioactive materials.

Energy Fuels officials added that those capabilities allowed it to begin rare-earth separation while other companies must develop processing facilities, expertise and regulatory approvals.

Whether that advantage translates into successful commercial magnet production will depend on engineering performance, financing, mineral supplies, manufacturing costs and completion of acquisitions.

Company disclosures acknowledge that its international strategy remains unfinished. Its proposed scale depends on construction, successful integration of acquired businesses and the ability to compete with established Chinese producers.

But its foundation already exists at White Mesa.

The company’s ability to pursue that transformation rests substantially on a uranium mill that survived when the rest of the conventional American milling industry disappeared.

text:
Thailand and Bhutan have signed three cooperation agreements covering healthcare, agricultural finance and clean energy as the countries seek to deepen economic ties, expand investment opportunities and promote sustainable development.

Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, who is also interior minister, witnessed the signing and exchange of the agreements in Thimphu on Saturday during his official visit to the Himalayan kingdom.

Government spokesman Ekkapob Pianpises said the agreements aim to boost the exchange of knowledge and technology, improve medical services, expand access to finance for farmers and small businesses, and support renewable energy development.

The first memorandum of understanding (MoU), between the Thai and Bhutanese public health ministries, covers universal healthcare, disease prevention and control, medical personnel development and medical research.

It also promotes cooperation in digital healthcare, telemedicine and artificial intelligence (AI), as well as arrangements for Bhutanese patients to receive treatment at Thai public hospitals.

The second agreement is a renewed MoU between the Bank for Agriculture and Agricultural Cooperatives (BAAC) and Bhutan Development Bank Ltd (BDBL) covering financial cooperation.

Areas of collaboration include green loans for sustainable agriculture, credit risk assessment, cross-border money transfers and trade in agricultural products and community-based goods. The aim is to improve access to finance for farmers and small enterprises in both countries.

The third document, a record of discussions on clean energy cooperation involving Thailand's Neighbouring Countries Economic Development Cooperation Agency (NEDA), Bhutan's Finance Ministry and Norion Renewable Energy Ltd, provides for technical assistance to review feasibility studies and detailed designs for a proposed 100-megawatt solar-agriculture project in Tareythang, Bhutan.

Mr Ekkapob said the agreements were testament to Thailand's commitment to translating its longstanding relationship with Bhutan into practical benefits for people in both countries.

The signing followed talks between Mr Anutin and Bhutanese Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay in Thimphu on Oct 30, during which the two leaders agreed to expand cooperation in trade, investment, infrastructure, healthcare, education and clean energy.

Both sides welcomed progress on a Thailand-Bhutan free trade agreement (FTA), which they hope will take effect on Jan 1, 2027. The agreement is expected to boost bilateral trade and investment.

text:
Space Exploration Technologies Corp.’s SPCX AI division, SpaceXAI, failed to get an NAACP Clean Air Act lawsuit thrown out, with a federal judge’s opinion released late Friday keeping the Mississippi case alive.

The dispute centers on gas-fired turbines used to supply electricity for AI data centers near Memphis.

The ruling comes as the Elon Musk-led company is working under an agreed timetable to wind down temporary units at its Southaven site, with the last mobile turbines scheduled to leave by July 2027.

The NAACP’s complaint, filed in April 2026, targets xAI and related entities now owned and run by SpaceX, and the court declined to accept the company’s bid to end the case, reported CNBC. The suit alleges the companies installed and operated 27 turbines in Southaven between August and December 2025 without an air permit.

Judge Rejects Company’s Defense

SpaceXAI has framed its turbine strategy as transitional, telling regulators it is moving toward a larger, permanent electricity setup for its Greater Memphis-area supercomputer project. In that update, the company tied the phaseout of temporary generators to a 1.2-gigawatt facility it says is being developed under a Clean Air Act permit.

The NAACP’s case was brought with the Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice acting as counsel.

The judge rejected the company’s core defenses and allowed the claims to continue, writing: "Because the plaintiffs have statutory standing under the Clean Air Act, because the combustion turbines are not ‘mobile sources’ under Mississippi’s SIP, and because the citizen suit provision does not violate Article II of the Constitution or the private nondelegation doctrine, the plaintiffs’ claims will proceed."

The decision followed another setback for the company in the same court roughly two weeks earlier, when a Justice Department request to end the case was turned away, according to the report.

SpaceX Calls It Mobile Equipment

In court filings, SpaceXAI argued the turbines should be treated as mobile equipment and therefore outside certain permitting rules, while also challenging the NAACP’s ability to sue under the statute. The judge disagreed, concluding the turbines did not qualify as mobile sources under Mississippi’s state implementation plan.

SpaceXAI said air monitoring shows local conditions continue to meet or exceed Environmental Protection Agency standards.

The permanent buildout described by SpaceXAI is larger than the temporary setup at the center of the lawsuit. The company said the long-term plant will use 41 turbines and that it received a Clean Air Act permit for that facility in March 2026.

title: AI's power bill could come at the planet's expense as US data centres push emissions ...
description:
Many data center developers are turning to natural gas to meet the immense electricity demand, relying on power sources that are both on and off the grid.
The Sierra Club’s estimate of the climate impacts of the data center buildout is higher than others released so far.
Other forecasts see US electricity continuing to decarbonize as economically competitive renewables outperform fossil fuels, despite the data center boom.
In 2009, thanks to advances in hydraulic fracturing, the US became the world’s largest natural gas producer.
The fracking boom in turn drove down the price of natural gas, displacing dirtier coal plants across the US.
text:
Many data center developers are turning to natural gas to meet the immense electricity demand, relying on power sources that are both on and off the grid. The bulk of the expected emissions by 2030 would come from sources that are not directly linked to the grid, often built by tech companies to avoid the long wait for a connection. These could exceed 460 million tons, Fisher said, roughly the same as the annual emissions of Mexico.

Helen Kou, a BloombergNEF analyst, said if there’s significant growth in gas power for new facilities, “you would presume emissions would increase from year to date.”

But how much is a difficult question to answer. There’s so much uncertainty in the projections for power emissions that the lowest and highest estimates differ by more electricity than the combined demand of California and Florida.

The Sierra Club’s estimate of the climate impacts of the data center buildout is higher than others released so far. The wide range of projections is due to questions around how many facilities will actually be built, what technologies they will ultimately use and how much renewable energy capacity comes online over the next few years.

The environmental nonprofit Union of Concerned Scientists in January projected that fossil-fuel-powered electricity for data centers could increase US power-sector emissions by 19% to 29%, or as much as 342 million tons a year by 2035. US and Canadian researchers in June published a journal article projecting a 28% rise in the sector’s emissions.

Other forecasts see US electricity continuing to decarbonize as economically competitive renewables outperform fossil fuels, despite the data center boom. Rhodium Group, a research firm that projects energy use and CO2, finds that in its highest-emission scenario for 2040 that the sector’s greenhouse gas emissions fall 24% below their 2025 level.

If the rush to build AI data centers leads to the upper bounds of the emissions projected by these researchers, it represents a reversal of a two-decade economic and policy trend toward less US power-sector climate pollution.

Electricity emissions peaked in 2007. In 2009, thanks to advances in hydraulic fracturing, the US became the world’s largest natural gas producer. The fracking boom in turn drove down the price of natural gas, displacing dirtier coal plants across the US. Meanwhile, the Environmental Protection Agency wrote regulations to dial down carbon from power plants, and former President Joe Biden aimed to decarbonize the grid completely by 2035.

Today, natural gas prices are historically low and President Donald Trump has undertaken a dramatic rollback of climate rules. That helped nudge US power-sector emissions back up in 2025.

The Sierra Club analysis draws on public filings and other groups’ data center projections, including the Environmental Integrity Project’s count of expected plants and emissions by 2030.

Grid-connected generators alone would increase 2030 baseline emissions by 10%, or 154 million tons of CO2. Then there are the bring-your-own-power projects. Four-fifths of the energy for those could come from natural gas, according to a separate analysis by Earthjustice and Better Data Center Project. The increased local air and climate pollution from such plants has already helped stoke opposition to data centers across the country.

If all the projected data centers do end up being built on time, and with new natural gas fueling inefficient turbines 24/7 at some facilities, that could drive power emissions up, said Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at Energy Innovation, a non-partisan energy and climate policy think tank.

“There’s certainly a risk that that’s enough emissions to push us back many years of our progress on reducing power-sector emissions,” he said. “But it’s not a foregone conclusion that that’s going to happen.”

But Pierpont said it’s challenging to model data-center emissions when little is known about factors like backlogs of gas turbine orders, wait times for grid connections or myriad other things that can slow or halt projects.

“There’s just enormous uncertainty, both around the scale of data center demand that ultimately gets built and gets added as well as the power supply strategy,” Pierpont said.

Many projects could be delayed or canceled. Just last month Oracle Corp. submitted a force majeure notice to the developer of its Project Jupiter data center in New Mexico, saying there is a risk that it won’t come online by 2028 as planned due to regulatory setbacks and community opposition.

“The big question of the day is trying to create an accurate forecast of project demand,” BloombergNEF’s Kou said.

name: Clean Energy
title: From students to career changers, this guide maps pathways for all in the renewables job boom
authors: Keeli Dyson, Claire Sams, Kellie O'Brien, Dione David, Joe Davis, Jen White, Lucy Ridge, Oliver Jacques, Michele Tydd, Jeremy Wilshire
description:
The region is set to host NSW’s first urban Renewable Energy Zone (REZ), leveraging local industry and existing infrastructure.
Crucially, the resource is tailored to connect a wide audience with these emerging pathways, including job seekers, career changers, students, First Nations people, career advisers and women considering careers in traditionally male-dominated trades.
The launch comes as state modelling forecasts more than 9000 jobs during peak construction activity and over 4450 ongoing operations and maintenance roles across NSW clean energy projects.
While the technology to decarbonise already exists, the clean energy boom faces an equally urgent challenge: building social licence.
Pathways are highlighted in UOW and Business Illawarra’s Illawarra Clean Energy Roadmap, and Wollongong City Council’s Energy Equity Framework.
text:
“It’s the best office in the world,” says wind farm operations manager Kacee Milnes — and a new state government guide is showing Illawarra residents how to claim a seat in it.

With the region positioned at the heart of New South Wales’ clean energy transition, the Illawarra Renewable Energy Jobs Guide aims to turn thousands of projected renewable energy roles into tangible careers for local workers.

The region is set to host NSW’s first urban Renewable Energy Zone (REZ), leveraging local industry and existing infrastructure. While the zone’s initial planned capacity is set at 1 gigawatt, that figure is expected to grow alongside emerging sectors such as green hydrogen and green steel manufacturing.

To support this growth, the guide maps out opportunities across the entire lifecycle of the industry — from initial construction and engineering to logistics, green manufacturing, environmental management and corporate roles. It breaks down the specific skills, training and qualifications required to secure positions in the state’s expanding project pipeline.

Crucially, the resource is tailored to connect a wide audience with these emerging pathways, including job seekers, career changers, students, First Nations people, career advisers and women considering careers in traditionally male-dominated trades.

The launch comes as state modelling forecasts more than 9000 jobs during peak construction activity and over 4450 ongoing operations and maintenance roles across NSW clean energy projects.

Ms Milnes, a former mining electrician who now oversees 37 turbines at Squadron Energy’s Crudine Ridge Wind Farm, says the industry offers unparalleled career growth and work-life balance.

“I feel like it’s part of my responsibility to try to motivate and encourage because I didn’t have a lot of role models when I was coming up through the industry,” she said. “Renewables are definitely the future. I think that’s the way it’s all going now and there’s so much room for growth … I would love to inspire the next generation to become involved in the industry.”

Ty Christopher, Director of the Energy Futures Network at the University of Wollongong (UOW), says the opportunities outlined in the state guide aren’t an exaggeration.

“I’d describe the guide as a good foundation and a good starting point,” Mr Christopher said. “If anything, it understates the breadth and depth of clean energy employment opportunities within the Illawarra.”

He points to the world-class industrial innovation taking place in the region, from clean-energy company Hysata to battery technology pioneer Sicona and gravitational energy storage outfit Green Gravity, as well as established local engineering firms such as Wise Energy.

At the same time, the region has become the national heartbeat for grassroots electrification. Driven by initiatives such as Rewiring Australia, Electrify 2515 and Hi Neighbour, everyday residents and businesses have spearheaded Australia’s world-leading rooftop solar and home battery uptake.

“That’s not a story of big industry and incumbent players doing the right thing. It’s the opposite: people taking control of their own communities and energy supply,” he says.

Yet Professor Christopher cautions that realising the region’s full economic transformation won’t just hinge on sparkies, engineers and heavy industry. While the technology to decarbonise already exists, the clean energy boom faces an equally urgent challenge: building social licence.

With disputes over transmission lines and debate surrounding offshore wind fresh in the public consciousness, he argues that one of the most critical, and overlooked, career frontiers lies in the humanities.

“We need social geographers. We need social scientists,” he said.

“Rather than consultants going out there and ‘doing community engagement’, what we need are people whose careers are about deeply understanding communities, how they operate and how they can work through change in a way that is participative and equitable.

“There’s no point arriving at the end of this journey driving an empty bus — even if the bus is electric.”

To help prepare the next generation for these diverse career paths, local institutions are already laying the groundwork. Pathways are highlighted in UOW and Business Illawarra’s Illawarra Clean Energy Roadmap, and Wollongong City Council’s Energy Equity Framework.

Education hubs are stepping up as well. At the UOW’s Science Space, the Energy Futures Zone was launched to demystify clean technology for school students and ignite early curiosity.

“The goal is to teach, not preach,” Mr Christopher said. “We want school kids to see how energy impacts our lives, so that out of the end of this, a lot more people realise there’s a huge future for their careers right here in the Illawarra — in clean energy, clean manufacturing and many other areas that are not front of mind.”

Download the Illawarra Renewable Energy Jobs Guide at EnergyCo.

text:
WASHINGTON — Losing more ground in the fight against climate change, humanity is heading for a hotter world than experts projected last year — and the United States is a big reason for that, a new United Nations report says.

If all the countries do what they promise to reduce heat-trapping emissions, Earth will likely still warm another 2.2 degrees Fahrenheit (1.2 degrees Celsius) above current temperatures, according to Wednesday's update of climate calculations by the United Nations Environment Programme. That's about two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit (0.1 degrees Celsius) more than last year's projections by the same science team.

"This is a worse outcome than expected last year, as a result of the formal withdrawal of the United States of America from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions," the report said. The report also blames the United States for increased emissions last year, saying all the other top 20 major economies reduced their carbon pollution or at least slowed the growth in how much carbon dioxide was spewed from the burning of coal, oil and gas.

"In terms of magnitude, the increase in the United States of America (133 megatons of CO2 equivalent) far exceeded that of all other countries and was driven by increased electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation," the report said. The 124 countries that increased emissions — not counting the 63 that decreased like most European nations — added 400 million tons of carbon dioxide in 2025, and 33% of that increase came from the U.S., according to the report.

The United States is going "hell-for-leather trying to block renewables while actively promoting and subsidizing dirty coal — and its diplomacy is trying to make other countries also pull back on action. It is looking at the fire, denying there is a fire, and then pouring more petrol on it," said Australian climate scientist Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics, which measures countries' climate fighting plans. He wasn't part of the U.N. report but, like several other outside scientists, said it was scientifically sound.

SHOOTING FAR PAST PARIS CLIMATE GOAL

The new calculations say that if countries do all they promise in the climate fighting plans they submitted to the United Nations, by 2100 the globe will be 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) hotter than pre-industrial times. If the world continues on its current path — without national promises — it will be 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than the last half of the 19th century, the same as last year's projection.

Both of those temperatures blow far past the goal of less than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) and preferably 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) adopted by the 2015 Paris climate pact. The world is now at about 1.4 degrees Celsius (2.5 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial times and earlier this year — and again in this report — United Nations officials conceded that there is no way of limiting warming to the 1.5-degree goal that they had embraced. Instead, officials are pinning their hopes of limiting warming to about 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) and then somehow pulling enough carbon dioxide out of the air to lower temperatures back down to 1.5 degrees.

The world is falling "dangerously short" of even those goals, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said, "but we have the tools to change course and pull back from the brink."

Drastically cutting global carbon emissions — by 18% by 2030 and 69% by 2040 — "is the only way that we can get back to a semblance of a reality that is still largely manageable without major impacts and therefore that makes every sense," said UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen.

"The report's message is clear," said climate scientist Adelle Thomas, vice chair of a United Nations scientific assessment on climate impacts. She wasn't part of this study. "We know what needs to be done. We have the tools to do it. And delay only makes the challenge more dangerous and more expensive for all."

AN ADDED TENTH OF A DEGREE OF DANGER

Report lead author Anne Olhoff, director of UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre, said the U.S. policy change will likely add one-tenth of a degree Celsius (nearly two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit) to global temperatures by the end of the century.

"This report shows that America's retreat isn't just a political embarrassment. It has real consequences for the planet and for millions of people around the world," said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, a climate organization. "An extra tenth of a degree might sound insignificant, but in climate terms it is enormous. It means more dangerous heat waves, more destructive floods, more failed harvests and more lives lost. For vulnerable communities in Africa, already living on the front lines of the climate crisis, every fraction of a degree matters. These are not abstract numbers. They are human lives."

Hare said that extra one-tenth of a degree pushes an additional 140 million people "into dangerously hot conditions" and increases the odds of the collapse of the Amazon rainforest or ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica. It also would cost the world and shave about $1.2 trillion from the global economy, said University of Pennsylvania climate scientist Michael Mann.

And the U.S. effect is probably even bigger than what the United Nations calculates because if the world's largest historical climate polluter doesn't do much to fight global warming other nations ease off in their efforts too, said Johan Rockstrom, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research in Germany.

"The rest of the world is exhausted when it comes to counting the damage that the U.S. is willingly doing to allies, multilateral structures, economic cooperation, disaster relief," Australian climate scientist Malte Meinshausen said. "The rest of the world should probably continue to focus even less on the U.S."

text:
German luxury car maker Audi will spend $4 billion to build its first US production facility near Macon, Georgia. The facility will be able to build 200,000 cars per year and will create 4,500 high paying jobs. Audi’s plant will be a four-hour drive south from Spartanburg, South Carolina where German rival BMW makes its X series vehicles. BMW is huge in South Carolina employing 11,000 workers at the company’s largest manufacturing facility anywhere in the world. BMW has invested $12 billion in Spartanburg.

There’s more to this auto industry boom in the American south. South Korea’s Hyundai is spending $12 billion on a huge plant near Savannah, Georgia’s Atlantic coast seaport. When it’s completed Hyundai in Georgia will employ 8,500 workers in a plant that can produce 500,000 cars per year. In addition, the American electric vehicle startup Rivian is building a plant near Atlanta. Online retailer Amazon and Volkswagen are major shareholders in Rivian.

“On October 28th Kevin Warsh, the new chairman of the US Federal Reserve, said there is an investment boom underway in the United States. Now most of that investment is in artificial intelligence (AI), things like data center and the like. But much of the investment is in manufacturing and most of that money is going to the American south, companies like Audi, Hyundai, Volvo, BMW.”

There are multiple factors explaining the boom in the South’s auto industry. One is the Trump administration high tariffs on imported vehicles. Another is the business-friendly environment in a region close to heavily populated consumer markets. Finally, there is an ample supply of workers and hostility to trade unions which have considerable power in the industrial Midwest, the Michigan and Ohio center of the American auto industry.

Workers at the Detroit Three—General Motors, Ford and Stellantis—are represented by the United Auto Workers union, which is unpopular with Asian and European manufacturers. None of the new auto plants In Georgia and South Carolina are unionized. Hostility to the UAW runs deep and centers on restrictive work rules more than compensation as pay and benefits at the transplant companies are in line with the Detroit Three.

These have been tough years for GM, Ford and Chrysler. Of the Detroit three only Ford escaped bankruptcy in the 2008 financial crisis. Ford avoided reorganization only because it sold off much of its overseas operation, including Sweden’s Volvo. The Detroit Three are laggards in EVs, where Tesla is dominant. By market value Tesla is the world’s richest car company.

In the year 2000 the Detroit Three accounted for 55% of all cars sold in US. Today their market share has shrunk to 36% with Asian manufacturers, imported and US produced, having a market share in excess of 50%. China is a non-factor as Chinese vehicles are neither built nor imported into the US.

There are 50 auto assembly plants in the US, 21 of which are foreign owned and they are mostly in the South. Toyota has several US factories including a massive facility in Georgetown, Kentucky that is Toyota’s biggest. In addition, Volvo, owned by China’s Geely, is in South Carolina, Mercedes is in Alabama and Nissan is in Tennessee. All together America’s auto industry employs 10 million people.

name: North Carolina Environment
title: Data centers, power bills, hurricanes: What's at stake for the environment in Florida's Senate race
description:
Instead of a broad climate debate, it shows up in specific fights over data centers, power bills, hurricane recovery and the fixes either candidate can offer.
Nixon’s sharpest environmental position is on data centers.
In June, Walton County commissioners voted unanimously to prohibit large data centers.
In September, she cosponsored the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would push utility regulators to make large data centers cover the grid costs of serving them.
Data center rules and power rates are largely set in Tallahassee, and Washington is pushing more disaster response onto the states, too.
text:
When asked to choose, Florida’s likely voters have picked protecting the environment over economic growth by more than 2 to 1, a margin that surprised even the pollster who asked the question.

In a University of North Florida poll released last week, 61 percent of respondents said state and local officials should prioritize the environment “even at the risk of curbing economic growth.” Twenty-six percent chose growth. Registered Republicans sided with the environment 48 percent to 35 percent, and so did a plurality of 2024 voters who backed Donald Trump.

“I expected probably [the] environment to win narrowly, but this was a blowout,” said Sean Freeder, who directs UNF’s Public Opinion Research Lab.

Less than two weeks before Election Day, that sentiment has echoed through Florida’s U.S. Senate race between Republican Ashley Moody, the incumbent, and Democrat Angie Nixon, a state representative. Instead of a broad climate debate, it shows up in specific fights over data centers, power bills, hurricane recovery and the fixes either candidate can offer.

The race is closer than many expected in a state Trump won by 13 points in 2024. The UNF poll showed Moody, whom Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed in 2025 to serve the rest of Marco Rubio’s term, ahead 49 percent to 45 percent, down 8 points from July. Nixon outraised Moody by nearly $2 million in the third quarter, but Moody and her affiliated committees had about $7.1 million on hand on Oct.1, compared with about $4.5 million for Nixon. The two will not debate.

Nixon’s sharpest environmental position is on data centers. “There needs to be a moratorium,” she told Inside Climate News. “You cannot build any more data centers.” Her campaign platform calls for no new construction “before there are real federal guardrails.”

The Sierra Club, whose political arm has endorsed Nixon, also wants federal rules. “Absent those, yes, we support a statewide moratorium,” said Susannah Randolph, director of Sierra Club Florida.

In June, Walton County commissioners voted unanimously to prohibit large data centers. In Polk County, residents are fighting a proposed $2.6 billion project on a former phosphate mine in Fort Meade, where Nixon held a town hall last month.

Moody, whose campaign did not respond to requests for comment, has said data center decisions belong to communities and states. “It needs to be up to the people of a community or a state to decide what works best for them,” she said in a Fox News interview last month. In September, she cosponsored the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would push utility regulators to make large data centers cover the grid costs of serving them.

“If billion-dollar tech companies want to build a massive data center, Floridians should not be left to foot the bill,” she said at the time.

The Ratepayer Protection Act, which passed the House 417-3 but has not cleared the Senate, would direct state utility regulators to consider standards requiring large data centers that draw more than 100 megawatts—roughly the electricity used by 65,000 Florida homes—to pay the full cost of new power plants, transmission lines and grid upgrades built to serve them. It would also have regulators consider requiring those customers to post financial guarantees before construction begins and to cover costs if they walk away from a contract early.

Florida’s new data center law, Senate Bill 484, signed in May, goes further. It already requires utilities to make large data center customers pay their full cost of service so those expenses don’t shift to other ratepayers, and it applies to more facilities than the federal bill.

“Anybody that would be covered by the Ratepayer Protection Act is already covered by Senate Bill 484,” said Ted Kury, director of energy studies at the University of Florida’s Public Utility Research Center. “When it comes to electricity, essentially all they’re saying is, ‘Hey, the state PSC has to do their job.’”

A national moratorium, he added, would likely be challenged by states that want data centers, “and the federal government would probably lose.” (The research center’s sponsors include Florida Power & Light and the Florida Public Service Commission.)

Randolph was blunter about Moody’s sponsorship weeks before the election: “The timing is really suspicious and doesn’t smell good.”

Both candidates also pitch themselves as capable of offering relief from rising power bills. Nixon said she would “call for investigations” when rate increases follow large utility campaign contributions. Moody has built her affordability message around the federal tax cuts she voted for.

Florida Power & Light customers are absorbing the biggest rate hike in the utility’s history, approved last November: $945 million in 2026 and $705 million in 2027, with more on the horizon. Retail rates are set by the Florida PSC, not Congress. “As far as electricity prices at the state level, there’s not a lot that a U.S. senator could do,” Kury said.

What a senator can affect is federal tax policy. Moody voted for Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which ended a 30 percent tax credit for homeowners who install rooftop solar and set earlier deadlines for utility-scale solar and wind projects to qualify for federal credits. Kury said the law’s effect on bills varies by utility, because taxpayers fund the credits, too. “The people always pay,” he said. “All the policymakers decide is how and when.”

Disaster recovery is the other pressure point in the race. Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin as a Category 2 storm on Oct. 9, and Moody is leading a congressional push for a major disaster declaration. She has also said she helped bring Florida $1.7 billion in Federal Emergency Management Agency reimbursements for past disaster recovery projects. Meanwhile, a Trump-appointed council has recommended further shrinking FEMA’s workforce and shifting disaster response to the states.

Nixon said she would restore FEMA jobs and keep the agency on the ground for months after storms. She also said a Democrat-led Congress should “hold on to the purse strings and not allow the states that are doing wrong environmentally” to receive certain federal funding. She did not say whether that would apply to Florida.

Moody is the lead sponsor of the American Shores Protection Act, which would bar oil and gas drilling off the coasts of Florida, Georgia and South Carolina, but has stalled in committee. She introduced it last October, and in December, Republican Sen. Mike Lee blocked her attempt to pass it by unanimous consent. Randolph gave Moody credit for introducing the bill but called it “a gimme,” since Florida’s economy depends on its beaches. Moody scored 0 percent on the League of Conservation Voters’ 2025 scorecard, with 35 votes the group counted as “anti-environment.”

Nixon traces her environmental politics to Brown’s Dump, a Jacksonville Superfund site where the city dumped incinerator ash and where homes and an elementary school were later built. Her grandmother bought one of those homes and Nixon was subsequently raised there. “That shaped me,” she said.

Each of the issues driving the race runs up against the same limit. Data center rules and power rates are largely set in Tallahassee, and Washington is pushing more disaster response onto the states, too. Kury said campaigns on both sides tend to blur those lines.

“In campaign season, you got a lot of folks on all sides making statements that, ‘I can do this, I can do that,’ when maybe they really can’t,” he said.

But he said that comes with the territory. “Nobody elects a politician who says, ‘Yeah, I realize you have all these problems, but there isn’t anything I can do about it.’”

text:
From urban forests and solar microgrids to women-led green enterprises, Shakti Foundation outlines how accessible finance, local partnerships and community-driven investment can strengthen Bangladesh’s climate resilience.

As Bangladesh prepares for the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, questions over climate finance accessibility, rising debt burdens and the slow delivery of international commitments are becoming increasingly urgent. For a climate-vulnerable country like Bangladesh, the challenge extends beyond securing funding to ensuring that it reaches frontline communities, particularly women and other marginalised groups. Shakti Foundation, which works on women’s economic empowerment, climate resilience, and community-based green initiatives, advocates grant-based adaptation finance, simplified funding procedures, and greater direct access for local organisations. In an exclusive pre-COP31 interview with Md Ibrahim Khalilullah, Executive Editor of The Climate Watch, Labiba Rahman, Joint Director, Climate Change Program at Shakti Foundation, discusses reforms to international climate funds, financing solutions for urban resilience, women-led green businesses, renewable energy investments and the role of community-driven initiatives in addressing Bangladesh’s climate challenges. The interview is part of the “Shakti–The Climate Watch COP31 Dialogue Series,” which aims to bring critical perspectives on climate action and justice into the global climate conversation.

The Climate Watch: What specific reforms to international climate funds, including simplified applications, direct access and faster disbursement, should Bangladesh advocate at COP31 to ensure that adaptation finance reaches local communities, particularly women-led organisations?

Labiba Rahman: This is meant to be the implementation COP. After ten years of pledges, the question is whether money reaches people. How can this process be made easier and more accessible, especially for a country like Bangladesh that already carries a significant debt burden? If we rely on loans, it will further cripple our country. Therefore, grants should really be the way to go.

Bangladesh should first demand the elimination of lengthy, complex and bureaucratic appraisal templates that shut grassroots groups out. A women’s group in a village can’t write a 100-page proposal. Second, direct access, so national and local organisations can receive funds without going through layers of international middlemen. Third, faster disbursement, with clear deadlines. Women’s labour force participation has fallen from 43 per cent in 2022 to 38 per cent in 2025 [source: World Bank], and climate shocks are part of that. So, for women specifically, we want ring-fenced windows and small grants for women-led organisations.

The Climate Watch: What concrete commitments should Bangladesh seek at COP31 to ensure that the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage provides timely, grant-based support to climate-affected households? How can transparency and direct community access be ensured?

Labiba Rahman: Our first problem is that we don’t speak with one voice. Look at Nepal. The fund approved $20 million for their floods just recently, in October. It’s still not disbursed, and it took about two months from the flood. That’s a first step, but it shows both the opportunity and the speed problem. So, Bangladesh needs a coordinated national position, and I’d ask for three things. It must be grants only. Since loss and damage results from historical emissions by developed countries, this funding is a matter of climate justice under the polluter-pays principle, not a debt-inducing assistance package. Bangladesh should also push for pre-agreed triggers, so money moves automatically after a disaster, like the parametric cyclone insurance Shakti launched in partnership with Sena Insurance PLC and K.M. Dastur & Company Limited. And it needs direct channels to trusted local organisations, with localised tracking so everyone can see whether the cash reached households.

The Climate Watch: Which financing instruments, such as green bonds, blended finance or public-private partnerships, offer the greatest potential for climate investment in Bangladesh? What safeguards would ensure that private capital also benefits low-income and climate-vulnerable communities?

Labiba Rahman: If I had to pick one, it’s public-private partnerships, because we’ve seen them work. Lautola Forest, Dhaka’s first human-made urban forest, happened because the city, private funders and Shakti each did their part. Green bonds and big blended-finance structures are still early for our financial system, so I’d start smaller, with blended models run through local lenders. Alongside that, there’s Zakat, which is large and underused in Bangladesh. Directed towards climate-vulnerable families, it could be debt-free support. Whatever we use, private capital needs safeguards: impact targets for jobs, clean energy access and housing for low-income people, and checks against greenwashing.

The Climate Watch: Drawing on Shakti Foundation’s experience, which financing models could most effectively support women-led green businesses and household adaptation? What practical barriers must be addressed to expand women’s access to affordable climate finance?

Labiba Rahman: Every Shakti programme is built around women, and 98 per cent of our borrowers are women. Our model isn’t just loans. It’s collateral-free credit combined with practical support, such as microfinance-linked green assets (like solar units) and mobile health clinics that bring healthcare directly to women in remote areas.

The practical barriers are huge. There’s a gender gap in digital financial inclusion, and many women lack formal documents. Disaster training and awareness data shows women are often left behind because they have to stay home caring for children and elderly family members. They can’t just walk out of the house easily. And when women do step up, the mindset of men in the community doesn’t always change. That’s why training has to be intergenerational and family-based, involving mothers, fathers and brothers, so everyone understands why women’s access to climate finance and green jobs matters. If we don’t address these social and structural barriers, funding and advanced projects won’t reach the women who need them most.

The Climate Watch: What three priority interventions should Dhaka and Chattogram implement over the next two to three years to protect low-income communities from extreme heat, flooding and waterlogging? How should their effectiveness be measured?

Labiba Rahman: Our study with the Center for Urban Studies found Dhaka lost 60.7 per cent of its vegetation between 2000 and 2025, while built-up area grew 59 per cent. This rapid urban development has intensified urban heat, while air pollution reduces life expectancy by 5.5 years across Bangladesh and 6.6 years in Dhaka [source: University of Chicago’s air quality index]. The people bearing the brunt of this are day labourers, rickshaw pullers and those in informal settlements.

To protect those most affected, first we must significantly scale up urban greening by expanding urban forests, pocket parks and Miyawaki-style forests, building on initiatives like Shakti Foundation’s Lautola Forest, which has helped bring local temperatures down by 2 to 3 degrees. Second, we need to restore canals and drainage systems and clear blocked waterways to prevent severe waterlogging from disrupting low-income neighbourhoods every time it rains. Third, heat-resilient housing, with cool roofs and shaded community spaces, to protect urban families during extreme heatwaves.

Of course, taking action is only half the battle. The real challenge is ensuring that these interventions deliver results. To measure their impact, we need to track clear, practical outcomes on the ground. This means measuring reductions in ambient temperatures using thermal monitoring tools, monitoring improvements in local Air Quality Index (AQI) levels, tracking how quickly water drains after heavy monsoon rains and assessing whether heat-related illnesses among vulnerable urban workers are declining.

The Climate Watch: What measurable outcomes has Shakti Foundation observed from its Lautola urban forest initiative in Dhaka, particularly regarding tree survival, temperature reduction, biodiversity and community benefits? What would be required to replicate this model in other cities?

Our Lautola urban forest initiative in Mohammadpur, Dhaka, demonstrates how urban blight can be transformed into a thriving ecosystem. Before our intervention, the site was an illegal truck terminal. Through a strategic public-private partnership (PPP), the canal was retrieved and we converted the area into Dhaka’s first dense, man-made urban forest.

We planted over 9,000 fruit-bearing, medicinal and native trees across multiple vegetation layers, using carefully prepared, organic-rich soil. This resulted in an exceptional survival rate of over 95 per cent, far exceeding what is typically achieved through conventional urban plantation drives. The dense canopy has helped reduce local temperatures by a verified 2 to 3 degrees Celsius, while the forest’s natural air-filtering capacity has contributed to a 10 to 20-point improvement in the localised Air Quality Index (AQI) compared to nearby areas. Home to over 73 native species of trees, plants and shrubs, the forest has also attracted pollinators, insects and bird species that had largely disappeared from the area. It also absorbs rainwater, which helps with local waterlogging.

The community benefits matter just as much. Residents now have a safe, green public space. And Lautola employs transgender gardeners from the hijra community, so it creates work for people who are often shut out of jobs.

Replicating this model in other major cities across Bangladesh requires strong public-private partnerships. City corporations provide land and help restore canals. Private companies provide capital, often through CSR funding. And organisations like Shakti provide technical expertise and oversee the work. Beyond that, you need proper soil restoration, native species and early engagement with local people so they feel ownership and protect the forest for the long term.

The Climate Watch: Which financing mechanisms could realistically help Bangladeshi cities invest in affordable cooling, heat-resilient housing and green infrastructure? What changes are needed to allow local governments to access international adaptation funds more directly?

Labiba Rahman: We have to face the reality that waiting around for traditional international climate grants just won’t cut it. First, as I mentioned earlier when talking about the Lautola Forest, public-private partnerships are a completely realistic and proven way forward.

Second, we can scale up green microfinance. A powerful model we are actively leveraging here is the ICCAP (Inclusive Climate Finance for Vulnerable Communities in the Asia-Pacific) project. Funded by Germany’s International Climate Initiative and led by the Stockholm Environment Institute alongside ADA and APRACA, this five-year regional programme channels public and private adaptation finance through local financial service providers like Shakti. Through this financing model, Shakti is developing client-centric green financial products that directly target 3,000 beneficiaries, with at least 50 per cent being low-income women, farmers and climate-vulnerable individuals who pay off these resilient upgrades through flexible instalments.

Third, as I touched on when discussing domestic climate finance, Zakat is a massive, untapped resource in Bangladesh that carries zero debt burdens, no foreign exchange risk and none of the heavy bureaucratic delays tied to international climate funds.

Now, as for getting international adaptation funds directly into the hands of local city governments, we need a few crucial shifts. City corporations need more financial autonomy, even to issue green bonds. At the same time, we have to build direct capacity within city corporations so they can meet the strict fiduciary and reporting standards required by global funders like the Green Climate Fund. And finally, international donors themselves need to establish dedicated sub-national funding windows that channel adaptation capital directly to local financial institutions and urban bodies where the heat and flooding are actually happening.

The Climate Watch: What three policy reforms or investment priorities are most critical to achieving Bangladesh’s NDC 3.0 renewable energy ambitions by 2035? What specific financial commitments, technologies and international partnerships should Bangladesh seek at COP31?

Labiba Rahman: Bangladesh can’t scale up renewables if our grid can’t handle solar and wind variability. So, the first priority should be to invest in smart grid infrastructure, battery storage and high-voltage transmission lines that ensure off-grid microgrids can feed back into our energy mix instead of staying isolated. This brings me to my second point: we need a comprehensive, streamlined net-metering framework that allows rooftop solar and microgrids to easily sell surplus electricity back to the grid. Lastly, we need to de-risk clean energy investments using blended finance. Standard commercial loans are far too expensive for green startups and low-income households. By pairing soft grants and concessional capital with microcredit, we can lower borrowing costs and make solar home systems, electric vehicle hubs and clean cooking affordable for marginalised communities.

As for COP31, we must demand grants for adaptation and concessional finance for mitigation. Alongside financial commitments, Bangladesh needs direct technology transfer and local manufacturing support. Finally, we must push for strategic international partnerships that establish direct funding windows for sub-national entities, local financial providers, civil society and municipal governments to ensure climate adaptation capital reaches frontline communities.

The Climate Watch: Based on Shakti Foundation’s solar energy and community-level experience, which clean-energy business models offer the greatest opportunities for women entrepreneurs and small businesses? How can these models become commercially sustainable while remaining affordable for low-income households?

Labiba Rahman: Alongside the environmental benefits, our motivation for deploying solar energy has always been about reaching the most remote communities while directly safeguarding women’s safety, supporting children’s education and protecting women and girls from gender-based violence. So far, we have deployed around 60,000 solar panels for households, schools and streetlights across Bangladesh.

When you look at which clean-energy business models offer the greatest opportunities for women entrepreneurs and small businesses, decentralised solar microgrids and productive-use energy models stand out the most. A prime example of what’s possible at the community level is our FCDO-funded project in Dhobaura, Mymensingh. Under a regulatory sandbox, 20 shop owners in a local market were equipped with interconnected solar panels as a microgrid, enabling them to trade excess power among themselves and even sell surplus electricity back to the national grid. Women and small business owners have leveraged this clean electricity to run solar irrigation pumps and three-wheeler charging stations, creating new green jobs and reliable, community-based revenue streams right within their communities.

To keep it affordable and sustainable, you have to connect clean technology directly with income generation and flexible financing. Offering collateral-free, flexible microcredit lets marginalised households and women-led enterprises acquire high-efficiency green technology over time without high upfront costs. They can then comfortably fund their loan repayments directly out of the savings made by displacing expensive fossil fuels, avoiding costly grid downtime and earning extra income through their solar-powered microenterprises.

The Climate Watch: Which green industries and skills should Bangladesh prioritise to create employment for women and young people? How can investments in renewable energy and energy-efficient cooling simultaneously generate jobs, reduce electricity costs and protect low-income households from extreme heat?

Labiba Rahman: I would prioritise industries close to where people already live and earn, and I’d make sure the jobs reach the people who are usually left out. First, decentralised solar, specifically solar installation, maintenance and microgrid operations. Having deployed around 60,000 solar panels, we’ve seen this impact firsthand. In Dhobaura, Mymensingh, our solar microgrid enables microenterprises to create reliable, home-based work.

Second, urban greening and reuse. Our Lautola Forest employs transgender gardeners from the hijra community, so it’s already creating work for people who are often shut out of jobs. Expanding on this, our Circle of Care project, supported by the Australian High Commission, is training 100 individuals from marginalised communities in urban forestry, tailoring and making bags from reused materials, while providing integrated health services and counselling. That combination of practical skills and holistic support is what empowers people to secure and maintain long-term employment.

Third is heat-resilient housing and green infrastructure, such as cool roofs and shaded community spaces, which offer practical, hands-on employment for trained local youth. Sustainable finance is what ties all of this together. Through collateral-free microcredit, families can invest in solar technology and pay in flexible instalments, funding their repayments directly out of fuel savings and extra income. Furthermore, under our ICCAP initiative, we are developing tailored green financial products for 3,000 beneficiaries, at least half of whom are low-income women, farmers and climate-vulnerable individuals. Ultimately, the exact same investment that lowers energy bills, makes cooling affordable and protects families from extreme heat is what gives women, youth and marginalised groups a dignified living.

text:
Americans head to the polls on Tuesday for midterm elections.

Ahead of the elections, here are The Jerusalem Post’s key Senate races to watch.

Michigan

The race between Democrat Dr. Abdul El-Sayed and MAGA favorite Mike Rogers has been the source of many national headlines.

El-Sayed has hammered his planks of universal healthcare and overall affordability in the state, but has gained significant attention for his criticism of Israel and outreach to Jewish voters.

Rogers’s platform mostly aligns with US President Donald Trump, and has specifically highlighted his plank of bringing manufacturing jobs back to America.

A poll recently released by CBS Detroit has El-Sayed leading by seven percentage points, or 51% to Rogers’s 44%.

Texas

Democrat James Talarico is poised to be the first Democrat to hold statewide office in conservative-stronghold Texas since the 1990s.

He is taking on the state’s Attorney-General Ken Paxton, a MAGA loyalist who has been plagued by scandals for the last decade.

Throughout the course of the campaign, Talarico has framed politics as a struggle between billionaires and working people. His platform includes raising the federal minimum wage, expanding universal childcare, raising public school teacher pay, creating pathways for long-term immigrants and DREAMers to gain US citizenship, and expanding pathways for legal immigration.

Paxton's platform includes Trump-aligned immigration policies, cutting taxes and government spending, America First foreign policy, and supporting crypto growth

Overall, Paxton promised to "carry the torch for Trump's agenda" on his website.

North Carolina

North Carolina could be one of the least competitive races on the ballot.

Though Trump endorsed ex-RNC chair Michael Whately in 2024, he admitted in October that he was “worried” about him.

Whately is running against two-term former governor Roy Cooper.

Whately’s platform is mostly focused on crime, immigration, and tax cuts. He supported Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill and has pledged to push Trump’s policies in the Senate.

Cooper’s “make stuff cost less” platform targets healthcare, child care, utility bills, and the standard cost of living in the state.

He’s pushed for expanded Medicaid access in the state, but has tried to pitch himself as an “independent voice” for voters on both sides of the aisle.

Cooper is currently leading in polls by 10 points, according to MS NOW.

Georgia

Jewish Sen. John Ossoff is defending his seat against GOP Congressman Mike Collins. Notably, Ossoff is the only Democrat in the Senate up for re-election in a state Trump won in the 2024 presidential race.

Ossoff’s platform calls for a ban on stock trading while in federal office, expanding rural broadband access, lowering housing prices, protecting abortion rights, and protecting voting rights. He is a critic of the war in Iran, but describes his support for Israel as “ironclad”, though he voted to block weapons sales in 2025.

Collins’s platform focuses on Trump-aligned immigration policies, rural hospital funding, reducing medicare spending, and other conservative fiscal policies that he claims will help small businesses.

Ossoff is up 52.6% to Collins’s 42.3% in the latest polls released by MS NOW.

Alaska

The race in Alaska has caused a stir after Republicans called for an investigation into a ballot-stacking scheme by Democrats.

Trump and his allies accused Democrat Mary Peltola of recruiting candidates with the same name as her and her opponent, Republican Dan Sullivan, to purposefully confuse voters when they cast their ballots.

Peltola has since denied the accusations and said that she is “not out soliciting more competition.”

“I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters.”

Federal prosecutors are now investigating the matter.

Peltola’s platform includes targeting corruption and influence in Washington, more benefits for Alaskan military families, balancing oil production with environmental protections, and supporting the state’s fishing industry.

Sullivan’s platform includes pieces on energy strategy and environmental standards to support the energy industry.

Peltola is up by two percentage points, 50.2% to Sullivan’s 48.4%, in the race.

Notably, Democrats would need to win seven seats to gain a 51-seat majority in the Senate.

text:
Auto component maker Sona BLW Precision Forgings Ltd (Sona Comstar) plans to increase its annual investments beyond the current ₹500-600 crore as it scales up operations, with a focus on research and development, capacity expansion and developing new capabilities.

“We are currently investing around ₹500-600 crore annually. This should increase as we grow over the decade,” Vivek Vikram Singh, Managing Director and Group CEO, Sona Comstar, told PTI in an interview.

Advt

The investments will be spread across the company's three business lines and cover R&D, capacity additions, new processes and capability development. Singh said the company was also working on developing entirely new products.

During the September quarter, Sona Comstar commercialised three new products: a helical limited-slip differential for electric vehicles, air springs for railway coaches and rear radar sensors for two-wheelers.

The company secured new orders worth ₹3,600 crore during the quarter, marking its third-best performance in terms of order bookings. Singh said the orders would convert into revenue over different timelines, depending on the stage of vehicle development and individual model cycles.

India to contribute 50-55% of business

India currently accounts for around half of Sona Comstar's business, and its contribution is expected to remain in the 50-55 per cent range as the company expands in other international markets.

“Orders already won will begin to convert, and North America should see good growth next year, with India keeping pace. India's contribution should remain in the 50-55 per cent range,” Singh said.

He also highlighted the opportunity for Indian auto component manufacturers as global companies look to diversify their supply chains away from China. However, he said domestic suppliers would need to strengthen their design and manufacturing capabilities to capture a larger share of this business.

Advt

“India could gain significantly, as companies are looking to diversify supply chains away from China. However, Indian suppliers must be capable of taking on that business. The ecosystem needs to demonstrate design capability and manufacturing quality,” Singh said.

He added that improvements in manufacturing standards across the domestic supplier ecosystem would be important in attracting more global business and production volumes to India.

Sona Comstar evaluating acquisitions

The company is also evaluating acquisition opportunities to strengthen its capabilities, including in technology-related areas.

“We are evaluating many opportunities, but there is nothing reportable that I can comment on at present. There are abundant opportunities, and it is important to be clear not only about what to pursue but also what not to pursue. M&A is something we are considering very seriously,” Singh said.

BEV revenue accounts for 51% of automotive revenue

Sona Comstar's battery electric vehicle (BEV) revenue, excluding hybrids, grew 129 per cent year on year in Q2 FY27 and accounted for 51 per cent of its automotive revenue.

Singh said the pace of electric vehicle adoption in India had been faster than the company's expectations, providing opportunities for its electric mobility-related product portfolio.

The company reported a 31 per cent year-on-year increase in consolidated profit to ₹223 crore in the September quarter, compared with ₹170 crore in the year-ago period. Revenue from operations rose to ₹1,535.84 crore from ₹1,138.29 crore in the corresponding quarter last fiscal.

text:
VE Commercial Vehicles (VECV), a subsidiary of Eicher Motors, reported a 36.9 per cent year-on-year increase in domestic sales to 9,676 units in October 2026, compared with 7,070 units in the corresponding month last year.

Domestic sales of SCV/LMD trucks (below 18.5 tonnes) grew 42.7 per cent to 6,053 units, while HD truck sales (18.5 tonnes and above) increased 44.9 per cent to 2,719 units.

Consequently, VECV's overall sales, including Volvo trucks and buses, rose 34.9 per cent to 10,861 units in October 2026, compared with 8,050 units in the year-ago month.

text:
Xiaomi delivered more than 50,000 vehicles in October 2026, according to Reuters and CnEVPost, and that is the best month the company has posted this year. The result lifts Xiaomi EV deliveries back above the level it first reached in December 2025, when it handed over 50,212 cars. It also ends a two-month run of year-on-year declines.

The headline is clean, but the details underneath are more interesting. Xiaomi has not published an exact October figure in the reports we reviewed, so the percentage gains below are minimums. The growth came largely from a brand-new extended-range lineup called Sky Nomad, not from the SU7 sedan or the YU7 SUV, whose sales have been sliding.

This analysis walks through what the number says, what it hides, how Xiaomi stacks up against Leapmotor, Xpeng, Nio and Li Auto, and why the company’s 550,000-vehicle goal for 2026 now looks like a stretch. For readers following the wider EV picture, our earlier look at how US EV sales fell 23.8% without tax credits shows how different the demand backdrop is in China.
