What Xiaomi Reported for October 2026

Reuters reported on November 1 that Xiaomi’s October EV deliveries topped 50,000 and marked a 2026 monthly high. CnEVPost, which tracks Chinese EV data closely, added that this is only the second time Xiaomi Auto has cleared 50,000 vehicles in a single month. The first was December 2025.

Cumulative deliveries for January through October reached about 336,000 vehicles, per the same reports. CnEVPost’s own tally puts the floor at 336,490. That equals roughly 61% of the company’s 550,000-vehicle target for the year.

Xiaomi’s choice to announce a round-number floor instead of an exact count matters here. CnEVPost calculated the growth rates against that floor, so the real October figure sits somewhere above 50,000. The month-on-month gain is at least 24.95%, and the year-on-year gain is at least 2.77%.

The Monthly Trajectory Behind the Record

Xiaomi’s year has not been a straight line. According to CnEVPost, the company topped 30,000 deliveries in June and again in July (31,267 units), which made it four straight months above that bar. It stayed above 30,000 in August, then jumped above 40,000 in September and above 50,000 in October.

Sources: CnEVPost and Reuters. October’s exact figure had not been published in the reports reviewed.

Look at the jump from July to October. Deliveries rose by roughly 19,000 units in three months, and a product that did not exist in August accounts for a large share of it. That is the heart of the story.

Why the Sky Nomad Matters More Than the Headline

Xiaomi launched the Sky Nomad SUV family on September 7, 2026. It is the company’s first extended-range electric vehicle (EREV) line, which pairs a battery-driven powertrain with an onboard generator. Until now Xiaomi sold only battery-electric cars, the SU7 and YU7.

Launch Pricing and Early Orders

CnEVPost reported that Sky Nomad pricing starts at 209,900 yuan, which converts to about $31,000. The lineup collected more than 10,000 locked-in orders within four minutes of going on sale, and more than 70,000 locked-in orders in its first 30 days. Notebookcheck’s launch coverage highlighted a combined range figure of 1,060 miles for the full-size hybrid SUV.

September Deliveries as the Proof Point

Xiaomi chief executive Lei Jun said on October 1 that Sky Nomad deliveries passed 10,000 in September, and CnEVPost’s count was 12,444. September was only a partial ramp, since sales began on the 7th. October gave the model a full month, and the roughly 10,000-unit jump in the overall total suggests Sky Nomad contributed a large share.

CnEVPost framed the pattern plainly. October’s return to growth suggests that Sky Nomad’s ramp is starting to offset falling SU7 and YU7 sales. Xiaomi did not break out model-level October numbers in the reports we saw, so that reading stays an inference.

Year-on-Year Growth Is Real but Thin

Compare October 2026 with October 2025 and the gain is slim. Xiaomi delivered 48,654 vehicles a year earlier, so a floor of 50,000 gives a gain of at least 2.77%. If the true number is 51,000, growth would be about 4.8%. That is growth, but not the kind of surge the 24.95% month-on-month rise might suggest.

The prior two months show why this matters. Xiaomi’s August and September deliveries both fell below year-ago levels, with September down 4.61%. A company that adds a new body style, an entirely new powertrain type and 70,000 locked-in orders, and still only edges past last October, is telling you something about its older models.

Cumulative numbers tell a similar story. January through October 2025 totaled 315,376 deliveries, so the 336,490 floor for 2026 is a 6.69% gain. Xiaomi is growing, but at a pace well below what it needs to hit its annual goal.

The 550,000 Target Math Gets Hard

Xiaomi set a 2026 goal of 550,000 vehicles. After ten months it sits at about 61.2% of that figure, which leaves up to 213,510 vehicles for November and December. That works out to roughly 106,755 per month, more than double October’s result.

The table below shows what a handful of plausible November and December paces would produce. These are our own arithmetic scenarios, built on CnEVPost’s 336,490 floor, and not company guidance.

Even an aggressive 80,000 a month leaves Xiaomi about 54,000 short. Xiaomi has reset goals before. Bloomberg reported in November 2025 that the company raised its 2025 delivery goal to 400,000 after reaching a profit breakeven on its EV business. A missed 2026 target would be a very different kind of headline, and Xiaomi has not said whether it plans to adjust.

Manufacturing capacity will decide how close Xiaomi can get. We could not confirm factory output figures from the reports reviewed, so we do not estimate a ceiling here. Western automakers face the same question from a different angle. Ford’s push to cut part counts, covered in our piece on Fathom’s 5,000 unicastings replacing 146 parts, shows how much of the output race now happens inside the factory.

October Scorecard: Xiaomi Against Its Chinese Rivals

Xiaomi’s October result lands in the middle of a crowded field. CnEVPost’s roundup of major Chinese automakers shows a market with a few clear winners and a lot of pressure on established names.

Source: CnEVPost October 2026 roundup. BYD, Tesla China and Aito/Seres were not included in the roundup we reviewed. SAIC-GM-Wuling led the broader list at 142,757 units.

On pure volume, Xiaomi ranks level with Xpeng and well behind Leapmotor. Because Xiaomi’s exact count is unpublished, we cannot say whether it edged out Xpeng’s 50,237. Reports describe the two as the month’s pair of 50,000-plus performers.

Leapmotor and Xpeng Set the Pace

Leapmotor delivered 106,127 vehicles in October, up about 51% from a year earlier, and marked a fourth consecutive month above 100,000. It is the volume leader among the independent EV makers in this dataset. Xiaomi’s best month is less than half of Leapmotor’s typical one.

Xpeng set a new company record at 50,237 deliveries. Its overseas business hit an all-time monthly high of 13,326 units, up 166% from a year earlier, according to Xpeng’s own announcement carried by StockTitan. About a quarter of Xpeng’s October volume went abroad, while Xiaomi’s EV business, based on the reports reviewed, remains focused on its home market.

That contrast shapes the next phase. Export growth gives Xpeng a second engine as domestic demand softens. Xiaomi has not disclosed a comparable overseas delivery figure.

The Squeezed Middle: Nio, Li Auto and Huawei HIMA

Nio delivered 34,246 vehicles, including 18,125 under the Nio brand and 8,383 under Onvo. Its total fell 15.23% year on year. Li Auto delivered 29,025, its lowest monthly total since February, and Huawei’s HIMA group fell more than 50% from a year earlier to 33,537.

Benzinga ran a late-October piece titled around a plunge in Nio, Li Auto, XPeng and BYD shares as China EV headwinds rise. We did not verify the share-price details, but the delivery data fits the theme. Winners are consolidating at the top and bottom, while mid-sized brands lose volume.

Xiaomi’s October result has to be read in that light. A 2.77% minimum gain in a market where Li Auto, Nio and HIMA all shrank is a respectable outcome. A strong new model launch is helping Xiaomi buck the trend, but the launch tailwind will fade as the Sky Nomad order backlog clears.

Tesla and BYD Provide the Wider Frame

Tesla’s China business posted its best month of 2026 in September, with wholesale sales up 5% to 95,366, per CnEVPost. Third-quarter China wholesale hit a record 275,111, up 13.73% year on year. Xiaomi’s 50,000-plus October month is about half of Tesla China’s September pace, though the two measure slightly different things (domestic deliveries versus wholesale including exports).

BYD remains far larger. It sold 3,131,576 EVs from January to September, down 3.9% on the same period of 2025, because a 30% drop in China outweighed a near doubling of overseas sales. We found no October figure for BYD in the sources reviewed, so we leave it out of the comparison table.

Tesla’s strategic attention is drifting toward autonomy and manufacturing, as our coverage of the Cybercab line with 25 stations and 78% automation shows. Xiaomi, by contrast, is still fighting for core volume in the mass market.

Market Impact for Hardware and Supply Chains

Xiaomi built its name on consumer electronics, which makes its car division a useful read for the wider hardware market. A phone and appliance brand that can ship more than 50,000 cars a month proves the consumer-tech playbook can scale into automotive. That raises the stakes for traditional carmakers and for parts suppliers who now sell to both camps.

The reports we reviewed did not include a Xiaomi share-price reaction, so we make no claim there. What we can say is that October’s data tightens the gap between Xiaomi and the volume leaders in China’s new-energy segment. It also adds pressure on mid-sized rivals already losing ground.

For suppliers, the shift toward extended-range vehicles matters. EREVs use a battery and a generator, which changes the mix of components compared with pure battery-electric models. Xiaomi’s decision to add one signals that even a company built around electrification sees a role for hybrid-style range solutions in 2026.

Historical Context: From 400,000 to 550,000

Xiaomi’s 2025 story set the stage. Bloomberg reported in November 2025 that the company lifted its annual goal to 400,000 vehicles after its EV unit broke even. December 2025 produced the 50,212-vehicle record that October 2026 has now matched or passed in the reports we saw.

The 2026 target of 550,000 sits about 37.5% above the 400,000 goal Xiaomi set for 2025. Ten months in, the company is growing cumulative deliveries about 6.69% year on year, using the 2025 comparison of 315,376 for January through October. The gap between those two growth rates is the clearest sign that the target was written for a stronger year than the market delivered.

By CnEVPost’s count, Xiaomi has delivered at least 887,798 vehicles since it began selling cars. Reaching nearly 900,000 cumulative units in a short time is a milestone, and it explains why investors treat each monthly number as a referendum on the whole project.

What It Means for Buyers and Western Automakers

For buyers in the US and Europe, the practical impact is limited today. Xiaomi sells its cars in China, and the Sky Nomad launched at 209,900 yuan for a full-size hybrid SUV. The price point shows how much vehicle Chinese brands now offer for roughly $31,000.

Western makers feel the effect indirectly through pricing pressure and export competition. Rivian’s third-quarter results, covered in our look at 19,248 deliveries and $2.155B in revenue, show a US-focused EV maker operating at a fraction of Xiaomi’s monthly scale. Shoppers weighing whether to switch should also read our breakdown of the old car versus new EV payback claim.

Robotaxi programs offer another angle. Waymo and Tesla are expanding service areas, as in our report on Tesla’s Houston zone reaching 254 square miles. Xiaomi is still competing on conventional car sales and has not announced anything comparable in the reports we checked.

Five Predictions for November and December

These are our judgments, based on the data above, not reported facts.

Xiaomi misses 550,000. Reaching the target needs about 106,755 a month. Nothing in the current trajectory points to doubling October’s output in 60 days, so expect a final 2026 total in the 440,000 to 500,000 range.

November stays above 50,000. With more than 70,000 locked-in Sky Nomad orders and a ramping production line, a drop below the October level would surprise us.

Xiaomi announces exact figures. Investors and analysts increasingly compare against precise counts, so pressure will build for Xiaomi to publish exact monthly numbers instead of floors.

Mid-sized rivals keep shrinking. Li Auto, Nio and HIMA face continuing declines unless new models land quickly, widening the gap with Leapmotor and Xpeng.

Xiaomi talks overseas. Xpeng’s 166% jump in overseas deliveries gives Xiaomi a template. Expect more questions about export plans in the next earnings call.

The Takeaway

Xiaomi’s October is a real milestone, because 50,000-plus deliveries put it in elite company among Chinese EV brands. But the number rests on one new product, the growth over last October is slim, and the annual target now demands a pace the company has never reached. Watch November’s figure and the model-level split. If Sky Nomad keeps carrying the load while the SU7 and YU7 slip, Xiaomi’s growth story is really a one-product story.

FAQ

How many EVs did Xiaomi deliver in October 2026? Xiaomi reported more than 50,000 vehicles, a 2026 monthly high, per Reuters and CnEVPost. The company did not publish an exact figure in the reports we reviewed.

Is this Xiaomi’s all-time record? Not necessarily. December 2025 produced 50,212 deliveries, and October 2026 is described as only the second month above 50,000. Without an exact October number, we cannot say which month is higher.

What is the Xiaomi Sky Nomad? It is Xiaomi’s first extended-range electric SUV lineup, launched on September 7, 2026, with a starting price of 209,900 yuan, per CnEVPost. It drew more than 70,000 locked-in orders in 30 days.

Will Xiaomi hit its 550,000-vehicle target for 2026? It would need about 213,510 deliveries in November and December combined, or roughly 106,755 a month. That is more than twice October’s pace, so a miss looks likely unless the target is revised.

How does Xiaomi compare with Xpeng and Leapmotor? Xpeng delivered 50,237 vehicles in October, roughly level with Xiaomi, while Leapmotor delivered 106,127, about double.

Did Xiaomi grow year on year in October? Yes, by at least 2.77% against 48,654 deliveries in October 2025. That ended two consecutive months of year-on-year declines.

name: Clean Energy
title: Column: Pragmatic policies must prevail for Virginia's energy needs - The Virginian-Pilot
description:
Yet, as this demand shock accelerates, state energy policy remains tethered to the VCEA.
Today, natural gas powers 59% of Virginia’s electric grid — outpacing every other energy source.
As lawmakers prepare for the 2027 General Assembly session, they should consider strengthening the 2026 Virginia Energy Plan in three specific ways.
Whether it’s managing severe weather or supporting substantial economic development, Virginia’s grid must be equipped to handle varying pressures.
To keep costs low, strengthen reliability and protect clean energy goals, the commonwealth must implement pragmatic solutions and marry natural gas with renewables.
text:
Although Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s carefully considered and well-intentioned 2026 Virginia Energy Plan sets ambitious goals, its modeling relies on assumptions that clash with physical grid realities, which could fail to deliver the energy affordability that Virginia desperately needs. If carried out to the letter, the proposal could even end up undermining power reliability and increasing costs for families and businesses at a moment we can ill afford.

A hard look at Virginia’s energy use projections and current power generation portfolio makes it difficult to envision the state realizing the 2026 Virginia Power Plan’s aspirations without significantly raising electricity prices or hamstringing the commonwealth’s economic potential. Specifically, the proposal’s focus on achieving the targets outlined in the Virginia Clean Economy Act (VCEA) would set Virginia back and leave it scrambling to add more than 90,000 megawatts to the grid.

Between 2019 and 2024, Virginia’s electricity consumption surged to 3.1% annually, more than three times the national average. Driven by Northern Virginia’s premier digital infrastructure hub, data centers already consume roughly 31% of the state’s electricity and will account for more than 90% of electricity demand growth over the next two decades. Yet, as this demand shock accelerates, state energy policy remains tethered to the VCEA. Enacted in 2020, during a vastly different economic era, the VCEA codified rigid technology quotas and mandated a complete phaseout of natural gas power by 2045 — parameters that risk blackouts, soaring power prices and mounting burdens on working families.

Natural gas has driven carbon emissions reductions in the commonwealth by facilitating the transition away from coal, and it remains essential for grid reliability while the state expands clean energy generation. Today, natural gas powers 59% of Virginia’s electric grid — outpacing every other energy source. Scaling up renewables in the next 20 years to meet the enormous power generation gap caused by a natural gas phaseout could cost the state hundreds of billions of dollars and cause monthly electric bills to spike far higher.

Perhaps most importantly, wind and solar can’t yet deliver on the 24/7 reliability that Virginia needs to keep its economy moving. The VCEA enacted policies modeled on outdated energy use targets, plotted well before today’s data center boom. These newfound pressures are putting the commonwealth’s obsolete policies to the ultimate test and revealing legitimate vulnerabilities.

Unlike coal and nuclear, natural gas can be dispatched instantly. This unique advantage can help Virginia and other states continue to phase out oil and coal and progress toward a renewable energy future, all while delivering reliable, uninterrupted power that won’t break the bank.

The governor’s blueprint also makes some challenging assumptions. This includes the prospect of constructing 39,600 megawatts of solar across the commonwealth by adding 1,800 megawatts every year through 2050, which would require developing roughly 277,000 acres of land, displacing 1.5% of Virginia’s farms, and affecting nearly 1% of its forests, a prospect already triggering zoning pushback from county boards.

As lawmakers prepare for the 2027 General Assembly session, they should consider strengthening the 2026 Virginia Energy Plan in three specific ways.

First, by amending the VCEA to place zero-carbon dispatchable technologies — such as advanced nuclear, fusion and geothermal energy — on equal footing with wind and solar. Second, by revising the VCEA’s reactive reliability exception so utilities and the State Corporation Commission can proactively maintain necessary natural gas capacity based on verified load growth and regional capacity warnings.

Third, by enforcing strict cost allocation on data center developers to shield families.

Whether it’s managing severe weather or supporting substantial economic development, Virginia’s grid must be equipped to handle varying pressures. To keep costs low, strengthen reliability and protect clean energy goals, the commonwealth must implement pragmatic solutions and marry natural gas with renewables. As lawmakers prepare for the 2027 session, I hope Spanberger’s administration and the state legislature consider these factors and prioritize solutions rooted in reality.

Neel Brown of Arlington is a managing director of the Progressive Policy Institute (PPI) in Washington, D.C.

text:
Hyundai Motor and Kia, grappling with severe domestic sales slumps, have launched year-end promotions featuring major discounts and interest-free installments for key models. The Kia Sorento offers up to approximately 5.5 million Korean won in discounts when combined with benefits for display vehicles, while the Hyundai Santa Fe provides up to 2 million Korean won in discounts. The Avante, which sparked price controversies, now offers a base discount of 1 million Korean won for its gasoline model, just three months after its pricing was announced. The Santa Fe and Palisade also provide interest-free installments of up to 60 months, including hybrid models.

Hyundai Motor and Kia announced these purchasing benefits on November 1 as part of the ‘2026 K Sale Festa.’ The K Sale Festa is a major domestic shopping festival led by the industry and supported by the government. Kia will apply discounts of up to 11% to 10,000 units of 16 models, including the Sorento and Carnival, released in November. The Sorento and Tasman receive up to 11% discounts, the K9, EV6, and Bongo EV up to 10%, and the Carnival, K5, K8, EV3, EV4, and EV9 up to 8%. All models offer up to 1 million Korean won in purchase benefits for 1,000 display vehicles. For the Sorento 2.2 Diesel Noblesse trim, combining all benefits results in a maximum discount of 5.5 million Korean won.

Hyundai applies discounts to three major popular models: the Avante, Grandeur, and Santa Fe. Until next month, the Santa Fe offers a base discount of 1 million Korean won plus an additional maximum discount of 1 million Korean won based on production timing. The Avante gasoline model receives a base discount of 1 million Korean won. The Genesis G80 and GV70, excluding electrified models, provide a base purchase benefit of 2 million Korean won and additional discounts of up to 5% and 3% based on production timing.

The Santa Fe and Palisade operate interest-free installments of up to 60 months. Compared to the existing 5.6% annual interest rate, the Santa Fe saves approximately 5.4 million Korean won in interest, the Santa Fe Hybrid 5.8 million Korean won, the Palisade 6.7 million Korean won, and the Palisade Hybrid 7.4 million Korean won. However, a 20% down payment is required using Hyundai-exclusive cards or Hyundai Card M-series cards, and benefits are limited to the first 2,000 units per model.

Certified used car discounts are also offered concurrently. Hyundai provides a 200,000 Korean won discount coupon to customers purchasing certified used Hyundai and Genesis vehicles in November. Kia offers 3–4% discounts on designated K-series, Sorento, Mohave, and Carnival models, and 2% discounts on electric vehicles. Contracts signed this month and finalized by December 15 receive an additional 200,000 Korean won charging voucher for electric vehicles or a digital Onnuri gift certificate for other models.

title: R-410A Refrigerant Isn't Banned, But Here's Why The AC Coolant Is Being Phased Out
description:
As the primary refrigerant used in air conditioners sold during this era, it was common for people to come across the R-410A label slapped across AC packaging.
Over time, as R-22 was gradually phased out around the 2010s, R-410A surged in popularity and eventually became the refrigerant of choice for AC manufacturers worldwide.
However, despite these new laws in place, existing R-410A air conditioners are very much legal.
In simpler terms, there is no outright "ban" on R-410A-based air conditioners, and existing R-410A-based equipment will continue to be able to use the refrigerant for the foreseeable future.
As existing R-410A air conditioners get older, they will eventually be replaced with newer systems that use more environmentally friendly refrigerants, thereby naturally reducing the number of R-410A systems in use.
text:
If you purchased an air conditioner from any of the major brands in the U.S. after 2010, chances are that you've come across the term R-410A. As the primary refrigerant used in air conditioners sold during this era, it was common for people to come across the R-410A label slapped across AC packaging. It was visible on AC outdoor units installed across the country, and consumers became familiar with the word as it was frequently used by technicians and those involved in the HVAC industry.

Having been around since the mid-'90s, R-410A came in as a replacement for R-22 (also known as Freon), which had gained notoriety during much of the '90s because of its ozone depletion potential and the resultant crisis. Upon its introduction, R-410A's major selling point was its zero ozone-depletion potential. Over time, as R-22 was gradually phased out around the 2010s, R-410A surged in popularity and eventually became the refrigerant of choice for AC manufacturers worldwide.

Fast forward to 2026, and R-410A finds itself in a similar position to that of R-22. While not completely banned, the coolant is being actively phased out in favor of newer, more environmentally friendly alternatives. While R-22 was phased out because of its adverse effects on the ozone layer, the case against R-410A is due to its high Global Warming Potential (GWP) numbers.

The beginning of the end for R-410A came with the American Innovation and Manufacturing (AIM) Act of 2020. This legislation led to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) instructing AC manufacturers in the U.S. to gradually cut down the production of R-410A-based equipment, while simultaneously transitioning to greener alternatives.

As outlined earlier, the primary reason for the ongoing phase-out of R-410A is its high Global Warming Potential. R-410A has a GWP of 2,088. To make sense of this number, it simply means that R-410A's warming effect is 2,088 times that of carbon dioxide (when measured over a 100-year period). The passing of the AIM Act in 2020 was only the first in a series of steps undertaken to ease the dependence on R-410A, and to give a fillip to the HVAC industry as a whole and look at other alternatives.

To ensure this transition happens as planned, the EPA came up with another set of rules aimed at equipment using these refrigerants. For new residential and light-commercial air conditioners, the EPA set an upper global-warming-potential limit of 700. This automatically pushed R-410A out of contention as far as newly manufactured AC systems are concerned, while encouraging manufacturers to switch to lower-GWP alternatives.

However, despite these new laws in place, existing R-410A air conditioners are very much legal. Homeowners can continue using and repairing them until it's time to completely replace them. The new set of rules is designed to gradually shrink R-410A's role as older models are replaced by a new generation of air conditioners. In simpler terms, there is no outright "ban" on R-410A-based air conditioners, and existing R-410A-based equipment will continue to be able to use the refrigerant for the foreseeable future.

For most homeowners, the R-410A phaseout will be a gradual process, and something they may not even notice. Those with freshly installed (and older) R-410A-based ACs will be able to use and service them for the next several years. The 700-GWP limit by the EPA, effective from January 1, 2025, prohibits manufacturers from importing residential and light commercial ACs based on R-410A. However, following a major rule change in May 2026, manufacturers and distributors in possession of older R-410A-based ACs will be able to sell this inventory to consumers.

So, as of October 2026, consumers can still buy and install R-410A-based ACs, all of which were manufactured or imported into the U.S. before January 1, 2025. As existing R-410A air conditioners get older, they will eventually be replaced with newer systems that use more environmentally friendly refrigerants, thereby naturally reducing the number of R-410A systems in use.

As for the replacements, there are two main contenders that will take the coveted spot currently occupied by R-410A. These are R-454B (GWP of 465) and R-32 (GWP of 675). These GWP numbers are much lower compared to R-410A's 2,088. In the U.S., R-454B has become a particularly common choice for new residential AC systems, while R-32 is also used by several manufacturers. It will be interesting to see which of these two refrigerants becomes dominant over the next few decades.

title: Copper Supply Agreement Signed by Prysmian and Aurubis - American Recycler
description:
Prysmian and Aurubis have signed a landmark agreement for the supply of copper wire rod, deepening a strategic partnership spanning more than 30 years.
Alberto Boffelli, chief operating officer at Prysmian, said, “As the world’s largest buyer of copper wire rod, Prysmian has both an opportunity and a responsibility to help shape the future of the copper value chain.
The company currently produces copper wire rod with approximately 36 percent recycled material content and a carbon footprint significantly below the global industry average.
All Aurubis rod mills have been awarded The Copper Mark, the leading independent assurance framework for responsible copper production, sourcing and recycling.
Strengthening Europe’s copper supply chain The agreement helps secure the materials needed for electrification, energy infrastructure and digital networks, while supporting Europe’s long-term industrial competitiveness.
text:
Prysmian and Aurubis have signed a landmark agreement for the supply of copper wire rod, deepening a strategic partnership spanning more than 30 years.

The agreement represents a significant step in securing one of the critical materials underpinning electrification, the energy transition, and digitalization. As copper demand grows, driven by the expansion of power grids, renewable energy, electrification and AI infrastructure, the agreement will enhance Europe’s production footprint, recycling capabilities and low-carbon copper rod and cable production.

Alberto Boffelli, chief operating officer at Prysmian, said, “As the world’s largest buyer of copper wire rod, Prysmian has both an opportunity and a responsibility to help shape the future of the copper value chain. This agreement with Aurubis gives us the reliable, flexible and increasingly sustainable supply our customers need, while strengthening Europe’s access to a material that is critical to its energy and digital future.”

As Europe’s largest vertically integrated low-carbon copper rod producer, Aurubis combines scale, quality and security of supply. The company currently produces copper wire rod with approximately 36 percent recycled material content and a carbon footprint significantly below the global industry average. Its four copper rod plants across Europe also provide Prysmian with flexibility and proximity to key markets.

Advancing more sustainable value chains

Prysmian and Aurubis share an ambition to advance electrification, the energy transition and digitalization through more sustainable value chains.

Prysmian is working to set best-in-class sustainability through its products and supply chain, while Aurubis contributes copper wire rod with an increasing share of recycled material and a carbon footprint significantly below the global average for comparable products.

All Aurubis rod mills have been awarded The Copper Mark, the leading independent assurance framework for responsible copper production, sourcing and recycling. Prysmian is also a member of The Copper Mark.

Together, the companies bring advanced recycling expertise, ambitious decarbonization efforts and high standards across the value chain to help meet growing demand for critical materials.

Strengthening Europe’s copper supply chain

The agreement helps secure the materials needed for electrification, energy infrastructure and digital networks, while supporting Europe’s long-term industrial competitiveness.

title: Winds of change: Laos looks up for renewables push - AFP.com
description:
Experts say wind is now set to take off, and point to Laos's 600-megawatt Monsoon Wind Power Project, which began operating in August 2025, as a bankable case study.
Spanning an area the size of Singapore, the $700-million scheme is the first cross-border wind project in Asia and the largest wind farm in Southeast Asia.
Through Monsoon, "wind power is being sold significantly cheaper to Vietnam than what Vietnam is buying wind power for locally", said Thomas Jakobsen, managing director at Indochina Energy Partners.
He estimated state utility Electricity Vietnam (EVN) was paying Monsoon around six cents per kilowatt-hour -- two to four cents less than the Vietnamese rate.
He insisted nobody was forced to relocate because of the project -- although public dissent is severely restricted in communist Laos.
text:
Rising from verdant ridgelines of southern Laos, 133 Chinese-built wind turbines help power Vietnam's surging growth and represent part of a regional rush to diversify energy sources.

"The view is beautiful. They're bigger than trees," 23-year-old Toukta Phonsala told AFP inside her wooden stilt house in Dak Wai village, her baby bouncing on her lap.

Hydroelectric dams have proliferated across Southeast Asia in recent years, but production drops off in the dry season and critics lament the ecological impacts.

Experts say wind is now set to take off, and point to Laos's 600-megawatt Monsoon Wind Power Project, which began operating in August 2025, as a bankable case study.

Spanning an area the size of Singapore, the $700-million scheme is the first cross-border wind project in Asia and the largest wind farm in Southeast Asia.

Built by a Chinese state firm and owned by a Thai-led consortium, it sells electricity exclusively to Vietnam's national grid via dedicated transmission lines.

Manufacturing hub Vietnam, Southeast Asia's fastest-growing economy, was already importing hydropower from Laos, its poorest neighbour.

But "the economics are moving in favour of wind", said Tristan Bellingham, technical programme lead at nonprofit EnergyLab Asia.

"Similar to hydro 20 to 30 years ago, there's a bit of a rush on to secure concessions and development rights" for new wind projects, he told AFP.

Laos already hosts 90 hydropower plants and there are dozens more in neighbouring nations, leaving few optimal sites remaining.

Bellingham said other wind farms were now riding "the coattails of Monsoon", with one Laos official pointing to 10 to 15 projects under development nationwide.

For Toukta, the 18 family members she lives with and other rice and coffee farmers residing near the turbines, Monsoon has brought new roads and improved access to fresh water and healthcare.

What it has not brought to her community, however, is power.

Residents say they still experience outages during heavy storms, as Laos's own electricity infrastructure is outdated and the state utility is heavily in debt.

Still, Toukta is glad Laos can send power abroad.

"It's better for development and can bring prosperity," she said.

For Vietnam, the project offers a reliable source of less costly energy.

There were severe blackouts in 2023 when drought cut into hydropower supply, and the government warned in September of the risk of electricity shortages from next year due to delays in planned power projects and increasing demand.

Through Monsoon, "wind power is being sold significantly cheaper to Vietnam than what Vietnam is buying wind power for locally", said Thomas Jakobsen, managing director at Indochina Energy Partners.

He estimated state utility Electricity Vietnam (EVN) was paying Monsoon around six cents per kilowatt-hour -- two to four cents less than the Vietnamese rate.

Representatives of Monsoon Wind, EVN and the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the Monsoon project's financial arranger, declined to share the rate during a press tour last week.

The project is also key to Vietnam reaching net-zero emissions targets by 2050, according to Ninh Xuan Hiep, an official at EVN's National Power Transmission Corporation.

At a substation in the Vietnamese capital Hanoi, he told AFP that by 2030, Laos imports would equal nearly 10 percent of Vietnam's total installed capacity -- its maximum possible production.

Monsoon Wind plans to boost capacity by 1,000 megawatts and is working to ensure some of this additional power is used inside Laos, according to general manager Narut Boakajorn.

"Laos has so much natural resources" -- wind, hydro and solar, Narut told AFP in an interview held below the spinning blades of a 110-metre-high turbine.

"Not many countries have all the good renewable energy in the same place. Laos has something unique."

The government was set to reap $180 million over the 25-year contract period, including taxes and community development and environmental protection funds, according to Narut.

He insisted nobody was forced to relocate because of the project -- although public dissent is severely restricted in communist Laos.

He said 1,600 grievances logged, mainly from farmers requesting compensation for construction impacts on their crops, were resolved.

In the shadow of the turbines, 23-year-old farmer Phonekhan Sengsopha said he was proud that electricity produced in his country was being sent to its neighbour, also a communist nation.

"Because Vietnam and Laos are like brothers. They help one another."

title: Energy Control and Resilience: Why Microgrids Matter
description:

text:
Energy is now a business risk. Here’s how to take back control.

For decades, energy was treated as a predictable operating expense. Power came from the grid, organizations paid the bill, and growth continued.

That model is changing.

Electrification is accelerating. Electricity demand is rising. Grid interconnection is slowing. Extreme events are disrupting operations. At the same time, volatile energy prices and decarbonization commitments are putting greater pressure on organizations to manage cost, reliability, and carbon performance together.

Energy is no longer just a facilities issue. It is a business risk, and increasingly, a source of competitive advantage.

From energy consumption to energy control

Most organizations still operate as passive energy consumers. They depend on the grid for capacity, reliability, and price stability, even as each becomes less certain.

A more resilient energy strategy starts by changing that relationship.

Microgrids give organizations greater control over how energy is generated, stored, managed, and consumed. By integrating on-site generation, battery energy storage, electrical distribution, flexible loads, and intelligent energy controls, a microgrid creates a connected energy ecosystem that can respond to changing conditions in real time.

When connected to the grid, a microgrid can optimize energy use, increase renewable self-consumption, and reduce exposure to high-cost periods. During a disruption, it can transition to islanded operation and continue supplying critical loads independently.

This is energy independence in practical terms. It does not necessarily mean disconnecting from the grid. It means having the flexibility and intelligence to make better energy decisions instead of relying on a single source of power.

One energy investment, multiple business outcomes

The value of a microgrid extends far beyond backup power. A well-designed system can address four priorities from one integrated investment: cost control, sustainability, resilience, and speed to power.

Gain greater control over energy costs

Energy prices fluctuate, tariff structures are becoming more complex, and peak-demand charges can significantly affect operating costs. Intelligent energy management helps organizations decide when to generate, store, purchase, or consume energy based on real-time conditions.

Rather than simply absorbing market volatility, organizations can take a more active role in managing their exposure.

Strengthen energy resilience

For hospitals, data centers, manufacturing facilities, transportation hubs, and other critical operations, an outage can quickly become a business continuity issue.

A microgrid can prioritize critical loads and balance available generation and storage when the grid is unavailable. This helps maintain essential operations and reduces dependence on manual intervention during a disruption.

Resilience is no longer only about recovering from an outage. It is about designing an energy system that can adapt before disruption becomes downtime.

Advance decarbonization without compromising performance

Organizations should not have to choose between reliable operations and carbon reduction.

Microgrids can integrate renewable energy and battery storage while intelligently managing their variability. This supports greater on-site renewable energy use, reduced Scope 2 emissions, lower generator fuel consumption, and more measurable sustainability reporting.

Decarbonization becomes part of the operating strategy rather than a separate initiative.

Move faster than the grid

For organizations expanding facilities, electrifying fleets, or adding energy-intensive operations, access to power can determine how quickly growth plans move forward.

Lengthening interconnection queues and required grid upgrades can delay projects. On-site distributed energy resources, coordinated through a microgrid, can provide an alternative path to additional capacity while improving operational flexibility and resilience.

The intelligence behind the infrastructure

A microgrid is more than a collection of solar panels, batteries, generators, and switchgear. Its real value comes from how effectively those resources work together.

The control system acts as the brain of the microgrid. It continuously monitors available resources and optimizes how energy is generated, stored, and consumed. Connected software, edge control, electrical distribution, and distributed energy resources must operate as one coherent system to deliver reliable performance.

That integration is what transforms physical infrastructure into an adaptive energy strategy.

It also explains why the path to a successful microgrid begins before equipment is selected. Organizations need to understand their load profile, operational priorities, resilience requirements, decarbonization goals, and financial objectives. The right solution should reflect the realities of the site and the outcomes the business needs to achieve.

Resilient today means ready tomorrow

The energy landscape will continue to evolve. Demand will grow, tariffs will change, new technologies will emerge, and pressure to decarbonize will intensify.

Organizations that take control of their energy are better positioned to adapt. With an intelligent microgrid, energy can shift from an unpredictable constraint to a managed strategic asset, supporting resilience, energy independence, cost optimization, and sustainable growth.

The question is no longer whether energy strategy belongs in the boardroom. It is how quickly your organization can turn energy risk into business advantage.
